en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Mahāniddesa in the Khuddakanikāya.
The Introduction to the Book:
He who, slaying the serpent of ignorance and uprooting delight and lust,
cultivated the Eightfold Path and touched the deathless state.
Having attained enlightenment, the Conqueror entered the Deer Park;
having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, he first [ordained] the Elder Koṇḍañña.
There, the Ascetic awakened eighteen koṭis of beings.
I pay homage with my head to Him, the supreme among all beings;
likewise to the Supreme Dhamma and the unsurpassed Saṅgha.
For that which was spoken in brief, I shall now explain in detail as the Wheel of Dhamma.
Sāriputta, of great wisdom, the son of the Conqueror who is like the Teacher himself,
having analyzed the Wheel of Dhamma, spoke the Mahāniddesa.
Its reading is distinguished as a detailed exposition (niddesa), and it is specified by that very name.
Having bowed down to that Sāriputta, the son of the Conqueror-King, the elder who is the abode of many steadfast virtues,
whose beautiful fame has risen through the power of his wisdom, and who is of most humble conduct—
[I shall speak] by means of one endowed with patience and the like, and who speaks what is appropriate and supreme.
Requested by the learned elder Deva,
[this work] was composed based on what should be accepted from the ancient commentaries, established for the recitation of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.
Not departing from his own tradition nor touching upon the traditions of others,
and appropriately incorporating the methods of the ancient commentaries and instructions, he [composed this work]—
that which brings about the various distinctions of knowledge and is practiced by many yogis.
Explaining the meaning that has not been explained before, and following the sequence of the suttas and their logical reasoning,
I shall begin this brief commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*,
out of great reverence for the True Dhamma and not out of a desire for self-glorification.
“I shall speak a commentary for the sake of people, for their welfare and for the long endurance of the True Dhamma.
Listen well and bear it in mind, O virtuous ones, for it is the illuminator of the True Dhamma.
In this regard, because it is said that “the reading is twofold: distinguished and specified by its name,” there are two kinds of reading: the reading of the phrasing (*byañjanapāṭha*), and...
And there is the textual reading (*pāṭha*) and the meaning (*attha*). Among these, the textual reading is sixfold, by way of:

syllables (*akkhara*), phrases (*pada*), words (*byañjana*), modes (*ākāra*), etymological definitions (*nirutti*), and detailed explanations (*niddesa*). The meaning is sixfold, by way of: making known (*saṅkāsanā*), manifesting (*pakāsanā*), explaining (*vivaraṇa*), analyzing (*vibhajana*), clarifying (*uttānīkaraṇa*), and establishing (*paññatti*).
Therein, the teaching that proceeds with a mind of pure compassion through the state of perfectly pure application in the three doors [of body, speech, and mind]...
Because it was not spoken by speech nor taught [orally], it is designated as "syllable" (akkhara).

This should be understood as "syllable" in the sense of the questions mentally asked by the Pārāyanika brahmins and the Great Treatise on the Foundations (Paṭṭhāna-mahāpakaraṇa) contemplated by the Blessed One while seated in the Jewel Chamber (Ratanaghara).
Alternatively, an incomplete word should be understood as a syllable (*akkhara*), as in cases such as "sixty thousand years" (*saṭṭhivassasahassāni*).
For here, the letters *s*, *n*, *s*, and so forth, are considered syllables; or some maintain that a single-syllable word is a syllable.
In passages such as "this craving which leads to renewed existence" (*yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā*), a cluster of syllables that expresses meaning through its case-ending is [to be understood].
A *pada* (phrase). In such cases as “name and form,” a phrase is that which is composed of many syllables. It clarifies a phrase stated in brief.
It is called *byañjana* because it expresses (*byañjayati*) what is signified by the *pada*, making it distinct (*byatta*) and manifest (*pākaṭa*); thus, it is simply the sentence itself.
[For example], regarding the meaning spoken in brief as “the four bases of psychic power” (*cattāro iddhipādā*), [one asks]: “Which four? Here,…”
In such passages as, “Monks, a monk develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving;

he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy, mind, and investigation and volitional formations of striving,” the term *byañjana* (the phrasing) refers to the state of making [the meaning] manifest.

The *ākāra* (the mode) is the clarification of the distinctions within that phrasing. In such passages as, “Therein, what is desire? It is desire, the state of desiring, the wish to act,” the phrasing is that which is spoken.
The act of making various distinctions is called *ākāra* (mode). The etymological analysis (*nibbacana*) of what is expressed by that mode is *nirutti* (language/definition).
In cases such as "contact" (*phassa*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*), the statement extracted according to the mode—namely, "it touches, thus it is contact;
it feels, thus it is feeling"—is called *nirutti*. A detailed exposition of the etymological analysis, taught exhaustively, is *niddesa* (explanation); for example: "It feels, thus it is feeling."
The detailed explanation of the meaning— “pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; it is pleasant because it pleases, painful because it pains,
and neither-painful-nor-pleasant because it neither pains nor pleases”— is called a *niddesa* (demonstration) because it has been stated in its entirety,
including the etymological derivation of the terms.

Having thus understood these six kinds of phrasing (*byañjanapada*), there is, in brief, exposition (*kāsanā*), illumination (*dīpanā*), and elucidation (*saṅkāsanā*) regarding the six points of meaning.
In such passages as, “Monk, one who conceives is bound by Māra;

one who does not conceive is freed from the Evil One,” there is what is called brief exposition and elucidation of the meaning. Now, this Elder [understood] this summary taught by the Blessed Buddha...
Having thus stated the matter, he penetrated [the truth] such that he was able to say, "It is understood, Blessed One; it is understood, Sugata.
Regarding the matter to be stated later, there is first the indication, the showing, and the making clear;

for instance, in passages such as "All, monks, is ablaze," the indicating and making clear by means of the initial statement of what is to be spoken later is called *dīpanā* and *pakāsanā*. Thus, first—
By further clarifying the meaning already illuminated through such explanations as, “And what, bhikkhus, is all that is aflame? The eye, bhikkhus, is aflame;

forms are aflame,” and so forth—and because it has been stated that “one of keen faculties penetrates what is spoken in brief”—these two sections on the meaning are spoken for the benefit of one with keen faculties.
Explanation (*vivaraṇa*) is the statement in detail of what was stated briefly, and the restatement of what was already said once;

it is the expansion by way of a detailed exposition of that which was set forth in brief as “wholesome states” (*kusalā dhammā*). For instance, the expansion by way of the answer—“Which states are wholesome?
At whatever time a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere has arisen”—is called explanation because it is spoken again by way of detail.

That making of distinctions is "analysis" (*vibhajana*); when the wholesome states have been disclosed by the phrase "at whatever time," the making of distinctions such as "at that time there is contact, there is feeling" is called analysis.

Making clear by means of an exposition for what has been disclosed and by means of an illustration for what has been analyzed is "elucidation" (*uttānīkaraṇa*); [this refers to] the meaning already disclosed by the exposition.
“What is contact at that time? It is that which at that time is contact, the act of contacting, the state of being contacted”—this is an explanation by way of detailed exposition;
and “Just as, monks, a cow without its hide, even so, monks, should the nutriment of contact be regarded,” this is an explanation by way of similes such as these.

"Making clear" (uttānīkaraṇa) is as follows: "Conceptualization" (paññatti) refers both to the production of manifold kinds of mental joy through the teaching of the Dhamma for those listening to the Dhamma, and to the making sharp of the manifold kinds of knowledge for those of keen intellect.

It is called "conceptualization" because it becomes manifest (paññāyati) to those listeners through the satisfaction of their minds and through the application of their minds. In this regard, the Blessed One—

"He makes it clear through syllables, he makes it manifest through phrases, he discloses it through phonemes, he analyzes it through modes, he makes it plain through etymologies, and he establishes it through definitions. What is meant by this?

The Blessed Buddhas, for certain disciples to be trained, perform the making clear of the meaning through syllables in a single teaching... [and so on] ...perform the establishing of the meaning through definitions.
"Making [them known]"—this is the intended meaning here.

Alternatively, having gathered [the meaning] together through syllables (*akkhara*), he makes it manifest through phrases (*pada*); having opened it up through phonemes (*byañjana*), he analyzes it through modes (*ākāra*);
having made it plain through etymologies (*nirutti*), he establishes it through detailed explanations (*niddesa*). What is meant? By such a teaching of the Dhamma...
He disciplines some of those to be trained in certain places.

Alternatively, he disciplines one who gains knowledge through condensed statements (*ugghaṭitaññu*) by disclosing the meaning through syllables and elucidating it through phrases; he disciplines one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññu*) by unveiling it through phonemes and analyzing it through grammatical forms (*ākāra*);
and he disciplines one who gains knowledge through explanations (*nippañcitaññu*) by making it clear through etymological definitions (*nirutti*) and detailed descriptions (*niddesa*).
By making [the meaning] known, he disciplines those who are to be guided. Thus, it must certainly be applied even according to the capacity of those to be trained (*vineya*).
As for the meaning here, what is the reading of the phrasing (*byañjanapāṭha*) and what is the reading of the meaning (*atthapāṭha*)?

When the Blessed Buddhas are teaching the Dhamma, that sound accompanied by intimation (*saviññattika-sadda*) which causes the understanding of the meaning is the reading of the phrasing. That which by it...
The Dhamma, together with its characteristics, functions, and so forth, is that which is to be fully realized; it should be understood as the "text of meaning" (*atthapāṭha*).

Furthermore, there are six kinds of texts: those spoken with intentional reference (*sandhāyabhāsita*), those spoken regarding the literal expression (*byañjanabhāsita*), those with a remainder (*sāvasesapāṭha*), those without remainder (*anavasesapāṭha*), the explicit (*nīta*), and the implicit (*neyya*).
Among these, that which is spoken with intentional reference is due to its having multiple meanings, such as: "Having slain mother and father, and two warrior-kings..."
And so forth. That which is expressed through synonyms because it has the same meaning is, for example, "mental phenomena are preceded by the mind" (*manopubbangamā dhammā*).

That which is incomplete is, for example, "All, O monks, is on fire. That which is the opposite—the complete—is, for example, "All phenomena in every aspect come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One. Just as the word [is used], so too...
That which is to be understood as "direct" (nīta) is such as "impermanent, suffering, non-self," and so forth.
That which is to be inferred through reasoning (neyya) is such as "There is one person, monks," and so forth.

Furthermore, the meaning (attha) is of many kinds: the literal meaning (pāṭhattha), the essential nature (sabhāvattha), the implied meaning (ñāyattha), that which conforms to the text (pāṭhānurūpa), and that which does not conform to the text (napāṭhānurūpa).

[The meanings are] "with remainder," "without remainder," "of explicit meaning" (*nītattha*), "of interpretable meaning" (*neyyattha*), and so forth. Among these, that which is uttered for the purpose of making known a limited meaning is the "literal meaning" (*pāṭhattha*), as in the expression "endowed with meaning and endowed with phrasing" (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*).

That which is the meaning consisting of the characteristics, functions, and intrinsic natures of material and immaterial phenomena is [the meaning] as in "he develops right view" (*sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti*) and so forth.
That which, when understood, leads to welfare, is "worthy of being known" (*ñātuṃ arahati*).
The meaning based on what is known (*ñāyattha*) is as in such passages as "one who speaks of the goal, one who speaks of the Dhamma.
That which is spoken according to the literal reading (*yathāpāṭha*) is in accordance with the text, as when the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, the eye is past karma. Therefore, even the eye is karma.

An interpretation that excludes the meaning by relying on the shadow of the phrasing (*byañjanacchāyā*) is not in accordance with the text; it is not authorized by the text, yet it has not been explicitly rejected.

"Detached" (*viyutta*): This is stated with a residual meaning (*sāvasesattha*), because it is expressed by leaving out what ought to be included or by not avoiding something that ought to be avoided—as in such passages as "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises" or "All tremble at punishment;
all fear death. The opposite of this is the non-residual meaning (*niravasesattha*).
“...the wandering and the transmigration of both myself and you. In that regard, bhikkhus, who is the thinker? Who is the believer?...

except for those who have seen the Dhamma,” as in such passages. That which is to be understood by way of the literal word alone is of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*), as in: “Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, and delightful tangibles.
That which is to be understood by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*) is of implicit meaning (*neyyārtha*), as in: “These four...”

"...as in the passages beginning with, 'Monks, persons are like clouds. Thus, having explained both the text and the meaning here, one stands firm and becomes unshakable by the proponents of other doctrines for a long time through dwelling in the [true] refuge.
By way of this unshakability, one is able to speak as far as the perfection of scripture and realization, according to the method of both summary and detail."
He is capable of making [others] understand through reasons, examples, and so forth.
Being such, he is pure because he is free from the stains of immorality and wrong views by virtue of his ability to purify both himself and others. For the immoral person harms himself;
consequently, his word is not to be trusted, and he is like a physician who is constantly ill and full of self-importance. One with wrong view harms others and cannot be a refuge.

And he becomes like a cluster of lotuses infested by predatory birds. But one who has failed in both respects is altogether unfit for attendance, like a charcoal-brand fallen into excrement, or like a black snake fallen into excrement.
One who has succeeded in both respects, however, is altogether fit for attendance and should be cultivated by the wise, like a treasure-mine free from danger; such is he.

Thus, he was free from stinginess and did not hold back his teachers' instructions. He was one who did not withhold the fourfold [teachings] known as the suttas, the teachings conforming to the suttas, the teachers' doctrines, and his own personal insights; it is by way of these that he is described.
"A categorical statement is a single [unit], while an analytical statement is a phrase."
“One should question the third [point] and set aside the fourth.
Or, one does not abandon these [qualities]. Because he is thus devoted to the welfare of his listeners, he remains untiring in making them understand. And it is said here:
“Firm in his knowledge of the meaning of the text, a speaker who is pure and free from stinginess;”

"One who does not abandon the four, and who is endowed with benefit for the teacher"—here, "of the teacher" (*desakassa*) means he is a teacher (*desako*), that is, one who should exist [as such]. "Endowed with benefit" (*hitānvito*) means following after what is beneficial, having a mind of benevolence.

Such a person is dear because of his pure heart; he is venerable because of his non-abandonment of the four; he is to be cultivated because of his unshakability; and he is a teacher because of his role as a guide.
He is dear, respected, and venerable; he speaks appropriately and is patient with what is said; he is a speaker of profound discourse because he has found out the meaning of the texts;
and because he is not envious, he does not urge others toward what is improper—thus:
"Dear, respected, and venerable, speaking appropriately and patient with what is said;"
“He shall deliver a profound discourse, yet not enjoin one toward what is improper.
“He has been designated as the teacher; now he is being addressed.
In this regard, out of reverence for the Dhamma, he does not disparage the discourse; out of reverence for the teacher, he does not disparage the speaker.
Because he is adorned with qualities such as faith and wisdom, he does not despise himself; because he is free from deceit and guile and is oriented toward the Deathless, his mind is undistracted;
and because he is wise, he attends to things thoroughly. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, one endowed with five qualities who hears the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness."
“Rightness regarding wholesome states. By what five [qualities]? He does not despise the discourse, he does not despise the speaker, he does not despise himself;
with an undistracted mind he listens to the Dhamma with a one-pointed mind, and he attends to it wisely.
Because he has attained those characteristics, he devotes himself to meditation. And it is said here:
“Revering the teacher of the Dhamma, adorned with the jewels of qualities such as faith and wisdom,
free from deceit and guile, the wise one is directed toward the Deathless.”—
Thus he speaks and thus he listens.

Having thus shown both the phrasing and the meaning of the aforementioned type, I shall now comment upon the *Mahāniddesa*. It is called the *Mahāniddesa* because it is "great" (*mahā*) due to being spoken with extreme excellence, and it is a "description" (*niddesa*); thus, it is like the great ocean and the great earth.
This *Mahāniddesa* is endowed with meaning and endowed with phrasing; it is profound, possessing a profound meaning;
it elucidates the supramundane, is associated with emptiness, accomplishes the distinctions of the path and fruit of practice, and refutes that which is contrary to the practice.
For the sake of providing consolation to practitioners of yoga by showing the means of escape from suffering to those who fear saṃsāra,
for the sake of destroying their opposites, and for the sake of gladdening the hearts of the virtuous through the exposition of the meaning of numerous profound passages from the Suttantas—

which serve as a mine of the supreme jewel of knowledge for those practicing yoga and as the cause of the particular splendor of the Dhamma-discourses for those who preach the Dhamma— [this work was composed].
By the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One— who, with the radiance of the great lamp of omniscient knowledge unimpeded in all respects,

and with the moisture of great compassion spread throughout all people, has kindled the great lamp of the True Dhamma for the purpose of dispelling the darkness of the defilements residing in the hearts of those to be trained—
one desires that it continue to burn for a very long time, five thousand years, by sprinkling the moisture that causes its intended meaning to blossom.
Having heard what was spoken by the Venerable Elder Sāriputta— the General of the Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, who is compassionate toward the world and like unto a Teacher—
the Venerable Ānanda, at the time of the First Great Council, committed it to the collection exactly as he had heard it.
Furthermore, among the three Piṭakas— the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka— this belongs to the Sutta Piṭaka.
Among the five great collections— the Dīghanikāya, Majjhimanikāya, Saṃyuttanikāya, Aṅguttaranikāya, and Khuddakanikāya— it is included within the Khuddaka Mahānikāya;
and among the nine factors of the Teacher’s dispensation— discourse (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), exposition (veyyākaraṇa), verse (gāthā), inspired utterance (udāna),
"thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical treatise (vedalla)— it belongs to these as appropriate.
It is comprised of two of the nine limbs of the Dhamma:
the Gāthā and the Veyyākaraṇa. As it is said:
“From the Buddha I received eighty-two thousand [teachings], from the Bhikkhus two thousand; thus eighty-four thousand are the teachings that have come down to me.”

Among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma acknowledged by the Elder Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika—who was designated as foremost in five respects—when they were received from the Bhikkhu, this [work] is comprised of many hundreds of Dhamma-sections within two of those eighty-four thousand sections.
It consists of two chapters: the Aṭṭhakavagga and the Pārāyanavagga, and the Khaggavisāṇasutta; in each chapter...
Having grouped them into sets of sixteen, there are thirty-three suttas beginning with the *Kāmasutta* and ending with the *Khaggavisāṇasutta*.
I shall now provide a word-by-word commentary on this *Mahāniddesa*, which has been established in these various ways.
Indeed, this *Mahāniddesa* should be recited with care by one who recites it both according to the text and according to the meaning.
It must be demonstrated, and it must be carefully learned and retained by one who studies it. For what reason?
Because of the profundity of this *Mahāniddesa*, it is for the benefit of the world and for its long endurance in the world.
1. The Chapter on the Eight Verses (*Aṭṭhakavagga*).
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Kāmasutta*. Therein, the *Kāmasutta* is first. Within that, the verse beginning “For one who desires sensual pleasures (*kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa*)” is first.

That [verse] exists in three ways: by way of enumeration (*uddesa*), exposition (*niddesa*), and further exposition (*paṭiniddesa*). “For one who desires sensual pleasures,” and so forth, is the enumeration. “Sensual pleasures (*kāmā*)—briefly stated, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures... [and so on].
The exposition is: “Sensual objects and sensual defilements. The counter-exposition is: “What are sensual objects? Agreeable forms,” and so forth.
In this context, *kāma* refers to the sensual object (*vatthukāma*), which consists of agreeable forms and other phenomena belonging to the three planes.

*Kāmayamānassa* means “of one who desires” or “of one who wishes for. *Tassa cetaṃ samijjhati* means that for that being who desires, this [object] consisting of sensual pleasure is successfully attained.
"If the basis succeeds" means, if he obtains it. "Surely his mind is joyful" means his heart is filled with one-pointed satisfaction.
"Having obtained" means having acquired. "A mortal" means a living being. "Whatever he desires" means whatever he wishes for.
This, however, is merely the connection between the words in brief; the detailed explanation follows the method set forth in the subsequent text.
It is to be understood. And just as in this case, so it is with all that follows hereafter.

"Kāma" (sensual pleasures) is the term to be indicated; "from the summary" (*uddānato*) is the term to be explained. "From the summary" means by way of sections (*vagga*), as in the cases of "the fish-summary" (*macchuddāna*) or "the kineyya-summary" (*kineyyā*).
Alternatively, it is a "summary" (*uddāna*) because of giving higher and higher, or because of purifying further and further upward (*uddham*).

It is like "cleansing" (*vodāna*) in the sense of purification (*byavadāna*). Or, it may be stated by supplying the word "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) and [explaining it] as being due to their expansive nature.
"Two" refers to the delimitation of number—neither one nor three. "And sensual objects" (*vatthukāmā*) means sensual objects consisting of agreeable forms and so forth;
and "defilement-sensualities" (*kilesakāmā*) in the sense of burning and in the sense of afflicting. Among these, the sensual object is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).
Sensual desire as defilement (*kilesakāma*) is to be abandoned. In this context, sensual desire as object (*vatthukāma*) is desired by means of sensual desire as defilement;

thus, because it is desired, it is called "kāma. Sensual desire as defilement is called "kāma" because it is the cause for the longing for sensual desires as objects, and because it is by means of this that one desires.

Therein, sensual desire as object is included within the aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, while sensual desire as defilement is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). [This occurs] through the six...

Sensual pleasure as an object (*vatthukāma*) is to be cognized by the [five] consciousnesses (*viññāṇa*); sensual pleasure as defilement (*kilesakāma*) is to be known by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).
Sensual pleasure as an object is so called in the sense of being a basis for defilements, in the sense of being a cause, and in the sense of being an objective support (*ārammaṇa*).
“Those variegated things in the world are not sensual pleasures; it is the passion of intention (*saṅkapparāga*) that is a person’s sensual pleasure.”
"Variegated things remain just as they are in the world; yet herein the wise subdue their desire.
The cases of the young brahmin Nanda, Soreyya the merchant’s son, and others serve as illustrations here.
*Kilesakāma* (the defilement-desire) is called "kāma" because it itself desires by way of burning and by way of afflicting. And this has been said: "O Brahmin, one who is impassioned by passion..."
The illustrations are such as: "One who is overcome and whose mind is obsessed intends for his own harm, intends for the harm of others, and intends for the harm of both";
and "One who is lustful, O Brahmin, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, and speaks falsehood," and so forth.
Desiring to explain that very same point in detail by way of a further exposition, he said: "What are sensual pleasures as objects? and so forth.
In this context, "what" (*katame*) is a question expressing a desire to speak. For there are five kinds of questions, and their classification will be made clear in the text itself below.
Among these, this is a question expressing a desire to speak. Therein, "pleasing" (*manāpikā*) means they nourish the mind (*manaṃ appāyanti*).
They are called "agreeable" (*manāpā*) because they increase what is pleasing; being agreeable, they are "the agreeable" (*manāpikā*).

"Forms" (*rūpā*) refers to objects of form arising from the fourfold origination—namely, by way of karma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment. They are called "forms" (*rūpā*) because they "form" (*rūpayanti*); the meaning is that, undergoing changes in color, they manifest their state as having entered the heart.
In this context, in what sense are they "form"? In the sense of being "formed" (*ruppana*). For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And what, bhikkhus, do you call ‘form’? It is deformed, bhikkhus, therefore it is called ‘form.

By what is it deformed? It is deformed by cold, it is deformed by heat, it is deformed by hunger, it is deformed by thirst, and it is deformed by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. It is deformed, bhikkhus.”
"Therefore it is called 'form' (rūpa).
In this context, "it is formed" (ruppati) means it is disturbed, struck, oppressed, and broken; such is the meaning. First, being formed by cold is evident in the Niraya of the World-Intervals.
It is likewise evident in regions such as the Mahimsaka country where snow falls and the climate is cold.
For there, beings whose bodies are split and cut by the cold even reach the end of their lives.

The ravaging by heat is evident in the Great Niraya of Avīci; for there, when beings are laid down upon a floor of red-hot iron and subjected to the fivefold torture and other punishments, they experience great suffering.
The ravaging by hunger is evident both in the realm of the *peta*s and during times of famine. Indeed, in the realm of the *peta*s—
Beings do not exist who, for two or three intervals between Buddhas, take even a small amount of food with their hands and put it into their mouths;
rather, their bellies are like hollow trees ablaze within. There is no measure to the number of beings who die from failing to obtain even a mere ladle of sour gruel during a famine.
The affliction by thirst is evident in such places as Kālakañjika;
for there, beings are unable to obtain even a single drop of water sufficient to moisten the heart or the tongue for two or three intervals between Buddhas.
When those who have gone to a river thinking, "We shall drink water," find that the water has turned into sand. This is true even for those who have entered the great ocean.
The ocean itself becomes like a slab of stone. As they dry up, tormented by powerful pain, they cry out.
Being afflicted by gadflies and the like is evident in places abounding with gadflies, flies, and so forth.
That, moreover, has been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma according to the method beginning: "What is that material form which is visible? It is impinging."
They are called *saddā* because they are sounded; the meaning is that they are articulated. Sounds have two origins: by way of the seasons (*utu*) and by way of the mind (*citta*).
They are called *gandhā* because they cause smelling; the meaning is that they indicate their own bases. They are called *rasā* because beings relish them; the meaning is that they provide enjoyment.
They are called *phoṭṭhabbā* because they are touched. These [objects] beginning with odors have only four origins. Their detailed classification has already been explained in the Abhidhamma.
Showing this same meaning in detail, he said: “Spreads and coverings,” and so forth. Therein, they are called *attharaṇā* because one lies down after spreading them out;
they are called *pāvuraṇā* because one wraps the body and covers oneself with them.

The four types beginning with those born in the house are female slaves, male slaves, and both female and male slaves. A field (*khetta*) is that in which grain grows; a site (*vatthu*) is that in which—
It is where other crops grow; or rather, that field is where both [crops] grow. A plot of ground prepared for that purpose is a site (*vatthu*).
By the terms "field" and "site," ponds, tanks, and so forth are also included here. "Silver" (*hirañña*) refers to the *kahāpaṇa* coin.
"Gold" (*suvaṇṇa*) refers to wrought gold (*jātarūpa*). By the inclusion of these two, all types of coins—including those made of iron, lac, and wood—are subsumed.
They go. Regarding "villages, market towns, and royal capitals": a village consists of a single hut and so forth; a market town (*nigama*) is one provided with shops;

a royal capital (*rājadhānī*) is the place where the commands of a single king are promulgated; a kingdom (*raṭṭha*) is a portion of a province (*janapada*); a province is a region such as Kāsi or Kosala;
a treasury (*kosa*) is fourfold—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; and a storehouse (*koṭṭhāgāra*) is threefold.

—The storehouse of wealth, the storehouse of grain, and the storehouse of cloth. "Whatever" is a term used to include everything without exception. "Lust-inducing" means in the sense of being fit to arouse lust.

Hereafter, in order to show [the analysis] by way of triads, [it is shown] by way of the triad of the past, the triad of the internal, the triad of the inferior, the triad of the occasion, the triad of conjunction, and the triad of the sense-sphere.

In the *Chattika* (Sixfold) [treatise], it is said: Regarding the "Past Triad" (*atītattika*) first, those that have passed away after reaching their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or the moments of arising and so forth are "past.
Those that have not yet arrived at either of these two are "future. Those that have arisen in dependence upon various causes are "present.
This is delimited by way of existence (*bhava*). For, starting from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), those produced in past existences [are past] in the immediately following existence...
Whether they have arisen at the end of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons or elsewhere, all those that have passed away are called "past.

Whether sensual desires are arising in future existences starting from the moment of death—whether in the immediately following existence or at the end of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons—all those are called "future.
Sensual desires that occur in the interval between death and rebirth-linking are called "present."

In the triad of internal [objects], those sensual pleasures that occur within one’s own continuity— occurring with the intention, as it were, “While proceeding thus, we shall be grasped as ‘self’”— are called internal sensual pleasures (*ajjhattā kāmā*).
Those, however, which exist outside of that, whether bound to the sense faculties or not bound to the sense faculties, are called external (*bahiddhā*).
The third category is stated by way of both [the inferior and the superior].
In the triad of the inferior, "inferior" means base. "Intermediate" means those that exist between the inferior and the superior.

The remainder are "superior" in the sense of being excellent. Furthermore, the states of being inferior, intermediate, and superior should be understood relative to one another. For instance, as compared to those in hell...
Sensual pleasures that have reached the limit are called "inferior. Compared to those, the sensual pleasures of the *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas* among the animals are called "exquisite.
The sensual pleasures of the remaining animals are called "middling. Even their sensual pleasures are inferior. Compared to those, the sensual pleasures of powerful *peta*s are called "exquisite.
The sensual pleasures of the rest are called "middling. Even their sensual pleasures are inferior. Compared to those, the sensual pleasures of the country folk...

Sensual pleasures are called "exquisite" [to some]. To those living in the borderlands, sensual pleasures are called "middling. Even for them, they are inferior. Compared to them, the sensual pleasures of village headmen are called "exquisite.
For their female attendants, sensual pleasures are called "middling. Even for them, they are inferior.
Compared to them, the sensual pleasures of provincial governors are called "exquisite. For their female attendants, sensual pleasures are called "middling. Even for them...

They are inferior. Compared to them, the sensual pleasures of regional kings are called superior. Compared to those, the sensual pleasures of their ministers are called middling. Compared even to those, they are inferior.

Compared to them, the sensual pleasures of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) are called superior. Compared to him, the sensual pleasures of his ministers are called middling. Compared even to those, they are inferior.
Compared to them, the sensual pleasures of the earth-dwelling devas are called superior. [Compared to] their female attendants...
The sensual pleasures of the gods are called "middling. Compared to those, even they are inferior.

Taking those as a basis, the sensual pleasures of the Cātumahārājika gods are "exquisite," and so on by way of this method, until the sensual pleasures of the Akaniṭṭha gods reach the pinnacle and are called "supreme.
In this manner, the states of inferior, middling, and exquisite should be understood by taking each preceding stage as a basis for comparison.

In the triad of opportunity (*okāsattika*): those who desire rebirth in the states of misery (*āpāyika-kāma*) are those who wish to be born in the four woeful states (*apāya*), which are devoid of life-force and reckoned as non-prosperity. Those who desire rebirth among humans are human (*mānusika*). Those who desire rebirth among the gods are divine (*dibba*).

In the triad of association (*saṃyogattika*): because of the enjoyment of present objects of desire, with the exception of those in hell, the desires of the remaining beings in the woeful states, of humans, and of the gods from the Cātumahārājika realm up to the Tusita heaven, are "present" (*paccupaṭṭhita*).

Regarding "desires" (*kāmā*): for the *Nimmānarati* devas, when they desire to enjoy themselves beyond what is provided by natural objects, they create and create objects according to their own liking and then enjoy them;
thus, the desires of the *Nimmānarati* devas are called "created desires" (*nimmitakāmā*).

For the *Paranimmitavasavatti* devas, having known their own inclination, they partake of objects created by others; thus, the desires of the *Paranimmitavasavatti* devas are "created-by-others" (*paranimmita*).
"Kāmas" means sensual pleasures. "Appropriated" refers to sensual pleasures grasped as "this is mine.

"Unappropriated" refers to those not so grasped, such as the sensual pleasures of the people of Uttarakuru. "Coveted" refers to those grasped as "this is mine" by way of craving. "Uncoveted" is the opposite of what was just mentioned.
"All phenomena of the sense-sphere" refers to the method beginning with "having made the Avīci hell the lower limit," and so forth.

They are included among the states belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) that have been mentioned. Herein, this is the explanation of the terms: briefly, there are two kinds of desire (*kāma*):
the object-desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*). Therein, in terms of meaning, defilement-desire is lustful craving (*chandarāga*).

Object-desire is the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) consisting of the three planes. Furthermore, defilement-desire is called *kāma* because it desires; the other is called *kāma* because it is desired. In whatever place these two types [of desire] exist—

Sensual desire (*kāma*) operates by way of its range of activity; since it operates within this elevenfold location consisting of the four woeful states, the human world, and the six celestial worlds, it is called "of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).
With reference to the phenomena included therein, it is said: "all phenomena of the sense-sphere. They are called "phenomena" (*dhammā*) because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

"Phenomena pertaining to the fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacara-dhammā) means that all phenomena are included within the fine-material sphere by way of those phenomena described in the manner beginning with: "having made the Brahma-world the lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha deities above," and so forth.
"Phenomena pertaining to the immaterial sphere" (arūpāvacara-dhammā) means [having made] the deities belonging to the base of infinite space the lower limit and above...

All phenomena belonging to the formless sphere (arūpāvacara) are included by way of the method stated in such passages as, “having included the gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,” and so forth.
In this context, they are called "form-sphere" (rūpāvacara) because they move within form; they are called "formless-sphere" (arūpāvacara) because they move within the formless.

They are "objects of craving" (taṇhāvatthuka) in the sense that they serve as the basis (vatthu) for craving, both as its foundation and as its cause. They are "objects of craving" (taṇhārammaṇa) by way of the occurrence of craving.
They are the objects of craving. "In the sense of being desirable" means in the sense of being something to be longed for.

"In the sense of being alluring" means in the sense of being fit to arouse passion. "In the sense of being intoxicating" means in the sense of producing intoxication such as pride of lineage and so forth.

In this context, beginning with "What are sensual objects as things? Agreeable forms... and ending with "...whatever thing is alluring," it is stated by way of both the animate and the inanimate. It should be understood that the remainder consists of the various sets of four and so on, up to the sixfold set.
Having thus shown sensual desire as an object (*vatthukāma*), he said, "What are sensual desires as defilements (*kilesakāma*)? and so forth, in order to show sensual desire as a defilement.
Therein, "desire" (*chanda*) is weak lust; "lust" (*rāga*) is stronger than that; the three [types of] lust mentioned below are even stronger than these.

"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) is desire consisting of sensual pleasure, not the desire for the wish to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*).
There is no desire for the Dhamma. By way of longing and by way of lust, "kāma" itself is lust;

thus it is "kāmarāga" (lust for sensual pleasure). By way of longing and by way of delight, "kāma" itself is delight; thus it is "kāmanandī" (delight in sensual pleasure). Having understood the meaning of "kāma" in all these instances, it is "kāmatanha" (craving for sensual pleasure) in the sense of running toward [objects].
It is "kāmasneha" (affection for sensual pleasure) in the sense of moistening. It is "kāmaparilāha" (fever of sensual pleasure) in the sense of burning. It is [craving] in the sense of infatuation...

*Kāmamucchā* (intoxication by sensual pleasures) is so called because it causes one to become infatuated with sense-desires. *Kāmajjhosāna* (clinging to sensual pleasures) is so called in the sense of swallowing and thoroughly consuming them.

It is called the *kāmogha* (flood of sensual pleasures) because it causes one to sink in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by means of the floods. It is called the *kāmayoga* (yoke of sensual pleasures) because it yokes one to the cycle of existence. Grasping at craving and views by way of their firmness is *upādāna* (clinging).
It is called a *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance) because it obstructs and envelops the mind.

"Addasanti" means "I saw. "Kāmā" is a form of address. "Te" means "your. "Mūlaṃ" means "foundation. "Saṅkappā" means "by way of conceptualization. "Na taṃ saṅkappayissāmi" means "I shall not perform that conceptualization. "Na hohisi" means "you shall not come to be.
"Icchamānassa" means "of one who expects. "Sādiyamānassa" means "of one who relishes. "Patthayamānassa" means "of one who arouses a longing.
"Pihayamānassa" means "of one who arouses the desire to attain. "Abhijappamānassa" means...
For one who produces satisfaction by means of craving; or alternatively, for one who approves [of it].
"Of a khattiya," and so forth, is stated by way of the four classes. "Of a householder or of one gone forth" is stated by way of gender (liṅga).
"Of a deva or of a human" is stated by way of rebirth (upapatti). "It succeeds" means it is accomplished.
"Samijjhati" means it is successfully accomplished. It "succeeds" (ijjhati) by way of obtaining a distinguished form; it "obtains" (labhati) by way of obtaining a beautiful form;
it "attains" (paṭilabhati) by way of obtaining a pleasing form; it "reaches" (adhigacchati) by way of obtaining a well-proportioned form;
it "finds" (vindati) by way of obtaining a radiant complexion. Alternatively, it succeeds through the greatness of merit, and through the greatness of birth.
He obtains it. He acquires it through the greatness of sovereignty. He attains it through the greatness of happiness. He finds it through the greatness of prosperity.

"One-sided statement" (*ekaṃsavacana*) means a statement consisting of a single portion. It is, for example, like the expressions "having arranged the robe on one shoulder" or "a question to be answered with a categorical (one-sided) reply," which serve as a negation of taking multiple sides.
"Statement free from doubt" (*nissaṃsayavacana*) means a statement devoid of uncertainty; it is a statement that negates hesitation.
*Attha*: the meaning. *Nikkaṅkhāvacanaṃ*: a statement that excludes doubt, [expressed as] "How could this be?
How could this be? *Advejjhavacanaṃ*: *Dvejjha* is a state of being twofold; by the absence of that, it is an "undivided statement.

Just as in such passages as "The Buddhas are undivided in speech," it is the exclusion of hesitation (*vimati*), being free from a state of duality. *Adveḷhakavacanaṃ*: it is "unwavering" due to the absence of a double heart.
“*Itihāsa*, *itihāsā*” is a statement for the rejection of doubt (*dveḷhaka*). “A definitive statement” (*niyoga-vacana*) means that two [contradictory] things are not possible in a single sense;
thus, it is a definitive statement that rejects a twofold path. Elsewhere, however, it is stated: “There are no definitive [conclusions] regarding future objects.
“An infallible statement” (*apaṇṇaka-vacana*) is a core statement free from fallacy (*palāsa*), a cause that is not contradicted—[this is called] “infallible.”
In phrases such as "some [say] it is a possibility," this is speech that has a firm foundation, like a jewel that is not subject to deception.
This statement is one of establishment; it is a settling and a placing that has descended and become firmly established.
Those words which have been assigned to their respective categories in this *Mahāniddesa*, while proceeding through those classifications, [are to be understood] by means of the three...
They undergo analysis through causes; becoming diverse, they become diverse by way of four causes.
Furthermore, in this context, the secondary exposition proceeds according to two points. How so? For those [terms] undergo analysis by way of these three causes:
by way of the phoneme (*byañjana*), by way of the prefix (*upasagga*), and by way of the meaning (*attha*). In that regard: "Anger (*kodha*) is the act of being angry, the state of being angry..."
"Fault, faultiness, the state of being faulty"—thus should the analysis according to verbal form (*byañjana*) be understood.
For therein, anger itself, as a single term, receives such an analysis merely through its verbal form.
However, "it succeeds, it is accomplished, it is obtained, it is acquired, it goes, it attains"—thus should the analysis according to prefixes (*upasagga*) be understood.
“Wisdom, skill, sagacity, discrimination, reflection, and investigation”—thus should the analysis be understood according to its meaning.
Among these, first, in the description of the term *pīti* (rapture), these three analyses are found: for instance, "rapture is gladness" is an analysis according to the phrasing (*byañjana*);
"delight, rejoicing, and laughter" is an analysis according to the prefixes (*upasagga*); and "vitality, satisfaction, and elation" [is an analysis according to the synonyms].
“Satisfaction” (*attamanatā*) is according to its meaning. In this manner, the application of grammatical case-endings (*vibhattigamana*) should be understood for all word-explanations.
Even though things are diverse, they are diverse by way of these four reasons: diversity of name, diversity of characteristic, diversity of function, and diversity of exclusion.
In that regard: “What, on that occasion, is ill-will (*byāpāda*)? That which on that occasion...”
In the passage, “At that time there was ill-will (*dosa*), corrupting (*dussanā*)”, both these terms—*byāpāda* (malevolence) and *dosa* (hatred)—are simply anger;
they differ only in name. Thus, their distinction should be understood as a distinction of names.

Furthermore, in the sense of a heap (*rāsa*), all five aggregates (*khandhā*) constitute a single aggregate. In this context, however, form (*rūpa*) has the characteristic of being affected (*ruppana*).
Feeling has the characteristic of being felt; perception has the characteristic of perceiving; volition has the characteristic of willing; consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
By this diversity of characteristics, there are five aggregates. Thus, diversity should be understood by way of the diversity of characteristics.
“The four right endeavours: here a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states...
[and so on] ...he exerts his mind and strives. Thus, it is a single energy that appears in four places due to the diversity of its functions.
In this way, the diversity [of energy] should be understood through the diversity of its functions.
However, in such passages as, “There are four things contrary to the true Dhamma: respect for anger, not respect for the true Dhamma;
respect for hypocrisy, not respect for the true Dhamma; respect for gain, not respect for the true Dhamma;
respect for honor, not respect for the true Dhamma,” the diversity [of the teaching] should be understood through the diversity of its negations.
However, these four diversities are not found in *pīti* alone; they are found in all [the aggregates] according to their respective occurrence.
For "rapture" (*pīti*) is the name for rapture, and "consciousness" (*citta*) is the name for consciousness.

Rapture has the characteristic of pervading; feeling has the characteristic of being felt; perception has the characteristic of perceiving; volition has the characteristic of willing; and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
Likewise, rapture has the function of pervading; feeling has the function of experiencing; perception has the function of perceiving; volition has the function of intending;

and consciousness has the function of cognizing. Thus, diversity should be understood by way of the diversity of functions. As for the diversity of opposition, this is not found in the section on rapture.
However, in the exposition of non-greed and so forth, it is found according to the method beginning with: "Non-greed is non-covetousness, the state of being uncovetous," and so on. Thus...

The diversity [of the terms] should be understood through the diversity of their prohibitions. Thus, in all explanations of the terms, the fourfold diversity should be understood according to what is applicable.
Furthermore, the further elucidation either serves as a praise of the term's meaning or as a reinforcement; thus it proceeds in two ways. [As for the phrase] "by the tip of a staff":
For if this term were uttered only once, as if being squeezed together, it would not be called "blossomed,
adorned, and embellished"; but when it is stated repeatedly— by way of its phonemes, its prefixes, and its meanings— as "rapture (pīti), gladness (pāmojja),
rejoicing (āmodanā), exultation (pamodanā), laughter (hāso), mirth (pahāso), and joy (vittī)," then it is indeed called "blossomed, adorned, and embellished."
For just as when a young boy has been bathed, dressed in beautiful garments, adorned with flowers, and his eyes anointed,
and then a single drop of *manosilā* is placed upon his forehead—
it does not yet become what is called a "mind-design" (*cittatilaka*) by that much alone; rather, it is only when drops have been made surrounded by various colors that it is called a "mind-design."
It is so. This should be understood as being exactly like that. This is called "explanation of the word-meaning" (*padatthuti*).
However, "strengthening" (*daḷhīkamma*) is simply the repeated utterance by way of prefix, particle, and meaning.
For example, when one says "friend," or "venerable sir," or "yakṣa," or "snake," [the repetition] constitutes strengthening.
When one says, "Friend, friend," "Venerable sir, venerable sir," "Yakṣa, yakṣa," or "Snake,
snake," there is what is called reinforcement; in the same way, when one merely says "rapture" (pīti) as if pressing down once with the tip of a stick, there is no reinforcement,
but rather [it is reinforced] through repetition by means of the phonemes, the prefixes, and the meanings of "rapture."
When it is said, “Gladness is rejoicing, delighting, laughter, hearty laughter, and cheerfulness,” this constitutes what is called “strengthening.
Thus, the further elucidation proceeds by way of two points. By means of this [method] as well, the meaning is to be understood in all instances of the explanations of the terms as they are obtained.
In this context, it "refreshes" (pīnati), thus it is *pīti*. Its characteristic is gladdening; its function is to refresh the body and mind, or its function is pervading;

it is manifested as elation. That which is associated with the five strands of sensual pleasure—that *pīti* which is connected to the fivefold division of sense objects such as visible forms—is "that which refreshes," thus it is *pīti*;
this is the term for its intrinsic nature. The state of one who is glad is *pāmojja*. Its mode is rejoicing.

*Āmodanā*. *Pamodanā* is the state of being delighted (*pamodanākāra*). Or, just as the mixing together of medicines, oils, hot water, or cold water is called "delighting" (*modanā*), so too this is "delighting" through the bringing together of states of joy (*pītidhamma*).
However, by means of a prefix, it is expressed as "delight" (*āmodanā*) and "exultation" (*pamodanā*).
It causes one to laugh, thus it is "laughter" (*hāsa*). It causes one to laugh aloud, thus it is "loud laughter" (*pahāsa*); this is a designation for the modes of being joyful and exultant.
"Vitti" means "vitta," which is a name for wealth. However, because it is a condition for mental joy (*somanassa*) and resembles wealth, it is called "vitti.
For just as joy arises in a wealthy person depending upon his wealth, so too does it arise in one possessed of rapture (*pīti*) depending upon that rapture.
Joy arises; therefore, it is called "vitti" (experience). "Tuṭṭhi" (contentment) is the name for joy established in its own nature.
However, a person possessing joy is called "udagga" (exultant) because of the upliftedness and elevated state of body and mind;
the state of being exultant is "odagya" (exultation).
"Self-satisfaction" (*attamanatā*) means being pleased with oneself. For the mind of one who is dissatisfied is not called "one's own mind" because it is a basis for suffering;
however, the mind of one who is satisfied is called "one's own mind" because it is a basis for happiness.

Thus, "self-satisfaction" (*attamanatā*) means being pleased with oneself (*sakamanatā*), the state of being pleased with oneself—this is the meaning. Furthermore, since that [satisfaction] does not belong to anyone else...
Self-satisfaction (*attamanatā*) is simply a state of consciousness, a mental factor (*cetasika dhamma*); therefore, it is called “self-satisfaction of the mind” (*attamanatā cittassa*).

It is called “mind” (*citta*) because of its variegated nature (*vicittatā*). It is called “intellect” (*mano*) because it measures and knows the object. “Mānasa” means the intellect itself; for in the passage, “The snare that moves through the air, which wanders as the intellectual (*mānaso*)”—here the associated mental factors are called “intellectual.
“How indeed, Blessed One, can your disciple, delighting in your teaching...”
“A trainee who has not yet attained his heart’s desire may pass away while listening to the teachings.
Here, “heart’s desire” (*mānasa*) refers to *arahatta* (Arahatship). But here, “mind” (*mano*) itself is “heart” (*mānasa*); this word has been expanded for the sake of euphony (*byañjana*).
“Heart” (*hadaya*) means consciousness (*citta*). As in the passage: “I will either hurl your mind [into the air] or split your heart open,” it refers to the chest (*uro*).
It is called "the heart" (*hadaya*). In the passage, "As if with heart to heart he knows and cleaves," it refers to consciousness (*citta*).
In the passage, "The kidneys and the heart," it refers to the physical heart-organ (*hadayavatthu*). But here, it is consciousness itself that is called "the heart" in the sense of being internal.

That very same [consciousness] is "bright" (*paṇḍara*) in the sense of being purified; this is said with reference to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). As it has been said: "This [mind] is luminous..."
“Monks, it is the mind, and it is defiled by adventitious defilements. However, because it has emerged from that [state],
even when unwholesome, it is described as “bright,” just as a river emerging from the Ganges is called the Ganges,
and one emerging from the Godhāvarī is called the Godhāvarī.
Regarding the phrase "mind as mind-base" (*mano manāyatanaṃ*): here, the inclusion of the word "mind" is for the purpose of showing that the mind itself constitutes the base. By this it is shown:

"This is not called the 'mind-base' because the mind is the base for something else, as in the case of a 'divine base' (*devāyatana*); rather, the mind itself is the base, hence it is the 'mind-base'.
In this context, [the term "base"] is used in the sense of a place of residence, a source, and a meeting place.
An *āyatana* should be understood in the sense of a place of birth (*sañjāti*) and in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).

For instance, in common usage, in such expressions as "the abode of Īśvara" (*issarāyatana*) or "the abode of Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāyatana*), the term "abode" (*āyatana*) refers to a dwelling place. In such expressions as "a mine of gold" (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) or "a mine of silver" (*rajatāyatana*), it refers to a source or mine.
However, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), in such passages as "In delightful abodes, they frequent the Vibhaṅga," it refers to a place of meeting or convergence (*samosaraṇa*).
In such passages as “The southern region is the breeding ground for cattle,” it refers to the place of origin.

In such passages as “In each respective instance, he attains the capacity for realization whenever there is a suitable occasion,” it refers to a cause. Here, however, it is appropriate in all three senses: as the place of origin, as the place of convergence, and as a cause.
For this is a *āyatana* in the sense of being the place where phenomena such as contact arise;
it is also an *āyatana* in the sense of being a meeting place, because external forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles converge here by way of being objects;
furthermore, it is an *āyatana* in the sense of being a cause, because it serves as the cause for contact and the rest through its status as a co-nascent condition and so forth.

It should be understood as follows. That which exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of mentalizing is a faculty (*indriya*); the mind itself as a faculty is the mind-faculty (*manindriya*). It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (*viññāṇa*);
consciousness itself as an aggregate is the consciousness-aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*). Its meaning should be understood by way of being a heap and so forth.
For in the passage, “It comes to be reckoned simply as a ‘great water-aggregate’,” the word *khandha* is used in the sense of a heap.

It is spoken of in the sense of a quality in such passages as "the aggregate of virtue" (sīlakkhandha) and "the aggregate of concentration" (samādhikkhandha). In the passage, "The Blessed One saw a large log of wood," it is spoken of in the sense of a mere designation (paṇṇattimatta). Here, however, "aggregate" (khandha) is spoken of in its conventional or metaphorical sense (ruḷhito).
For in the sense of a heap (rāsa), a single instance of consciousness is but one part of the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, just as one who cuts a single part of a tree...

Just as one says, “he cuts down a tree,” even so, a single instance of consciousness that constitutes a portion of the aggregate of consciousness is conventionally called the “aggregate of consciousness.
“The corresponding mind-consciousness element” refers to the mind-consciousness element that is suitable for those phenomena such as contact and the rest.
For in this passage, a single consciousness is described by three names: it is called *mano* in the sense of measuring; *viññāṇa* in the sense of cognizing;
and *dhātu* in the sense of intrinsic nature or, alternatively, in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being. *Sahagata* means not abandoned. *Sahajāta* means arisen together.
*Saṃsaṭṭha* means existing in a state of association. *Sampayutta* means conjoined equally through various modes. By which [modes]?
"In what ways? By way of simultaneous arising and so forth. "Are there no states that are associated with any other states? Yes, [there are].
Thus, in the refutation of this question, one should state:

"Is it not the case that there are some states which are co-existent, conascent, conjoined, simultaneously arisen, simultaneously ceased, having the same basis, and having the same object? In this manner, [one establishes] simultaneous arising and the rest.

By means of this [term], the meaning of association (*sampayoga*) has been stated. Thus, that which is joined by these modes, such as simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*), is "associated" (*sampayutta*).
"Simultaneous arising" means arisen together; the sense is "not apart. "Simultaneous cessation" means ceased together.

"Having a single basis" (*ekavatthuka*) means having a single basis by way of the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). "Having a single object" (*ekārammaṇa*) means having a single object by way of visible form and so forth.
In this context, the word *sahagata* is seen in the Word of the Conqueror (*jinavacana*) in five senses: identity, being mixed, object, support, and association.
In the passage, “This craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust,” it should be understood in the sense of identity;
the meaning is “consisting of delight and lust. In the passage, “That investigation, monks, which is accompanied by indolence, associated with indolence,” [it is used in the sense of association].
In this context, "intermingled" means intermingled with indolence arising here and there.

Regarding the phrase, “He is an obtainer of attainments accompanied by the form [realm] or attainments accompanied by the formless [realm],” the meaning here is “having form as their object” or “having the formless as their object.
[And regarding the phrase,] “the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by the perception of a skeleton...”
In the phrase "he develops," it refers to a support; the meaning is that [the perception] was obtained by relying upon the perception of a skeleton and having developed that perception of a skeleton.
In the phrase "this pleasure is accompanied by, co-arisen with, and associated with this joy," it refers to being conjoined;
the meaning is "mixed together. In this instance as well, "conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭha) is what has been used.
The word *sahajāta* (co-nascent) is used in the sense of "co-nascent," as in the passage: "co-nascent, pre-nascent, post-nascent.
The word *saṃsaṭṭha* (associated) is used in the sense of "association," as in "associated with householders" and "thus associated, venerable sir.
However, in the phrase "having avoided the lean and the fat, the horses were yoked in association (*saṃsaṭṭhā*)," it is used in the sense of "similarity."
“O Dadhivāhana, the *pucimanda* tree is surrounded by mangoes;
root is conjoined with root, and branch serves branch.
Here [the term] refers to those that have accumulated (*upacita*). In the phrase “states conjoined with mind,” it refers to states associated with mind (*cittasampayutta*). But here, however...
In the granting of its fruit, it is called "associated" because it is of a nature not to be dissociated, having arisen simultaneously and so forth, without being separated.

It has that as its object. Alternatively, after saying "accompanied," the term "co-arisen" is stated to show that it is not like something that follows behind, as in a sutta where things arrive one after another;
for it is not like form and non-form that arise separately from one another.
To show this, it is said: "associated" (*saṃsaṭṭha*).
And to show that he is not like milk and water [inseparable], it is said: "conjoined" (*sampayutta*).
For there are also phenomena that arise together which, though conjoined, cannot be separated, like milk and oil. Likewise...

Even though they are dissociated, they are like butter extracted from milk. Thus, in order to show that what is associated by way of characteristic possesses precisely the characteristics of simultaneous arising and so forth, it is said:
"simultaneous arising" (*ekuppāda*), and so on. Herein, what is the difference between simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*) and co-arising (*sahajāta*)?
Simultaneous arising is that which is devoid of any interval in its arising. Butter is made manifest through churning, even in the case of curd that has been separated from the time of the milk.

To show that it is not as if it were produced over the course of a single day—such as by way of a morning meal and an afternoon meal—it is said to be "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*), meaning it arises in a single moment.
It is "of one basis" (*ekavatthuka*) in the sense of having a single foundation or delimitation;
like two monks sharing a single dwelling, it is devoid of any difference in location. It is "of one object" (*ekārammaṇa*); this does not mean its object is restricted to one specific thing.
“Like eye-consciousness”—thus some explain it.
*Macca* is the root word. One who is attached to, clinging to, and stuck in forms and so forth is a *satta*.
For this has been said: “Venerable sir, it is said ‘a being, a being. In what way, venerable sir, is one called ‘a being’? In regard to form, Rādha...”

“Whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving—therein one is stuck, therein one is fastened; therefore, one is called ‘stuck’ (satta). Or else, one is “stuck” (satta) by way of being bound to existence.
One who wanders through happy and miserable destinies is a “man” (naro). One who is the son of Manu is a “mānava. One who nourishes oneself with requisites is a “person” (poso).
“Pum” refers to hell; one who swallows that is a “puggala. One who sustains the life-faculty is [a *jīvita*].
It is a *jīva* (living being). It goes from death to birth, thus it is a *jāgu*. It lives, thus it is a *jantu*. It goes by means of the sense faculties (*indriya*), thus it is an *indagu*.
Alternatively, it goes by means of karma that has become like Indra (*inda*), thus it is an *indagu*.

There is also the Pāli reading *hindagu*; they drive toward death, and it goes toward that, thus it is a *hindagu*. It is born from the mind, thus it is a *manuja*. That which it relishes refers to whatever form and so forth it finds gratifying.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. Concluding the matter already explained, the Blessed One said:
“Though one may desire sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...having obtained what a mortal desires.
From here on, without saying even this much more, we shall speak only of the specific distinction.
2. "If, while desiring sensual pleasures" means: if that person is wishing for sensual pleasures, or is striving through sensual desire.
"One in whom craving has arisen" means one in whom *taṇhā* (craving) has been born. "A living being" means a sentient being (*satta*). "Those sensual pleasures decline" means:
if those sensual pleasures should indeed diminish. "He is tormented like one pierced by an arrow" means: then he is oppressed as if pierced by an arrow made of iron or other materials. From this...
Setting aside what has already been stated, I shall explain each point that remains unexplained.

It "goes" (yāti) or proceeds by reaching an object that delights the eye. It "leads" (niyyati) because it brings about dearness through its quality of being beautiful and satisfies [the mind] by way of the object.
Having become something worth hearing, it delights the ear-cavity by way of the object.
"Parikaḍḍhati" means it is carried away. Because it is something to be remembered, and because it is brought forth by being grasped as an object that gladdens the mind, it is "saṃharīyati.
"Yathā" is a particle used in the sense of a simile. "By an elephant vehicle" means one travels or goes by means of an elephant vehicle;
"vā" has the sense of an alternative. "By a horse vehicle" means one travels or goes by means of a horse vehicle. "Goyuttaṃ" refers to a vehicle such as a cart yoked with oxen.
A vehicle; by that vehicle. The same method applies to “goat-cart” (ajayāna) and so forth. Born through the influence of what is desirable is “born” (sañjāta).
Produced through the state of being dear to the object is “produced” (abhinibbatta). Manifested by way of the agreeableness of the object.
Alternatively, born through the influence of sensual lust is “born”; produced through the delight in sensual pleasures is “produced. Through the influence of sensual craving...
It should be understood that [lust] has manifested by way of affection for sensual pleasures, by way of desire for sensual pleasures, and by way of feverish craving for sensual pleasures.

"Those sensual pleasures wane" means those objects of sensual pleasure and so forth wane and disappear. "Or he wanes from sensual pleasures" means this person, such as a kshatriya, wanes and disappears from sensual pleasures consisting of objects and so forth. "Previously... [etc.]
As in such passages as: “Wealth leaves the mortal; the mortal leaves wealth first. How? In what manner?
“While he still stands” means while he is still alive. “Those enjoyments” refers to those material objects of desire and so forth.
“Kings” refers to kings of the earth and so on. “Carry off” means they take and go away, or they plunder. “Or thieves” means...
"Breaking the joints," and so forth. "Fire" refers to forest fires and the like. "Burns" means it consumes, reducing things to ashes. "Water" refers to floods and the like.
"Carries away" means it takes [them] and brings them to the great ocean. "Unpleasant ones" means those who are undesirable and disagreeable.
"Heirs take [the wealth]" means those who are deprived of their inheritance and have no owner take it. "Or what is deposited" means that which has been set aside after being made into a store.

“Does not attain” means he does not find, does not acquire, or does not see; such is the meaning. “Ill-employed” refers to occupations such as agriculture and trade that are engaged in through improper application.
“Are broken” means they reach a state of ruin; they do not proceed successfully—this is the meaning.
The sense of occurrence (sambhava) should be understood from such examples as, “Those who do not drive [properly] break the chariot.”
"A family-doomer arises in a family" means that one who burns the lineage, the last person in the family, is reborn in a family such as those of the khattiyas.
There is also a reading "one who brings ruin to the family. "He squanders those riches" means he exhausts the wealth, such as gold and so forth, belonging to that family.
"He scatters" means he causes separation; he casts it far away. "He destroys" means he ruins it, bringing it to non-appearance.
He causes [it] to go away. Alternatively, it should be construed as follows: having become a woman-gambler, he scatters;
having become a liquor-gambler, he dissipates; having become a dice-gambler, he ruins. Or, "scatters" means by not knowing the income that has arisen;
"dissipates" means by not knowing the methods of distribution; "ruins" means by failing to provide protection for the place where it was deposited, and so forth.
"Impermanence itself is the eighth" means that the very nature of destruction is the eighth. "They fade away" means they go out of sight.
"They waste away" means they are no longer perceived. "They burn away" means they depart from their place. "They fall away" means they flow down.
"They disappear" means they go to disappearance, which is to say, out of sight. "They crumble apart" means they depart having become reduced to dust and powder.
“Those enjoyments remain” means while those riches are still present; it is used here as in such passages as “while they remain or even when they have perished.
“He” refers to that person who is the owner of the enjoyments. He “falls away” from the world of the devas; he “dies” from the world of humans;
he “perishes” from the worlds of nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth. Alternatively, he “diminishes” by way of his storehouses of grain; he “declines” by way of his storehouses of wealth.
It is worn away by way of elephants, cattle, horses, and so forth; it falls away by way of female and male slaves;
it disappears by way of wives and ornaments; some explain that it perishes by way of water and the like.
"Made of iron" means produced from black iron and the like. "By a dart" means by an arrow. "Made of bone" means excluding human bone.
By the remainder. "Made of ivory" means made of elephant tusks and so forth. "Made of horn" means made of cow horns and so forth. "Made of wood" means made of bamboo and so forth.
"Struck" means hit by one or another of the aforementioned types of arrows. "Is afflicted" (*ruppati*) means it is scattered; it undergoes transformation.
"Is disturbed" (*kuppati*) means it wavers; it gives rise to agitation. "Is struck" (*ghaṭṭīyati*) means it has been struck.
It becomes so. "It is oppressed" means it is oppressed; the wound that has received a blow becomes inflamed.
"On the third day, after inserting the probe, it is irritated at the time of washing. It is oppressed by the application of caustic. Or it is lacerated during the washing of the blow.
It becomes inflamed by that production of pain. It is oppressed by the insertion of the probe. It is irritated by the application of caustic"—thus some explain it.
"Afflicted by disease" means being oppressed after having received a blow. "Dejected" means having fallen into a state of mental distress (*domanassa*).
"Through change and alteration" refers to that which, having abandoned its natural state, is brought into a different condition;

namely, sorrow such as internal grief and the like, lamentation which is verbal wailing, suffering which is bodily oppression and the like, dejection which is mental oppression and the like, intense exertion, and despair. These...
The aforementioned types of sorrow and so forth arise and become manifest. 3.

The summary meaning of the third verse is as follows: But that bhikkhu who, by means of suppressing or by means of uprooting desire and lust for these sensual pleasures, avoids them with his own foot as one would avoid the head of a snake—he [traverses] the entire world.
"Having expanded [his mind], being mindful, he transcends craving—which is reckoned as 'clinging in the world'—by means of equanimity.
The word "yo" (who) is the term to be analyzed. "Yo yādiso" (whoever such as this), etc., are the terms that analyze it.
And here, since "yo" is a term for a person (*atthapada*), and it indicates a person without restriction, therefore, in order to show its meaning, [the commentator] speaks without restriction:
The word *yo* (who) alone indicates the person (*puggala*). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: *yo* means "whosoever.

Since whosoever is called by that name is necessarily manifested in a single mode by way of being endowed with those phenomena that have reached their respective gender, connection, designation, appearance, and state, [the author] spoke the words beginning with *yādiso* (of such a kind) in order to make that known there, while clarifying that specific distinction.
In this context, "of whatever kind" means by way of gender: whether he be such or such, long or short, black or white, hairy-skinned or lean, or stout;
that is the meaning. "According to his application" means by way of practice:
whether he be engaged in one way or another, engaged in building work or engaged in recitation.
Or, the meaning is that he is engaged in the burden of providing lodging. "As appointed" means as established by way of being the overseer of new construction and so forth.
"According to his function" means as established by way of being a lamp-bearer, a guide, and so forth.
"Having attained a particular position" means having reached a certain station, such as the position of a general or a treasurer. "Endowed with which quality" means by which quality...
It has arrived by way of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) and so forth.
"By suppression" means by means of access and absorption concentration, through the removal of the defilements, just as moss is removed by striking with a jar.
"By eradication" means by making them not arise again, [it is attained] through the path by way of the absolute destruction of the defilements.

"Cut off at the root" means either by way of abandoning or by way of total eradication. The eleven phrases beginning with "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton" are stated by way of insight (vipassanā).
The six phrases beginning with "Even while developing the recollection of the Buddha" refer to one who develops the recollection of death (maraṇassati) and the recollection of peace (upasamānussati).

"Even while developing" refers to these [practices] by way of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*). "Even while developing mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*)," "even while developing mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*)," "even while developing the first jhāna," and so on, up to "even while developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti*)," are stated by way of absorption concentration (*appanā-jhāna*).
In that context, "sensuous pleasures are like a skeleton" is well-expressed.
“A skeleton, stripped of flesh and smeared with blood”—this is the simile for these sensual pleasures; thus, sensual pleasures are "likened to a skeleton.
"In the sense of providing little gratification" means in the sense of seeing that "the gratification of pleasure here is slight and limited, while the danger is greater.
"Perceiving" means [seeing] with the eye of knowledge: "Insofar as that dog would merely partake of exhaustion and distress."
“Walking about. “He avoids” means he goes far away. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Householder, suppose there were a dog, overcome by hunger and weakness, standing before the slaughterhouse of a butcher;
then a skillful butcher or a butcher’s apprentice would present him with a well-cut skeleton of bones.”

“Suppose it were smeared with blood and devoid of flesh. What do you think, householder, would that dog, while licking our well-pulped, well-extracted bone—devoid of flesh and smeared with blood—be able to overcome its hunger and weakness?
