“No, indeed, venerable sir. “And for what reason? “Because, venerable sir, that bone is nothing more than a mere skeleton.”
“Venerable sir, that skeleton, well-boned and stripped of flesh, smeared with blood—this would only result in exhaustion and distress for that dog.
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a skeleton; they bring much suffering and much despair.’”
“The danger here is even greater. Having seen this as it truly is with correct wisdom,
one avoids that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity, and develops instead that equanimity which is unified and based on unity,
wherein the clinging to worldly material things ceases without remainder.
They are "flesh-meat similes" because a piece of flesh is common to vultures and other scavengers; they are "common to many" in the sense of being shared by many.
They are "firebrand similes" because a burning grass-torch is their simile; "in the sense of burning along" means in the sense of burning the hands and so forth.
They are "charnel-pit similes" because a pit full of glowing embers—devoid of smoke and reduced to ashes—that measures more than a man's height, is their simile.
They are like glowing coals in the sense that they involve great burning. They are like dreams because gardens, groves, and such things are merely dream-like similes for them.
They are like borrowed goods in the sense that they remain only for a short duration, without being reached or attained.
They are like borrowed items such as vehicles and so forth obtained through begging; they are temporary in nature.
In the sense of being unattached. They are "likened to tree fruits" because a tree with fully ripened fruit is their simile.
"In the sense of breaking and crushing" means both in the sense of breaking the branches and in the sense of felling the tree by breaking it down on all sides.

They are "likened to a sword and a butcher’s block" because a sword and a butcher’s block are their simile. "In the sense of hacking" means in the sense of cutting. They are "likened to a spear and a stake."
"These are like spears and spikes" means in the sense of piercing through; "in the sense of falling upon and striking.
These are "like the heads of snakes" in the sense of producing fear; "in the sense of being accompanied by fear when facing them.
These are "like a mass of fire" in the sense of producing suffering; "in the sense of great scorching."
"He avoids sensual pleasures in the sense that they produce great distress and bodily affliction. For this has been said:
"Householder, suppose a vulture, a heron, or a hawk were to fly up carrying a piece of meat;
then other vultures, herons, and hawks would pursue it again and again, tearing at it and snatching it away. What do you think..."
“What do you think, householder? If that vulture, or hawk, or falcon were not to let go of that piece of meat quickly, would it come to death on that account, or to suffering amounting to death?
“Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘The pieces of meat are like this.’”
"Sensual pleasures have been described by the Blessed One... [as before] ...he develops that very equanimity.
Householder, it is just as if a man were to take a burning grass torch and walk against the wind. What do you think, householder?
If that man did not quickly let go of that burning grass torch, would that burning grass torch not burn his hand or..."
“...it might burn his hand, or it might burn his arm, or it might burn some other limb or member, and because of that he would meet death or suffering amounting to death?”—“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a grass torch; they bring much suffering.’”
“Full of many dangers... [and so on] ... he develops that very equanimity. Householder, suppose there were a charcoal pit more than a man’s height deep, full of glowing coals, free from smoke.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not desiring death, desiring pleasure, averse to pain; and two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him toward that charcoal pit.”
“They would drag him toward it. What do you think, householder, would that man bend his body toward that thought?
“Yes, venerable sir. “For what reason? “Because, venerable sir, it is known to that man:
‘I shall fall into this pit of embers; on account of that, I will meet death or suffering as painful as death.’”
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a pit of glowing embers… [as above] …he develops that very equanimity.
Householder, it is just as if a man were to see in a dream a delightful park, a delightful grove, a delightful landscape, or a delightful lotus pond; then, having woken up, he [reflects upon it].”
One would not perceive anything at all. In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
“Sensual pleasures have been compared to a dream by the Blessed One... [as before] ...he develops that very equanimity.
Householder, it is just as if a man, having requested borrowed wealth—such as a carriage fit for a gentleman or excellent jeweled earrings—were to use those borrowed goods.
Honored and surrounded by a retinue, he might enter the marketplace. When people saw him, they would say, "What a wealthy man indeed! Such is how the wealthy enjoy their riches!
Yet wherever his owners saw those goods, they would take them away from that very spot. What do you think, householder?

“Would that man not indeed undergo a change of state? “Yes, venerable sir. “For what reason? “Because, venerable sir, they are taken away by their owners. “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared to borrowed goods by the Blessed One… [as previously stated] …he develops that very equanimity. Just as, householder, if a king’s frontier fortress were well-provided with provisions, well-stocked with grass, wood, and water, and well-guarded with strong gates and bolts; and if a man from the countryside, having entered it, were to take whatever he needed for his journey—such as food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps—and having taken these things, were to depart from that fortress by the eastern gate, the western gate, the northern gate, or the southern gate, would that man not indeed undergo a change of state?
“Yes, venerable sir. “For what reason? “Because, venerable sir, they are taken away by their owners. “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘Sensual pleasures have been compared to borrowed goods by the Blessed One… [as previously stated] …he develops that very equanimity.’”
Not far from a village or a town there was a dense grove of trees, and in it was a tree that was laden with fruit and possessed of ripe fruit, yet not a single fruit had fallen to the ground.
Then a man might come seeking fruit, searching for fruit, wandering in quest of fruit; he would enter deep into that grove.
He might see that tree with its fruit both abundant and fully developed. It would occur to him:
"This tree indeed has abundant and fully developed fruit, yet not a single fruit has fallen to the ground;
moreover, I know how to climb a tree. What if I were to climb this tree and [take] as much as I need?"
‘I shall eat and fill my lap. He would climb that tree and eat as much as he desired and fill his lap.
Then a second person would come, seeking fruit, searching for fruit, wandering in quest of fruit, carrying a sharp axe. Having entered deep into that forest grove, he would see that tree.
It has both abundant fruit and well-developed fruit. It might occur to him:
"This tree indeed has both abundant and well-developed fruit, yet no fruits have fallen to the ground; moreover, I do not know how to climb the tree.
Suppose now that I were to cut this tree down at its root and eat as much as I need."
"And let me fill my lap. He would cut that tree right at its root. What do you think, householder?
That man who first climbed the tree—if he did not descend quickly—would that tree, as it fell, break his hand or break his foot, or some other limb or another?
“...he might break his limbs and joints, and because of that he would meet death or suffering amounting to death?
“Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:

‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to the fruits of a tree; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater. Thus he understands this as it really is.”
“Having seen this with right wisdom, one avoids that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity,
and develops that very equanimity which is unified and based on unity, wherein the clinging to worldly material things ceases without remainder.

Having thus shown insight (vipassanā) starting from the skeleton and ending with the simile of the mass of fire, he now says, “Developing the recollection of the Buddha,” etc., in order to show access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).
In this context, *anussati* is simply *sati* (mindfulness) because it arises again and again;

and it is called *anussati* because it is mindfulness appropriate for a clansman who has gone forth through faith, occurring precisely in the place where it ought to occur. *Buddhānussati* is the mindfulness arisen with reference to the Buddha.
This is a designation for that mindfulness which has the qualities of the Buddha—such as his state of being an Arahant—as its object. That...
"Recollection of the Buddha": developing it means increasing and expanding it. Recollection arisen with reference to the Dhamma is "recollection of the Dhamma";

this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-expounded. Recollection arisen with reference to the Saṅgha is "recollection of the Saṅgha";
this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its being well-practiced.
Recollection arisen with reference to virtue is *sīlānussati*; this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object one’s own qualities of virtue, such as being unbroken.
Recollection arisen with reference to generosity is *cāgānussati*; this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object one’s own qualities of generosity, such as being free-handed.
Recollection arisen with reference to deities is *devatānussati*; [this refers to] deities standing in the position of witnesses.
This is a designation for mindfulness that has one’s own qualities such as faith as its object. Mindfulness arisen with reference to inhalation and exhalation is *ānāpānassati*;
this is a designation for mindfulness that has the sign of inhalation and exhalation as its object.

Mindfulness arisen with reference to death is *maraṇassati*; [it is so called] because it has as its object death, which is defined as the cutting off of the life-faculty included within a single existence.
This is a designation for mindfulness (*sati*).

Mindfulness that has gone to, or is active within, the body—which is known as the "body" because it is dependent upon and composed of the loathsome and repulsive things such as hair and so forth—is "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*).
Alternatively, when mindfulness has gone to such a body, it should be called "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatasati*), though it is abbreviated [to *kāyagatāsati*].

Without making [the compound], it is stated as “mindfulness directed to the body” (*kāyagatāsati*). This is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the sign of repulsiveness regarding the bodily parts beginning with the head-hairs.
It is a recollection arisen with reference to peace (*upasama*). “Recollection of peace” (*upasamānussati*) is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the subsiding of all suffering.
He develops the first jhāna, which is associated with applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
He develops the second jhāna, which is associated with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. He develops the third jhāna, which is associated with happiness and one-pointedness of mind.

He develops the fourth jhāna, which is associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind... and so on... even while developing the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he avoids sensual pleasures.

Having shown the abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), he now says, "While developing the path of stream-entry," and so forth, in order to show the abandoning of sensual desires by eradication (*samuccheda*).
In that context, "stream-entry" (*sotāpatti*) is the entering into the stream of the path; the path to stream-entry is the "path of stream-entry.
Regarding "sensual desires leading to the states of deprivation": those by which one goes to the states of deprivation are the "sensual desires leading to the states of deprivation."
By means of complete eradication, one who develops the path of stream-entry abandons [the fetters].

Because he returns to this world only once more by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), he is a "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*); his path is the "path of the once-returner. One who develops that path [abandons the fetters].

"Gross" (*oḷārika*) means having reached a state of feverish intensity. Because he does not return to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) even by way of rebirth-linking, he is a "non-returner" (*anāgāmī*); his path is the "path of the non-returner."

Cultivating that path. "Anusahagata" means having reached a state of subtlety. He is an *arahant* because he is far removed from defilements (*kilesa*), because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements, because he has slain the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because there is no opportunity (*raha*) for him to do evil, and because he is worthy (*araha*) of the requisites and so forth.
The state of an *arahant* is *arahatta*. What is that? It is the fruit of *arahantship*. The path to *arahantship* is the *arahattamagga*.
He is developing that path to arahantship. "In every way, all" means in every manner, all. "In every respect, all" means in every aspect, all.
"Without remainder, without residue" means leaving nothing behind, not even a scent. Alternatively, "in every way, all" refers to it by way of its roots;
"in every respect, all" refers to it by way of its aspects and details; "without remainder, without residue" [means the same].
By way of the absence of cultivation; likewise, by the first [term], there is the absence of misconduct; by the second, the absence of obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*);
and by the third, the absence of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Thus some explain it.
"Serpent" (*sappa*) is said to mean "any creature that moves crawling. "In what sense" (*kenaṭṭhena*) means "by what meaning. "Crawling" (*saṃsappanto*).
It is called a *sappa* because it goes (*gacchati*) as it wanders rightly (*sammā*). It is called a *bhujango* because it moves crookedly (*vaṅkavaṅko hutvā*).

It is called a *pannaso* because it has its head lying down (*nipannasīso hutvā*). It is called a *siraso* because it sleeps with its head; that is, by way of sleeping with its head placed between its coils, it sleeps with its head (*sirasā supati*), thus it is a *sarīsapo*.
It is called a *bilāsayo* because it dwells in a hole (*bile sayati*). There is also a textual reading (*pāḷi*) of "bilasayo," which is more elegant.
"He lies in a cave" means he is a cave-dweller (*guhāsayo*). "His fangs are his weapon" means that the snake has two fangs which are considered weapons in the form of striking instruments.
"Its venom is terrible" means the snake's venom, known as pervasive, is fierce and harsh.
"Its tongue is twofold" means that the snake has a double-tongue. "It tastes flavor with its two tongues" means with those two [tongues].
With the tongue one knows taste; one finds gratification and relishes it. One who desires to live is "one desiring life" (*jīvitukāma*).
One who desires not to die is "one desiring immortality" (*amaritukāma*). One who desires pleasure is "one desiring happiness" (*sukhakāma*). "Averse to suffering" means not wishing for suffering.
"With the foot" means with one's own foot. "The serpent's head" means the head of a snake. "One should avoid" means one should avoid it from afar.
"Vivajjeyya" means by its measure. "Parivajjeyya" means on all sides. "Abhinivajjeyya" means by the fourth measure.
Alternatively, by the first [measure] one avoids it from the front; by the second and third, from the two sides; and by the fourth, from behind.

Furthermore, for one who has not attained sensual pleasures, one should avoid them because they are the basis for the suffering rooted in seeking; for one who has attained them, because they are the basis for the suffering rooted in guarding them.

"One should avoid it; one should shun it because it is a basis for the suffering of the fever of ignorance; one should steer clear of it because it is a basis for the suffering of separation from the beloved, even at the gateway to destruction"—thus some explain.
It is *rāga* (lust) by way of coloring; it is *sārāga* (passion) in the sense of being a powerful coloring. Because it leads sentient beings along, step by step, toward sense objects...

*Anunaya* means "following after. *Anurujjhati* (he conforms) thus it is *anurodha*; the meaning is "he desires. Sentient beings rejoice in this in whatever state of existence they may be, thus it is *nandī*;
or, it itself rejoices, thus it is *nandī*. That which is both *nandī* and *rāga* in the sense of "coloring" (*rañjana*) is *nandirāga*.
In this context, craving that arises once toward a single object is *nandī*, while that which arises again and again is *nandirāga*.

It is called "lust of the mind" (*cittassa sārāgo*). That which was previously described as "lust in the sense of intense coloring" does not belong to a being, but rather is the lust of the mind itself;
this is the meaning. They desire objects by means of it, thus it is "desire" (*icchā*). Living beings become infatuated through its state of thick defilement, thus it is "infatuation" (*mucchā*).

*Ajjhosaṇa* (cleaving) is the state of attachment by way of swallowing and finishing [the object] through grasping. Because beings "gild" (*gijjhanti*)—that is, fall into greed—it is called *gedha* (greed).
Or, in the sense of being thick or dense, it is *gedha*; for it is said, "Or *gedha* is a thicket of trees," precisely in the sense of density.
The following term is augmented by means of a prefix; or, greed that is all-pervasive is *paligedha*. They adhere (*sajjanti*).

By this [craving] there is attachment (*saṅga*). Or, in the sense of clinging, it is attachment; in the sense of sinking down, it is mud (*paṅka*); in the sense of dragging along, it is the pull (*ejā*). For it is said:
"This pull drags this person along toward the production of this or that state of existence.
In the sense of deceiving, it is illusion (*māyā*); in the sense of generating beings within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is the progenitor (*janikā*). "Craving generates the person..."
For it is said: “His mind runs wild. It is called *sañjananī* (the producer) because it produces beings by joining them with suffering within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

It is called *sibbinī* (the seamstress) in the sense of binding together. For this [craving] sews and joins beings in the round of existence by means of death and rebirth-linking, just as a tailor sews one piece of cloth to another;
therefore, it is called *sibbinī* in the sense of binding together.
It is called *jālinī* (the net-like) because it possesses a net consisting of the manifold web of sense-objects, which is known as the agitation and settling of craving;
or because it has such a net. It is called *saritā* (the flowing) because, in the sense of dragging [one along], it is like a swift-flowing stream;
or it is called *saritā* in the sense of being moist. For this has been said: "The joys of a person are flowing and affectionate. Thus, they are both moist and smooth.
This is the meaning here. It is called a "thread" (*sutta*) because, in the sense of leading to ruin and disaster, it is like a spider’s thread.
For this has been said: "‘Thread,’ monks, is a designation for delight-and-lust. It is "crawling" (*visatā*) in the sense of spreading out over forms and so forth.

It is "pulling-in" (*āyūhinī*) because it causes beings to exert themselves for the sake of obtaining this or that [object]. Because it does not allow one to become weary [of saṃsāra], it is called "not-yet-wearyed."
In the sense of being a companion, it is the second [craving]. For this does not allow beings to become weary of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra);
rather, like a dear friend, it causes them to take delight wherever they go. Therefore it is said:
"Accompanied by craving, a person wanders through the long journey of saṃsāra."
“From this state to another state, one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Aspiration (*paṇidhi*) is so called by way of its being an aspiration. “The guide to existence” (*bhavanetti*) means the rope of existence (*bhavarajju*).
For by means of this rope, beings are led to whatever place they desire, like oxen bound by the neck with a rope. It “desires” (*vanati*) and clings to various objects.
It is called *vana* because it clings (*allīyati*), or because it seeks and entreats (*vanati yācati*). The word *vanatha* is formed by extending the term through the addition of the suffix *-tha*.
Alternatively, it is called *vana* because, in the sense of being the originator of harm and suffering and in the sense of being a thicket, it is like a forest (*vana*).
This is a name for powerful craving (*taṇhā*). However, in the sense of being more difficult to penetrate, that which is even stronger than this is called *vanatha*. Therefore it was said:
“Cut down the forest, not the tree; from the forest fear is born.
Having cut down both the forest and the undergrowth, become forest-free, O bhikkhus.
Here, *saṃstava* (familiarity) means intimacy through association; it signifies social contact. That is twofold: intimacy through craving and intimacy with friends.
Among these, it is here the intimacy of craving (*taṇhā-santhava*) that is intended. It is "affection" (*sneha*) by way of endearment.

It is "regard" (*apekkhā*) because one looks back with longing while being shaken by the act of forming an attachment (*ālaya-karaṇa*). And this has been said: "O King, here are these eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī;
O King, generate desire for them, have regard for life. Here, the meaning is: "Form an attachment (*ālayaṃ karohi*)."

It is called *paṭibandhu* because it binds [the mind] to each respective object (*ārammaṇa*). Alternatively, it is also called *paṭibandhu* because it is a relative (*bandhu*) in the sense of being distinct (*pāṭiyekka*).
Indeed, for sentient beings, there is no relative equal to craving (*taṇhā*) in the sense of constant dependence. It is called *āsā* because it does not abandon objects;
the meaning is that it consumes [objects] by both overwhelming them and by seeking satisfaction. By way of longing (*āsīsanā*),...
*Āsīsanā*. The state of having wished for something is *āsīsitattaṃ*.
Now, in order to show the sphere of its occurrence, the passage beginning with “desire for form” (*rūpāsā*) was stated.

Therein, because it is a desire by way of wishing, taking the meaning as “desire,” there is a desire for form, which is *rūpāsā*. In this way, all nine terms are to be understood. And here, the preceding ones...

The first five are stated by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), while the sixth is by way of greed for requisites (*parikkhāra*). That [sixth] pertains specifically to those who have gone forth;
the three following it pertain to householders by way of objects that never bring satisfaction.
For them, there is nothing dearer than wealth, children, and life. [They think: "This is mine, this is mine," or "This was given to me by such-and-such a person, this..."
"Jappā" means that which causes beings to long for in this way, "let it be given. The next two terms are augmented by prefixes;
because they are then begun to be analyzed in another manner, the word "jappā" is stated once again.
"Jappanā" is the mode of longing. "Jappitattaṃ" is the state of having longed. "Lolupo" refers to one who repeatedly tears at or draws toward an object.
Loluppa is the state of being greedy. Loluppāyanā is the manner of greediness. Loluppāyitatta is the state of one possessing greediness.
Pucchañjikatā is the name for that craving by which people wander about shaking and trembling like dogs wagging their tails at places where they expect gain;
it refers to that craving characterized by such shaking. One who lusts after objects that are desirable and pleasing is called *sādhukāmo*.
The state of that [desire] is *sādhukamyatā* (the desire for excellence). Lust for an improper object, such as one’s mother or maternal aunt, is *adhammarāga* (unrighteous lust).
Greed that arises even toward a proper object, but with excessive intensity, is *visamalobha* (improper greed).

Alternatively, according to such statements as “lust is improper,” the desire-lust (*chandarāga*) that arises toward either a proper or an improper object is *adhammarāga* in the sense of being unrighteous, and it is *visamalobha* in the sense of being improper.
It is to be understood as follows: *nikanti* is the inclination toward objects by way of desiring them; the mode of desiring is *nikāmanā*. *Patthanā* is the state of longing;
*pihanā* is the state of yearning. Intense longing is *sampatthanā*. Craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure is *kāmataṇhā*;
craving for existence in the realms of form and the formless is *bhavataṇhā*; craving for non-existence, which is reckoned as annihilation, is [vibhavataṇhā].

Craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*). Craving specifically for existence in the pure form realm is craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*). Craving for existence in the formless realm is craving for the formless (*arūpataṇhā*).
Lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism is craving for cessation (*nirodhataṇhā*). Craving for visible forms is craving for form; craving for sounds is craving for sound.
The same principle applies to craving for odors and so forth. The floods (*ogha*) and other such categories have meanings already explained.
It is called an *āvaraṇa* (obstruction) because it obstructs wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). It is called a *chadana* (covering) by virtue of its function of covering.

It is called a *bandhana* (bond) because it binds sentient beings to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). It is called an *upakkilesa* (corruption) because, having afflicted the mind, it becomes defiled and makes it impure.

It is called an *anusaya* (latent tendency) because it lies down closely (*anu-anu-seti*) in the sense of being firmly established. It is called a *pariyuṭṭhāna* (outburst) because it overwhelms the arising mind; [it is so called] in order to arise.
The meaning is that one seizes the side of the wholesome by means of the *apadāna*. For in such passages as “Thieves beset the road; scoundrels beset the road,” the meaning is “they seized the road.
In the same way, here too, *pariyuṭṭhāna* (obsession) should be understood in the sense of seizing.
It is called a *latā* (creeper) because it is like a creeper in the sense of entwining. Even in the passage where it is said, “The creeper arises and stands,” this craving is called a creeper.
"Viviccha" means desiring various things. "Root of the suffering of the round" means the root of suffering (*dukkhamūla*).
"Source of that very suffering" means the source of suffering (*dukkhanidāna*). "That suffering originates from this" means the origin of suffering (*dukkhappabhava*).

It is like a snare in the sense of being a bond, thus a "snare" (*pāsa*); specifically, it is the "Mara-snare" (*mārapāsa*). It is like a hook in the sense of being difficult to swallow, thus a "hook" (*baḷisa*).

The snare of Māra is the *mārabalisa*. Because those overcome by craving do not transcend the domain of Māra, and because Māra exercises power over them—by this method it is called "the domain of Māra" (*māravisaya*).

In the sense of flowing, craving itself is the river; thus, it is the "craving-river" (*taṇhānadī*). In the sense of overwhelming, craving itself is the net; thus, it is the "craving-net" (*taṇhājāla*). Just as dogs...
Just as those bound by a leather thong (gaddūla) are led wherever one wishes, so too are beings bound by craving;
thus, in the sense of being a firm bond, it is like a leather thong, and therefore it is called "gaddūla. Craving itself is the leather thong, hence "taṇhāgaddūla.
In the sense of being difficult to fill, craving itself is the ocean, hence "taṇhāsamudda. In the sense of coveting, it is "abhijjhā. By means of this they are corrupted, or it itself is corrupted.
Or, "greed" (*lobha*) is simply the state of being greedy. It is a "root" (*mūla*) in the sense of being the foundation for the unwholesome states associated with it.
Regarding the term "clinging" (*visattikā*): what is its meaning? By what intrinsic nature? It is "stretched out" (*visatā*) over forms and so forth; it is "wide" (*visālā*), meaning extensive;
it is "spread out" (*visaṭā*), meaning it spreads throughout the three planes of existence. [The variant] *visattikā* is merely the first word with the letter *t* [changed].
It is stated after making the letter *ṭ* and making a division of the consonants. "Visakkati" means it creeps along (*parisappati*) or endures (*sahati*).
For one who is lustful, even when struck with the foot—the object of his lust—he endures it. Some also say that "visakkana" refers to retreating or quivering.
Some commentators explain it as "the opponent of the wholesome and unwholesome. "Visaṃharati" means [to distribute] in such and such ways among sensual pleasures.
Seeing the benefits, one collects and contracts the mind by directing it toward renunciation in various ways;
"removes" means it carries away or bears off suffering, which is like poison.
It is "deceptive" because it deceives by grasping at the impermanent and so forth as permanent. It has "poison as its root" because it is the cause of karma that produces suffering.
It is "poison-rooted" (*visamūlā*) because its root consists of feelings that are of the nature of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) and so forth.

It is "poison-fruited" (*visaphalā*) because its fruit is poison due to being the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*). That craving by which there is the enjoyment of suffering itself—such as form (*rūpa*) and so on—and not of the Deathless (*amata*), is called "the enjoyment of poison" (*visaparibhogā*).
In all cases, the derivation of the terms should be understood according to their etymological analysis (*nirutti*).
Desiring to show its objective sphere, he said, "Furthermore, that craving is vast regarding forms," and so forth.

Therein, "furthermore, it is vast" means that craving is indeed great in the sense of being a vehicle for desire. The five beginning with "forms" are stated by way of attachment to the fivefold qualities of sensual pleasure.
The eleven phrases beginning with "clan" and "group" are stated by way of greediness. The triad of the sense-sphere element is stated by way of the round of kamma.
The triad of sense-sphere existence is analyzed by way of the round of resultants; the triad of perception-existence is analyzed by way of perception;
the triad of one-aggregate existence is analyzed by way of the aggregates. The triad of the past is analyzed by way of time; the tetrad of views is analyzed by way of objects;
the triad of states of deprivation is analyzed by way of location; and the triad of aggregates is analyzed by way of being devoid of a self and a soul.
It should be understood. Herein, this is the brief explanation of the meaning and its analysis:

"In that regard, what is the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*)? Taking the Avīci hell as its lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas above, whatever aggregates, elements, and bases have their range and are included within this interval."
“Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu).

“In that regard, what is the fine-material element (rūpadhātu)? Taking the Brahma-world as its lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha devas above, whatever exists within this interval, which belongs there and is included therein, for one who has attained [meditative absorption]...”
“The mental states and mental factors of one who has been reborn there, or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life—this is called the form realm (rūpadhātu).
“In that regard, what is the formless realm (arūpadhātu)?

Taking as its limit the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space below, and including within it the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception above—whatever exists in this interval, and whatever belongs to this range [is the formless realm].”

“Herein, the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained [a meditative absorption], or one who has been reborn [therein], or one who dwells in happiness in this very life—all these included phenomena are called the formless element (arūpadhātu).
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it says: “The sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu) is sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava);

the five aggregates are found there. The fine-material element (rūpadhātu) is fine-material existence (rūpabhava); the five aggregates are found there. The formless element (arūpadhātu) is formless existence (arūpabhava);”
It is said: “The four aggregates are found.
Alternatively, the element associated with *kāma*—which is defined as sensual lust—is the *kāmadhātu*; or else, the element that is itself defined as *kāma* is the *kāmadhātu*.
The element associated with form (*rūpa*), having abandoned *kāma*, is the *rūpadhātu*; or else, the element that is itself defined as form is the *rūpadhātu*. And *kāma*...
Having abandoned form, that which is associated with the formless is the formless element (*arūpadhātu*); or, the element known as the formless is the formless element.
Those same elements are further described by way of the cycle of existence (*bhava*). For they are called "existence" (*bhava*) because they come to be (*bhavanti*).

Existence associated with perception is "perceptual existence" (*saññābhava*), or the existence of those possessing perception, or the existence in which perception exists; this is sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*).
And there is the form existence (rūpabhava) which is free from non-perception, and the formless existence (arūpabhava) which is free from neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is not a state of perception, nor is it a state of non-perception; it is a portion of form existence. Because of the absence of grossness, it is "neither-perception";

because of its presence through subtlety, it is "nor non-perception"—thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Existence associated with that is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence" (nevasaññānāsaññābhava). Now...
Or, because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, there is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" in this existence; thus it is called *nevasaññānāsaññābhava*.
This is a portion of the formless existence (*arūpabhava*). An existence mixed with one aggregate of form is, or has, one "mixture" (*vokāra*);
thus it is *ekavokārabhava*, which is indeed the same as non-percipient existence (*asaññābhava*). An existence mixed with four formless aggregates, or having four mixtures...
"Becoming with four bases" (*catuvokārabhava*) means that this becoming has four bases; it is exclusively formless becoming (*arūpabhava*).

"Becoming with five bases" (*pañcavokārabhava*) means that this becoming is mixed with the five aggregates, or that this becoming has five bases; it consists of sense-sphere becoming (*kāmabhava*) and a portion of fine-material becoming (*rūpabhava*).
The triad of the past is to be understood in the same manner as explained above. "Seen" refers to a visible object (*rūpārammaṇa*) arising from the four [great] elements.

"Seen" (*suta*) refers to the sound-object, which arises from two sources. "Sensed" (*muta*) refers to the objects of smell, taste, and touch, which are to be grasped by contact and arise from four sources.
"Cognized" (*viññāta*) refers to the mental-object (*dhamma*), which is to be known by the mind.
Among those phenomena—seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—"dispersed" (*visaṭā*) means extensive, vast, and widespread.

Regarding "the world of the states of misery" (*apāyaloka*): it is called *apāya* because of the absence of the "iron" (*aya*) known as prosperity; [it refers] to that world of the states of misery. Regarding "the world of the aggregates" (*khandhaloka*):

in the sense of being a heap (*rāsa*), the five aggregates—form and so forth—are themselves the world. Regarding "the world of the elements" (*dhātuloka*): in the sense of emptiness (*suññata*), the eighteen elements—the eye element and so forth—are themselves the world.
Regarding "the world of the bases" (*āyatanaloka*): by way of such reasons as being bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases themselves [are the world].

The world (*loka*). All things are called the "world" in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. "Clinging" (*visattikā*) means they are spread out and extended within the world of the aforementioned kind.
"Mindful" (*sato*): one who remembers is mindful; thus, mindfulness (*sati*) is stated by way of the person.
In this context, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering. By means of it, people remember, or it itself remembers, or it is simply that which consists of remembering.
It exists. Furthermore, this mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away; its function is non-forgetfulness; it is manifested as protection, or as being directed toward the object;
its proximate cause is firm perception, or the foundations of mindfulness such as the body.
Because it is firmly established upon its object, it should be regarded as like a pillar; because it guards the eye-door and so forth, it should be regarded as like a gatekeeper.

Showing the sphere of its occurrence, he spoke of the fourfold foundation of mindfulness by way of the method beginning: "Being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body in the body.
Therein, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*).

For here, the material body—being a collection of the limbs and members and of such phenomena as head-hairs—is intended by the term "body" in the sense of a mass, just like a "body of elephants" or a "body of chariots."

And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too it is in the sense of the origin of things that are loathsome. For that is the "origin" (āya) of those things that are loathsome, even of those most utterly disgusting;
thus it is called the "body" (kāya). "Origin" (āya) means the place of arising. Herein, this is the etymological derivation: they arise from there, thus it is an "origin" (āya).
What arises? Loathsome things such as hair and so forth. Thus, the body is the origin of those loathsome things, hair and the rest.
“Contemplation of the body” (*kāyānupassanā*) means contemplation of the body, or contemplation upon the body.

Although the word “body” has already been stated, the second mention of the word “body” in the compound *kāyānupassanā* should be understood as being made for the purpose of showing the distinctness, the definition, the resolution of the compact mass, and so forth.
By this, it is shown that there is no contemplation of feelings, mind, or mental objects within the body, but rather only contemplation of the body itself.
By the demonstration of the mode of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanākāra*) alone upon the physical basis designated as "body," its distinct determination is shown through non-confusion.

Likewise, there is no contemplation of a single phenomenon apart from the limbs and members of the body, nor is there contemplation of a woman or a man apart from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth.

Furthermore, even regarding that which is called "body"—the aggregate of primary elements and derived matter consisting of hair, body hair, and so on—there is no contemplation of a single phenomenon apart from those primary elements and derived matter.
Now, the contemplation of the body as a designation for a collection of things occurs precisely through the mode of a collection:

like one observing the various parts of a chariot, it is the contemplation of the collection of limbs and members; like one observing the components of a city, it is the contemplation of the collection of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth;
and like one who splits open the leaf-sheaths of a plantain trunk or one who unbinds an empty fist, it is the contemplation of the collection of primary elements and derived matter.
By showing [them] in various ways, the analysis of the compact mass is demonstrated.
For herein, neither a body, nor a woman, nor a man, nor any other phenomenon whatsoever is perceived apart from the aforementioned collection;
rather, beings merely upon that collection of phenomena as previously described form their false attachments in this or that manner. Thus said the ancients:
"What one sees, that is not seen; what is seen, that one does not see.
Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, he is not released.

This is said for the purpose of demonstrating the resolution of the compact mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), this further meaning is also to be understood here.
For this is indeed contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) upon this very body, and not contemplation of other phenomena.

Just as there is a contemplation of water even in a mirage that is devoid of water, so too, in this body—which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul—there is no contemplation of permanence, pleasure, selfhood, or beauty;
rather, it is said that contemplation of the body is precisely the contemplation of the collection of modes such as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.
Alternatively, there is the body described in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* by way of the passage beginning, “Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest...
he breathes in mindfully,” which extends from the inhalations and exhalations down to the final stage of the bones produced from the pulverization [of the body];
and that which is mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* in the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness: “Here, a certain person contemplates the earth-body as impermanent.”

The "body" is spoken of as: the water-element body, the fire-element body, the air-element body, the hair-of-the-head body, the hair-of-the-body body, the skin body, the hide body, the flesh body, the blood body, the sinew body, the bone body, and the bone-marrow body.
Since one contemplates all of these within this very body, it should also be understood that the meaning is "contemplation of the body in the body."
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows:

because it is the contemplation of whatever might be grasped in the body as "I" or "mine," and because it is the contemplation of each respective collection of various phenomena such as head-hairs and body-hairs, it is called "contemplation of the body as a collection of head-hairs and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said: "In this body he contemplates impermanence, not permanence," and so on.

Furthermore, the meaning should also be understood as "contemplation of the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassanā*) by way of contemplating the entire collection of aspects—beginning with the characteristic of impermanence and so forth—as they are presented in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. This, however, is the meaning common to all four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Regarding the term *satipaṭṭhāna*:
there are three foundations of mindfulness, and it is also the range of mindfulness; it is the Teacher’s [mindfulness] toward his disciples who have practiced in the three ways.

It is also because of the state of having transcended aversion and attachment. For in such passages as: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness;
listen to that and pay close attention... And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of the body?
With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of the body,” the object of mindfulness is called a “foundation of mindfulness.”
It is so stated. Likewise in such passages as: “The body is the foundation (upaṭṭhāna), but not the mindfulness;

mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness. The meaning of this is as follows: it is called *paṭṭhāna* because mindfulness is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) in it. What is established? Mindfulness. The foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*.
Alternatively, *paṭṭhāna* means a primary place (*padhānaṭṭhāna*). The foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*, just like the terms *hatthiṭṭhāna* (elephant-place) or *assaṭṭhāna* (horse-place).

Regarding the statement: “The three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, by cultivating which the Noble One is worthy to instruct a following as a Teacher”—here, the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways is called “foundation of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Its meaning is as follows: it is a “foundation” (*paṭṭhāna*) because it is to be established; that is to say, it is to be set in motion. By whom is it to be established? By the Teacher.

“Foundation of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhāna*) means the establishing (*paṭṭhāna*) of mindfulness (*sati*). However, in such passages as, “The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,” it is mindfulness itself that is called “foundation of mindfulness.

Its meaning is as follows: it is called “foundation” (*paṭṭhāna*) because it establishes (*patiṭṭhāti*); the meaning is that it stands near (*upaṭṭhāti*), having entered and plunged into [the object], and thus proceeds. It is mindfulness itself.
*Paṭṭhāna* means the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Alternatively, it is *sati* in the sense of remembering (*saraṇa*) and *paṭṭhāna* in the sense of establishing (*upaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, it is "mindfulness" and it is also "foundation," hence *satipaṭṭhāna*. This is what is intended here. That is the foundation of mindfulness.
"Developing" means increasing it. And herein, regarding the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways:
It was said, “the foundations of mindfulness”; that [term] is to be understood by means of this sutta. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is fit to instruct a group.
Now, with reference to what was this said? Here, monks, the Teacher [instructs] his disciples...
The Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma out of compassion, seeking their welfare and motivated by kindness, saying: "This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness.

Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understanding, and they proceed contrary to the Teacher’s instruction. In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor...
And he experiences displeasure, yet he dwells uncorrupted, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness, which a noble one...
[as before] ...is worthy of. "Furthermore, monks, the Teacher... [as before] ...'This will lead to your happiness. Yet some of his disciples do not wish to listen... [as before]..."
They conduct themselves accordingly. Some disciples listen attentively... [and so on] ...and they do not act contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
In this regard, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure;
nor is he pleased nor does he experience pleasure. [Such is] both displeasure and pleasure.
And having avoided both of these, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is called the second [Tathāgata-power]...
[as before] ... "Furthermore... 'This will lead to your happiness. His disciples listen... [as before] ... they conduct themselves accordingly.
In that regard, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences pleasure; he is untainted."
"And he dwells mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is called the third [foundation of mindfulness].

Thus, being untainted by aversion and attraction, and having transcended both through the constant establishment of mindfulness, it is called "the foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). It is said that only Buddhas possess this constant establishment of mindfulness, and not Paccekabuddhas and others.

Regarding the purpose of repeating the mention of "feeling" and so forth in the phrases "contemplation of feelings in feelings" and so on, [it serves] in the context of the contemplation of the body...
This should be understood by applying it appropriately according to the method already stated. This too is a common meaning.

There is the contemplation of each individual feeling—such as pleasure and so forth, which are of many kinds—as impermanent and so on. There is the contemplation of each individual state of consciousness—such as those with lust and so forth, which are of sixteen kinds—as impermanent and so on.
[And there is the contemplation] of the remaining states belonging to the three planes, excluding the body, feelings, and consciousness.

The contemplation of each individual phenomenon, such as impermanence and so forth, is the "contemplation of phenomena" (dhammānupassanā) regarding the hindrances and other factors, according to the method taught in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*.

Furthermore, in this context, the singular form "body" (*kāye*) is used because the body is a single entity; the singular form "mind" (*citte*) should be understood as being employed by way of a class-reference (*jātiggahaṇa*), since there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of the mind.
And just as feeling and the other aggregates are to be contemplated, one who contemplates them in that manner—
It should be understood that there is contemplation of feelings in feelings, contemplation of the mind in the mind, and contemplation of phenomena in phenomena.

How should feelings be contemplated? First, pleasant feeling should be contemplated as suffering; painful feeling as a dart; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it has been said:
“He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and has seen suffering as a dart,
and has seen the peaceful state that is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as impermanent—
he indeed is a bhikkhu with right vision; he fully understands feelings.”
All these indeed should be contemplated as suffering. For it has been said: "Whatever is felt, that I declare to be suffering.
And they should also be contemplated as both pleasure and pain. As it was said: "A pleasant feeling is pleasant in its persistence, but painful in its change;
a painful feeling is painful in its persistence, but pleasant in its change; a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant through knowledge, but painful through ignorance."

Moreover, they should also be contemplated by way of the sevenfold insight into impermanence and so forth. Regarding mental states (*cittadhamma*), first, consciousness (*citta*) should be contemplated by way of the sevenfold contemplation of impermanence and so forth, according to its various divisions such as object-condition, predominance-condition, conascence-condition, plane, kamma-resultant, and functional;

and also by way of the sixteenfold divisions such as "with lust" and so forth. As for mental factors (*dhammā*), they are to be contemplated by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).
They should be contemplated by way of the contemplations on impermanence and so forth regarding the phenomenon of emptiness, as well as by way of the peaceful and unpeaceful, and so on.
These four foundations of mindfulness are found in various states of mind during the preliminary stage;
for one contemplates the body with one state of mind, feeling with another, the mind with another, and mental phenomena with yet another. At the moment of the supramundane path, however—
However, these are obtained within a single moment of consciousness.

For, when one has first grasped the body and arrived [at insight], the mindfulness associated with insight is called "contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupassanā*); a person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one who contemplates the body.
When one has intensified insight and attained the Noble Path, at the moment of the path, the mindfulness associated with the path is "contemplation of the body."
A person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one who contemplates the body.

Having comprehended feelings, having comprehended the mind, and having comprehended mental phenomena, the mindfulness associated with insight that has arisen is called "contemplation of mental phenomena";
a person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one who contemplates mental phenomena. [This is] insight.
For one who has exerted effort and attained the Noble Path, at the moment of that path, mindfulness associated with the path is called "contemplation of phenomena" (*dhammānupassanā*).
A person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one contemplating phenomena. Thus, for the time being, the teaching rests upon the person.
However, regarding the body, mindfulness that grasps the body succeeds through the path by means of abandoning the perversion that [views it] as beautiful (*subha*).

Contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) is so called. Contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*) is so called because mindfulness that grasps feelings succeeds through the Path by abandoning the perversion [of perceiving] feeling as "pleasure.
Contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*) is so called because mindfulness that grasps the mind succeeds through the Path by abandoning the perversion [of perceiving] the mind as "permanent.
[Contemplation of phenomena is so called] by abandoning the perversion [of perceiving] phenomena as "self" (*attā*).
Mindfulness that grasps phenomena succeeds by means of the Path; this is called "contemplation of phenomena.
Thus, mindfulness itself, when associated with the Path, receives four names in the sense of accomplishing the four functions. Therefore it was said:
"But at the moment of the supramundane Path, they are obtained within a single consciousness alone."
Furthermore, three other tetrads have been stated by way of assistance, by way of non-decline, and by way of qualities.
Therein, "by way of avoiding what is absent" (*asatiparivajjanāya*): "absence" (*asati*) means not being present, or it is that wherein mindfulness (*sati*) is absent;
this is a designation for forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassati*). "By way of avoidance" (*parivajjanāya*) means by way of shunning from all sides. [It is] like a crow perched upon food.

Indeed, mindfulness arises through avoiding persons who are forgetful, by associating with persons who possess established mindfulness, by the purpose of arousing mindfulness during standing, sitting, and so forth, and by the mind’s being inclined, leaning, and bent toward it.

"Of the things to be done by mindfulness" means of those things which are to be performed by means of mindfulness. "By having been done" means by way of their having been accomplished. Of the four paths...

The meaning is "because of having been performed" and "because of having been developed. "Because of the destruction of states that obstruct mindfulness" means by way of the elimination of sensual desire and so forth.
"Because of the non-forgetfulness of states that are the signs of mindfulness" means by way of the non-loss of the objects of the body and so forth, which are the causes of mindfulness.

"Because of being endowed with mindfulness" means because of having properly attained mindfulness and because of its non-decline. "Because of mastery" means by one who has attained the state of mastery.
“By proficiency” means by way of being skilled. “By non-retrogression” means by way of not turning back or not falling away.

“By existence” means by way of existing as an intrinsic nature. “By peace” means by way of having the nature of being extinguished (*nibbuta*). “By tranquility” means by way of the state of having the defilements stilled.
“By being endowed with the qualities of peace” means by way of not being devoid of the qualities of a true person (*sappurisa*). [These include] the recollection of the Buddha and so forth.
The method is exactly as stated below. "Mindfulness" (*sati*) is by way of remembering; this is the term for the intrinsic nature of mindfulness.
"Recollection" (*anussati*) is by way of recollecting through repeated remembering. "Re-collection" (*paṭissati*) is by way of re-remembering as if having gone forward toward it.

Or, it is merely an expansion [of the meaning] by means of prefixes. The mode of remembering is "the state of remembering" (*saraṇatā*). Since, however, "the state of remembering" refers to the three...
Since "recollection" (*saraṇā*) is also a name for mindfulness, the term *sati* is mentioned again in order to exclude that [other meaning].

Here, the meaning is: "mindfulness" (*sati*) is what is intended by "recollection" (*saraṇatā*). It is "retention" (*dhāraṇatā*) because it possesses the state of retaining what has been heard and mastered.

It is "non-floating" (*apilāpanatā*) in the sense of plunging in, which is reckoned as entering deeply. For just as gourds and the like float upon water, [mindfulness does not float away from the object].
They do not enter [into the object], nor do they remain [fixed] upon the object in that way. For this [faculty] enters into the object; therefore, it is called "non-forgetfulness" (*apilāpanatā*).
It is "non-forgetfulness" (*asammussanatā*) because of the state of not forgetting what was done long ago or spoken long ago.

It is a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) with respect to the characteristic of establishing and the characteristic of illuminating; thus, the faculty known as mindfulness is the "mindfulness-faculty" (*satindriya*).

"It does not waver through negligence" refers to the power of mindfulness (*satibala*). "Mindfulness that dwells according to reality," "mindfulness of deliverance," and "wholesome mindfulness" refer to right mindfulness (*sammāsati*).

It is called a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is a limb for one who is awakening; or, it is a praised or beautiful factor of enlightenment, thus a "perfect enlightenment factor" (*sambojjhaṅga*); mindfulness itself as a perfect enlightenment factor is the "mindfulness-enlightenment-factor" (*satisambojjhaṅga*).
"The path with a single way" means a single path; the meaning should be understood as: this path is not a forked road. Now...
It is "the path traversed by one" (ekāyana) because it is to be traversed by one alone. "By one" means by one who has abandoned the company of the crowd, whose mind is secluded and withdrawn.
It is to be traversed or practiced; or else, it is a "path" (ayana) because one goes by means of it—the meaning being that one goes from saṃsāra to Nibbāna.
The path of one is the "ekāyana. "Of one" means of the best. The Blessed One is indeed the best among all beings; therefore, [it refers to] "of the Blessed One."
This is what is meant. For although others also go by that path, even so it is the path of the Blessed One alone, because it was brought forth by him.
As it is said: "For that Blessed One, brahmin, is the arouser of the unarisen path," and so forth. Or, it is called a "path" (ayana) because one goes (ayati) by it;
the meaning is that one proceeds or moves along it. A path for one person is a "single-path" (ekāyana). In this very [context]...
It is said that it proceeds within this Dhamma and Vinaya, and not elsewhere.
As it was said: "In this Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found. For this is merely a difference in teaching; in meaning, however, it is one and the same.

Furthermore, it is called "the sole way" (ekāyana) because it goes to a single goal. Although in its preliminary stages it proceeds by way of various methods of cultivation, [it leads to a single destination].
In the end, it is said that one goes to nothing but Nibbāna. As Brahmā Sahampati said:
“The one who sees the destruction of birth understands the path leading to the goal alone; the compassionate one, out of pity for welfare, knows this path.
By this path, those of old have crossed over, and those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood do so by this very way.”
In what sense is "maggā" (the path) called "magga"? It is so called in the sense of going toward Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.
"Upeto" means having gone near. "Samupeto" means having gone even nearer than that. By both terms, the meaning is that one has not fallen away from mindfulness.
"Upagato" means standing after having approached. "Samupagato" means standing while being associated [with it]. "Upāgato samupāgato" is also used in this sense.

Pāli: By both [terms], the meaning is that one has come into the vicinity of mindfulness. *Upapanna* means having attained non-separation. *Samupapanna* means perfected. *Samannāgata* means complete and present.
"Endowed (*upeta*) and fully endowed (*samupeta*)"—by these two terms, the process (*pavatta*) is described.

"Approached (*upagata*) and fully approached (*samupagata*)"—by these two terms, penetration (*paṭivedha*) is described. "Attained (*upapanna*), fully attained (*samupapanna*), and possessed (*samannāgata*)"—[these describe the fruit].
"Acquisition is explained by three terms"—thus some describe it.

"Or, that attachment is in the world": the meaning is that this attachment, which has been described in many ways, exists only in the world of the aggregates (*khandha-loka*) and does not occur apart from the aggregates. "Or, that attachment is in the world": [it exists] only in the world of the aggregates.
This is the occurrence of craving, which is designated as "clinging" (*visattikā*). One "crosses over" by avoiding sensual pleasures;

one "crosses beyond" by abandoning the defilements (*kilesa*); one "crosses over quickly" by cutting off their basis; one "transcends" by transcending *saṃsāra*; and one "goes beyond" by making rebirth impossible.
Alternatively, one "crosses over" and "crosses beyond" by means of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).
One crosses over by means of the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*). One transcends by means of the contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*).

Alternatively, one crosses by means of virtue (*sīla*), one surmounts by means of concentration (*samādhi*), one crosses over by means of insight (*vipassanā*), and one transcends by means of the path (*magga*);
one goes beyond by means of the fruit (*phala*)—it should be applied in such ways as these.

4. This is the summary meaning of the fourth verse: whoever [desires] a single field such as a rice-field and so forth, or a site for a house and so forth, or gold reckoned as *kahāpaṇa* coins, or cattle and horses distinguished by their types, or slaves born within the household and so forth, or laborers such as hired servants, or women designated as "women," or kinsmen and relatives, or other manifold objects of desire that are pleasing to the mind—
"Anugijjhati" means he covets. "Sālikhettaṃ" is where rice grows. The same method applies to fields of barley (*vīhi*) and so forth.
"Vīhī" refers to the remaining types of barley. "Modayati" means mung bean (*mugga*). "Gharavatthuṃ" is the portion of ground, whether prepared or unprepared, for the purpose of establishing a house.
The same method applies to the site for a granary (*koṭṭhaka*) and so forth. "Koṭṭhaka" refers to a gate-tower (*dvārakoṭṭha*) and the like. "Pure" means in front of the house.
"Behind" means behind the house. It is called an *ārāma* because they delight the mind there;
the meaning is that they rejoice in it through its flowers, fruits, shade, and water.
"Dogs and so forth" refers to sheep and the like. "Born inside" means born from the womb of a female slave within the house. "Bought with wealth" means...
"Having been bought with wealth" means having been acquired through exchange. "Of his own accord" (*sāmaṃ*) means by himself. "Slavery" (*dāsabyaṃ*) is the state of being a slave;

that is slavery. "Enters into" (*upeti*) means he goes toward it. "Or against his will" (*akāmako vā*) means either by his own lack of desire or having been brought there as a convict (*karamarānīto*).
To show those four types again, he said: "Some even become slaves for a debt. "Slaves for a debt" (*āmāya dāsā*) refers to slaves born in the house.

“In that place where a slave born of a mother who is a slave remains and goes about with his master”—here too, these same [categories] are mentioned. “Bought with wealth” refers to slaves purchased for money.
“And some themselves” refers to those who are slaves by their own accord. “Driven away by fear” refers to unwilling slaves; they are driven away—that is, cast out—by fear.

“Hired laborers” refers to those who live by wages. “Workmen” refers to those who perform tasks such as plowing and so forth. “Dependents” refers to those who live by approaching [a patron] through flattery and the like, making him their support.

"A woman" (*itthī*): she is called a woman because the womb (*gabbha*) resides within her. "A relative by marriage" (*pariggaha*): a female companion who has a husband. "Relatives by blood" (*ñātibandhu*): mother, father, and kinsmen.

"Relatives by clan" (*sagotta*): those of the same lineage. "Relatives by mantras" (*mantabandhu*): those who have studied under the same teacher or who possess the same birth-rite, or those who have mastered the same mantras.
"Relatives by craft" (*sippabandhu*): one who has learned together in archery, arts, and so forth. "And relatives by friends" (*mittabandhavā*)—these too are "relatives."
In some manuscripts, the following reading is seen:
"Gijjhati" means he longs for with the desire of defilement (*kilesakāma*). "Anugijjhati" means he longs after repeatedly; he desires again and again.
"Paligijjhati" means he desires all around. "Palibajjhati" means he desires specifically. "By way of grossness..."
“By way of grasping at signs one covets; by way of coveting one further covets; by way of grasping at secondary characteristics one is obsessed and fettered”—thus some explain it.
In the fifth verse, this is the summarized meaning: weak defilements overpower, overcome, and crush that person.
Or, because he is devoid of the powers such as faith, that person is weak, and weak defilements overpower him due to his weakness.

The meaning is "they grow stronger. Alternatively, both the lion and other such manifest dangers, as well as the non-manifest dangers such as bodily misconduct and so forth, crush that person who is greedy for sensual pleasures, intoxicated by sensual pleasures, and seeking after sensual pleasures.
Then, like water following a broken boat, the suffering of birth and so on follows that person who has been overcome by those non-manifest dangers.

They are "weak" (*abala*) because they have no strength; thus they are devoid of power. They are "feeble" (*dubbala*) because their application is sluggish and they lack the strength required for the task to be performed.
They are "of little strength" (*appabala*) because their strength is small or limited; thus they are incapable of fighting.

They are "of little stamina" (*appathāmaka*) because their stamina—their exertion or effort—is small or limited. They are "inferior" (*hīna*) and "debased" (*nihīna*) due to their inferiority of application.
"Omakā" means inferior in strength. "Lāmakā" means inferior in supporting conditions. "Chatukkā" means inferior in aspiration. "Parittā" means inferior in conviction.
"They overcome" (*sahanti*) means they crush and produce friction. "They overwhelm" (*parisahanti*) means they crush from all sides.
"They surpass" (*abhibhavanti*) by way of arising again and again. "They overspread" (*ajjhottharanti*) by way of arising repeatedly. "They consume" (*pariyādiyanti*).
They "dry up" by means of their station. They "crush" by obstructing the arising of wholesome states.
Faith-power (*saddhābala*): It is called faith because one has faith by means of it, or because it itself has faith, or because its essence is merely the act of having faith.
Its characteristic is that of having faith, or its characteristic is that of conviction (*okappana*). Its function is to clarify, like a water-clearing gem.
It has the function of plunging in, like one crossing a flood. Its manifestation is as unshakability, or its manifestation is as resolute confidence (*adhimutti*).
Its proximate cause is a matter worthy of faith, or its proximate cause is the factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅga*).

It should be regarded as being like hands, wealth, and seeds. It is the power of faith because it does not waver in the face of lack of faith. Regarding the power of energy (*vīriyabala*): energy (*vīriya*) is the state of a hero (*vīra*).
Viriya is the action or energy of heroes; or it is called viriya because it must be set in motion and activated by means of method, principle, or strategy.
Furthermore, this viriya has the characteristic of supporting and the characteristic of exerting; its function is to support co-nascent states, and it is manifested as the state of non-collapse.
This is according to the statement: "One who is moved by a sense of spiritual urgency strives with wise application."

It has the state of spiritual urgency as its proximate cause, or the basis for the arousal of energy as its proximate cause. It should be understood that when rightly undertaken, it is the root of all success.
It does not waver in the face of indolence; thus it is the power of energy (*vīriya-bala*). The characteristics and other qualities of mindfulness have already been stated.

It does not waver in the face of forgetfulness; thus it is the power of mindfulness (*sati-bala*). That which is co-nascent [with the other factors] and rightly places or establishes them is concentration (*samādhi*).
Thus, characterized by pre-eminence or by non-distraction, its function is to unify the co-nascent states upon their object, like water with bath-powder;

it is manifested as tranquility or as knowledge, for it is said: "One who is concentrated understands and sees things as they truly are. Specifically, its proximate cause is happiness, like a lamp in a windless place.
The stability of the mind should be understood as "stability" (*ṭhiti*) itself. It does not waver due to restlessness; this is the power of concentration (*samādhi*). It understands (*pajānāti*);
this is wisdom (*paññā*). What does it understand? The Noble Truths, by way of the method beginning with "This is suffering.

Its characteristic is the penetration of things according to their true nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer. Its function is the illumination of the object.
Like a lamp, it has non-delusion as its manifestation, like a guide who has traveled through the forest. "It does not waver because of ignorance" refers to the power of wisdom (*paññābala*).
Regarding the power of moral shame (*hiribala*) and the power of moral dread (*ottappabala*): "It does not waver because of shamelessness" is the power of moral shame;

"it does not waver because of lack of moral dread" is the power of moral dread. This is the explanation of the meaning according to both [aspects]. "One feels shame on account of bodily misconduct and so forth"—this is the power of moral shame.
*Hirī* is a designation for shame (*lajjā*). *Ottappaṃ* is that by which one is ashamed; it is a designation for dread of wrongdoing.
To illustrate the distinction between these two, this summary outline was established: “By origin, by predominance, and by such characteristics as shame”;
and following this, the detailed exposition was spoken: “*Hirī* has its origin within oneself (*ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā*), while [the other] has its origin externally (*bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ*).”
This is called *ottappa* (moral dread). *Hirī* (moral shame) has self as its dominant influence; *ottappa* has the world as its dominant influence.

*Hirī* is established in the nature of modesty; *ottappa* is established in the nature of fear. *Hirī* has the characteristic of having a sense of propriety; *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing danger and fearing blame.
Therein, one arouses *hirī*, which originates from within oneself, by four means: by reflecting upon birth...
We [should act] after reflecting, reflecting on our courage, and reflecting on our great learning.
How so? First, by reflecting on birth thus: "This doing of evil is not the work of those endowed with noble birth; this is the work of low-born people such as fishermen and the like.
It is not fitting for one like me, who is endowed with noble birth, to do such a deed. Thus, first, one reflects on birth.
By refraining from evil such as the taking of life, one arouses moral shame (*hiri*). Likewise, by reflecting on one’s age—thinking, "This doing of evil is a deed fit for the young;

it is not proper for one like me, established in this stage of life, to perform such an act"—one refrains from evil such as the taking of life and arouses moral shame. Likewise, [reflecting that] "this is indeed an evil deed..."

"This is the work of those of weak nature; it is not fitting for one like me, endowed with courage, to perform such an act"—reflecting thus on his own courage, he arouses a sense of moral shame (*hiri*) by refraining from evil deeds such as the taking of life. Likewise:
"This evil deed is the work of blind fools, not of the wise. It is not for one like me, a wise man of great learning..."
"This action is not fit to be done"—thus, by reflecting on his great learning (*bāhusacca*) and refraining from evil such as the taking of life, he arouses moral shame (*hiri*).
In this way, he arouses internally-arisen moral shame through four causes.
Having aroused it, he introduces moral shame into his own mind and does not commit an evil deed. Thus is the internally-arisen [shame].
There is that which is called moral shame (*hirī*). How is it that there is that which is called moral dread (*ottappa*) arising from external factors?
"If you commit an evil deed, you will become an object of reproach in the four assemblies:
'The wise will reproach you, like an impure citizen.'"
“Shunned by those who possess virtue, how will you fare as a bhikkhu?
Reflecting in this way, one does not commit an evil deed through a sense of moral dread (*ottappa*) that arises from external factors; such is what is called moral dread arising from the external.
How is it that shame (*hirī*) has oneself as its dominant influence? Here, a certain son of good family, making himself his own dominant authority and leader, [reflects: “I myself am noble...”
“An evil deed is not fitting for one like me—one who has gone forth out of faith, who is learned, and who maintains the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)—” thinking thus, he does not commit evil.
This is what is called self-sovereignty as moral shame (attādhipati hirī). Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having made himself alone his sovereign, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and [cultivates] the blameless.”
“He develops it and preserves himself in purity.
What is called moral dread (*ottappa*) with respect to the world? Here, a certain son of good family, making the world his authority and his elder, does not commit an evil deed. As it is said:
“Great indeed is this world-dwelling; and in this great world-dwelling there are recluses and brahmins...”
Those who possess supernormal powers, those with the divine eye, and those who know the minds of others—though they see from afar, they do not see when one is near;
they also know the mind with their own minds. They too might perceive me thus:
"Look, sirs, at this clansman who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells entangled in evil, unwholesome states."
There are also deities who possess supernormal powers, who have the divine eye, and who know the minds of others;
they see from afar and are not seen even when nearby, and they know the mind with their own mind. They too would perceive me thus:
"Look, sirs, at this clansman who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells entangled in evil things."
‘from unwholesome states. He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused and unflagging;
my mindfulness will be established and unconfused; my body will be tranquil and unaroused; my mind will be concentrated and one-pointed.
Taking the world itself as his authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, [abandoning] what is blameworthy...
“He abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and preserves himself in purity.
Thus, *ottappa* (moral dread) is called the lord of the world. Regarding the statement, “*Hirī* is established in the nature of shame;
*ottappa* is established in the nature of fear”: here, “shame” (*lajjā*) is the mode of being ashamed; *hirī* is established by that very nature. “Fear” (*bhaya*)...
The fear of the states of misery (*apāya-bhaya*) is the sense of shame (*ottappa*) established by that very nature. Both of these become manifest in the avoidance of evil.

For just as a certain son of good family, while performing the functions of defecation and urination, might become overcome with a sense of shame and feel abashed upon seeing someone who ought to be shunned, so too does one, having internalized the quality of shame (*lajjī-dhamma*), [avoid evil].
One does not commit an evil deed. A certain person, being terrified by the fear of the states of misery, does not commit an evil deed.
Here is a simile for this: suppose there were two iron balls; one were cold but smeared with excrement, and the other were hot and glowing.
In that case, the wise man, loathing the cold one because it is smeared with excrement, would not take it; [he would take] the other.
