Out of fear of burning. In this context, just as one does not take up cool excrement due to the loathsomeness of being smeared by it, so should the non-committing of evil after having descended into the nature of internal shame be understood;
and just as one does not take it up out of fear of burning heat, so should the non-committing of evil out of fear of the states of deprivation (apāya) be understood.
“*Hirī* has the characteristic of reverence; *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is blameworthy”—this pair also becomes manifest specifically in the avoidance of evil.

For a certain person possesses the characteristic of reverence by means of four reasons: reflection on the greatness of one’s birth, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, and reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.

Having aroused a sense of shame (*hiri*), one does not commit evil. A certain person, having aroused a sense of moral dread (*ottappa*)—which is characterized by the perception of fear regarding blameworthy conduct through four modes, namely: fear of self-reproach, fear of reproach by others, fear of punishment, and fear of an unhappy rebirth—does not commit evil.
In this context, there are both the reflections on the greatness of one's birth and so forth, as well as the fears of self-reproach and the rest.
These should be explained in detail. Thus, for whichever person these seven kinds of power do not exist, those defilements overcome that person... [as before] ...they exhaust and crush him.
"Two dangers" means there are exactly two calamities, according to their manifest and unmanifest nature; they are neither one nor three. As for their classification:
In order to show this, he said: “Which are the manifest dangers? and so forth. Therein, *kokā* means *kekā* (cranes); or rather, this very reading (*kokā*) is correct.
*Corā* are those engaged in the work of thievery. *Māṇavā* are those engaged in acts of violence. *Katakammā* are those who have already committed acts of theft such as housebreaking.
*Akatakammā* are those who have set out to commit such an act. Here, *assu* means “there might be. *Cakkhurogo* (eye disease) means...

A disease that has arisen in the eye; it is called a "disease" (*roga*) because it causes pain. "Eye-disease" and so forth are to be understood by way of their physical bases (*vatthu*), for there is no such thing as a disease in the translucent visual faculty (*pasāda*) itself once it has been produced. "Ear-disease" refers to a disease of the external ear. "Mouth-disease" is a disease that has arisen in the mouth.
"Tooth-disease" is toothache. "Cough" (*kāsa*) is a disease of the throat. "Sneeze" (*sāsa*) is a gasping or belching disease. "Catarrh" (*pināsa*)—
A disease of the nose. "Burning" (*ḍāha*) is a heat arising within. "Fainting" (*mucchā*) refers to those states that cause the loss of mindfulness.
"Diarrhea" (*pakkhandikā*) is bloody diarrhea or dysentery. "Colic" (*sūla*) is abdominal pain or stomach wind.

"Cholera" (*visūcikā*) is a severe purging. "Leprosy" (*kilāsa*) is a spotted skin disease. "Consumption" (*sosa*) is a wasting disease characterized by drying up. "Apasmāra" is possession by non-human spirits.
*Veriyakkhābādho*: a disease caused by the *verī* (poisonous) *yakṣa*. *Daddū*: a *daddu*-boil. *Kaṇḍū*: a small boil. *Kacchū*: a large itch (*mahākacchu*). *Rakhasā*:
a disease that arises in places scratched with the fingernails. There is also a textual reading of "nakhasā. *Vitacchikā*:
a disease that arises when one scrapes the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet repeatedly with a sharp tool. *Lohitapitta*: blood-bile; *rattapitta* means the same.
This has been said. *Madhumeha* is a severe disease within the interior of the body; for it is said: "Moreover, the disease *madhumeha* is severe.
*Aṃsa* refers to the disease *arisā*. *Pīḷaka* refers to blood-blisters (*lohitapīḷakā*). It is called *bhagandala* because it causes the *bhaga* (the anus) to split;
the meaning is that it tears open the path of excrement. *Pittasamuṭṭhānā* means those whose origin or arising is from bile (*pitta*).
These, it is said, are thirty-two. The same method applies to those arising from phlegm (*semha*) and so forth.

"Arising from a combination" (*sannipātika*) means arisen through the coming together and unification of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm. "In the sense of an affliction" (*ābādha*) they are called "afflictions" (*ābādhā*). "Arising from a change in climate" (*utupariṇāmaja*) means [diseases] arisen by means of a change in climate.

"Excessive heat" refers to diseases produced by cold. "Arising from an irregular lifestyle" (*visamaparihāraja*) means [diseases] arisen through an irregular lifestyle, such as standing or sitting in improper postures.

"Born. "Produced by means of an external agent" (*opakkamikā*) means born through such means as killing, binding, and so forth. "Born of the ripening of kamma" (*kammavipākajā*) means produced from the ripening of powerful kamma.

Cold, heat... [and so on]... contact—these are indeed obvious. "Thus, moreover" (*iti vā*) means "in this way, moreover. He spoke thus while concluding: "These are called... He asks: "Which are the concealed perils?
meaning, which are those that are not obvious, whose afflictions are hidden? Regarding that:
Bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) should be understood as the volition of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.

Verbal misconduct (*vacīduccarita*) should be understood as the volition of false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. Mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*) should be understood as covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
It is called "misconduct" because it is a bad conduct occurring in the body, or proceeding from the body, or because it is rotten with defilements (*kilesa*).
"Bad conduct" (*duṭṭhucarita*) refers to bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*). The same principle applies to verbal and mental misconduct as well.

They are "desired" (*kāmīyanti*), thus they are "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*); these are the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*). "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) is the desire (*chanda*) for sensual pleasures. Alternatively, one who desires is "desire" (*kāma*);

"sensual desire" is simply the desire for sensual pleasures, not the desire for action (*kattukamyatāchanda*), nor the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammachanda*). It is precisely craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).

"Named so-and-so. It is called an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance) because it hinders wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). Sensual desire itself is the hindrance; thus, it is "the hindrance of sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*). The same applies to the others.
It is called ill-will (*byāpāda*) because by means of it the mind becomes putrid, or because it causes harm to the discipline, conduct, physical perfection, welfare, happiness, and so forth.
Sloth (*thina*) is the state of being slothful. Torpor (*middha*) is the state of being drowsy; it is the lack of exertion, the lack of firmness, and the impairment of strength.
This is the meaning. *Thīna* (sloth) and *middha* (torpor) together constitute *thinamiddha*. Therein, *thīna* has the characteristic of lack of exertion;
its function is the dispelling of energy; it is manifested as a state of sinking. *Middha* has the characteristic of unworkability; its function is shrouding;

it is manifested as a state of sluggishness, or alternatively, as nodding and sleep. Both have unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) as their proximate cause, occurring in such states as boredom, languor, and stretching the limbs.
Agitation (*uddhacca*) is the state of one who is agitated. Its characteristic is lack of tranquility, like water stirred by the impact of the wind;
its function is instability, like a banner or a flag fluttering in the wind; it is manifested as restlessness, like ashes thrown up by the impact of a stone;
its proximate cause is lack of tranquility of mind and improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). It should be understood as mental distraction.

That which is done badly is *kukata*; the state of that is *kukkucca* (remorse). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; its function is to sorrow over what has been done and left undone; it is manifested as remorse; its proximate cause is what has been done and left undone;
it should be regarded like slavery. Restlessness (*uddhacca*) and remorse (*kukkucca*) together are *uddhaccakukkucca*.
Doubt (*vicikicchā*) is the absence of investigation (*cikkhā*); or, it is so called because it investigates (*vicinanto*) the true nature [of things].

It is called *vicikicchā* because one is troubled and exhausted by it. It has the characteristic of doubt; its function is to waver; it is manifested as indecision, or as the grasping of multiple alternatives;
its proximate cause is unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). It should be regarded as an obstacle to practice.
Lust has the characteristic of being excited. Hatred has the characteristic of being corrupt. Delusion has the characteristic of being bewildered. Anger has the characteristic of being irascible.
Anger has the characteristic of ferocity, the function of causing resentment, and the manifestation of defilement.
Resentment has the characteristic of persistent attachment, the function of not relinquishing enmity, and the manifestation of being a state of following after anger. And this has been said:
"Anger is at an earlier time; resentment is at a later time," and so forth.
Flattery (*makkha*) has the characteristic of smearing over the good qualities of others; its function is their destruction, and it is manifested as concealing those [faults].

Slander (*paḷāsa*) has the characteristic of seizing both sides; its function is to equalize one’s own qualities with the qualities of others, and it is manifested as appearing according to the measure of others’ qualities.
Envy (*issā*) has the characteristic of being dissatisfied with the success of others, or the characteristic of intolerance toward it; its function is a lack of delight therein.
Therefore, it has the manifestation of being averse [to others]. Stinginess (*macchariya*) has the characteristic of concealing one’s own prosperity;
its function is the inability to endure others sharing in one’s own prosperity; its manifestation is contraction.
Deceit (*māyā*) has the characteristic of concealing the evil one has done; its function is the hiding of that [evil]; its manifestation is the obstruction of it. One’s own...

Deceit (*sāṭheyya*) has the characteristic of manifesting qualities that do not exist; its function is the proclaiming of those [qualities]; it is manifested as making those [qualities] appear through bodily gestures.

Rigidity (*thambha*) has the characteristic of inflation of the mind; its function is conduct without deference; it is manifested as lack of gentleness (*amaddava*). Aggression (*sārambha*) has the characteristic of taking oneself as superior; its function is opposition; it is manifested as disrespect (*agārava*).

Conceit has the characteristic of swelling up; its function is the sense of "I am"; it is manifested as a state of inflation. Excessive conceit has the characteristic of being excessively swollen up; its function is an excessive sense of "I am"; it is manifested as a state of extreme inflation.

Intoxication has the characteristic of a state of being intoxicated; its function is the grasping of intoxication; it is manifested as madness. Negligence has the characteristic of the mind’s relinquishment toward the five cords of sensual pleasure;
its function is the non-provision of that relinquishment; it is manifested as the absence of mindfulness.
In this way, the characteristics and other qualities of these phenomena are to be understood. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Vibhaṅga* beginning with, "Therein, what is anger?
Furthermore, specifically in this context, one who is greedy for material things becomes angry at another who receives a gain that he himself does not obtain. Once [that anger arises]...
The anger that has arisen is simply anger; beyond that is resentment (*upanāha*).
Being thus angry and resentful, he defames the virtues of another who is even peaceful and successful, thinking, "I am just like him," and he adopts a competitive attitude.

This constitutes his hypocrisy (*makkha*) and spite (*palāsa*); being thus hypocritical and spiteful, regarding that person's gains, honor, and so forth, he thinks, "What does this man have to do with this?"
He envies and seeks to corrupt; this is his envy (*issā*). But if he possesses some success, he cannot endure its being shared with others;
this is his stinginess (*macchariya*). Furthermore, for the sake of gain, he conceals his own existing faults;
this is his deceit (*māyā*). He proclaims qualities that do not exist; this is his craftiness (*sāṭheyya*). Practicing in this manner, if...
However, when he obtains gain according to his desire, he becomes stiff and hard-hearted;
unable to be exhorted with the words, "This should not be done in this way," this is his stubbornness (*thambha*).
But if someone says something to him, such as, "This should not be done in this way," he becomes agitated in mind, with a frowning face, speaking insolently: "Who are you to me?"
This is his agitation (*sārambha*). Then, through stubbornness (*thambha*), thinking "I alone am better," he becomes conceited (*mānī*).
Through agitation, thinking "Who are these? while despising others, he becomes over-conceited (*atimānī*); this is his conceit (*māna*) and over-conceit (*atimāna*).

By means of those conceits and over-conceits, he generates intoxication (*mada*) in many forms, such as pride in birth and so forth. Being intoxicated, he becomes heedless regarding objects consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure and the like.
This should be understood as his intoxication and negligence.
"All defilements" refers to all unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*). They are called defilements (*kilesa*) in the sense of burning and in the sense of afflicting.
Because they are rotten with defilement, they are misconducts (*duccarita*). In the sense of causing distress, they are torments (*daratha*). In the sense of causing internal burning and so forth...

*Parilāhā* (fevers). They are *santāpā* (torments) in the sense of constant burning. All unwholesome volitional formations (*akusalābhisaṅkhārā*) are so called in the sense of being produced by lack of skill and in the sense of volitional construction.
"In what sense? means "in what meaning. To show the threefold meaning beginning with "overpowering," he said: "They overwhelm, thus they are perils (*parissayā*)," and so forth.
"They afflict" means they produce suffering and overcome [the practitioner]. "They lead to decline" means they lead to the abandonment of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).
"Therein they lie latent" means that unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) lie latent—that is, they dwell and arise—within that body.
"Those dangers" refers to calamities such as bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*). Of the wholesome...
"For the obstruction of states" means for the disappearance and non-appearance of those states to be described hereafter that arise from skillfulness, such as right practice and so forth.
"Right practice" means a beautiful or praiseworthy practice, not a wrong practice. "Conformable practice" means a practice that is not contrary, not a reverse practice.
"By a practice that is not contrary" means by a practice that is not opposed, by a practice that is not hostile.

"By a practice that conforms to the goal" means by a practice that follows the goal, by a practice that increases further and further. What is meant is: by a practice that should be undertaken in accordance with the goal.
There is also a textual reading, "by a practice for one's own benefit," but that is not good. "By a practice that conforms to the Dhamma and its sequel" means...

"Dhamma" refers to the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*). "Anudhamma" refers to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and so forth. The practice of Dhamma that is in conformity with that Dhamma is "practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipadā*); [the phrase] "of that practice in accordance with the Dhamma" [is used].
"By being one who fulfills the precepts" means by remaining having brought the precepts of the Pātimokkha to completion. "By guarding the doors of the sense faculties" means...
Regarding the state of having well-guarded doors among the six sense faculties, including the mind, as described by the method beginning with “having seen a form with the eye”;
regarding moderation in eating, which is the state of being proportionate in measure in receiving [alms] and so forth, and eating moderately after discarding things such as extra robes;
and regarding devotion to wakefulness, as expressed by the passage beginning: “During the day, by means of walking and sitting, one should purify the mind of obstructive states.”
By way of the practice of the five factors of wakefulness. "Of mindfulness and clear comprehension" means:
of that mindfulness and clear comprehension which is beneficial at all times to all yogis who are devoted to the cultivation of any meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Of the foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānānaṃ*): it is called a "foundation" (*paṭṭhāna*) because it enters into and leaps upon its objects; it is simply mindfulness itself.
"Foundation" (paṭṭhāna) refers to the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).

However, because it functions by way of grasping the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—and because it accomplishes the task of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self—it possesses a fourfold classification.
This refers to those four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the phrase "of the four right endeavors" (*catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ*): it is called an "endeavor" (*padhāna*) because one exerts oneself by means of it.
A "right endeavor" (*sammappadhāna*) is an excellent endeavor; or alternatively, it is a right endeavor because one exerts oneself rightly by means of it.

Or else, it is "excellent" (*sobhana*) because it is free from the deformity of the defilements, and it is an "endeavor" (*padhāna*) in the sense that it produces welfare and happiness, brings about a state of excellence, and effects the state of being an endeavor.
"Right exertion" (*sammappadhāna*) is a designation for energy (*vīriya*).

However, its fourfold classification occurs by way of accomplishing the functions of abandoning, non-arising, arising, and maintaining, respectively, with respect to the four unwholesome and wholesome states as they have arisen or not yet arisen.
These are the four right exertions.
Regarding the phrase "of the four bases of psychic power" (*catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ*):

here, each one among zeal (*chanda*), energy (*vīriya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is called "psychic power" (*iddhi*) because it succeeds, is accomplished, or is brought to fruition.
Alternatively, by the first sense, it is "psychic power" itself that is the "base" (*pāda*), meaning a constituent part of psychic power. By the second sense, [it is the basis for beings].
*Iddhipāda* means the basis of success (*iddhi*). "Basis" (*pāda*) means a foundation or a means of attainment; this is the meaning.
It is called a "basis" because by means of it one goes toward, that is, reaches, success characterized by successive distinctions.

Of those four bases of success. Regarding the "seven factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*): they are factors of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or factors belonging to enlightenment; thus they are "factors of enlightenment. This is what is meant:

This harmony of factors (*dhammasāmaggī*)— consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity— which, when arising at the moment of the supramundane path, serves as the antidote to numerous calamities such as dullness and agitation,
striving for stability, striving for exertion, devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism—
is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) because by means of this harmony of factors the noble disciple awakens; he awakens from the sleep of the continuity of defilements.
One either exerts oneself, penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself.

These are called "factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅgā) because they are factors of that enlightenment (bodhi) which consists in the harmony of these states (dhamma-sāmaggī), just as in the case of the factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, and so forth.
Furthermore, the noble disciple is called "enlightenment" (bodhi) because he awakens by means of this aforementioned harmony of states.

They are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because they are the limbs of that enlightenment, just as one speaks of the limbs of an army or the parts of a chariot. Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said:
"They are factors of enlightenment because they are the limbs of the person who is awakening. Of those seven factors of enlightenment.
"Of the Noble Eightfold Path": "Noble" (*ariya*) means being far removed from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, and because it brings about the state of a noble one.
And it is "noble" (ariya) because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruits (ariyaphala). It is "eightfold" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it possesses eight factors (aṭṭhaṅga).
This [path], like a fourfold army or a fivefold musical ensemble, consists merely of its constituent parts; there is nothing apart from those parts.
It is called the "path" (magga) because it seeks out (maggati) Nibbāna, or because it proceeds while slaying the defilements (kilesa). Of that noble eightfold [path]...
Of the application to the development of the path. "Of these wholesome states" refers to the wholesome states, both mundane and supramundane, of the kind already described.
"For the obstruction" means for the obstruction and disappearance of the supramundane wholesome states, and for the relinquishing of the mundane wholesome states.
Among them, they are called dangers (*parissaya*) in the sense that they do not allow the supramundane wholesome states to arise; for once they have arisen, [they cause those states to disappear].
When they cease, they do not bring about calamity. "In that" means in that personal existence (*attabhāva*). "These" refers to those [defilements]. "Evil" means base or inferior.

"Dependent on the personal existence" means they arise depending upon and taking as their object the personal existence; thus they are called "dependent on the personal existence. "In water" means in water. "For it has been said" means for this has indeed been stated.

"One who dwells with a pupil" (*sāntevāsika*) means one who dwells together with the defilement known as the "pupil"; thus he is "one who dwells with a pupil. "One who dwells with a teacher" (*sācariyaka*) means one who dwells together with the defilement known as "conduct" (*samudācaraṇa*); thus he is "one who dwells with a teacher."

"Having seen a form with the eye" means having perceived a form by means of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*). The same method applies to the subsequent phrases such as "having heard a sound with the ear," and so forth.
"Arise" means they manifest. "Discursive thoughts accompanied by memories" (*sarasaṅkappa*) refers to conceptualizations that have arisen through wandering among various objects.
"Conducive to fetters" (*saṃyojaniya*) means that, having become objects, they lead to being bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
They are conducive to the fetters (*saṃyojana*). "Of him" means of that person who possesses those evil qualities. "Dwell within" means they reside inside the mind.
"Flow along" means that having followed the continuum of defilements (*kilesa*), they flow intensely and persist.
"They strike" means these unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) afflict that person. "They assail" means they act together or proceed [against him]; this is the meaning.

They are "stains" (*mala*) in the sense of defiling. They are "enemies" (*amitta*) in the sense of being hostile. They are "rivals" (*sapatta*) in the sense of being adversaries. They are "slayers" (*vadhaka*) in the sense of killing.
They are "foes" (*paccatthika*) in the sense of being opponents. Alternatively, they are stains like the clouds that are the sun’s impurities;
enemies are like the smoke of the sun; rivals are like the frost of the sun; and slayers are like the dust of the sun.
Enemies are like Rāhu to the sun. They are like impurities that obscure the luster of gold;
they are enemies that destroy the clarity of the mind, like the dross of black iron that destroys the smoothness of the metal.

They are adversaries who ruin the qualities established in the mind, like rival warriors fighting in close combat. They are executioners who destroy the Dhamma, like murderers who kill human beings. They are adversaries.
Some describe it thus: "It is like the destruction of one who has approached a king; it is an obstructer of the path to liberation. Regarding the phrase *anatthajanano*:
"not-benefit" (*anattha*) is the opposite of benefit (*attha*); that which produces such non-benefit is *anatthajanano*.
What is it? Greed (*lobha*). Regarding *cittappakopano*: it is that which agitates and disturbs the mind; having warded off the wholesome, it obstructs the mind.
Meaning: "Fear born from within" means it has arisen within one's own mind itself, being the cause of fear such as the production of misfortune.
"People do not understand that" means the foolish masses, having descended [into the world], do not comprehend or know that fear.
"One greedy for gain" means a person who does not know the mundane and supramundane welfare (*attha*). "The Dhamma" refers to its cause. "Blind darkness" means...
"Thick darkness": because they go [into it], or toward such a person. "Overcomes" means it overpowers. "Internally" means within one's own continuum (*saṃtāna*).
"Arising, they arise" means that arising from the past onward, they arise for one's detriment and for suffering.
By both of these, there is an uncomfortable dwelling. "For one's detriment" means for the sake of mental suffering.

“For the sake of suffering” means for the sake of bodily pain. “For the sake of an uncomfortable dwelling” means for the sake of a dwelling that is not pleasant due to both [bodily and mental suffering].
Alternatively, some explain it thus: “They are called ‘arising’ from the movement of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) up until the stage of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*);
however, having reached the stage of determining, they are called ‘arising’ by virtue of their non-retrogression.”
They burst asunder by their own fruit, like a bamboo-stem known as *tacasāra* which has been deprived of its core.
"Discontent" (*arati*) means a state of weariness toward wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*). "Delight" (*rati*) means attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"Horripilation" (*lomahaṃsa*) refers to one whose body hair stands erect like thorns. "Having this as their source" (*itonidāna*) means that this personal existence (*attabhāva*) is the source or condition for these things.
"Born from this": born from this personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Thoughts of mind arising from this":
just as boys, having tied a crow's foot with a long string, release it after winding the end of that string around their finger;
and though it flies far away, it falls back again at the very feet of those boys—exactly so, thoughts arise from this personal existence.
Evil thoughts let go of the mind.
The first sutta, beginning with “One who has pupils,” was spoken with reference to dwelling together with the defilements.
The second, beginning with “Bhikkhus, there are these three internal stains,” was spoken by way of making wholesome states impure, [and] regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful.
And [the first] is by way of ignorance. It should be understood that the third, beginning with “Great King, three things arising internally in a person,” is by way of destroying one’s own support;
and the fourth, beginning with “Lust and hatred arise from this source,” is stated by way of showing the foundation of the defilements.
"From this or that peril" means from various calamities. "That person" refers to a person possessed of the aforementioned defilements.
"Suffering follows" means suffering follows after him, just as one who drinks milk follows behind his mother.
"It goes along with" means it approaches him, like an executioner approaching one who has reached the place of execution. "It becomes attached" means it clings to him, like a knot tied in a thread.
It is like a delimitation. Regarding "the suffering of birth" (*jātidukkha*), many meanings have been proclaimed for the word *jāti*.
As it is said: "Existence, clan, category, virtue, designation, characteristic, And procreation, as well as junction—these are the meanings proclaimed for *jāti*."
For instance, in such passages as “one birth, two births,” etc., the meaning is *bhava* (existence).
In the passage “uncensured and unreviled regarding one’s birth (*jāti*”), it refers to *kula* (clan). In the passage “There are, Visākhā, recluses called Nigaṇṭhas,” it refers to *nikāya* (sect).
In the passage “Sister, since I was born with the noble birth (*ariyāya jātiyā*), I do not recall...,” it refers to *ariyasīla* (noble virtue). [In the passage] “Tiriyā by name...”
In the passage, “Having grown from the navel of the grass-heap, it stood reaching up to the sky,” there is *paññatti* (designation).

In the passage, “Birth is comprised within two aggregates (*khandha*),” there is the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*). In the passage, “The Bodhisatta was just born, Ānanda,” there is *pasūti* (birth as emergence).
And in the passages, “With existence as condition, birth” and “Birth, too, is suffering,” there is, by way of figurative expression (*pariyāyato*), the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhikkhaṇa*).
In the ultimate sense (*nippariyāya*), however, birth is the first manifestation of whichever aggregates appear for beings as they are reborn here and there.
Why, then, is this birth suffering? Because it is the basis for many kinds of suffering. For indeed, there are many sufferings.
That is to say: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, figurative suffering, and non-figurative suffering.
Among these, bodily and mental painful feelings are called "the suffering of suffering" because they are suffering both by their intrinsic nature and by name.

Pleasant feeling is suffering due to change because it is the cause for the arising of suffering through transformation; thus, it is "suffering due to change. Both neutral feeling and all remaining formations belonging to the three planes are "suffering due to formations" because they are oppressed by arising and passing away.

Physical and mental affliction—such as earache, toothache, or the fever born of lust, hatred, and delusion—is "concealed suffering" because it must be known by asking [others] and because its mode of occurrence is not manifest; it is also called "unmanifest suffering."

Illness arising from the thirty-two tortures and so forth is "unconcealed suffering" because it must be known even without being asked about and because its cause is evident; it is also called "manifest suffering.

With the exception of the suffering of suffering itself, all other factors such as birth mentioned in the *Vibhaṅga* of the Truth of Suffering are "figurative suffering," since they serve as the basis for various types of suffering. However, the suffering of suffering is said to be "non-figurative suffering."

In this context, "birth" is called suffering because it serves as the basis for that suffering pertaining to the states of misery— which was illustrated by the Blessed One through similes in such discourses as the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*—
as well as for the various types of suffering that arise even in the happy destinies within the human world, beginning with the descent into the womb.
In this regard, this is the suffering beginning with the descent into the womb:
for when this being is being reborn in the mother’s womb, he is not reborn among blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and so forth;

rather, he is between the stomach below and the intestines above, amidst the ribs and the backbone, in the midst of extreme confinement, in utter darkness, and permeated by the stench of various kinds of filth.

He is born like a worm in a place that is utterly foul, pervaded by winds of supreme stench, and exceedingly loathsome—a region of the belly containing putrid fish, rotten gruel, cesspools, and the like.
Having been born there, for ten months he is cooked like a wrapped-offering by the heat produced within the mother’s womb;
he is steamed like a lump of dough, deprived of the ability to contract or extend his limbs, and [suffers] excessively.
"He experiences suffering"— this, first of all, is the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb.
Furthermore, when his mother suddenly stumbles, moves, sits down, stands up, turns over, and so forth,
he is subjected to being dragged hither and thither, shaken and tossed about, like a goat in the hands of a drunkard or a young snake in the hands of a snake-charmer.
Through such exertion, one experiences intense suffering: when the mother drinks cold water, he experiences suffering like that of one reborn in a cold hell;
when she consumes hot gruel, rice, and so forth, he experiences suffering like one surrounded by a rain of glowing coals;

and when she consumes salty, sour, and other such foods, he experiences sharp suffering like one subjected to the torture of being smeared with caustic lye. This is the suffering rooted in the maintenance of the womb.

Furthermore, the suffering that arises for a mother whose womb is obstructed— suffering caused by cutting, tearing, and so forth at a place of birth inaccessible even to friends, ministers, and kinsmen— is the suffering rooted in the failure of the womb. Then there is the suffering of the mother giving birth,
as the fetus is turned by the winds born of karma and led through the birth canal—
which is as terrifying as a fall into hell— and through the extremely narrow opening of the womb, which is like the hole of a palm-wood pestle.
When the great elephant is being dragged out, suffering arises for him as if he were a creature in hell being crushed by colliding mountains;
this is the suffering rooted in birth.
Furthermore, when the newborn’s delicate body—resembling a fresh wound—is being grasped by the hand, bathed, washed, rubbed with cloth, and so forth, [suffering arises].
Suffering arises similar to being pierced by needle-tips or split by razor-edges; this is the suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb.

Furthermore, there is the suffering for one who, during the course of existence, strikes himself with his own hand, or who is devoted to the practice of self-mortification and tormenting oneself through such means as the naked ascetic’s observances.
For one who does not eat due to anger and who hangs himself, there is suffering; this is suffering rooted in self-aggression (*attūpakkamamūlaka*).
However, the suffering that arises for one experiencing killing, binding, and so forth at the hands of others, is suffering rooted in aggression by another (*parūpakkamamūlaka*).
Thus, for all this suffering, birth (*jāti*) alone is the basis; this follows upon the suffering of birth.
Regarding "the suffering of aging," there are two kinds of aging: the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), which is recognized as decrepitude and so forth;
and the state of the aggregates (*khandha*) becoming worn out within a single continuity (*santati*) belonging to one existence. It is this latter kind that is intended here.

Furthermore, this [aging] is suffering both because it is of the nature of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and because it is a basis for suffering. For it consists in the loosening of the limbs and members, and the disfigurement resulting from the transformation of the sense faculties.
Physical and mental suffering arises due to numerous conditions such as the destruction of youth, the impairment of strength, the loss of mindfulness and intelligence, and being overcome by others;
aging is its basis. Therefore, this is said:
“Because of the loosening of the limbs, because of the transformation of the faculties...”
Through the destruction of youth, through the impairment of strength,
through separation from one's hundred [virtues] and so forth, from one's children and wife,
through being untrustworthy, and furthermore, through falling into greater foolishness.
“The suffering that a mortal attains, both physical and likewise mental—all this has aging as its cause;
therefore, aging is suffering. This is the connection: [the phrase] “this suffering of aging follows.

Regarding “disease” (*byādhi*): it is called *byādhi* because it brings forth (*ā-dahati*) or burns up (*vi-dahati*) manifold suffering. Or, it is called *byādhi* because it afflicts (*byādhayati*), torments (*tāpayati*), or causes trembling (*kampayati*).

Regarding "the suffering of death," here too there are two kinds of death: the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), with reference to which it was said, "Old age and death are comprised within two aggregates";

and the severance of the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) included within a single existence, with reference to which it was said, "There is constant fear of death. It is the latter that is intended here. With birth as condition...
Death, intentional death, natural death, death through the exhaustion of the life-span, and death through the exhaustion of merit—these are also names for that same phenomenon.
Furthermore, this distinction should also be understood: momentary death, conventional death, and death as total cessation.
The dissolution of material and immaterial phenomena during the course of existence is called momentary death. "Tissa is dead," "Phussa is dead"—this is... [conventional death].

Since, in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), there is no such thing as a "being," the expressions "the crop is dead" or "the tree is dead" are also called conventional death (*sammutimaraṇa*) due to the absence of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
The passing away of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) without rebirth-linking is called death by eradication (*samucchedamaraṇa*).
Excluding external conventional death, the other types of conventional death are included here by way of the cessation of the aforementioned continuity.
It is included [in the category of suffering], but it is called "suffering" because it is the basis for suffering.
Therefore, this is said: "For one who contemplates evil as the cause of evil kamma and so forth, and who cannot endure the separation from beloved objects—though he be fortunate—"
The mental suffering experienced by one being measured is, for the most part, without distinction [from that of others]. And likewise,
the bodily suffering arising from the cutting of joints and ligaments, which occurs to those whose vital points (*marmans*) are being pierced, is the same for all.
“Because this is an unbearable and incurable basis for suffering,
namely death, it is therefore described simply as ‘suffering. Regarding the phrase “the suffering of sorrow,
lamentation, pain, grief, and despair,” herein, among sorrow and the others, “sorrow” (soka) refers to [the distress] caused by the loss of relatives and so forth.
Grief has the characteristic of inward brooding when one is touched [by suffering];
it is painful both because it is the suffering of suffering itself and because it serves as the basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“Grief pierces the hearts of beings like a dart.”
The essence of fire itself is not the arrow, yet it burns even more fiercely. Furthermore,
because it brings about disease, decay, death, and dissolution,
and because it entails manifold suffering, it is therefore called "suffering."

Lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outpouring of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and other such misfortunes. It is suffering because it is of the nature of the suffering of *saṃsāra* and because it is a basis for suffering.

Therefore, this is said: “Struck by the dart of sorrow and lamenting, one undergoes even greater and excessive suffering produced by the parching of the throat, lips, and palate; therefore, the Blessed One called lamentation ‘suffering’.”

Suffering (dukkha) is bodily suffering characterized by oppression of the body. It is called "suffering" both because it is the suffering of suffering itself and because it brings about mental suffering. Therefore, this is said:
"This bodily suffering oppresses, and it brings about even greater mental suffering;
since it generates [both], it is therefore specifically called 'suffering.'"
Mental grief (*domanassa*) is mental suffering characterized by the affliction of the mind.

It is suffering both because it is suffering-as-suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) in itself and because it brings about physical suffering. For those possessed by mental suffering, they tear out their hair and weep;
they beat their breasts, wring their hands, and roll back and forth; they throw themselves down precipices, take up weapons, [or consume] poison...
They eat [themselves], they hang by ropes, they enter fire, and they experience various kinds of suffering. Therefore this is said:
“Since it oppresses the mind and brings about oppression of the body, it is called ‘suffering’ (dukkha) and also ‘mental distress’ (domanassa); from that, mental distress arose.”

Despair (*upāyāsa*) is simply the corruption produced by excessive mental suffering in one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth. Some say it is a single phenomenon included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
It is suffering, however, because of its nature as the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), because it burns the mind, and because it afflicts the body.
Therefore, this is said:
“Because it burns the mind and because it destroys the body to an extreme degree,
the suffering that arises from despair is therefore called ‘suffering. And here,
sorrow is like the cooking of food inside a vessel by a mild fire, whereas [despair] is like that of one being roasted in a vessel by a fierce fire.

Lamentation should be seen as like going outside; despair should be seen as like the cooking of what remains after one has gone outside, which, being unable even to go out, continues to cook within the vessel until its total exhaustion.
"Hellish suffering" refers to the suffering consisting of the fivefold bondage and so forth that follows one in hell; this should be illustrated by the *Devadūta Sutta*. Therefore, this is said:
“If a being were not to be born in the hells, where could it find a footing for the suffering that is difficult to endure, such as the burning by fire? Thus the Sage said here: ‘Birth is suffering.

Regarding the suffering of the animal realm: various kinds of suffering, such as being struck with whips, sticks, and goads, and being pierced, follow those in the animal womb. This should be understood from the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*. Therefore, this is said:
“In the animal realm, suffering is manifold, consisting of being struck by whips, goads, sticks, and so forth.
How could that [suffering] exist there without birth? Indeed, even apart from that, birth itself is suffering.

As for the suffering of the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisayika*): it follows upon the suffering produced among the *petas* by hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and the like, as well as the suffering of unbearable cold and so forth in the dense darkness of other worlds. Therefore, this is said:
“Furthermore, among animals, suffering is manifold, arising from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and so forth;
since that does not exist for one who is unborn, the Sage therefore called birth itself suffering.
And the suffering among the Asuras in the world-intervening realms—characterized by intense darkness and unbearable cold—”
“There would be no becoming there, nor would there be birth; yet from whatever this birth arises, even that is suffering.
“Human suffering” refers to the suffering among humans such as killing, imprisonment, and so forth. “Suffering rooted in descent into the womb” refers to [the passage] beginning with:
“For when this being is being reborn in the mother’s womb, he is not reborn in blue, red, or white lotuses, and so on.”
The suffering of birth mentioned by way of this method follows upon the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb.

As for the intense suffering mentioned by way of the method beginning with, "When he suddenly stumbles, moves, or sits of his mother," that follows upon the suffering rooted in remaining in the womb. From the womb...

"Suffering rooted in birth" refers to the suffering described in the following manner: "Furthermore, for a mother whose fetus has died, there arises suffering even at a place where she ought not to be seen by friends, companions, kinsmen, and others.
This [suffering] follows upon the suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb. Therefore, this is said:—
“And even that which is like dwelling in a womb as if in a pit of excrement,
and the suffering that a being experiences when, after staying there for a long time,
it undergoes the most terrible pain upon emerging from it— this too does not exist [in that state].”
“Even ‘without birth’—for this birth is suffering.
What is the use of much speaking?
Is there not indeed some kind of suffering here or there at any time?”
"There is nothing, O Great Sage, that is more wretched than birth;
for this reason, you declared at the very outset that 'birth is suffering.
Birth is the bond of suffering; it is the suffering involved in the maintenance of one who is born, such as bathing, anointing, eating, drinking, and so forth.
It follows. "The suffering of being dependent on another" means that the suffering of powerlessness, which is contingent upon another—that is, someone else—follows one.

For it has been said: "All that is under the control of another is suffering. "The suffering of self-exertion" refers to the suffering of one who, by his own hand, subjects himself to the practice of mortification and self-torment through such ascetic observances as those of the naked ascetics (acelakas), or who, out of anger, refuses to eat.
And for one who hangs oneself, there is suffering; this follows as the suffering of self-inflicted action (*attūpakkama-dukkha*).

As for "suffering inflicted by others" (*parūpakkama-dukkha*), that which arises for one experiencing slaughter, bondage, and so forth from another follows as the suffering of action inflicted by others.
"Suffering-as-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*) refers to bodily and mental painful feelings, because they are suffering both by their intrinsic nature and by name.
Suffering as suffering (*dukkhadukkha*): this follows upon suffering as suffering.

Suffering due to formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*): both the feeling of equanimity and the remaining formations of the three planes are suffering due to formations because they are oppressed by arising and passing away; this follows upon suffering due to formations. Suffering due to change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*):
pleasant feeling is suffering due to change by way of being the cause of suffering due to change; this [follows upon] suffering due to change.
The suffering of change follows.
"Death of the mother" means the death of one's mother. "Death of the father" means the death of one's father. "Death of brothers" means the death of elder and younger brothers.
"Death of sisters" means the death of elder and younger sisters. "Death of sons" means [the death] of sons.
Death. "The death of a daughter" means the death of daughters. "The suffering of loss of relatives" means the misfortune of relatives;
the destruction or loss of relatives through thieves, disease, fear, and so forth—this is the meaning of "the ruin of relatives.
For one who is touched, overwhelmed, and overcome by that loss of relatives, the suffering that arises is the "suffering of loss of relatives"; that suffering of loss of relatives follows after him.
The same method applies to the others as well. However, this is the distinction: the misfortune of wealth (*bhogabyasana*) is the ruin of wealth;
it means the depletion of wealth through kings, thieves, and so forth, or the destruction of wealth. In the manner already stated, that misfortune of wealth follows after suffering.
The misfortune of disease (*rogabyasana*) is disease itself as a misfortune. For disease is a "misfortune" (*byasana*) because it ruins or destroys health (*ārogya*); in the manner already stated...
That calamity of disease is followed by suffering. Regarding "the calamity of virtue is suffering":
the calamity of virtue is a "calamity of virtue" (*sīlabyasana*); this is a name for immorality (*dussīlya*). In the manner already stated, that calamity of virtue is followed by suffering.
A view that has arisen which destroys right view is itself the calamity; thus it is a "calamity of view" (*diṭṭhibyasana*). In the manner already stated, that calamity of view is suffering.
It follows. And herein, the first two are unconditioned (*anipphanna*), while the latter three are conditioned (*nipphanna*) and struck by the three characteristics.
Furthermore, the first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the pair consisting of the ruin of virtue and the ruin of view is unwholesome.
"Yathā" means in comparison. "A broken ship" refers to a ship with loose fastenings or one that has become dilapidated and riddled with cracks.

Or: *dakamesinī* means one that seeks water, one that enters the water, or one that causes water to enter. "It follows the water from here and there" means it enters the water from various broken points.
"From the front" means even from the forward part of the boat. "From the back" means even from its rear part.
"From below" means even from the lower part. "From the sides" means even from both sides. Whatever has not been stated in between [should be understood accordingly].
This should be understood according to the reading of the text.
Therefore, by means of the development of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) and so forth, a person, being constantly mindful, should avoid sensual pleasures;
avoiding all forms of defiled desire (*kilesakāma*) regarding the objects of desire such as visible forms (*rūpa*), etc., by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and eradication (*samuccheda*).
Thus, having abandoned those sensual pleasures, by means of the very path that effects their abandonment, one would cross— be able to cross— the fourfold flood. Then, just as a man,
having bailed out water from a heavy boat, would reach the further shore with little difficulty by means of a light boat, even so,
having bailed out the water of the defilements from the boat of one's own person, by means of the light [boat]...
One would become a master through one’s own person. One would have gone to the further shore of all phenomena, which is Nibbāna;
one would go for the attainment of Arahantship by means of final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue—thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because this suffering, beginning with birth, follows after this person; therefore. This also applies to such phrases as "for that reason" (*taṃkāraṇā*) and "for that cause" (*taṃhetu*).
The same method applies here. The word-order (*padayojanā*) should be made as follows: "Because this [suffering] follows it, therefore it is its cause (*hetu*);
because it follows it, therefore it is its condition (*paccaya*); because it follows it, therefore it is its source (*nidāna*). *Hetu*, etc., are synonyms for "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

For a cause is called *hetu* because by means of it the fruit is led forth (*hinoti*) or brought into occurrence. It is called *paccaya* because depending upon that [cause], the fruit comes (*eti*) or occurs.
“Condition” (*paccaya*). It is called “source” (*nidāna*) because it points toward its own fruit as if saying, “Come, take this!

“By that cause” (*taṃkāraṇā*) is a negation of [the terms] *akāraṇa* (non-cause) and *nikkāraṇa* (without cause). “By that reason” (*taṃhetu*) is a negation of [the terms] *ahetu* (no-reason), *mahābhūtahetu* (reason of the great elements), and *hetu* (cause).

“By that condition” (*tappaccayā*) is a negation of conditions not shared with the *appaccaya* (conditionless). “By that source” (*taṃnidānā*) is a negation of sources consisting of scripture and realization, along with the *anidāna* (sourceless).”
Thus some explain it. "Seeing this danger" means seeing and perceiving with the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) this aforementioned calamity.
"Always" is the root word; "again, always" is the word for the meaning. "Always" means every day. "At all times" means at all [occasions].
"At the proper time. "At all times" means at every time, such as the morning and so forth. "Constantly" means day after day. "Perpetually" means without interruption.
"Continually" means without interval. "Unified" means become one. "Uninterrupted" means unmixed with anything else.
"In succession, link after link" means joined in a continuous sequence, as in the expressions "link after link it appears unbroken," and so forth.
“Like water-moss” means like the waves of water that has arisen. “Avīci” means without interval. “Santati” means uninterrupted.
“Sahita” means joined or unified, as in such expressions as “this is suitable for me, that is not suitable for you.
“Phassita” means touched, as in such expressions as “in a windless place, with a touch of dew. “Before the meal” and “after the meal.”
Two terms are stated by way of the division of the day: the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch—these three are by way of the division of the night.
"In the dark [half]" and "in the bright [half]" are by way of the half-month. "In the rainy season," etc., and "in the summer"—these three are by way of the seasons.
"In the first stage of life," etc., and "in the last stage of life"—it should be understood that these three are stated by way of the divisions of age.

“Mindful” (*sato*) means mindful by way of four reasons. The meanings of such passages as “Developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body in the body, he is mindful,” up to the conclusion, “Thus he should avoid sensual pleasures by way of eradication,” have already been explained. Furthermore, he is mindful because of his steadfastness (*satatta*);
that is, either by way of his steadfastness in the three bases, or by way of his being a spear (*satti*) capable of driving away the three defilements.

"Sato" (mindful): "Because of being calmed" means because he is calmed by having expelled the defilements and secondary defilements, and by having been liberated through both his state and his object.
"Because of being stilled" means because he is stilled by merit that yields desirable fruits and by the absence of evil that yields undesirable fruits.
"Endowed with peaceful qualities" means because of cultivating the qualities of true persons and because of attending upon noble individuals such as the Buddhas.
He is "mindful" because he is endowed with the qualities of mindfulness.

"Having fully understood sense-desires as objects" means having known these aforementioned sense-desires pertaining to the three planes through the full understanding of scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*).

"Having abandoned" means having relinquished sense-desires as defilements through the full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*). "Having cast off" means having discarded them. What is this refuse?
"Is it like a basket? "No, rather, having dispelled it, crossed over it, pierced it, and extracted it. "Is it like a goad-stick for an ox?
"No, rather, having made it disappear, having made it reach its end—having done so in such a way that not even its interior remains, not even so much as a mere fragment. But how [is it done]?
How is it done in that way? By taking it to non-existence (*anabhāva*) and leading it to subsequent non-existence (*anu-abhāva*). What is meant is:

having acted so that it is completely severed through abandonment by cutting off (*samuccheda-pahāna*). This same method applies to the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) and the others.

Regarding the "flood of sensual desires" (*kāma-ogha*) and so forth, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the "flood of sensual desires" in the sense of sinking down. The "flood of existence" (*bhava-ogha*)...
In the realms of form and formlessness, there is sensual desire and lust, as well as attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*).

The "flood of views" (*diṭṭhogha*) is simply the aspiration for existence accompanied by eternalist views and the like; thus, the flood of views merges into the flood of existence itself. The "flood of ignorance" (*avijjogha*) is non-knowing regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Among these, for one who attends to the strands of sense pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) as gratifying, the unarisen flood of sensuality arises, and that which has already arisen...
And the flood of sensual desire increases. For one who attends to the sublime states as gratification, the unarisen flood of existence arises and the arisen increases.

It should be understood that through the state of being the basis for the four perversions regarding phenomena of the three planes, the unarisen flood of ignorance arises and the arisen increases. This is by way of the opposite of the method already stated.
The bright side [of the practice] should be explained in detail.

One practicing the desireless liberation would cross the flood of sensual desire; one practicing the signless liberation, the flood of existence; and one practicing the emptiness liberation, the flood of ignorance.
One would cross by means of the first path and emerge by means of the second path.
One might cross by means of the third path, transcend by means of the fourth path, and pass beyond by means of the fruit.

Alternatively, some explain it thus: "One might cross by means of the flood of sensuality, emerge by means of the flood of existence, cross over by means of the flood of views, transcend by means of the flood of ignorance, and pass beyond by means of all floods."
"Heavy" means not light. "Heavy" refers to a heavy load; it is called "heavy" because they place it there.
"Having sprinkled water" means having poured water. "Having drenched" means having poured excessively. "Having discarded" means having cast down.
"Lightly" means very lightly. "Swiftly" means quickly. "Immediately" means at that very moment. "Without difficulty" means without pain.
“The further shore” (pāra) is said to be the deathless Nibbāna; thus, it is the further shore that stands beyond the world of personal existence (sakkāya).

Nibbāna is described as having emerged from the flood of craving (taṇhāvāna). “He who” (yo so) refers to this very person. The entire passage beginning with “the stilling of all formations” (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha) refers to Nibbāna alone.
For since all the stirrings of formations (saṅkhāra-vipphanditāni) are stilled—that is, completely pacified—by coming to it, it is therefore called “the stilling of all formations.”

It is so called because, by depending upon this, all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all craving (taṇhā) is exhausted, all stains of defilement (kilesa-raja) are removed, and all suffering (dukkha) ceases;

therefore, it is called "the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation. Furthermore, as for this craving which leads from existence to existence and from fruit to fruit...
It is called *vāna* because it weaves or sews together action (*kamma*) with [craving]. That which has emerged from that is *nibbāna*.

One would go to the further shore (*pāra*) by means of the sign; that is, one would reach the further shore of *nibbāna* through the knowledge of emergence and the knowledge of change-of-lineage occurring on one side.
One would attain the further shore of *nibbāna* through the knowledge of the path of emergence on both sides, by means of the sign and the occurrence [of the sign].
One would especially reach [it]. One would touch the further shore of Nibbāna by way of the resultant consciousness that has Nibbāna as its object.
One would realize it by way of its qualities; having touched it, one would make the further shore of Nibbāna directly manifest through the knowledge of review.
Alternatively: "By the first path one would go to the further shore; by the second one would attain it; by the third one would touch it."

"One should realize it by means of the fourth"—thus some explain. Furthermore, "one who desires to go to the further shore" refers to any person established in insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) who desires to go to the further shore of Nibbāna;
such a one is a "far-reeled" (*pāragū*) because they will certainly go there. For this has been said:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death, in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs," and so forth.
In the preliminary stage, by way of aspiration and through the practice of insight, one is also called "one who has gone beyond.
Furthermore, he who goes to the further shore—that is, the possessor of the path who goes to the further shore of Nibbāna—is also called "one who has gone beyond.

And he who has gone to the further shore—that is, he who, having completed what was to be done by means of the path, stands in the fruit and has reached the further shore of Nibbāna—is also called "one who has gone beyond."

To demonstrate this by means of the Conqueror’s word, he said: “For this was also said by the Blessed One: ‘The brahmin has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land’,” and so forth.
“One who has reached the further shore through direct knowledge (*abhiññāpāragū*)”: desiring to go to the further shore of Nibbāna, one goes by means of the knowledge already attained;

having gone, one is “one who has reached the further shore. “One who has reached the further shore through full understanding (*pariññāpāragū*”)”: by means of the full understanding that consists in the investigation of all phenomena...

"Having transcended," as stated by the method already described, he has "gone to the further shore. "One who has gone to the further shore through abandoning" means that, having transcended the defilements belonging to the side of origination by means of the full understanding of abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*), he has, according to the stated method, gone to the further shore.
For whoever fully understands all phenomena, he understands them by means of three kinds of full understanding:

by the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*), by the full understanding of scrutinization (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and by the full understanding of abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). In this context, what is the full understanding of the known?
One knows all phenomena thus: "These are internal, these are external; this is their characteristic, these are their taste, manifestation, and proximate cause.

This is full understanding by knowledge (*ñātapariññā*). What is full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*)? Having thus gained such knowledge, one scrutinizes all phenomena according to how they are found, by way of [contemplating them as] impermanent, suffering, a disease, and so forth. This is full understanding by scrutinization. What is full understanding by abandoning (*pahānapariññā*)?
Having thus investigated, one abandons desire and lust for phenomena by means of the supreme path; this is "full understanding as abandonment.

It is with reference to these full understandings that it was said: "He has reached the further shore through direct knowledge, he has reached the further shore through full understanding, he has reached the further shore through abandonment.

"One who has reached the further shore through development" means having reached the pinnacle of development, one has gone to the further shore of Nibbāna by way of the path. "One who has reached the further shore through realization" means...
By way of the fruit of Nibbāna, he has gone to the further shore of the realization-fruit of Nibbāna.

"One who has reached the further shore of attainments" means one who has attained the further shore of the eight attainments. "Of all phenomena" means of all phenomena such as the five aggregates and so forth.

"Of all sufferings" means of all sufferings such as the suffering of birth and so forth. "Of all defilements" means of all defilements such as bodily misconduct and so forth. "Of noble paths" means...
Of the four noble paths, beginning with the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). Of cessation (*nirodha*) means of *nibbāna*.

Of all attainments (*samāpatti*) means of all eight attainments of the form and formless realms. "He" (*so*) refers to that noble one (*ariya*). "One who has attained mastery" (*vasippatta*) means one who has reached the state of mastery (*vasībhāva*).

Alternatively, it means one who has reached the state of being desirable, the state of sovereignty, and the state of perfection. "One who has attained the further shore" (*pāramippatta*): "further shore" (*pāramī*)...
He has reached the end, the conclusion, or the supreme state. To the question "Where has he reached it?", he says: "In noble virtue," and so forth.
Therein, "in noble virtue" means in faultless virtue. "In noble concentration" means in faultless concentration.
"By noble wisdom" means by faultless wisdom. "By noble liberation" means by the faultless liberation that is the fruit.

It should be understood that by the first [term], right speech, action, and livelihood are included; by the second, right effort, mindfulness, and concentration; by the third, right thought and right view;
and by the fourth, the remaining factors associated with them.

"One who has gone to the end" means one who has reached the end of the world of formations by means of the Path. "One who has attained the end" means one who has reached that very end of the world by means of the Fruit.

"Reached the limit" (*koṭigata*) means having reached the limit of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārakoṭi*) by means of the path. "Attained the limit" (*koṭippatta*) means having attained that very limit by means of the fruit (*phala*).
"Reached the boundary" (*pariyantagata*) means having gone after having established a demarcation and enclosure around the world—the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth—by means of the path.

"Attained the boundary" (*pariyantappatta*) means having attained that very world after having made it a boundary by means of the fruit. "Reached the consummation" (*vosānagata*) means having reached the end by means of the path.
"Attained to the end" means having reached the conclusion by means of the fruit (*phala*). "Gone to refuge" means gone to protection by means of the path (*magga*).

"Attained to refuge" means attained to protection by means of the fruit. "Gone to a shelter" means gone to concealment by means of the path. "Attained to a shelter" means attained to that concealment by means of the fruit.
"Gone to a resort" means gone to a firm foundation by means of the path. "Attained to a resort" means [attained] to a resort by means of the fruit.

*Patto*: "One who has gone to fearlessness" means one who has reached the state of being fearless by means of the path. "One who has attained fearlessness" means one who has reached the fearlessness of Nibbāna by means of the fruit (*phala*).

"One who has gone to the deathless" means one who has reached Nibbāna, which is devoid of death, by means of the path. "One who has attained the deathless" means one who has reached that [Nibbāna] by means of the fruit.

"One who has gone to the immortal" means one who has reached Nibbāna, which is free from death, by means of the path. "One who has attained the immortal" means one who has reached that [Nibbāna] by means of the fruit.

"Attained. "Gone to Nibbāna" means he has gone by way of the path to Nibbāna, which has emerged from the flood of craving. "Reached Nibbāna" means he has reached that very same state through its fruit.
"One who has dwelt [in the training]" refers to that Arahant who has dwelt, fully dwelt, and lived out the ten noble dwellings;
he has emerged from them, and thus he is one who has "dwelt. "One who has practiced the conduct" means he has mastered the eight meditative attainments together with virtue.

One who has practiced the conduct (*ciṇṇacaraṇa*). One who has gone beyond the stream (*gataddha*) means one who has transcended the course of *saṃsāra*. One who has gone to the direction (*gatadisa*) means one who has gone to the direction of *nibbāna*, which has never been gone to even in a dream.

One who has reached the limit (*gatakoṭika*) means one who stands having reached the limit of *nibbāna* without remainder (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). One who has guarded the holy life (*pālitabrahmacariya*) means one whose holy life has been protected.
One who has attained the supreme view (*uttamadiṭṭhippatto*) means one who has attained the supreme right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). One who has penetrated the unshakable (*paṭividdhākuppo*)...
Having penetrated the unshakable, immovable fruit of arhatship, he stands firm. "One who has realized cessation" means he stands having realized cessation, which is Nibbāna.
"Suffering has been fully understood by him" means that the threefold suffering has been transcended and thoroughly delimited by him. "That which is to be directly known..."
It is to be known in a beautiful manner by way of awakening to its specific characteristic (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*).

"Fully known" (*abhiññāta*) means known by superior knowledge (*adhika-ñāṇa*). "To be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) means it is to be thoroughly understood by way of awakening to its general characteristic (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*) and by way of fulfilling its function (*kicca*).
"Fully understood" (*pariññāta*) means known all around. "To be developed" (*bhāvetabba*) means to be increased.
"To be realized" means to be made directly evident. For realization is twofold: realization as attainment and realization as the object.
"With the crossbar lifted":
here, the "crossbar" refers to ignorance rooted in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). For this [ignorance] is called a "crossbar" in the sense that it causes one to suffer.

It is said thus. For that reason, because the crossbar has been lifted from it, he is called "one who has lifted the crossbar" (*ukkhitapaligho*). Regarding "one whose moat has been filled" (*saṃkiṇṇaparikho*):

"moat" (*parikhā*) refers to the formative volitional action of karma (*kammābhisaṅkhāra*), which is the condition for the aggregates of renewed existence (*punabbhavakkhandhā*)—those which, by way of being born and wandering through various states of existence, have received the name "the cycle of birth" (*jātisaṃsāro*). For that [karma] brings about repeated arising.

Because it stands surrounding [the city], it is called a "moat" (*parikhā*). Therefore, because that moat has been filled in and scattered, it is described as "having its moat filled and scattered" (*saṃkiṇṇaparikho*).
"With the pillar pulled out" (*abbūḷhesiko*): the "pillar" (*esikā*) is craving, which has a rounded base. For this [craving] is called a "pillar" in the sense of being deep-reaching.
Therefore, because that pillar has been pulled out—uprooted and discarded—it is called "with the pillar pulled out. "Without a bolt" (*niraggaḷo*)...
"Bar" (aggaḷa) refers to the lower fetters (orambhāgiya), which are the conditions for rebirth in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava).
For these are called "bars" because they stand closing off the mind, like a great door-bolt blocking the city gate.
Therefore, because these have been removed and broken, he is called "one who is without bars" (niraggaḷa). "Noble" (ariya) means free from defilements and completely purified.

"Pannaddhaja" means one who has caused the banner of conceit (māna) to fall. "Pannabhāra" means one by whom the burden of the aggregates (khandha), the burden of defilements (kilesa), the burden of volitional formations (abhisankhāra), and the burden of the five strands of sensual pleasure (pañca-kāmaguṇa) have been laid down;
thus he is "pannabhāra. Furthermore, in this context, he is intended as "pannabhāra" specifically because the burden of conceit alone has been laid down.
"Visaṃyutta" means detached from the four bonds (yoga) and from all defilements; however, in this instance, it refers specifically to the bond of conceit.
Because he is dissociated [from defilements], he is intended as "dissociated.

Up to this point, the Elder has shown the time when, having exhausted the defilements by means of the path, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)—having entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object—dwells having gone to the excellent bed of cessation (nirodha).
For just as there are two cities, one being a city of thieves, [the other a city of peace].
There was one secure city. Then, suppose a desire should arise in a certain great warrior:
"As long as this robber-city remains, this secure city will not be freed from fear. I shall turn the robber-city into a non-city.
Having donned his armor and taken up his sword, he approaches the robber-city and stands at the city gate by the raised pillar.
Having cut through with his sword, broken down the door-panel along with the door-posts, lifted up the crossbar, breached the rampart, filled in the moat,
lowered the flags that had been raised for the sake of the city’s beauty, and set the city ablaze, he entered the city of Khema; then,
ascending the upper terrace of the palace, surrounded by a circle of kinsmen, [he partook of] delicious food.
He would eat. In this way, the city of personal existence (sakkāya) is like a city of thieves, Nibbāna is like a city of security, and the practitioner (yogāvacara) is like a great warrior.

It occurs to him: "As long as the cycle of personal existence continues, there is no liberation from the thirty-two tortures, the ninety-eight diseases, and the twenty-five great fears. Thus, that great warrior...
Having donned the armor of virtue as if it were actual mail and grasping the sharp sword of wisdom,
he cut through the shaft of craving with the path of arahantship as if cutting through a wooden post with a sword;
that warrior then shattered the bolt of the five lower fetters as if it were a city gate-bar, and [overcame] the crossbar of ignorance as if it were a physical bar.
Having hurled it, that warrior, like one breaking down a rampart, broke through the rampart of the formative forces of karma (*saṃskāra*) and filled up the moat of the cycle of birth and rebirth;
like a warrior felling a banner raised for the sake of beautifying a city, he cast down the banner of pride,
burned down the city of the five aggregates (*sakkāya*), and having entered the city of security, stood upon the upper terrace of the palace.

As if eating a meal of divine flavor, having entered the city of Nibbāna, he passes his time experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), which has the cessation of the deathless as its object. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"And how, monks, is a monk one who has lifted the crossbar? Here, monks, for a monk, ignorance..."
It has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk has the crossbar lifted. “And how, monks, is a monk one who has filled the moat?
Here, monks, a monk’s cycle of birth leading to renewed existence has been abandoned... [as before] ...It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has filled the moat.”
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has pulled out the pillar? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s craving has been abandoned... Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has pulled out the pillar.
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who is without bolts? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s five lower fetters have been abandoned... Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who is without bolts.
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu noble, with banner lowered, with burden dropped, unfettered? Here, bhikkhus...”

“Monks, when a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising—in this way, monks, a bhikkhu is noble, with his banner lowered, his burden dropped, and unyoked.

Monks, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, even the gods together with Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati, though searching for it, do not find it, thinking: ‘Upon what is the consciousness of the Tathāgata supported?’”
"Abandoning the five factors" means that he stands having abandoned the five factors, beginning with sensual desire, by various means. For this has been said:

"And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has abandoned the five factors? Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, has abandoned ill will, has abandoned sloth and torpor, has abandoned restlessness and remorse..."
“Doubt has been abandoned. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors.

Regarding “endowed with six factors”: having fulfilled the six factors by dwelling mindful and clearly comprehending through the mode of equanimity—having avoided aversion and attraction toward objects such as forms at the six sense doors—one fulfills and completes the six factors.
Because he remains established [in this way], he is called "endowed with the six factors. For it has been said:
"And how, friends, is a bhikkhu endowed with the six factors? Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither glad nor sad;
he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear..."

“Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, having touched a tangible object with the body, and having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad; one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
It is in this way, friend, that a bhikkhu is endowed with the six factors.”
"Having a single guard" (*ekārakkho*) means: he has a single, supreme guard, which is mindfulness;
