thus he is "one-guarded. For this has been said: "And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one-guarded? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one-guarded.
"Four-sided" (*caturāpasso*) refers to the four aspects by way of wisdom: namely, reflecting upon, avoiding, dispelling, and abandoning.
It is called "four-sided" by way of those who do not turn from side to side while lying down; it stands having reached them. For this has been said:
"And how, friends, is a bhikkhu four-sided? Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having reflected, pursues one thing;
having reflected, he avoids another; having reflected, he dispels one thing; having reflected, he abandons one thing. It should be elaborated in this manner and so forth.

"One who has discarded individual truths" (*paṇunnapaccekasacca*) means one by whom the "individual truths"—that is, views considered as separate truths in the sense of "only this is truth, only this is truth"—have been discarded, removed, and abandoned; thus he is "one who has discarded individual truths.
"One who has thoroughly relinquished all quests" (*samavayasaṭṭhesana*): here, *avaya* means "not deficient" (*anūna*), and *saṭṭha* means "relinquished" (*vissaṭṭha*).

One for whom all quests have been properly and completely relinquished is "one who has thoroughly relinquished all quests"; the meaning is "one who has properly and fully cast off every search. "Perfect" (*kevalī*) means complete (*paripuṇṇa*).
"Vusitavā" means one who has lived the holy life (*brahmacariya*); he is one who has dwelt in the company of the teachers, on the Noble Path, and in the ten noble dwellings.
"Uttamapurisa" means a distinguished person because his defilements have been exhausted; it means a person of noble breeding.

"Paramapurisa" means the supreme person, or one who has attained the highest attainment; having reached the attainment of Arahantship which is the most excellent thing to be attained, he has become an unsurpassed field of merit.

He is a supreme person (*uttamapurisa*); for that same reason, he is a transcendent person (*paramapurisa*). Because he has attained the acquisition of the deathless by entering the unsurpassed attainment, he is one who has reached the supreme attainment (*paramapattippatta*).
Alternatively, he is a supreme person because, having perceived the danger in the household life, he enters the Dispensation;
he is a transcendent person because, having perceived the danger in personal existence, he enters into insight (*vipassanā*).
Some explain it thus: having recognized the danger in the defilements (kilesa), he has entered the interior of the noble plane (ariyabhūmi) and attained the supreme attainment;
therefore, he "does not accumulate" because, having abandoned both the wholesome and the unwholesome, he does not increase their fruition (vipāka).

He "does not disperse" because, being established in the fruit (phala), he does not destroy it. He is "established after having dispersed" because he stands in the abandonment through subsiding (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna) of the defilements.
He stands having shattered [them]. From here on, the following three phrases should also be applied by way of the path and its fruition (*magga-phala*) alone.
"Does not abandon" means that he does not abandon the defilements because there is nothing left to be abandoned.

"Does not grasp" means that because there is nothing to be grasped by craving, conceit, and views, he does not take hold of them through those. "Stands having abandoned" means he stands having relinquished them. "Does not bind together" means that, by way of craving, he does not...

"He sews together" (*saṃsibbati*). "He does not cast up" (*na ussineti*) means he does not elevate himself through conceit (*māna*). "Standing having unraveled" (*visinitvā ṭhito*) means standing without having performed the sewing of craving (*taṇhā*);
thus some explain it. "Neither fanning out" (*neva vidhūpeti*) means he does not extinguish the fire of the defilements (*kilesaggi*).

"Nor kindling" (*na sandhūpeti*) means he does not cause the fire of the defilements to blaze up. "Standing having fanned out" (*vidhūpetvā ṭhito*) means standing after having extinguished that [fire].

"By means of the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (*asekha*)," means: because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue consisting of speech, action, and livelihood—which is "beyond training" in the sense that there is nothing further to be trained in—he stands firm;
he stands firm by way of not falling away from it. "By means of the aggregate of concentration" means:

by means of concentration associated with effort and mindfulness. "By means of the aggregate of liberation" means: by means of the aggregate associated with the liberation of fruition (*phala-vimutti*). "By means of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation" means...

By means of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). "Having fully realized the truth" means having established and penetrated the Four Noble Truths within one's own continuum according to their intrinsic nature.
"Having transcended agitation" means having transcended the craving that causes trembling.
"The fire of the defilements" refers to the fire of defilements such as lust (*rāga*). "Having consumed" means having exhausted and extinguished it. "By way of non-recurrence" means...
"In the state of not going back into saṃsāra" means by way of not returning again. "Having taken up the task" means having undertaken the pursuit of victory.

"By way of practicing liberation" means by way of practicing the engagement with objects such as forms after being liberated from all defilements; or else, by way of practicing the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which is liberated from all defilements.
"By way of the purity of loving-kindness" means [the purity] freed from secondary defilements (upakkilesa).
He stands in loving-kindness (*mettā*) established in its state of complete purity. The same method applies to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others as well.
"By means of absolute purity" means having reached the limit of purity through a state of purity that has transcended [ordinary] purity.
"By means of non-identification" (*atammayatā*): craving, views, and conceit are called "identifications" (*tammaya*). The absence of these is "non-identification"; by means of that.
He stands by virtue of being free from craving, views, and conceit. For this has been said:
"Such a wise sage, knower of the world, is not attached to any phenomena. Here too, the meaning is that he is free from craving, conceit, and views.

"By way of liberation" means by way of being released from all defilements. "By way of contentment" means by way of contentment with whatever is obtained, whatever strength one possesses, and whatever is appropriate.
He stands by way of being contented.
Regarding "at the end of the aggregates": having consumed the one, four, or five aggregates with the three fires of full understanding (*pariññā*), he stands at the conclusion or the limit;
or, that which has no end is the "limit" (*pariyanta*), and he stands within that limit. This also applies to the phrases "at the end of the elements" and so forth.
The method is the same. However, this is the distinction: "limit of elements" (*dhātupariyanta*) refers to the limit of the eighteen elements;
"limit of bases" (*āyatanapariyanta*) refers to the twelve bases; "limit of destinations" (*gatipariyanta*) refers to the five destinations beginning with hell;

"limit of rebirths" (*upapattipariyanta*) refers to being born in happy or miserable states; and "limit of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhipariyanta*) refers to the realms of sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence.
At rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). At the end of existence (*bhavapariyante*):

at the conclusion of the single-aggregate, four-perception, five-perception, non-percipient, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, sensual, fine-material, and immaterial existences. At the end of the cycle of wandering (*saṃsārapariyante*): at the cessation of the uninterrupted occurrence of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

At the end of the round (*vaṭṭapariyante*): at the conclusion of the rounds of karma, its result, and the defilements. In the final existence (*antime bhave*): in the last birth-existence. In the final...
"Standing upon the heap" means standing upon the heap at the end, that is, upon the body. "Bearing the final body" means he bears the final, ultimate body; thus, he is one who bears the final body.

"Arahant" [is so called] because he is far from (*ārakattā*) enemies (*arīnaṃ*), because his spokes (*arānaṃ*) have been destroyed, because he is worthy (*arahattā*) of requisites and so forth, and because there is no opportunity (*rahābhāvā*) for him to do evil; thus, he is an Arahant.
“This is his last body”: for that one whose taints are exhausted, this physical aggregate—the personal existence—is the finality.
“The last”: like the final morsel of food, it is small and meager; it is like the very last mouthful. Referring to the absence of further rebirth-linking, he said:
“There is no wandering in birth and death; for him there is no more becoming. Birth is the act of being born; they die by means of it.
For that one whose taints are exhausted, there is no more death, nor the uninterrupted wandering in saṃsāra of the aggregates and so forth;
thus, concluding the verse, the Blessed One said:
“Therefore, a person... having climbed onto the boat, has reached the further shore.”
In this sutta, whatever has not been stated here and there should be understood by following the sequence of the text.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Kāma Sutta from the Saddhammappajjotikā,
the commentary on the Mahāniddesa, is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta 7.

Regarding the second [verse]: "A being" (*satta*) refers to one who is attached. "In the cave" (*guhāyaṃ*) means in the body. For the body is called a "cave" because it is the dwelling place for the wild beasts of passion and the other defilements.
"Covered by much" (*bahunābhichanno*) means covered by the many kinds of defilements such as passion. By this—
The internal bond has been described. He stands by way of passion (*rāga*) and the other [defilements]. "Plunged into delusion" (*mohana*):
here, "delusion" refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), for gods and humans are deluded therein, having plunged deep into them;
by this, the external bond is described. For such a person is far from seclusion; such a man is thus in three ways...
The seclusions of body and so forth are distant, not near. For what reason? Because sensual desires in the world are not easily abandoned;
this is what is meant by the statement that they are not easily abandoned in the world.
"A being" (satta) is indeed spoken of—meaning it is described in such ways as "a being," "a man," or "a youth. The cave (guhā).
“First it should be described” means that the cave should first be explained. Regarding the phrases “or as ‘the body’” and so forth, this is the construction of the words:

“or as ‘the body,’ or as ‘the cave’... pe ... or as ‘the jar. Therein, “the body” has already been explained below in the discussion on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) as “the body (*kāya*) because it is the coming (*āya*) of things that are vile (*kucchita*).
It is a “cave” (*guhā*) in the sense of being a dwelling place for the wild beasts of lust and so forth; it is also [a cave] in the sense of concealment.
Some [say it is] like in such passages as: “Far-reaching, wandering alone, bodiless, dwelling in a cave. In the sense of being consumed by passion and so forth, it is the *deha* (body), as in:
“Having abandoned that human *deha*,” and so on. In the sense of causing negligence, it is the *sandeha* (doubt/body), as in:
“The putrid *sandeha* breaks apart; for life ends in death,” and so on. In the sense of wandering through *saṃsāra*, it is the *nāvā* (boat), as in: “Empty it... [etc.]
As in such passages as, "Monk, this boat, when launched by you, will go swiftly";
where the *ratha* (chariot) is used in the sense of the presence of the postures, as in, "The chariot is the equipment of virtue, with jhāna for its axle and energy for its wheels";
and where it is used in the sense of being loftily raised, as in, "The banner is the sign of the chariot."

The term "ant-hill" (*vammika*) refers to its being the dwelling place of mongooses (*kimikulānaṃ*). As it is said in such passages as, "Bhikkhu, 'ant-hill' is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements," and so forth.

Just as an external ant-hill is called an "ant-hill" for four reasons—namely, that it "vomits" (*vamati*), it is "vomited upon" (*vantaka*), it is a "nest of what has been vomited" (*vantussaya*), and it is "bound together by the moisture of what has been vomited" (*vantasinehasambaddha*)—so too, this [body] is inhabited by snakes, mongooses, rats, house-lizards, and the like.
It is called a *vammika* (anthill) because it vomits forth various kinds of creatures; it is called an anthill because it is vomited up by termites.
It is called an anthill because it is heaped up—by the dust and powder tossed up by the snouts of the termites after they have vomited it out—to the height of a hip or even to the height of a man.
Because it is bound together by the moisture of the saliva vomited by the termites, it does not crumble even when it rains for seven days and seven nights.
Even in the heat of summer, if one takes a handful of dust from there and squeezes it with the fist, moisture comes forth;
thus, because it is bound together by vomited moisture, it is called a "termite mound" (*vammika*).

Likewise, this body is also a "termite mound" because it vomits various kinds of impure filth in the manner described by the passage beginning, "From the eye, a fire-dung [excrement]," and so forth. The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed...
Because they have abandoned this personal existence and departed by means of the exhaustion of attachment to it, the anthill is called "vomited-up" (*vantaka*) by the Noble Ones.
Furthermore, because all that by which this [body]— propped up by three hundred bones, bound together with sinews, smeared with flesh, covered with moist skin, and colored by the outer integument—
deceives sentient beings has been vomited up by the Noble Ones, the anthill is also called "a resting place for what has been vomited" (*vantassaya*).

“Craving gives birth to a person; his mind runs hither and thither. Because it is produced by craving in this way, and because it moves while bound by the moisture of craving—which has been vomited out by the Noble Ones—it is called a “vomit-moisture-bound anthill” (*vanta-sineha-sambaddho*).
And just as within an anthill various kinds of creatures are born right there, void excrement and urine are deposited, and the sick lie down, so too is this [body].
The dead fall down. Thus, for them, it becomes a maternity home, a latrine, a sickroom, and a charnel ground.
In the same way, regarding the body of a wealthy noble or others, one should not think, "This body was protected by a father and mother;

this is a decorated and adorned body of great power," but rather consider the creatures dwelling in the skin, the creatures dwelling in the hide, the creatures dwelling in the flesh, and the creatures dwelling in the sinews.
There are creatures dwelling in the bones, creatures dwelling in the bone-marrow, and creatures [dwelling in other parts of the body].

Thus, by way of counting their species, about eighty thousand families of worms are born right within the internal body; they discharge excrement and urine, they lie down afflicted by disease, and they fall down dead or dying.
Thus, this [body] serves as a maternity home, a latrine, a sickroom, and a charnel ground for those creatures.
“Vammiko” (anthill) is a conventional designation.
It is a city in the sense of being a place where the agreeable and disagreeable fall, as in expressions such as “the city of *sakkāya*.

It is a nest in the sense of being a dwelling-place for diseases and so forth, and in the sense of being a hollow, as in expressions such as “the fragile nest of disease. It is a dwelling-house in the sense of being the abode of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
“Hut” (*kuṭi*) is used, as in such passages as: “Having approached this hut with five doors. “A boil” (*gaṇḍa*) is used in the sense of putrefaction, as in such passages as:
“‘A disease,’ monks, ‘a boil,’ monks, ‘an arrow,’ monks—this is a designation for this body. “A jar” (*kumbha*) is used in the sense of being subject to breaking, as in such passages as:
“Having understood this body to be like a jar. “This is a designation for the body”: this [is what is meant].
This is a designation for the influx of base phenomena composed of the four great elements as previously described;

the meaning is "how [does it come about]? "In the cave" means within the body. "Attached" (satta) means clinging. "Entangled" (visatta) means clinging in various ways by way of passion for beauty and so forth.
"Adhered" (āsatta) means stuck by way of passion for shape. "Clung" (lagga) means stuck by way of perceiving that very place as beautiful and pleasant.
"Attached" means stuck by way of grasping at a self. "Obstructed" means remaining without releasing due to attachment to contact.
"On a wall-nail" means on a peg driven into a wall. "On a peg" means likewise on a curved rod resembling an elephant's tusk.
"Attached" refers to that which is stuck on a wall-nail. "Clinging" refers to that which is stuck on a peg. "Adhering" refers to that which is stuck on a robe-stand. "Stuck" [is the general term].
"Attached by a robe-string": "attached" means attached to the feet of a bench. "Obstructed" means attached to the feet of a bed;
in this manner, it should be applied according to the same principle.
"A designation for attachment" is a specific term for clinging. "Shrouded" means covered by the defilements of the kind already mentioned.
"Covered over again and again" (*ucchanna*) means covered higher and higher by way of repeated arising. "Shrouded" (*āvuta*) means enclosed. "Concealed" (*nivuta*) means obstructed.
"Overwhelmed" (*ophuta*) means covered after having been spread over. "Closed off" (*pihita*) means wrapped around like the mouth of a cooking pot with a lid.
"Hidden" (*paṭicchanna*) means veiled. "Inverted" (*paṭikujjita*) means placed face down. In that context, it refers to what is covered with grass, leaves, and so forth.
"Covered" (channa) is like being concealed. "Over-covered" (ucchanna) is like a dam blocking a river. "Obstructed" (āvuta) is like a barrier blocking a path for the movement of people.

"Bound by the army of conceit" (vinibaddho mānavasena) means that having become bound to various objects of perception through various kinds of conceit and over-conceit (mānātimāna), it remains there.
"Grasped by way of views" (parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhivasena) means grasped—that is, touched—by way of the sixty-two types of views.
"Seized": having reached or arrived at distraction by way of restlessness, that is, by way of not remaining steady upon the object.
"Not having reached a conclusion": by way of doubt, that is, by way of doubt characterized as uncertainty regarding the Triple Gem and so forth;
it has not attained certainty. "Firmly rooted": by way of underlying tendencies, that is, by way of underlying tendencies that are difficult to remove and have not been abandoned.
Having reached and attained a state of stability, it remains.
"They approach form" means having approached form by way of craving and views, they take it as an object.
"Consciousness remains while remaining" means that consciousness, with form as its object, remains while remaining upon that object. [It has] form as its object.
"Established in form": having taken form itself as the object and having made form itself the foundation. "Smeared with delight":
consciousness that has been sprinkled with the water of craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*). "Growth": the state of increasing. "Increase":
the state of further growth by way of impulsion (*javana*). "Expansion": expansion by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*).
"There is lust," and so forth, are synonyms for greed (*lobha*). For it is called "lust" (*rāga*) by way of coloring; "delight" (*nandī*) by way of rejoicing;

and "craving" (*taṇhā*) by way of thirsting. "Consciousness has become established and grown there" means that, having impelled karma, it is both "established" and "grown" by virtue of its capacity to draw in rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Wherein" refers to the round of existence consisting of the three planes.
The locative case (*bhummam*). Or rather, in all instances, this is the locative of the preceding word.

"Therein there is an increase of formations" (*saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhi*)—this was said with reference to the formations that are the causes for the future cycle of existence for one who stands within this wheel of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*).
"Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future" (*yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti*) means: in whatever place there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
In this regard, it should be understood that the first sutta was spoken by way of clinging to objects such as form; the second sutta was spoken by way of delighting in those same objects;
the third was spoken by way of the stationing of consciousness; and the fourth was spoken by way of the fourfold nutriment and the stationing of wholesome and unwholesome consciousness.
"Mostly" means for the most part. "They are deluded" means they fall into delusion. "They are thoroughly deluded" means they are especially deluded.

"They are completely deluded" means they are deluded in every way. Alternatively, they are deluded depending on the object of visible form; they are thoroughly deluded depending on the object of sound;
they are completely deluded depending on the object of smell. "Blinded by ignorance" refers to [the eight]...

They are blinded by ignorance (*avijjā*) due to lack of knowledge regarding these points. Alternatively, the reading is "gone" (*gatā*); the meaning is that they have entered into a state of blindness.

"Plunged" (*pagāḷho*) means entered. "Submerged" (*ogāḷho*) means entered into the lower part. "Deeply submerged" (*ajjhogāḷho*) means having gone down into it, having spread across it, having especially entered, or being drowned;
that is, having entered with the face downward. Or else, through contact with vision...
*Ogāḷho*: plunged deep by association with listening; submerged by association with speech; or plunged because deprived of association with true persons (*sappurisa*);
plunged deep because deprived of devotion to the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*); or submerged because deprived of practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*).
*Viveka*: seclusion (*vivitti*) or the act of being secluded (*viviccana*). *Tayo*: a delimitation by way of number. *Kāyaviveka*: seclusion by means of the body.
Seclusion (*viveka*) means departing and withdrawing. This same principle applies to mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*) and the others as well. "Here, a bhikkhu" means in this teaching.
He is called a *bhikkhu* because he looks upon (*ikkhati*) the danger (*bhaya*) in *saṃsāra*. "Secluded" (*vivitta*) means empty; the meaning is that it is quiet and free from noise.
It is with reference to this very point that the *Vibhaṅga* states: "'Secluded' means even if the lodging is near, it is not crowded."
It is said: "Because it is secluded from householders and those who have gone forth. It is called a *senāsana* because one lies down (*seti*) and sits (*āsati*) there;
this is a designation for beds, chairs, and so forth. Thus he said: "A *senāsana* is a bed, a chair... a mattress... a pillow... a monastery cell... a gabled house..."
"A palace... a watchtower... a multi-storied building... a cave... a grotto... the foot of a tree... a bamboo thicket...
or wherever else monks retire—that is all 'lodging' (senāsana).
Furthermore, a vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, and a guhā—this is called "vihāra-lodging. A bed, a chair...
“Cushion and pillow”—this is called bedding for beds and chairs. “Canvas, a piece of hide, a grass mat, and a leaf mat”—this is called bedding for mats.
Or else, “wherever monks withdraw”—this is called bedding for open spaces.
Thus there are four kinds of bedding; all of them are indeed included by the term “bedding.”
Now, showing the suitable lodging for this bird-like bhikkhu who wanders in the four directions, he said:

"The forest, the foot of a tree," and so forth. Therein, regarding "the forest" (*arañña*), the definition "having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is the forest" is given according to the rule for bhikkhunīs.
"A forest-dwelling lodging (*āraññakaṃ senāsanaṃ*) is [a place] five hundred bow-lengths (*dhanusatika*)... [and so on].
"Last" (pacchima) refers here to what is appropriate for this bhikkhu. Its characteristics are described in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
"At the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*) means any secluded spot at the base of a tree that provides cool shade. "A mountain" (*pabbata*) means a rocky peak;
for there, having performed one's water-related duties by the mountain springs, one sits in the cool shade of the trees while [the sounds of] various directions...
While being eaten [by insects], his mind becomes one-pointed as he is fanned by a cool breeze.
A *kandara* is so called because it is "torn" (*kaṃ*)—that is, split—by water; it is a mountain region broken open by water. It is what people call a "river-pool" or a "river-glen.
For there, the sand is like silver plates, and at its head is a dense forest thicket like a canopy of jewels.

Water flows like a mass of jewels. Having descended into such a cave, having drunk the water, having cooled his limbs, having strewn sand and spread out his rag-robe (*paṃsukūlacīvara*), the mind of one who sits and practices the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) becomes one-pointed.
A "mountain cave" (*giriguhā*) is the space between two mountains, or even within a single mountain.
A great hollow resembling a mountain cleft. The characteristics of a charnel ground (*susāna*) are described in the *Visuddhimagga*.
A forest retreat (*vanapattha*) is a place beyond the village boundary where people do not frequent, where they neither plow nor sow.
For this very reason it is said: "‘Forest retreat’ is a designation for remote lodgings," and so forth. An open space (*abbhokāsa*).
It is uncovered. However, if one so desires, one may build a robe-tent there and dwell. "A heap of straw" means a pile of straw.
For they take straw out from a large heap of straw and construct a dwelling resembling a mountain cave or a rock shelter;
or, having thrown straw over bushes, thickets, and the like, they practice the duties of a recluse while sitting underneath. All this is with reference to these [practices].
It is said: “He dwells secluded by body,” and so forth. “One undertakes the walking meditation” means one sets it in motion.
“He moves about” means he maintains the postures. “He conducts himself” means he brings about the functioning of the postures.
“He preserves” means he guards the postures. “He sustains” means he supports [the body]. “He maintains” means he keeps [the body] going.

“Of one who has attained the first jhāna” means: of one possessing a wholesome jhāna. Although the mind is secluded from the hindrances even by way of access concentration (upacāra), it is said, “of one who has attained the first jhāna the mind is secluded from the hindrances,” in order to show that within the state of absorption (appanā) it is thoroughly secluded.

The same method applies to those who have attained the second, third, and fourth jhānas through applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and pain (*dukkha*).
"Of the perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) means the perception of the fifteen fine-material-sphere jhānas by way of the wholesome, resultant, and functional [consciousness].

"Of the perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*) means the perception comprised of the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, which arises through the impact of the eye and visible forms, etc., by way of the wholesome and unwholesome resultants.

And from the perception of resistance. "From the perception of diversity" means that the mind becomes secluded and empty of the forty-four types of sense-sphere perceptions that occur with respect to diverse objects.
"Of one who has attained the base of infinite space": here, that which has no end is "infinite" (ananta); infinite space is "space-infinity" (ākāsānanta).

"Space-infinity" (ākāsānañca) is simply infinite space; that infinity of space is the "base" (āyatana) in the sense of being a foundation for the associated states of this jhāna, just as the "divine base" is for the gods—thus it is the "base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana).
This is a designation for the jhāna that has as its object the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa. That base of infinite space belongs to one who has attained the wholesome functional jhāna.
"Perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhāna by way of its generic term "perception," and to its object.

For the fine-material-sphere jhāna itself is called "form" in such passages as "possessing form, he sees forms," and its object is also called "form" in such passages as "he sees external forms, beautiful and ugly.
Therefore, here "perception of form" means perception regarding form; thus it is stated by way of the generic term "perception."
This is a designation for fine-material-sphere jhāna. "Having perception of form" means *rūpasaññaṃ*; what is meant is that "form is its name.
Thus, it should be understood that this is also a designation for that which has the earth-kasiṇa and so forth as its object.
By means of this fifteenfold perception of form—comprised of jhāna according to the wholesome, resultant, and functional modes. By means of this...
And [it is the cessation] of the eightfold perception of form (*rūpasaññā*), which consists of objects such as the earth-kasina and so forth. Regarding "perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*):
perception that arises through the impact (*paṭighāta*) of the bases, such as the eye, and their objects, such as visible forms, is "perception of resistance";
this is a designation for the perceptions of form and so on. As it is said: "In this context, what is perception of resistance?"
“Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, and perception of tangibles—these are called perceptions of resistance (paṭighasaññā).
These consist of five that are wholesome-resultants and five that are unwholesome-resultants; it is by means of this perception of resistance.
“By means of perception of diversity (nānattasaññā)” means by means of perception occurring with respect to a diverse object, or by means of diverse perception. As it has been said:

—“In this context, what is diversity-perception (*nānattasaññā*)? The perception, perceiving, and state of having perceived of one who has not attained meditative absorption and who possesses either the mind-element (*manodhātu*) or the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—these are called diversity-perceptions. Having thus analyzed it in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated there.
Those [perceptions] are intended here. They are the perceptions comprised within the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element of one who has not attained absorption.
They proceed with respect to a manifold range that is diverse in form, sound, and so forth, and possesses various intrinsic natures. And because these forty-four perceptions— namely,
the eight wholesome perceptions of the sense-sphere, the twelve unwholesome perceptions, the eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense-sphere,
the two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and the eleven functional perceptions of the sense-sphere— are thus manifold and of various intrinsic natures, they are mutually distinct.
Because they are incomparable, they are called "perceptions of diversity. By means of that perception of diversity, the mind becomes secluded;

that is, for one who has attained the base of infinite space, the meditative consciousness becomes secluded from, separated from, and withdrawn from the perceptions known as perception of form, perception of resistance, and perception of diversity. This is the base of infinite consciousness.
This very consciousness has that [space] as its base in the sense of a foundation, thus it is the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*);

this is a designation for the jhāna whose object is the consciousness occurring in space. For one who has attained that jhāna, the mind becomes secluded from the perception of the base of infinite space of the aforementioned type.
Regarding the term *ākiñcaññāyatana*: here, "nothing" (*akiñcana*) means that there is nothing whatsoever belonging to it;
what is meant is that not even so much as a mere fragment remains. The state of being nothing is *ākiñcañña*;

this is a designation for the departure from the consciousness of the base of infinite space. That base of nothingness (*ākiñcañña*) is its "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of a foundation; thus it is the *ākiñcaññāyatana*. [In the case of] space...

This is a designation for the jhāna that has as its object the departure from the consciousness that was occurring. For one who has attained that base of nothingness, the mind is secluded from that perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
As for the term "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," it is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" because of the presence of that perception therein.
It is said: in order to show how that perception arises for one who has practiced accordingly, the *Vibhaṅga* first cites the term "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" and then explains it thus:
"He attends to the base of nothingness as peace; he develops the attainment with a residue of formations.
Therefore, he is called 'neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient'. In this context, "he attends to it as peace" means:
“This attainment is indeed peaceful, in that one dwells having made even non-existence the object.

Thus, by way of its peaceful object, he attends to it as “peaceful. For one who has entered and is seated in that base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the meditative consciousness becomes empty of that perception of the base of nothingness.

“Of one who has entered the stream” means of one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). “Of personality-view” (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) means of the personality-view consisting of twenty bases.

“Of doubt” (*vicikicchā*) means of uncertainty regarding eight points. “Of the misapprehension of rules and observances” (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) means the view that arises from misapprehending that “purification comes through rules” and “purification comes through observances.
“Of the underlying tendency to views” (*diṭṭhānusaya*) means that which lies latent within the continuum in the sense of being unabandoned.
The underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*). Likewise, the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*). And by those "associated with them" (*tadekaṭṭhehi*):
that is, by those factors such as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) which stand together with them. They "torment" and "afflict," thus they are called defilements (*kilesa*).

By those defilements, such as the view of a self-identity, the mind becomes secluded and empty. Here, "associated with them" (*tadekaṭṭha*) is twofold: association through abandonment (*pahānekaṭṭha*) and association through co-arising (*sahajekaṭṭha*).
For as long as the defilements leading to the states of misery have not been abandoned by means of the stream-entry path, they remain together with wrong view and doubt within a single individual;
thus, they are "to be abandoned together. Of the ten defilements, only wrong view and doubt are mentioned here.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the underlying tendency of wrong view and the underlying tendency of doubt are mentioned. As for the remaining [defilements], they lead to the states of misery...
The eight defilements— greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness— being abandoned together with wrong view and doubt,
are abandoned by the path of stream-entry along with the two underlying tendencies.

Alternatively, among the one thousand five hundred defilements headed by greed, hatred, and delusion, when wrong view is being abandoned by the path of stream-entry, they are abandoned together with that wrong view.
Doubt is abandoned; along with it, all defilements leading to states of misery—which are associated with the underlying tendencies of views and doubt—are abandoned by way of being abandoned together.
However, the remaining defilements that coexist with each individual consciousness, along with views and doubt, are abandoned by way of being abandoned simultaneously.
By the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), five types of consciousness are abandoned: the four associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) and that associated with doubt (*vicikicchā*).

Therein, when the two types of non-volitional (*asaṅkhārika*) consciousness associated with wrong view are being abandoned, the defilements—namely greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*)—are abandoned by way of their being conascent and bound up with them.

When the two types of view-associating spontaneous consciousnesses (*diṭṭhisampayutta-sasaṅkhārika-citta*) are abandoned, the defilements— namely greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), sloth (*thina*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*),

and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*)— which arise simultaneously with them, are abandoned by way of being co-existent and co-operative. When the doubt-accompanied consciousness (*vicikicchāsahagata-citta*) is abandoned,
the defilements— namely delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing— which arise simultaneously with it, [are abandoned] by way of being co-existent and co-operative.
They are abandoned. Because the mind is secluded from those defilements—which are grouped together as two types—the path-consciousness is secluded;
the meaning is that the fruition-consciousness becomes secluded, detached, withdrawn, and empty.
For the once-returner, the "gross fetters of sensual lust" refers to those which have become gross by acting as conditions for transgression through the door of the body.
The fetters (*saññojana*) consist of lust for sexual intercourse, which is termed "thick" (*thūla*). For it fetters one within the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), thus it is called a "fetter.
The "fetter of repulsion" (*paṭighasaññojana*) is the fetter of ill-will (*byāpādasaññojana*). For it strikes against the object (*ārammaṇa*), thus it is called "repulsion" (*paṭigha*).

These very same [fetters], because they persist in the continuum (*santāna*) in the sense of having become firmly established, are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*). "Accompanied by atoms" (*aṇusahagata*) means having become subtle.
The fetters of sensual lust and aversion, and the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion that remain as subtle residues—
these are the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion that have become subtle by way of lying latent within the continuum in the sense of being unabandoned.
By means of the two kinds of defilements mentioned as "associated with those" (*tadekaṭṭha*), the mind is secluded and empty.

"Arahant" refers to one who has obtained the name "Arahant" because the enemies that are the defilements (kilesa) have been slain. "Attachment to form" (rūparāga) means desire and lust for the form realm (rūpabhava). "Attachment to the formless" (arūparāga) means desire and lust for the formless realm (arūpabhava).

"Pride" (māna) refers specifically to those types of pride to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Likewise, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendencies of pride, and so forth, are to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship.
Among these, pride has the characteristic of loftiness (unnati). Restlessness has the characteristic of lack of tranquility (avūpasama). Ignorance has the characteristic of blindness (andhabhāva).
Ignorance (*avijjā*). The underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), which occurs by way of lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms.
And "together with those associated therewith" means together with the defilements that stand in association with them.

And "with all external signs" means with all signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāranimitta*) that occur externally, having released the internal [mind] and being reckoned as "external" in relation to the unwholesome aggregates within one's own internal mental continuum.
The path-consciousness is secluded, becomes separate, and withdraws; the fruition-consciousness is secluded, dissociated, and withdrawn.
In this regard, the absence of underlying tendencies (anusaya) should be understood in two ways: by way of the sequence of defilements and by way of the sequence of the paths.

For, by way of the sequence of defilements, the absence of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion occurs with the third path, while that of the underlying tendency to conceit [occurs with the fourth].

By the fourth path, the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) are abandoned; by the first path, the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) are abandoned;
and by the fourth path alone, [the remaining tendencies are abandoned]. Furthermore, according to the sequence of the paths:

by the first path, there is the non-existence of the underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt; by the second path, there is the attenuation (*tanubhāva*) of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*); and by the third path...

Complete non-existence: through the fourth path, there is the non-existence of the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), and the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*).
“Seclusion of mind” (*cittaviveka*) means the state of being empty of defilements in the case of exalted and supramundane minds; the meaning is its state of being void.

“Seclusion from acquisitions” (*upadhiviveka*) means the state of being empty of acquisitions (*upadhi*), which consist of defilements, aggregates, and volitional formations. [Regarding] acquisition...

To show this, he said: "The 'substrata' (upadhi) are called both the defilements (kilesā) and... and so forth. They are called "defilements" because they afflict and obstruct that in which they arise, such as lust and the rest.

They are also the five aggregates, beginning with form, which are the objective sphere of clinging (upādāna). And they are the volitional formations (saṅkhāra) of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable, which are produced by clinging.
It is "deathless" (amata) because there is no death—meaning the state of dying—in it; thus it is the deathless.
Because it is the antidote to the poison of the defilements (*kilesa*), it is also called the "antidote" (*agada*) and the "deathless" (*amata*).

It is called "craving" (*taṇhā*) because it binds and weaves together within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the womb-origins (*yoni*), the destinies (*gati*), the bases of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*); since that [craving] is absent therein, it is *nibbāna*.

"Of those whose bodies are secluded" (*vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ*) means of those whose persons are removed from the company of crowds. "Delighting in renunciation" (*nekkhammābhiratānaṃ*) means [delighting] in renunciation, which has emerged from sensual desires and so forth.
"For those who delight in and are inclined toward the first jhāna and so forth. "Having attained the fruit of supreme purity" means having reached and remained in the state of ultimate purification.
"For those whose minds are purified by the absence of defilements, and who have attained supreme purity through being liberated from the defilements;
for those whose minds are purified by the abandoning [of defilements] through suppression, and [purified] by the abandoning [of them] through eradication..."
"Of those who have attained supreme exertion"—thus some explain. "Free from substrate" (*nirūpadhi*) means those from whom the substrate has departed.
"Gone to the unconditioned" (*visaṅkhāragata*) means those who, having abandoned conditioned phenomena as objects, have approached Nibbāna—which is free from conditioning—as their object.
For here too, in the phrase "the mind gone to the unconditioned," it is Nibbāna alone that is called "the unconditioned."
*Vidūreti* means variously distant. *Suvidūreti* means very far away. *Na santiketi* means not near.
*Na sāmantāti* means not on one side. *Anāsanneti* means not in immediate proximity. *Vivekaṭṭheti* means extremely distant; the meaning is "separated. *Tādisoti* means similar to that.
*Tassaṇṭhitoti* means standing in that manner. *Tappakāroti* means standing in that way. *Tappaṭibhāgoti* [means having a resemblance to that].
It is like a storehouse. Or alternatively, some explain it thus: "It is like that because of its clinging to the cave of the personal existence (*attabhāva*);

it is established as such because of being covered by defilements; it is of that nature because of being submerged in delusion; and it resembles that because of being far removed from the three kinds of seclusion.
"Difficult to abandon" means they are not easily abandoned. "Difficult to give up" means they cannot be relinquished with ease. "Difficult to renounce" means...
They cannot be abandoned in every way. "Difficult to subdue" means they cannot be made free from intoxication or pride.
"Difficult to disentangle" means it is impossible to effect their release or liberation. "Difficult to cross" means they cannot be crossed over and transcended.
"Difficult to traverse" means they cannot be traversed with distinction. "Difficult to transcend" means they must be passed beyond with great difficulty. "Difficult to turn back."
Or alternatively, some explain it thus: "It is difficult to turn back from suffering. Or rather, by its very nature, it is difficult to relinquish;

like a bull's tether, it is difficult to subdue; like an elephant's tether, it is difficult to untie; like a desert wilderness in the summer season, it is difficult to cross and difficult to traverse;
like a forest infested by tigers, it is difficult to pass beyond; and like the waves of the ocean, it is difficult to turn back. Thus they describe it.

8. Having thus established in the first verse that “such a person is indeed far from seclusion,” he spoke the verse beginning with “The source of desire” (*icchānidānā*) to reveal the natural law (*dhammatā*) of such beings.
Therein, “the source of desire” means having craving as their cause.
“Bound by attachment to existence” (*bhavasātabaddhā*) means bound by the attachment to existence found in pleasant feelings and so forth. “They are difficult to release.”
These phenomena are the basis for the flood of existence (*bhava*). Or rather, beings who are bound to them by the root of craving are difficult to liberate.
"Not by another's liberation" means that others are not able to liberate them; or this is a statement of reason: those beings are difficult to release. Why?
Because they cannot be liberated by another. If beings were to be liberated, they would be liberated by their own power.
This is its meaning: "Looking back or forward" means looking with longing toward sensual pleasures (*kāma*) of the future or the past.
"They crave these very pleasures or those former ones" means they yearn with powerful craving for both types—whether the present sensual pleasures or the former ones of the past and future.
And regarding these two phrases, [it is said]: "They are hard to release, for there is no other liberation."

The connection [of this verse] should be understood with this very [preceding one]. Otherwise, if they were considered independently, it would not be known what the "mutterings" (jappa) do or what they have done.
"Bound by attachment to existence" (bhavasātabaddhā):
attachment to existence is *bhavasāta*; being bound by that attachment to existence—that is, by the relish of pleasure—[they are so called].
[The text] stands [thus]. To demonstrate that by dividing it, he said: "One is the delight in existence—pleasant feeling," and so forth.
Youthfulness is *yobbañña*. Healthiness is *ārogya*. The state of the life-faculty's occurrence is *jīvita*.
"Gain" (*lābha*) is the acquisition of the four requisites. "Fame" (*yasa*) is a retinue. "Praise" (*pasaṃsā*) is reputation. "Happiness" (*sukha*) is bodily and mental happiness.
“Pleasant forms” means forms that increase delight. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
“Eye-perfection” means the perfection of the eye. It is called “eye-perfection” with reference to the relish of pleasure that arises when one thinks, “My eye is perfect;
it appears like an open lion-window in a jeweled palace. The same applies to ear-perfection and the others.
The same method applies here. "Bound to pleasant feeling" (*sukhāya vedanāya sātabaddhā*)... [etc. ... "bound in various ways" (*vibaddhā*) means bound in manifold modes.

"Tightly bound" (*ābaddhā*) means especially bound from the very beginning. "Attached" (*laggā*) means stuck fast to the object. "Adhering" (*laggitā*) means adhering like a vessel of molasses on a peg.
And whatever is not mentioned here should be understood according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "a being, clinging" (*satto visatto*).

"Na hi aññamokkhā" means not liberated by others. Or, "they are difficult to release from the basis of the flood of existence" means that those phenomena which have become the basis for the relish of pleasure in existence are difficult to abandon.
Or, "beings are difficult to release from this" means that beings themselves are difficult to liberate from this basis of the flood of existence.
"Duruddharā" means difficult to pull out. "Dussamuddharā" refers to one who has fallen into the pit of hell with its banks cut away on all sides.
They are difficult to lift up, as if one were trying to pull something out after having turned it upward. They are difficult to rouse; they are difficult to cause to stand up.
They are exceedingly difficult to raise up, like attempting to establish a subtle form upon the earth.
Being themselves stuck fast and mired in the mud, submerged in deep mire up to their very heads, they are unable to help another.
"Unable to pull out one who has sunk deep into the mud": they were unable to grasp him by the hand or the head while he was submerged in that very way, pull him out, and establish him on dry land.

"That person indeed, Cunda"—this is a designation of a person using the form "he. Having brought forward the demonstrative term "who" for that [person], it means: "O Cunda, that person who himself has sunk deep into the mud..."
"Thinking, 'I shall pull out another who is stuck fast in the mud. In this way, the connection should be understood for the remaining phrases.
"Stuck fast in the mud" (*palipapalipanno*) refers to one who is submerged in deep mire.

Just as if, Cunda, some man were submerged in deep mire up to his head, and [thinking] he would pull out another who was likewise submerged by grasping them by the hand or the head—this is not possible.
It is possible that there is no cause by which he, having lifted him up, might establish him on dry land. Furthermore, regarding the terms "undisciplined," "untrained," and "not fully extinguished":
here, one should understand that he is "undisciplined" (*adanta*) due to a lack of practice; "untrained" (*avinīta*) due to a lack of training in discipline (*vinaya*);
and "not fully extinguished" (*aparinibbuta*) due to the non-extinction of the defilements (*kilesa*). Being such as this, how could he tame another, making them free from defilement?
He will act; he will discipline; he will train [others] in the three trainings. He will cause [them] to attain parinibbāna; he will extinguish their defilements.
"There is no other" means there is no other person capable of liberating [them]. "By his own power" means by the power of his own knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
"By strength" means by the strength of knowledge. "By energy" means by the mental energy associated with knowledge. "By human exertion" means...
By means of great energy, through ascending to higher and higher states.

"I will not endure" means "I will not endure, I am unable," or "I will not exert myself. "For the sake of liberation" means for the purpose of liberating. "With doubt" means with uncertainty. "Dhotaka" is a form of address. "You would cross" means you might cross.
"Indeed, by oneself is evil done; by oneself is one defiled..."
“By oneself alone is evil done; by oneself is one purified.
Purity and impurity belong to oneself; no one can purify another.”—In this context, the meaning is as follows:
he by whom unwholesome karma has been performed will experience suffering in the four states of misery.
Experiencing [the results] by oneself, one is defiled by oneself.
But he who has not committed evil himself, while going to both a good destination and a bad destination, is purified by himself.

Purity, which consists in wholesome action, and impurity, which consists in unwholesome action, ripen within the very self of the individual beings who perform them; one person does not [purify or defile] another person.
It is said that it does not purify, nor does it cause purification; it does not defile.
"Nibbāna remains" means that the great Nibbāna of the Deathless remains. "The path leading to Nibbāna" refers to the Noble Path beginning from preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā).
"I remain as one who encourages" means that I remain as one who causes others to take up [the practice] and establishes them in it.
"Being thus exhorted and thus instructed" means being exhorted and instructed by me in this way.
Here, one is said to "exhort" when speaking regarding a matter that has already arisen;
one is said to "instruct" when, regarding a matter not yet arisen, one points out the future by saying, "This too will happen to you," and so forth. One also exhorts when speaking in one's presence.
"Admonishes" means instructing either in person or by sending a messenger with a message when one is absent. "Counsels" means speaking once;
"instructs" means speaking repeatedly. Or, "instructs" may mean simply admonishing.

"Some" (*appekacce*) means "even some" (*api ekacce*), which signifies "certain ones. "Attaining the ultimate goal, Nibbāna" refers to reaching the end characterized by the destruction and passing away [of defilements].

"Past" (*atīta*) means "absolute" (*accanta*); and because it is the place where all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) absolutely cease to function, it is "the absolute goal" (*accanta-niṭṭha*), meaning the "exclusive goal" (*ekanta-niṭṭha*) or the "constant goal" (*satata-niṭṭha*). They "achieve" (*ārādhenti*) that absolute nibbāna;
they "do not achieve" (*nārādhenti*) it means they do not accomplish it, they do not obtain it—this is the meaning. Herein, *kyāhaṃ* means "among these."

"What am I? What shall I do? is the meaning. "One who proclaims the path" means one who proclaims the path of practice (*paṭipadā-magga*). "He explains" means he tells. "May they be liberated by practicing themselves" means: "by practicing, may we be liberated.
"With reference to the past" means depending upon the past. "How does he look back to what was before? means in what manner does he look?
He performs an observation. "He was of such a form" means: by way of being long, short, slender, stout, and so forth, he was of such a kind and of such a form.
In that regard, "he brings about delight" means: he correctly brings and leads craving toward that objective support of form.
This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
He spoke thus, beginning with “‘This is my eye,’” in order to show the arising of craving by way of the basis and the object.
“Thus [regarding] forms” means “thus [regarding] these forms.

In that context, “bound by desire and lust” means bound to and clinging to those eyes and forms by means of desire—which is termed weak—and lust—which is termed strong. “Consciousness” refers to the impulsion-consciousness (*javana-citta*).
"Because consciousness is bound by desire and lust" means that the impulsive consciousness (javana-viññāṇa) is bound by the state of being fettered through desire and lust.
"He delights in that" means he delights in that object by way of craving (taṇhā).
"Those which are his" means those which belong to him. "In the past" means in the past time. "Together with" means simultaneously. "Smiling, talking, and playing" means...
These include smiles with bared teeth and the like, speech consisting of various utterances, and play involving physical frolics and the like.
"He relishes it" means he finds gratification in it, experiences its flavor, and approves of it. "He desires it" means he longs for it and looks forward to it.
"He attains satisfaction" means he reaches a state of contentment.

“May I be” means “May I exist. “For the sake of obtaining what has not yet been obtained” means for the purpose of reaching what has not yet been reached. “He fixes his mind” means he establishes the mind. “By reason of the mind’s aspiration” means by way of the cause of establishing the mind.
“By virtue” means by virtue such as the five precepts and so forth. “By observance” means by the undertaking of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). “By austerity” means by the undertaking of energy.
“By the holy life” means by abstaining from sexual intercourse. “A deva” means one of great power.
“Or the king of the gods” means one among those [gods].

“Uttering prayers” means speaking by way of their qualities. “Uttering fervent prayers” means speaking in a specific manner. “Uttering intense prayers” means speaking with distinction, or [a term] augmented by a prefix. 9.

Having thus established in the first verse that “for such a person is far from seclusion,” and having revealed the natural state of such persons in the second verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with “Lustful for sense pleasures” (kāmesu giddhā) in order to reveal their commission of evil deeds.
The meaning of this is as follows: those beings are greedy for the craving of enjoyment regarding sense-pleasures;

they are intent upon seeking and so forth; they are bewildered because they have fallen into delusion; they are unworthy of offerings because of their lack of discernment, their stinginess, and their refusal to accept the words of the Buddha and others;
they are settled in the unevenness of bodily misconduct and the like; at the end of their time, they are brought to the suffering of death, [thinking], "What indeed..."
“We shall become [something] after passing away from here,” they lamented.
“Greedily attached” (giddhā) means greedily attached by way of sensual lust. “Infatuated” (gadhitā) means infatuated because they have formed expectations through the passion of intention.
“Deluded” (mucchitā) means overcome by the delusion of sensual craving. “Clinging” (ajjhosannā) means clinging to or overwhelmed by the delight of sensual pleasures.

They cling by means of the moisture of sensual desire; they adhere by being joined together through the fever of sensual desire; they are obstructed by being entangled in the perception of sensual desire.
Alternatively: they are greedy for the viewing of [sexual] views; they are lustful for frequent viewing; they are infatuated with the act of physical contact;
they are obsessed with the act of intimacy; they cling to the smoothness of affection; and [they cling] to the union of the couple.
"Having become attached, they are obstructed by not letting go of one thing after another"—thus some explain it.
"Seeking" means they expect; "searching" means they pursue; "seeking out" means they desire and long for in every way.
Alternatively, regarding a visible object, they seek whether beauty or ugliness exists or does not exist; regarding beautiful or ugly objects...
Having made [the object] manifest before them, they seek it while cherishing it for the sake of enjoyment. They search by way of the mind; they seek by way of application;
they pursue by way of performance. Because they descend and move about depending on these two kinds of sensual pleasure, they are "those whose conduct is such" (*taccarita*).

And because they frequently and predominantly increase and set those sensual pleasures in motion, they are "those for whom that is predominant" (*tabbahula*). And because they hold those sensual pleasures in high esteem...

They are called *taggaruka* because they dwell having made those [sensual pleasures] their object of reverence. They are called *tanninna* because they dwell inclined toward and bent over those sensual pleasures.

They are called *tappoṇa* because they dwell leaning toward and sloping toward those sensual pleasures. They are called *tappabbhāra* because they dwell hanging over, bent down toward, and weighted down by those very sensual pleasures.
They are called so because they speak while being overwhelmed by infatuation and addicted to those sensual pleasures.
They are resolved upon that; and because they dwell having made sensual pleasures their dominant influence and their chief, they are "dominated by those" (*tad-adhipateyyā*).
Alternatively: "Because of the desirable nature of the object, they are characterized by that (*taccaritā*); because of the lovely nature of the object, they abound in that (*tabbahulā*);

because of the agreeable nature of the object, they hold that in high esteem (*taggarukā*); because of the dear nature of the object, they are inclined toward that (*tanninnā*); because of the object's association with sensual desire..."
"Inclined toward that" means leaning toward the object because of its quality of being alluring. "Directed toward that" means being intent upon the object because of its quality of being enthralling.
"Governed by that" means having the object as its dominant influence because of its quality of being binding.

Thus some explain it. Regarding the phrases "they seek after form," and so forth: "seeking" refers to the act of searching for the sake of obtaining what has not yet been obtained. "Obtaining" refers to...
"By way of having come into one's hand. "They enjoy" should be understood as being said by way of utilizing [the object].
"One who creates strife and dispute" is a *kalahakāraka*. "Devoted to that" means intent upon strife (*kalahapasuta*). The same method applies to the *kammakāraka* and others as well.

"Wandering in his resort" means wandering in resorts such as those of prostitutes, or wandering in resorts such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). "Devoted to those" means intent upon those resorts (*gocarapasuta*).
One who possesses *jhāna* by way of sustained contemplation upon an object is a *jhāyī*. One who is intent upon that is *jhānapasuta*.
"They go" means they go to a state of woe (*apāya*). "Misers" means those who conceal their own prosperity.
"Speech" means talking. "Discourse-path" means the path of sentences. "Teaching" means an answer or instruction. "Instruction" means guidance.
“*Nādiyanti*” means they do not take up [the teachings] and do not hold them in high regard. Alternatively, the reading is “*na paṭissantī*,” which has the same meaning.
To demonstrate stinginess in terms of its objects, it is said: “The five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding residence (*āvāsamacchariya*),” and so forth.
Therein, stinginess regarding a residence is “stinginess regarding residence. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"Abode" (*āvāsa*) means the entire monastery, a courtyard, even a single hut, or the night-quarters and so forth.

Those dwelling in these places live happily and obtain the necessary requisites. If one bhikkhu does not wish for the arrival of another well-behaved and virtuous bhikkhu there, and even when he has arrived, thinks, "Let him depart quickly," this is the stinginess regarding an abode (*āvāsamacchariya*).
[This is] the name [of that greed]. However, for those who cause quarrels and so forth, if they do not desire to dwell there, it is not called "dwelling-greed" (*āvāsamacchariya*).
As for "family" (*kula*), it refers both to a family of supporters and a family of kinsmen. Therein, for one who does not desire another person's approach, it is "family-greed" (*kulamacchariya*).
But even for one who does not desire the approach of a wicked person, it is not called "greed. He...

For he acts for the sake of destroying their confidence. However, for a monk who is capable of protecting that confidence, it is called stinginess (macchariya) when he does not wish others to approach him there.
"Gain" (lābha) refers specifically to the gain of the four requisites. It is [stinginess] when one thinks, "May another not obtain this," while another virtuous person is actually receiving it.

There is stinginess regarding gain. However, there is no such thing as stinginess for one who thinks, upon seeing a gift of faith being wasted—destroyed through non-use, improper use, and so forth, or even going to rot—not giving it to another:
"If this person does not receive it, may another virtuous person receive it and put it to use."

“Color” (vaṇṇa) refers both to physical beauty and to the praise of virtues. In this regard, one who is envious of physical beauty does not wish to speak when it is said of another, “He is pleasing to look at and handsome.
One who is envious of the praise of virtues does not wish to speak of another’s praise for their virtue, ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), way of progress, or conduct.

"Dhamma" refers both to the dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and the dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha-dhamma*). In this regard, noble disciples do not harbor stinginess regarding the dhamma of realization;
they desire that the world with its devas realize the very dhamma they themselves have realized.
Furthermore, they desire that others know of that realization. However, it is only regarding the dhamma of the scriptures (*tantidhamma*) that there exists the stinginess of dhamma.
This is what is meant by [the term]. A person endowed with this quality does not wish others to know whatever secret text or method of discourse they themselves know.

However, one who does not grant [teachings] either because they have examined the person but lack support for the Dhamma, or because they have examined the Dhamma but lack support for the person, is not called "one who is stingy with the Dhamma. In this regard:
A certain person is fickle; at one time he is a *śramaṇa*, at another a *brāhmaṇa*, and at another a *nigaṇṭha*.

For when a monk, thinking, "This person will disrupt the subtle and delicate tradition of the lineage by breaking apart the distinct Dharma," does not grant [the teaching], this is called not granting it out of a lack of examination of the person and a lack of support through the Dharma.
However, if one does not give [the teaching] thinking, "This Dhamma is subtle and delicate;

if this person were to grasp it, they would reveal themselves by declaring final knowledge and thus be lost," this is called not giving out of a desire to favor the person after having examined the Dhamma.
Furthermore, if one thinks, "If this person grasps this Dhamma, they will break our tradition..."
If one does not give because of the thought, "He will become capable," this is called stinginess regarding the Dhamma (*dhammamacchariya*).

Among these five types of stinginess, first, by way of stinginess regarding one's dwelling (*āvāsamacchariya*), one becomes a *yakkha* or a *peta* and wanders about with the refuse of that very dwelling carried upon one's head.
By way of stinginess regarding families (*kulamacchariya*), toward others in that family...
Seeing others performing acts such as giving and honoring, one who thinks, "Alas, this family of mine is divided," may have blood gush from his mouth,
suffer purging from his stomach, or even have his internal organs come out in pieces. Through stinginess regarding gains,
having been envious of gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group, and having used them as if they were for private personal use—
He is reborn as a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or a great python.

However, through envy regarding his own physical beauty and qualities, as well as envy regarding the Dhamma he has mastered, he praises his own appearance while speaking of various faults in the appearance of others, asking, "What kind of beauty is this?
Furthermore, by not giving any portion of the mastered Dhamma to anyone else, he becomes ugly and deaf-mute.
Moreover, through stinginess regarding dwellings one is cooked in the Iron House; through stinginess regarding families one has little gain;
through stinginess regarding gains one is reborn in the Excrement Hell; through stinginess regarding physical beauty, in whatever existence one is reborn, one lacks beauty;
and through stinginess regarding the Dhamma one is reborn in the Kukkuḷa Hell.
It is *macchariya* (stinginess) by way of being stingy (*maccharāyana*). The state of being stingy is *maccharāyanā*.

The state of one who is stingy, of one who possesses stinginess, is *maccharāyitatta*. One is *veviccha* because they do not wish to extend any of their own successes to others, thinking, "Let these be mine alone;
let them not belong to another. The state of one who is *veviccha* is *veviccha*; this refers to mild stinginess.
This is the name. One who is *kadariya* is called disrespectful; the state of being such is *kadariya*, which is a term for stubborn stinginess.
A person endowed with that quality even prevents another from giving to others. And this has been said:
"The stingy one, of evil intent, possessing wrong view and lacking respect..."
“He restrains one who is giving food to those who beg.
One whose mind turns away or contracts with a sense of bitterness upon seeing a beggar is called *kaṭukañcuka*; the state of being such is *kaṭukañcukatā*.
According to another method, *kaṭukañcukatā* refers to the grasping of the ladle (*kaṭacchuggāha*). For when a pot is filled to the brim, [one must grasp the ladle to prevent it from overflowing].
When one receiving almsfood takes it with a tip-spoon that is contracted on all sides, one is unable to take it after filling [the bowl];
in this way, the mind of a person who is miserly contracts. When that [mind] has contracted, the body likewise contracts, shrinks back, recoils, and does not extend;
thus, miserliness is called "bitter shyness" (*kaṭukañcukatā*).
"Seizing upon the mind": this refers to the state of the mind having been seized by obstructing it so that it does not flow away through acts such as giving when performing a service for others.
For a person who is stingy desires not to give his own possessions to others, but rather desires to take the possessions of others; therefore, [he thinks], "Let this wonder belong to me alone."
"May it not belong to another"—by way of this [thought], its characteristic of concealing one's own excellence and its characteristic of grasping at the excellence of others should be understood.
Stinginess regarding the aggregates (*khandhamacchariya*) is also stinginess;

that is, the stinginess occurring with the thought, "May this wonderful thing consisting of my own five aggregates—my state of rebirth—not be shared by others, but be mine alone. This is stinginess regarding the aggregates.
[This is] the name. The same principle applies to stinginess regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense bases (*āyatana*). "Grasping" (*gāha*) means taking hold by way of a firm resolve.
"By way of not being communicative" (*avadaññutāya*) means by way of not understanding even what has been spoken by the All-Knowing Buddhas.

For one who does not give to supplicants indeed does not understand what they have said. "People are negligent" (*janā pamattā*) means people whose mindfulness has departed. "Speech" (*vacana*) is a concise statement. "Discourse" (*byappatha*)...

"Extensive statement" (*vitthāravacanaṃ*): this refers to a discourse that shows a simile and demonstrates the meaning. "Instruction" (*desanā*): this refers to a discourse that points out the meaning after having shown it.
"Admonition" (*anusitthi*): this refers to a discourse that causes one to observe repeatedly. Alternatively, speaking after having shown [the meaning] is called "statement" (*vacana*).

Speaking after having caused [one] to grasp [the meaning] is called "expression" (*byappatha*). Speaking after having satisfied [one] is called "teaching" (*desanā*). Speaking after having made [the meaning] clear is called "admonition" (*anusitthi*).
Alternatively, speech that destroys the suffering of distress is called *vacana*; speech that destroys the suffering of feverish burning is called *byappatha*;
speech that destroys the suffering of the woeful states is called *desanā*; and speech that destroys the suffering of existence is called *anusāsani*.

Alternatively, it is speech associated with the penetration of the full understanding of the truth of suffering; speech associated with the penetration of the abandonment of the truth of the origin [of suffering].
Some explain it in this manner: "conduct" refers to behavior; "teaching" is instruction connected with the penetration and realization of the truth of cessation;
and "advice" is instruction connected with the penetration and cultivation of the truth of the path.
"They do not wish to hear" means they do not listen. "They do not lend an ear" means they do not apply their auditory faculty for the purpose of hearing.
“They do not establish their minds on understanding” means they do not settle their minds for the sake of knowing. “Disobedient” means not listening to instruction.
“Non-compliant” means that even though they listen, they do not carry out what is said; thus they are non-compliant. “Acting contrary” means behaving as obstacles.
“They turn their faces away” means that even while acting, they do not show their faces; this is the meaning.

It is "uneven" (*visama*) because it is the opposite of the evenness consisting of good conduct of body and so forth; [the phrase] "in that unevenness" means in that which is uneven. "Established" (*niviṭṭhā*) means entered and difficult to extract.
"In bodily action" (*kāyakamme*) means occurring from the body, or in bodily action occurring by means of the body. The same method applies to verbal action and the rest as well.
Therein, bodily, verbal, and mental actions are analyzed by way of misconduct, and by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action beginning with the destruction of life.
It should be understood that [the term] is analyzed [as follows]. This, first, is the commentary on the common terms here. Regarding the uncommon terms, however:

the taking away of life (pāṇa) is "killing of living beings" (pāṇātipāta); the slaying of life is "destruction of living beings" (pāṇaghāta)—this is what is meant. Herein, from the conventional standpoint (*vohāra*), "living being" (*pāṇa*) refers to a sentient being;

from the ultimate standpoint (*paramattha*), it refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). Now, with regard to that living being, for one who perceives it as a living being, [the act] originated by an effort that severs the life-faculty...
Killing is the volition of killing that proceeds through either the door of body or the door of speech.
It is less blameworthy when directed toward small creatures among animals and other beings devoid of special qualities, and more blameworthy when directed toward large-bodied beings. Why?

Because of the greatness of the effort; and even when the effort is equal, because of the greatness of the object. Among those possessing qualities, such as humans, it is less blameworthy when directed toward those with few qualities.
In regard to living beings, [killing] is slightly blameworthy when the being is of little value, and greatly blameworthy when it is of great value.

However, when there is equality in the value of the body, it should be understood that it is slightly blameworthy if the defilements and the means employed are mild, and greatly blameworthy if they are intense.
It has five constituent factors: the living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intent to kill, the means employed, and death by that means.
The six methods of application (chappayoga) are: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishment, by persistence, by means of knowledge, and by means of supernormal power.
However, if this matter were to be explained in detail, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we shall not elaborate upon it.
Other matters of this kind should likewise be understood by those who desire them by consulting the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
Taking what is not given is *adinnādāna*; it is said to be the seizing of another’s property, theft, or robbery.
In this context, "what is not given" refers to that which is owned by another, such that if one were to exercise control over it as one pleases, one would incur neither punishment nor blame.
Regarding that which is owned by another, for one who perceives it as being owned by another, [the offense] arises from the effort of taking it.
The volition of theft is taking what is not given. That [offense] is less blameworthy when the object is the property of an inferior person, and more blameworthy when it is that of a superior person.
Why? Because of the superiority of the object; for when the object is of equal value, it is more blameworthy when it belongs to one who possesses superior qualities.
Depending on each respective superior quality, it is less blameworthy when the object belongs to one whose qualities are inferior compared to that [superior person].

For this [offense], there are five constituent factors: another’s possession, the perception that it is another’s possession, the intention to steal, the exertion, and the carrying away by means of that [exertion].
There are six modes of application, beginning with "by one's own hand" and so forth.
These, moreover, correspond respectively to these five types of theft: theft by taking, theft by force, theft by concealment, theft by artifice, and theft by trickery.
