Here, however, because it is not overwhelmed by applied thought, sustained thought (*vicāra*), and rapture (*pīti*), it has become fully manifest in its function, as if with its head held high; therefore, it is said to be "spoken of.

Regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending" (*sato ca sampajāno*): here, one who remembers is "mindful" (*sato*); one who clearly understands is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*). Thus, mindfulness is [a quality] of the person.
And mindfulness and clear comprehension have been mentioned. Therein, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering; its function is non-forgetfulness; it is manifested as protection.
Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion; its function is investigating; it is manifested as discrimination.
Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas, for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking in clear comprehension—
Not even mere access concentration is achieved, let alone absorption. However, because those jhānas are gross, the movement of the mind is easy, like that of a man walking on level ground;

thus, the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not required there. But because this jhāna is subtle due to the abandoning of its gross factors, it is like a man walking on the edge of a razor’s blade, and must be sustained by the application of the functions of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
It is stated right here that such a course for the mind must be desired. Moreover:

just as a calf accustomed to its mother, if removed from her and left unprotected, returns once more to the cow, so too this bliss of the third jhāna, though removed from rapture (*pīti*), would—if not protected by the safeguard of mindfulness and clear comprehension—return once more to rapture.
It may be associated with joy (*pīti*) alone, for beings are attached even to pleasure (*sukha*), and this [pleasure] is exceedingly sweet because there is no pleasure beyond it.

However, it should be understood that this very point was stated here to show this specific distinction: that through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), there is no attachment to pleasure in this state, whereas otherwise there would be.
Now, regarding the phrase "he experiences pleasure with the body": although there is no mental application (*abhoga*) for the experience of pleasure in one who possesses the third jhāna,
nevertheless, because that pleasure is associated with his mental body (*nāmakāya*),
and because his physical body (*rūpakāya*) is pervaded by an exceedingly refined matter produced by that pleasure associated with the mental body— due to which pervasion [the phrase is used].
Even when emerged from jhāna, one would experience pleasure; therefore, in order to show this meaning, he said: "and he experiences pleasure with the body.
Now, regarding that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, equanimous and mindful," herein, because of the jhāna—

Because of that third jhāna, the Noble Ones—the Buddhas and so forth—proclaim, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and expound the person who possesses that third jhāna; the intention is that they praise him. How so?
As "one who dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous. Thus one enters upon and abides in that third jhāna.
The application [of the terms] here should be understood in this way.
But why do they praise it in such a manner? Because it is worthy of praise.

For although this [state] has reached the perfection of happiness in the extremely sweet bliss of the third jhāna, one remains equanimous there; one is not dragged away by attachment to that happiness.

And because he is mindful through the presence of mindfulness such that rapture does not arise, and because he experiences with his mental body that undefiled happiness which is beloved by the Noble Ones and cultivated by the Noble Ones,

he is worthy of praise. Thus, because he is worthy of praise, the Noble Ones, manifesting those very qualities that serve as the cause for such praise, describe him as "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness."
It should be understood that they praise it in this way. "The third" means the third in the numerical sequence; it is also called the third because it arises as the third.
"With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain" means with the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain.
"Previously" means indeed before [the fourth jhāna], not at the moment of the fourth jhāna. "With the disappearance of mental joy and mental grief."
Regarding these two—mental pleasure and mental pain—it is said that they have already "disappeared" and been "abandoned" even before [the attainment of the first jhāna].
But when does their abandonment occur? It occurs at the moment of the access concentration (upacāra) of the four jhānas.

For mental joy (somanassa) is abandoned precisely at the moment of access to the fourth jhāna; while suffering, mental grief, and physical pleasure are abandoned at the moments of access to the first, second, and third jhānas respectively.

Thus, although not mentioned here according to the sequence of their abandonment, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief—which are indeed mentioned here according to the order of enumeration of the faculties in the *Indriya-vibhaṅga*—should be understood.
But if these are abandoned at the very moment of the access concentration (*upacāra*) of each respective jhāna, then why [is it said]: "Where..."?
Where does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as above] ...enters and dwells in the first jhāna; there the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.
Where does the arisen faculty of grief... the faculty of pleasure... the faculty of joy cease without remainder?
"Does it cease? Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [etc] ...a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
And herein, the arisen faculty of mental joy ceases without remainder. Thus, cessation is stated specifically in reference to the jhānas.
This is because their cessation is absolute; for their cessation is indeed absolute in the first jhāna and the others, but not elsewhere.
It is cessation indeed. However, at the moment of access (upacāra), it is not an absolute cessation.

For instance, even when the pain faculty has ceased during the access to the first jhāna through the exclusion of various objects of thought, it may still arise due to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or from the affliction of an uneven seat;
but this does not happen within the state of absorption (appanā). Even though this [pain] has ceased in access, [it can still reappear].

It is not completely ceased because it has not been struck down by its opposite. However, within the access concentration (antoppanā), the entire body becomes suffused with happiness through the pervasion of rapture;
and for one whose body is suffused with happiness, the faculty of pain is completely ceased because it has been struck down by its opposite.
And even in the preliminary stage (upacāra) of the second jhāna, through various acts of adverting, the faculty of mental grief—which had already been abandoned—[is likewise suppressed].

Because this arises even when there are conditions of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), provided there is bodily fatigue and mental affliction, yet it does not arise in the absence of applied and sustained thought;
and where it does arise, it is only where applied and sustained thought exist.
Furthermore, since applied and sustained thought have not yet been abandoned in the vicinity of the second jhāna, its arising might occur there, but certainly not in the second jhāna itself.

Because its condition has been abandoned. Likewise, although the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) has been abandoned in the vicinity of the third jhāna, it might still arise for one whose body is touched by the sublime matter produced by joy (pīti);
however, this is not the case in the third jhāna itself, because in the third jhāna, the joy that serves as the condition for pleasure has ceased entirely.
Similarly, although the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) has been abandoned in the vicinity of the fourth jhāna, [it might still arise] due to its proximity.

And because it has not been properly transcended due to the absence of equanimity that has reached absorption (appanā), there might be its arising; but this is certainly not the case in the fourth jhāna.
For this very reason, the term "without remainder" (aparisesa) is employed in various places [in the Suttas], as in: "The faculty of pain that has arisen here ceases without remainder.
Here it may be asked: "If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access (upacāra) stage of each respective jhāna, why are they brought together here?"
For the purpose of easy apprehension. For that feeling which is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" here is subtle and difficult to discern;
it cannot be easily grasped. Therefore, just as a cowherd, for the sake of easily catching a bull that is wild and impossible to catch by approaching it in one way or another, [might use a device...]
Just as a cowherd gathers all his cattle together and, while driving them out one by one, causes even the last one that comes in order to be seized, saying, "Seize this one too!";
even so, the Blessed One gathered all these [feelings] for the sake of easy comprehension. Having thus shown them as they were gathered, he said:
"That which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither mental joy (*somanassa*) nor mental grief (*domanassa*)," and so forth.
"This is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"—it is possible to grasp it in this way.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these [terms] were also spoken for the purpose of showing the conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*).
For the abandoning of pain and so forth are its conditions. As it is said: "There are, friend, four conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant..."

"Friends, there are these four conditions for the attainment of the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Here, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
These, friends, are the four conditions for the attainment of the liberation of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Or, just as elsewhere, even though the view of a self-entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth have already been abandoned, they are mentioned again for the purpose of praising the third path.
It should be understood that these [factors] are mentioned here for the purpose of praising this jhāna, even though they have already been described as "abandoned" therein.
Alternatively, it should be understood that they are mentioned here to show the extreme remoteness of lust and hatred from this state due to the destruction of their conditions.
For among these, pleasure is the condition for joy, joy for lust, and pain for grief.
Mental distress [is the nutriment] for hatred. Because greed and hatred, along with their conditions, have been destroyed by the destruction of pleasure and so forth, they become exceedingly remote.

"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" means not painful due to the absence of pain, and not pleasant due to the absence of pleasure. By this, he indicates here the third type of feeling which is the opposite of pleasure and pain, rather than a mere absence of pain and pleasure.
The third feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukhā*).

It is also called equanimity (*upekkhā*). It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing what is pleasant and unpleasant in an impartial manner, the function of neutrality, the manifestation of non-manifestation, and the proximate cause of the cessation of pleasure.
"Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" means the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity; for in this jhāna, mindfulness is perfectly pure.
The purity of that mindfulness which exists is produced by equanimity and not by anything else; therefore, this is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
And as for the equanimity by means of which mindfulness here becomes pure, it should be understood in its actual sense as "neither-aversion-nor-favour" (tatramajjhattatā).
Not only is mindfulness purified by it, but all associated mental states are purified as well.
However, the teaching was spoken by one who is preeminent in mindfulness.
In this regard, although this equanimity exists even in the three lower jhānas, just as during the day the sun’s radiance prevails,
and because of its gentle nature or its helpfulness to itself, it does not find a corresponding counterpart in the night, so too, although it exists during the day...
Just as the crescent of the moon is impure and unpurified, so too this crescent of equanimity toward the middle [state] is impure within the various stages of the first jhāna and so forth;

for although it exists, it is overwhelmed by the heat of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*), and because it has not yet attained its corresponding feeling of equanimity and delight, it remains impure. And while that [equanimity] is impure during the day...
Just as the light of an impure crescent moon is itself impure, so too mindfulness (*sati*) and the other factors, even though they are co-nascent, remain impure.
Therefore, not even one of them is described as "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*).

However, here, because this crescent-moon-like equanimity of "onlooking-equanimity" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) is free from the overpowering heat of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*), and because it has attained a corresponding affection for the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*), it is exceedingly—
It is completely pure; because of that purity, even the co-nascent factors such as mindfulness and so forth become pure and radiant, like the light of the completely pure crescent moon.
Therefore, it should be understood that this alone is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
It is "the fourth" in the sequence of counting; it is also called "the fourth" because it arises as the fourth.
"Endowed with wisdom" (*paññavā*) means one who possesses wisdom (*paññā*).

"Leading to arising and passing away" (*udayatthagāmini*) means leading both to arising and to passing away. "Possessed of" (*samannāgato*) means complete. "Noble" (*ariyāya*) means faultless. "Penetrative" (*nibbedhikāya*) means conducive to penetration.
"Leading to the destruction of suffering" (*dukkhakkhayagāmini*) means leading to *nibbāna*. In such passages as "This is suffering," [it is understood that] "this much is suffering..."
"There is nothing beyond this": by means of the penetration of its intrinsic characteristic, one understands and penetrates the entire truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) as it truly is.
One understands the craving that produces that suffering as "this is the origin of suffering" (dukkhasamudaya).
And that state where both of these cease, the non-occurrence of them—Nirvana—one understands as "this is the cessation of suffering" (dukkhanirodha).

And regarding the Noble Path that leads to its attainment, one understands and penetrates it as it truly is through the penetration of its essential characteristic, thinking: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is how the meaning should be understood.

Having thus shown the Truths according to their specific nature, he now speaks the words beginning with "These are the taints" (ime āsavā) in order to show them by way of the defilements (kilesa) as a figurative exposition (pariyāya).

These should be understood in the manner already stated. Having thus shown the three trainings, he now says, "One should train while adverting to these three trainings," etc., in order to show the sequence for their fulfillment. Its meaning is as follows:
one should train even while adverting to each one individually for the sake of fulfilling it; and one should also train while knowing, after having adverted, "This is such-and-such a training."
Having known it, one should train even while seeing it again and again; having seen it, one should train even while reviewing it as it was seen;
having reviewed it, one should train even while making the mind immovable and establishing it right there;

one should train even while performing their respective functions through faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom associated with each specific training; and one should train even while performing those respective functions at the time of directly knowing what is to be directly known.

One should train in the three trainings: one should practice higher virtue (*adhisīla*), conduct oneself rightly in higher mind (*adhicitta*), and proceed having undertaken higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).

"Herein" (*idha*) is the foundational term. By means of the ten terms beginning with "of this view" (*imissā diṭṭhiyā*), it is precisely the teaching of the Omniscient Buddha, known as the Three Trainings, that is spoken of.
For that is called "view" (*diṭṭhi*) because it was seen by the Blessed Buddha; and by way of its being acceptable to him...

It is called *khanti* (patience/endurance) by way of being agreeable; *ruci* (liking) by way of being pleasing; *ādāyo* (taking up) by way of grasping; *dhamma* (the Teaching) in the sense of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*);

*vinaya* (the Discipline) in the sense of that which is to be trained in; *dhammavinaya* (the Teaching and Discipline) by both these meanings; *pāvacana* (the Word) by way of what has been spoken; *brahmacariya* (the Holy Life) in the sense of the best conduct;
and *satthusāsana* (the Teacher’s Dispensation) by way of the giving of instruction. Therefore, in such phrases as "of this view" (*imissā diṭṭhiyā*), [it refers to] this...
In this vision of the Buddha, in this acceptance of the Buddha, in this preference for the Buddha,
in this guidance of the Buddha, in this Dhamma of the Buddha,
in this Vinaya of the Buddha: “Those qualities, Gotamī, that you might know as ‘these qualities lead to passion, not to dispassion;’”
They lead to bondage, not to liberation; they lead to accumulation, not to diminution; they lead to great desire, not to fewness of wishes;
they lead to lack of contentment, not to contentment; they lead to social entanglement, not to seclusion;
they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to being difficult to support.
“They lead, Gotamī, not to being easy to support. You should categorically understand, Gotamī: “This is not the Dhamma; this is not the Vinaya;
this is not the Teacher’s instruction. “But those teachings, Gotamī, which you should know as leading to dispassion, not to passion... [and so on]...”
“They lead to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support. “In this way, Gotamī, you should categorically hold:
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.
When this was said, the meaning should be understood as follows: in this Buddha-Dhamma-Vinaya, in this word of the Buddha, in this holy life of the Buddha, in this teaching of the Buddha.

Moreover, this entire teaching, known as the three trainings, is "view" (diṭṭhi) because it was seen by the Blessed One, because it has right view as its condition, and because it is preceded by right view. It is "patience" (khanti) by virtue of being acceptable to the Blessed One. It is "inclination" (ruci) by virtue of being pleasing to him.
It is "adoption" (ādāya) by virtue of being grasped by him. And it is "Dhamma" because it sustains one's maker by preventing him from falling into the states of misery.
It is called *vinaya* because it leads away (*vineti*) the side of defilement. It is both *dhamma* and *vinaya*, hence *dhammavinaya*.
Alternatively, it is *dhammavinaya* because it is the leading away (*vinaya*) of unwholesome states by means of wholesome states. For this very reason it was said:

"And those things, Gotamī, that you should know as 'these things lead to dispassion, not to passion... [etc.]... you should, Gotamī, hold with absolute certainty: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction."'"*
The discipline is by means of the Dhamma, not by means of punishment and so forth; thus it is called "Dhamma-discipline" (*dhammavinaya*). And this has been said:
"Some tame by means of punishment, And with goads and whips;
But the Naga was tamed by the Great Seer Without punishment and without a sword."
Likewise:
"For those who are led by the Dhamma, what envy can there be for one who understands?

Or, the discipline (vinaya) for the sake of the Dhamma is "Dhamma-vinaya. For this discipline is for the purpose of the faultless Dhamma, not for the sake of the bait of existence and worldly enjoyment.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “This holy life, bhikkhus, is not lived for the sake of deceiving people,” and so forth in detail.
The Elder Puṇṇa also said: “Friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
Or, it leads to distinction, thus it is the Vinaya. Discipline according to the Dhamma is *dhammavinaya*. For [it leads] from the phenomena of saṃsāra, such as the phenomena of sorrow and so forth...
Or, it leads to the distinguished Nibbāna. Or, it is the discipline (vinaya) of the Dhamma, not of other founders of sects; thus it is "Dhamma-vinaya.
For the Blessed One is the embodiment of the Dhamma, and his alone is the discipline.
Or, because it is the phenomena (dhammas) themselves that are to be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized.
Therefore, because this is a discipline (*vinaya*) regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), and not regarding sentient beings (*satta*) or living entities (*jīva*), it is called *dhammavinaya*.

It is called *pavacana* because it is the preeminent teaching due to its possession of both meaning and phrasing (*sāttha-sabyañjana*), as distinguished from the words of others; being a teaching (*vavana*), it is thus *pāvacana*.
It is called *brahmacariya* because it is a conduct distinguished by all forms of noble practice. It is the instruction (*sāsana*) of the Blessed One, who has become the Teacher of gods and humans.
It is the Teacher’s instruction (*satthusāsana*). Alternatively, it is the instruction that has become the Teacher; thus it is the "Teacher’s instruction.
For it has been said: "After my passing, the Dhamma and Vinaya alone shall be your teacher"—it is in this way that the meaning of these terms should be understood.

Furthermore, because in this very dispensation (*sāsana*) alone—and not elsewhere—is a monk seen who can produce all types of jhāna, one should understand that the restriction using the words "of this" (*imissā*) and "in this" (*imasmiṃ*) was made in various places for that reason.
It is called *jīvita* (life) because the states associated with it live by means of it.

It is called *indriya* (faculty) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of preservation. Life itself as a faculty is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). It is the predominant factor over the continuity of the process of existence.
Furthermore, among the states inseparable from itself according to their characteristics and so forth, the life-faculty has the characteristic of preserving them.
Their function is to cause those very states to proceed; their manifestation is the stabilization of those same states;

their proximate cause is the phenomena that are to be maintained. And although there is a formal arrangement characterized by protection and so forth, it protects those states only at the very moment they exist, just as water [supports] lotuses and the like.
Furthermore, even though the states have arisen through their own respective conditions, it protects them, just as a nurse [protects] an infant.
It proceeds by way of its own connection with the dhamma that has set it in motion, like a pilot [steering] a ship.
It does not cause it to proceed after the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅga*), because of the absence of both itself and that which is to be caused to proceed.

Nor does it establish it at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself dissolving, like the wick of a lamp when the oil in the bowl is being exhausted; yet it is not devoid of the power of preservation, causing to proceed, and establishing.
It should be understood that [the cause] is the means of accomplishing each respective [effect] at the moment already described.

"Due to the limitedness of its duration" (ṭhitiparittatāya) means due to the weakness or meagreness of the moment of its existence. "Small" (appakaṃ) means weak, inferior, or low-quality. "Due to the limitedness of its own essence" (sarasaparittatāya) means due to the deficiency or weakness of its own conditions or of the functions and attainments belonging to it.
In order to show the distinction between these two reasons, he said: “How, by the limitedness of duration...,” and so forth.
Therein, [the phrase] “‘He lived in the past mental moment’ and so on” refers to the time when consciousness ceases during the process of existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*);
even though all material and immaterial phenomena have not ceased, the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpajīvita*) exists by virtue of the immaterial being the foundation for the material.

It should be understood that this was said with reference to the death-consciousness (cuticitta) in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava), considering the state of cessation of all form and non-form [phenomena] along with the death-consciousness;
and it was said with reference to the four-aggregate existence (catuvokārabhava), considering the absence of form therein.
"In the past mental moment" means at the time when one possesses the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of a past consciousness; at that time, the person possessing it—
It is permissible to say, “he lived. It is not permissible to say, “he lives,” because he does not live. It is not permissible to say, “he will live,” because he will not live.
However, it is permissible to say, “he will live,” at the time when one possesses the non-arising moment of a future consciousness, in the sense that he will live in a future conscious moment.
It is not permissible to say, “he lives,” because he does not live.

It is not permissible to say, "He lived. It is also not permissible to say, "He lived," [meaning] "he lived" (*jīvittha*). At the present moment of consciousness—that is, at the time one possesses the present moment of consciousness—it is permissible to say, "He lives," meaning "he lives now.
It is not permissible to say, "He lived. It is also not permissible to say, "He will live," meaning "he will live" (*jīvissati*).

It should be understood that this verse—“Life, the personal existence, and pleasure and pain”—is spoken with reference specifically to the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), because it takes up painful feeling as something obtainable without relinquishing the five-aggregate existence. How so?
"Life" refers to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) by way of the headword "life. "Personal existence" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). But as for equanimity...
Because it is stated, “When agitated, it is simply called ‘pleasure’,” the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) includes equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) along with pleasure and pain.

The term “mind” (*citta*) refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*). Precisely because these four aggregates have been explained, the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*) is also included by virtue of having the same characteristic as the characteristic of the aggregates, through its mode of characteristic.

It should be understood as "spoken. When the five aggregates have been thus described, by excluding the immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma), the predominance of the immaterial is stated through the fact that materiality—whether produced by kamma and so forth—does not occur in association with a single moment of consciousness.
How so? In the case of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), even materiality proceeds without relinquishing the power of accumulated kamma;
likewise, in those who have attained cessation (nirodhasamāpanna), even materiality [proceeds] without relinquishing the power of the attainment first entered.

It proceeds without ever being released. Thus, even in a place where matter does not exist for itself, the immaterial dhamma—which has the nature of proceeding by making the occurrence of matter its own property—proceeds as being "associated with a single consciousness" (ekacittasamāyutta) because it serves as the primary cause for the occurrence of matter in its own place of occurrence.
It should be understood that the primacy of consciousness is thus stated.

Thus, in the course of existence within the five-aggregate realm (pañcavokārabhava), when form is still persisting, there occurs what is called the "cessation" of those [mental states] that have arisen through the cessation of the mind—the primary factor for the occurrence of form. Therefore, it is said with reference to immaterial phenomena alone: "The moment passes swiftly.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this was spoken with reference to the death-consciousness (cuticitta) in the five-aggregate realm. When it is explained in this way:
"And both pleasure and pain" refers to bodily and mental pleasant feelings as well as bodily and mental painful feelings;
although these do not exist at the moment of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), they are said to cease together with the death-consciousness by way of a single continuity (*ekasantati*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that this was said with reference to existence in the fourfold plane (*catuvokārabhava*). How so? In another context, "individuality" (*attabhāva*) refers to the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*).
By virtue of being what has been described, "selfhood" (attabhāva) refers specifically to the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha).

It should be understood that although bodily pleasure, pain, and mental grief do not exist in the Brahma-world, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is included there because it is obtained through the commonality of the term "pleasure and pain.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated. And in these three alternatives, there is absolutely no permanence, pleasure, beauty, or self.

They exist entirely unmixed with one another. According to the method already stated, "a moment passes swiftly," because of its duration being a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*), the moment of life and so forth passes as something light and exceedingly brief.
Demonstrating that two moments of consciousness do not arise simultaneously, he spoke the verse beginning with "eighty-four thousand. Eighty-four thousand...
"Those who abide as Maruts and those hosts of gods remain for eighty-four thousand aeons, having taken up a lifespan in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
There is also a textual variant: *ye narā* (those men). Yet even they do not truly live;
for they are 'conjoined by two minds'—meaning those gods, being conjoined by two minds and becoming one through a yoked mind, do not live in that way individually."
The meaning is: "they live by means of the mind.
Now, showing the time of death, he spoke the verse beginning with "those that have ceased. Therein, "those that have ceased" refers to those aggregates (*khandhā*) that have ceased and passed away.
"Of one dying" means of one who has died. "Or of one standing" means of one who is still living. All [of these].

"Similar aggregates": whether they be aggregates that have ceased after death or aggregates that have ceased during the course of existence, all aggregates are "similar" in the sense that they cannot be reassembled.
"Gone without reconnection": because there is no returning of ceased aggregates to form a new rebirth-linking, it is said that they have "gone without reconnection."
Now, in order to show that there is no diversity among the aggregates (khandhas) ceased at the three times, he spoke the verse beginning with "anantarā.
Therein, "those which have been broken without interval" (anantarā ca ye bhaggā) refers to those aggregates which, having become immediately past, were split and ceased;

and "those which are broken in the future" (ye ca bhaggā anāgatā) refers to those future aggregates that will be split. "In the interval between them" (tadantare) means within the interval of those [past and future ones] that have ceased.
Of the present aggregates. "Vesamaṃ natthi lakkhaṇe" means that there is no unevenness (*vesama*) in their characteristic;

the state of being uneven is *vesama*, and that *vesama* does not exist—meaning there is no diversity among them. It is called a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized (*lakkhīyati*);
[the phrase refers] to that characteristic. Now, explaining how future aggregates are unmixed with present aggregates, he says: "By that which has not yet arisen..."
He spoke this verse: “He is not born. By “not born,” it is meant that he is not born—that is, not produced—by the unborn, unmanifested future aggregate (*anāgata-khandha*).
By this, he explains the state of the future aggregate being unmixed with the present aggregate.
“He lives by means of the present” means he lives by the present aggregate existing at this very moment (*khaṇa-paccuppanna*). By this...

It is stated that one does not live with two consciousnesses at a single moment. "Dead through the breaking of consciousness" means dead by way of the cessation of consciousness (*cittabhaṅga*) due to the state of not living with two consciousnesses at a single moment.
There is also a textual reading, “*uparito cittabhaṅgā*,” which is straightforward [in meaning]. Regarding the phrase “conventional designation (*paññatti*) is the ultimate reality (*paramattha*)”:
it is according to the sequence of the statement, “The physical form (*rūpa*) of mortals decays, but name-and-lineage (*nāmagotta*) does not decay.”

“Mere designation” (*paṇṇattimattaṃ*): its supreme stability (*paramā ṭhiti*) does not consist in the nature of decaying; thus it is “ultimate” (*paramatthiyā*). The meaning is “stability of intrinsic nature” (*sabhāvaṭṭhitikā*).
For when one says, “Datta is dead, Mitta is dead,” only the mere designation remains. Alternatively, *paramatthiyā* means *paramatthikā*.
It is “ultimate” (*paramatthikā*) because its object (*attha*) is supreme (*parama*). [The phrase] “space without core” (*ajaṭākāsa*) refers to a non-existent phenomenon by way of designation.

Just as the expression "he is dead" is a designation (paññatti) dependent upon a non-existent state, it is not spoken in dependence on a non-existent phenomenon; rather, it is spoken in dependence on the phenomenon known as the dissolution of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).
"They have gone to non-deposit, they are broken" means that those aggregates which are shattered do not go to a deposit, a store, or an accumulation.
"Stored away": there is no accumulation or massing of them in the future; thus, even in the future, they possess neither the state of being a heap nor the state of being a collection.
"They remain only as they have arisen": by way of the present, having arisen, they remain while still subject to the nature of decay at the very moment of their stability.
Like what? "Like a mustard seed on the point of an awl"—like a mustard seed on the tip of a needle.
Now, demonstrating the nature of the aggregates as objects of vision, he spoke the verse beginning with “of those that have arisen.
Therein, “of phenomena that have arisen” refers to the present aggregates. “Their dissolution is placed before them” means that their disintegration has been set forth as preceding.
“Subject to disintegration” means having the inherent nature of perishing. “Supported by those that were prior” means supported by those that arose previously.
They are neither mixed with nor in contact with the aggregates.
Now, showing the state of the non-perception of the aggregates, he spoke this verse:
"They come from non-perception. In that context, "they come from non-perception" means they arrive and arise while remaining imperceptible. "They go to perception through dissolution."
The various divisions, after their dissolution, go beyond the state of being visible.

"Like the appearance of lightning in the sky" means like the flashing of a bolt of lightning in the open sky. "They arise and pass away" means they arise from the past and break apart—that is, they perish—just as in expressions such as, "The moon rises, it waxes, and it wanes."

Having thus shown the limited nature of duration (*ṭhitiparittatā*), he now speaks the passage beginning with "How is it limited by its own nature? (*sarasaparittatā*) in order to show the limited nature of its own essence.
Therein, "life bound up with inhalation" (*assāsūpanibandhaṃ jīvitaṃ*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) dependent upon the inward-moving breath of the nose.

"Exhalation" (*passāsa*) is the outward-moving breath of the nose. "Inhalation and exhalation" (*assāsapassāsa*) is both of these together. "Bound up with the great primary elements" (*mahābhūtūpanibandhaṃ*)...
Life is bound to the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—which arise from the fourfold origination.

It is "bound by the nutriment of physical food" (*kabaḷīkārāhārūpanibandha*) in the sense that it is maintained by the nutriment of physical food consisting of what is eaten, drunk, and so forth. It is "bound by heat" (*usmūpanibandha*) in the sense that it is maintained by the heat element born of karma.

It is "bound by consciousness" (*viññāṇūpanibandha*) in the sense that it is maintained by the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgaviññāṇa*). With reference to this, it was said: "Vitality and heat..."
“...consciousness, when it abandons this body.
Now, showing their weak cause, he said: “The root of these is also weak,” and so forth. Therein, “the root also” means that which has become the root in the sense of being a foundation.
For the physical body is the root of the in-breaths and out-breaths; [and] of the primary elements, etc.

Ignorance, karma, and craving are the nutriments. "Of these" refers to the aforementioned types—inspiration and so forth—which have been described as the causes for the functioning of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
For if any one of these is absent, the life-faculty does not persist. "Weak" means lacking in strength.

"Past causes" refers to ignorance, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), craving, clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*), which served as the causes and conditions for this cycle of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*) in a previous birth.
"Those conditions which are weak are also weak" refers to the common conditions such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and so forth.

"Productive" (*pabhāvika*) means that craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) arises as the primary factor. "Co-existent" (*sahabhū*) refers to both material and immaterial phenomena that arise together. "Associated" (*sampayoga*) refers to immaterial phenomena that are conjoined with one another.
"Conascent" (*sahaja*) refers to those that have arisen together within a single moment of consciousness. "That which is also instigating" (*payojikā*)...

"Applying" means being engaged in order to connect [the process] by way of rebirth-linking and death; thus, it is craving that acts as the motivator, having the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) as its root. For this has been said: "A person has craving as his companion.
"Always weak" means constantly weak. "Unstable" means not stable; having descended, they do not remain.
"They cause to fall" means these [factors] cause one another to fall and exhaust one another. "Of one another" means...
"Another for another, one for one"—this is the meaning. *Hi* is a particle used in the sense of a reason.
"There is no protector" (*tāyana*) means there is no guardian. "Nor do they establish one another" means others are not able to establish another.
"Even he who produces them is not found" means that even the phenomenon which is their producer does not exist now.
"And no one is diminished by anyone" means that not even a single person is deprived of anything through the influence of another.
"And all these are 'gandhabbas'" means that all these aggregates (khandhas) are fit to reach dissolution in every respect.

"These are manifested by the former" means that these presently occurring [aggregates] are produced by prior causes and conditions. "And those which manifest" refers to those [future aggregates] as well.
These present productive [factors] have prior causes as their condition.
"They died earlier" means that those conditions of the aforementioned type met with death even before reaching the present state. Both the former and the latter:
the former refers to the prior causal conditions, and the latter refers to those arisen from conditions in the present. They are never mutually [opposed].
"Never before seen by us"—the *ma* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasaṇḍhi*).

Regarding "the gods of the Four Great Kings" (*cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ*): they are called *cātumahārājikā* because the four great kings—namely Dhatarattha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera—are their lords (*issara*).
They are called *devā* because they sport and play with forms and other such things. They [dwell] on Mount Sineru...
They are situated in the midst [of the world]. Among them, some are mountain-dwelling and some are space-dwelling;
their succession reaches as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.

The Khiḍḍāpadosika, Manopadosika, Sītavalāhaka, Uṇhavalāhaka, Candima the son of a god, and Suriya the son of a god—all these belong to the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), being the subjects of those Four Great Kings.
"Life. "Dependent upon" means by way of condition (*paṭicca*). "Limited" is a negation of increase. "Brief" refers to a short duration, a negation of long days.
"Momentary" refers to a short duration, a negation of any other interval of time. "Light" means very light, a negation of sluggishness.
"The other" is a negation of swiftness and strength. "Not to be traversed" means, by way of time, not capable of enduring a journey. "Not long-lasting."
"Of short duration" (*naciraṭṭhitika*) means it does not remain for long even by day; this is a negation of its lasting through the day.
"Of the Thirty-three" (*tāvatiṃsānaṃ*): thirty-three people have been reborn there, thus they are called the Thirty-three.
Furthermore, it is also said that "Thirty-three" is simply the name of those deities. Among them, some dwell on mountains and some dwell in the sky; such is their succession.

They have reached the Cakkavāḷa mountain. The same applies to the Yāmas and the others. For even within a single world-system, there is no succession of deities that has not reached the Cakkavāḷa mountain.

They are called *Yāmas* because they have gone (*yātā*), proceeded (*payātā*), and arrived (*sampattā*) at divine bliss. They are called *Tusitas* because they are contented (*tuṭṭhā*) and delighted (*pahaṭṭhā*).
They are called *Nimmānaratis* because they take delight after creating, according to their own wish, enjoyments that exceed the objects provided by nature.

*Nimmānaratī* (Delighting in Creations). Because they exercise control over enjoyments created by others after knowing their mental inclinations, they are called *Paranimmitavasavattī* (Masters over the Creations of Others).
Those who are connected with the assembly of Brahmas in the Brahma-vessel are *Brahmakāyikā* (Retainers of the Brahma-Body); this includes all Brahmas of the fivefold realm (*pañcavokāra*).
A *gandhabba* is one who is "to be gone to" (*gamaniyo*). *Samparāyo* is the world beyond (*paraloko*). "Monks, he who lives long lives for a hundred years."
"One who remains for a long time" means he remains for about a hundred years. "Or even less" means there is no one remaining beyond a hundred years, nor anyone remaining for two hundred years.
"One would despise it" means one would treat that life with contempt, thinking of it as something base.
They also read "hīḷeyyāna. "They pass away" means they transcend [that limit].
"Days and nights" refers to the divisions of night and day. "Is cut off" means that the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) ceases and reaches non-existence.
"The lifespan of mortals wastes away" means that the life-constituent (*āyusaṅkhāra*) of sentient beings goes to its destruction.

"Like the water of small streams": just as the water of a small stream whose flow has been cut off [evaporates], so too does the lifespan of mortals waste away. In the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*).
For the moment of existence of sentient beings is exceedingly brief, lasting for only a single thought-moment (*cittakkhaṇa*).

Just as a chariot wheel, even while rolling, rolls upon only one point of the rim, and even while standing still, stands upon only one point, even so the life of sentient beings lasts for only a single thought-moment;
as soon as that thought has ceased, the being is said to have ceased.
“Wise, most wise”: again, “wise” means *paṇḍita* (learned). “Possessing wisdom” (*dhitimā*): one who has wisdom (*dhiti*) is “possessing wisdom.
“Endowed with wisdom” means possessed of learning (*paṇḍicca*). “One whose evil is censured” (*dhīkatapāpa*): one whose evil is condemned.

To show this very same method of explanation, he said, “Wisdom (*dhī*) is called discernment (*paññā*),” and so forth. In that context, it is “discernment” (*paññā*) because it discerns (*pajānāti*). What does it discern? “This is suffering,” and so on.
[It is] the Noble Truths by way of method. In the Commentary, however, it is stated: "Wisdom is so called by way of making known. How does it make known?
It makes known [them] as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self. That very [wisdom] is a faculty (indriya) in the sense of being dominant because it overcomes ignorance;
or alternatively, it is a faculty because it exercises the lordship (indaṭṭha) in the characteristic of seeing. Wisdom itself as a faculty is the "faculty of wisdom" (paññindriya).

Furthermore, this [wisdom] has the characteristic of illuminating and the characteristic of understanding. For just as in a house with four walls, when a lamp is lit during the night, darkness ceases and light becomes manifest, even so wisdom has the characteristic of illuminating.
There is no illumination equal to the illumination of wisdom. Indeed, for one possessed of wisdom sitting cross-legged, the ten-thousandfold world system—
There is a single light. Therefore the Elder said:

“Great King, just as if a man were to bring an oil lamp into a house that is in darkness, once the lamp has been brought in, it destroys the darkness, produces radiance, makes light manifest, and renders forms visible; even so...”

“Indeed, Great King, when wisdom arises, it shatters the darkness of ignorance, generates the light of true knowledge, reveals the radiance of understanding, and makes the Noble Truths manifest. Thus, Great King, wisdom has the characteristic of illumination.
Furthermore, just as a skilled physician knows which foods and other things are suitable or unsuitable for his patients, so too is wisdom.

As they arise, one understands wholesome and unwholesome states, those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, the inferior and the superior, the dark and the bright, and those with a counterpart and those without a counterpart.
And this has been said by the General of the Dhamma: “One understands, one understands—therefore, friend, one is called ‘possessed of wisdom.
What does one understand? One understands: ‘This is suffering’”—this should be expanded in detail.
Thus its characteristic of understanding should be known.

Another method: wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer.
Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp. It is manifested as non-delusion.
Like a bird that has gone to the forest. "Wise in the aggregates" (*khandhadhīrā*):

they are wise in the aggregates because they cause knowledge to proceed regarding the five aggregates. "Wise in the elements" (*dhātudhīrā*): they are wise in the elements because they cause knowledge to proceed regarding the eighteen elements.
The meaning should be understood in the same manner for the remaining terms as well. Those wise ones spoke thus.
These wise ones spoke thus. "They speak" means they say, "It is small and limited.
"They utter" means they declare, "It is trifling and momentary. "They illuminate" means they establish it as, "It is light and brief.
"They express" means they describe it in various ways as, "It is not lasting and does not endure for long."
11. Now, showing the arising of calamity for those who do not act in such a way, he spoke the verse beginning with “I see.
Therein, “I see” means I perceive with the fleshly eye and so forth. “In the world” means in the realms of misery (apāya) and so on.
“Trembling” means quivering here and there. “This generation” refers to this body of beings. “Gone with craving” means one who has gone under the influence of craving.

The intended meaning is that they have been overcome and cast down. "In existences" (*bhaveṣu*) means in the realms of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth. "Lowly men" (*hīnā narā*) refers to men of inferior conduct.

"Lamenting in the mouth of death" (*maccumukhe lapanti*) means they wail when the time of death has arrived at the threshold of death. "Those whose craving has not departed" (*avītataṇhāse*) means those from whom craving has not vanished.

"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to sensual existence and the like. "In existences" (*bhaveṣu*) refers to sensual existence and so forth. Alternatively, it may mean "in various states of existence" (*bhavābhavesu*).
"In various states of existence" means in successive births.
"I see" means that one sees even with the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*). There are two kinds of fleshly eye: the composite eye (*sasambhāracakkhu*) and the sensitive eye (*pasādacakkhu*).
Of these, that which is established in the eye-socket, below by the bone of the eye-socket and above by the bone of the eyebrow—
The mass of flesh, variegated with white and black circles, which is demarcated externally by the two eye-sockets and the eyelashes,
and which is fastened to the brain by a cord of sinews protruding from the middle of the eye-socket—

this is called the "eye with its constituent parts" (*sasambhāra-cakkhu*). Furthermore, that sensitivity (*pasāda*) derived from the four great elements which is situated here and bound here— this is...

This is what is intended by the term "eye of sensitivity" (pasādacakkhu). It is located in the center of the black circle (kaṇhamaṇḍala) surrounded by a white circle (setamaṇḍala) of that eye together with its constituent parts;

it is situated in the region where the shape of the body appears to those standing directly in front, and in terms of its size, it extends across the seven layers of the eye-filaments (khipapaṭala), just as oil poured over the layers of a cotton wick permeates those layers.
The head of the *ū* vowel remains, establishing itself as the appropriate basis (*vatthu*) and door (*dvāra*) for eye-consciousness and the others.
It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees; thus, "I see with that fleshly eye.
"With the divine eye" means with such a divine eye as [the Buddha] said: "Bhikkhus, with the purified divine eye, I saw... "With the wisdom-eye" means...
“By the eye of wisdom” means by the eye of wisdom as it has come down in the passage: “The dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose.
“By the Buddha-eye” means by the Buddha-eye as it has come down in the passage: “Bhikkhus, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw...
“By the universal eye” means by the universal eye as it has come down in the passage: “The ‘universal eye’ is a term for omniscient knowledge.”
"I see" means that with the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), I see forms as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of the hand.

"I perceive" means that with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), I am conscious of the passing away and rebirth [of beings]. "I survey" means that with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), I look upon the Four Noble Truths.
"I contemplate" means that with the eye of the Buddha (*buddhacakkhu*), I reflect upon the faculties beginning with faith as the fifth. "I examine" means...
"I look all around and search with the universal eye at the five paths of guidance.
"Trembling with the quivering of craving" means trembling due to the movement of craving.

From this point on, the sequence ending with "trembling with the calamity of views" and so forth is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained. "Trembling repeatedly" means again and again.
“Trembling” (*phandamānaṃ*). “Quivering” (*vipphandamānaṃ*) means moving in various ways. “Shaking” (*vedhamānaṃ*) means trembling. “Shaking violently” (*pavedhamānaṃ*) means trembling with effort.
“Shaking intensely” (*sampavedhamānaṃ*) means trembling again and again; or the word is extended by means of a prefix. “Followed by craving” (*taṇhānugataṃ*) means entered by craving.
“Beset by craving” (*taṇhāyānusaṭaṃ*) means overwhelmed by craving. “Proximate to craving” (*taṇhāyāsannaṃ*)...
"Sunk in craving" means fallen by way of craving; "cast down" (*khitta*) by craving—or alternatively, the reading is *paripātita* (overthrown).

"Overcome" means crushed and overwhelmed by craving. "With mind consumed" means a mind seized after being exhausted [by craving]. Alternatively, it is "gone with craving" as if carried away by a flood;
it is "followed by craving" as if having fallen and gone due to the conditions of appropriated form.
Like a spread-out dark-blue mat covering the surface of the water, it is pervaded by craving. Like one submerged in a cesspool, it is close to craving.
Like one who has fallen from the top of a tree into hell, it is cast down by craving.

Like a physical form subject to grasping (upādiṇṇaka-rūpa) being overwhelmed by a union, it is overcome by craving. [This is] the insight that has arisen in one who comprehends the physical form subject to grasping.
Or alternatively: "one whose mind is overwhelmed by craving" means: through sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), it has reached craving;

through thirst for sense-pleasures (*kāmapipāsā*), it is followed by craving; through the taint of sense-pleasures (*kāmāsava*), it is permeated by craving; through the fever of sense-pleasures (*kāmapariḷāha*), it is near to craving; through attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmajjhosāna*), it is cast down by craving;
through the flood of sense-pleasures (*kāmogha*), it is overcome by craving; through clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), its mind is overwhelmed by craving—thus some explain it.

"In the realm of sense-desire" (*kāmabhava*) means in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). "In the realm of form" (*rūpabhava*) means in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). "In the formless realm" (*arūpabhava*) means in the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).

Their distinctions have already been explained below. "In various existences" (*bhavābhavesu*): "existence and non-existence" (*bhavābhava*)—here "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), and "non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to the fine-material and immaterial elements (*rūpārūpadhātu*). Alternatively, "existence" (*bhava*)...

The realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). "Non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). Among those various existences (*bhava*), "kamma-existence" (*kammabhava*) refers to the round of kamma.

"Re-existence" (*punabbhava*) refers to the round of resultant [existence] which leads to renewed becoming. "Sensual existence" (*kāmabhava*) refers to the realm of desire. "Kamma-existence" refers to the round of kamma.
Therein, it is called "existence" (*bhava*) because kamma-existence causes one to come into being. "Re-existence in sensual existence" refers to rebirth-existence within the realm of desire.
In the cycle of kamma-result (vipākavaṭṭa). It is called "existence" (bhava) because resultant existence comes to be. This same method applies to the existence of form (rūpabhava) and so forth.

And here, the phrases "in the existence of sense-sphere desire (kāmabhava), in the existence of form (rūpabhava), in the existence of the formless (arūpabhava)" are stated with reference to existence as location (okāsabhava). In all three cases, "kamma-existence" (kammabhava) refers to kamma-existence;
likewise, "renewed existence" (punabbhava) is stated with reference to rebirth-existence (upapattibhava). "Again and again existence" (punappunabbhava) means from one [life] to another.

"In rebirth" (*uppattiyaṃ*). "In a destination" (*gatiyā*) means in any one of the five destinations. "In the production of a personal existence" (*attabhāvābhinibbattiyaṃ*) means in the manifestation of personal existences.

"Not free from craving" (*avītataṇhā*): this is the root term. "Those whose craving has not departed" (*avigatataṇhā*): like momentary concentration, their craving has not departed because there is no momentary abandoning;

thus they are "those whose craving has not departed. "Those who have not cast off craving" (*acattataṇhā*): their craving has not been relinquished because there is no abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*).
"Craving not vomited up" (*avanta-taṇhā*) means that because there is an absence of abandonment by suppression, craving has not been vomited up.

"Craving not released" (*amutta-taṇhā*) means that because there is an absence of abandonment by absolute eradication, craving has not been released. "Craving not abandoned" (*appaḥīna-taṇhā*) means that because there is an absence of abandonment by subsiding, craving has not been abandoned.
"Craving not relinquished" (*appaṭinissaṭṭha-taṇhā*) means that because there is an absence of abandonment by escape, it remains established in existence (*bhava*).
Because they remain without relinquishing the underlying defilements (*anusaya-kilesa*), there is "unrelinquished craving" (*appaṭinissaṭṭha-taṇhā*). 12.

Now, since it is precisely through this unrelinquished craving that beings thus quiver and prattle, he spoke the verse beginning with "In what is cherished" (*mamāyite*) in order to encourage them toward the subduing of craving.
Therein, "in what is cherished" (*mamāyite*) refers to that which has been grasped as "mine" by means of craving, views, and the conceit of "mine-ness."
"In the matter" (*vatthusmiṃ*). "Behold! he said, addressing the listeners. "This too"—that is, this danger as well. The rest is quite clear.
"Two notions of 'mine'" (*dve mamattā*) means two attachments (*ālayā*). "As far as" (*yāvatā*) is a particle used in the sense of a limit or restriction.

"By what is reckoned as craving" (*taṇhāsaṅkhātena*) means by a portion of craving; *saṅkhā* and *saṅkhāta* are identical in meaning, as in such passages as "for the conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) is reckoned by perception (*saññānidānā*)," and so forth.
"Delimited" (*sīmakata*) means made into a boundary that is free from the fault of lack of demarcation, as in such passages as "one should designate a boundary not exceeding three *yojanas*.
"Defined" (*odhikata*) means made into a defined limit that is free from the fault of verbal indeterminacy, like a boundary-tree (*sīmantarikarukkha*).
"Circumscribed" (*pariyantakata*) means made into a defined limit. However, the boundary-tree is common to both [the delimited and the defined].
But this is "made bounded" (pariyantakata), like a single continuous row of palm trees.

"Appropriated" (pariggahita) means taken in every way, having relinquished dependence on others even for the sake of future time. "Coveted" (mamāyita) means treated as a personal possession, like a dwelling place where one has entered for the rains.
"This is mine" refers to what stands nearby; "that is mine" refers to what stands at a distance. "So much" is the delimitation of requisites.
“...as if one were not even to speak so much. *Ettāvatā* is a particle used in the sense of a limit, as in “*ettāvatā kho mahānāma*” (Thus far, Mahānāma).
*Kevalampi mahāpathaviṃ* means the entire great earth.
*Aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritaṃ* means the hundred-and-eightfold expansion of the movements of craving. Hundred-and-eightfold.
If one asks how this occurs: craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*)... [and so on] ...craving for mental phenomena (*dhammataṇhā*).

Thus, craving that proceeds through the cognitive process (*javanavīthi*) in the doors of the eye and so forth is like a son who receives his name from his father—such as "the merchant’s son" or "the brahmin’s son"—and has arisen with an object similar to his father.
And herein, craving for form is *rūpataṇhā* because it has form as its object; it relishes form by way of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).

Craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*) is that which proceeds by finding gratification through the state of lust accompanied by the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), thinking: "Form is permanent, stable, and eternal.

Craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is that which proceeds by finding gratification through the state of lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), thinking: "Form is annihilated, destroyed, and will cease to exist.
Craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) is that which proceeds by finding gratification in such a manner. Thus [it is said].
It is threefold. Just as there is craving for forms, so too are there cravings for sounds and the rest; thus these constitute eighteen modes of craving.
These are eighteen with respect to internal forms and so forth, and eighteen with respect to external forms and so forth, making thirty-six.
Thus, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present, totaling one hundred and eight. Of the internal...
Based on [internal objects], there arise such thoughts as “I am” or “I am thus,” totaling eighteen based on internal form and so forth.
Based on external [objects], there arise such thoughts as “I am by means of this” or “I am thus by means of this,” totaling eighteen based on external form and so forth;
thus, there are thirty-six. Likewise, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present.
"Thirty-six"— in this way, there are one hundred and eight modes of craving's wandering.
"Sakkāya-diṭṭhi with twenty bases" means that by taking each of the five aggregates— form and so forth—
as a basis according to the method beginning with "one regards form as self," they arise in four ways through the mode of grasping.
In the sense of being present, "view" regarding the body—consisting of the five aggregates—is "personality-belief" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
"Wrong view with ten bases" refers to wrong view proceeding in such a manner as "there is no giving, there is no sacrifice," and so forth;

it is a "wrong view" because it is a view that is not according to reality, or because it is a "perverse view" due to grasping erroneously, or because it is "contemptible" to the wise since it brings about what is harmful.

"View" (*diṭṭhi*) refers to wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). It has the characteristic of irrational adherence, the function of misapprehension, the manifestation of false adherence, and its proximate cause is the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones and so forth;
it should be regarded as the supreme fault. "The ten-based view of extremes" (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*) refers to views occurring in such a manner as:
"the world is eternal," "the world is non-eternal," "the world is finite," and so on, each taking one side [of the dichotomy].
The view that proceeds by way of grasping after having established a foundation is the "view with ten bases" (dasavatthukā diṭṭhi), which is a "view of extremes" (antaggāhikā diṭṭhi).
"Such a view as this" means a view of such a nature. "A resort of views" (diṭṭhigata) means gone among views.
This perspective is called a "resort of views" because it is included within the sixty-two views; it is a "thicket" (gahana) in the sense that the view itself is difficult to transcend.
The thicket of views is like a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, and a thicket of mountains.
In the sense of being fraught with danger and peril, it is like a wilderness of bandits, a wilderness of wild beasts, a waterless wilderness, and a wilderness of famine.
It is called the "perplexity of views" in the sense that it pierces through right view and in the sense that it causes confusion; for when wrong vision arises—

Right vision pierces through and opposes [wrong view]. Because it sometimes grasps at eternalism and sometimes at annihilationism, it is called "the vacillation of views" (*diṭṭhivipphandita*) due to its distorted flickering.
For one who follows a wrong view cannot remain established in a single position; sometimes he recollects eternalism, and sometimes annihilationism. View itself, in the sense of being a bond—
"Fetter" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the fetter of views. It is "grasping" (*gāha*) because, like crocodiles and other such creatures, it firmly seizes its object.
It is "fixation" (*patiṭṭhāha*) because of its state of being firmly established; for this [view] seizes by establishing itself through its powerful mode of occurrence.
It is "adherence" (*abhinivesa*) because it adheres by way of permanence and so forth, having transcended the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) through such modes as permanence.

"Grasping at others" (*parāmāsa*) means grasping from another. It is a "bad path" (*kummagga*) because it brings about what is harmful, or because it is the path to the wretched states of existence (*apāya*).

It is a "wrong path" (*micchāpatha*) because it is not the true way. For just as one who is confused about directions may be told, "This is the path to such-and-such a village," yet it does not lead him there, so too [is it with this path] when a proponent of wrong views [claims], "This is the path to a happy destination."
Even when grasped, this view does not lead to a happy destination; thus, from the perspective of being a path that is not according to reality, it is a "wrong path" (*micchā-patha*).

Because its intrinsic nature is wrong, it is "wrongness" (*micchatta*). Because fools wander about therein, it is a "ford" (*tittha*); and because it is both a ford and a source of misfortunes, it is a "ford-source" (*titthāyatana*).
Alternatively, it is the dwelling place of the sectarians (*titthiya*) in the sense of being their birthplace and their abode.
“Āyatana” also refers to a sectarian standpoint (*titthāyatana*). A grasp that has become perverted, or a grasp by way of perversion, is “perversion-grasp” (*vipariyesaggāha*).
A grasp of what is not the true nature is “perverse grasp” (*viparītaggāha*). A grasp that proceeds by way of such modes as “the impermanent is permanent” is “inversion-grasp” (*vipallāsaggāha*).
A grasp of an improper means is “wrong grasp” (*micchāgāha*). This occurs with respect to a matter that is not as it truly is, not its actual nature.
Grasping at a basis as "true," "as it really is," or "of its own nature" is the grasping [of what] "is not as it really is" as "as it really is.
"As many as" means however many. "The sixty-two views" refers to the sixty-two types of views found in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
"Even those who fear being cut off tremble" means even those who have developed the fear that [the king] will cut them off, overpowering them and seizing them by force.

They move. "Even when being taken away" means even when being cut off in the manner already described. "Even when taken away" means even when it has been cut off and seized in the manner already described.
"Even when apprehensive of change" means even when apprehensive of its being turned over and becoming otherwise. "Even when changing" means even at the time of turning over.
"Even when changed" means even when it has been turned over. "Quiver" means they move. "Tremble violently" means...
They move in every way. "They quiver" means they throb in various ways. "They tremble" means they shake upon seeing fear.

"They shudder" means they shake intensely due to the specific state of being paralyzed by fear. "They quiver violently" means they shake in every way due to the fear that causes the hair to stand on end.
"Phandamāne" is the accusative plural form. "Appodake" means having little water. "Parittodake" means...
"In water that is stirred up. "Upon the exhaustion of the water" means when the water has run dry.

"By cranes" refers to the remaining species of birds mentioned. "Being harassed" means being harmed, struck, or agitated. "Being tossed up" means being pulled out from within the mud or being swallowed.
"Being devoured" means being eaten. They quiver because of the crows; they writhe because of the hawks.
They quiver with their feathers; they tremble when seized by the beak due to the onset of death; they shake violently at the moment of being pierced;

they convulse as death approaches. "Having seen" means having seen the faults. "Having weighed" means having weighed the merits and faults. "Having scrutinized" means [having scrutinized] the merits and faults.
Having expanded upon it. "Having analyzed" means having set aside and excluded that which pertains to the loss of the basis (*vatthu-hāna-bhāgi*).

"Having made manifest" means having brought it to completion and having made it distinct. Alternatively, it means having released the fault of confusion by seeing through the differentiation of the basis;
having released the fault of lack of delimitation by weighing it through the determination of its measure; and having released the fault of the basis itself.
Having determined it by way of making a division; having freed it from the fault of delusion and having clarified it by way of making a supreme division;
having freed it from the fault of density and having made it manifest by means of making a natural division. "Having abandoned" means having relinquished. "Having given up" means having renounced.
"Not being possessive" means not making a home for it through craving and views. "Not grasping" refers to the stage prior to [wrong] view.
"Not grasping it through wisdom. "Not misapprehending" means not performing an estimation by way of applied thought (*vitakka*).
"Not adhering" means not entering [into it] by way of the view that enters the fixed course (*niyāma*).
"Not making" means not acting by way of the craving for appropriation (*pariggāha-taṇhā*). "Not generating" means [not acting] by way of the craving for renewed existence (*ponobhavika-taṇhā*).
"Not producing" (*ajanayamāno*): "not producing at all" (*asañjanayamāno*) means not producing specifically. "Not generating" (*anibbattayamāno*):
not generating by way of the craving for aspiration (*paṭṭhanā-taṇhā*). "Not causing to arise" (*anabhinibbattayamāno*): not causing to arise in every respect.
Alternatively, these terms have been augmented by means of prefixes (*upasagga*). Thus, herein is the gratification (*assāda*) of the first verse.

13. Having shown the danger (*ādīnava*) by means of the four verses following that, he now speaks the pair of verses beginning with "In both extremes" (*ubhosu antesu*) in order to show the escape (*nissaraṇa*) together with its method, as well as the benefit of that escape (*nissaraṇānisansa*);

or alternatively, having shown by all these [verses] the danger, the degradation, and the defilement (*saṃkilesa*) of sensual pleasures (*kāma*), he now speaks this pair of verses to show the benefit of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
Therein, "in both extremes" refers to contact (*phassa*), the arising of contact, and so forth.
"In two, in two delimitations. "Having removed desire" means having removed the lust of desire (*chandarāga*). "Having fully understood contact" means:

having thoroughly understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*) the entire complex of name-and-form—namely, contact such as eye-contact and so forth; or, following from contact, all immaterial phenomena associated with it; and, by way of their bases, doors, and objects, all material phenomena.

"Free from craving" (*anānugiddho*) means not being greedy for any phenomena, such as forms and the rest. "Not doing what he censures himself for" (*yadattagarahī tadakubbamāno*) means not performing that which he himself reproaches.

"The wise one is not smeared by what is seen or heard" (*na limpatī diṭṭhasutesu dhīro*) means that such a wise person, endowed with steadfastness (*dhitisampanno*), is not smeared by even one of the two kinds of taints regarding things seen or heard, just like the sky.
He is undefiled and has attained ultimate purity.
Contact is one extreme; contact is a single delimitation. It touches, thus it is "contact" (*phassa*).

This contact has the characteristic of touching, the function of impingement, the manifestation of a coming together, and its proximate cause is the object that has come into the range of the senses. For although this is an immaterial phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*),...
Because it proceeds toward its object in the very mode of touching, it has the characteristic of touching (*phusanalakkhaṇa*).

Although it does not adhere to its object even partially—just as the eye [does not adhere] to visible form, nor the ear to sound—it nevertheless strikes together the consciousness and the object, like a visual organ striking a visible form or an auditory organ striking a sound;

thus it has the function of striking together (*saṅghaṭṭanarasa*). Alternatively, because it arises from the striking together of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object, it is called "having the function of striking together" in the sense of attainment (*sampatti*).
This should be understood. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“There is no contact belonging to the four planes that does not have the characteristic of touching; however, only that which pertains to the five doors has the function of impingement.
For that which pertains to the five doors is named both ‘having the characteristic of touching’ and ‘having the function of impingement. But for that which pertains to the mind-door...”
"It has the characteristic of touching alone; its function is not that of physical impact.
Having said this, he cited this sutta:
"Great King, just as two rams might fight, so should the eye be regarded, like one of those rams."
Just as with the second ram, so should form be regarded. Just as their coming together, so should contact (phassa) be regarded.
Thus, contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impingement.
Great King, just as two people might strike one another, or two hands might strike one another—just as one hand, so should the eye be regarded; just as the second hand, so should [form be regarded].
“Form is to be seen; contact is to be seen as the meeting of those [three].
Thus, contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impingement,” so it is said in detail.
Or, just as in such passages as “having seen a form with the eye,” eye-consciousness and the rest are expressed by the names of the eye and so forth.
In the same way, it should be understood that here too they are spoken of by the names "eye" and so forth.
Therefore, in such passages as "the eye should be seen thus," the meaning should be understood according to this method: "eye-consciousness should be seen thus.

This being the case, because of the impact between the mind and its object, even in this sutta, by virtue of its function (kicca), it is established as having the "taste of impact" (saṅghaṭṭanarasa). [This refers to] the triad known as the coming together (sannipāta)...
However, because it is explained by way of its own cause, it has "convergence" as its manifestation. For in various places it is explained precisely by way of the cause thus:
"The meeting of the three is contact. And the meaning of this scriptural passage is that contact is the convergence of the three, not mere convergence itself.
Because it has been proclaimed in this way, it manifests in that very manner; thus it is said to have "convergence as its manifestation.
However, by way of its fruit as its manifestation, it is called "having feeling as its manifestation," for it brings feeling into manifestation—that is to say, it causes it to arise.

And while causing it to arise, just as [the color red] exists externally dependent on the substance known as lac even though the conditions for heat are present, [so too does this consciousness arise].
Heat produces softness in its own support, but not in the external heat-conditioned state known as glowing embers.
Likewise, although the object-base is an external condition, because it depends upon consciousness,
this arising of feeling occurs only in the consciousness that serves as its own support, and not in the base which serves as its condition.

It should be understood as "in the object" (*ārammaṇe va*). However, because it arises without obstruction when the object has been prepared by the corresponding attention and the faculty, this [contact] is called "having the object that has come into the range as its proximate cause" (*āpāthagata-visaya-padaṭṭhāna*).

That from which contact originates and arises is called "the origin of contact" (*phassa-samudaya*). For this has been said: "With the six sense bases as condition... (*saḷāyatana-paccayā*)... [and so on].
“Contact. The pair on the past is stated by way of time. The pair on feeling is stated by way of pleasure and pain, having taken equanimous feeling as pleasure itself because it was said:
“But equanimity, because of its peacefulness, is spoken of as pleasure. The pair on name-and-form is stated by way of the material and the immaterial.
The pair on the sense bases is stated by way of the process of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). The pair on personality (*sakkāya*) is stated by way of the five aggregates.
It should be understood as "spoken. In this context: it brings happiness, thus it is *sukhā* (pleasure); it is felt, thus it is *vedanā* (feeling); it causes suffering, thus it is *dukkhā* (pain).
That which has the characteristic of bending is *nāma* (name); that which has the characteristic of being affected (by change) is *rūpa* (form).

The six internal bases, beginning with the eye-base, are internal; the six external bases, beginning with the form-base, are external. The five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form, are *sakkāya* (personality) in the sense of existing.
Ignorance, kamma, craving, nutriment, contact, and name-and-form are the origin of the personal existence (sakkāya).
