Regarding "eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*): it is called the "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees; the meaning is that it enjoys and discerns visible forms.

Contact that proceeds from the eye is "eye-contact. Furthermore, by way of its co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance [conditions], it relates to the feeling associated with itself.

The condition is eightfold. "Hears" refers to the ear. This [ear] resides within the ear-canal along with its constituent parts, in a location shaped like a finger-ring and covered with fine, tawny hairs;
there it functions as the appropriate basis and door for ear-consciousness and the rest.
Contact that proceeds from the ear is "ear-contact. The same method applies to nose-contact and the others as well.

It smells, thus it is the nose (*ghāna*). It remains within the cavity of its physical base, in a location shaped like a goat’s hoof, establishing itself as the appropriate basis and door for nose-consciousness and the rest.
It draws life toward itself, thus it is the tongue (*jivhā*); or, in the sense of tasting, it is the tongue.
Excluding the very tip, the root, and the sides of the tongue along with their physical bases, it occupies the middle of the upper surface, in a shape like the point of a split lotus petal.
In its respective location, it remains establishing itself as the basis and door for tongue-consciousness and the rest.
It is called the "body" (kāya) because it is the source (āya) of base, tainted phenomena; "source" (āya) here means the place of arising.

To whatever extent there is the occurrence of what is clung-to (upādiṇṇa) within this body, therein the body-sensitivity (kāyappasāda) generally serves as the basis and door for body-consciousness and the rest, as appropriate.

"He remains accomplishing" means he stays engaged in practice. "He thinks" (munāti) is *mano*; the meaning is that it cognizes. *Mano* includes both the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Mental contact (*manosamphassa*) is the contact that proceeds from the mind.
To show that even the sixfold contact is of only two kinds, [the text says]: "designation-contact (*adhivacana-samphassa*) and resistance-contact (*paṭigha-samphassa*)."

He said: Contact associated with the mind-door is "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃphassa*). Contact associated with the five doors is "resistance-contact" (*paṭigha-saṃphassa*), because it arises through resistance toward the physical bases, objects, and so forth.

That which is to be experienced as pleasant when its object is a pleasant feeling is "to-be-experienced-as-pleasant. That which is to be experienced as painful when its object is a painful feeling is "to-be-experienced-as-painful.

That which is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant when its object is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is "to-be-experienced-as-neither-painful-nor-pleasant. In this context, "pleasure" (*sukha*) means that which pleases; one for whom it arises is "pleased" (*sukhita*).
The meaning is "it makes. Or, it thoroughly digs up and devours afflictions of body and mind; thus it is "ease" (*sukha*). It causes suffering;
thus it is "suffering" (*dukkha*), meaning that which arises makes one who possesses it suffer. "Neither suffering nor ease" is *adukkhamasukha*;
the letter *m* is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).

“Wholesome,” and so forth, are stated by way of their classification. Therein, “wholesome” is associated with the twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses; “unwholesome” is associated with the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses; and “indeterminate” is associated with the remaining indeterminate consciousnesses, which are resultant or functional.

Again, explaining by way of the divisions of existence, he says “belonging to the sense sphere” and so forth. That which is associated with the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Having abandoned the sense sphere, it courses in the fine-material realm, thus it is “belonging to the fine-material sphere” (*rūpāvacara*); it is associated with the fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses by way of being wholesome or indeterminate.

Having abandoned both the sensual and the fine-material, it moves in the immaterial; thus it is "immaterial-sphere" (*arūpāvacara*). It is associated with twelve types of immaterial-sphere consciousness by way of being wholesome or indeterminate.
Now, showing [the three doors] by way of misapprehension (*abhinivesa*), he says: "Emptiness" (*suññato*), and so forth. Therein, it is "emptiness" because it is empty of lust, hatred, and delusion.
It is "signless" (*animitta*) because it is signless of the signs of lust, hatred, and delusion. Of the aspirations (*paṇidhi*) for lust, hatred, and delusion...
Because it is non-existent, it is called "wishless" (*appaṇihita*).
Now, showing [the distinction] by way of what is included within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and what is not included, he says "mundane" (*lokiya*), and so forth.

"World" (*loka*) is said to be the cycle of existence in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating; that which is connected to the world by virtue of being included therein is "mundane. "Transcended" (*uttiṇṇo*)...
"Uttara" means "transcending the world" because it is not included within the world; thus it is "supramundane" (lokuttara). "Phusana" refers to the mode of touching.
"Samphusana" and "samphusitatta" are terms expanded by the addition of a prefix.
"Having made it known in this way" means making it manifest while knowing it; one "delimits" (tīreti) it, that is, one delimits it according to the manner to be described hereafter.
He reflects: he evaluates it as impermanent because its end is impermanence and because it has a beginning and an end;
as suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away and because it is the basis for suffering; as a disease because it is maintained by conditions and because it is the root of disease;
as a boil because it is joined with the sting of suffering, because it drips with the impurity of defilements, and because through arising, aging, and dissolution it is swollen, ripened, and burst.

It is "a dart" (salla) because it produces affliction, pierces within, and is difficult to extract; because it is to be censured, brings about non-prosperity, and is the basis for misfortune, it is "misery" (agha);
because it produces a state of lack of mastery and is the proximate cause of disease, it is "affliction" (ābādha);

because it is not subject to one's own control and is not compliant, it is "external" (para); and because it is broken down and disintegrated by sickness, old age, and death, it is "dissolution" (paloka).
It is a plague (*īti*) because it brings about manifold calamities. It is a misfortune (*upaddava*) because it brings about vast, unknown evils and because it serves as the basis for all adversities.
It is a terror (*bhaya*) because it is a source of all fears and because it is the opposite of the supreme consolation known as the subsiding of suffering.
It is afflicted by hatred (*dosa*) because it is pursued by manifold evils.
It is called an "affliction" (*upasagga*) because it is subject to non-endurance, like an external calamity.

It is "fickle" (*cala*) because it is shaken by the world-conditions (*lokadhamma*) such as disease, aging, death, gain, and so forth. It is "perishable" (*pabhaṅgu*) because its nature is to fall into dissolution both through external attack and by its own inherent essence.
It is "unstable" (*adhuvato*) because it falls away in every state and lacks any state of permanence. It is [called] "non-protection" (*atāyanatāya*)...

It is "without refuge" because it offers no safety that can be obtained; it is "without shelter" because it is unfit for reliance and because even those who rely upon it fail to perform the function of a shelter;

it is "without a resort" because it lacks the quality of being a support for those who depend on it from fear; it is "empty" because it is void of the permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood as they are imagined;
it is "vain" precisely because of that emptiness, or else because of its insignificance—for in the world, even that which is insignificant is called "vain."
It is called "empty" (suññata) because it is devoid of an owner, an inhabitant, an experiencer, a doer, and a controller.

It is called "non-self" (anattato) because it itself lacks the state of being owned and so forth. It is called "disadvantageous" (ādīnavato) because of the suffering inherent in its occurrence and because of the peril of suffering.
Alternatively, it is called "disadvantageous" (ādīnavo) because it "goes toward" (vāti) or "proceeds toward" misfortune (ādi); this is a term for a wretched person.
It is a designation. They are "from the perspective of disadvantage" because aggregates are likewise miserable, due to their similarity in being disadvantageous.

They are "of a nature to change" because they possess a twofold tendency toward transformation through both aging and death. They are "insubstantial" because of their weakness and because they are easily broken like pith.
They are "the root of misfortune" because they are the cause of misfortune. They are "murderers" because they betray trust, like a friend with a treacherous face.

It is "from non-existence" (*vibhavato*) because it is devoid of becoming and has arisen from the absence of becoming. It is "with taints" (*sāsavato*) because it is the basis for the taints (*āsava*).

It is "conditioned" (*saṅkhatato*) because it is constructed by causes and conditions. It is "the bait of Māra" (*mārāmisato*) because it serves as the material sustenance for the Māra of death and the Māra of defilements.

It is "subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death" (*jātijarābyādhimaraṇadhammato*) because its nature consists of birth, aging, sickness, and death. It is "subject to sorrow, lamentation, despair, and anguish" (*sokaparidevaupāyāsadhammato*) because it is the cause of sorrow, lamentation, despair, and anguish.
He scrutinizes them as a state of defilement because craving, views, and misconduct are by nature subject to defilement;

as origination because they arise by way of ignorance, karma, craving, and the six sense bases; as passing away because of their absence; as gratification because of the sweet taste of desire and lust for contact;
as danger because of the transformation of contact; and as escape because of the renunciation of both. Thus he scrutinizes them.
In all these instances, the phrase "he crosses over" (*tīreti*) should be understood as the remainder of the reading.
"He abandons" (*pajahati*) means he draws [it] out from his own continuum. "He dispels" (*vinodeti*) means he strikes it away. "He makes it vanish" (*byantiṃ karoti*) means he makes it reach its end.

"He brings it to non-existence" (*anabhāvaṃ gameti*) means he causes it to go to non-existence little by little. It is severed by the sword of the Noble Path—the [sword] consisting of craving and ignorance.
"They have their root cut" means their root has been severed. "They have had their base made like a palm stump" (*tālāvatthukatā*):
just as when a palmyra tree is uprooted along with its roots and only its base remains in that spot, the regrowth of that palm is no longer perceived;
even so, having uprooted the "flavors" of form and so forth together with their roots by means of the weapon of the Noble Path—
When their mental continuity has been established as a mere basis by virtue of having previously arisen in the past, all of them are called "made like the trunk of a palmyra tree" (*tālāvatthukatā*).
"Of whomsoever" (*yasseso*) means of whichever person this greed belongs. "Cut off" (*samucchinno*) means severed.
"Calmed" (*vūpasanto*) means calmed by its fruit. "Allayed" (*paṭipassaddho*) means become tranquil through the abandonment of agitation. [This is] by means of the prefix (*upasaggena*).
Or the state has increased. "Incapable of arising" means incapable of arising again. "Burnt by the fire of knowledge" means consumed by the fire of path-knowledge.
Alternatively, it is abandoned together with its basis, like a vessel containing poison that has been discarded along with the poison itself.
It is "completely cut off" (samucchinna) like a poisonous creeper whose roots have been severed. [It is like] water on a hearth...
Some describe it thus: it is calmed like embers extinguished by being sprinkled with water;
it is tranquilized like a drop of water fallen upon extinguished embers; it is incapable of arising again like a seed whose cause for sprouting has been cut off;
and it is burnt up by the fire of knowledge like a tree struck down by a lightning bolt.
"Free from lust" (*vītagedha*) is said by way of relinquishing one's own being. "Devoid of lust" (*vigatagedha*) is by way of relinquishing the state of attachment toward an object.
"Abandoned lust" (*cattagedha*) is by way of showing the state of not taking it up again. "Released from lust" (*muttagedha*) is by way of liberation from the continuity [of craving].
"Lust abandoned" (*pahīnagedha*) is by way of showing that even for one who is released, there is no lingering anywhere. "Renounced lust" (*paṭinissaṭṭhagedha*)...

This is stated by way of showing the relinquishment (*nissagga*) of what was previously taken up. It should be applied according to the method already explained for the terms "one free from passion" (*vītarāgo*), "one whose passion has departed" (*vigatarāgo*), and "one whose passion is cut off" (*cattarāgo*).
In this context, *gedha* (greed) is so called by way of grasping; *rāga* (passion) is so called by way of coloring or attachment.

*Nicchāto* means one who is without craving (*nittaṇho*). There is also a reading *nicchado*; the meaning is "devoid of the covering of craving" (*taṇhāchadanavirahito*). *Nibbuto* means one whose nature is extinguished (*nibbutasabhāvo*).
"Cool-become" means having a nature that is cool. "Experiencing happiness" means having a nature that experiences bodily and mental happiness.
"By being become-Brahma" means by way of a supreme nature. "By oneself" means by the mind.

"And because of what has been done" means because of the state of having performed evil kamma. "And because of what has not been done" means because of the state of not having performed wholesome [kamma].

"‘I have committed bodily misconduct; I have not performed good bodily conduct,’ and so forth, are stated by way of the doors, by way of non-abstinence and abstinence, and by way of the courses of kamma.

‘One who does not fulfill the precepts,’ and so forth, are stated by way of the fourfold purification of virtue. ‘One who is not devoted to wakefulness’ is stated by way of the five kinds of wakefulness.
‘By means of mindfulness and clear comprehension’ is stated by way of clear comprehension of what is beneficial, and so forth."
It should be understood that the factors conducive to enlightenment, beginning with the "four foundations of mindfulness," are taught according to both the mundane and supramundane levels;
whereas those beginning with "Suffering has not been fully understood by me" are stated according to the four noble truths.
Their meaning is already evident, as they follow the methods explained in their respective places.
The terms *dhīra* (steadfast) and *paṇḍita* (wise) have meanings already explained by the seven [preceding] terms. Furthermore, he is *dhīra* in the sense of being unshakable regarding suffering;

*paṇḍita* in the sense of not being swept away by pleasure; *paññavā* (possessed of wisdom) in the sense of having cultivated familiarity with matters pertaining to the present life and the future life;

*buddhimā* (intelligent) in the sense of being immovable regarding his own welfare and the welfare of others; and *ñāṇī* (possessed of knowledge) in the sense of not retreating from the profound and the shallow.

It is *vibhāvī* (discerning) in the sense of illuminating meanings that are hidden and concealed. It is *medhāvī* (wise) in the sense of being like a scale in its stainless purification (*nikkilesa-vyavadāna*).
"It is not smeared" (*na limpati*) means it is not smeared by its own kind, like a line drawn in the sky.

"It is not thoroughly smeared" (*na palimpati*) means it is not smeared in a particular way. "It is not completely smeared" (*na upalimpati*) means even when there is contact, it is not smeared, like a line on the palm of the hand. "Unsmeared" (*alitta*)—
Even when in contact, it is not defiled, like a precious gem placed upon a cloth from Kāśī.
"Unburnt" (apalitta) means it is especially not defiled, like a cloth wrapped around a precious gem.
"Untainted" (anupalitta) means that even having approached, it does not adhere, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. "Departed" (nikkhanta) means having gone out from prison.
"Like one who has fled": "escaped" means one who has abandoned evil, like a defiled object entrusted to an enemy.
"Completely liberated" means well-freed, like one who, having destroyed their attachment to an object that could be seized, does not return again.

"Dissociated" means not joined with the defilements, like a sick person released from a disease. "With a mind free from boundaries" means with a mind from which the boundaries [of the defilements] have departed.
"By mind" means by a mind liberated from all states of existence, all objects, and all defilements.
In the verse beginning with "The full understanding of perception," this is the summary of the meaning:

it is not only contact that is meant, but rather perception—divided into the categories of sensual perception and so forth—or, according to the method previously explained, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) following upon perception.
Having fully understood through the three kinds of full comprehension, one may cross over even the fourfold flood by means of this practice.

Then, having crossed the flood, that sage whose taints are destroyed—being unstained by the grasping of craving and views due to the abandonment of the defilements of craving and views—is "one whose arrow is extracted" because he has pulled out the arrows of passion and the rest;
and being diligent, he moves about having attained the perfection of mindfulness. In the prior stage...

Or, practicing with diligence, having extracted the arrow by means of that diligent practice, he does not long for this world or the next—consisting of his own future personal existence and so forth—but rather, with the cessation of the final consciousness, he attains Parinibbāna like a fire without fuel.
Thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship, establishing the guide of the Dhamma; but not by this [other method].
He produced either the path or the fruit through the teaching, because it was taught to one whose taints were exhausted.
Perception (saññā) is so called because it perceives an object distinguished by blue and other colors. It has the characteristic of perceiving and the function of recognition.
Indeed, there is no perception belonging to the four planes that does not have the characteristic of perceiving; all perceptions have precisely the characteristic of perceiving. That which...
In this context, when one recognizes [something] by means of a mark (*abhijñāṇa*), that is called "the function of subsequent recognition" (*paccābhijñāṇarasa*).
For example, when a carpenter has made a mark on a piece of wood and later recognizes it again by that very mark;
or when a man observes a mark such as a black mole and later identifies him by that mark, saying, "This is so-and-so."
The sequence of events should be understood as occurring at the time of recognition: when the king’s treasurer, who guards his ornaments,
has tied a name-tag to each particular ornament and says, "Bring such-and-such an ornament," [the man] lights a lamp,
enters the inner chamber, reads the tag, and brings that very ornament.
Another method: In its comprehensive sense, perception has the characteristic of perceiving.

Its function is to make a sign as a condition for subsequent perception, like carpenters and others with respect to timber and so forth. Its manifestation is the forming of an adherence according to the sign as it was grasped, like a blind man who has seen an elephant;
or its manifestation is non-abiding for long, because its mode of existence does not penetrate deeply into the object, like a flash of lightning.
It is like the perception of "men" that arises in young deer regarding grass figures of men, which has the appearance of the object as its proximate cause.

Furthermore, that [perception] which is associated with knowledge follows knowledge alone; it should be understood as being like the remaining properties following the earth and so forth in the case of "earth" and so on when they include their constituent parts.
Perception associated with sensual desire is perception of sensual desire. Perception associated with ill will is perception of ill will. Perception associated with cruelty is perception of cruelty.

Among these, two arise both in relation to sentient beings and in relation to formations. For perception of sensual desire arises in one who is thinking of a dear and pleasing sentient being or formation; perception of ill will [arises] in relation to what is not dear or pleasing.
Having become angry with either sentient beings or formations, it arises from the moment of looking [at them] until their destruction.
The perception of cruelty does not arise toward formations, for there is no such thing as a formation that can be made to suffer.
However, it arises toward sentient beings at the time of thinking, "May these beings be killed, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they cease to exist."
Perception associated with renunciation is "perception of renunciation. This is sense-sphere perception during the preliminary stage of the foul (asubha);

it is fine-material-sphere perception during the foul meditative absorption (jhāna); and it is supramundane perception at the time of the arising of the path and fruit when that absorption has been made the basis.

Perception associated with non-ill will is "perception of non-ill will. This is sense-sphere perception during the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā); [it is fine-material-sphere perception] during the loving-kindness absorption...
The fine-material-sphere [perception] is that which arises when that jhāna is made the basis; at the time of the arising of the path and fruit, it is supramundane.

Perception associated with non-cruelty is "non-cruelty perception"; that is fine-material-sphere during the preliminary stage of compassion, fine-material-sphere during the compassion-jhāna, and supramundane at the time of the arising of the path and fruit when that jhāna is made the basis. When non-greed is the head [of the wholesome root], then...
The other two follow along with that. When loving-kindness (*mettā*) is predominant, the other two follow along with it;
when compassion (*karuṇā*) is predominant, the other two follow along with it.

Perception arisen by taking visible forms as its object is "perception of forms" (*rūpasaññā*). The same method applies to the perception of sounds and so forth. This [is defined] precisely from the perspective of its object.
This is the name. Because the objects have been stated, the bases for eye-contact and so forth are also implicitly stated.
"Whatever perception is of such a kind" should be understood as including other types such as "perception born of impingement-contact" and "perception born of designation-contact.
In this context, even "perception born of designation-contact" is, by way of a figurative expression, simply sixfold, pertaining to the six doors.

For the three formless aggregates, having themselves become the backbone, give the name "perception born of designation-contact" (*adhivacana-samphassajā saññā*) to the perception co-nascent with themselves.

However, in the direct sense, "perception born of impingement-contact" (*paṭigha-samphassajā saññā*) refers to perception belonging to the five doors, while "perception born of designation-contact" refers to perception belonging to the mind door.
It should be understood that these [three] are included within "excessive perception."
*Saṇñā* is a name for its own nature. *Sañjānanā* is the mode of perceiving. *Sañjānitattaṃ* is the state of having perceived. Regarding *avijjogha*:
in the sense of being unfit to be filled, bodily misconduct and so forth are called *avindiya*, meaning "unobtainable.
One finds (*vindati*) that which is *avindiya*; thus it is *avijjā*. Conversely, bodily good conduct and so forth are called *vindiya*; that which is *vindiya*...

It is called ignorance (*avijjā*) because one does not find [the truth]. It is also ignorance because it makes unknown the meaning of the aggregates as a "heap," the meaning of the sense-bases as a "base," the meaning of the elements as "emptiness," the meaning of the faculties as "predominance," and the meaning of the truths as "suchness.

Furthermore, it is ignorance because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning—suffering and so forth—as described by way of oppression and so on. [It is ignorance] regarding that which is devoid of extremes...

It is called *avijjā* (ignorance) because it causes sentient beings to speed along (*javāpeti*) within saṃsāra—through the various wombs, destinies, states of existence, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

Etymologically, it is ignorance because it speeds toward things that do not exist in the ultimate sense, such as "woman" or "man," while it does not speed toward things that do exist, such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
Furthermore, [it is ignorance] regarding the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and the rest, and regarding dependent origination and dependently originated phenomena.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it conceals phenomena; that is the flood of ignorance. One might cross over by means of the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*);

one might swim across by means of the flood of existence (*bhavogha*); one might transcend by means of the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*); and one might pass beyond by means of the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*).

Alternatively, one might cross over by way of abandoning through the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*); one might swim across by way of abandoning through the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*).
One would transcend it by means of abandonment through the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga). One would pass beyond it by means of abandonment through the path of arahantship (arahattamagga).

Alternatively, some say that "the five terms beginning with 'cross over' (tareyya) should be connected with the five kinds of abandonment beginning with 'abandonment by means of its own nature' (tadaṅgappahāna).
Having stated that "mona is called knowledge" (ñāṇa), he said "that which is wisdom, understanding," and so forth, in order to show its classifications.

Setting aside that which has been explained in the same manner, there is the phrase: “Non-delusion is the investigation of phenomena. Non-delusion is the antidote to the non-cultivation of wholesome states and is the cause for their cultivation.
Through non-delusion, one grasps things without error, because one who is deluded grasps things erroneously.

By means of non-delusion, bearing things as they truly are according to their true nature, one proceeds in accordance with the actual mode of being. For the deluded person [perceives] the real as unreal...
One grasps at what is not true as true; thus, there is no suffering from failing to obtain what was desired.
For one who is undeluded, because such reflections as "How could that be obtained here? are possible, there is no suffering of death.

Indeed, dying in a state of delusion is suffering, and that does not occur for one who is undeluded. For those who have gone forth, it is pleasant to dwell together; [this is not so] in the animal realm.
Rebirth does not occur. For it is through delusion that those who are perpetually bewildered are reborn in the animal realm.
Non-delusion (*amoha*), being the opposite of delusion, prevents the state of lack of balance caused by delusion.
Through non-delusion, there arises the perception of non-harming, the perception of elements, the practice of the middle way, and the breaking of the latter two fetters. The latter...
By the power of that very [non-delusion], two foundations of mindfulness are accomplished. Non-delusion is a condition for long life.
For one who is undeluded, having understood what is beneficial and what is harmful, avoids the harmful and pursues the beneficial, becomes long-lived, and does not fall away from his own excellence.
Indeed, by doing only what is beneficial for himself, the undeluded person perfects himself.
It is a condition for the noble abiding; one becomes extinguished amidst those on the side of equanimity because of the absence of all clinging due to non-delusion.

Through non-delusion, there is the vision of non-self. For one who is undeluded, skilled in grasping things as they truly are, awakens to the five aggregates—which lack a leader—as being without a leader.
And just as through this there is the vision of non-self, so too [is there] the vision of self.
"By delusion. For who indeed, having awakened to the emptiness of self, would again fall into confusion?
"Endowed with that knowledge" means one who has become possessed of the kind of knowledge described above—the sage (muni) who is still in training (sekkha), and so forth.
"Attained to sagehood" means having acquired knowledge and reached the state of a sage. "Three" is the numerical limit. "Sage-qualities" (moneyyāni): [text fragment].
The states that constitute the practice leading to the state of a sage and to sagehood are the qualities of the Dhamma.

Among these, bodily sagehood (*kāyamoneyya*) is to be understood by way of the body as intimation and the material body; verbal sagehood (*vacīmoneyya*) is to be understood by way of speech as intimation and speech as sound;
and mental sagehood (*manomoneyya*) is to be understood by way of the mind-door consciousness and so forth. It is the abandoning of the three kinds of bodily misconduct.

The abandoning of misconduct occurring through the body, such as the performance of killing living beings and so forth. Bodily good conduct (*kāyasucarita*) is wholesome conduct occurring through the body.
Knowledge regarding the body (*kāyārammaṇe ñāṇa*) is knowledge that occurs with respect to the body as its object by way of [contemplating it as] impermanent and so forth.
Full understanding of the body (*kāyapariññā*) is by way of knowing the body through the full understandings of the known, the scrutinized, and the abandoned.

"Knowledge that has occurred": the path accompanied by full understanding (*pariññā*). "The path produced after having comprehended the internal body" means the path generated after having reflected upon the internal body.
"The abandoning of desire and lust for the body" means the relinquishing of craving, desire, and lust for the body.
"The cessation of bodily formations" means the stopping and suppression of inhalation and exhalation; it is the attainment of the fourth jhāna.
"Cessation of verbal formations" refers to the cessation and suppression of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), which is the attainment of the second *jhāna*.

"Cessation of mental formations" refers to the cessation and suppression of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedanā*), which is the attainment of the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding the first verse, in the phrases "silent in body" and so forth, one is "silent in body" by virtue of abandoning bodily misconduct. By virtue of abandoning verbal misconduct... [the one is silent in speech].

He is a sage of speech (*vācāmuni*). He is a sage of mind (*manomuni*) by virtue of abandoning mental misconduct. He is a sage free from taints (*anāsavamuni*) by virtue of abandoning all that is unwholesome.
"Endowed with sagacity" (*moneyyasampanna*) means that having known what is to be known, he is endowed with sagacity because he abides in the fruit [of liberation].
"They call him the abandoner of all" means they speak of him as the abandoner of all because he abides having abandoned all defilements.

Regarding the second verse, *ninhātapāpako* should be understood as follows: one who, by means of the knowledge of the Path (*maggañāṇa*), has washed away and cleansed all evils—which are capable of arising through internal and external objects within every sense-sphere (*āyatana*) designated as "internal" and "external"—is thus called "one whose evils have been washed away.
Those dwelling in the midst of a household are "householder sages" (*agāramunino*); those who have gone forth into homelessness are "homeless sages" (*anagāramunino*).

In this context, those in training (*sekkhā*) are the sages of training (*sekkhamunino*). The arahants are the sages beyond training (*asekkhamunino*). The paccekabuddhas are the solitary sages (*paccekamunino*).
The perfectly enlightened buddhas (*sammāsambuddhā*) are the sages of sages (*munimunino*).

Again, by way of a question arising from a desire to speak further, he asked: "Who are the household sages (*agāramunino*)? [The answer is: "Householders (*agārikā*)" refers to those engaged in household tasks such as plowing and cattle-herding.
*Niyyutta*: those who are directed toward [the goal]. *Diṭṭhapada*: those who have seen Nibbāna. *Viññātasāsana*:

those for whom the teaching of the three trainings has been understood; thus they are called "those who have understood the teaching. *Anagāra*: those who have no householders' work such as plowing or cattle-tending; having gone forth, they are called "homeless ones" (*anagārā*). *Satta sekkhā*:
the seven types of trainees, beginning with the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). They are so called because they train in the three trainings (*tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhanti*).

Those in training are *sekkhā*. Those who do not train are *asekkhā*. Because they have awakened to the Four Noble Truths entirely by themselves and without a teacher, depending on various causes, they are called *paccekabuddhas* or *paccekamunis*.
Regarding the statement that "Tathāgatas are called *munimunino*," here the Blessed One is a Tathāgata for eight reasons—namely, *tathā*...
He is a *tathāgata* because he has come (*āgata*) in suchness; he is a *tathāgata* because he has gone (*gata*) in suchness; he is a *tathāgata* because he has come to the characteristic of suchness;

he is a *tathāgata* because he has perfectly awakened to the phenomena of suchness as they truly are; he is a *tathāgata* by virtue of seeing things as they are; he is a *tathāgata* by virtue of speaking things as they are;
he is a *tathāgata* by virtue of acting things as they are; and he is a *tathāgata* in the sense of overcoming.

How is it that the Blessed One is a “Tathāgata” because he has come in such a way? It is because he has come in the same manner as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones who exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world.
What is meant by this? By the very same aspiration through which the previous Blessed Ones came, our Blessed One has also come.

Alternatively, it is because he has come in the same manner as the previous Blessed Ones [who practiced] what is known as generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity.
Having fulfilled the thirty perfections— namely, the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten near-perfections (*upapāramī*),
and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)— and having made the five great renunciations, namely the relinquishing of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, children, and wife;
and having fulfilled the preliminary practices, former conduct, teaching of the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of others, and so forth, he reached the pinnacle of the practice of wisdom.
Just as they came, so too has our Blessed One come. And just as the previous Blessed Ones came having developed and fulfilled the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
and the noble eightfold path, so too has our Blessed One come.
Thus he has come in that way, therefore he is the Tathāgata.
And as the sages beginning with Buddha Dīpaṅkara have come here to the state of omniscience, so too this Sage of the Sakyas has come;
for that reason, the Visionary One is called the Tathāgata.
How is he a Tathāgata because he has gone thus (tathā-gata)? He has gone in the same way that the previous Blessed Ones went when they were newly born.
And how did they go? For as soon as they were born, having stood upon the earth with level feet, they went seven steps toward the north. As it is said:
"Ānanda, as soon as the Bodhisatta was born, having stood upon the earth with level feet, facing the north..."
He walks with the stride of a lion; while a white parasol is held over him, he surveys all directions and utters this lion’s roar:
“I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world;
this is the final birth; now there is no more renewed existence.”
And that gait of his was true and not false, serving as a precursor to many distinguished attainments.
For the fact that he stood with level feet immediately upon birth was a precursor to his acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
His facing toward the north, moreover, was a precursor to his state of being supreme over the entire world. His stride of seven steps—

The obtaining of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*sattabojjhaṅga*). Furthermore, the waving of the yak-tail whisks mentioned here in the phrase "Yak-tail whisks with golden handles are waved" signifies the crushing of all rival teachers.
The holding of the white parasol signifies the obtaining of the supreme, stainless white parasol of the liberation of Arahantship.
The surveying of all directions signifies the obtaining of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇa*). As for the uttering of the voice of a bull (*āsabhivācā*):

This was the omen of his setting in motion the irreversible, supreme Wheel of Dhamma. Thus the Blessed One departed, and that departure was true and not false, insofar as it served as the omen for those very specific attainments. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"Just as soon as he was born, the Lord of Kine touched the earth with his even feet;”
Thus Gotama strode seven steps, and the gods held up a white parasol for him.
Having gone those seven steps, Gotama surveyed the quarters all around.
He uttered a voice endowed with eight factors, like a lion standing upon the peak of a mountain.
Thus he has come (tathā-āgata) is a Tathāgata.
Alternatively, just as the previous Blessed Ones did, this Blessed One likewise [overcame] sensual desire through renunciation...

[and so on]... the hindrances through the first jhāna... [and so on]... the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence... [and so on]... all defilements through the path of Arahatship.
Having abandoned [defilements] and gone, he is thus "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone).
How is he "Tathāgata" as one who has come to the true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇa*)? The characteristic of hardness in the earth element is true and not false;
the characteristic of trickling in the water element, the characteristic of heat in the fire element, and the characteristic of motion in the wind element...

The characteristic of distension belongs to the space element; the characteristic of non-obstruction belongs to the space element; the characteristic of cognizing belongs to the consciousness element.

The characteristic of being afflicted belongs to form; the characteristic of being felt belongs to feeling; the characteristic of perceiving belongs to perception; the characteristic of volitional formation belongs to mental formations; the characteristic of cognizing belongs to consciousness.

Applied thought has the characteristic of directing the mind; sustained thought has the characteristic of examining; rapture has the characteristic of pervading; pleasure has the characteristic of gratification; one-pointedness of mind has the characteristic of non-distraction;

contact has the characteristic of touching. The faculty of faith has the characteristic of resolution; the faculty of energy has the characteristic of exertion; the faculty of mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; the faculty of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction; the faculty of wisdom has the characteristic of understanding.

The characteristic of the power of faith is unshakability by lack of faith; that of the power of energy is unshakability by laziness; that of the power of mindfulness is unshakability by forgetfulness; that of the power of concentration is unshakability by restlessness; and that of the power of wisdom is unshakability by ignorance.

The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor is establishing; that of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is investigating; that of the energy enlightenment factor is exerting;
that of the rapture enlightenment factor is pervading; that of the tranquility enlightenment factor is...

The characteristic of tranquility belongs to the enlightenment factor of concentration; the characteristic of non-distraction belongs to the enlightenment factor of equanimity; and the characteristic of reflective discernment belongs to the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Right view has the characteristic of seeing; right intention has the characteristic of directing onto; and right speech has the characteristic of...
The characteristic of right action is undertaking; the characteristic of right livelihood is purification; the characteristic of right effort is exertion;
the characteristic of right mindfulness is establishing; the characteristic of right concentration is non-distraction.
The characteristic of ignorance is unknowing; the characteristic of volitional formations is intending; the characteristic of consciousness is cognizing.
The characteristic of name-and-form is bending; the characteristic of form is being affected; the characteristic of the six sense bases is being a base;
the characteristic of contact is touching; the characteristic of feeling is being felt; the characteristic of craving is being a cause; the characteristic of clinging is grasping;
the characteristic of becoming is accumulating; the characteristic of birth is arising; the characteristic of aging is decaying.

Death has the characteristic of passing away; the elements have the characteristic of emptiness; the sense bases have the characteristic of being bases; the foundations of mindfulness have the characteristic of establishing;
the right efforts have the characteristic of exertion; the bases of psychic power have the characteristic of succeeding; the faculties have the characteristic of predominance.

The powers have the characteristic of being unshakable; the factors of enlightenment have the characteristic of leading out; the path has the characteristic of being a cause. The truths have the characteristic of being suchness;
serenity has the characteristic of non-distraction; insight has the characteristic of contemplation; serenity and insight have the characteristic of having a single flavor;

the pair-yoked [practice] has the characteristic of not overstepping one another. Purification of virtue has the characteristic of restraint; purification of mind has the characteristic of non-distraction; purification of view...
The characteristic of vision is the characteristic of the knowledge of destruction; the characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is the characteristic of tranquility;
the characteristic of zeal is the characteristic of the root.

The characteristic of attention is the characteristic of origination; the characteristic of contact is the characteristic of convergence; the characteristic of feeling is the characteristic of meeting.

Concentration has the characteristic of being foremost; mindfulness has the characteristic of sovereignty; wisdom has the characteristic of being superior to that; liberation has the characteristic of being the core;
and Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, has the characteristic of being the ultimate goal—this is true and not otherwise.
This is the "characteristic of suchness" (*tathalakkhaṇa*). Because he has come by way of the course of knowledge, having reached and attained it without missing it, he is the Tathāgata. Thus...
He is called the Tathāgata because he has come to the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*).
How is he the Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of things as they really are (*yāthāvato*)? The "true things" (*tathadhammā*) are the Four Noble Truths.
As it is said in detail: "Monks, these four are true, not untrue, not otherwise. Which four? 'This is suffering,' monks—this is true, this is not untrue, this is not otherwise," and so forth.
And because the Blessed One has fully awakened to those [truths], he is called the "Tathāgata" due to his having thus fully awakened; for here the word *gata* has the sense of "fully awakened.
Furthermore, the meaning of the arising and the coming-to-be of aging-and-death through the condition of birth is *tatha* (thus), not otherwise, not different...
[and so on] ...the meaning of the arising and the coming-to-be of volitional formations through the condition of ignorance is *tatha*, not otherwise, not different. Thus, regarding ignorance...
The meaning of conditionality for volitional formations... [and so on] ...the meaning of conditionality for birth and for aging-and-death is such, not otherwise, not different.
The Blessed One has fully awakened to all that; because he has fully awakened to those "suchnesses" (*tathatā*), he is the Tathāgata.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the suchness of phenomena exactly as they are.

How is the Tathāgata “one who sees things as they truly are”? In the world with its devas... [as in the standard formula] ...among the generation including devas and humans, whatever form-object there is that comes within the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One knows and sees it in all its aspects.
By knowing and seeing it thus, he [discerns it] by way of the desirable, the undesirable, and so forth.

Or, by way of the terms available among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, it is analyzed through numerous names—thirteen sections and fifty-two methods—in such a manner as: "What is that form which is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)?
It is that form derived from the four great elements which possesses visible appearance, is with resistance, and is blue, yellow," and so forth.
It is exactly so; it is not otherwise. This same principle applies to sounds and other objects that come within the range of the ear-door and the rest.
And this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... [and] among the generation with its devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed..."
“Whatever has been cognized, attained, sought after, or explored by the mind—that I know... [and so on] ...that I have directly known.
That is known by the Tathāgata; that does not stand before the Tathāgata. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they truly are (*tathadassitā*).
In this context, the derivation of the term *Tathāgata* should be understood in the sense of “one who sees things as they truly are.”
In what sense is the Tathāgata one who speaks truthfully? From the night the Blessed One sat upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment and,
having crushed the heads of the four Māras, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
until the night he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue between the twin Sāla trees— in this interval spanning forty-five years— [he spoke only that which is so].

In the first, middle, and last dispensations, whatever discourse (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), and so forth, up to the analytical exposition (vedalla) was spoken by the Blessed One—at all times—that is entirely irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing;
it is neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect, and it crushes the intoxication of lust, hatred, and delusion. Not even a hair’s breadth exists therein [of fault].

When it is compared, all of it is exactly the same—neither false nor otherwise—just as if it were stamped with a single seal, measured by a single scale, or weighed on a single balance. As it is said:
"Cunda, between the night when the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night [when he passes away]..."
“He attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue. Whatever he speaks, utters, or explains during this interval—all that is exactly so and not otherwise;
therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata. Here, the word *gata* has the sense of “spoken. Thus, he is a Tathāgata by virtue of being one who speaks truthfully.

Moreover, *āgada* means "coming" (*āgata*), which signifies "speech. Since his coming—that is, his speech—is "thus" (*tatha*), meaning unerring, by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, one forms the term *Tathāgata*. In this sense, the derivation of the word should be understood.
How is he a *Tathāgata* by virtue of acting accordingly (*tathākāritā*)? For the Blessed One’s body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body.
Therefore, he is one who acts as he speaks, and speaks as he acts. And for one who has become such, just as...
The meaning is that speech has gone thus, and the body likewise proceeds thus. And just as the body has gone thus, speech also proceeds thus;
therefore he is the Tathāgata. For this very reason it was said: "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata acts in accordance with his word, and speaks in accordance with his action.
Thus, acting in accordance with his word and speaking in accordance with his action, he is called the 'Tathāgata'. Thus...
He is the Tathāgata because of acting accordingly.

In what sense is he the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits, he overcomes all beings throughout immeasurable world-systems across the horizontal by means of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation.
By virtue of his knowledge and vision of liberation, there is for him no measure or limit;
rather, he is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed—the king of kings, the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās. Therefore it was said:

"Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... [and so on] ...in this generation with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power; therefore he is called the 'Tathāgata'."

In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like a "remedy" (*agada*), thus it is called a "remedy. But what is this? It is both the splendor of the teaching and the accumulation of merit.
For by means of that, this Great Being, the Physician, just as one might overcome snakes with a divine remedy, overcomes all rival teachers and the world with its devas.
Thus, in the overcoming of the entire world, it is "true" (*tatha*)—that is, non-erroneous—and consists of the splendor of the teaching.

And by changing the letter *da* to *ta* in the phrase "may he be a medicine consisting of merit," one should understand him as the Tathāgata. Thus, the Tathāgata is so called in the sense of "overcoming.
Furthermore, he is the Tathāgata because he has gone (*gato*) to suchness (*tathāya*); he is the Tathāgata because he has gone to reality (*tathaṃ*).
"Gone" means understood, transcended, attained, and entered. In this context, he has gone to and understood suchness by means of the full understanding through investigation of the entire world.
The Tathāgata is so called because he has gone (gato) to suchness (tathā) by means of the full understanding of abandonment regarding the origin of the world;

he is so called because he has gone to and attained suchness by means of the realization of the cessation of the world; he is so called because he has gone to and entered upon the true path leading to the cessation of the world.
Therefore, as it was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world.
The origin of the world, bhikkhus, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata.
The cessation of the world, bhikkhus, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. The way leading to the cessation of the world...”
“Bhikkhus, the path to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata.
Whatever, bhikkhus, has been mentally explored in the world with its devas… [as before] … all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is called the ‘Tathāgata.’”
Its meaning should be understood in this way as well. And even this is merely a small portion of the Tathāgata’s state of being a Tathāgata, illustrated by means of a lamp.

Only a Tathāgata himself could describe the state of being a Tathāgata of a Tathāgata in its entirety. However, because all Buddhas are exactly equal in their qualities as Tathāgatas, he spoke of them as "Tathāgatas" by way of including them all.

"An Arahant" means: because he is far removed from defilements (*kilesa*); because he has slain the enemies (*ari*) and their arrows (*ara*); because he is worthy of receiving requisites and the like;

and because he is devoid of secrecy (*raha*) in the performance of evil—the Tathāgata is thus "Arahant. For he stands far, very far indeed, away from all defilements, since the defilements along with their latent tendencies have been destroyed by the Path; thus, because of being "far removed," he is an Arahant.
“Thus, he is called ‘far removed’ (āraka) because of his lack of association with those [defilements];
and since the Protector is free from faults, he is therefore considered ‘Worthy’ (arahaṃ).
Furthermore, because these enemies—the defilements—have been slain by him through the Path, he is also ‘Worthy’ (arahaṃ) due to the slaying of his enemies.”
“Because all enemies, reckoned as lust and the rest,
have been slain by the Protector with the sword of wisdom, for that reason too he is considered an *Arahaṃ*.
And as for this wheel whose hub consists of ignorance, becoming, and craving, whose rim is aging and death, and which is made of the accumulation of the taints (*āsava*)...

Having pierced with the axle the wheel of saṃsāra—which has been set in motion since beginningless time and is yoked to the chariot of the three realms—he stood upon the earth of virtue with the feet of energy at the seat of awakening;
then, taking up with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma, he shattered all its spokes. Thus, he is an *arahaṃ*.
“Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed by the sword of knowledge by the Lord of the World, for that reason he is called ‘Arahant.
Furthermore, because he is the most worthy of offerings, he is worthy of the requisites such as robes and of special honor; and thus, when the Tathāgata has appeared...”
Whosoever among gods and humans are of great influence do not offer worship elsewhere. For instance, Brahmā Sahampati honored the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland as large as Mount Sineru;
likewise did others—gods and humans such as King Bimbisāra, King Kosala, and so forth—according to their respective means.
And even for the Blessed One who has attained final Nibbāna, ninety-six koṭis of wealth [were offered].
Having bestowed [his wealth], the Great King Aśoka established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
What need is there to mention other special offerings? Because he is worthy even of the requisites and so forth, he is an *arhat*.
“Since this Lord of the World is worthy of special offerings together with the requisites, [he is therefore called an *arhat*].”
“In this world, those who are worthy of their status according to their qualities are called *arahant*; therefore, the Victor (*Jina*) is worthy of this name.

Furthermore, just as in the world some fools who pride themselves on being wise commit evil deeds in secret out of fear of ill-repute, he never commits evil in such a way; thus, because he lacks any secrecy regarding the performance of evil, he is an *arahant*.
“For there is no such thing as secrecy for one such as him regarding evil deeds.”
“Because he has abandoned [defilements] by their very absence, he is renowned as ‘Arahant.
Thus, in every respect:
‘Because he is far removed and because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements, that Sage—’”
“Having destroyed the wheel of saṃsāra, and being worthy of the requisites and so forth, he does not commit secret evils; therefore he is called ‘Arahant.
Furthermore, because all Buddhas are exactly equal even in the quality of arahantship, they are all [collectively] called “Arahants.”
He said: "Sammāsambuddha" means he is a *sammāsambuddha* because he has awakened (*buddhattā*) rightly (*sammā*) and by himself (*sāmañca*) to all phenomena (*sabbadhammānaṃ*).
For in this way he has fully awakened to all phenomena: to phenomena that are to be directly known, as things to be directly known;

to phenomena that are to be fully understood, as things to be fully understood; to phenomena that are to be abandoned, as things to be abandoned; and to phenomena that are to be realized, as things to be realized.
Because the states that are to be developed have been developed. For this very reason it was said:
"That which was to be directly known has been directly known, and that which was to be developed has been developed;
that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O Brahmins, I am a Buddha."
Alternatively, the eye is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that originates it by being its root cause is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*);
the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the path that leads to the realization of cessation is the truth of the way (*maggasacca*).
Thus, by extracting each term individually, he has perfectly and directly awakened to all phenomena. This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. And by this very method...
The six bases, beginning with form; the six classes of consciousness, beginning with eye-consciousness;

the six types of contact, beginning with eye-contact; the six types of feeling born of contact, beginning with feeling born of eye-contact; the six types of perception, beginning with perception of form;

the six types of volition, beginning with volition regarding form; the six groups of craving, beginning with craving for form; the six types of applied thought, beginning with applied thought regarding form; and the six types of sustained thought, beginning with sustained thought regarding form.
The six types of investigation; the five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form; the ten kasiṇas; the ten recollections;
the ten perceptions, beginning with the perception of a bloated corpse; the thirty-two aspects, beginning with head-hair; the twelve bases; the eighteen elements;
the nine existences, beginning with the existence of sense-desire; the four jhānas, beginning with the first; the four immeasurables, beginning with the development of loving-kindness; the four...
The formless attainments, the factors of dependent origination in reverse order beginning with aging-and-death, and in forward order beginning with ignorance, should be applied.
Herein, this is the application of single terms: aging-and-death is the truth of suffering; birth is the truth of the origin;
the escape from both is the truth of cessation; and the way leading to the realization of cessation is the truth of the path. Thus, by extracting each term individually...
The Buddha has perfectly awakened to, awakened to by himself, and penetrated all phenomena.
Or rather, because he has perfectly awakened to whatever is to be known, he is the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddha*) by virtue of the knowledge pertaining to liberation.
Their distinction will be made clear further on. Furthermore, since all Buddhas are equal in their quality as Perfectly Enlightened Ones, they are identical.
Therefore, he says "Perfectly Enlightened Ones" (Sammāsambuddhā) with reference to all [of them].

Regarding "by means of silence" (monena): although one is called a sage (muni) by means of the sagehood-knowledge (moneyya-paṭipadā) consisting of the knowledge of the Path, here it is said "not by means of silence" (na monena) with reference to the state of being silent (tuṇhībhāva). "Of deluded form" (mūḷharūpa) means of empty form. "Ignorant" (aviddasu) means lacking understanding.
For one who is merely silent like this is not truly called a "muni. Alternatively, he is not a muni in the sense of possessing *moneyya* (wisdom);
the meaning is that he is empty and ignorant. And as for the phrase "like one who has taken up a scale":
just as one standing with a scale in hand takes away what is excessive and adds to what is deficient, even so, he is like one taking away what is excessive.
He removes evil and avoids it, and he fulfills the wholesome by adding to what is deficient, as if pouring more into a vessel that is short.
And while acting in this way, taking up the excellent and supreme—namely, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—he avoids sinful, unwholesome deeds;
such a one is called a "muni. For that reason, he is a muni. But why?
If it is asked, "Why is he a sage (*muni*)?"—the meaning is that he is a sage for the reasons stated below. "He who measures both worlds":
that person, as if weighing them on a scale in this world of aggregates and so forth, measures these two matters according to the method beginning with, "These are internal aggregates;
these are external. "He is called a sage because of that": furthermore, by that...
The meaning is that for this reason he is indeed called a "Muni.
Regarding the verse beginning with "Of the non-existent and the existent," this is the summary of the meaning:

that which is the Dhamma distinguished as unwholesome and wholesome, both of the non-existent and the existent—that [Dhamma] is, by means of the knowledge of investigation (*pavicaya-ñāṇa*), [discerned] within and without in this entire world, both as non-existent and as existent.

Having known the Dhamma. Because of that very knowledge, he has transcended—having gone beyond—the sevenfold attachment divided into passion and the rest, as well as the two-fold net divided into craving and views;

thus he is a sage (*muni*) because he is endowed with that investigative knowledge termed "silence. "Worshipped by gods and humans" is a word of praise for him, for he is a sage whose taints are exhausted.
He becomes worthy of worship by gods and humans; therefore, it is said thus. "Arrow" (*salla*) is the root term.
"Seven arrows" (*satta sallāni*) is the delimitation by number. "The arrow of lust" (*rāgasalla*):

lust is called an "arrow" because it is colored (or impassioned), because it causes affliction, because it pierces within, and because it is difficult to extract; thus it is the "arrow of lust. The same applies to the "arrow of hatred" (*dosasalla*) and the others.
The same method applies here. “One who has pulled out the dart” (*abbūḷhasalla*) is the basic term. “One who has extracted the dart” (*abbahitasalla*) means one from whom the dart has been removed.

“One who has drawn out the dart” (*uddhatasalla*) means one from whom the dart has been pulled upward or extracted. “One who has completely drawn out the dart” (*samuddhatasalla*) is stated by way of the prefix (*upasagga*). “One who has torn out the dart” (*uppāṭitasalla*) means one from whom the dart has been plucked out.
“One who has completely torn out the dart” (*samuppāṭitasalla*) is likewise by way of the prefix.

"One who acts with thoroughness" (*sakkaccakārī*) means one who acts with thoroughness by way of performing the cultivation of wholesome states such as giving, whether toward a person or toward the object to be given.
One who acts with constancy (*sātaccakārī*) does so by practicing them continuously. One who acts with steadfastness (*aṭṭhitakārī*) does so by practicing them without ceasing.
Just as, for example, a *kakaṇṭaka* bird goes a little and then stops, rather than going without interruption; [so too is this].

In the same way, a person who gives a gift, performs an act of worship, hears the Dhamma, or practices the duty of a recluse on a single day, but then does so again only after a long interval, does not carry it out continuously.
Such a person is called "one who acts without persistence" (*asātaccakārī*) and "one who acts without stability" (*anaṭṭhitakārī*).

He is called "one who acts without stability" because he does not act in this manner [continuously]. "One of unflagging conduct" (*anōlīnavuttiko*) refers to one whose practice is characterized by continuity.
"Of unremitting conduct" means one whose conduct is not sluggish due to the state of being expansive.
"One who has not cast aside his desire" means one who has not cast aside the desire for effort (*vīriya-chanda*) in performing what is wholesome, by virtue of not having abandoned that desire.
"One who has not laid down the burden" means one who has not laid down the burden of effort; the meaning is that his mind has not slackened. Whatever desire and exertion there is therein—
And what is that? It is the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*) consisting in the wish to act toward those wholesome states, and the effort (*vāyāma*) designated as exertion;
it is "endeavor" (*ussāha*) by way of striving, and "perseverance" (*ussoḷhi*) by way of supreme striving. This effort is so called in the sense of going to the further shore;
this endeavor in the sense of being a precursor; and this perseverance in the sense of being preeminent. And "irreversibility" means non-retrogression.
"And mindfulness and clear comprehension": it is "mindfulness" (*sati*) because one remembers; it is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*) because one comprehends thoroughly.

The meaning is that one knows by means of all-around modes. The classification of this clear comprehension should be understood according to these four types: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion.
"Ardor" (*ātappa*) is the energy that scorches the defilements. "Exertion" (*padhāna*)...
Supreme vigor (*uttamavīriya*). "Resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is the state of being established in the performance of what is wholesome. "Application" (*anuyoga*) is the act of applying oneself.
"Diligence" (*appamāda*) is non-negligence, which is the non-separation from mindfulness.
"He does not long for this world" is the root phrase. "His own personal existence" (*sakattabhāva*) means his own individuality. "The personal existence of another" (*parattabhāva*)...

The self-body in the next world. One's own five aggregates—consisting of one's own form, feeling, and so forth—and the five aggregates in the next world—consisting of the form, feeling, and so forth of others.

"The sense-sphere realm" (kāmadhātu) means existence in the sense-sphere (kāmabhava). "The fine-material realm" (rūpadhātu) means existence in the fine-material sphere (rūpabhava). "The immaterial realm" (arūpadhātu) means existence in the immaterial sphere (arūpabhava).
Furthermore, in order to show a dyad by way of the material and the immaterial, the sense-sphere realm and the fine-material realm are combined as one.
The formless realm (*arūpadhātu*) is mentioned by being treated as one. "Or as a destiny" (*gati*) refers to the five destinies by way of their status as places of establishment.

"Or as a rebirth" (*upapatti*) refers to the four modes of birth (*yoni*) by way of their manifestation. "Or as rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) refers to rebirth-linking by way of the connection of the three types of existence (*bhava*).
"Or as existence" (*bhava*) refers to it by way of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*). "Or as saṃsāra" refers to it by way of the uninterrupted continuity of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
"He does not wish for the round" means he does not desire the round of the three planes of existence.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta* in the *Saddhammappajjotikā*,
the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka-sutta* 15.
Regarding the first verse of the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka*: "There they speak" means they revile both the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
"Some with minds corrupted" (*duṭṭhamanāpi eke*) refers to those with corrupt hearts; "and yet others truly know" (*athopi ve saccamanāti*) refers to some who perceive things as they actually are.
Having made the offering, the sectarians were satisfied in mind; the intention is that those who heard them believed it was true.

"And the dispute has arisen" refers to the abusive dispute that broke out. "The Sage does not approach us" means that, because of his state of non-doing and his state of being unshakable, the Buddha-Sage does not approach [us].
Therefore, "for this reason, there is no resentment anywhere for this Sage."
It should be understood that for those with the barrenness of lust and so forth, there is no barrenness anywhere.

"With corrupted minds" means those whose hearts are defiled by arisen hatreds. "With hostile minds" means those whose hearts are obstructed by those defilements, not allowing an opening for the wholesome.
"With thoroughly hostile minds" is an extension of the term by means of the prefix *paṭi*. "With struck-down minds" [means...]

“Those whose minds are struck by aversion” (*āhatamanā*) means those whose minds are struck by resentment (*paṭigha*). “Those whose minds are struck back at” (*paccāhatamanā*) is due to the prefix alone.

“Those whose minds are provoked” (*āghātitamanā*) means those whose minds are provoked by malice (*vihiṃsā*); “those whose minds are provoked back at” (*paccāghātitamanā*) is likewise due to the prefix alone.
Alternatively, they are “those with corrupted minds through anger,” “those with defiled minds through enmity,” and “those with hostile minds through slander.”
“With a mind hostile through resentment, with a mind struck and counter-striken through hatred, with a mind provoked and counter-provoked through ill will;
with a mind corrupted and vitiated by the non-attainment of requisites, with a mind hostile and resentful because of infamy,
with a mind struck and counter-striken because of censure, and with a mind provoked and counter-provoked due to being possessed of painful feelings.”
In this manner and others like it, some explain [the passage]. "They revile" means they produce censure. "By what is untrue" means by that which does not exist.
"Believing" means generating faith by way of confidence (*pasāda*). "Accepting" means descending and establishing [their view] by way of its qualities (*guṇa*).
"Resolving" means making a firm determination through serene confidence (*sampasādana*) and thus tolerating their words. "Taking as truth" means...
“Tacchamanā” means those who speak truthfully. “Saccasaññino” means those who perceive things as they truly are. “Tathamanā” means those whose minds are not perverted.
“Bhūtamanā” means those whose minds are directed toward the actual reality. “Yāthāvamanā” means those whose minds are unshakable. “Aviparītamanā” means those whose minds are free from doubt.
In this context, “saccamanā saccasaññino” refers to the quality of being a speaker of truth; “tathamanā tathasaññino” refers to the quality of having faith in the truth; and “bhūtamanā”...

It should be understood that the quality of being established is expressed by “perceiving [them] as they have become”; the quality of being reliable is expressed by “having a mind according to reality and perceiving according to reality”;
and the quality of non-deceptiveness is expressed by “having an unperverted mind and perceiving without perversion.
“The voice of another” refers to a sound arising from the presence of others. “Abuse” refers to any one among the ten types of abuse, such as those concerning birth and so forth.
"One who enters into dispute" is a person who approaches with censure. "Or an offender" means one who has committed a fault.
"By way of being an offender" means being called or spoken of as such because of the state of having committed a fault. "Being censured" means being found guilty of a fault.
"Is provoked" means he gives way to anger.

"Nor is there 'stump-grown-ness'" means: one who has a "stump grown"—that is, one for whom the "stump of resistance," consisting of the state of mental bondage and the state of mental refuse, has grown—is called *khilajāto*;
the state of being such is *khilajātatā*, and that too does not exist, it is not present.

The five "stumps of the mind" (*cetokhila*) are: one who is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; one who is not free from lust for the body; one who is not free from lust for forms; and one who, having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full...
He does not dwell addicted to the pleasure of sleeping, the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of drowsiness;
nor does he lead the holy life aspiring for some order of devas, thinking, "By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva or some kind of deva.
Such mental barrenness—consisting of five things that bind the mind and are reckoned as its refuse—is absent in him.
16. Having spoken this verse, the Blessed One asked the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, when bhikkhus are thus reviled and disparaged, what do they say? “Nothing at all, Blessed One.
“Ānanda, one who thinks ‘I am virtuous’ should not remain silent in every situation. For in the world, they do not recognize one who does not speak out; such a person is confused with fools.”
Having said, "He is wise," [the Buddha] spoke this verse—"The speaker of falsehood goes to hell"—for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, saying, "Ānanda, let the monks thus rebuke those people.
The Elder, having learned it, said to the monks, "People should be rebuked by you with this verse. The monks did so. Wise people...
They remained silent. The king, having dispatched his royal officers everywhere, apprehended those scoundrels who had given bribes to the heretics to have him killed;
having seized them and learned the facts of the matter, he rebuked the heretics.
When people saw the heretics, they struck them with clods of earth and covered them with dust, saying, "They have brought infamy upon the Blessed One."
When the Elder Ānanda saw this, he informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One spoke this verse to the Elder:
“Sakañhi diṭṭhiṃ... pe... vadeyyā.

The meaning of this is as follows: This view held by the followers of other sects—that after murdering Sundarī, [the blame should be laid upon] the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans—[is their own view]. They would say it thus.
“Having proclaimed dispraise, we shall accept the honor obtained by this means”—how could such a person overcome that view?
Indeed, he returns to those very same followers of other sects, being unable to transcend that view.
Or how could one who holds views such as eternalism (sassatavāda) transcend their own view? It is because of that very desire for such views.
He was won over by that view and inclination and became settled in it;
nevertheless, while performing those views as if they were complete in themselves, he would speak exactly as he knew them to be, making those views appear perfect.
"Having manifested dispraise" means having made the lack of virtue manifest. "Honoring" means the careful provision of the four requisites.
"Honoring" means showing great respect with the mind. "We shall bring back" means we shall produce such gains and so forth. "Holding such a view" means having such a conviction.

Just as they have this conviction, namely, "we shall produce gains and so forth," so too does it suit and please them that "I possess the Dhamma of the kind described"; it is of precisely such a nature.
Or their mind [thinks], "I have a mind. At that time, for them there is either a view, or an inclination (khanti) together with the view,

or a preference (ruci) together with the view and the inclination, or an adherence (laddhi) together with the view, the inclination, and the preference, or an underlying tendency (ajjhāsaya) together with the view,
the inclination, the preference, and the adherence, or an intention (adhippāya) together with the view, the inclination, the preference, the adherence, and the underlying tendency.
Showing [this], he said: “Having such a view... [and so on] ...having such an intention. His own view (*sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ*) means his own seeing.
His own acceptance (*sakaṃ khantiṃ*) means his own forbearance. His own preference (*sakaṃ ruciṃ*) means his own liking. His own conviction (*sakaṃ laddhiṃ*) means his own belief.
His own inclination (*sakaṃ ajjhāsaṃ*) means his own disposition. His own intention (*sakaṃ adhippāyaṃ*) means his own state of mind.
*Atikkamituṃ* means to transcend. *Atha kho sveva ayaso* means that very infamy is, in every respect, [infamy]. *Te paccāgato* means returned to them.
*Te* is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*).
*Atha vā* indicates a change of subject matter. *Sassato* means eternal, permanent, and stable. *Loko* refers to the personal existence (*attabhāvo*). "This alone is the truth..."
"They think it is vain"—this alone is true and real; the other is empty. "Fully undertaken" means completely fulfilled.
"Adopted" means correctly taken up. "Grasped" means grasped by way of approach.

"Clung to" means grasped after having clung to it in every aspect. "Adhered to" means having specifically gained a firm footing. "Non-eternal" should be understood as the opposite of what was stated [previously].
“Finite” means having an end. “Infinite” means increasing without end. “That which is the soul is the self” (*taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ jīvaṃ*); here a grammatical inversion of gender has been made.
“Soul” (*jīva*) refers to the self itself. “Tathāgata” refers to a sentient being; some say it means “the Worthy One” (*araha*). “After death” means beyond death; the meaning is “in the next world.
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death” means that he does not exist beyond death. “He exists... [and so forth].
"Neither exists nor does not exist after death": after death, he both exists and does not exist.
