"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death": he does not exist by way of annihilationism (*uccheda*), and he does not not exist by way of speculative reasoning (*takka*).
"By means of his own view," and so forth, are instrumental expressions. "Adhered" means become one with it.

"He makes himself complete" means that, having freed himself from deficiency, he rightly makes himself complete (*samatta*). "Perfect" (*paripuṇṇa*) means having freed it from the fault of excess, it is fully complete.
"Unexcelled" (*anoma*) means having freed it from the fault of inferiority, it is without blemish. "Foremost" (*agga*) means the beginning. "Best" (*seṭṭha*) means preeminent and faultless.
"Superior" (*visesa*) means the eldest or most excellent. "Preeminent" (*pāmokkha*) means superior. "Supreme" (*uttama*)...

It does not make the lower [levels] superior. "He makes it excellent" means he makes it pre-eminent by way of excess. Alternatively: "By releasing one from the fault of the underlying tendency (*āsaya*), he makes it foremost (*agga*);
by releasing one from the fault of defilement (*saṃkilesa*), he makes it best (*seṭṭha*); by releasing one from the fault of secondary defilement (*upakkilesa*), he makes it distinguished (*visesa*);

by releasing one from the fault of negligence (*pamatta*), he makes it pre-eminent (*pāmokkha*); by releasing one from the fault of the middling, he makes it supreme (*uttama*); and by releasing one from the fault of the highest-middling, he makes it excellent (*pavara*)."
Thus some describe it: "This Teacher is omniscient" means that our Teacher is omniscient by virtue of knowing all things.
"This Dhamma is well-expounded" means that our Dhamma is well-proclaimed.
"This Saṅgha has practiced well" means that our Saṅgha has practiced excellently. "This view is auspicious" means that our own doctrine is beautiful.
"This way of practice is well-proclaimed" means that this way of practice beginning with our own self-development has been properly proclaimed by us.
"This path is leading-out" means that this path of ours which leads to liberation makes it known for itself that it is leading-out.

One might say, "The world is eternal"; one might declare, "Only this is true, anything else is false"; one might illuminate, "The world is finite"; or one might speak in various ways to cause others to grasp [views], such as, "It both exists and does not exist."
17. Then, after seven days had passed, the king had that corpse removed.
In the evening, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said: “Venerable sir, when such a calamity had arisen, should it not have been reported to me as well?
When this was said, the Blessed One replied: “Great king, one should not report to others, ‘I am virtuous and endowed with good qualities.’”
Having said, "This is worthy of the Noble Ones," he spoke the remaining verses on that occasion, beginning with "One's own virtuous practices.

Therein, "virtuous practices" (*sīlavatāni*) refers to the precepts such as the *Pātimokkha*, and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) such as dwelling in the forest. "Unasked" (*anānupuṭṭho*) means not having been questioned.
"He speaks out" (*pāvāti vadati*). "The wise call that ignoble conduct" (*anariyadhammaṃ... āhu*): they call it ignoble conduct when one speaks out for oneself without being asked.
When someone speaks of themselves in this way, the wise declare that such a claim is "un-Ariyan.
"There is both virtue (*sīla*) and observance (*vata*): there is virtue in the sense of 'conduct' (*sīlana*), and there is observance in the sense of 'undertaking' (*samādāna*).
There is observance that is not virtue; this refers to what has been stated as 'observance, but not virtue. What is it?"—this is a question asked out of a desire to explain.

Here, "the bhikkhu is virtuous," and so forth, are to be understood in the manner already stated. "In the sense of restraint" means in the sense of restraining, that is, in the sense of closing the door to transgression.
"In the sense of undertaking" means in the sense of correctly undertaking each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

"The forest-dweller’s factor" (*āraññikaṅga*): one whose habit is dwelling in the forest is a forest-dweller (*āraññika*); his factor is the forest-dweller’s factor. "The alms-food-eater’s factor" (*piṇḍapātikaṅga*)...
*Piṇḍapāta* means the falling (*pāta*) of morsels of food (*piṇḍa*) belonging to others, reckoned as alms;
what is meant is that the morsels given by others fall into the bowl. One who *uñchati*—that is, approaches and seeks—that *piṇḍapāta* from various families is a *piṇḍapātika*.
Alternatively, one whose practice (*vata*) is to fall for morsels is a *piṇḍapātī*. To "fall" means to wander for alms. Thus, he is a *piṇḍapātī*.
Thus, he is a *piṇḍapātika*; the factor of that [practice] is the *piṇḍapātik-aṅga*. "Factor" (*aṅga*) is said to mean a cause.
Therefore, it should be understood as a designation for that undertaking by which one becomes a *piṇḍapātika*.

By this same method, because he stands upon dust anywhere—such as on carriage tracks, charnel grounds, heaps of refuse, and so forth—in the sense of being elevated (*abbhuggata*), [he is called an *ekāsanika*].
Among these, "like refuse-rags" means *paṃsukūla*. Alternatively, it is called *paṃsukūla* because it goes (*ulati*) toward a state of contemptibility (*kucchitabhāva*), as if toward dust (*paṃsu*);
that is to say, it becomes something contemptible. The wearing of such refuse-rags, whose derivation is thus established, is *paṃsukūla*.
One for whom this *paṃsukūla* is a habit (*sīla*) is a *paṃsukūlika*. A factor of the *paṃsukūlika* is a *paṃsukūlika-aṅga*.
One who possesses the three robes—consisting of the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the inner garment (*antaravāsaka*)—is called a *tecīvarika*.
The practice of such a person is the *tecīvarika-aṅga* (the factor of the three-robed one). Regarding the *sapadānacārika-aṅga*: "giving" (*dāna*) means breaking (*avakhaṇḍana*).
That which is away from giving is *apadāna*, meaning non-breaking. Together with *apadāna* is *sapadāna*; it is that which is devoid of breaking.
"It flows along" is what is meant. "One who goes from house to house" (*sapadānacārī*) means this is his habit; one who is such a goer is a "house-to-house-goer" (*sapadānacāriko*);
the factor of that [practice] is the "house-to-house-going factor" (*sapadānacārikaṅga*). Regarding the "factor of eating only one meal" (*khalupacchābhattikaṅga*):
*khalu* is a particle used in the sense of prohibition. "After-meal food" (*pacchābhattaṃ*) refers to food obtained after one has already been invited to eat.

"Meal after the proper time" (*pacchābhattabhojana*) means food eaten after the meal; having formed the perception of "after the meal" regarding that meal after the proper time, one whose virtue (*sīla*) consists in [eating] after the meal is called a "one who eats after the meal" (*pacchābhattika*). One who is not such is a "one who eats only at the proper time" (*khalupacchābhattika*);
this is the name for one who has rejected extra food by way of formal undertaking. A factor of that is the "factor of eating only at the proper time" (*khalupacchābhattikaṅga*).
The *nesajjikanga* (the practice of never lying down): one who has the habit of dwelling in a sitting posture after rejecting reclining is a *nesajjiko*;
his practice is the *nesajjikanga*. The *yathāsanthatikanga* (the practice of accepting whatever seat is assigned): *yathāsanthata* means "as spread out";
this is a designation for the lodging that has been first assigned with the words, "This seat falls to you. In that regard...
"One whose nature it is to dwell according to whatever seat is provided" is a *yathāsañthatika*; the "factor of that" is the *yathāsañthatika-aṅga*.
All of these, however, are factors (*aṅga*) of a monk who has shaken off the defilements (*dhuta-kilesa*) by means of various such undertakings;

or alternatively, they are called "ascetic factors" (*dhutaṅga*) because knowledge—which has acquired the designation "shaken off" (*dhuta*) due to its shaking of the defilements—is their factor. Or else:
They are called *dhutaṅgas* because they shake off (*dhunana*) opposing qualities and because they are factors (*aṅga*) of practice;
thus should the analysis of their meaning be understood here. Furthermore, all of these have the characteristic of volition consisting in undertaking.

And this has been said: "He who undertakes is the person. That by which he undertakes are these states, namely, consciousness and mental factors. The volition of undertaking is the *dhutaṅga*. That which he rejects is the basis."

And all [these qualities] have the function of destroying greed; they are manifested as the state of being free from greed; and their proximate cause is the noble quality of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth. In this way, the analysis of these [qualities] should be understood by means of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and other criteria.

"Also the undertaking of energy" (*vīriyasamādānam-pi*): the inclusion of the word "energy" (*vīriya*). "Kāmam": an indeclinable particle used in the sense of "certainly. "Skin and sinews" (*taco ca nhāru ca*):
the outer skin and the cords of sinew. "Bones" (*aṭṭhi ca*): all the bones. "Let it remain" (*avasissatū*): let it stay. "Let it dry up" (*upasussatu*).
“Flesh and blood”: let all the flesh and blood dry up. “Skin” is one factor; “sinews” is one; “bones” is one;
“let the flesh and blood dry up” is one factor. The word *yaṃ* (which) connects with the phrase to be stated above.
“By manly strength” means by a man’s physical power; “by power” means by the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). “By energy” means...

By the power of mental factors, knowledge, and energy. "With exertion" means by advancing to higher and higher stages through energy that has attained enthusiasm. "That which is to be reached" refers to whatever is to be attained. "Without reaching that" means without having attained that which is to be reached.
"There will be no slackening of energy" means there will be no laxity or sinking of the energy described in the aforementioned manner.
“Paṭṭhāna” is also a reading; it has this very same meaning. “He uplifts the mind” means he causes the mind to take up enthusiasm.
“He exerts” means he establishes [the mind].
“I will not eat” means I will not chew, I will not consume, I will not partake of food. “I will not drink” means I will not drink rice-gruel and so forth.
"I shall not cause him to leave the monastery; I shall not go outside the lodging. Nor shall they let him fall;
I shall not effect his falling or placing [on the ground] upon the couch, the chair, the floor, or the straw mat.
"While the arrow of craving has not been extracted" means while the shaft known as craving has not been pulled out; the meaning is "while it has not departed."
"This cross-legged posture" means sitting with the legs folded all around, with the thighs locked together. "I will not break it" means I will not abandon it.
"Until for me there is no grasping" means without taking hold by means of the four types of clinging (*upādāna*).

"From the taints" means from the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*). "Will be liberated" means he will be liberated through the liberation of total eradication (*samucchedavimutti*). "Not yet from this... [he continues:]... I shall not rise from this seat.
Beginning with "I shall rise from my seat," up to "I shall go out to the foot of a tree," these are stated by way of place.
Beginning with "At this very time of morning I shall bring forth the Noble Dhamma," up to "I shall heat [myself]," these are stated by way of time.
"In the first stage of life," and so forth, are stated by way of age. In that context, "I shall not rise from my seat" [is stated by way of resolve].
"I shall not rise from my seat. *Aḍḍhayoga* refers to houses with gabled roofs. *Pāsāda* refers to long palaces. *Hammiya* refers to houses with flat roofs.
*Guha* refers to a cave made of earth. *Leṇa* refers to mountain caves with defined boundaries and openings. *Kuṭi* refers to a hut plastered over and so forth.
*Kūṭāgāra* refers to a house constructed with a peaked roof (*kaṇṇika*). *Aṭṭa* refers to watchtowers at the gates.
*Māḷā* refers to circular houses. An *uddaṇḍa* is a particular type of dwelling; some say it is a "house with a triple roof.
An *upaṭṭhānasālā* is an assembly hall or a dining hall. *Maṇḍapas* and so forth are well known.

*Ariyadhamma* means the blameless Dhamma, or the Dhamma of the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha. *Āharissāmi* means "I shall bring [it] into the vicinity of my mind."
"I shall bring it by means of virtue" (*sīlena*); "I shall collect it"—this means I shall specifically bring it by means of concentration (*samādhinā*).

"I shall attain it"—this means I shall go toward it by way of acquisition (*paṭilābhavasena*) through its specific factor (*tadaṅgena*). "I shall touch it"—this means I shall touch it by means of the path (*maggena*).

"I shall realize it"—this means I shall make it manifest (*paccakkhaṃ karissāmi*) by means of the fruit (*phalena*). Alternatively, I shall bring it by means of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimaggena*); [I shall bring it] by means of the once-returning path (*sakadāgāmimaggena*).
"I shall collect [them]; I shall attain them by means of the path of non-returning; I shall touch them by means of the path of arahantship; I shall realize them through review.
In both methods, "I shall touch" means that I shall touch Nibbāna with the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
"Unasked" (*apuṭṭho*) is the root term; its meaning is "not questioned" (*apucchito*). "Not questioned" means not made known. "Unsolicited" (*ayācito*) means not requested.
*Anajjhesito*: not requested; some say "not desired. *Apasādito*: not made to have faith. *Pāvadati*: speaks. *Ahamasmi*: "I am," I exist. *Jātiyā vā*:
either by birth, such as the birth-status of a khattiya or a brāhmaṇa. *Gottena vā*: or by clan, such as the Gotama clan and so forth.
*Kolaputtiyena vā*: or by being a son of good family. *Vaṇṇapokkharatāya*: by the excellence of one's complexion.
Or by the beauty of the body; or by wealth, that is, by the possession of riches; or by study, that is, by the act of reciting;
or by the sphere of action—that is, action itself is the sphere of action—by that sphere of action, such as the work of plowing or cattle-herding;
or by the sphere of craft, such as the craft of archery and so forth; or by a branch of knowledge, that is, by one of the eighteen branches of learning (*vijjāṭṭhāna*).

Or by lineage; or by the quality of being well-versed in the scriptures (*bahussuta*); or by eloquence, which is to say, by the knowledge characterized as the discernment of what is appropriate and inappropriate;
or by any one of various grounds, such as birth and so forth.
"From high-born families" refers to Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa families; by this, he illustrates the greatness of birth and clan (*jāti-gotta-mahatta*). "From wealthy families" means...
"From great landed householder families": by this he indicates wealth. "Families of noble possessions": these are the remaining families, such as the *vessa* and others;
by this he indicates an abundance of gold, silver, and so forth—for even *caṇḍālas* may possess noble wealth. "Renowned" means well-known. "Possessing glory" means endowed with a retinue.
"A master of the Suttantas" means one engaged in the Suttanta Piṭaka. "A bearer of the Vinaya" means one who masters the Vinaya Piṭaka.
“Dhammakathika” means one who is versed in the Abhidhamma. “Āraññika” and the others are mentioned for the purpose of showing the practice that has the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*) as its precursor.
“One who has attained the first jhāna” and so forth are mentioned by way of demonstrating penetration after having shown the eight attainments of the fine-material and immaterial realms.
“Pāvadati” is the root word. “Katheti” means he declares, “I am a teacher of the Piṭakas. “Bhaṇati” means [he declares], “I am a possessor of the ascetic virtues.”

He makes it manifest. "He illuminates" means he fully demonstrates, "I am an attainer of the fine-material jhānas. "He speaks" means he formulates the distinction in speech, "I am an attainer of the immaterial jhānas.

"Skilled in the aggregates" means they are proficient in the five aggregates regarding their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), by way of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning.

"Skilled" (kusala) means "proficient. This same method applies to the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and so forth. "Skilled in Nibbāna" means proficient in Nibbāna.
"Of the ignoble ones" (anariyānaṃ) means not of the noble ones (ariya). "This Dhamma" means this nature. "Of the fools" (bālānaṃ) means of those who are unwise.
"Of the bad persons" (asappurisānaṃ) means not of beautiful persons. "Self" (attā) means oneself (attānaṃ).
18. They are "peaceful" (*santa*) because of the subsiding of defilements such as lust. Likewise, they are "fully extinguished in nature" (*abhinibbutatta*).
"Thus he does not boast about his virtues" means that he does not boast regarding his virtues in such a manner as "I am endowed with virtue," and so forth;
what is meant is that he does not utter speech referring to himself on account of his virtue. "The skilled ones speak of that noble quality" refers to his lack of boasting.
“The noble Dhamma is this”: the Buddhas and others who are skilled in the aggregates and so forth declare this.
“For whom there is no haughtiness anywhere in the world”: for that one whose taints are destroyed, the seven kinds of haughtiness—lust and the rest—do not exist anywhere in the world.
The connection is that the skilled ones declare that such non-boasting on his part is “the noble Dhamma.”
“Peaceful” (*santa*) is the root term. “Because of the calming of lust” (*rāgassa samitattā*) means by way of the state of having calmed lust, which is characterized by passion.

The same method applies to hatred (*dosa*) and the rest as well. “Because of its being extinguished” (*vijjhātattā*) means because all fevers (*pariḷāha*) have been burnt away. “Because of its being quenched” (*nibbutattā*) means by way of the state of having caused all torments (*santāpa*) to cease.
“Because of its being departed” (*vigatattā*) means by way of the state of having departed from, or being distant from, all unwholesome volitional formations (*akusalābhisaṅkhāra*).
"Because of being completely subsided" means by way of being incapable of arising in any manner whatsoever.

"A bhikkhu because of the breaking of seven things" means a bhikkhu by virtue of having broken and stood apart from the seven things that will be mentioned below. These three defilements—personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*)—are broken by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
These two defilements—lust (*rāga*) and hatred (*dosa*)—are gross and are [broken] by the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*).

Those [defilements] were already broken; those very same ones associated with the subtle (anu-sahagata) were broken by the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-mārga); these two defilements, delusion (moha) and conceit (māna), were broken by the path of arhatship (arahatta-mārga).
To show the remaining defilements, he said: "His evil, unwholesome states (pāpakā akusalā dhammā) are broken.

"Corrupting" (saṃkilesika) means having defilement as their condition. "Leading to renewed existence" (ponobhavika) means bringing about rebirth. "With fever" (sadarā) means that the fevers of defilement (kilesa-daratha) exist therein.
“With distress” (*sadarā*); there is also a reading *saddarā*, meaning “with torment” (*sahadaratha*). “Having suffering as their result” means they give rise to suffering at the time of fruition.
“Leading to birth, aging, and death in the future” means they are the conditions for birth, aging, and death in the future.
The summarized meaning of the verse beginning with “By one’s own path made” is this: [it refers to] that by which one attains final nibbāna through a path developed by oneself.
He has gone; he has attained the final nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*); and because he has indeed reached that final nibbāna, he has crossed over doubt.

Having utterly abandoned both existence (*bhava*) and non-existence (*vibhava*)—which are distinguished by misfortune and success, loss and gain, annihilationism and eternalism, demerit and merit—he has dwelt in the dwelling of the Path and exhausted further rebirth. Such a bhikkhu is worthy of these words of praise.
Regarding the phrase *itihan*, there are two readings: *idahan* and *itihan*. Taking into account the euphonic combinations (*padasandhi*) and so forth, one should understand the reading as *idahan*.
They do not find pleasure [in it]. In this context, "iti" refers to what has been stated. "Padasandhi" (junction of words) means the junction (*sandhi*) of words;

the meaning is the connection (*ghaṭanā*) of words. "Padasaṃsagga" (conjunction of words) is the unification of words. "Padapāripūrī" (completion of words) is the fulfillment of words, the unification of two words.
"Akkharasamavāya" (combination of syllables) is that which, though unified, is still incomplete; this [term] is not like that. Of syllables...
He said "a combination of syllables" (*akkharasamavāyo*) for the purpose of showing that a coming together (*sannipāta*) is a coalescence (*samavāya*).

"Smoothness of phonemes" (*byañjanasiliṭṭhatā*) refers to the softness of the recitation due to the sweetness of the phonemes—those phonemes which are called "words" (*pada*) as a collection (*samuccaya*), or which manifest the meaning, or which cause the clarity of the meaning.
"The sequence of words is my [measure]" (*padānupubbatā metan*): this is the state of following the sequence of words.
The meaning is "the sequential order of words" or "the state of the succession of words.
*Metam* is this [word]. If one asks, "What is it? it is this word *iti*. Here, the letter *m* in *metam* is used for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).

"One who boasts" (*katthī*) means one whose habit is to speak by exalting oneself, thinking, "I am endowed with virtue. "He boasts" (*katthati*) means he speaks in the manner already described. "He boasts excessively" (*vikatthati*)...
"Vividhā" means "various. "Kathana" means "speaking. "Ārata" means "delighting from afar. "Virata" means "delighting by way of having departed," through the shifting of one's position.
"Paṭivirata" means "delighting after having turned back from that," being detached in every respect.
In this context, one who has fled upon seeing [the object] like a piśāca is "ārata. One who has run away like someone fleeing from an elephant that is trampling is "virata."
"Abstinent": having struck and crushed [the defilements] like a warrior in combat, he has gone forth as one who has turned away from them.

"Of one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavassa*): of one whose taints of the defilements (*kilesāsava*) have been destroyed. "The swelling of karma" (*kammussada*): the swelling, the abundance, of karmas consisting of the formative forces of merit (*puññābhisankhāra*), the formative forces of demerit (*apuññābhisankhāra*), and the formative forces of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisankhāra*). "In whom these [exist]" (*yassime*): in whom, that one whose taints are destroyed, these swellings exist. 19.
Having thus shown the practice of one whose taints are destroyed, [the text now shows] the practice of the sectarian teachers who hold to views.

Explaining this, he said: "Fabricated and conditioned. Therein, "fabricated" (*pakappitā*) means thoroughly imagined (*parikappitā*). "Conditioned" (*saṅkhatā*) means constructed by conditions (*paccayābhisaṅkhatā*).
"Of whom" (*yassa*) refers to any given holder of views. "Ideas" (*dhammā*) refers to views. "Placed before" (*purakkhatā*) means made foremost.
"Exist" (*santi*) means they are found. "Unclean" (*avīvadātā*) means not purified. Whatever benefit one sees within oneself, one relies upon that.

"Peace dependent on what is unstable": because one for whom these views regarding phenomena (*diṭṭhadhammā*)—which are unwholesome and unpurified—are prioritized, such a person perceives within themselves the benefits of those views, both pertaining to the present life, such as honor and the like, and pertaining to future lives, such as excellence in rebirth;
therefore, [the Blessed One spoke of] that benefit and its instability, and its being dependently arisen.
And because of his adherence to conventional existence and to the view known as "existence dependent on the unstable," he relies upon that [view].
Due to that reliance, he might exalt himself or disparage others by means of qualities or defects that do not even exist.
"Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) is the root term. "Conditioned" means made by coming together through conditions. By virtue of the prefix, it becomes a term [meaning "that which has been constructed"].
"Augmented": produced by conditions. "Constructed": brought about by conditions. "Formed": properly established by means of conditions alone. "Impermanent":
because of the non-existence of that which has come to be. "Dependently arisen": arisen in dependence upon a physical basis and an object.
"Subject to destruction": having the inherent nature of gradual destruction. "Subject to vanishing": having the inherent nature of falling away through the course of its occurrence.
"Subject to fading away" (*virāgadhamma*) means having the nature of disappearing without returning. "Subject to cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing;

the meaning is that they have the nature of ceasing after having become subject to non-arising. "Of one who holds views" (*diṭṭhigatika*) refers to a person who stands having grasped the sixty-two views.
*Purekkhārā* means "placed before. *Taṇhādhaja*: in the sense of being raised up, it is the "banner of craving"; it is called *taṇhādhaja* because it has craving as its flag. *Taṇhāketu*:
it is called *taṇhāketu* because craving itself is its crest (*ketu*) in the sense of going ahead. *Taṇhādhipateyyo*: it is dominated by craving by way of the predominance of desire (*chanda*);
or, it is called *taṇhādhipateyyo* because it comes from craving as the dominant factor; or else, craving is the dominant factor.
"Having this as its dominant influence" means having craving as its dominant influence. The same method applies to the "banner of views" and so forth.
"Impure" means not completely purified. "Defiled" means defiled in itself. "Corrupting" means that which leads to torment.
"He sees two benefits" means he perceives two qualities. "The benefit pertaining to the present life" means in this very [life].
And the benefit of the visible dhamma within one’s own person. "Belonging to the future life" means the benefit to be attained in the world beyond.
"Whatever view the Teacher holds" means that the Teacher comes to possess whatever [conviction] he has acquired.

"The disciples hold that same view" means that the disciples, hearing his word, also come to possess that same [conviction]. "They honor him" means they perform acts of veneration toward him who has been honored.
“They show respect” means they bring about that which has reached the state of being respected. “They honor” means they hold dear with the mind.
“They worship” means they worship with the offering of the four requisites. “They pay homage” means they bring about that which has reached the state of being paid homage.
In this context, he for whom one gives the four requisites after honoring them and making them well-prepared and excellent is “honored. He toward whom one establishes a sense of reverence...
He whom they honor with the body is "honored" (*sakkata*). He whom they respect with speech is "respected" (*garukata*). He whom they love even with the mind is "venerated" (*mānita*).

He for whom they perform all these things is "worshiped" (*pūjita*). He for whom they perform the highest form of service by way of prostration, attendance, joining the palms in salutation, and so forth, is "revered" (*apacita*).
Some say: "They honor him with the body, they respect him with speech, they venerate him with the mind, they worship him..."
They explain it thus: "By means of gain. "Sufficient for being a *nāga*" means sufficient or adequate for the state of a *nāga*, or for the state of a *nāga* king.
"For being a *supaṇṇ*" means for the state of a *supaṇṇa* king. "For being a *yakkha*" means for the state of a *yakkha* general. "For being an *asura*" means for the state of an *asura*.
"For being a *gandhabba*" means for the state of being reborn in the assembly of the *gandhabba* devas. "For being a Great King..."
"Vāti" means for the sake of becoming one of the four Great Kings. "Indattāya vāti" means for the sake of the state of Sakka.

"Brahmattāya vāti" means for the sake of becoming one of the various classes of deities such as those of the Brahma-world. "Devattāya vāti" means for the sake of becoming one of the various types of conventional deities (*sammutideva*).
"Suddhiyā" means sufficient or adequate for the sake of a state of complete purity. "Visuddhiyā" means for the sake of an absolutely pure state free from all defilements.
"Parisuddhiyā" means for the sake of complete purity in every respect.

In that regard, it is for the sake of purification (*suddhi*) with reference to oneself in the animal realm; for the sake of thorough purification (*visuddhi*) with reference to oneself in the world of the devas;
and for the sake of total purity (*parisuddhi*) with reference to oneself in the Brahma-world, for the purpose of being liberated after eighty-four thousand eons have passed.
"By liberation": for the purpose of being liberated through the absence of obstacles, by means of *vimutti*. "By complete liberation": by way of liberation in every aspect, that is, *parimutti*.
"They are purified" (*sujjhanti*): at that time, they attain purity by virtue of their state as renunciants. "They are thoroughly purified" (*visujjhanti*):
having taken up renunciation, they are purified in various ways through being devoted to the practice. "They are completely purified" (*parisujjhanti*): [they reach] perfection...

Having reached [the goal], they are purified in every way. They are released by means of their own respective doctrines. They are liberated by the exhortation of this Teacher. They are fully emancipated by the instruction of this Teacher.

"I shall be purified," and so forth, are stated with reference to the future. "Expecting a fruit in the future" means desiring the result of maturation in the future. This is the view of those who follow wrong paths.
It is merely a matter of desire. For when a speculative view succeeds, it produces either hell or the animal realm.

"Ultimate peace" (*accanta-santi*) means the peace of final transcendence. "Peace by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga-santi*): because the factor of defilement, such as the hindrances, is stilled by the factor of excellence, such as the first jhāna, the jhāna is "peace by substitution of opposites.
"Conventional peace" (*sammuti-santi*) refers to the peace of views by way of conventional designation. These, according to their divisions—
In order to demonstrate this, he said, "What is ultimate peace? and so forth. Terms such as "the deathless" and "nibbāna" have already had their meaning explained above.
Statements such as "for one who has attained the first jhāna, the hindrances are stilled" are spoken with reference to the excellence found within the state of absorption (appanā).
Furthermore, in this context, "peace" (santi) is intended in the sense of conventional peace (sammuti-santi), having set aside the other two types of peace.

It illuminates only conventional peace (*sammuti-santi*). "Shaking peace" (*kuppasanti*) refers to a peace that is unstable due to the production of karmic results and through the process of transformation.
"Greatly shaking peace" (*pakuppasanti*) refers to one that is especially unstable. "Agitated peace" (*eritasanti*) refers to a peace that is trembling.

"Violently agitated peace" (*sameritasanti*) refers to one that is especially violently trembling. "Moving peace" (*calitasanti*) is a synonym for that very same state. "Struck peace" (*ghaṭṭitasanti*) refers to a peace that is oppressed.
“Dependent on peace” means dependent on the peace known as [right] view. “Resorted to” means settled upon or specifically dependent.
“Clinged to” means become one with it. 20. Regarding those thus dependent, in the passage beginning “The settling on views...
and grasps at phenomena,” there “settling on views” refers to the fixations on views characterized by the adherence that thinks “this alone is the truth. Indeed, they are not easily transcended.
They do not exist. Regarding the phrase "having discerned and grasped among phenomena" (*dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītaṃ*):

it is said that because one does not transcend them, the adherence to views—which proceeds after having discerned and become attached to various grasped phenomena among the sixty-two types of speculative views—does not indeed pass beyond them.
Therefore, the verse says: "Therefore, a person, amidst those attachments, both rejects and takes up phenomena. This is because he does not transcend them.
Therefore, a person, within those very same fixed views, rejects and adopts, abandons and grasps various doctrines—

such as the teacher, the preaching of the Dhamma, and the various groups— and likewise practices the "goat-virtue," "ox-virtue," "dog-virtue," the five fires, the desert, the leap, the squatting posture, the exertion, and the bed of thorns;
it is said that he is like a forest monkey that seizes one branch after another.
Thus, by rejecting and adopting [qualities] with an unstable mind, one might produce fame or infamy for oneself or for another through qualities or faults that do not even exist.
"Difficult to overcome" (*durativatta*) means difficult to transcend. "Difficult to cross" (*duttara*) means difficult to get across.
"Difficult to pass over," "difficult to surmount," and "difficult to turn back" are expanded by the addition of prefixes (*upasagga*).

“Having determined” (*nicchinitvā*) means having made a determination by way of eternalism. “Having discriminated” (*vinicchinitvā*) means having made a discrimination in various ways by way of a self (*atta*).
“Having sought” (*vicinitvā*) means having searched. “Having thoroughly sought” (*pavicinitvā*) means having searched in every manner by way of what belongs to a self (*attaniya*).

There is also a reading: “having sifted” (*nicinitvā*) and “having winnowed” (*viccinitvā*). “Grasping by way of a limit” (*odhiggāha*) means grasping after having fixed a boundary. “Grasping by way of a pit” (*bilaggāha*)...
Grasping by way of parts (*koṭṭhāsa*) is, as in the phrase "having analyzed part by part" (*bilaso vibhajitvā*), grasping according to its constituent portions.

Grasping the best (*varaggāha*) is grasping the supreme. Grasping by components (*koṭṭhāsaggāha*) is grasping by way of its members. Grasping by accumulation (*uccayaggāha*) is grasping by way of a heap. Grasping by collection (*samuccayaggāha*) is grasping by way of both parts and heaps.
"This is the truth" (*idaṃ saccaṃ*) means this alone is the true nature (*sabhāva*). "Suchness" (*tatha*) means the state of being thus, the non-perverted nature.
"Tathā" means free from change (*vipariṇāma*). "Bhūta" means existing (*vijjamāna*). "Yāthāva" means according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāva*). "Aviparīta" means not inverted (*na viparīta*).
"Nirassati" means he casts away (*niassati*) or distracts (*vikkhipati*). "By way of being cut off by others" means by being made to relinquish by others.
"Not being able to endure" means not reaching it, or being unable to maintain it, he relinquishes it. "Another cuts him off" means another person effects a separation.
"Natthettha" means "there is not here. "Not fulfilling virtue" means not accomplishing virtue. "He rejects virtue" means he abandons virtue.
This same method applies to the following cases as well.
21. But as for this one who is "shaken off" (*dhona*) because he is endowed with the wisdom that shakes off all faults such as the various types of views (*diṭṭhigata*), his...

"For the one who is cleansed... he is without attachment. What is this saying? For the one who is cleansed—endowed with the qualities of cleansing and having shaken off all evil—the Arahant, there is no intention or view regarding any part of the world or any of those various states of existence.

Because of the absence of such views, and because of that [absence] by which the sectarian teachers, while concealing the evil karma they themselves have committed, act through either deceit or pride...
Thus they go to a bad destination; but having abandoned both that illusion and pride, by what means could the one who is free from stain go?
In this very life or in the future, by what means could he be reckoned among the various destinations such as the hells?
He is "without resort" (*anūpaya*), for he is without resort due to the absence of the two resorts of craving and views.
"By what cause? means for what reason. "Why is wisdom called 'dhona'? means for what reason is wisdom so designated?

"By that wisdom, bodily misconduct" means: by that aforementioned kind of wisdom, that which proceeds from the body—being "bad" (duṭṭhu) because it is rotten with defilements, or being "conduct" (carita)—is "bodily misconduct" (kāyaduccarita). "Shaken off and washed away" means both shaken and cleansed.
"Sandhotañca" means well-washed. "Niddhotañca" means especially and thoroughly washed.
"Rāgo dhuto ca" (lust shaken off) and so forth should be applied according to the four paths.
Regarding "By right view, wrong view is shaken off": by right view associated with the path, wrong view [is shaken off].
“Shaken,” “moved,” and “washed away. This same method applies to right intention and the others as well.
For this Sutta should be quoted in detail: “Bhikkhus, for one of right view, wrong view is worn away.

By “right knowledge” is meant either knowledge associated with the Path or reviewing knowledge. “Wrong knowledge” is perverted knowledge, knowledge that is not according to reality, occurring by way of preoccupation with evil deeds.
Delusion that arises in the manner of reviewing after having committed evil, thinking, "I have done well. Regarding "wrong liberation" as opposed to "right liberation":
it is precisely the perverted, non-factual liberation that is contrary to liberation by total eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*), yet is designated as "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*).
An *arahant* stands far removed from these defilements such as lust, and thus is called an *arahant* because of these aforementioned qualities that are to be shaken off.
He is endowed with qualities that wash away the defilements (*dhona*). "Washed" (*dhona*) refers to a person who has washed [away impurities];

for this very reason, it is said, "he is one whose lust is washed away," and so forth. *Māyā* is called a deceptive practice; thus, one who possesses the act of deceiving or the performance of deception is "one of deceptive practice.
"For the sake of concealing those" means for the purpose of not revealing those misdeeds. "He entertains an evil wish" means:
He establishes a base aspiration. "He desires that 'they may not know me'" means he expects, "May others not know the evil I have committed.

"He intends" means he arouses a thought. "He speaks words" means that a monk who knowingly transgresses a designation (paṇṇatti) commits a grave offense. [Thinking,] "There is no ground for our transgression," [he acts].
He speaks as if he were peaceful. "He exerts himself with the body" means that he performs physical actions with the thought, "Let no one know that this evil deed was done by me.
Because he conceals existing faults, he possesses "deceit which deludes the eye"; thus he is a deceiver (*māyāvī*).

The state of being a deceiver is "deceitfulness" (*māyāvitā*). Because a being remembers excessively (*aticca*) after having committed an evil deed for the sake of concealing it again, [it is called *macchariya*].
*Accasarā*. It is *vañcanā* (deceit) because one deceives by appearing otherwise through actions of body and speech.

It is *nikati* (guile) because beings disparage one another by means of it; the meaning is that they act wrongly. It is *nikiraṇā* (dissimulation) because one diverts blame for evils by saying, "I did not do this.

It is *pariharaṇā* (concealment) because one avoids [the truth] by saying, "I did not do this. It is *gūhanā* (covering up) because one hides [one's faults] by means of body and so forth. By way of evenness...
*Gūhanā* is concealing; *parigūhanā* is thorough concealing. It is called *chādanā* because one covers over evil with bodily and verbal actions, as if covering excrement with grass and leaves.
*Paricchādanā* is concealing on all sides. Because one does not show it by making it plain, it is called *anuttānikamma*.
Because one does not show it by making it manifest, it is called *anāvikamma*. *Vocchādanā* is excellent concealing. By way of having performed such concealment—
Furthermore, it is from the performance of evil that there is "evil-doing.

This is called "deceit" (māyā), which is defined by the characteristic of concealing what has been done; a person endowed with this is like a coal covered by ashes, like a stump hidden by water, or like a sword wrapped in a rag.

Pride as a single type is pride by way of a single delimitation, a single portion. "That which is the loftiness of the mind" means that which is the elevation of the mind; this is the meaning of pride. Here, pride is spoken of simply as it arises, without referring to a specific person.

Pride of self-exaltation is the pride that places oneself in a superior position. Pride of disparaging others is the pride that treats others as inferior. These two types of pride are generally stated according to their predominant mode of manifestation.
“*Seyyohamasmī*” (I am superior) conceit is the conceit that arises based on birth and so forth, thinking “I am superior.

The same method applies to the conceits of equality and inferiority as well. Thus, these three types of conceit are described according to their mode of occurrence without depending on a specific distinction of person.
Among them, each one arises in relation to all three—those who are superior, equal, and inferior. Therein, the conceit “I am superior” arises only for one who is superior.

Pride regarding one who is inferior is pride that is in accordance with reality (*yāthāvamāna*) toward those who are inferior; toward others, it is pride that is not in accordance with reality. The pride thinking, "I am equal," is pride that is in accordance with reality toward one who is equal;
toward others, it is pride that is not in accordance with reality. The pride thinking, "I am inferior," is pride that is in accordance with reality toward one who is inferior;

toward others, it is pride that is not in accordance with reality. Pride has been explained in four ways according to the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). Pride has been explained in five ways according to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). Pride has been explained in six ways according to the excellence of the eye and the other [senses]. In this context, "he generates pride" means he produces pride.
In the exposition of the sevenfold conceit (*māna*), "conceit" (*māna*) means loftiness (*unnama*). "Excessive conceit" (*atimāna*) is conceit arisen by way of overestimation, thinking:
"There is no one equal to me in birth and so forth. "Conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*) is conceit arisen [thinking]:
"This person was equal to me in the past, but now I am superior and this person is inferior. This is like a burden upon a burden, compared to the previous conceit of equality.
In order to show that which is called "conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*) based on [a certain basis], he said "conceit beyond conceit. "Inferiority-conceit" (*omāna*) is inferior conceit.

That which is called conceit in the sense of "I am inferior" is what is known as inferiority-conceit. Furthermore, in this context [the following is said]: "You have a birth; your birth is like that of a crow. You have a clan;
your clan is like that of a *caṇḍāla*. You have a voice; your voice is like that of a crow."
Thus, by way of proceeding while placing oneself below others, this should be understood as "inferiority-conceit" (*omāna*).

"Excessive conceit" (*adhimāna*) refers to one who perceives themselves as having attained what they have not attained regarding the Four Truths; one who perceives themselves as having performed what is to be done through the four paths when it has not yet been performed;

one who perceives themselves as having mastered the Dhamma of the Four Truths when it has not been mastered; and one who perceives themselves as having realized Arahatship when it has not been realized.
The conceit that has arisen upon attaining [a state] is called overweening conceit (*adhimāna*). Now, for whom does this arise, and for whom does it not arise?

First of all, it does not arise in a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). For he, having become joyful through the reviewing of the defilements abandoned by the path, fruit, and Nibbāna, as well as those remaining defilements, is free from doubt regarding the penetration of the noble qualities; therefore, for stream-enterers and others, [conceit such as] "I am a once-returner" and so forth [does not arise].
Conceit does not arise; nor does it arise in one who is immoral, for he has no hope at all of attaining the noble qualities.
Nor does it arise in one who possesses virtue but has abandoned his meditation subject and is devoted to the pleasure of sleep and so forth.
However, it does not arise in one whose virtue is purified, who is diligent in his meditation subject, and who, having defined name-and-form, has crossed over doubt by discerning the conditions.
This arises for one who has applied the three characteristics and is contemplating formations while practicing insight;
and once it has arisen, one who has attained pure serenity or pure insight stops in the interim.
For he, not seeing the manifestation of defilements for ten years, twenty years, thirty years, or even eighty years, thinks: "I..."
He does not conceive of one as a "stream-enterer," a "once-returner," or a "non-returner"; rather, he establishes only those who have attained serenity and insight in the state of Arahantship.
For in him, the defilements are suppressed by the power of concentration and the formations are thoroughly grasped by the power of insight;
therefore, even for sixty years, eighty years, or a hundred years, the defilements [do not arise].
They do not manifest; his mental conduct is that of one whose taints are exhausted.
Not seeing the manifestation of defilements for so long, he does not stop midway and conceives the thought, "I am an arahant.
"The conceit 'I am'" (asmimāna) is the pride arisen in regard to the five aggregates—such as form—in the manner of "I am [form]," etc., thinking, "I am form and so forth."

"Wrong conceit" (*micchāmāna*) is the conceit arisen through evil spheres of action (*kammāyatana*), spheres of craft (*sippāyatana*), fields of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*), learning, eloquence, and rules and observances (*sīlabbata*), as well as through wrong view (*diṭṭhi*).

In this context, an "evil sphere of action" refers to the work of fishermen, fishers, hunters, and the like. An "evil sphere of craft" refers to casting nets for fish, making traps, setting snares, laying pits, impaling on stakes, and so forth.

And there is cleverness. A "base branch of knowledge" refers to any science that involves harming others. "Base learning" refers to that which is connected with the *Mahābhārata*, the abduction of Sītā, and so forth.
"Base ingenuity" refers to ingenuity connected with ill-spoken words, such as the fabrications of plays and lamentations.
"Base virtue" refers to the "vow of the goat" (*aja-sīla*) and the "vow of the cow" (*go-sīla*). Their "practice" (*vata*) likewise consists only of the "goat-practice" and the "cow-practice."

An evil view (*pāpikā diṭṭhi*), however, is any view whatsoever among the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*). The eightfold conceit (*māna*) has its meaning already explained in plain terms.
In the exposition of the ninefold conceit (*navavidha-māna-niddesa*), the nine types of conceit—beginning with "I am superior" (*seyyo 'ham asmi*)—are stated with reference to a person.
Among these, the conceit "I am superior" arises in both kings and those who have gone forth (*pabbajita*).
For a king conceives this conceit: "In terms of kingdom or wealth and vehicles, who is there equal to me? Even one who has gone forth conceives this conceit:
"In terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so forth, who is there equal to me?
The conceit "I am equal" arises for those very same [types of persons]. For a king [thinks], "In terms of kingdom or wealth and vehicles..."
He conceives this conceit: "What difference is there between me and other kings? Even when he has gone forth, he conceives this conceit:
"What difference is there between me and another bhikkhu in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so forth?
The conceit "I am inferior" also arises in these very persons. For instance, [the conceit arises] regarding a king's kingdom, wealth, vehicles, and so on...
Or if they are not very abundant, he conceives this pride, thinking: "The title 'king' is for me merely a convenience of worldly convention; what is this so-called 'king,' am I not [the king]?

Even when gone forth, one who receives little gain and honor conceives this pride, thinking: "'I am an expounder of the Dhamma,' 'I am learned,' 'I am a great elder'—this is mere talk. What am I, an 'expounder of the Dhamma'? What am I, a 'learned one'? What...
One who thinks, "I am a great elder (mahāthera), yet for me there is no gain or honor," conceives this pride (*māna*).

In one who is equal [to another], such things as the pride "I am superior" arise in ministers and others. For a minister or a provincial official might think, "What other royal person is my equal in terms of wealth, vehicles, mounts, and so forth? or, "Compared to others, mine..."
Or he conceives the pride: "What is the difference between me and him? Or: "I have the mere title of 'minister,' yet I do not even have enough food and clothing; what kind of minister am I?
Such prides arise in one who is inferior, such as the pride "I am superior," which arises in those like slaves. For instance, a slave [thinks] regarding his mother or father...
Or [thinking]: "What other slave indeed is there equal to me? Others have become slaves because they were unable to live otherwise due to the womb;
but I am superior because it has come down through my lineage"; or [thinking]:

"What difference is there for me between this and such-and-such a slave, since we both share the status of being slaves by lineage and are doubly pure slaves"; or [thinking]: "I entered into slavery by way of the womb..."
Furthermore, one develops these conceits, thinking: "I have no place among ten million parents; how could I be a slave?
Just as with a slave, so too do outcasts, scavengers, and others develop such conceits.
And herein, the conceit that arises in one who is superior, thinking "I am superior," is a conceit based on reality (*yāthāvamāna*); the other two are conceits not based on reality (*ayāthāvamāna*).
Likewise, the conceit that arises in one who is equal, thinking “I am equal,” or in one who is inferior, thinking “I am inferior,” is conceit according to reality (*yāthāvamāna*);
the other two are conceits not according to reality (*ayāthāvamāna*). Among these, the conceits according to reality are to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship;

the conceits not according to reality are to be abandoned by the path of Stream-entry. And herein, the conceit of one who is superior, thinking “I am superior,” refers to one who is supreme in the sense of being supreme, [thinking] “I am superior.”
The conceit "I am equal" arising toward one who is superior; the conceit "I am equal" arising toward one who is supreme by way of equality;

and the conceit "I am inferior" arising toward one who is superior by way of being base—thinking "I am inferior"—thus these three types of conceit arise in one who is superior. Specifically: the conceit "I am equal" toward one who is superior; the conceit "I am equal" toward one who is supreme;

and the conceit "I am inferior" toward one who is supreme by way of being base—thinking "I am inferior"—thus these three conceits arise in one who is superior. These three conceits—the conceit of superiority, the conceit of equality, and the conceit of inferiority—arise in one who is superior.

In one who is equal, three types of conceit arise: "I am better," "I am equal," or "I am inferior. In one who is inferior, three types of conceit also arise: "I am inferior," "I am equal," or "I am better. Regarding the exposition of the tenfold conceit:
"here someone generates conceit" means that a certain person generates conceit. [This occurs] by way of birth...
"By means of the excellence of birth," such as the status of a khattiya (noble) and so forth; "or by clan," such as the Gotama clan or other distinguished clans;
"or by family lineage," meaning by being of a great family; "or by the beauty of complexion," meaning by having a body endowed with a beautiful complexion.
For the body is called "pokkhara"; thus, the meaning is: by the state of being handsome through the perfection of the body's complexion.
“By wealth” means either by the possession of wealth; the meaning is that there is no limit to my wealth stored as a treasure.

“Or by recitation” means by way of study. “Or by the sphere of action” means thinking, “The rest of beings are like crows with clipped wings, but I am of great psychic power and great majesty,” or “Whatever work I undertake, all of it succeeds.”
Or by the sphere of action (*kammāyatana*) proceeding in such a manner as this; or by the sphere of craft (*sippāyatana*) proceeding in such a manner as this:
"The rest of beings are without craft, but I am possessed of craft"; or by the field of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*), which is in the same manner as explained below;
or by learning (*suta*) proceeding in such a manner as this: "The rest of beings have little learning, but I am one of great learning."
Or by way of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*): that is, by such ingenuity as, "The remaining beings are lacking in ingenuity, but for me there is no limit to my ingenuity," and so forth.
Or by way of some other basis (*vatthu*): that is, by another unstated basis.

"Whatever conceit of such a kind" refers to conceit (*māna*) by way of the act of conceiving. "Conceiving" (*maññanā*) and "the state of conceiving" (*maññitatta*) are terms describing its mode and its nature.
In the sense of being raised high, it is *unnati*. That which arises makes a person lofty, lifting them up and establishing them there, thus it is *unnāma*.
In the sense of being well-raised, it is a *dhaja* (banner). In the sense of uplifting, it thoroughly seizes the mind, thus it is *sampaggāha*.
*Ketu* refers to the highest-raised banner among many banners. Pride (*māna*), arising again and again, is so called in the sense of being loftily elevated by taking up successive [objects].
A banner (*ketu*) is that which flies abroad (*viyāti*); one who desires that banner is "one desirous of a banner" (*ketukamyam*); the state of being such is "desire for a banner" (*ketukamyatā*).

However, that belongs to the mind, not to oneself. Therefore it is said: "Desire for a banner of the mind. For the mind associated with conceit (*māna*) desires a banner; its state is conceit, which is designated as a "banner.
Having abandoned and relinquished both deceit (*māyā*) and conceit (*māna*), the one who is "shaken off" (*dhona*)—that is, purified—[is so called].

That ascetic, an Arahant—who stands having abandoned the defilements by means of their removal, bringing them to an end, and so forth, in the manner described above—would go with those defilements such as lust and the rest.
"Or one bound for hell" means a being reborn in hell; the same method applies to those born in the animal womb and so forth. He...
"There is no cause" means that there is no productive cause by which one might be reborn in the various realms of existence and so forth.
"Condition" is a synonym for that same thing. "Reason" (*kāraṇa*) means a basis (*ṭhāna*).

For a reason is called the "basis" of its own fruit because the latter's existence is dependent upon it. Therefore, there is no such reason or condition by which one might be reborn in the various realms of existence and so forth.
22. Furthermore, as for that approach (*upāya*) which exists through the state of these two approaches, that approach is indeed...
[as before] ... "all is view in this very world. In this context, "approach" (*upāya*) is dependent upon craving and views.

One "approaches" a doctrine regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), saying "one is lustful" or "one is hateful," thus approaching a doctrine regarding this or that phenomenon. How could one speak of a non-approach (*anupāya*)? How could one speak of it?
But by the abandoning of craving and views, how could one say that the one whose taints are exhausted—who is beyond all means—“is impassioned” or “is corrupted” on account of lust or hatred?
And since he is thus beyond reproach, the intention [of the verse] is: why would he be like the sectarians who practice concealment?
For "neither self nor non-self exists for him," because for him there is neither the view of a self nor the view of annihilation.
There is neither grasping nor releasing, nor even that which is designated as "self" or "non-self.
If one asks why they do not exist, it is because: "He has washed away every view right here.

Since he, in this very state of existence, has washed away, abandoned, and dispelled all speculative views with the water of knowledge—thus concluding the teaching at the pinnacle of Arahantship—the King, having heard this, was delighted.
"Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he departed.
"Red" means either red with passion (*rāga*) or red [in color]. The same method applies to the phrases "corrupt," and so forth.

"Those volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) have not been abandoned" refers to those volitional formations of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable (*āneñja*), which have not been abandoned. "Because the volitional formations have not been abandoned" [is the reason for the result].
It is because those aforementioned formations of kamma have not been abandoned. "He enters into a dispute regarding a destination" means he approaches the assertion of one of the five destinations.
For this very reason, it is said: "He enters into, that is, approaches, the claim that 'one is a denizen of hell'...
[and so on]... or 'one is a deva'. "He might say" means he might speak. "There is nothing taken" means there is nothing to be grasped.
"There is nothing to be released" means that because one stands having already released [the grasping], there is nothing further to be released.
"For whom there is grasping" refers to that person for whom there is grasping in the form of "I" and "mine.
"For him there is something to be released" means that for that person there is something to be released. The subsequent phrases should be applied by reversing the terms. Grasping...
"Having transcended by releasing": the Arahant has transcended grasping and release. "Having passed beyond the decline of intelligence":

this refers to that which proceeds having gone beyond both increase and decline. From "He is one who has dwelt [in the rains]" and so forth, down to the conclusion "burnt away by the fire of knowledge," the method is exactly as explained below.
"Adho-sī" means you shake off. "Dhuni, sandhuni, niddhunī": the word-form has been expanded by means of prefixes.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Discourse on the Eightfold Corruption (*Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa*) in the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed. 4.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Discourse on the Eightfold Purity (*Suddhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa*).
23. Regarding the first verse of the fourth set of eight pure verses, the meaning is as follows:
"Monks, purity does not come from such a vision; rather, it is impure because it is defiled by the stains of the *kilesas*.

Having encountered the diseases of the *kilesas*, one sees the Brahmin Candābha—or anyone else of that sort—as being truly diseased. Upon seeing him, the foolish one who is caught in wrong views thinks: 'I see...'"
"Pure, supreme, and healthy; by that vision known as seeing, a person attains complete purification.
Knowing this, he understands that vision to be "supreme"; while contemplating purity within that vision, he regards that vision as "knowledge of the path.
Yet, that is not actually knowledge of the path.
"Attained to supreme health" means having reached and established oneself in the highest state of freedom from disease. "Attained to protection" means likewise having reached a state of preservation.
"Attained to a shelter" means having reached a place of refuge. "Attained to a resort" means having reached a firm foundation, or having reached that which destroys suffering.
"Attained to fearlessness" means having reached a state free from dread. "Attained to the deathless" means having reached the state of immortality. "Attained to the ambrosia" means...
The deathless Great Nibbāna has been attained. Or, "one who has attained Nibbāna" means one who has attained that which is free from craving (*taṇhā*).

"One who knows directly" (*abhijānanto*) means knowing with distinction. "One who understands" (*ājānanto*) means understanding. "One who discerns" (*vijānanto*) means knowing in manifold ways. "One who penetrates" (*paṭivijānanto*) means discerning in dependence upon this or that. "One who pierces through" (*paṭivijjhanto*) means making it one's own within the heart.
"Eye-consciousness by the seeing of forms" means the seeing of forms by means of eye-consciousness. "Wisdom" (*paññā*) is so called because it realizes (*pacceti*) knowledge.
Thus he has faith. He resolves, "It is the path," meaning he has faith that it is the "means. "Path" (patha) means a way of proceeding.
It is called "leading out" (niyyāna) because one goes by taking hold of it; alternatively, the reading is "niyyānaṃ. 24.
"If purity is through what is seen" is the second verse. Its meaning is: by that which is called "seen," namely, the seeing of forms...

If a person attains purification from defilements through that knowledge, and if by means of that knowledge he abandons the suffering of birth and so forth, then—this being the case—he would be purified by a path of impurity other than the Noble Path;

and while still possessing the acquisitions (upadhi) such as lust and the rest, he would incur the state of being called "purified," yet one who is of such a nature is not truly purified. Therefore, this is a [wrong] view.
Indeed, because he speaks in such a way, that very view declares of him, "This one is a holder of wrong view";
for he speaks accordingly, in such and such ways, according to his view, by way of [asserting] "the world is eternal," and so forth.
It is called *sarāga* because it exists together with lust (*rāga*); the meaning is "one who possesses lust. The same method applies to the terms *sadosa* and the others as well.

25. "Not by birth is one a brahmin" is the third verse. Its meaning is as follows: He who is a brahmin because he has banished evil is a *khīṇāsava*-brahmin (a brahmin whose taints are destroyed) who has attained the destruction of the taints through the Path.

Apart from the knowledge of the Noble Path, he does not regard as a true auspicious sign (*abhimaṅgala*) what is called a "seen" object—such as the form of an elephant or a lute—and likewise what is called a "heard" sound, nor does he rely on virtue (*sīla*) defined as non-transgression, nor on the various [superstitions] such as elephant-sacrifices and so forth.
He does not attain purity through wrong knowledge arisen regarding wind, or the various [elements] such as earth, or regarding what is sensed.
The rest is stated by way of praising this brahmin. For he is unsullied by all merit within the three realms and by all evil;
why? Because of his having abandoned that view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), and because of his having abandoned any grasping whatsoever, he has relinquished the self (*attañjaho*).
Because he does not perform volitional formations of merit and so forth, he is said to be "one who does nothing here. Therefore, praising him in this way, the Blessed One said:

"Untainted by both merit and evil, having abandoned the self, one who does nothing here—a brahmin does not seek purity from elsewhere. The connection of all this should be understood with the first line:
"Untainted by merit and by evil, having abandoned the self, one who does nothing here—a brahmin does not seek purity from elsewhere. *Na* is a negation; it is a prohibition.
The meaning of the verse "Having cast out all evils" is as follows: it is said that he who, by means of the fourth path, has cast out all evils and stands firm is one whose self is established.
Precisely because he has cast out evil, he is stainless (*vimalo*); he has attained the state of being stainless, the state of Brahma, the supreme state.

By means of the concentration of the fruit of the highest path, which has relinquished the stains of the defilements that cause the distraction of concentration, he is well-composed (*sādhusamāhito*).
By having transcended saṃsāra through the surmounting of its causes, he is called "the Perfect One" (*kevalī*) because his task is fully accomplished;

by not being dependent on craving or views, he is called "the Independent One" (*anissito*); and by remaining unshaken by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), he is called "the Neutral One" (*tādī*). Thus, he is indeed worthy of praise as "the Brahmā," "the Brāhmaṇa."
"Apart from the foundations of mindfulness" means having set aside the four foundations of mindfulness. The same method applies to the right efforts and so forth.
"There being some recluses and brahmins" means that there exist certain individuals who, by worldly convention, have acquired the designation "recluses and brahmins.
"Those who seek purity through views" means those desiring purification by means of what is seen. They [hold] that it is the seeing of certain forms...

"Purification through what is seen" means the looking at these objects of form. "They prescribe auspiciousness" means they establish the cause of success, the cause of wisdom, and the cause of all prosperity.
"They prescribe inauspiciousness" means they establish the cause of failure, the cause of lack of wisdom, and the cause of lack of prosperity.
"Having emerged from their time" means that these proponents of auspiciousness based on what is seen [emerge] even beforehand.
Having risen. "Abhimaṅgalagatāni" means those things that have become specifically causes for prosperity. "Passantī rūpāni" means they will see various kinds of visible objects as sense-objects.
"Cāṭakasakuṇaṃ" refers to a bird of that name. "Phussaveḷuvalaṭṭhiṃ" means a young bamboo stalk produced under the constellation Phussa.
"Gabbhinitthiṃ" means a pregnant woman. "Kumārakaṃ khandhe" [means a boy on the shoulder].
"Carrying off" means going while lifting a young child upon one's shoulder. "Full jar" means a jar filled with water.
"Red fish" means a red *rohitaka* fish. "Chariot of thoroughbreds" means a chariot yoked with Sindhava horses.
"Bull" means an auspicious bull. "Tawny cow" means a tawny-colored cow.
“A heap of straw” means a pile of chaff. “A pot of buttermilk” means a vessel filled with buttermilk and so forth. “An empty pot” means a hollow pot. “Actors” refers to actors and the like;
some say it means “the conduct of rogues. “A naked ascetic” means a monk who goes about without clothes. “A donkey” means a camel.
“A donkey-cart” means a cart such as a *vayha* yoked to a donkey. “A single-yoked vehicle” means a vehicle drawn by a single beast of burden.
A connected vehicle. "One-eyed" means one who is blind in one eye or both eyes. "Lame" means one with a lame foot or a foot that moves horizontally.
"Palsy-stricken" means a cripple. "Decrepit" means worn out by old age. "Afflicted" means oppressed by disease. "Dead" means one who has passed away.
"Those seeking purity through hearing" means those desiring purification by what is heard through auditory consciousness. "The hearing of sounds" means [the hearing] of sound-objects.
*Sa-vanaṃ*. [The words] *vaḍḍhati*, *vāti*, and so forth, are spoken by taking up merely those sounds that occur in the world.
However, inauspiciousness consists precisely of the sounds expressed by various names such as "the one-eyed" (*kāṇo*) and so on.

Or, it is [the sound] "cut" (*chinda*), meaning "with hands, feet, etc., cut off"; or "split" (*bhinda*), meaning "with head, etc., split open"; or "burnt" (*daḍḍha*), meaning "consumed by fire"; or "lost" (*naṭṭha*).
"Is blown away" means destroyed by thieves and the like. "There is not" means it does not exist.
"Those who seek purity through virtue" (sīlasuddhika) are those who desire purification by means of virtue. "By mere virtue" means by mere restraint. "By mere self-control" means by mere cessation.
"By mere restraint" means by mere closing of the doors [of the senses]. "By mere non-transgression" means by the mere fact of not having transgressed.
"Śramaṇa Muṇḍikāputta" is the name he received from his mother. "Endowed with skill" means possessing complete skill.
"Supremely skilled" means possessing the highest skill. "Having attained the supreme attainment" means having reached and remained in the state of the supreme goal, Arhatship.
"Invincible" means a śramaṇa who cannot be defeated.
“Those who desire purity through vows” (*vatasuddhikā*) means those who seek purity by means of an undertaken vow (*samādāna-vata*).
“Those who possess the elephant-vow” (*hatthivatikā*) means those for whom there exists an undertaken elephant-vow; the meaning is that they perform every action of an elephant.
How so? With the thought, “From today onward, I shall do what is to be done by elephants,” their minds having thus arisen, [they imitate] the manner of walking of elephants...

They exhibit the manner of standing, the manner of sitting, the manner of lying down, and the manner of voiding excrement and urine; and upon seeing other elephants, they raise their trunks and display all the behaviors of walking—thus they are "elephant-like" (*hatthivatikā*).
In the case of the "horse-like" (*assavatikā*) and others as well, the application should be made accordingly based on what is observed.
Among these, at the end, the "quarter-like" (*disāvatikā*) are mentioned by way of paying homage to the directions, such as the east and so forth.
The undertaking of vows by these ascetics and brahmins who have undertaken the directions [of conduct],
when successful, leads to companionship with elephants and other such beings. However, if he holds wrong view— thinking, "By this undertaking of virtue, vows, and holy life,
may I become a god or some other kind of deity"— then for one who thinks thus, it results in rebirth in either hell or the animal realm.
This should be understood. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Here, Puṇṇa, a certain person develops the dog-vow, complete and uninterrupted;
he develops the dog-conduct, complete and uninterrupted; he develops the dog-mind, complete and uninterrupted; he develops the dog-appearance..."
He develops it fully and uninterruptedly. Having developed the dog-vow fully and uninterruptedly,
having developed the dog-ethic fully and uninterruptedly, having developed the dog-mind fully and uninterruptedly,
and having developed the dog-appearance fully and uninterruptedly, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of dogs.
But if he holds such a view as this: "By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or some other kind of deity," that is his wrong view.
For one with wrong view, Puṇṇa, I declare one of two destinations: either hell or the animal realm.
"Thus, Puṇṇa, when practiced successfully, the dog-vow leads to companionship with dogs; when practiced unsuccessfully, it leads to hell.

The meaning should not be taken as that those who practice the Gandhabba-vow and so forth attain companionship with Gandhabbas and so forth; rather, because they have grasped a wrong view, it should be understood that they go only to hell or the animal realm.
"Mutasuddhikā" means pure by means of a spray. "Touching the earth" refers to the great earth together with its constituent parts.
They touch with the body. "Green" means having fresh, green blades of grass. "Cow-dung" means the dung of cows and other such animals.
"Tortoise" refers to various kinds, such as the bony tortoise. "They tread upon the ploughshare" means they crush the iron ploughshare.
"A cartload of sesame" means a cart of sesame or a heap of sesame. "They eat auspicious sesame" means they eat sesame associated with auspicious rites. "Auspicious oil" [is mentioned].
"They massage" means they apply such sesame oil as an unguent for the body. "A tooth-stick" means a tooth-cleanser.
"They bathe with clay" means they bathe after rubbing their bodies with fine clay such as *kuṅkuma* (saffron) and the like.
"They put on a garment" means they wear cloth associated with auspiciousness. "They wrap a turban" means...
They place head-wrappings—cloths such as *paṭṭuṇṇa* and so forth—upon their heads and fasten them.

"Volitional formations of the three realms that are wholesome" refers to the condition-based volitional formations produced by skill (*kosalla*) that bestow rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, and the immaterial realm.
"All unwholesome [volitional formations]" refers to the twelvefold types produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*).

It is unwholesome (*akusala*). "When" (*yato*) means when those tenfold volitional formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), twelvefold volitional formations of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), and fourfold volitional formations of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) have been abandoned through their respective abandonment by complete eradication (*samucchedappahāna*). "One who has abandoned the view of self" (*attadiṭṭhijaha*) means one who has abandoned the view grasped as "this is my self.
"One who has abandoned grasping" (*gāhajaha*) means [one who has abandoned] the grasping [of the conceit] "I am this."
The inclusion of "associated with the mind" (*mānasampayutta*) is to be abandoned.

Furthermore, "one who has abandoned self" (*attajaha*) refers to that which was grasped by way of craving and by way of views as "this is mine," as well as what was touched upon subsequently, what was adhered to therein, what was swallowed and clung to through the power of strong craving, and what was strongly infatuated with—all that is abandoned; these and other points follow the same method already explained.

26. Having thus stated that “a brahmin does not find purity through another,” he now spoke the verse beginning with “having abandoned what is prior” to demonstrate that the views of those proponents of wrong views who claim purity through another do not lead to Nibbāna.
Its meaning is as follows: although they are proponents of purity through another, because they have not abandoned a particular view, there remains for them the grasping and releasing [of objects].
Having abandoned the former teacher and others by means of that [craving], they have relied upon another;

followed and overcome by craving—which is designated as *ejā*—they do not cross over the attachment consisting of the divisions of lust and so forth. And not crossing over that, they grasp at and let go of various phenomena, just as a monkey grasps one branch and then another.

"Having abandoned the former teacher" means having rejected the status of being a teacher previously accepted. "Dependent on another teacher" means dependent upon, attached to, another status of being a teacher. The same method applies to the phrases "having abandoned the former teaching of the Dhamma," and so forth.

"Followers of craving" (*ejānugā*) means those who follow after craving (*taṇhā*). "Those gone along with craving" (*ejānugatā*) means those who have followed after craving. "Those who have entered into craving" (*ejānusaṭā*) means those who have entered into or plunged into craving. "Those fallen into and cast down by craving" (*ejāya pannā patitā*) means those who are submerged and laid low by craving.
“Makkaṭo” means a monkey. “Araññe” means in the forest. “Pavane” means in the great woods. “Caramāno” means while walking.
“Evameva” is the application of the simile. “Puthū” means various. “Puthudiṭṭhigatāni” means various kinds of speculative views.
“Gaṇhanti ca muñcanti ca” means they grasp by way of seizing and they release by way of letting go; they take up and they cast off.
And they create obstacles, abandon [the practice], and cast it aside.
27. The connection with the fifth verse: "And he who was called 'for views indeed lead him astray when he speaks thus,' he himself takes them up.
In that context, *sayam* means by oneself. *Samādāya* means having taken up. *Vatāni* refers to the vows such as the elephant-vow (*hatthivata*) and others.
"High and low" means from one teacher to another, or from inferior to superior teachers. "One who clings to perceptions" refers to one who is attached to sensual perceptions and the like.

"And the wise one, having fully understood the Dhamma through knowledge" means that the Arahant, wise in the ultimate sense, has fully realized the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the four kinds of knowledge of the paths. The rest is self-evident.
*Samādāya*: having taken up by oneself. *Ādāya*: having taken up, having grasped. *Samādāya*: having properly taken up.
*Ādiyitvā*: having made an obstacle. *Samādiyitvā*: having properly made an obstacle. *Gaṇhitvā*: having seized, not letting go.
*Parāmasitvā*: having shown. *Abhinivisitvā*: having established. The perceptions of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) and so forth are exactly as described by the aforementioned method.
*Vidvā* means wise (*medhāvī*). *Vijjāgato* means having attained the state of knowing. *Ñāṇī* means endowed with wisdom (*paññā*). *Vibhāvī* means one who investigates by means of knowledge.
*Medhāvī* means one whose knowledge has weighed [the truths] such as impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth. *Paññā* and the other terms are exactly as explained below.
