"One investigates the Dhamma of the Four Truths" refers to the enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*). The meaning of "enlightenment factor" (*bojjhaṅga*) has already been explained above.
"Investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) is precisely wisdom that investigates the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; for it is said: "Investigation is the contemplation of the Dhamma.

"Insight" (*vipassanā*) is precisely wisdom that sees in various modes associated with the Path. "Right View" (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is the beautiful, praised, and excellent right view associated with the Path.
"By these knowledges" means by these very four kinds of path-knowledge. "One who has reached the end" (*antagata*)...
He has reached the end of birth, aging, and death. "One who has reached the limit" (*koṭigata*) and so forth are to be understood according to the method explained below.
Or, "one who has gone to the end of the Vedas" (*vedānam antagata*) means one who has reached the conclusion of all that is to be known.

Or, "one who has gone to the end by means of the Vedas" (*vedehi antagata*) means one who has reached Nibbāna—which is designated as the "end" because it constitutes the boundary of the suffering of saṃsāra—by means of the four kinds of knowledge of the paths (*maggañāṇa*). "By way of being known" (*viditattā*) means by way of having been known, that is, by way of having been understood.
The meaning of the verse, “Having scrutinized the Vedas in their entirety,” is as follows:
he who has gone by means of the four knowledges and insights of the paths, effecting the destruction of the defilements, is called a *vedagu* (one who has reached the Vedas) in the ultimate sense.

He, by that very cultivation of the path, having scrutinized through its function the Vedas—designated as the "weapons" of all recluses and brahmins—by way of their impermanence and so forth, [attains liberation] through the abandoning of desire and lust for them.
Having transcended all that feeling, as well as whatever feelings arise on account of the Vedas or otherwise, he is free from lust for all those feelings.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate this meaning, when asked, "What is it that they call a 'Vedaga'?", he did not say, "This is a Vedaga," but rather said, "Having investigated the Vedas... [he is] a Vedaga. Or alternatively, because one who, by means of investigative wisdom—
Having discerned the Vedas, by abandoning desire and lust for them, he proceeds having transcended all knowledge.

Having reached and known those things called "Vedas," he has indeed gone beyond. One who is free from passion regarding feelings (*vedanā*) has likewise reached and transcended those things called "Vedas";
because he has gone to the "beyond-feeling" (*ativedanā*), he is a "Veda-knower" (*vedagū*). Therefore, showing this meaning as well, [the Blessed One said]: "This is the attainment."
Having said, “...having investigated the Vedas... he is a master of knowledge,” [the Buddha] spoke.

“Having fully understood” (*samecca*) means having come together with wisdom. “Having penetrated” (*abhisamecca*) means having pierced through with wisdom. “The Dhamma” refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
“All conditioned phenomena” (*sabbe saṅkhārā*) refers to all phenomena that possess conditions; for these are indeed called “conditioned formations” (*saṅkhatasaṅkhārā*). By means of conditions...

They are called *saṅkhārā* because they are produced by coming together (*saṅgamma karīyanti*). Because they are thus produced by conditions coming together, they are specifically designated as "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*).
In the commentaries, it is stated: "The material and immaterial phenomena of the three planes produced by kamma are conditioned formations (*abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhārā*).
These too are included among the conditioned formations in such passages as, "Impermanent indeed are conditioned formations."

In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, when this person, immersed in ignorance, performs a meritorious volitional formation,” it is specifically formations that have come down as conditioned by ignorance. Volitions consisting of wholesome and unwholesome consciousness belonging to the three planes are called “formations that perform volitional construction.
In such passages as, “Having gone as far as the range of volitional construction, it stood as if struck by a pin,” [it refers to the same].
The bodily and mental energy that has arisen is called the "volitional formation of application" (*payogābhisaṅkhāra*).

In such passages as, “Friend Visākha, for a bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, first the verbal formation ceases, then the bodily formation, then the mental formation,” it is stated that applied thought and sustained thought form speech; thus they are called “verbal formations” (*vacīsaṅkhāra*).
In-breaths and out-breaths are "bodily formations" because they are conditioned by the body; perception and feeling are "mental formations" because they are conditioned by the mind.
Here, however, it is the conditioned formations that are intended. They are impermanent in the sense of having no existence after having come to be;
they are suffering in the sense of being oppressed; and "all phenomena" is said including even Nibbāna. They are non-self in the sense of being devoid of mastery.
Regarding the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*): here, that depending upon which a result comes about is the "condition" (*paccaya*).

"Depending upon" (*paṭicca*) means not without [it], that is, not excluding it. "Comes about" (*eti*) means both arises and occurs. Furthermore, the meaning of "condition" is the sense of being beneficial or supportive.
Ignorance is both itself and a condition, thus it is "ignorance-condition"; from that, "with ignorance as condition. "Volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*).
“They arise” means they are produced; in this way, the word *sambhavanti* (they arise) should also be construed with the remaining terms.

Therein, what is ignorance (*avijjā*)? It is non-knowing regarding suffering, non-knowing regarding the origin of suffering, non-knowing regarding the cessation of suffering, non-knowing regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, non-knowing regarding the past, non-knowing regarding the future, and non-knowing regarding both the past and the future.
Ignorance: ignorance regarding these phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions. What are volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)?

The meritorious volitional formation, the non-meritorious volitional formation, and the imperturbable volitional formation; the bodily volitional formation, the verbal volitional formation, and the mental volitional formation;
the eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere, the five wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere—these are the meritorious volitional formation—and the twelve unwholesome volitions.
The formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) consists of the four types of wholesome volition pertaining to the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*).

The imperturbable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) consists of bodily volition as bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), verbal volition as verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*), and mental volition as mental formation (*manosaṅkhāra*).
Herein, it may be asked: how is it to be known that "these formations have ignorance as their condition"? [It is known] from the absence of ignorance.

By way of its nature: for one in whom the ignorance known as nescience regarding suffering and the other truths has not been abandoned, he—through that nescience regarding suffering as well as the past and so forth—grasps the suffering of saṃsāra with the perception of pleasure and initiates the three kinds of volitional formations which are the cause of that very suffering.
Through nescience regarding the origin, he [regards] the volitional formations conditioned by craving—which are actually causes of suffering—as causes of pleasure.

One undertakes [volitional formations] through conceiving. However, regarding cessation and the path, due to ignorance, one perceives as the cessation of suffering those specific states of existence that are not actually the cessation of suffering;

and perceiving as the path to cessation those things such as sacrifice, self-mortification, and austerity that are not actually the path to cessation, one undertakes all three kinds of volitional formations by way of sacrifice, self-mortification, and austerity while aspiring for the cessation of suffering.
Moreover, because of that ignorance which has not been abandoned regarding the Four Truths, he—

failing to recognize as suffering even that suffering known as the fruit of merit, which is interspersed with manifold disadvantages such as birth, aging, sickness, and death— undertakes the volitional formation of merit consisting of bodily, vocal, and mental activities for its attainment,
just like one who desires celestial nymphs might leap from a precipice on Mount Meru. This is true even of that which is considered pleasure.
And even though he does not perceive the suffering of change and the lack of satisfaction inherent in that meritorious fruit— which at its end produces great fever—
he nevertheless initiates the aforementioned volitional formation of merit for its sake, like a moth flying into the flame of a lamp,
or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking the edge of a sword blade smeared with honey.

Furthermore, failing to see the danger in the pursuit of sensual pleasures and other such states that entail karmic results, and being both deceived by the perception of pleasure and overwhelmed by the defilements,
one initiates unwholesome volitional formations even through the three doors— just as a fool engages in playing with excrement, or like one wishing to die who consumes poison. And likewise,
failing to comprehend the suffering inherent in the transformation and decay of conditioned phenomena, even regarding the results of the formless attainments...
Through the perversion of eternalism and so forth, one initiates the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), which is a mental volitional formation,

like a person who has lost his way setting out on a path toward a city of demons. Thus, because the state of being a formation arises precisely from the existence of ignorance and not from its absence,
it should be understood that "these formations have ignorance as their condition."
Here it is asked: Let us grant for now that "ignorance is a condition for volitional formations.
But is this ignorance alone the condition for volitional formations, or are there other conditions as well? What follows from this?

If it were ignorance alone, one would fall into the doctrine of a single cause. If, on the other hand, there are others, then the singular designation "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" [would be incorrect].
Does it not arise? It does not fail to arise. Why? Because:
“One is not from one here, nor is the many from the many, nor is the one from the many;
there is a fruit, and yet there is a purpose in illustrating the relationship between cause and fruit.”
For the Blessed One, depending on whether it is for the sake of emphasis, clarity, or uniqueness, and in accordance with the elegance of his teaching and the dispositions of those to be trained,
illustrates either a single cause or a single fruit. Therefore, although other bases, objects, co-nascent factors,
and so forth exist as causes of volitional formations, here ignorance alone is [singled out] for one who contemplates gratification.

It should be understood that ignorance is explained as the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) because it is the primary cause among other causes such as craving, according to the statements, "Craving increases" and "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints (*āsava*");

because it is evident from the passage, "Bhikkhus, one who is ignorant and immersed in ignorance performs even a meritorious volitional formation"; and because it is unique [to all types of formations].

And by this very statement regarding the refutation of the explanation of each individual cause and fruit, the purpose for explaining each individual cause and fruit in all instances should be understood.

Here it is asked: Even if this is so, how is it logical that ignorance—which has exclusively undesirable fruits and is reprehensible—should be a condition for the formations of merit and the imperturbable?
For sugar-cane does not arise from a nimba seed. How could it not be logical? For in the world—
“Contradictory and non-contradictory, likewise similar and dissimilar—
such is established as the condition for phenomena, yet they are not themselves kamma-results. Thus,
this ignorance is exclusively undesirable in terms of its result, and it is also blameworthy by way of its own intrinsic nature.

It should be understood that for all these—meritorious formations and so forth—there is a conditionality according to their respective suitability, by way of conditions that are compatible or incompatible with their location, function, and intrinsic nature, and by way of similar and dissimilar conditions. Furthermore, there is this other method:
"In death and rebirth, in saṃsāra, and in the characteristics of formations;..."
He who is deluded regarding dependently arisen phenomena constructs these three kinds of volitional formations;
therefore, ignorance is the condition for those three types as well.
“Just as a man born blind, having no guide,
Sometimes goes by the right path and sometimes by the wrong path; So the fool, wandering in saṃsāra, being without a guide, [Sometimes goes by the right path and sometimes by the wrong path.]”
At one time he performs merit, and at another time even demerit.
But when, having understood the Dhamma, he realizes the Truths, then,
through the subsiding of ignorance, he will live in peace, being stilled.

“With volitional formations as condition, consciousness”: this refers to the six classes of consciousness—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
Therein, eye-consciousness is twofold: wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant.
The same applies to ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. Mind-consciousness, however, consists of the two resultant mind-elements (*vipākamanodhātu*).

The twenty-two types [of resultant consciousness] consist of: the three rootless resultant mind-consciousness elements, the eight root-possessing resultant consciousnesses, the five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses, and the four immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses. Thus, there are thirty-two worldly resultant consciousnesses in total.
Herein, it may be asked: how is it to be known that this aforementioned consciousness has formations as its condition?
“Does it exist? Because there is no result in the absence of accumulated kamma. For this is a result, and a result does not arise in the absence of accumulated kamma;
if it were to arise [without such a cause], the results of all beings would arise for everyone.

Since they do not so arise, it should be understood that “this consciousness exists with volitional formations as its condition. Indeed, all of this occurs by way of both the process of existence (*pavatti*) and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

It occurs in two ways. Among these, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*), the two mind-elements (*manodhātu*), and the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—these thirteen occur only during the course of existence (*pavatti*) in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*).
The remaining nineteen occur, as appropriate, both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) across the three realms of existence.
“‘Having obtained conditions’—this is merely a phenomenon (dhamma) that enters into another state of being;
it does not transmigrate from there, nor does it exist without a cause from there.
Thus, this mere phenomenon, whether material or immaterial, which arises having obtained conditions, is said to “enter into another state of being.”
It is said that there is neither a being nor a soul. There is no transmigration of this [being] from a past existence to this one, nor is there its manifestation here without a cause.
In this context, the former is called "death" (cuti) because of the passing away, and the latter is called "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) because of the linking to the beginning of another existence.

Here it is asked: "If, in this way, there is manifestation without transmigration, then since the aggregates belonging to this human existence have ceased, and since the karma that is the condition for the fruit does not go there, that fruit would be something else arising from something else.
Furthermore, if there is no experiencer, to whom would that fruit belong? Therefore, this formulation is not sound. To this, it is said:
“That fruit which exists in the continuum belongs neither to another nor from another;
the conditioning of seeds is the means for accomplishing this fact.
It is precisely through the arising of the fruit that the conventional designation of an ‘enjoyer’ is established.”
"Just as the conventional designation 'the tree bears fruit' occurs through the production of the fruit.
One might also say: "Even if this were so, these formations would have to be either existent or non-existent conditions for the fruit.
If they were existent, their result (vipāka) would have to occur at the very moment of their arising. But if they are non-existent,"
“If these were causes that existed both before and after [the action], they would always bring about their fruit. He should be told:
“These conditions exist because of what has been done; they do not always bring about their fruit.
In this regard, examples such as surety-bonds and the like should be understood.”
"Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form": here, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations are "name";
the four great elements and the derived matter of the four great elements are "form.

For those born from a womb without a physical basis (as in the case of apparitional beings) and for those born from an egg, at the moment of rebirth-linking there are twenty material phenomena—the tenfold sense-base of the heart (vatthudasaka) and the tenfold body-base (kāyadasaka)—together with the three immaterial aggregates.
These twenty-three factors should be understood as "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness. When the material decads of intrinsic nature are added, there are thirty-three.

Among beings of spontaneous birth, at the moment of rebirth-linking for those such as the Brahmakāyika deities, there are thirty-nine material phenomena—namely, the decads of the eye, ear, and physical base, and the nonad of the life-faculty—and the three immaterial aggregates. These...
Forty-eight states should be understood as "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.

Furthermore, in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), for the remaining types of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) or for moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) whose sense bases are naturally complete, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), there are the seven decads consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the heart-base;
these are seventy material phenomena, together with the three immaterial aggregates—these seventy-three states are [conditioned by consciousness].

These should be understood as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). This is the maximum; however, by way of deficiency, for those lacking various decads, one should understand the designation of "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness" at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) after successively subtracting [the factors] according to each case.

For those in the formless realms (*arūpī*), there are only the three formless aggregates (*khandha*). For those without perception (*asaññī*), there is only the nonad of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) from among the material phenomena.
This, first of all, is the method regarding rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

However, during the course of existence (*pavatta*), in every place where matter arises, at the moment of the presence of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the temperature-born (*utusamuṭṭhāna*) pure octad appears together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. From the first bhavaṅga onwards...
The mind-originated [materiality] is the pure octad; at the time of the manifestation of sound, there is the sound nonad, which arises from both temperature and mind;
and for those living on edible food, there is the nutriment-originated pure octad.
Thus, by way of the nutriment-originated pure octad and the two nonads originating from temperature and mind, it is twenty-sixfold.
In each single consciousness, ninety-six kinds of material phenomena arise— namely, the seventy kinds produced by the aforementioned kamma that arise three times,

along with the other material phenomena— and together with the three immaterial aggregates, these ninety-nine states should be understood as "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness," according to their respective occurrence.
In this regard, it might be asked: "How is it to be known that the name-and-form of rebirth-linking has consciousness as its condition?

It is to be known from both scripture (sutta) and reasoning (yutti). For in the Suttas, the fact that feeling and the other mental factors have consciousness as their condition is established in many ways, such as by the method beginning with the phrase, "states that follow upon the mind. As for reasoning:
“For by means of the form born of mind, which is seen here, success is achieved;
for even though that form is unseen, consciousness is its condition.
Thus, the name “the sixfold sense base conditioned by mind-and-form” has already been stated. Here, however, form is, by necessity, the four great elements.

The six bases consist of the life-faculty; thus, there are eleven types. As for the sixfold base (*saḷāyatana*), it consists of the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base.

Herein, one might ask: "How is it to be known that 'name-and-form is the condition for the sixfold base'? Because they exist when name-and-form exists. For each respective sense-base comes into being when its corresponding name and form exist, and not otherwise.
"With the sixfold base as condition, contact [arises]"— [End of excerpt]
“There are six contacts in brief: eye-contact and so forth;
in detail, they become thirty-two, just like consciousness. Thus:
“With contact as condition, feeling arises.”
“Feeling is said to be from the doors, such as that born of eye-contact and so forth;
those six, when divided further, are the thirty-two kinds of feeling here.
With feeling as condition, craving [arises].”
“Here, craving is explained as sixfold, divided by craving for form and so forth;
each of these is considered threefold therein according to its mode of occurrence.
One who is suffering yearns for happiness; one who is happy desires even more.”
But because equanimity is peaceful, it is described simply as "pleasure.
Therefore, the three kinds of feeling arise with craving as their condition;
and with feeling as their condition, craving arises—so it was said by the Great Seer.
"Conditioned by craving, clinging": there are four kinds of clinging—clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
"Conditioned by clinging, existence": here, "existence" (bhava) is intended as kamma-existence;

however, rebirth-existence is mentioned for the sake of the sequence of terms. "Conditioned by existence, birth": conditioned by kamma-existence, birth is the manifestation of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking.
In this regard, it might be asked: "How, then, is it to be known that 'existence is a condition for birth'?
It is because even when external conditions are equal, distinctions such as inferiority and superiority are observed.

For even among beings—such as twins—even when the external conditions of the father, mother, semen, blood, food, and so forth are equal, a distinction of inferiority, superiority, and so on is seen. And that [distinction] is not without a cause.

Because it is absent for all [beings] at all times, and because there is no other cause within the internal continuum of those beings who are produced by it—other than kamma-existence—it has kamma-existence as its sole cause.

For kamma is the cause of the distinctions among beings, such as their inferiority and superiority. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Kamma divides beings, that is to say, by way of inferiority and superiority."
Therefore, this should be understood: "Becoming is the condition for birth.

Regarding the statement "With birth as condition, aging-and-death," and so forth: because when birth is absent, the phenomena of aging-and-death as well as sorrow and the rest do not exist, whereas when birth exists, there is aging-and-death, and for one touched by the painful phenomenon known as aging-and-death...

In the case of a fool, there arise states such as sorrow, either through connection with aging, death, and so forth, or through being touched by various phenomena of suffering. Therefore, it is said: "With birth as condition, aging and death.
"Having fully and completely realized the Dhamma" means having approached it through knowledge and having penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

Having thus shown the occurrence of the conditionality formula in twelve steps, he now says, "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; having fully understood and realized this Dhamma," etc., for the purpose of showing the cessation of ignorance and the rest by way of turning away (*vivaṭṭa*).

Therein, "with the cessation of ignorance" means with the cessation consisting in the non-arising of ignorance, that is, its cessation through not occurring again. "Cessation of volitional formations" means...

There is the non-arising and cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*). The same applies to the remaining sections. "This is suffering," and so forth, follow the method already explained previously.

"These phenomena are to be directly known" means that these phenomena belonging to the three planes are to be known by way of their intrinsic nature through the awakening to their specific characteristics, either in a beautiful manner or by means of superior knowledge (*adhika-ñāṇa*). "They are to be fully understood" means by way of the awakening to their general characteristics.
And they should be understood as being pervasive by way of the fulfillment of duties.
"These states are to be abandoned" means that these states belonging to the side of origination are to be abandoned through this or that specific quality. "To be developed" means to be increased.
"To be realized" means to be made directly manifest. There are two kinds of realization: realization as acquisition and realization as object. Of the six...
"Of the spheres of contact" means of the six spheres, beginning with the eye. "Both their arising and their passing away" means both their origination and their cessation.

"One of vast wisdom" (*bhūripañña*): it is "vast" (*bhūri*) because it is like the vast [earth]; one who is endowed with that vast wisdom is "one of vast wisdom. In phrases such as "one of great wisdom," the meaning is "endowed with great wisdom" and so forth.
Herein, this is the distinction between "great wisdom" and the others: what is great wisdom? It is that which grasps great meanings.
"Of great wisdom": because she comprehends great phenomena... [and so on] ...great modes of expression... and great inspired insights, she is "of great wisdom.
Because she comprehends the great aggregate of virtue, she is "of great wisdom. Because she comprehends the great aggregate of concentration...
[and so on] ...the aggregate of wisdom... the aggregate of liberation... and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, she is "of great wisdom."
Great are the right and wrong courses of action... great are the meditative attainments of the Great Monastery... great are the Noble Truths... the great foundations of mindfulness...
the right efforts... the bases of psychic power... the great faculties... the powers...
the factors of enlightenment... the great Noble Path... the great fruits of recluseship... the great direct knowledges... the great ultimate goal.
One who grasps Nibbāna is one of great wisdom (*mahāpaññā*). What is wide wisdom (*puthupaññā*)?
Knowledge that proceeds with respect to various and diverse aggregates (*khandha*) is wide wisdom. [Knowledge that proceeds] with respect to various and diverse elements (*dhātu*)...

[and so on] ...with respect to various and diverse sense bases (*āyatana*)... with respect to various and diverse dependent originations (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)... with respect to various and diverse emptinesses and non-apprehensions (*suññatamanupalambha*)... is wide wisdom.
...in various and diverse meanings... in phenomena... in definitions... in inspired eloquence... in various and diverse aggregates of virtue...

in various and diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation... in various and diverse points and non-points... in various and diverse abidings and attainments... in various and diverse noble truths...
in various and diverse foundations of mindfulness... in right efforts... in bases of psychic power... in faculties... in powers... in factors of enlightenment... in various and diverse noble paths...
In the fruits of recluseship... in the direct knowledges... having transcended those qualities shared by various and diverse people, knowledge proceeds toward Nibbāna as the ultimate truth;
thus it is "wide wisdom" (*puthupaññā*).
What is "joyful wisdom" (*hāsapaññā*)? Here, someone is full of laughter, full of rapture, full of contentment, and full of gladness, [and] virtue...
He fulfills it. He fulfills restraint of the sense faculties. [He fulfills] moderation in eating... [and so on] ...the application of wakefulness...

the aggregate of virtue... the aggregate of concentration... the aggregate of wisdom... the aggregate of liberation... he fulfills the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is "wisdom of laughter" (hāsapaññā).
Abounding in laughter... [and so on] ...abounding in gladness, he penetrates what is possible and what is impossible—this is "wisdom of laughter."

Wisdom through laughter is that by which one, abounding in laughter, fulfills the dwellings and attainments; wisdom through laughter is that by which one, abounding in laughter, penetrates the Noble Truths.

Wisdom through laughter is that by which one develops the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path;
wisdom through laughter is that by which one, abounding in laughter, realizes the fruits of recluseship.
One penetrates the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*); thus it is "wisdom of laughter" (*hāsapaññā*). One realizes the ultimate truth, Nibbāna, by means of abundant laughter;
thus it is "wisdom of laughter. What is "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*)? Whatever form (*rūpa*) there is—whether past, future, or present;
internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that form...
It flashes swiftly upon [things] as impermanent; thus it is "swift wisdom. It flashes swiftly upon [them] as suffering and as non-self; thus it is "swift wisdom.
Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever formations... whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present...
whether far or near—all consciousness flashes swiftly upon as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self; thus it is "swift wisdom."

Swift wisdom (*javanapaññā*). Because it swiftly impels [the mind] toward the eye... [and so on] ...up to aging-and-death, as impermanent, suffering, and non-self—whether past, future, or present—it is called swift wisdom.
Form, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of being coreless.
Having weighed, having scrutinized, having analyzed, and having made manifest the cessation of form—that is, Nibbāna—one swiftly courses toward it; thus it is "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*).
Having weighed feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness... the eye... and so on...

up to aging-and-death—past, future, and present—as impermanent in the sense of destruction, as suffering in the sense of terror, and as non-self in the sense of corelessness; having weighed [them]... and having made them manifest... [one swiftly courses toward their cessation].
Because it runs swiftly toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death, it is called "swift wisdom" (javanapaññā).
Having weighed form—whether past, future, or present—as impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation...
[and so on] ...having made it manifest, one runs swiftly toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of form.

It is called "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*) because it swiftly speeds toward Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death. Having weighed feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness... the eye... and so on...

up to aging and death as impermanent in the past, future, and present... and so on... having made them manifest as phenomena subject to cessation, it swiftly speeds toward the cessation of aging and death, which is Nibbāna; thus it is called swift wisdom.
What is sharp wisdom? It is called sharp wisdom because it swiftly cuts off the defilements. One does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen;

one does not tolerate a thought of ill will that has arisen… a thought of cruelty that has arisen… evil, unwholesome states as they arise… lust that has arisen… hatred that has arisen… delusion… anger… resentment… disparagement… [that have arisen].

She does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and eliminates all envy, ill will, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations, and all karmas leading to existence; thus she is one of keen wisdom. In one...

On this seat, the four noble paths, the four fruits of asceticism, the four analytical knowledges, and the six direct knowledges have been attained, realized, touched, and verified by wisdom; thus, one is called "one of sharp wisdom.
What is "penetrative wisdom"? Here, a certain person is full of urgency and full of terror toward all conditioned formations.
Abounding in longing, abounding in discontent, and abounding in lack of delight, one who looks outward finds no pleasure in all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Because it pierces and shatters the mass of greed (*lobhakkhandha*) never before pierced or shattered, it is called "penetrating wisdom" (*nibbedhikapaññā*).

[It likewise pierces and shatters] the mass of hatred (*dosakkhandha*) never before pierced or shattered... the mass of delusion (*mohakkhandha*)... anger (*kodha*)... resentment (*upanāha*)... and so forth.
It is "penetrating wisdom" because it becomes disillusioned with and shatters all kamma that leads to further existence.
He who has become free from enmity toward all phenomena—whatever is seen, heard, or sensed—is one of vast wisdom whose taints are exhausted;
having destroyed Māra’s army among all those phenomena, whatever is seen, heard, or sensed.
"By his state of stability, he has become free from the army [of defilements]. "To him who sees that very thing" means to him who sees that very purity.
"Moving about with [his eyes] open" means moving about having become open through the removal of the veil of craving and so forth. "Who here in the world could conceptualize him? means:

who in this world could conceptualize him by means of the conceptualization of craving or the conceptualization of views? Or rather, because those have been abandoned, no one could do so by means of passion and so forth, as previously stated.
In the four verses beginning with “Sensual pleasures are your first army,” this is the meaning:
because from the very beginning, while beings are still householders, the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesakāma) delude them regarding the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma);
and having overcome those [objects], for those who have entered the homeless life, either in remote lodgings or in various other superior wholesome states, a lack of delight (arati) arises.
And this has been said: "Friend, it is difficult for one who has gone forth to find delight.
Then, because their livelihood is dependent on others, hunger and thirst afflict them; being afflicted by these, the craving for seeking exhausts the mind.
Then, when their minds are exhausted, sloth and torpor descend upon them. Consequently, failing to attain distinction, they find it difficult to progress through those things that are hard to master.
For those dwelling in dwellings in forest and woodland groves, a sense of trepidation and fear arises;

for them, as they dwell with suspicion and apprehension, yet finding satisfaction in the flavor of seclusion over a long period, doubt regarding the practice arises, thinking, "Could this not be the path?
Having dispelled that, as they dwell [further], there arise conceit, disparagement, and rigidity due to even a slight attainment of distinction.
Even having dispelled those [defilements], as you dwell on, there arise gains, honor, and fame based on a further attainment of distinction.
Intoxicated by gain and the rest, proclaiming counterfeit versions of the Dhamma, they acquire false renown;

established therein, they exalt themselves through birth and other such factors and disparage others. Therefore, one should understand that sensual desire and the rest constitute the first army and so forth.

Having thus pointed out this tenfold army, because it leads to the assistance of Kaṇha Namuci due to its being endowed with dark qualities (kaṇhadhamma), he described it as "your army," saying: "This is your army, O Namuci, the assailant of Kaṇha.
In that context, "assailant" (abhippahārinī) means the slayer and the crusher of recluses and brahmins.
The meaning is "one who creates obstacles. "A coward does not conquer it;

only by conquering it does one obtain happiness"—thus, a cowardly person who is anxious about his body and life does not conquer your army, but a hero does conquer it, and having conquered, he attains the happiness of the path and the happiness of the fruit.
"By means of the four noble paths" (*yato catūhi ariyamaggehi*) means when, by means of the four paths characterized as faultless and leading to the attainment of *nibbāna*.

"The army of Māra" (*mārasenā*) refers to the defilements (*kilesa*) that carry out Māra’s commands. "Acting as adversaries" (*paṭisenikarā*) means acting as opponents. "And conquered" (*jitā ca*) means being defeated and struck down.
"And vanquished" (*parājitā ca*) means being suppressed. "Broken" (*bhaggā*) means shattered. "Completely shattered" (*vippaluggā*) means pulverized into dust.
"Facing away" (*parammukhā*) means having been made to turn away. "Becoming free from enemies" (*visenibhūto*) means standing having become free from defilements (*nikileso*).
"One of pure vision" (*vodātadassi*) means one who sees with clarity (*byavadātadassi*). "Those coverings" (*tāni chadanāni*) refers to these coverings of defilements such as craving (*taṇhā*).
"Opened up" (*vivaṭāni*) means made manifest. "Shattered" (*viddhaṃsitāni*) means removed from their place of abiding. "Lifted open" (*ugghāṭitāni*) means torn apart.
"Completely eradicated" means they have been specifically uprooted.
Regarding the verse "They do not fashion," the connection and the meaning are as follows:
Furthermore, being such as they are, they do not fashion or prioritize two things—namely, the [two] kalpas and the two types of esteem (*purekkhāra*). This is the ultimate sense.
Because they have attained ultimate purity, they do not call the views of non-action and eternalism—which are themselves not ultimately pure—"ultimate purity.

Having "abandoned the bond of grasping" means that, by means of the sword of the Noble Path, one has severed and released the fourfold bond of grasping for form and so forth, which was knotted and bound within one's own mental continuum. The rest is self-evident.
"Ultimate purity" (*accantasuddhi*) means purity that is ultimate and supreme. "Purity from saṃsāra" (*saṃsārasuddhi*) means purity from the cycle of existence.
"The view of non-action" (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*) is the view that "evil is not done by one who acts.
"Eternalism" (*sassatavāda*) is the statement that "[the self] is permanent, stable, and eternal. They do not speak; they do not say.
They are called "fetterings" (*gantha*) because they fetter the mental body (*nāmakāya*), and because they join one to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of death and rebirth-linking.
Covetousness is both covetousness and a fetter by way of joining the mental body; thus it is the "bodily-fetter of covetousness. It destroys welfare and happiness, thus it is ill-will (*byāpāda*).
Ill-will is both ill-will and a fetter by the method already stated; thus it is the "bodily-fetter of ill-will. Adherence to rules and observances...
“Purity through virtue and purity through conduct [is found] among the recluses and brahmins outside of this [teaching]”—this is the dogmatic assertion (*āmāsa*) of others.
“Adherence to the view that ‘this alone is the truth’” means that even after rejecting what has been spoken by the Omniscient One, one adheres in this manner: “The world is eternal;
this alone is the truth, all else is false. “Attachment to one’s own view” means having adhered to it oneself...
In regard to a view that has been adopted, there is desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*). "Ill-will toward the doctrines of others" means anger toward the words of another.
"Dissatisfaction" (*appaccaya*) is a state of being discontented. "One's own virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the virtue one has undertaken for oneself, such as the cow-vow (*gosīla*) and so forth.
"One's own view" (*diṭṭhi*) is the view that one has adopted and clung to. "By those bonds" (*gantha*) refers to these aforementioned constructions of the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
“They take up form” means they take up and seize the object of form arising from the four [causes]. “They cling to” means they seize by approaching through the grasping of craving (*taṇhā*).
“They misapprehend” means through the grasping of views (*diṭṭhi*). “They adhere” means through the grasping of conceit (*māna*).
“The round” refers to the round of existence in the three realms. “Ties” refers to bonds.
*Vosajjitvā* means having properly released. *Gathita* means bound. *Ganthita* means bound by means of a bond (*ganthana*).
*Vibandha* means a specific kind of binding. *Ābandha* means binding in many ways. *Palibuddha* means not released.
*Bandhane poṭayitvā* means having shattered the bonds of craving, conceit, and views. *Visajja* means having abandoned.

Furthermore, it is appropriate to present these four bodily ties (kāyagantha) according to either the sequence of the defilements (kilesa) or the sequence of the paths (magga). According to the sequence of the defilements:
the bodily tie of covetousness is abandoned by the path of Arahantship; the bodily tie of ill will by the path of Non-returning;
the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances by the path of Stream-entry; and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth" by the path of Stream-entry.
In the sequence of the paths: the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances and the bodily tie of insistence on "this alone is the truth" are severed by the path of stream-entry;
the bodily tie of ill will is severed by the path of non-returning; and the bodily tie of covetousness is severed by the path of arahantship.
These four ties, when present in a person, bind and constrain them within the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) by means of death and rebirth-linking.
The fetters (*gantha*). They are of four kinds. It is called *abhijjhā* because by means of it one covets, or because it itself covets, or because its mere nature is that of coveting.
Greed itself fetters the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and joins it to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) through death and rebirth-linking; thus it is the "body-fetter" (*kāyagantha*).
By means of it the mind becomes corrupted, or it causes harm to the discipline, conduct, beauty, welfare, happiness, and so forth; thus it is "ill-will" (*byāpāda*).

Ill will (*vyāpāda*). Clinging to the notion that “for recluses and brahmins outside of this [teaching], purity comes through virtue and purity comes through observances” is adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
Rejecting even what has been spoken by the Omniscient One, one becomes dogmatically attached in such ways as “the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false”;
this is adherence to the view that “this is the truth” (*idamsaccābhinivesa*). As in the passage beginning with “like a cart,” etc.
He spoke thus, providing a simile for the disintegration of the fetters in order to bring about their separation.
"They do not generate" means they do not cause to arise. "They do not produce" means they do not cause to be manifested. "They do not bring forth" is a phrase expanded by means of a prefix.
"They do not produce" refers to the moment of arising; "they do not manifest" and "they do not bring forth" [refer to the moments of presence and growth].
This was said with reference to the moment of occurrence (*pavattikkhaṇa*).
30. The verse beginning "One who has crossed the boundary" (*sīmātiga*) is spoken as a teaching based upon a single individual. Its connection, however, is exactly like that of the preceding [verse];
it should be understood together with the following commentary on the meaning—what more is there to say? Such is he, possessed of vast wisdom (*bhūripañña*).
Because he has transcended the four boundaries of defilement, he is "one who has gone beyond the boundary" (sīmatiga); and because he has warded off evil, he is a "brahmin" (brāhmaṇa).

For one who has become such as this, there is nothing whatsoever grasped—meaning adhered to—either by knowing through the knowledge of others' minds or the recollection of past lives, or by seeing with the fleshly eye or the divine eye. Furthermore, due to the absence of sensual lust, he is not "one who is lustful" (rāgarāgī).
Because he is devoid of lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, he is not "one who delights in dispassion.
Since there is nothing whatsoever grasped here by him as "this is supreme," the Teacher brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

"The four boundaries" means the four delimitations. "Latent tendency of views" (*diṭṭhānusaya*) refers to both the view itself and the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) in the sense of being unabandoned.

...and thus there is the underlying tendency of views. The same method applies to the underlying tendencies of doubt and the rest. In what sense are they called "underlying tendencies" (*anusaya*)? In the sense of lying latent (*anusayana*).
What is this so-called sense of "lying latent"? It is the sense of being unabandoned. For these, by virtue of being unabandoned, are said to lie latent within this or that continuity;
therefore, they are called "underlying tendencies. They "lie latent" in the sense that, having obtained a suitable condition, they arise.
This is the meaning. Now, it might be argued: "The state of being a latent tendency (*anusaya*) is a mode of non-abandonment, and it is not logical to say that a mode of non-abandonment 'arises';
therefore, latent tendencies do not arise. To this, the reply is as follows: A latent tendency is a mode of non-abandonment;
however, by way of its non-abandoned state, the term "latent tendency" refers to defilements that have become firmly established. It is associated with the mind (*cittasampayutta*).
Having an object, being with a cause in the sense of having a condition, and being exclusively unwholesome, it exists in the past, the future, and the present;
therefore, it is appropriate to say that it "arises.
Herein, this is the proof: in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, in the discourse on clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*), it says, "One abandons defilements in the present."
Having asked [this], because of the existence of the present state of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), it is said: "One abandons an entrenched underlying tendency.
In the word-commentary on delusion (*moha*) in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, regarding the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), it says:

"The underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of ignorance, the snare of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root—this, at that time, is delusion," thus [showing] the underlying tendency to ignorance together with the unwholesome consciousness.

The state of having arisen (*uppannabhāva*) has been stated. In the *Kathāvatthu*, all propositions such as "the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are indeterminate," "the underlying tendencies are rootless," and "the underlying tendencies are dissociated from consciousness" have been refuted.
In the section on arising within one of the seven great chapters of the *Anusayayamaka*, it is stated:
"In whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust arises, in him does the underlying tendency of aversion arise? and so forth. Therefore...

Regarding what was stated—that “they ‘lie along’ (anusenti) because they arise having obtained a corresponding cause”—this should be understood as well-expressed according to this scriptural authority.
Furthermore, that which was stated—“associated with consciousness, possessing an object,” and so forth—is also well-expressed.
For it must be concluded here that this so-called *anusaya* is a fully established, unwholesome dhamma associated with consciousness.

In this context, the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) [arises] in the four consciousnesses associated with views; the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) in those accompanied by doubt;

and the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) in the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, both by way of co-nascence and by way of object. Furthermore, these three—view, doubt, and delusion—also exist in the remaining states of the three planes by way of object.
And here, the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) exists in the consciousnesses accompanied by greed by way of co-nascence.
And by way of object: greed arising by way of object toward agreeable remaining sense-sphere phenomena;
the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) arising by way of co-nascence and by way of object in consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure;

hatred (doso) arising solely by way of object toward disagreeable remaining sense-sphere phenomena; and the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) in consciousnesses associated with greed but dissociated from views.

Conceit (*māna*) arises both by way of co-nascence and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*); it arises solely by way of object with respect to all remaining sense-sphere phenomena—excluding those associated with painful feeling—as well as with respect to fine-material and immaterial-sphere phenomena.
The underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), although arising even in the four [mental states] dissociated from views, is stated here by way of co-nascence;
however, greed (*lobha*) arising with respect to fine-material and immaterial-sphere phenomena is stated solely by way of object.
In this context, the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) refers to the sixty-two types of views.

The underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) refers to doubt consisting of eight bases, as well as the defilements associated with it; these stand together by virtue of being co-nascent and associated with views and doubt.

The underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*) refers to the ninefold conceit. Or, "having known through the knowledge of the ultimate truth" means by means of the wisdom that knows the mental conduct of others.

"Having known"—this means having known by means of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*). "Or by means of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*)" means having known by means of the knowledge that recollects the aggregates that have resided in the past.
"By the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*)" means by the natural eye.
"By the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*)" means having seen by means of the divine eye, which resembles the divine or is dependent upon the divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*). "Dyed with lust (*rāgaratta*)"—

"Stained by passion": those who [are stained] in regard to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), that is, in regard to the five constituent parts of desire consisting of visible forms and so forth. "Delighting in dispassion":

excessively attached to and clinging to the attainments of the form and formless realms, which are designated as "dispassion. "And when there is passion for sense-desires": when there is passion for the realm of sense-desires (*kāma-bhava*);
the same principle applies to passion for the realms of form and the formless.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Sutta of the Pure Octad within the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed. 5.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Sutta of the Supreme Octad.

31. In the fifth discourse, the *Paramaṭṭhakasutta*, the phrase "dwelling in extremes among views" (*paramanti diṭṭhīsu paribbasāno*) means that, having grasped this as the "extreme," one dwells under the sway of one's own respective view.
"He makes that which is beyond it his best" (*yaduttariṃ kurute*) means that he regards his own teacher and so forth as supreme.
"He calls all others inferior to that" (*hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāha*) means that, setting aside his own teacher and so forth, he calls everyone else inferior to them.
"These are inferior," he said. Therefore, "not having transcended disputes": for that reason, he has indeed not transcended the quarrels over views (*diṭṭhikalahā*).
"Dwell" (*vasanti*) means they dwell by way of the views that first arose. "Dwell within" (*pavasantī*) means they dwell having entered [into them].
"Dwell on" (*āvasantī*) means they dwell specifically. "Dwell around" (*parivasantī*) means they dwell in every respect. Demonstrating this by means of a simile: "Just as..."
He said, “Or householders,” and so forth. “Householders” means owners of homes. “Dwelling in houses” means they live in their own homes free from apprehension.
“One who has committed an offense” means one who has many offenses. “One who has defilements” means one who has many defilements such as lust.
“He does more” means he exceeds [the limit]. “This Teacher is omniscient” means, “This Teacher of ours knows everything.”

"He casts aside all other doctrines" means he discards all other convictions. "He throws up" means he removes them. "He surrounds" means he places them behind him. "Destroyers of views" means those who cause the destruction of views.

The meaning of the second verse is as follows: And one who has not thus transcended, seeing in these four things—what is seen, heard, the precepts, and vows—the aforementioned kind of benefit in the self consisting of the views that have arisen therein.
Having adhered to that very thing as its benefit with his own view, thinking, "This is the best," he regards everything else—such as other teachers and so forth—as inferior.
"He sees two benefits" means he observes two qualities. "And pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammika*) refers to the visible, immediate personal existence.
The cause of ripening. "And pertaining to the future" means the qualities to be obtained in the next world.
"A teacher with such a view" means one who holds such a doctrine, the master of that religious system. "Sufficient for the state of a Nāga" means adequate for the status of a Nāga king;
the same method applies to the states of a Supaṇṇa and so forth. "For the state of a deva" means for the status of a conventional deva and so on. "Anticipating a fruit in the future."
"He becomes" means he becomes one who aspires for the fruit of ripening in the future.

"He sees two benefits even in purity through what is seen" means that because purity is caused by the visible base (rūpāyatana) perceived by eye-consciousness, he observes two qualities by means of his own apprehension of what has been grasped.
The same method applies to purity through what is heard, and so forth.

33. The meaning of the third verse: For one who sees in this way, whatever inferiority they perceive in another teacher and so forth compared to their own teacher and so forth—that very perception, the skilled ones call a "bond"; it is said to be a fetter.
Since this is so, therefore a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen or heard or sensed, nor on rules and observances.
"One should not adhere" is what is meant.
"Skilled" means clever in knowing the aggregates and so forth. "Skilled in the aggregates" means skilled in the five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*).

[They are also skilled] in the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), the path (*magga*), the fruits (*phala*), and nibbāna.
The same method applies here. In this context, "skilled in the paths" means skilled in the four paths. "Skilled in the fruits" means skilled in the four fruits.
"Skilled in Nibbāna" means adept in the two kinds of Nibbāna. "Those who are skilled" means those who are proficient in these aforementioned categories.

"Speak thus" means they say this. For one who perceives that "this is a bond," there is reliance on one's own teacher and so forth, as well as the perception of another, such as the teachers of other sects.
They say that this is a lowly view and a fetter, a bond. It is a "clinging" because it hangs downward like something caught on a peg as previously described.
It is a "binding" because, in the sense of being difficult to sever, it is a bond like a shackle or similar restraint.
It is an "impediment" because [it prevents] one from departing from saṃsāra.
In the sense of being a non-giving, this is an impediment.

34. The meaning of the fourth verse: Not only should one not rely on what is seen, heard, and so forth, but furthermore, one should not construct—that is, one should not generate—any further unarisen views regarding the world. Of what kind?
Whether by means of knowledge or by means of virtuous conduct—whether by knowledge such as that of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or by virtuous conduct—one should not fashion this view.

Not only should one not fashion such a view, but furthermore, one should not, through pride based on grounds such as birth and so forth, represent oneself as equal; nor should one think of oneself as inferior or superior.
"Or by the knowledge of the eight attainments" means by the wisdom associated with the eight attainments, beginning with the first jhāna.
"Or by the knowledge of the five superknowledges" means by the wisdom associated with the five mundane superknowledges (abhiññā).
"Or by wrong knowledge" means by the wrong knowledge that has arisen such as, "He who is not liberated sees one who is liberated," which occurs with a perverted nature.

35. The meaning of the fifth verse: Thus, not forming such views and not conceiving [a self], having abandoned the self and not grasping at it, having abandoned what was previously grasped and not grasping at anything else, he does not establish a twofold support even for that aforementioned knowledge.
And by not doing so, among beings who are divided by various distinct views, he indeed—among those who are discerning—[is truly wise].
"Not following a faction" means that, being one who does not go along by way of desire and so forth, he does not resort to any view among the sixty-two views;
"does not return to them" is what is meant.

"By the four clingings" means by the four intense graspings, beginning with sensual-clinging (*kāmupādāna*). "In those that are distinguished" refers to those things determined by that person. "In those that are split" means split into two parts.
36. Now, in order to provide a description of that one who has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava), as mentioned in this verse, [the Buddha] spoke three verses beginning with “yassūbhayante.
Therein, in the first verse, "yassūbhayante" refers to the aforementioned categories such as contact (phassa) and so forth.
"Paṇidhi" means craving (taṇhā). "Bhavābhavāya" means for the sake of repeated becoming. "Idha vā huraṃ vā" refers to the distinctions between one's own individual existence and other states.
"Here" refers to this present life, or "elsewhere" to other states of existence and so forth.
"Contact is one extreme": contact, such as visual contact and the rest, is one portion. "The arising of contact" refers to the physical basis and the object;
that from which it arises or originates is the "arising. "The second extreme" is the second portion. "Past" means... [the remainder of the sentence is cut off].
"Past" means gone by; it is said to be "transcended. "Future" means not yet come; it is said to be "unarisen.

"Pleasant feeling" and so forth are [distinguished] by way of their dissimilarity. The dyad of "name-and-form" is [distinguished] by way of bending and being disturbed. "Internal" and so forth are [distinguished] by way of being internal and external.
It should be understood that "personality" (*sakkāya*) and so forth are stated by way of the occurrence and origination of the five aggregates.
"One's own state of being" (*sakattabhāvo*) means one's own personal existence (*attano attabhāvo*). "Another's state of being" (*parattabhāvo*) means another person's personal existence.

In the second verse, "in what is seen" (*diṭṭhe vā*) refers to purification through views regarding what is seen. The same method applies to what is heard and so forth. "Perception" (*saññā*) refers to the view that gives rise to such perception.

"Without misapprehending" (*aparāmasantaṃ*) means not grasping [the object] by way of craving, conceit, or views. "Without adhering" (*anabhinivesantaṃ*) means not becoming attached to it by those very same factors.
“Bound” (*vinibaddho*) means bound by conceit (*māna*). “Grasped” (*parāmaṭṭho*) means grasped as being permanent, pleasant, beautiful, and so forth.
“Fallen into distraction” (*vikkhepagato*) is by way of restlessness (*uddhacca*). “Fallen into the undesirable” (*aniṭṭhaṅgato*) is by way of doubt (*vicikicchā*).
“Firmly established” (*thāmagato*) is by way of underlying tendency (*anusaya*). “In a destination” (*gatiyā*) is by way of that which is to be gone to.

38. In the third verse, "even the teachings were not accepted by them" means that even the teachings of the sixty-two types of views were not accepted by them [with the thought], "This alone is the truth;

all else is vain. "One who has gone to the further shore does not return, such a one" means that having gone to the further shore of Nibbāna, he does not return again to the defilements abandoned by each respective path; and he is "such a one" (tādī) by way of five aspects. The rest is self-evident.

The twenty-based view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is the view that occurs with respect to the existing body, established upon the five aggregates by means of four aspects for each aggregate, according to the method beginning with "one regards form as self.
The ten-based wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is the view occurring according to the method beginning with "there is no giving. The view of grasping at extremes (*antaggāhikādiṭṭhi*)...

The view that occurs in such a manner as “the world is eternal, this alone is true, all else is vain,” and so forth—proceeding by grasping one or another extreme as existing—is the definition of *diṭṭhi*.
This phrase, “whatever view it may be,” is the root term common to the nineteen terms that will now be mentioned.
Whatever is a view (*diṭṭhi*), that itself is a "state of views" (*diṭṭhigata*); whatever is a view, that itself is a "thicket of views" (*diṭṭhigahana*). [This applies] to all of them.

A connection must be made. That which is "view" (*diṭṭhi*) in the sense of seeing things as they are not, is itself "gone among views" (*diṭṭhigata*) because it is included within the sixty-two views;
thus it is "gone among views. Its meaning has already been explained above.
It is also called "gone among views" because it has gone exclusively toward two extremes. In that context, "eternal" (*sassata*) means permanent. "The world" (*loka*) means the self (*attā*).
They imagine: "In this case, only the body perishes, but the self remains both here and in the hereafter.
For, taking it as something that looks by itself, they imagine it to be the "world" (*loka*). "Non-eternal" means impermanent. They imagine: "The self perishes together with the body.
"Finite" means having produced jhāna upon a limited kasiṇa, [they take] that volition which has the limited kasiṇa as its object...

They conceive: "The self is finite. Or they conceive: "It is infinite. Having arisen in jhāna upon an immeasurable kasiṇa, they conceive that volition which has the immeasurable kasiṇa as its object thus:
"The self is infinite. "That life-principle is that body" means that the life-principle and the body are one and the same.
"Life-principle" refers to the self; the neuter gender is used here by way of a grammatical shift in gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).

The "body" (*sarīra*) is the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) in the sense of a mass (*rāsa*). "The soul is one thing, the body another" means that the soul is one thing and the pentad of aggregates is another.

"A Tathāgata exists after death" means that while the aggregates perish right here, the sentient being (*satta*) exists and persists after death and does not perish; "Tathāgata" is a designation for such a sentient being. However, some [interpret] "Tathāgata" as...
"They are arahants," they say. Having seen the fault in the position that "he does not exist," they grasp it thus:
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death"; [they think] the aggregates perish right here, and the Tathāgata does not exist beyond death;

he is annihilated. Having seen the fault in the position that "he exists," they grasp it thus: "He exists. "He both exists and does not exist"—these [views] arise from grasping each side individually.

Seeing the faults in both positions, they take up both sides. Seeing that in the grasping of both sides—namely, "it neither exists nor does not exist"—there is the occurrence of both faults, they take up the position of the Eel-Wriggler (*amarāvikkhepa*), saying "it both exists and does not exist" and "it neither exists nor does not exist.
Herein, however, this is the method of the Commentary: the classification of views consists precisely of ten modes, beginning with "the world is eternal," and so forth.

Thus it was said. Therein, "the world is eternal" is the view that arises in the mode of grasping as eternal for one who, taking the five aggregates to be the world, apprehends: "This world is permanent, stable, and everlasting.
"It is not eternal" is the view that arises in the mode of grasping as annihilation for one who apprehends that very same world as being "cut off and destroyed. "It is finite" [is the view...].
For one who has attained a limited kasiṇa— whether it be the size of a thumb-joint or a saucer— and who, while in meditative absorption,
perceives the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within that attainment as "the world" and as "finite" by way of the boundaries of the kasiṇa,
there arises the view "the world is finite. That view is both an eternalist view and an annihilationist view.
However, for one who has attained the vast *kasiṇa* and has entered into that *kasiṇa*, there arises the view consisting in the mode of apprehension:

"The world is infinite. This occurs when one perceives the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within the attainment as "the world," and because they extend to the limits of the *kasiṇa*, perceives them as "infinite.

That [view] is an eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), and it is also an annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). [It is the same as the view] that "the soul is the same as the body" regarding that which is subject to disintegration.

Because the body itself is grasped as the "living being" (jīva), the view that arises in the mode of grasping at annihilationism is: "When the body is annihilated, the living being is also annihilated.
Because a living being distinct from the body is grasped by the second phrase, the view that arises in the mode of grasping at eternalism is:
"Even when the body is annihilated, the living being is not annihilated. In the passages beginning with "The Tathāgata exists," [the reference is to] a "being" (satta).
For one who grasps, "The Tathāgata exists after death," there is the first eternalist view (*sassataditthi*).

For one who grasps, "He does not exist," there is the second annihilationist view (*ucchedaditthi*). For one who grasps, "He both exists and does not exist," there is the third partial-eternalist view (*ekaccasassataditthi*).
For one who grasps, "He neither exists nor does not exist," there is the fourth eel-wriggling view (*amarāvikkhepaditthi*). Thus, there are ten types as described.
"View. It is twofold, as appropriate: the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) and the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
The meaning is that not even one of these is accepted by those whose taints are destroyed.
"Those defilements" refers to those defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry. "He does not return" means he does not come back again.
"Does not return" (*na pacceti*) means that having been reborn again, one does not go back; one does not return to a subsequent existence (*paccabhave*).
"Such-like" (*tādī*) in five ways means similar by way of five causes or factors.

"Such-like toward the desirable and undesirable" (*iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī*) means that because one stands having released both attachment and aversion toward both desirable and undesirable objects, one is equal regarding the two. "One who has cast off" (*cattāvī*) refers to the defilements (*kilesa*).

“Conquered” (*cajitavā*) means one who has overcome [the defilements]. “Crossed over” (*tiṇṇāvī*) means one who has transcended *saṃsāra*. “Freed” (*muttāvī*) means one who is liberated from passion and the rest.

“One who is similar by way of that description” (*taṃniddesā tādī*) means he is similar because he is to be described by repeatedly describing him through various qualities such as virtue, faith, and so forth.
Desiring to explain those five types in detail, he said: “In what way is the Arahant ‘similar’ (*tādī*) toward the desirable and the undesirable? and so on.
In that context: "even in gain" means even when there is the acquisition of the four requisites;

"even in loss" means even when there is no such acquisition. "Even in fame" means even when there is a retinue; "even in disrepute" means even when there is a failure of retinue. "Even in praise" means even when there is the speaking of one's virtues;
"even in blame" means even when there is censure. "Even in pleasure" means even in bodily pleasure; "even in pain" means even in bodily pain. "If one arm with perfume..."
"Let them smear it" means that if they were to apply a coating of four kinds of fragrant scents over and over again upon one arm.
"Let them carve it with an adze" means that if carpenters were to repeatedly shave one arm with an adze until it becomes thin.
"In this there is no lust" means that there is no affection, no attachment, found therein. "In this there is no aversion" means...
In that [state], there is no resistance—meaning anger characterized by striking back—when he is being carved with an adze; it does not exist, nor is it found.
"One who has abandoned attraction and repulsion" means one who stands having relinquished both affection and anger.

"One who has transcended favoring and disfavoring" means one who stands having gone beyond both the favoring that comes through attraction and the disfavoring that comes through repulsion. "One who has completely surmounted approval and opposition."
He has rightly transcended both attraction and aversion.

"When virtue exists" means when virtue is present. "Virtuous" means endowed with virtue. One who receives an explanation or description by means of that is called "one of such a nature" (*tādī*). This same method applies to such cases as "when faith exists, one is faithful," and so forth.
[From] the *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammapajjotikā*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Paramaṭṭhaka-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Jarā-sutta*:
In the sixth discourse, the *Jarā-sutta*, regarding the phrase "Truly, this life is short," it means that the life of human beings is indeed brief.
This is according to the method stated even in the *Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta*: "limited" by way of limited duration and limited essence.

"Even before a hundred years he dies" means he dies even during the period of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, prior to a hundred years. "After [a hundred years]" means having exceeded a hundred years.
"He dies through old age" means he dies by means of aging. Hereafter follows the commentary on the *Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta*.
It should be understood in the manner already stated.
"Little" means slight. "The future world is to be gone to" means the next world is to be traversed. Regarding the phrase "even at the time of the *kalala*":
here, the "time of the *kalala*" refers to that which, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), is as clear as a drop of oil placed on the tip of a thread spun by three spiders.
The *kalala* becomes perfectly clear. With reference to this, it was said:
"Just as a drop of sesame oil, or the unclouded cream of ghee, so too is the *kalala* described as having a corresponding color."
Even at that time of the *kalala* (embryonic stage). "Falls away" (*cavati*) means the life-force ebbs away. "Dies" (*marati*) means one undergoes separation from life.
"Vanishes" (*antaradhāyati*) means one reaches the state of invisibility. "Is dissolved" (*vippalujjati*) means one is cut off. Some explain it thus: "One falls away from the egg-born womb;
one dies from the womb-born womb; one vanishes from the moisture-born womb; one is dissolved from the spontaneously born womb."

"Even the *abbuda* stage": after seven days have passed since the *kalala*, that which is called *abbuda* has the color of water used for washing meat, and the name "kalala" disappears. And this has been said:
"For seven days it is *kalala*; when fully matured, it is removed."
"As it continues to evolve, that state becomes what is called the *abbuda*.
During that stage of the *abbuda*, "the *pesi* also" means that after another seven days have passed, from that *abbuda*, something called the *pesi* arises, resembling a mass of melted fat.
This should be illustrated by the example of pepper and molasses. For when village girls [eat] well-ripened peppers...
Having taken it, they form it into a bundle at the edge of their cloth, squeeze it, take the essence, place it in a bowl, and set it out in the sun;
as it dries, it exudes from all sides. Such is the *pesi*; the name *abbuda* disappears. And this has been said:
“For seven days it is the *abbuda*; when fully matured, it is removed.”
“As it turns, it produces what is called the *pesi* (embryo-mass).

Even at that stage of the *pesi*, and also at the stage of the *ghana* (solid mass): after another seven days have passed from the *pesi* stage, a lump of flesh shaped like a hen’s egg arises, which is called the *ghana*, and the name *pesi* disappears. And this has also been said:
“For seven days it remains a *pesi*; when fully matured, it becomes a *ghana*.”
As it evolves, that state comes to be known as a "solid mass" (ghana).
"Just as a hen’s egg is perfectly round all over,
so too is the shape of the solid mass produced through the condition of kamma."
At that time of density (*ghanakāla*) as well. At the time of the *pasākhaka* as well means:
on the fifth week, five swellings arise for the two hands, the two feet, and the head; with reference to this it was said:
"Monks, on the fifth week five swellings are formed through karma. At that time of the *pasākhaka* as well. Beyond that, the sixth, seventh, and so forth.

After seven days had passed, having condensed the teaching, [he spoke of] the period of forty-two weeks when [the fetus] was fully developed, and the time when the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth arise.
Furthermore, a tube arising from its navel is connected as one with the lining of the mother’s womb;
it is perforated like the stalk of a lotus, and through it the essence of food flows, giving rise to the material form produced by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).
Thus he sustains himself for ten months; instead of describing all of that, [the Buddha] said, "in the birth-chamber. With reference to this, it was said:
"Hair, body hair, and nails," and, "Whatever food, drink, and nourishment his mother eats."
“By that he sustains himself there, the man dwelling in the mother’s womb.

Here, “in the birth-chamber” (*sūtighare*) means in the lying-in chamber, the place of delivery; alternatively, the reading is “*sūtikāghare*,” which is analyzed as “of the woman in labor” (*sūtikāya*).
“Even half-monthly” (*addhamāsiko*) means that from the day of birth, a half-month belongs to him.
"Fortnightly" (*addhamāsiko*). The same method applies to "every two months" (*dvemāsiko*) and so forth. "Annual" (*saṃvacchariko*) means that it possesses one year starting from the day of birth.
The same method applies to "biennial" (*dvivassiko*) and so forth above that.
"When he has grown old" (*yadā jiṇṇo hoti*) means when he becomes worn out by aging, decrepit. "Aged" (*vuddho*) means advanced in years.
"Mahallaka" means one who is advanced in years. "Addhagata" means one who has passed through three stages of life (*addhā*). "Vayo-anuppatta" means one who has reached the third stage of life.

"Khaṇḍadanta" means one whose teeth have become broken due to the power of old age—having gaps between them where they have fallen out and being cracked—the teeth having become fragmented, thus he is "khaṇḍadanta. "Palitakesa" means one with white hair. "Vilūna" means having plucked out.
