"Like one whose hair has been plucked," refers to one with a bald head (*khalati-siro*). "One with a bald head" means one whose head is largely bald. "Wrinkled" means having wrinkles that have formed.
"A body covered with moles" means a body strewn with white and black moles. "Bent" means broken; by this, his crookedness is also indicated.

"Dependent on a staff" means relying on a staff, having a staff as a companion. "He, by old age... [he... (Note: The final fragment *so jarāyapi* appears to be an incomplete phrase from the source text.)
A person dies overcome by old age. "There is no escape from death" means that no means for liberation from death exists or is found.
"As with ripe fruits, there is fear of falling at dawn" refers to ripe jackfruit and other such fruits that have reached full maturity and have loosened stalks.
"At dawn they will surely perish," [they think] like those who fear their own masters. "Thus for mortals born, there is constant fear of death":
in this very way, for beings who have arisen, there is perpetual fear of death, which is designated as *maccu*.
"Just as for a potter" means, for example, as for one making earthenware vessels. "The earthen vessel has been made" [is said].
"A vessel finished by him": "All ends in breaking" means that everything, whether cooked or uncooked, has breaking as its limit;
it has breaking as its final end. "In this way, the life of mortals" means exactly so for the life-force (*āyu-saṅkhāra*) of sentient beings.
"Both the young and the old" means both the tender and the aged. "Those who are fools and those who are wise" refers to those who are dependent upon inhalation and exhalation.
"Both fools and those endowed with wisdom, such as the Buddhas and others—all go under the power of death.
This means that all these aforementioned beings, from the young to the old, come under the sovereignty of death.
"Of those seized by death" means of those surrounded by death. "Going to the other world" means from this human world.
"For those going to the other world": "The father does not protect the son" means the father does not guard the son.
"Nor do kinsmen their kin" means that even kinsmen on the side of the mother and father are unable to protect those very kinsmen.
"While the kinsmen look on" means while the kinsmen are looking on, while they are gazing, while they are watching—referring precisely to the manner already described.
"Behold the many who wail" (*passa lālappataṃ puthu*): this is an address. "Of the many who wail and lament in various ways.
"Each one alone among mortals is led away like a bull for slaughter":
just as a single ox is led away to its execution, so too each being is led away and reaches death. "Thus is the world struck down": in this very way, the world of beings is violently struck.
"By death and by old age" means overcome by both death and old age.

"That which is cherished" refers to the objects of attachment. "They know it as subject to separation" means that this existing thing is indeed subject to separation; the sense is that it is impossible for it not to be separated.
"They grieve" means they perform grieving with the mind. "They weary" means they undergo exhaustion of the body. "They lament" means...
They utter various kinds of lamentations with their voices. "Beating their breasts and wailing" means they beat their chests again and again while crying out.
"Falling into delusion" means they reach a state of bewilderment.
"Impermanent" is in the sense of non-existence after having existed. "Conditioned" means produced by the coming together of conditions. "Dependently arisen" means...

It has arisen together with [its causes], not having been rejected, in dependence upon the completeness of conditions. "Subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*) means its nature is to go toward destruction.
"Subject to vanishing" (*vayadhamma*) means its nature is to go toward vanishing; the meaning is that its nature is to go toward dissolution by way of breaking up.
"Subject to fading away" (*virāgadhamma*) means its nature is to fade away. "Subject to cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*) means its nature is to cease. This which...
“Possession” (*pariggaha*) refers to that which is a possession. There is also a reading, “by which there is possession,” and this is the correct word-division (*padaccheda*).

“Eternal” (*nicca*) means lasting at all times. “Permanent” (*dhruva*) means stable. “Everlasting” (*sassata*) means unchanging. “Of a nature not subject to transformation” (*avipariṇāmadhamma*) means having a natural character that does not abandon its original state.
“It will remain forever, the same, and just so” means it would persist like the moon, the sun, Mount Sineru, the great ocean, the earth, the mountains, and so forth.

"Diversity" (*nānābhāva*) means diversity by way of birth. "Separation" (*vinābhāva*) means the state of dissociation through death. "Alteration" (*aññathābhāva*) means becoming otherwise than one's original state.
"Of each preceding aggregate" (*purimānaṃ purimānaṃ khandhānaṃ*) refers to the aggregates that arose in the immediately preceding moment.

"Alteration through transformation" (*vipariṇāmaññathābhāva*) means by way of becoming otherwise after having abandoned its natural state. "The subsequent aggregates, etc. (*pacchimā pacchimā khandhādayo*).
The connection is: "they proceed" means "they arise.
"All the impediments of household life" refers to the entire tangle of the householder's state.

"The impediments of relatives, friends, and companions" refers to relatives on the side of one's mother and father, friends as associates, and ministers as attendants. "Having cut through the impediment of hoarding" refers to the tangle of stored wealth. "Hair and beard..."
“Having shaved off” means having removed the hair of the head and the beard. “Yellow robes” means garments dyed with an astringent (kasāya) substance.
“My own” means one who has come to be reckoned as my lay follower or my monk; or, it refers to one who regards the Buddha and other such objects as his own.
“Of this and that being” is a collective designation for many beings. “The death of Yaññadatta... [is an example].
"the death of Somadatta"—for even if one were to speak in this manner for an entire day, sentient beings would not be exhausted, nor would the complete demonstration of otherness be accomplished.
However, by means of these two phrases, no sentient being remains unaccounted for, and nothing fails to be accomplished in demonstrating otherness.
The phrase "from here and there" refers to the various states of existence (*gati*).
This is a common exposition for the schools (*nikāya*). "The groups of beings" (*sattanikāyā*) means the groups of beings, the multitudes of beings, the aggregates of beings;
such is the meaning. "Death" (*cuti*) is stated by way of the process of passing away. This is a general term for death consisting of one, four, or five aggregates.

"The state of passing away" (*cavanatā*) indicates the characteristic by means of an abstract noun. "Dissolution" (*bhedo*) is an illustration of the arising of the breakup of the aggregates at the moment of death.
"Disappearance" (*antaradhāna*) is a description of the non-existence of the broken aggregates in any manner whatsoever, like a broken jar.
"Death by death" (*maccumaraṇa*) is death characterized as death; it is not momentary death. "Time" (*kāla*) means the Ender (*Antaka*);
"the act of that" is "the act of time" (*kālakiriyā*). Up to this point, conventional death (*sammutimaraṇa*) has been illustrated. Now...

In order to illustrate this according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), he said, "the breaking up of the aggregates," and so forth. For according to the ultimate sense, it is only the aggregates that break up;
no so-called "being" dies. However, when the aggregates are breaking up, one says "the being dies," and when they have broken up, there is the conventional expression "dead.
And herein, the breaking up of the aggregates occurs by way of the fourfold and fivefold bases, while the breaking up of the physical body occurs by way of the single base.

The laying down [of the body]. The differentiation of the aggregates according to the fourfold plane (catuvokāra), and the laying down of the physical frame (kaḷevara) according to the remaining two planes, should be understood.
Why? Because in both the realms of sense-desire (kāma-bhava) and fine-materiality (rūpa-bhava), there exists the physical frame known as the material body (rūpakāya).

Or alternatively, because in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth, the aggregates merely break up and nothing at all is laid down; therefore, for those [planes], [the term "laying down" does not apply].
By way of this [cessation], there is the dissolution of the aggregates and the casting off of the physical body among humans and others.

And here, death is called "the casting off of the physical body" because it is the act of casting off the physical body. By the phrase "the cutting off of the life-faculty," he shows that what is called "death" occurs only for that which is bound by faculties;
there is no such thing as the "death" of that which is not bound by faculties. "The crop is dead."

The phrase "the tree is dead" is merely a conventional expression (*vohāramatta*). In terms of actual meaning (*attha*), however, such statements simply illustrate the state of exhaustion and decay of things like grain.
"Form-ness" (*rūpagata*) means form itself; the same method applies to "feeling-ness" (*vedanāgata*) and so forth.
In that context, "wealth leaves the mortal even before" means that possessions abandon the mortal person even earlier, at the very outset. The mortal...
"Or rather, they abandon their wealth even earlier. "O seeker of sensual pleasures"—this is how he addresses the king of thieves. "O you who desire sensual pleasures, O seeker of sensual pleasures!
In this world, wealth is indeed impermanent; or when wealth is lost, those who still live become non-wealthy.
Or, having abandoned their wealth, they themselves perish. Therefore, the meaning is: 'Even in a time of sorrow for the great multitude, I do not grieve.'"
"O Sattuka, I have understood the worldly conditions," he said, addressing the king of thieves.
"O Sattuka, I have understood the worldly conditions such as gain and loss, fame and disrepute. For just as the moon rises, waxes full, and then wanes again;
and just as the sun, dispelling the darkness, shines upon the vast regions of the world—"
"Again, in the evening it sets, goes to its end, and is no longer seen; even so, possessions arise and perish.
What is the use of grieving for that? Therefore, I do not grieve"—this is the meaning.
"He conceives through the conceiving of craving" means he conceives through the conceiving of pride produced by craving. "He forms pride through the conceiving of views."

By means of the conceiving that has arisen based on the underlying tendency toward views (*diṭṭhi*). "By conceiving through conceit" means by conceiving through conceit that is co-nascent (*sahajāta*).
"By conceiving through defilement" means one conceives by means of the conceiving through defilement—which is of the aforementioned type—in the sense of burning (*upatāpana*).
"Deceivers" (*kuha*) are those who cause wonder. "Stubborn" (*thaddha*) are those as stubborn as a stump. "Chatterers" (*lapa*) are those who chatter by means of the signs of conditions.
42. *Saṅgataṃ* means come together; seen or touched. *Piyāyitaṃ* means made dear. *Saṅgataṃ* means present before one's eyes.
*Samāgataṃ* means come into proximity. *Samāhitaṃ* means become unified. *Sannipatitaṃ* means gathered as a mass.
*Supinagato* means entered into a dream. *Senābyūhaṃ passati* means he sees the array of an army.
“Delightful with groves” (*ārāmarāmaṇeyyaka*) refers to the delightful nature of flower gardens and the like. The same principle applies to “delightful with woods” (*vanarāmaṇeyyaka*) and so forth.
“Passed away” (*peta*) means gone from here to the other world. “Deceased” (*kālaṅkata*) means dead.

“Only the name remains, as something to be spoken of” (*nāmamevāvasis-sati akkheyyan*): all categories of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest are abandoned; only a mere name remains, such as “Buddharakkhita” or “Dhammarakkhita,” to be spoken and declared.
"Those produced by eye-consciousness" refers to those forms arising from four causes that have been personally produced, gathered together, and seen by one's own eye-consciousness.
"Produced by ear-consciousness" refers to sounds arising from two causes that have been heard and gathered together by the ear-consciousness through the voice of another.
44. "Sages" (munayo) refers to sages whose taints are exhausted. "Seers of security" (khemadassino) refers to those who see Nibbāna.
Regarding "sorrow" (soko): in the exposition of sorrow—*byasatīti byasanaṃ*; the meaning is that it casts away or destroys welfare and happiness.
"Calamity of relatives" (ñātibyasanaṃ) means the calamity of relatives; the meaning is the loss or destruction of relatives through thieves, disease, fear, and so forth. By that...
"By the loss of kinsmen": *phuṭṭhassa* means being overwhelmed, overcome, or possessed;
this is the meaning. The same method applies to the others as well. However, this is the distinction: the loss of wealth is "loss of wealth" (*bhogabyasana*);
the meaning is the depletion or destruction of wealth through kings, thieves, and so forth. Sickness itself is the "loss" (*byasana*); for sickness is the opposite of health.
It is called *byasana* because it ruins (*vināseti*) or destroys (*byasati*). The ruin of virtue (*sīla*) is "ruin of virtue" (*sīlabyasana*); this is a name for immorality (*dussīlya*).
A view that arises destroying right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is itself the ruin; thus it is "ruin of view" (*diṭṭhibyasana*).
Herein, the first two are unconditioned (*anipphanna*), while the latter three are conditioned (*nipphanna*) and struck by the three characteristics. And the first three—
Neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the two calamities of virtue and view are unwholesome.
"By one or another" means by whichever among those mentioned—or even among those not mentioned, such as the calamity of friends or relatives—that [calamity] occurs.
"Of one who is possessed" means of one who is pursued by it and is not liberated from it. "By one or another painful phenomenon" means...
By whatever cause sorrow and suffering arise. "Sorrow" (*soka*) is so called by way of the act of grieving. This is the specific intrinsic nature of the sorrow that arises through those causes.
"Grieving" (*socanā*) is the mode of grieving. "The state of having grieved" (*socitatta*) is the condition of having grieved.
"Internal sorrow" (*antosoka*) is internal grief; the second term is augmented by a prefix, for it dries up what is within.
Because it arises as if drying up and as if withering away, it is called "inner grief" (*antosoka*) and "inner desolation" (*antoparisoka*).

"Inner burning" (*antodāha*) means internal combustion. The second term is augmented by a prefix. "The burning of the mind" (*cetaso parijjhāyanā*) refers to the manner in which the consciousness is consumed.
For when grief arises, it burns and consumes the mind like a fire, such that one thinks: "My mind is being consumed."
He causes [the person] to say, "Nothing occurs to me. The mind is pained and dejected; the state of that is *domanassa* (grief).
In the sense of having entered [into the heart], sorrow itself is a dart; thus it is the "dart of sorrow" (*sokasalla*). In the description of lamentation (*parideva*):
they wail and weep, repeatedly pointing [at the deceased], saying, "My daughter! My son! and so forth.
"By this they cry out," thus it is *ādeva*. "By crying out again and again after having praised various qualities, they cry out," thus it is *parideva*.
The following two pairs of words are stated by way of describing the manner and the cultivation of the preceding two. *Vācā* means speech.
*Palāpa* is empty, meaningless speech. It is "disfigured" (*virūpa*) by way of being half-spoken, spoken otherwise, and so forth.
*Palāpa* means empty chatter. *Lālappa* is speaking again and again. *Lālappanā* is the manner of such repeated speaking.

*Lālappitattaṃ* is the state of one who has spoken thus. *Macchariya* (avarice) and the others have already been explained in their respective places. 45. This seventh verse is spoken for the purpose of showing the appropriate course of conduct in a world struck by death. Therein:
"Of one who lives withdrawn" means: of one who walks about having made the mind withdrawn from this and that.
"A bhikkhu" refers to either a noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) or one in training (*sekkha*). "They say that is his harmony" means:

they say this is fitting for him who does not show himself in existence—namely, for one who has practiced in such a way that he does not show himself in existence, which is divided into the realms of hell and so forth. For it is thus that he...
The intention is: "May he be released from this death.
They are called "those who live withdrawn" (paṭilīnacarā) because they are said to have a mental conduct that is withdrawn from here and there.

"Seven trainees" (satta sekkhā) refers to those who train in the three trainings—higher virtue and so forth; beginning with one standing on the path of stream-entry up to one standing on the path of arhatship, these are the seven.
“Those in training” (*sekkhā*). An “Arahat” is one who stands at the fruit; he is withdrawn because his mind has reached its consummation.
Showing the reason for the state of those in training being “withdrawn in conduct,” he says, “For what reason?

and so forth. “They withdraw their minds from this and that” means those seven persons in training withdraw their minds from various objects, making their own minds retreat. “They shrink back” means they contract [the mind].
“Turning back” means folding [the mind] like a mat of straw. “Restraining” means restraining it.
“Restraining firmly” means exercising control. “Preventing” means warding off. “Guarding” means exercising protection.
“Protecting” means keeping [it] safe within the casket of the mind.
Now, showing [the classification] by way of the doors, he says, "In the eye-door," and so forth. Therein, "eye-door" means the door of eye-consciousness.

The same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well. Regarding the term "bhikkhu," rather than explaining the etymological meaning of the word *bhikkhu*—whether it refers to a bhikkhu who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*) or a bhikkhu who is a trainee (*sekha*)—only the bhikkhu intended here is indicated.

In this context, he is a "worldling" (*puthujjana*) because the defilements have not been eradicated, and he is "excellent" (*kalyāṇa*) because he is engaged in the practice of virtue and so forth; thus, he is a "worldling-excellent-one," a *puthujjanakalyāṇaka*.
One who trains in the higher virtue and so forth is a "trainee" (*sekkha*); [the term refers] to such a trainee, or to a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner.
It is called a *āsana* because they sit (*nisīdanti*) upon it. "Upon which" means upon those things such as beds (*mañca*) and chairs (*pīṭha*). "Bed," etc., are terms for the various types of seats.

For even a bed is included here among the seats because it provides a place for sitting; it is one of the following: a stuffed bed, one bound with cotton-wool, one with legs shaped like a crab, or one with removable legs.
A chair is likewise one of those same types. A "cushion" (*bhisi*) refers to a woolen cushion, a cloth cushion, a grass-cushion, or a straw-cushion.
"Of leaf-mats" means of any one of them. "A mat" (*taṭṭikā*) is one made by weaving palm leaves and so forth.
"A piece of hide" (*cammakhaṇḍo*) is any piece of hide suitable for sitting upon. "Grass mats and so forth" are those made by bunching together grass and other materials.
"By seeing unsuitable forms" means by looking at undesirable, attractive objects. "Empty" (*rittam*) means hollow within. "Secluded" (*vivittam*) means by the absence of entry from the outside.
"Empty. "Secluded" means it is particularly empty because no householder is there.
The same method applies even to the hearing of unsuitable sounds. "By the five strands of sensual pleasure" refers to the five divisions of sensual desire:
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are pleasing to the mind. And this has been said: "Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, and tangibles that are delightful..."
"The five strands of sensual pleasure in the world are seen in the form of women.
"Bhajato" means for one who practices cultivation with the mind. "Sambhajato" means for one who practices correctly. "Sevato" means for one who approaches.
"Nisevato" means for one who practices by making them a support. "Saṃsevato" means for one who practices thoroughly. "Paṭisevato" means... [for one who practices repeatedly].
For one who approaches again and again.

"Harmony of the group" (*gaṇasāmaggī*) means the state of unity and concord among ascetics. "Harmony of the Dhamma" (*dhammasāmaggī*) means the collective state of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*).
"Harmony of non-rebirth" (*anabhinibbattisāmaggī*) refers to those things that are not being produced and do not arise, [leading] to the state of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa*).
A multitude of Arahants who have attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna. "In harmony" means they are not separated from one another in body.
"In mutual affection" means they are well-pleased and satisfied with one another in mind. "Without dispute" means they do not engage in verbal contention.
"Become like milk and water" means they are blended together like water mixed with milk.

“They leap up together” means that those factors conducive to enlightenment enter into a single object. “They become serene” means they attain serenity toward that very same object. “Without residue” (anupādisesāya) means devoid of fuel (upādi).
“In the element of Nibbāna” means in the great element of Nibbāna, which is the deathless. “Deficiency” (ūnattaṃ): here, the state of being deficient is deficiency;

the meaning is the state of being incomplete. “Fullness” (puṇṇattaṃ): the state of being complete is fullness, or the state of being full; the meaning is that it is not perceived, or that it does not exist.

"Of those bound for hell (*nerayikānan*): because of the existence of kamma that causes rebirth in hell. They are called *nerayikā* because they deserve hell; [the phrase] "of those *nerayikā*" refers to them.
Hell is their existence (*bhavana*): hell itself is their dwelling place and home. The same method applies to the phrases "of those born as animals" (*tiracchānayonikānan*) and so forth.
"This is his concordance" (*tasse sā sāmaggī*): this is the concordance with Nibbāna for that one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "This is covered" (*etaṃ channaṃ*)."
"This is appropriate" (*anucchavikaṃ*). "Suitable" (*patirūpaṃ*) means similar and corresponding; it is not dissimilar or non-corresponding.
"Appropriate" means it is suitable for the qualities of recluses and brahmins, or for the qualities of the Dhamma consisting of the Path, the Fruits, and Nibbāna.
It follows and conforms to their skin, their luster, and their beauty; indeed, it comes from their very presence.
And it is called "conformable" (*anuloma*) precisely because it is consistent with those qualities; it conforms to them, and is thus neither contrary nor standing in opposition to them.
46. Now, having thus described the one whose taints are exhausted by the words, "He who would not display himself in becoming," for the purpose of praising him:
He spoke three verses following this. Therein, in the first verse, the phrase "in all places" (*sabbattha*) refers to the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding the expression "he makes neither dear nor undear," in the *Niddesa*, "dear" (*piya*) means those things that produce joy in the mind.

Showing their classification, he said: "Which beings are dear? Here, those who belong to one. In that context, "those who belong to one" (*yassa te*) means "those which are his" (*ye assa te*). "Belong" (*honti*) means...
[They] exist. "Desiring welfare" means desiring prosperity. "Desiring benefit" means desiring happiness. "Desiring comfort" means desiring a state of ease.
"Desiring security from bondage" means desiring that which is secure and fearless from the four bondages. "She nurses" thus she is a mother (*mātā*). "He loves" thus he is a father (*pitā*).
"He shares" thus he is a brother (*bhātā*). The same principle applies here for "sister" (*bhaginī*). A son (*putta*) is one who protects and guards (*puṃ tāyati rakkhati*).

She who maintains the family lineage is a daughter (*dhītā*). Friends (*mittā*) are companions. Ministers (*amaccā*) are attendants. Kinsmen (*ñātī*) are those on the father’s side. Blood-relations (*sālohitā*) are those on the mother’s side.
These beings are dear means these beings are producers of joy. By the reverse of what has been stated, those who are not dear are to be understood. 47.

Regarding the phrase “in regard to what is seen, heard, or sensed” (*yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutamutesu*): here, the connection should be understood as follows—“in regard to these things, namely what is seen and heard, or in regard to things that are sensed (*mutesu*)”; thus, “the sage is not defiled. Thus the construction is to be understood.
“A mere drop of water” means a small amount of water. There is also a reading: “Udakatthevako. Regarding “on a lotus leaf,” it means on a lotus petal. 48.

“The one who is cleansed does not conceive on account of that, namely, what is seen, heard, or sensed”—here too, the connection should be understood in this way: he does not conceive on account of that object, namely, what is seen or heard, nor does he conceive regarding the phenomena that are sensed.
"He is not impassioned, nor is he dispassionate": unlike the foolish worldling (*bālaputhujjana*), he is not impassioned;

unlike the noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) and those in training (*sekkha*), he is not dispassionate. Because lust has been exhausted, he is reckoned simply as "dispassionate. The rest is self-evident.
By that wisdom—or by the preliminary wisdom associated with it—bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) is to be comprehended.
Grasping [this], the yogi shakes off the threefold misconduct of body by way of its total eradication.

And this person, when the phenomena that have failed are being shaken off among the phenomena of the teaching, is said to "shake off" even the person who possesses those phenomena. Furthermore, one who has begun to shake off those very phenomena within oneself at the moment of their occurrence by means of wisdom is called *dhuta*, just as...
When one has begun to eat, it is said that "he has eaten. The definition here, however, should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
*Dhuta* is an agentive noun (*kattusādhana*). It is "shaken off" (*dhuta*) by the first path; "washed away" (*dhota*) by the second path; "completely washed away" (*sandhota*) by the third path;
and "thoroughly washed away" (*niddhota*) by the fourth path.

“He does not conceive what is seen” means that the Arahant does not conceive, by way of the three types of conceiving, the visible object-base (rūpāyatana) seen with the fleshly eye or seen with the divine eye.

How so? Seeing the visible object-base through the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure, he does not generate desire-and-lust for it, does not relish it, and does not delight in it; thus, he does not conceive the seen by way of the conceiving of craving (taṇhāmaññanā).
He does not conceive [it]. Nor does he bring about delight here [with the thought], "In this way may my form be so in the future.
Or, desiring excellence of form, he does not give gifts, does not undertake virtue, and does not perform the observance-day duties.
Thus, even in this way, he does not conceive through the conceiving of craving regarding what is seen; yet he [observes] the excellence and the failure of his own and others' forms.
Relying on this, one does not give rise to conceit. One does not conceive through the conceiving of views, thinking: "By means of this, I am superior," or "I am equal," or "I am inferior.
Furthermore, one does not conceive of the sphere of visible forms as "permanent, stable, or eternal.
One does not conceive of the self as "belonging to a self. One does not conceive of an auspicious thing as "inauspicious."

Thus, one does not conceive of what is seen by means of the conceiving of views. "One does not conceive in regard to the seen" means that one does not conceive in regard to the seen by way of regarding form as a self;

or, just as there is milk in the udder, so too, by not conceiving that passion and so forth exist in form, one does not conceive in regard to the seen. Furthermore, in that very same [state], by means of the conceiving of views...
It should be understood that for one who does not give rise to affection or conceit regarding an object of conceiving, there is likewise no craving, conceit, or conceiving.
Thus, "he does not conceive in what is seen. Regarding the phrase "he does not conceive from what is seen," here "from what is seen" (*diṭṭhato*) is an ablative expression.
Therefore, it refers to the arising [of views] from what is seen—according to the aforementioned classifications—as belonging either to oneself or to another, along with its causal basis.
Or, not conceiving of anything other than what is seen as a self—whether it be a conclusion or something else—he should be understood as "not conceiving from the standpoint of views.

This is his non-conceiving regarding views. Furthermore, because he does not give rise to affection or pride toward that very basis which was not conceived through the conceiving of views, his non-conceiving regarding craving and pride should also be understood.

Regarding the phrase "He does not conceive 'I have seen'": here, not conceiving through the influence of craving in the form of "this is mine," he does not conceive the seen by way of the conceiving of craving.
"Hearing" (suta) refers to what is heard through the physical ear and what is heard through the divine ear;

it is a designation for the sense-base of sound. "Known" (muta) means that which is grasped after having been sensed and reflected upon; the meaning is "having struck against" or "having approached. [This refers to] the faculties.
It is said that they are "cognized" as the mutual defilement of objects; this is a designation for the sense bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles.
"Cognized" means cognized by the mind; this is a designation for the remaining seven sense bases, or for the mental object (dhammārammaṇa).
However, in this context, only that which is included within the personality-group (sakkāya) is obtained. The detailed exposition here is as follows:
It should be understood according to the method explained in the section on views (*diṭṭhavāra*).
Now, demonstrating by means of the suttas spoken by the Blessed One, he said: "‘I am,’ monks,” and so forth. Therein, “I am” (*asmīti*) means “I exist”;
this is a designation for that which is permanent. “This is a conceiving” (*maññitametan*) means this is a conceptualization of views (*diṭṭhikappana*). “This I am” (*ayamahamasmīti*)...
"This is I; I am. "Apart from the foundations of mindfulness" means excluding the four foundations of mindfulness.
"All foolish worldlings are attached" means that all blind fools, various kinds of people, cling [to this]. The seven trainees (*śaikṣa*).
"They become dispassionate" means that the seven types of noble persons, beginning with the stream-enterer, attain dispassion (*virāga*).
"The arahant neither lusts nor becomes dispassionate" means that because the defilements have been extinguished (*parinibbāpita*), he performs neither of these two.
"Through the destruction of lust," and so forth—these three [phrases] refer to Nibbāna itself.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Jarāsutta from the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the sub-commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed. 7.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Tissa-metteyya-sutta.

49. In the seventh discourse, the *Tissametteyya-sutta*, the phrase "one who is devoted to sexual intercourse" (*methunamanuyutta*) means one who is engaged in the practice of sexual union (*methunadhamma*).
"Thus" (*iti*) means "in this way. "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment. "Tissa" is the name of that elder; for he was indeed known by the name Tissa.
"Metteyya" is his clan name (*gotta*); it was precisely through his clan name that he became well-known. Therefore, it is stated in the introduction (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
“Two companions named Tissa and Metteyya. *Vighātam* means affliction or injury. *Brūhi* means explain. *Mārisa* is a term of affection;
it means “one who is free from suffering. *Sutvāna tava sāsanam* means having heard your word.
When he says, “We shall train in seclusion,” he speaks while requesting a teaching on the Dhamma concerning his companion, though that companion was already one who had trained in the training.
"Sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*)" is the introductory term for the sexual act that is to be defined.
"Not the Dhamma of the good" (*asaddhamma*) means the practice of the wicked, the base folk. "The village practice" (*gāmadhamma*) means the practice of those who dwell in villages.

"The practice of outcasts" (*vasaladhamma*) means the practice of outcasts; or, because it rains down defilements, it is itself an outcast practice, thus "the practice of outcasts. "Vile" (*duṭṭhulla*)...
It is "vulgar" (*duṭṭhulla*) because it is corrupted by defilements (*kilesa*) and because it is coarse due to its lack of subtlety.
Furthermore, since even the looking at, grasping, touching, feeling, or rubbing that serves as an accompaniment to that act is vulgar, for that reason too sexual intercourse is called "vulgar.
It is "near water" (*odakantika*) because one takes water near it for the purpose of purification.
"Water's edge" (*udakanta*); one who belongs to that [practice] is "one who goes to the water's edge" (*odakantika*). "In secret" (*rahasso*) means because it is to be done in a concealed place.
In the *Vinaya*, however, the reading is: "The grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*) is 'water's edge' and 'in secret'.

Therein, among the three phrases, by changing the word "he" (*yo so*) to "that which" (*yaṃ taṃ*) and connecting them accordingly: "That which is the grave offense is the act of sexual intercourse; that which..."

"In that which is 'near water' (odakantika), that is the act of sexual intercourse; in that which is 'in secret' (rahassa), that is the act of sexual intercourse. But here, the construction should be understood thus:

"That which is contrary to the true Dhamma (asaddhamma) is the act of sexual intercourse... [and so on] ...that which is in secret is the act of sexual intercourse. It is called "attainment by way of pairs" (dvayadvayasamāpatti) because it is to be entered into by means of two [persons] with two [persons]. The construction there is as follows:
"That which is the union of pairs is what is called the 'act of sexual intercourse'. For what reason is it called "the act of sexual intercourse"?
By what cause, by what method is it spoken of as "the act of sexual intercourse"? Demonstrating that reason, he said: "Of both who are impassioned," and so forth.
In this context, "of both who are impassioned" means of two people—a woman and a man—who are colored by passion (*rāga*).
*Sārattānaṃ* means those who are especially and thoroughly impassioned. *Avassutānaṃ* means those who are soaked with defilement (*kilesa*).
*Pariyuṭṭhitānaṃ* means those who stand having exhausted and crushed wholesome conduct (*kusalācāra*), as in expressions such as "thieves have beset the road.
*Pariyādinnacittānaṃ* means those whose minds stand having exhausted and depleted the wholesome mind. Of both [these types].
"Similar" means similar in terms of defilement (*kilesa*). "Dhamma" means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "For that reason" means for that cause.
Establishing this by means of a simile, he said, "Both are quarrelsome," and so forth. In that context, "both quarrelsome" refers to two who were quarrelsome in the prior stage.
"They are called 'sexual partners'" means they are called "similar. "Quarrelsome" refers to those therein—
Having gone there, they engage in quarreling. "Bhaṣsakārakā" means those who engage in verbal strife. "Vivādakārakā" means those who utter various [contradictory] statements.
"Adhikaraṇakārakā" means those who create the specific causes that lead to formal legal proceedings.
"Vādino" refers to those who argue and counter-argue. "Sallāpakā" refers to those who speak words; this is a comparison by way of analogy, meaning "just so."
"Yuttassa" means associated with it. "Payuttassa" means applied with diligence.
"Āyuttassa" means especially applied. "Samāyuttassa" means joined together with it. "Taccaritassa" means practicing that conduct.
"Tabbahulassa" means making that predominant. "Taggarukassa" means holding that as important. "Tanninnassa" means having one's mind inclined toward that.

*Tappoṇassa* means: of one whose body is bent toward that. *Tappabbhārassa* means: of one whose body is directed toward that. *Tadadhimuttassa* means: of one who is intent upon that. *Tadadhipateyyassa* means:
of one who proceeds having made that the dominant influence (*adhipati*) and the foremost (*jeṭṭhaka*).
*Vighātaṃ* is the statement of the summary (*uddesa*) for the detailed exposition (*niddesa*). *Vighātaṃ* means oppression (*pīḷana*). *Upaghātaṃ* means having brought [it] near.
“Affliction” (pīḷana): affliction means striking; striking means affliction. All these are synonyms for one another. “Calamity” (upaddava) means injury.
“Misfortune” (upasagga) means the manner of afflicting by approaching here and there. “Speak” (brūhi) means tell. “Explain” (ācikkha) means answer.
“Teach” (desesi) means show. “Describe” (paññapehi) means make known. “Establish” (paṭṭhapehi) means set forth. “Reveal” (vivarā) means—
"Make manifest" means: analyze it; divide it; "make clear" means: bring it to the shore [of understanding]; "reveal" means: make manifest. "Your word" means: your speech.
"Utterance" means: speech. "Teaching" means: explaining. "Instruction" means: advice. "Admonition" means:
instruction. "Having heard" means: having heard with the ear. "Having listened" is a synonym for that same thing.
"Having grasped" means having correctly taken up. "Having held fast" means not letting it perish.
"Having characterized" means having discerned. "Or else the Dispensation perishes": both aspects of the Dispensation—the scriptural teaching (*pariyatti*) and the practice (*paṭipatti*)—are lost.
"Or" is used merely as a filler word. "This is ignoble in him": in that person, this is ignoble, namely, this wrong practice.

"Gāravādhivacanaṃ" (the designation for veneration) means the designation for the highest veneration and respect shown toward all beings who possess distinguished qualities. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"Bhagavā" is the best word; "Bhagavā" is the supreme word.
He is venerable and worthy of veneration; therefore, he is called "Bhagavā."
Or name is fourfold: situational (*āvatthika*), indicative (*liṅgika*), symbolic (*nemittika*), and fortuitously arisen (*adhiccasamuppanna*).
That which is called "fortuitously arisen" is what is referred to in worldly parlance as "at will. Among these, names such as "calf," "ox to be tamed," and "bullock" are situational;

names such as "staff-bearer," "umbrella-bearer," "crest-wearer," and "ear-ringed" are indicative; [names such as] "one possessing the three knowledges" and "one possessing the six direct knowledges" are... [symbolic].

Such [names] as "Nemittika" (the Fortunate) and "Sirivaḍḍhaka" (Prosperity-Increaser), "Dhanavaḍḍhaka" (Wealth-Increaser), and so forth, are adventitious, occurring without regard for the meaning of the words.
However, this name "Bhagavā" is *nemittika* (indicative of a specific cause);
it was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana, nor by the eighty thousand kinsmen, nor by distinguished deities such as Sakka or Santusita.

It has been said [thus]. And he will say: “‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother... [etc. ...it is a designation based on realization due to his attainment, namely ‘the Blessed One’ (Bhagavā).
“He possesses fortune (bhāgya), he has overcome (bhagga) [defilements], he is endowed with the [eight] fortunes (bhaga), and he is distinguished by them;
he has enjoyed (bhatta) and has cast out (vanta) [craving], and has gone beyond (gamana) states of existence (bhava)—therefore he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā).”
In this regard:
“The addition of a syllable, the substitution of a syllable, two others—the modification and elision of a syllable;
and the connection with an excellence of meaning of the roots—this is called the fivefold etymological interpretation (nirutti).”
The derivation of words should be understood by taking the characteristics of linguistic convention as they have been stated.

In this regard, the addition of a non-existent syllable, such as the insertion of the letter *ra* in the phrase “like the king of stars among the stars,” is called *vaṇṇāgamo* (the addition of a phoneme).

The transposition of existing syllables, one above or below the other, as in the case of calling something a “lion” (*sīho*) when it should be called “killing” (*hiṃsanā*) or “a killer” (*hiṃso*), is [called *parivattanā*].

The "reversal of phonemes" (*vaṇṇavipariyāyo*) refers to the substitution of one phoneme for another, such as the change of the letter *a* to *e* in the expression “a gift is given in a new hut” (*nave channake dānaṃ diyyati*).
The "modification of phonemes" (*vaṇṇavikāro*) refers to the alteration of one phoneme into another.

The "destruction of phonemes" (*vaṇṇavināso*) refers to the disappearance of existing phonemes, such as the loss of the letters *v* and *n* when one ought to say “the death of a living being” (*jīvanassa mūto jīvanamūto*), but instead says “cloud” (*jīmūto*).
“Name. In the passage, “O prince, you speak to me with harsh words, attacking me,” the word *pakubbamāno* is explained as having the sense of *abhibhavamāno* (overpowering).
In various instances, the application of a specific meaning according to the context is called the "application of a preponderant meaning" (*atthātisayena yogo*) to verbal roots (*dhātu*).

Thus, having grasped the characteristic of etymological derivation (*niruttilakkhaṇa*) according to the method of phonetics (*saddanaya*), or having grasped the characteristic of inclusion in the *pisodarādi* group— on the basis that it is established [therein]—

it should be understood that because he possesses the fortune (*bhāgya*) consisting of the perfection of the perfections such as generosity and virtue which produces mundane and supramundane happiness,
he is called "Bhagavā" when it would otherwise be said "bhāgyavā" (possessing fortune).
But because [it is free from] greed, hatred, delusion, distorted attention,

lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, haughtiness, intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the threefold unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains,
uneven perceptions, discursive thoughts, conceptual proliferation, the fourfold perversions, taints, fetters, floods, bonds, and wrong courses—
The hundreds of thousands of defilements consisting of suffering and fever— beginning with craving, arising, grasping, the five heart-pins,

fetters, hindrances, delight, the root of vexation and dispute, the body of craving, the underlying tendencies toward beings, the eight wrong views, the nine roots of craving, the ten unwholesome paths of action, the sixty-two types of speculative views, and the eighty-four thousand modes of craving;
or, in brief, the five aggregates of defilement, the Māra of volitional formations, the Māra of the devaputta, and the Māra of death.
He has broken [them]; therefore, because these perils have been broken, although he should be called "Bhaggavā" (the One who has Broken), he is called "Bhagavā. And it is said in this regard:
"He has broken lust, broken hatred, broken delusion, and is free from taints;
his evil states have been broken—therefore he is called Bhagavā."

By his fortunate nature, the excellence of his physical body, endowed with the hundred marks of merit, is illustrated; by his state of having overcome faults, the excellence of his Dhamma-body [is shown].

Likewise, there is his being highly esteemed by those in the world who are his peers, his accessibility to both householders and renunciants, and his capacity to remove the suffering of body and mind from those who approach him through both the giving of material gifts and the giving of the Dhamma.
Beneficence is shown, as well as the capacity to provide both mundane and supramundane happiness.

Furthermore, because the word *bhaga* occurs in the world with reference to six things—sovereignty, virtue, fame, glory, desire, and effort—and because his sovereignty over his own mind is supreme, or else his mundane qualities such as *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and so forth, are complete in every respect and esteemed by the world; [therefore he is called Bhagavā].
There exists, likewise, the supramundane Dhamma; there is a fame attained through qualities as they truly are that pervades the three worlds and is exceedingly pure;
there is the splendor of all limbs and members, complete in every aspect, capable of producing delight in the eyes of people intent on beholding the physical body;
and because whatever benefit for oneself or others he has desired or prayed for has been accomplished exactly so.
There is desire, known as the accomplishment of whatever is wished for, and there is effort, termed right exertion,

which serves as the cause for attaining a state of being honored by the whole world; therefore, because he is endowed with these "blessings" (bhaga), he is called "Bhagavā" in the sense that "the blessings belong to him."

Furthermore, because all phenomena are categorized by distinctions such as the wholesome and so forth; or because wholesome and other phenomena are categorized by aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so on;

or because the Noble Truth of Suffering is understood in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changeability; the Origin in the sense of accumulation, source, bondage, and obstruction;
Cessation in the sense of escape, seclusion, being unconditioned, and the deathless; and the Path in the sense of leading out, cause, vision, and predominance—[all these are included].
"Vibhattavā" means one who has analyzed, opened up, and taught the path; therefore, although "vibhattavā" should be said, he is called "Bhagavā.
And because he [dwells] in the divine, brahma, and noble abidings; in the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites; and in the void, the wishless, and the signless liberations—
Furthermore, because he cultivated, frequented, and practiced extensively other mundane and supramundane states that transcend the human condition (*uttarimanussadhamma*),
he is called "Bhagavā" when what should be said is "Bhattavā.

Moreover, because the going (*gamana*)— consisting of craving (*taṇhā*)— within the three realms of existence (*bhava*) has been vomited out (*vanta*) by him, he is [called] "one who has vomited out the going within the realms of existence" (*bhavesu vantagamano*).
It should be stated that by taking the letter *bha* from the word *bhava*, the letter *ga* from the word *gamana*, and the letter *va* from the word *vanta*, and lengthening them, one says "Bhagavā.
This is just as in the world, where when it should be said "a garland for the mehana (the penis) and the kha (the mouth)," one says "mekhalā" (a girdle).
Furthermore, demonstrating another method, he said: "Moreover, he is called Bhagavā because he has destroyed passion (*bhaggarāgo*)," and so forth. In that regard:
"One whose passion is broken" (*bhaggarāgo*) means one for whom passion has been shattered. The same method applies to "one whose hatred is broken" (*bhaggadoso*), and so forth.
"Thorns" (*kaṇḍaka*) refers specifically to the defilements (*kilesa*) in the sense of piercing.

"He divided" (*bhaji*) means he divided by way of enumeration (*uddesa*). "He analyzed" (*vibhaji*) means he divided in various ways by way of exposition (*niddesa*). "He analyzed in detail" (*pavibhaji*) means he divided in a specific manner by way of further exposition (*paṭiniddesa*). [This is] for those who understand through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

He honored it by way of those who understand through brief exposition; he analyzed it by way of those who understand through detailed exposition; he fully analyzed it by way of those who require guidance.
Regarding the "jewel of the Dhamma":
"It is esteemed and of great value, incomparable, and rare to behold."
“Because it is enjoyed by beings without equal, it is therefore called a ‘jewel.
Thus he divided the jewel of the Dhamma, described in this way, into three kinds.

“One who makes an end of existence” means one who effects the delimitation, the limit, and the enclosure of the nine existences, beginning with sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). “One whose body is cultivated” means one whose body has been developed.

The same applies to the others as well. *Bhajati* means to cultivate or frequent. *Araññavanapatthāni*: the forest (*arañña*) is that which lies outside the boundary pillar (*indakhīla*) of a village or a town.
Wooded thickets (*vanapatthāni*) are forest groves that extend beyond the reach of human habitation.
*Pantāni* refers to remote lodgings where people neither plow nor sow. Some, however, [explain] "wooded thickets" (*vanapattāni*) because where...
"There are tigers and other [wild animals]; they protect and guard that forest; therefore, because it is protected by them, they are called 'forest-dwellers' (vanappatā)," they say.
"Resting places" (*senāsanāni*) means those where one both lies down and sits.

"Quiet" (*appasaddāni*) means quiet with respect to the sound of speech. "Silent" (*appanigghosāni*) means silent with respect to the noise of villages and cities. "Free from the breath of people" (*vijanavātāni*)...
They were devoid of the body-wind of people moving about inside. There is also a reading, “vijanavādāni,” meaning “devoid of the speech of those inside.

There is also a reading, “vijanapātāni,” meaning “devoid of the movement of people. “Manussarāhasseyyakāni” means places for people to act in secret. “Paṭisallānasāruppāni” means suitable for seclusion. “Bhāgī vā” means...
"One who has a share (*bhāga*)—that is, a portion such as robes and so forth—is a 'possessor of a share' (*bhāgī*).

"One who has a share by way of acquisition—that is, a share consisting of the flavor of the meaning (*attharasa*) and so forth—is a 'possessor of a share'. "Of the flavor of the meaning" means of the flavor of the meaning comprised of the perfection of cause and fruit.

"Of the flavor of the Dhamma" means of the flavor of the Dhamma comprised of the perfection of the cause. For this has been said: "Knowledge regarding cause and fruit is the analytical knowledge of the meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)."

“Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā). Regarding “the flavor of liberation”: this refers to the flavor of liberation characterized by the attainment of the fruit.
And it has been said: “The term ‘flavor’ is used in the sense of the successful accomplishment of what is to be done.
“Of the four jhānas”: of the four jhānas beginning with the first jhāna. “Of the four immeasurables”...
Of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) that lack the pervasion and measure [of their objects], such as loving-kindness (mettā) and the rest;
of the four formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti), namely the four formless jhānas beginning with the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana);
of the eight liberations (vimokkha), which are liberated from objects and described by the method beginning with “one possessing form sees forms”; and of the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana).
The "bases of mastery" (abhibhāyatana) are those meditative absorptions (jhānas) in which the sense-bases (āyatanas) have been mastered.
Here, "bases" refers to the kasiṇa objects designated as bases in the sense of being a foundation. For a person who is preeminent in knowledge is one of clear wisdom;
thus, what need is there here for an object to be attained? [He thinks: "There is no burden upon me regarding the production of one-pointedness of mind. Thus, these...
One enters attainment having overcome the objects. The meaning is that here one produces absorption (appanā) simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
The jhānas produced in this way are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhāyatana).

Of these eight bases of mastery and of the nine successive dwellings in attainment (anupubbavihārasamāpatti)—the term *anupubba* means "one after another," because they are to be dwelt in successively.
"Attainable by successive stages" (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*) means that they are to be attained in regular succession;
[this refers] to those nine successive dwellings in attainment (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*).

"Of the ten developments of perception" (*saññābhāvanā*) refers to the ten developments of perception, such as the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), mentioned in the *Girimānanda Sutta*. "Of the ten kasiṇa attainments" (*kasiṇasamāpatti*)...
In the sense of being complete, [it refers] to the ten jhānas reckoned as *kasiṇa*, beginning with the earth-*kasiṇa* jhāna.

"Of concentration through mindfulness of breathing" means of the concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing. "Of the attainment of the foul" means of the attainment of the jhāna on the foul.
"Of the ten powers of a Tathāgata" means of the ten powers that constitute the tenfold power. "Of the four grounds of self-confidence" means of the states of fearlessness.
Of the four kinds of intrepidities. Of the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) means of the four types of knowledge of analytical insight.
Of the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) means of the six direct knowledges beginning with the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).

Of the six qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhamma*) means of the six qualities of a Buddha that appear later in the text according to the method beginning with, "All bodily action follows after knowledge."
Therein, the triad beginning with the robe (*cīvara*) is stated by way of the perfection of fortune; the triad of the essence of meaning (*attharasa*) is stated by way of penetration (*paṭivedha*);

the triad of higher virtue (*adhisīla*) is stated by way of practice (*paṭipatti*); the triad of jhāna is stated by way of fine-material and immaterial jhānas; the triad of liberation (*vimokkha*) is stated by way of attainment (*samāpatti*);

the tetrad of perception (*saññā*) is stated by way of access and absorption; and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth are stated by way of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).
It should be understood that the phrases beginning with "the powers of a Tathāgata" are stated by way of the unique qualities (āveṇika-dhamma).
From here on, the passage beginning with "Bhagavā is not merely this name" is stated for the purpose of making known that "this designation follows the actual meaning.
In that context, "recluses" (samaṇā) are those who have gone forth into homelessness; "brahmins" (brāhmaṇā) are those who address others as "bho," or those who have stilled evil and cast out evil.

The deities are Sakka and others, as well as the Brahmās. "Ending with liberation" (*vimokkhantika*) means that liberation is the path to arahantship, and the end of liberation is the fruit of arahantship; that which exists at the end of liberation is called "ending with liberation.
For omniscience is accomplished by means of the path to arahantship, and it becomes perfected through the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, omniscience...
At the end of liberation, there is existence. That name, though called "indicative" (*nemittika*), becomes "existence at the end of liberation. Therefore it is said:
"This [name] of the Blessed Buddhas is 'pertaining to the end of liberation' (*vimokkhantika*). "At the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with the acquisition of omniscience" means:
together with the acquisition of omniscience at the aforementioned moment at the root of the Great Bodhi Tree.
"Designation by realization" (*sacchikā paññatti*) refers to the designation arising from the realization of the fruit of arahantship or the realization of all phenomena.
"That is to say, 'the Blessed One'" (*yadidaṃ bhagavā*) refers to this very designation "the Blessed One.

"By two reasons" (*dvīhi kāraṇehi*) means by two components. "The teaching of the scriptures" (*pariyattisāsana*) is the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tipiṭaka*). "Practice" (*paṭipatti*)...

"Practice" (*paṭipatti*) is that by which one practices. "That which has been mastered by him" (*yaṃ tassa pariyāpuṭaṃ*): the genitive case is used here in the sense of the instrument, meaning that which has been mastered or recited by that person.
There is also a reading, *pariyāpuṭṭaṃ*. "Discourse" (*sutta*) refers to the two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesas, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra;
the Maṅgala-sutta, Ratana-sutta, and Tuvaṭaka-sutta from the Sutta-nipāta; and whatever other word of the Tathāgata is named a "discourse."
It should be understood as *sutta*. As for *geyya*, it should be understood that all *sutta* accompanied by verses (*sagāthaka*) is *geyya*;
specifically, the entire Sagāthāvagga in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* is so designated.

*Veyyākaraṇa* refers to the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, all *sutta* without verses (*niggāthaka*), and whatever other word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) is not included within the other eight factors (*aṅga*). That is called *veyyākaraṇa*.

It should be understood as follows: *Gāthā* refers to the *Dhammapada*, the *Theragāthā*, the *Therīgāthā*, and those verses in the *Suttanipāta* not designated as individual suttas—these are to be understood as "verses" (*gāthā*).
*Udāna* refers to the eighty-two discourses connected with verses consisting of joy and wisdom; these are to be understood as "inspired utterances" (*udāna*).
*Itivuttaka* refers to those discourses that proceed according to the formula beginning, "Thus it was said by the Blessed One."

The one hundred and ten discourses should be understood as the *Itivuttaka*. As for the *Jātaka*, the more than five hundred birth stories, beginning with the *Apaṇṇakajātaka*, should be understood as the *Jātaka*.

As for the *Adbhutadharma* (Marvels), all those connected with marvelous and extraordinary qualities that proceed according to the method beginning with, “Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities are in Ānanda,” should be understood as such.
The Suttantas should be understood as the "Marvelous Teachings" (*abbhutadhamma*). As for the "Vedalla":

all those Suttantas that have been requested again and again until satisfaction and joy are attained—such as the *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sammādiṭṭhi*, *Sakkapañha*, *Saṅkhārabhājaniya*, *Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta*, and so forth—should be understood as the "Vedalla.
This is the Dispensation of the Scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*); this refers to the aforementioned categories.
The word of the Buddha contained in the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka) is called "the teaching" (pariyatti) in the sense of being mastered, and "the dispensation" (sāsana) in the sense of instruction;
thus it is the "teaching-dispensation" (pariyattisāsana). "He forgets that" means that even this teaching-dispensation perishes.
"He forgets thoroughly" means it perishes from the beginning. "He becomes an outsider" means he stands outside [the community].

What is the teaching on practice (*paṭipattisāsana*)? That which precedes the supramundane state (*lokuttara-dhamma*) is "practice" (*paṭipatti*), because one practices for its sake. It is called "teaching" (*sāsana*) because those to be trained (*veneyya*) are taught therein. "Right practice" (*sammā-paṭipadā*) and so forth are exactly as described by the aforementioned method.
"He takes life" means he destroys the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "He takes what is not given" means he seizes property belonging to another.
"He breaks into a dwelling" means he breaks into the structure of a house. "He commits robbery" means...

Having plundered a village, he even commits great looting. He makes it a house-by-house raid means that, having surrounded even fifty or sixty houses and seized them by force of life, he causes their wealth to be brought out. He stands on the road means he performs the work of highway robbery.
He goes to another’s wife means he engages in sexual misconduct with the wives of others. He speaks falsehood means he utters speech that destroys one’s welfare.
The Buddha also says this. "Un-Aryan nature" (*anariya-dhamma*) means the character of one who is not an Aryan. 51.
"Having previously wandered alone" means having formerly lived in the world either by way of the life of a renunciant (*pabbajjā*) or by way of being released from the crowd.
"Like a wandering vehicle in the world, they call him base, a worldling"—this refers to that person who has fallen away.
Just as one who mounts an untrained vehicle, such as an elephant-carriage, falls upon uneven ground, breaks the vehicle while ascending, or tumbles down a precipice— so too,

by mounting the unevenness of bodily misconduct and the like, one falls into the realms of hell and so forth; and by the breaking of one's welfare and falling into the precipice of birth and so forth,
the world calls the ordinary person (puthujjana) "unsteady," just like that vehicle.

“By what is reckoned as going forth” means either by the category of going forth, or by the designation “the ascetic has gone forth” through the application of a numerical count. “Or by the state of being the senior of a group” means either by having relinquished the delight in the company of a group, or by the state of being the senior [of the rainy-season retreat].
“He goes back alone” means he returns from the village by himself. “Who indulges” is the introductory phrase for the detailed explanation.
“At another time” means at a different period, at a later stage. “The Buddha” means the Omniscient Buddha. “The Dhamma” means...
The Dhamma endowed with qualities such as being well-expounded; the Saṅgha endowed with qualities such as practicing rightly;

the training—that which is to be trained in, namely the training in higher virtue and so forth. Having renounced means having rejected the Buddha and the others. For the low means for the sake of the base state of a householder.
Having turned back means having returned. He indulges means he indulges once. He practices repeatedly means he indulges in manifold ways.
He serves; he attends upon; having approached, he serves. He pursues; he serves repeatedly. "Wandering" means straying.
"Untamed" means not brought to the state of being tamed. "Untrained" means not taught the performance of what is well-trained.
"Undisciplined" means not disciplined, not trained in the perfection of conduct. "He takes to a bypath" means:
A vehicle of the kind described, when yoked to an untamed horse, goes astray upon an uneven road.
It "ascends uneven stumps and rocks" means that it climbs over rough stumps situated on uneven ground, as well as mountains and boulders.
It "breaks both the vehicle and the rider" means that for one riding or driving a vehicle such as a cart, it breaks their hands, feet, and so forth.
"He falls over a precipice" means he causes one to fall even over a precipice that is a sheer cliff with a single break.
"He is a wanderer" means he is one who has turned back from the path. "Resembling a swerving vehicle" means it is like a vehicle that is unsteady.

"He takes to a byway" means having retreated from the wholesome courses of action (*kusalakammapatha*), he enters a byway, a wrong path, which is a path leading to the states of misery (*apāya*). "He mounts upon uneven bodily action" means...
The uneven bodily action known as bodily misconduct, which is the opposite of evenness, ascends [to him]. The same method applies to the others as well.
"He destroys himself in hell" means that he reduces his personal existence to powder in hell, which is characterized by a lack of satisfaction.
"He destroys himself in the world of men" means that he is destroyed by means of various forms of punishment. In the world of the gods...

"He destroys himself" means by way of the suffering of separation from what is dear and so forth. "He causes even the precipice of birth to fall" means he causes one to fall even into the precipice of birth;
the same method applies to the precipices of old age and the rest. "In the world of men" indicates precisely the world intended here.
"Ordinary persons" (*puthujjana*) is the summary term for the detailed explanation. In that regard, "ordinary persons" (*puthujjana*)—
A "puthujjana" (worldling) is so called because of various causes such as being born among many, or because this person is a multitude of diverse types.
Indeed, he is a worldling by reason of generating, etc., various kinds of defilements and so forth. To analyze this:

To demonstrate this, he said, "They generate various defilements," and so forth. In that context, they are called *puthujjana* because they have not destroyed (*avihatattā*) the many diverse types of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), or because those [defilements] are generated by them, or because they are generated by those [beliefs]. The word *jana* expresses precisely this sense of "not destroyed.

Regarding the phrase "they look toward the faces of various teachers (*puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikā*"), here "various" (*puthu*) means that these people have various different teachers who claim to be such.
This is the etymological analysis of the term *puthujjana*. Regarding the phrase "separate from all destinies" (*puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitā*):

here, *janā* refers to those who are to be born, or those by whom birth is produced; that is, the destinies (*gatiyo*). Those for whom there are many such destinies are *puthujjanā*. Alternatively, those beyond this [world] are born by means of these;
that is, the formative volitions (*abhisaṅkhārā*) and so forth. Since these exist in them, they are *puthujjanā*. Or else, the word *jana* itself carries the sense of "formative volition" and so on.
It should be understood as follows: "Tormented by various fevers" refers to the fevers of the fire of lust and so forth;

or rather, those very [fires], or all the defilements (*kilesa*), are the fevers (*pariḷāha*). "Among the five diverse strands of sensual pleasure": here, one who is born is a "person" (*jana*); lust, greed, and so forth are such things.

Those in whom there is a diverse person are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*). Alternatively, the word *jana* has the same meaning as lust and so forth, in the sense that they are "born diverse" (*puthu jātā*) [in their passions].
It should be seen. *Palibuddhā* means bound together. *Āvutā* means obstructed. *Nivutā* means hindered. *Ovutā* means covered from above.
*Pihitā* means covered by the lower part. *Paṭicchannā* means concealed. *Paṭikujjitā* means turned face downwards.
Alternatively, [it refers to] those who are many, beyond the path of calculation, averse to the noble Dhamma, and practitioners of base conduct.
They are called "puthujjana" (worldlings) because they are included among the masses of people (*janānaṃ antogadhattā*). Alternatively, this person has gone to a separate reckoning (*puthu*);
thus, a *puthujjana* is one who is detached from the Noble Ones (*ariya*) who are endowed with virtues such as moral discipline and learning.
Thus, those who—
“Two types of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
one is the blind worldling, and the other is the worldling of noble character.
Thus it should be understood that two types of worldlings were indeed spoken of, among whom the blind worldling is the one referred to here.
52. "Fame and renown" means gain, honor, and praise. "In the past" refers to the state of having gone forth into homelessness.
"Or even his fame wanes" means that for one who has fallen away from the holy life, both that fame and that renown diminish.
"Seeing this too" means seeing both the previous acquisition of fame and renown and their subsequent loss. Therefore, one should train oneself to utterly abandon sexual intercourse.
One should train in the three trainings. For what reason? "In order to abandon sexual intercourse"—that is, for the sake of abandoning sexual intercourse—this is what is meant.

"Possessed of praise" means the Blessed One is praised; the meaning is that he speaks while uplifting both his reputation and his virtues. "A speaker with insight" (*cittakathī*) means one who possesses speech according to various methods. "Of beautiful eloquence" (*kalyāṇapaṭibhāno*) means one of excellent wisdom. "Is diminished" (*hāyati*) is the summary term for the detailed explanation.
"Is falling away" (*parihāyati*) means it falls away on all sides. "Is being consumed" (*paridhaṃsati*) [means it goes] down to the earth.
It falls away. "Falls away completely" means it departs from all sides. "Vanishes" means it goes out of sight. "Is utterly destroyed" means it is cut off.
"The minor aggregate of virtue" refers to offenses such as *thullaccaya*. "The great aggregate of virtue" refers to *pārājika* and *saṃghādisesa* offenses.

"For the abandoning of sexual intercourse" means for the purpose of abandoning it through the abandonment of its constituent factors (*tadaṅga*) and so forth. "For the subsiding" refers to the stains.
"For the sake of pacification" means for the purpose of calming. "For the sake of relinquishment" means for the purpose of the relinquishment consisting of leaping forward and total letting go.
"For the sake of subsiding" means for the sake of the fruit known as subsiding.

53. He who does not abandon sexual intercourse through his thoughts... [as before] ...is such a person. In this context, "possessed by" means endowed with. "The reproach of others" refers to words of censure from preceptors and others. "Becomes dejected" means he becomes dispirited.
"By thoughts of sensual desire" means by a thought connected with sensual desire. The same method applies to the subsequent terms as well.
"Touched" means touched by thoughts. "Assailed" means not having escaped [them]. "Overwhelmed" means completely overcome, having entered within.
"Like a wretched man" means like a person of miserable lot. "Like one dull-witted" means like one who lacks knowledge. "Like one utterly bewildered" means become completely deluded.
"Jhāyati" means he thinks. "Pajjhāyati" means he thinks intensely. "Nijjhāyati" means he thinks in various ways.
"Apajjhāyati" means he thinks having moved away from that. "Ulūko" refers to the bird-owl. "On a tree branch" means on a branch grown upon a tree, or on a bough.
"Magayamāno" means seeking a mouse; it is also [spelled] "maggayamāno."

They recite [the following]. *Kotthu* means jackal; *biḷāra* means cat. *Sandhi-samala-saṅkaṭire* refers to the space between two houses, the place where water drains and mud and refuse are deposited, and the bare ground.
*Vahacchinno* means one whose flesh on the back and neck has been cut away. The verses following this have an obvious connection.
54. Regarding those [actions], "weapons" refers to bodily misconduct and so forth. For these are called "weapons" in the sense that they cut both oneself and others.
Among these, he first of all specifically employs the weapon of false speech, saying, "For this reason I have left the Order.
Therefore it was said: "This is indeed his great snare; he plunges into the transgression of lying."
In this context, *esa khvassa* means "this indeed belongs to him. *Mahāgedho* means a great bond. If one asks what it is:
it is that which plunges into false speech; this immersion in lying is to be understood as the "great bond.
*Tīṇi satthāni* means three cutting instruments. Bodily misconduct is the bodily weapon. The same applies to verbal weapons and so forth.
This is the method. To show its classification, he said: "The threefold misconduct of body is the weapon of the body.

"He speaks falsehood knowingly" means that being aware, he utters empty speech. "I was delighted, venerable sir, with the going-forth" means that I was free from lack of delight in the going-forth within the Teaching.
"My mother is to be supported by me" means my mother is to be maintained by me.
"He says, 'I am one who has gone astray'" means he speaks thus: "For that reason, I have departed.
The same principle applies to such statements as "My father must be supported.
"This is his great debt" means this is a great bond for that person. "A great forest" means a vast, wicked forest.
“Thicket” means difficult to traverse. “Jungle” is like a jungle of thieves and the like.
“Uneven” is uneven with thorns. “Crooked” is like a winding mountain pass. “Mire” is like a swamp. “Quagmire” is like mud. “Obstruction” is great suffering.
“Great bond” is a large bond that is difficult to release. “Namely, intentional lying” refers to this very act of intentional lying.
"Having gone to an assembly" means standing in an assembly. "Having gone to a gathering" means standing in a village gathering.
"Having gone into the midst of kinsmen" means standing in the midst of heirs. "Having gone into the midst of a guild" means standing in the midst of a company of merchants.

"Having gone into the midst of the royal court" means standing in the midst of the royal court during a great legal proceeding. "Being brought forward" means being led forth for the purpose of interrogation.
"Sakkhipuṭṭho" means questioned while being made a witness. "Ehambho purisa" is a form of address.
"Attahetu vā parahetu vā" means for one's own sake or for another's sake, such as for the sake of one's hands, feet, and so forth, or for the sake of wealth.
"Āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā": here, "āmisa" is intended to mean gain (lābha). "Kiñcikkha" means something trifling or insignificant, even down to the smallest thing.
The meaning is: "for the sake of even a mere gain such as a partridge, a bowl, a lump of ghee, or a lump of butter. "He speaks a deliberate lie" means he commits a falsehood while fully aware of it.
Furthermore, showing another method, he said: "Moreover, there are three ways in which a lie occurs: first, it occurs to him beforehand," and so forth.
In this context, "by three ways" means by the three factors that constitute the constituent parts of a conscious lie (*sampajāna-musāvāda*).
"He thinks it beforehand" means that even prior to the act, this person thinks: "I shall speak a lie. "It occurs while he is speaking" means it occurs as he is in the process of speaking.
"It occurs when he has spoken" means it occurs once he has finished speaking; the meaning is that it occurs when what was to be said has been uttered.
Alternatively, "of one who has spoken" means that it occurs for one who has uttered and finished speaking. Thus, this meaning is shown here:
whoever knows even in the preliminary stage, knows while speaking, and knows afterwards—thinking, "I have spoken falsely"—is bound by the kamma of false speech when speaking in such a manner.
Although this has been shown, there is nevertheless this distinction here:
First, there is the question: Is there the preliminary stage of thinking, "I will speak falsely," but the subsequent stage of thinking, "I have spoken falsely," is absent?
For if someone forgets immediately after speaking, does he commit false speech (musāvāda), or not?
This was answered in the Commentaries as follows: In the preliminary stage, there is the thought, "I will speak falsely," and while speaking, there is the thought, "I am speaking falsely."
And for one who knows [the truth] at the conclusion, it cannot be that "I have spoken falsely" does not occur;
even if it does not occur, it is still false speech (*musāvāda*). For the first two factors alone are the criterion.

Even for one who has no prior intention in the earlier stage, thinking "I will speak falsely," but while speaking knows "I am speaking falsely," and after speaking knows "I have spoken falsely"—[in this case too, it is false speech].
He knows it. He should not be made to undergo [the penalty] on account of that false speech. For the preliminary stage is more significant.
In its absence, it is either spoken playfully or spoken in jest.
And here, both the state of knowing that [preliminary stage] and the convergence of knowledges must be relinquished. "The state of knowing that must be relinquished" means:

If one were to claim that by the very same consciousness one knows, "I shall speak falsely," and by that same [consciousness] one knows, "I am speaking falsely," and "Falsehood has been spoken by me"—
thus knowing all three moments with a single consciousness— this notion of "knowing that" must be abandoned.
For it is not possible for that very consciousness to know itself, just as it is not possible for a sword to cut that very same sword.
"To cut off": each preceding consciousness ceases by acting as a condition for the arising of each subsequent consciousness in that manner. Therefore, this is said:
"The prior stage alone is the measure; when that exists, [the subsequent] will not come to be."
“There is no such thing as two cognitions [occurring together]; the word ‘mind’ refers to three factors.

One should not grasp the idea that these three types of consciousness arise simultaneously, thinking that the convergence of knowledge must be abandoned. For this so-called “consciousness” is defined thus:
“While the first has not ceased, the subsequent does not arise.”
"Because it arises without interval, it appears as if it were one.

Beyond this, however, regarding one who speaks a deliberate lie (*sampajāna-musā*) in the manner of "I know," even though he does not know—since he holds the view that "this is unreal"—for him, this conviction indeed exists. Likewise, "this..."
"It is unreal"—thus it is both approved and liked by him. Such is his perception, and his mind is of such a nature that he thinks, "This is unreal.

But when he wishes to speak falsely, then he [holds] that view, or approval together with the view, or liking together with the view and approval, or perception together with the view, approval, and liking.
Or, having distorted, set aside, concealed, and fabricated a state of being together with views, inclinations, and perceptions, one speaks.
Therefore, in order to show the differentiation of factors (aṅga) by way of these as well, it is said: "Moreover, in four ways," and so forth.
