And here, "having distorted a view" is stated by way of distorting a powerful factor; "having distorted an inclination," and so on, [should be understood similarly].
Then, by way of misrepresenting even the very weakest [of the factors]. "Misrepresenting the perception" (vinidhāya saññaṃ), however, refers here to misrepresenting even the weakest of all phenomena.
It is impossible that one would speak a deliberate lie without misrepresenting even a mere perception.

55. "The dull-witted one is tormented": one who commits the killing of living beings and so forth, and experiences the suffering resulting therefrom, as well as those involved in the pursuit and protection of wealth, is tormented like a fool.
"Kings seize him and inflict various punishments" means that it is not the kings themselves who act, but men dependent on the king who inflict various kinds of punishments.
"They flog him with whips" means they strike him with whips made of leather strips.
"With canes" means with rattan creepers. "With clubs" means with mallets; or, for the purpose of striking, a four-cubit staff.
"Having cut [the head] in two with seized clubs. "The *bilaṅgathālika* [torture]" refers to the punishment of being forced to stand in a cauldron of sour gruel.
While undergoing that, they gouge out the skull, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and throw it therein;
by this, the brain matter boils over and flows upward. "The *saṅkhamuṇḍika* [torture]" refers to the punishment of having the head shaved like a conch shell.
While performing this, they cut the skin along the demarcations of the upper lip, both ears, the crown of the head, and the nape of the neck;
having gathered all the hair together into a knot and bound it with a stick, they tear it out, and the skin comes away with the hair.
Then, rubbing the skull with large pebbles while washing it, they make it the color of a conch shell. "The mouth of Rāhu" means...
The "torture of Rāhu’s mouth": while undergoing this, they force open the mouth with a lever and light a lamp inside it;
or, starting from the ears and the crown of the head, they gouge the mouth with a chisel until blood flows out and fills the mouth.
The "garland of fire": having wrapped the entire body in oil-soaked rags, they set them on fire. The "hand-torches": [they hold flaming torches in their hands].
They wrap his hands in an oil-soaked cloth and set them ablaze like a lamp. Regarding the "erakavattika" (the eraka-cord torture):
they perform this by cutting strips of skin starting from below the neck and pulling them down to the ankles.
Then, having bound him with ropes, they drag him along. As he does so, he repeatedly steps on his own strips of skin and falls. Regarding the "cirakavāsika" (the long-dweller torture)...
The *cirakavāsika* torture: while performing this, they cut [the skin] right there on a leather strap and place it upon the waist;

then, starting from the waist, they cut it down and place it upon the ankles. Thus, by means of the upper [straps], the lower part of the body becomes as if clothed in a garment worn for a long time (*cirakanivāsana*).
The *eṇeyyaka* [torture]: the *eṇeyyaka* torture. While performing this, [they cut] on both elbows and on both...
Having placed iron rings on his kneecaps, they drive iron spikes into them; he stands upon the ground supported by four iron spikes.
Then, surrounding him, they kindle a fire. This very same account is also stated in the passage where it says, "Like the deer-hunter Jotipariggaha.
Having removed the spikes from each joint, they leave him standing on the four ends of his bones alone.
There are no such punishments as these.
"The fish-hook" means that having struck them with hooks on both ends, they tear away the skin, flesh, and sinews.
"The copper coin" means that they shave the entire body with sharp axes, starting from the head, removing it bit by bit, the size of a copper coin.
They pound them. Regarding "the scourge of caustic lye": having struck the body here and there with weapons, they rub it with caustic lye using brushes;
skin, flesh, and sinews ooze out and flow away, until only the skeleton remains. Regarding "the revolving bar":
having made [the victim] lie on one side, they drive an iron spike through the ear-hole and turn it.
They make it one with the earth. Then, seizing it by the feet, they pull it away. "A straw mat":
skilled executioners, having stripped off the skin and flesh, cut the bones with small saws, and then, seizing it by the hair, they lift it up;
there remains only a heap of flesh. Then, they take hold of it by wrapping it around with the very hair; [this is] the straw mat.
They wrap it around [the body] as if making it their own. "By dogs" means that for several days they give no food and have it eaten by hungry dogs;
in a mere moment, they reduce it to a skeleton. "Is worn away" (*parikissati*) means it reaches a state of exhaustion.
"Completely worn away" (*parikissati*) means it reaches a state of exhaustion in every respect. "Completely defiled" (*parikilissati*) means it reaches a state of torment.

Showing another reason, he said: “Or else, overcome by craving for sensual pleasures,” and so forth. Therein, “by craving for sensual pleasures” means by greed for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇika-lobha*).
“Overcome” means crushed by that. “With mind consumed” means having exhausted his virtuous conduct, his mind is seized [by craving].
“Seeking wealth” means searching for riches. “By ship across the great ocean.”
"He leaps forth" means he enters the great salt ocean by means of a boat known as a ferry.
"With cold before him" means having placed cold in front of him. "With heat before him" means having placed heat in front of him.

"Gnats" refers to brown flies. "Mosquitoes" refers to mosquitoes themselves. "Being afflicted" means being tormented by the contact of gnats and the like. "Perishing through hunger and thirst" means...
"Dying of hunger and thirst" refers to the twenty-four phrases beginning with "he goes to the *tigumba* forest" and ending with "he goes to the root-land," which are spoken by way of country names.
"He goes to the desert wilderness" means he goes through a sandy wilderness perceiving it as a starry sky.
"The knee-path" is a path to be traveled on the knees. "The goat-path" is a path to be traveled by goats.
The same method applies to the path of the ram as well.
Regarding the "path of stakes" (*saṅkupatha*): this refers to a path of stakes that must be climbed by knocking together wooden posts;
one traveling along it stands at the foot of the mountain, ties an iron hook to a rope, hurls it upward so that it catches on the mountain, and then climbs up by means of that rope.
Having pierced a mountain with an iron rod tipped with a diamond, having crushed it into a stump, standing there,
having pulled up a crossbeam and fixed it back in place above, standing there again, having hung down a leather rope,
and taking hold of it, he descended; having tied it to the lower stump, he took the rope in his left hand and held a club in his right hand.
Having struck the rope and pulled out the stake, he climbs back up again. By this same method,
having climbed to the summit of the mountain and descending on the other side, he first strikes a stake at the mountain top in the same manner as before,
ties the rope to a leather bag, winds it around the stake, sits himself inside the bag, [and lets it down] for the monkeys.
One descends by uncoiling the rope in the manner of releasing a thread from a spindle. Therefore it is said:

"The 'stump-path' is a path that must be climbed up by means of stumps after they have been hewn out. The "parasol-path" is a path that must be descended upon like birds, having caused a leather parasol to catch the wind.
The "bamboo-path" is [a path] where one has cut through a thicket of bamboo with a knife for cutting bamboo. A tree...

It should be understood that the expression "he goes along the bamboo path" is said with reference to the path he must take by cutting down a bamboo with an axe while making a road, constructing a ladder in the Bamboo Grove, climbing into a bamboo thicket, cutting a bamboo, dropping it onto another bamboo thicket, and thus proceeding right over the top of the bamboo thicket.
"Seeking, he does not find": he experiences sorrow and dejection rooted in non-acquisition; that is, he encounters physical and mental suffering rooted in failure to obtain.
"Having obtained": having acquired. "Rooted in guarding": meaning rooted in protection.
"How might my wealth... refers to: "By what means might kings not seize my wealth... [and so on]... nor might unpleasant heirs seize it? "Guarding": by means of caskets and the like.
"Of one who conceals [it]. "They fall apart" means they perish. 56.
"Knowing this danger, the sage [considers] what comes before and after here"—referring to what is stated from this point onward, beginning with:

"Whatever fame and reputation he had before, that too diminishes for him," the sage considers what comes before and after here in this teaching (*sāsana*), from the former state up to the subsequent state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*).
"Having understood the danger in the state of being a wanderer, the Sage [said]:

'One should make it firm. This is the introductory phrase for the explanatory passage. "One should make it steadfast" means one should make it not lax. "One who has firmly undertaken [the training]" means one who possesses a firm promise. "One whose undertaking is stable" means one whose promise is resolute.
(57) "'This is the supreme of the Noble Ones'": this refers to the practice of seclusion; this is the supreme among the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others.
Therefore, the intention is: "One should train in solitude alone.

"One should not think oneself superior because of that" means that one should not, on account of that solitude, think of oneself, "I am superior"; what is meant is that one should not become stiff with conceit (*māna*) because of it.

"Elevation" (*unnati*) is the act of raising up. "Exalting" (*unnamanti*) is the act of setting up after having risen up. "Conceit" (*māna*) is the sense of "I-am-ness" (*ahaṃkāra*). "Stiffness" (*thāma*)...
*Balakkāram*: by force. *Thambham*: making stiff. *Thaddho*: unyielding. *Patthaddho*: especially unyielding.
*Paggahitasiro*: with head held up. *Sāmanta*: not far away. *Āsanne*: not distant.
*Avidūre*: in close proximity. *Upakaṭṭhe*: nearby.
"58. Of one who is secluded (*rittassa*) means of one who is isolated, devoid of bodily misconduct and so forth.

'The folk, clinging to sensual pleasures, envy him who has crossed the flood'—beings attached to objective sensual pleasures envy that one who has crossed the four floods, just as debtors envy one who is free from debt.
Thus he concludes the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship."
"Empty" (*rittassa*) means empty of all defilements. "Secluded" (*vivittassa*) means void. "Withdrawn" (*pavivittassa*) means alone.
Now, showing those things by which he is empty, he says, "empty of bodily misconduct," and so forth.

In this regard, emptiness should be understood in two ways: according to the sequence of the defilements and according to the sequence of the paths. First, according to the sequence of the defilements: lust, delusion, and rigidity...
With the six defilements—sārambha, conceit, intoxication, hatred, anger, and resentment—one is emptied by the path of arahantship;
with the four defilements—hatred, anger, enmity, and negligence—one is emptied by the path of non-returning;
with the seven defilements—excessive pride, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, and craftiness—one is emptied by the path of stream-entry.
Furthermore, according to the sequence of the paths: by the stream-entry path, one is empty of these seven—conceit, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, guile, and deceit;
by the non-returning path, one is empty of these four—hatred, anger, enmity, and negligence;
and by the path of arhatship, one is empty of lust, delusion, rigidity, resentment, conceit, and arrogance.
By these six [factors], one is empty. The remaining [factors] should also be applied accordingly in the manner beginning with "the three types of misconduct by way of all defilements.

Having fully understood sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) means having known the sensual pleasures belonging to the three planes through the attainment of the full understandings of knowing and scrutinizing.
Having abandoned sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*) means having relinquished the defilements such as desire through the full understanding of abandoning. *Byantiṃ*...
"Having made" means having made it free from end and free from limit.

"Of one who has crossed the flood of sensual desire" means of one who stands having crossed the flood of sensual desire, which is reckoned as the finality, by means of the path of non-returning. "The flood of existence" [is crossed] by means of the path of arahantship.
"The flood of views" by means of the path of stream-entry. "The flood of ignorance" by means of the path of arahantship. All.

"Having crossed the path of saṃsāra"—this refers to one who stands having crossed the path consisting of the successive sequence of all aggregates, elements, and bases by means of the path of Arahantship alone:
having crossed over it by means of the stream-entry path; having completely crossed over it by means of the once-return path;

having transcended the sense-sphere element by means of the non-return path; and having completely transcended all existence by means of the path of Arahantship. By way of the attainment of fruition...
"Of one who has transcended. "One who has gone to the further shore," and so forth, are stated with reference to Nibbāna.
Just as debtors, wandering about while still carrying increased interest, long for freedom from debt—that is, they generate a longing for it. "The sick [long for] health":
one afflicted by diseases such as bile-disorder (pitta) longs for health for the sake of pacifying that disease through the administration of medicine. Just as...
"Bound in fetters" refers to those men bound in the prison on the day of a festival. Just as slaves long for freedom—
because free men do whatever they wish and no one can forcibly turn them back from it, and therefore slaves yearn for the state of being free— so too,
just as those who have set out on a journey through a wilderness long for safety, because they are strong...
Men, taking up their loads and equipped with weapons, set out across the wilderness with their retinues;
seeing them from afar, the bandits flee. Having safely crossed the wilderness and reached a place of safety, they are joyful and elated.
Therefore, those who have entered the wilderness long for the land of security. At the conclusion of the teaching, the three attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having attained [this state] and subsequently gone forth, he realized arhatship.
The commentary on the exposition of the Tissametteyya Sutta from the *Saddhammapajjotikā*,
the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pasūra Sutta 59.
Regarding the eighth [section], the exposition of the *Pasūra Sutta*: first, the summary of the initial verse is as follows.
These proponents of views (*diṭṭhigatika*), referring to their own view, say, "Purity is found right here. However, they do not acknowledge purity in other phenomena.

Thus, those many ascetics and brahmins who rely on their own teachers and others, holding the view that "this doctrine alone is beautiful," become proponents of beauty (subhavāda) and settle upon individual truths such as "the world is eternal.
They "cast aside all other doctrines" means they discard all other convictions. They "throw away" means they cast them far off.
*Parikkhipantīti* means they throw [them] all around. *Subhāvādā* is the summary term for the detailed explanation;
it means those who speak of beauty, saying, "This is excellent. *Paṇḍitavādā* means those who speak thus: "We are wise. *Thiravādā* means those who speak thus:
"We speak words free from fault. *Ñāyavādā* means those who speak thus: "We speak words that are logical. *Hetuvādā* means...
“Proponents of causes” are those who say, “We speak with supporting reasons. “Proponents of characteristics” are those who say, “We speak of what is to be observed.
“Proponents of reasons” are those who say, “We speak words joined with illustrative examples. “Proponents of positions” are those who say, “We speak words from which it is impossible to depart.
“Adhered to” means having entered within; “established” means standing right there.
60. And thus established, they are described as "those who desire debate" in the second verse.

In that context, "they mutually perceive each other as fools" means that both persons, thinking "this one is a fool, this one is a fool," perceive each other as fools; they view one another as being foolish.
"They speak a dispute dependent on others" means that, relying on various teachers and so forth, they engage in quarreling. They are "desirous of praise."
"Those who proclaim what is wholesome" means that both, desiring praise, perceive themselves thus: "We are proclaimers of the wholesome, speakers of wisdom.

"Desirous of debate" means those who have need for debate. "Intent on debate" means those whose underlying disposition is toward debate. "Making debate their primary aim" means those who conduct themselves having placed debate itself foremost.
"Wandering in search of debate" means wandering about seeking out debate alone. "Having plunged into" means...
"Having entered. "Having plunged" means having descended. "Having immersed" means having submerged. "Having entered" means having gone inside. "Lacking *ojā*" means having inferior *ojā*;

the meaning is being devoid of vitality (*tejas*). "That speech" refers to this word. "Speaking empty talk" means speaking that which is devoid of vitality. And while they were speaking thus, one [of them] was necessarily... 61. The verse beginning with "Engaged in talk":
therein, "engaged in talk" means striving in discursive debate; "desiring praise..."

"Is struck down" (*vinighāti hoti*): one who desires praise for oneself becomes "one who is struck down" (*vinighātī*)—meaning one who is full of doubt even before the debate begins—by way of thinking, "How indeed shall I refute him? and so forth. "In that which has been refuted" (*apāhatasmiṃ*):

when the argument has been seized away by those who examine the questions, by way of saying, "Your statement is devoid of meaning," "Your statement is devoid of phrasing," and so forth. By this censure...
"He becomes angry" means that he becomes angry at the censure arising when his argument has been thus refuted. "Seeking a flaw" means one who is searching for nothing but a flaw in the other.
"Praise" (thomana) is the speaking of commendation. "Fame" (kitti) is making oneself well-known. "Gathering of praise" (vaṇṇahāriya) is the increase of one's virtues. Previously...
“From conversation” means prior to the conversation itself. One who has *kathaṃkathā*—that is, doubt (*kathaṃkathā*) such as “How is this?
How is this?”—is a *kathaṃkathī*. “Victory for me” means my victory. “How will they refute me? means in what manner will there be a refutation.
“I shall perform a counter-measure” means I shall purify my own position. “Distinction” means superiority. “Counter-distinction” means...
"Again and again, [I shall achieve] distinction. "I will wrap around" means I will encircle.
"Unwrapping" means my release, liberation, or emergence from that encirclement. "Cutting" means the severing of the debate.
"The circle" means the assembly of the debate. "The attendants" means the followers. "The challengers" means those who raise legal objections. "Carrying off" means warding off.
*Atthāpagatan* means departed from the meaning; that is, "there is no meaning. *Atthato apaharantī* means they exclude [the opponent] from the meaning.
*Attho te dunnīto* means your meaning has not been correctly established. *Byañjanaṃ te duropitan* means your phrasing has been poorly formulated.
*Niggaho te akato* means no refutation has been made by you. *Paṭikammaṃ te dukkaṭan* means your counter-argument is ill-executed.
By her, the establishment of her own tenet was poorly done. "Ill-spoken" means it was not spoken correctly.
"Badly uttered" means even while speaking, it was spoken badly. "Poorly explained" means it was not correctly answered.
"Ill-stated" means it was stated otherwise than [the truth]. "Ill-proclaimed" means it was proclaimed in an unseemly manner.

"By censure" means by reproaching. "By reviling" means by speaking of faults. "By disparaging" means by speaking of non-virtues. "By bringing disrepute" means by increasing the perception of non-virtue.
"Is agitated" means that, having abandoned its natural state, it wavers. "Becomes corrupted" means that, through the influence of hatred (*dosa*), it reaches a state of putrefaction.
"Becomes established" means that, through the influence of anger (*kopa*), it takes on a mass-like density. "And anger" refers to the state of being enraged. "And hatred" refers to...
*Dūsanaṃ*: finding fault. *Apaccayañca*: and lack of confidence, meaning a state of dissatisfaction. *Pātukaroti*: makes manifest, renders evident. *Randhamesī*: one who seeks out internal flaws.
*Virandhamesī*: one who seeks out defects or holes. *Aparaddhamesī*: one who, having set aside virtues, seeks only faults.
*Khalitamesī*: one who seeks out stumbles. *Gaḷitamesī*: one who seeks out falls. "Ghaṭṭitamesī" is also [a term for] one who seeks out collisions.
*Pāṭho*: the meaning is "one who seeks its affliction. *Vivaramesi*: one who seeks a flaw. 62.
Not only does he become angry, but furthermore there is the verse beginning with “*yamassa vādan*.

Therein, “they say it is deficient” means they say it is deficient because it has been discarded in terms of both meaning and phrasing (*atthabyañjana*). “He laments” means [he laments] on account of that.
Thus he raves with such thoughts as, "Something else was intended by me. He grieves means that he grieves on account of things such as, "His victory.
He laments, "He has surpassed me," means that he raves even more intensely in the manner of, "He has outstripped me in debate," and so forth.
"Neglected" means not increased. "Another thing was adverted to by me" means another reason was brought forward by me.
"Thought about" means investigated. "One with a great faction" means one who has a large circle of kinsmen; thus he is "one with a great faction. "A great retinue" means a retinue of many attendants.
"A great following" means a following of many male and female slaves. And this assembly is divided. And this...
The assembly is divided, not one. "I will break it again" means "I will split it again.
63. "These disputes among recluses": here, "recluses" refers to outside wanderers (*paribbājaka*).

"Among these there is the striking down and the striking up" means that in these debates, by way of victory and defeat, one experiences the striking down or the striking up of the mind; thus, it is called "striking down" (*ugghāti*).
And it becomes a destruction. "One should abstain from quarreling" means one should abandon strife.

"There is no other purpose than praise and gain" means that there is indeed no purpose here other than praise and gain. "Superficial" means not deep, as in such passages as "these five strands of sensual pleasure."
"Deep" means difficult to enter, like dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), which has no fixed footing.
"Hidden" means remaining concealed, as in such passages as "Rejoice, Nanda! I am your guarantor.
"Concealed" means not manifest, as in such passages as "Having slain mother and father... "To be drawn out" means to be explained by being elicited, as in "one who is faithless, ungrateful..."

In phrases such as "and so forth" (cā’ti-ādīsu), it is like that. "Led" (nīto) means it should be explained according to the established order of the Pāḷi, as in "Monks, there are these four noble lineages" (cattārome, bhikkhave, ariyavaṃsā).
"Blameless" (anavajjo) has the sense of being faultless, as in "wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā). "Free from defilement" (nikkileso) means devoid of defilements, like insight (vipassanā).
"Pure" (vodāno) means completely purified, like the supramundane (lokuttara). "The ultimate meaning" (paramattho).
The supreme goal blows [upon them]; the goal that has become the supreme goal, such as the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and Nibbāna.

64. The meaning of the sixth verse: Since there is no gain of praise from being killed, therefore, even when one obtains the highest gain, if one is praised because of the view that "this is beautiful," he [is still subject to that state]. Thus, regarding that doctrine...
Having proclaimed this in the midst of the assembly, he then laughs, either out of satisfaction with that victory or by baring his teeth;
and through pride, he becomes uplifted. For what reason? Because, having attained that victory, he has become as he desired.
"Having stiffened" means having filled it. "Having cultivated" means having increased it. The explanation of this verse is clear in meaning.
65. Thus, regarding the verse beginning with “That which is loftiness,” it says: “But he speaks of conceit and over-conceit.
This means that he, failing to understand that very loftiness as a ground of affliction, speaks of conceit (*māna*) and over-conceit (*atimāna*).
In this way, the explanation of this verse is clear in its meaning.
66. Having thus shown the fault in that position, he now spoke the verse beginning with “A hero” (*sūro*), not accepting that argument.
Therein, “for the king’s food” (*rājakhādāya*) means by way of the king’s solid food; that is to say, by way of his meal and wages. “He comes roaring” (*abhigajjamāno*):
they seek a counter-hero, and just as one seeking a counter-hero comes roaring, so does the holder of a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatiko*).
He shows that [the opponent] is one who holds wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*). "Go by the very same way he went" means: go by the same path as that of your adversary.
"There was nothing previously for this battle" shows that whatever kind of defilement (*kilesa*) there might have been for the sake of combat, that did not exist here even before;
it shows that it was abandoned by him right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

"Sūra" is the term of reference (uddesapada) for the subsequent explanation (niddesa). "Sūra" means one whose chest (*ura*) is excellent; it signifies one with a broad chest or a well-developed chest.
"Vīra" means one who possesses prowess. "Vikkanta" means one who enters into battle.

"Abhīru" and so forth are exactly as previously explained. "Puṭṭha" is the term of reference for the subsequent explanation. "Posita" means made stout. "Āpādita" means brought to half-strength or fully established. "Vaḍḍhita" means developed from various [causes].
"Roaring" means roaring with an unskilled voice. "Loudly roaring" means making a shout of triumph.
"Utterly roaring" means letting out a lion’s roar. "He comes" means he arrives. "He approaches" means he goes near from there.
"He draws near" means having gone near from there, he does not turn back. "A rival" means one who is fearless. "An adversary" means an enemy person.
*Paṭisattuṃ*: standing face-to-face as an enemy (*sattu*). *Paṭimallaṃ*: fighting as an opponent (*paṭisedha*).
*Icchanto*: desiring or wishing.
*Palehi*: go away. *Vāja mā*: do not stay. *Gaccha*: approach nearby. *Abhikkama*: exert yourself.
"At the root of enlightenment" means in the vicinity of the Great Bodhi tree. "Those defilements which act as adversaries" refers to those defilements that function as opposites.
"Those that act contrarily" means those that act as obstacles (*paṭāṇī*). "Those that act as thorns" means those that pierce through. "Those that act as enemies" means those that act as foes. 67.
From here on, the remaining verses have a self-evident connection. In that context, "they dispute" means they argue. "Because of acting as adversaries... [and so forth].
Those who act perversely. "Dispute" (*vivāda*) is contradictory speech in the manner of saying, "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya," and so forth.
"My word is consistent" (*sahitaṃ me*) means my word is connected with benefit. "Your word is inconsistent" (*asahitaṃ te*) means your word is not connected with benefit.

"That which you have long practiced is overturned" (*adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ*): that which has been practiced for a long time and thus made proficient through repeated cultivation—that very thing [is overturned].
"Having come to my challenge, you have turned back. You have been defeated in debate; that is, the fault has been attributed to you by me.
'Go about for the sake of release from the debate' means: take your bowl of alms and wander from place to place, seeking a reply for the purpose of escaping the debate.
'Or refute it' means: otherwise, free yourself from the fault attributed by me. If...
“*Pahosī*” means “if you are able.

*Āveṭhiyāya āveṭhiyanti* means turning back by means of winding around; *nibbeṭhiyāya nibbeṭhiyanti* means releasing by means of freeing from faults. Because expressions such as *chedena chedanti* (cutting by cutting) have been explained in the manner stated below, they should be applied accordingly.
68. *Visenikatvā* means having destroyed the army of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Kiṃ labhetha* means “what rival will you find?”—that is, what will you obtain?
Pasūra addresses that wanderer. "Yesīdha natthi" means "for those who have nothing here. The explanation for this verse is also of plain meaning. 69.
"Pavitakkaṃ" means while thinking such thoughts as, "Will there be victory for me? "Dhonena yugaṃ samāgamo" means [meeting] with the one who has shaken off [defilements].
"He has entered into a contest of speed with the Buddha who has shaken off the defilements. For you will not be able to go along with him"—

this means that, like the jackals and others with the lions and others, you will not be able to take even a single step together with the one who has shaken off [the defilements], nor will you be able to achieve such a contest of speed.

"Mano" is the term for the summary (uddesa) of the detailed exposition (niddesa). "Citta" means "consciousness" by virtue of its cognizance (cittatā). "Mano" is so called because it "measures" (minamāna) and "knows" the object.
"Mānasa" is simply "mano. For in the passage, "The snare that moves in the sky is this which moves as the mental (mānaso)," the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) are referred to as "mānasa."

“How indeed, O Blessed One, could a disciple of yours, delighting in your teaching, a trainee who has not yet attained the goal, pass away while still known among men?”—here, *mānasa* is said to mean “arahantship.
But here, *mānasa* means simply “mind”; this word has been expanded for the sake of the meter.
*Hadaya* means mind (*citta*). In the passage, “I will either throw your mind (heart) into confusion or split your heart (chest),” it refers to the chest.
In the passage, “As if knowing heart by heart, he pierces it,” it refers to the mind. In the passage, “Kidney and heart,” it refers to the physical heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).
But here, it is the mind itself that is called “heart” in the sense of being internal.
It is in the sense of being completely pure that it is called "bright"; this was said with reference to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). As it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.

However, because it has emerged from that [luminosity], even the unwholesome is like the Ganges River when it has emerged from the Ganges, or like the Godhāvarī River when it has emerged from the Godhāvarī.
And it is described as "white" (paṇḍara) as it were.
As for the term "mind-base" (manāyatana), the mention of "mind" here is for the purpose of indicating that the mind itself constitutes the base. By this, he demonstrates:
"This is not called the 'mind-base' because the mind is the base for something else, like the 'deva-base'; rather, it is the mind itself [that is the base]."
“...the sphere, the mind-sphere. In this context, *āyatana* (sphere) should be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, a source, a meeting place, a place of birth, and a cause.

For instance, in common usage, in such expressions as “the abode of Īśvara” (*issarāyatana*) or “the abode of Vāsudeva” (*vāsudevāyatana*), a dwelling place is called an *āyatana*. Likewise, in such expressions as “the gold-mine” (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) or “the silver-mine” (*rajatāyatana*), [it refers to a source].
It means a mine. In the Dispensation, however, in such passages as “In a delightful abode, birds frequent it,” it means a place of assembly.
In such passages as “The southern region is the abode of cattle,” it means a place of origin.

In such passages as “In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion (sati sati-āyatane),” it means a cause. But here, it is used in the sense of a place of origin and in the sense of a place of assembly.
"In the sense of cause" applies in all three ways.
Since phenomena such as contact arise therein, it is a *āyatana* in the sense of being the place of birth (*sañjātidesa*).

Furthermore, since external visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles converge therein by way of being objects, it is also [an *āyatana*] in the sense of being a meeting place (*samosaraṇaṭṭhāna*).

It is a *āyatana* (base). Furthermore, because it acts as a cause for contact (*phassa*) and the other factors by way of being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth, it should be understood as a *āyatana* in the sense of a cause as well.
The meaning of the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) has already been explained.

It is called consciousness (*viññāṇa*) because it cognizes (*vijānāti*). Consciousness itself is the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*). Its meaning is to be understood in terms of its being a heap (*rāsi*) and so forth.
It should be understood as follows: in the phrase "it is reckoned simply as a great mass of water," *khandha* is used in the sense of a heap (*rāsa*).

In such expressions as "the aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*) and "the aggregate of concentration" (*samādhikkhandha*), it is used in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*). In the passage "The Blessed One saw a large log of wood," it is used in the sense of a mere designation (*paṇṇattimatta*).
Here, however, *khandha* is used in its conventional sense (*rūḷhi*), in the sense of a heap. It is used in the sense of a heap.

For a single consciousness is indeed one part of the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, just as one who cuts a single part of a tree is said to be "cutting the tree," so too, even a single consciousness— which is but one part of the aggregate of consciousness—
is conventionally referred to as "the aggregate of consciousness."
"The mind-consciousness element born thereof" means the mind-consciousness element that is suitable for those states beginning with contact.

For in this term, a single state of consciousness is described by three names: it is "mind" (*mano*) in the sense of measuring; "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) in the sense of cognizing; and "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of its own-nature or in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being.
"Together" means they come together at one and the same time. "Having come together" means having arrived.
"Having taken hold of the yoke" means having grasped what corresponds to the yoke. "To converse" means to speak with one another. "To talk" means to engage in conversation.
"To enter into discussion" means to undertake speaking together. This is the reason for their lack of capability.

To demonstrate this, he said: “For what reason? Because the wanderer Pasūra is inferior,” and so forth. For that Blessed One is “the foremost” (agga) both because he is the foremost in incomparable giving and because he is designated as peerless.
He is “the best” (seṭṭha) in the sense of being without equal in all virtues.
He is “liberation” (mokkha) because he is freed from the defilements along with their latent tendencies. He is “supreme” (uttama) because of his own...
It is "supreme" (uttama) because it is devoid of anything superior. It is "excellent" (pavara) because it is desired by the entire world.
"By the intoxicated Mātaṅga" means by an elephant with rut-fluid flowing.
"The old jackal" (kotthuṅka) means an aged jackal. "Together with the lion, the king of beasts" means together with the maned lion, the monarch of animals.
A young koṭi is a bow-possessor; a young dhenu is a milk-drinker. "By a bull" means by a bull esteemed as auspicious.
"Together with a moving kunāla" means together with a kunāla that is moving. "Dhaṅka" means a crow. "Together with a garuḷa, a son of Veṇatā":
here, "garuḷa" is the name according to his birth, and "son of Veṇatā" (Venateyya) is according to his lineage. "Caṇḍāla" means...
*Chavacaṇḍāla*: by a universal monarch (*cakkavattin*), that is, a wheel-turning monarch of the four continents.
*Paṃsupisāca*: a spirit (*yakkha*) born in a place where sweepings are discarded. *With Indra, the king of the gods*: together with Sakka, the king of the devas.
Those six phrases beginning with "That Blessed One is of great wisdom" have been explained in detail below. Therein, "skilled in the analysis of wisdom" refers to his own...
He is skilled in the manifold divisions of wisdom (*paññā*) with its infinite conceptualizations. "One whose knowledge is manifold" means one who has attained knowledge of infinite distinctions.

By this, he shows that even while being skilled in the divisions of wisdom, those wisdoms possess infinite variety. "One who has attained the analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidā*) means one who has acquired the supreme knowledge of the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*).
"One who has reached the four grounds of self-confidence" (*vesārajja*) means one who has attained the four kinds of knowledge characterized by fearlessness. As it is said:
“Monks, regarding my claim to be a perfectly awakened Buddha, I do not perceive any ground on which any ascetic,
brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me by saying,
‘These things have not been fully awakened to by you. Not perceiving such a ground, monks, I— ”
“I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence.
Regarding you who claim to be one whose taints are destroyed: ‘These taints are not yet exhausted’...

[and so on] ...‘As for those things called obstructive by you, their use is not sufficient to constitute an obstruction’... [and so on] ...Regarding that purpose for which the Dhamma was taught by you...”

"‘This has been taught; it does not lead the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering’—in this regard, monks, I do not see any ground on which any ascetic or brahmin, or god, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, could rightfully challenge me. Not seeing such a ground, monks..."
“I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.

“One who possesses the power of the Ten Powers”: those who possess ten powers are the “Ten-Powered Ones” (*dasabala*); the powers of the Ten-Powered Ones are the “powers of the Ten-Powered Ones” (*dasabalabala*); one who maintains those powers of the Ten-Powered Ones is “one who possesses the power of the Ten-Powered Ones,” which means one who possesses the power of the knowledge of the Ten-Powered One.
By these three terms, a mere glimpse of the divisions of those things to be known (*neyya*), which possess infinite distinctions, has been shown.

By virtue of his application of wisdom (*paññāyogavasena*), he is a "bull among men" (*purisāsabha*) in the sense of being highly auspicious and esteemed. He is a "lion among men" (*purisasīha*) in the sense of being fearless. He is an "elephant among men" (*purisanāga*) in the sense of greatness.
He is a "thoroughbred among men" (*purisājañña*) in the sense of understanding. He is a "sturdy ox among men" (*purisadhorayha*) in the sense of bearing the burden of the world's duties.

Now, desiring to show the specific qualities such as splendor (tejas) obtained from infinite knowledge, and demonstrating that these qualities like splendor have their root in infinite knowledge, he said "one of infinite knowledge" (*anantañāṇo*) and then spoke "one of infinite splendor" (*anantatejo*), and so forth.
In this context, "one of infinite knowledge" means one whose knowledge is devoid of limits both in terms of numerical calculation and in terms of its power.
"One of infinite splendor" means [one who possesses splendor] by dispelling the darkness of delusion within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
Infinite knowledge and splendor. Infinite fame means that through the very qualities of his wisdom, the sound of his infinite renown has spread throughout the three worlds.
Prosperous means enriched by the abundance of the wealth of wisdom. Of great wealth:

even though the wealth of his wisdom increases, it is called "of great wealth" because he possesses a vast amount of currently active wisdom-wealth; alternatively, the reading is *mahādhano*. Possessing wealth: because he abounds in the praiseworthy wealth of wisdom.
He is "wealthy" (dhanavā) because of his possession of the wealth of wisdom (paññādhanavatta) through its preeminent nature, being endowed with constant wisdom.
For among these three meanings, scholars of grammar maintain that this term [dhanavā] applies here.

Thus, having shown the accomplishment of the Blessed One’s personal perfection through the quality of wisdom, he again shows the accomplishment of the perfection of benefit for the world through that very same quality of wisdom.

Showing this, he said, "The Leader," and so forth. Therein, he is the "Leader" because he leads those to be trained from the place of fear known as *saṃsāra* to the place of safety known as *nibbāna*.
At the very time of leading them there, he is the "Discipliner" by means of the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*) and the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*).
At the very time of teaching the Dhamma, he is the "Persuader" by cutting through their doubts. Having cut through their doubts, he is the one who must make them understand.
He is one who makes known the meaning. He is one who causes others to reflect upon the meaning thus made known by means of reaching a definitive conclusion.

He is one who observes the purpose of the practice regarding the meaning thus reflected upon. He is one who inspires confidence in those who have practiced accordingly through the power of that practice.
In the phrase "So hi Bhagavā," the particle *hi* is a grammatical indeclinable used to indicate the reason for the meaning stated immediately preceding it.

"Producer of the unarisen Path": one who produced at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the welfare of the world, within his own continuum, the Noble Path that had never previously arisen in his own continuum and which serves as the cause for the sixfold uncommon knowledge (*cha-asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa*). "Generator of the ungenerated Path":

[one who generates] within the continua of those to be trained (*veneyya*), the Noble Path that had never previously arisen in their continua and which serves as the cause for the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (*sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa*).
From the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma until the present day, he is the one who generates [the noble path] within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
For even in the case of disciples to be trained, the Blessed One is called "the generator" because he generates the noble path within their continuums by means of his very words.
He is "the proclaimer of the unproclaimed path" for the sake of attaining Buddhahood for those endowed with the eight qualities.

Having given the prophecy for the attainment of Buddhahood to Bodhisattas who had made their formal resolve through discourse, he was the one who, by the mere act of prophesying "he will become a Buddha," taught the Noble Path that must arise at the foot of the Bodhi tree—the path of the perfections (pāramitā) never before proclaimed.
This same principle applies even to the prophecy concerning a Pacceka-Bodhisatta. He is called "the Knower of the Path" (maggaññū).

He is a "knower of the path" (maggajānī) by virtue of knowing the noble path he has himself produced through review. He is a "knower of the path" (maggavidū) because he is skilled in generating the noble path within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
He is a "connoisseur of the path" (maggakovido) because he is discerning regarding the path to be proclaimed for Bodhisattvas.

Alternatively, he is a "knower of the path" (maggaññū) in regard to the practice leading to perfect enlightenment (abhisambodhi); a "knower of the path" (maggavidū) in regard to the practice leading to solitary enlightenment (paccekabodhi); and [a knower of the path] in regard to the practice leading to the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi).
Skilled in the path. Or alternatively:
"By this path those of old crossed over, and those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood."
According to the word [of the Buddha], they apply the interpretation here in due order:

by way of the paths of the past, future, and present Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples; by way of the paths of emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*appaṇihita*);

and by way of the paths of persons who are "to be known through a brief indication" (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and "to be known through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*). And furthermore, it follows the path of the Blessed One.

"Having become followers of the path already traveled. Here, the particle *ca* is a grammatical indeclinable (*nipāta*) used in the sense of a reason; by this, the Blessed One has stated the reason for attaining qualities such as the arising of the Path.
The particle *pana* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "having done"; by this, the Blessed One’s act of making the path—that is, his practice—is expressed.
"Endowed with [qualities] afterwards" means that they are endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) after the Blessed One had first gone [along the path].

Thus the Elder spoke of his qualities based specifically on the path of arahantship, because all the Blessed One’s qualities—beginning with “the arouser of the unarisen path”—have come about by depending upon that very path of arahantship.
“He knows what should be known” means he knows whatever is to be known; through his omniscience, there is nothing whatsoever that ought to be known by wisdom which he does not know.
The meaning is that he knows all of that—which consists of the five paths of the knowable—by means of wisdom (*paññā*). "Seeing, he sees" means he sees what is to be seen;
by virtue of his all-seeing nature, making that very path of the knowable appear as if seen with the eye, he sees it with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
Or, just as someone who grasps things perversely does not know even though they know, nor see even though they see...
He does not see; it is not thus for the Blessed One. Rather, the Blessed One, grasping things according to their true nature, knows simply by knowing and sees simply by seeing.
Thus, in the sense of being a leader and a guide, he has become vision (*cakkhubhūta*). In the sense of being known and so forth, he has become knowledge (*ñāṇabhūta*).
Or, in the sense of the unerring nature of reality, having reflected with his heart upon the turning of the Dharma of the scriptures...
Or, he is "consisting of Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) because he has uttered the Dhamma with his speech; or he is "become the Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) in the sense of being supreme.
Alternatively, he is "become the eye" (*cakkhubhūta*) because he is like an eye; he is "become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*) because he is like knowledge;

he is "become the Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) because he is like the unerring Dhamma; and he is "become Brahma" (*brahmabhūta*) because he is like Brahma. This refers to him who, through the speaking and the practicing of the Dhamma...
Or he is a speaker (*vattā*). He is one who proceeds (*pavattā*) by means of speaking and acting in various ways.
He is a guide to the meaning (*atthassa ninnetā*) because he extracts and demonstrates the meaning.

He is a giver of the Deathless (*amatassa dātā*) because he teaches the Dhamma that leads to the attainment of the Deathless, or because through his teaching of the Dhamma that reveals the Deathless, he causes others to attain it. Because he has generated the supramundane Dhamma, [he acts] in accordance with those to be trained...
Because he gives the supramundane Dhamma at will, he is the Lord of the Dhamma and thus the Master of the Dhamma (*dhammassāmī*). The meaning of the term *Tathāgata* has been explained above.

Now, wishing to demonstrate his specific quality of omniscience by distinguishing it from the qualities described by such phrases as "knowing what should be known," and thereby establishing that omniscience, [the author] says, "There is nothing...
and so forth. For such is that Blessed One, perfected through the radiance produced by the fruit of the merits of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Because all phenomena—including their underlying tendencies—have been destroyed by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, there is nothing that has not been fully known through the absence of delusion.
Likewise, because all phenomena have been seen with the eye of knowledge as if with a physical eye, there is nothing that has not been seen.
Because they have been reached by means of knowledge, there is nothing that has not been realized. This is the realization of non-delusion.
Because it has been realized, there is nothing that is not realized. Because it has been touched by non-delusive wisdom, there is nothing that is not touched by wisdom.
"Present" refers either to the present time or to present phenomena. "Having taken" (*upādāya*) means having grasped or having included within.
By the very word "having taken," even *nibbāna*, which is independent of time, is indeed included. And the expressions "past" and so forth...

They are connected by the very words beginning with “there is not,” or by the words beginning with “all. “All phenomena” (*sabbe dhammā*) is a complete inclusion of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

“In every aspect” (*sabbākārena*) is a complete inclusion of all aspects, such as impermanence and so forth, for each individual phenomenon among all phenomena. “At the gateway of knowledge” (*ñāṇamukhe*) means facing toward knowledge.
“Come into range” (*āpāthaṃ āgacchanti*) means they enter into the field of approach. “That which is to be known” (*jānitabbaṃ*) is the word [referring to the object].
This was stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the term *neyya*.
In the phrases "one's own welfare" (*attattho*) and so forth, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction. "One's own welfare" means one's own benefit.
"The welfare of others" (*parattho*) means the benefit of others—the three worlds. "The welfare of both" (*ubhayattho*) means the benefit of both oneself and others simultaneously.

*Diṭṭhadhammika* means that which is connected with the present life, or a matter whose purpose lies in the present life. *Samparāyika* means that which is connected with the future life, or that whose purpose lies in the future life.
Regarding the terms "shallow" (*uttāna*) and so forth: it is called "shallow" because it is easily established when expressed by way of conventional usage (*vohāra*).
It is called "deep" (*gambhīra*) because it is difficult to establish when expressed by transcending conventional usage and being associated with emptiness (*suññatā*).
The supramundane is "hidden" because it is extremely concealed. The [truths] such as impermanence and so forth are "concealed" because they are covered by the [notions of] solidity and so on.
It is "to be inferred" (neyya) because it must be understood through its underlying intention rather than being taken literally, as it cannot be expressed by common parlance.

It is "inferred" (nīta) because its intention is already drawn out by mere words, as it can be expressed by common parlance. Its purpose is the complete purification of virtue, concentration, and insight.
It is blameless (*anavajja*) because it is free from fault by way of suppressing its constituent parts.

It is without defilement (*nakkilesa*) because it is the state of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) due to the total eradication of the defilements. It is purification (*vodāna*) because it is the state of the Noble Fruit (*ariyaphala*) due to the subsiding of the defilements.

Nibbāna is the ultimate reality (*paramattha*) because it is the supreme dhamma among both the conditioned and the unconditioned. It "revolves" (*parivattati*) within the Buddha-knowledge because, being the object of that knowledge, it is not external to it.
It functions by pervading, or by surrounding, or by adorning, or by distinguishing.
By the words “all bodily action,” etc., he shows that it is within the range of the Blessed One’s knowledge. “Accompanying knowledge” means that knowledge accompanies it;
the sense is that it is never devoid of knowledge. “Unobstructed” shows its state of being free from hindrances.
Desiring again to establish omniscience by means of a simile, he said, "As far as," and so forth. In this context, that which is to be known is the "knowable" (*neyya*).

That which has the limit of the knowable, the end of the knowable, is "limited by the knowable" (*neyyapariyantika*). However, for those who are not omniscient, there is no such thing as the end of the knowable.
The same method applies to that which is limited by knowledge (*ñāṇapariyantika*). Having distinguished the meaning already stated in the previous Yamaka by means of this Yamaka:

He shows it; by means of the third pair (yamaka), he shows it having determined it through negation. And herein, the "knowable" (*neyya*) is the "path of the knowable" (*neyyapatha*) because it is the range of knowledge.
"Abiding at each other's limits" means that they are disposed to stand at the mutual limit of one another after both the knowable and knowledge have been exhausted from their respective positions.

"Dependent on adverting" means dependent on mind-door adverting; the meaning is that it knows immediately after [the object] has been adverted to. "Dependent on desire" means dependent on inclination;
the meaning is that it knows by way of impulsion-knowledge immediately after adverting.
The other two phrases are stated for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of these two phrases respectively. Regarding the phrase "it knows the disposition," here they... [disposition].

"Āsaya" (abode) means that which they abide in; this is a designation for the mental continuum (*santāna*) that has been permeated by either wrong view or right view, or by sensual desire and so forth, or by renunciation and so forth.
"Anusaya" (latent tendency) means that they follow along with and continue to flow within the mental continuum of beings;

this is a designation specifically for those [defilements] such as sensual lust that have become firmly established. "He knows the latent tendencies"—the discussion regarding latent tendencies has already been explained above.
*Caritaṃ* refers to past wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed. *Adhimutti* is the present mental inclination toward the wholesome or the unwholesome.

*Apparajakkhā* means those for whom there is little dust of passion and so forth in the eye consisting of wisdom; thus they are *apparajakkhā*. Alternatively, those for whom there is little dust of passion and so forth are *apparajakkhā*;
these are the ones with little dust. *Mahārajakkhā* means [those for whom there is] great [dust] in the eye consisting of knowledge.

Those who possess the dust of passion and so forth are "those with great defilement" (*mahārajakkhā*). Alternatively, those for whom the dust of passion and so forth is great are "those with great defilement";

such are the *mahārajakkhā*. Regarding "those with sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriya*) and "those with dull faculties" (*mudindriya*): those for whom the faculties of faith and so forth are sharp are "those with sharp faculties.

Those for whom the faculties of faith and so forth are dull are "those with dull faculties. Regarding "those of good conduct" (*svākāra*) and "those of bad conduct" (*dvākāra*): those whose faith and so forth are excellent...

Those who have good modes (ākāra) and parts (koṭṭhāsa) are "those of good character" (svākāra). Those who have base and censurable modes and parts, such as lack of faith and so forth, are "those of two-fold character" (dvākāra).
Regarding "easy to instruct" and "difficult to instruct": those who perceive the reason stated [by the teacher] and can be instructed with ease are "easy to instruct.
Those who are the opposite of that are "difficult to instruct. Regarding "capable" and "incapable": in the case of the capable...
And those who are incapable (*abhabba*). They are called "capable" (*bhabba*) because they exist and are being born through noble birth.
The use of the present tense here refers to what is proximate to the present; thus, "capable" means they will exist or will be born, that is, they are fit vessels.

Those who are suitable for the penetration of the Noble Path and are endowed with the requisite conditions (*upanissaya*) are capable. Those who possess the opposite of what has been stated are incapable.
“He understands beings”: he understands beings who are attached and clinging to objects such as form and so forth. “The world with its devas”: together with the devas, it is *sadevaka*.
Together with Māra, it is *samāraka*. Together with Brahmā, it is *sabrahmaka*. Together with recluses and brahmins, it is *sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī*.
Because they have been born (*pajātattā*), they are called “beings” (*pajā*). Together with devas and humans, it is *sadevamanussā*. “Beings” (*pajā*) refers to the world of sentient beings.
This is a figurative expression. In this context, by the term "together with devas" (sadevaka), there is the inclusion of the devas of the five sense-sphere realms;

by the term "together with Māras" (samāraka), there is the inclusion of the devas of the sixth sense-sphere realm; by the term "together with Brahmas" (sabrahmaka), there is the inclusion of the Brahmās such as those of the Brahmakāyika realm;

and by the term "together with recluses and brahmins" (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī), there is the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the Teaching, as well as those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil.
By the term "the world of beings" (pajā), the world of sentient beings is included. By the term "with its devas and humans," conventional devas and the remaining humans are included.
Thus, it should be understood that here, by three terms, the world of space is grasped, and by two terms, the world of beings is grasped.

According to another method: by the inclusion of "with its devas," the formless realm (arūpāvacara) is grasped; by the inclusion of "with its Māras," the six sense-sphere realms (kāmāvacara) are grasped.

By the inclusion of "together with Brahmā," the world of the fine-material-sphere Brahmās is meant; by the inclusion of "together with recluses and brahmins," etc., it refers either to the human world together with conventional deities according to the four assemblies, or to the entire world of all remaining beings.

Furthermore, here, by the expression "together with devas," [the Buddha] establishes, by way of the highest possible limit, that the entire world is encompassed within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Then, for those who might think, "Māra is of great power, the lord of the six classes of sense-sphere deities, and possesses sovereign control;

could even he be included within the Buddha’s knowledge?"—in order to dispel their doubt, [the Blessed One] said, "together with Māra" (*samāraka*). Furthermore, for those who might think, "Brahmā is of great power;
with a single finger he radiates light throughout a thousand world-systems. With two... [and so on]... up to ten..."
“With his fingers he radiates light throughout ten thousand world-systems and experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative attainment;
does he too revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge? To dispel their doubt, he said, “together with Brahmā.
Then, for those who might think, “There are many ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the teaching; do they also revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge? [he said...]
To dispel their doubt, he said, "This generation, together with its recluses and brahmins.
Having thus demonstrated that even those at the highest level are included within the Buddha’s knowledge, he then showed— in terms of the highest possible limit—
that the rest of the world of beings, including the conventional deities and all other humans, is likewise included within the Buddha’s knowledge.
Explaining this, he said, "together with gods and humans. This is the sequence of the connection here. However, the ancients have said:
"Together with gods" means the remaining world together with the deities; "together with Māra" means the remaining world together with Māra;

"together with Brahmā" means the remaining world together with the Brahmās. Thus, all beings included within the three realms of existence [are encompassed] by these three modes in these three locations.

Having included [the world] again, it was stated that it is "together with its recluses and brahmins, its generation with its devas and humans," in order to exhaust it by means of two further aspects.
Thus, by these five phrases and in those respective ways, the threefold realm itself is exhausted.
"Antamaso" means down to the very limit. Regarding "timitimiṅgala": here, *timi* is a species of fish; in order to swallow a *timi*, [one must be as large as a *timitimiṅgala*].
Capable of swallowing even that is the species of fish named *timiṅgala*, which has a body five hundred leagues long;

capable of swallowing even a *timiṅgala* is the species of fish named *timitimiṅgala*, which has a body five hundred leagues long. It should be understood that here the singular number is used by way of referring to the genus.
Regarding the phrase "the *garuḷa* called *venateyya*," here "*garuḷa*" is a name based on the genus, while "*venateyya*" is [a specific epithet].
By way of clan. "In one place" means in a single location. It should be understood that the phrase "equal to Sāriputta" is said by taking the Elder Dhammasenāpati as the standard for all Buddhas;
for among the remaining disciples, there is no one who can truly be called equal to the Elder Dhammasenāpati in wisdom.
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus of great wisdom, namely this one."
“Sāriputta. And it is said in the Commentary:
“Setting aside the Lord of the World, whatever other living beings there may be, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of Sāriputta’s wisdom.”
"Having pervaded" means that the Buddha’s knowledge, having reached the wisdom of all gods and humans, stands having pervaded—that is, having spread across—their wisdom from its own basis.

"Having overcome" means that it stands having transcended the wisdom of all gods and humans, and having overcome the entire range of the knowable (neyya), which is not even within their domain; such is the meaning.
In the *Paṭisambhidā*, however, the reading is “having struck through” (*atighaṃsitvā*); the meaning is “having struck and having pierced.
By the words “those who...,” etc., he shows the means of making the state directly manifest by thus encompassing and overcoming [the object]. Therein, “wise” (*paṇḍita*) means endowed with wisdom.
“Clever” (*nipuṇa*) means those whose intellects are subtle and refined, capable of penetrating subtle points of meaning.
"Having mastered the doctrines of others" means they have both understood the doctrines of others and gained proficiency in debate with them.

"Like hair-splitting archers" means they are like archers who can pierce a single hair. "They move about, as it were, piercing the positions of views with the weapon of wisdom" means that, like a hair-splitter piercing a hair, they pierce even the most subtle positions of others' views with their own course of wisdom.

The meaning is "moving as it were. Alternatively, just as in the expressions "gone to excrement" (*gūthagata*) or "gone to urine" (*muttagata*), so too wisdom itself is "gone to wisdom" (*paññāgata*).

Views themselves are "gone to views" (*diṭṭhigatāni*). Having formulated and formulated questions—having composed inquiries consisting of two lines, three lines, or four lines—the word "twice" is used for the sake of including all of them, because those questions are exceedingly numerous.
It has been said. The phrase "categories of meaning that are hidden and concealed" is the remainder of the text.
Because it was intended by the Blessed One that they would ask questions formulated by themselves after seeing the Vinaya in such a manner, they ask questions.
However, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to those who approach him without even giving others the opportunity to ask questions, as it is said:
“They formulate a question, thinking: ‘Having approached the ascetic Gotama, we will ask him this question.
If the ascetic Gotama, being asked thus, answers thus, we will refute his argument in such a way;
and if, being asked thus, he answers otherwise, we will refute his argument in that way. They hear [of this].”
‘The ascetic Gotama has indeed arrived at such-and-such a village or town. They approach the ascetic Gotama.
The ascetic Gotama instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a discourse on the Dhamma, they...
"Though they have been thus encouraged and cheered, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama a question; how then will they refute his doctrine?
On the contrary, they simply become disciples of the ascetic Gotama himself.
If one asks why they do not ask questions, it is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly, he [overwhelmed] the assembly...
He observes their intention, and then he sees: "These wise ones have come having made this question hidden, secret, and like the core of a palm fruit.
Even before being asked by them, he thinks: "In the posing of this question there are so many faults; in the answering, so many;
in the meaning, the phrases, and the syllables, so many [possibilities]. One asking this question should ask thus; one answering..."

"One should answer thus. Having thus made the core of the matter [the *ovaṭṭika-sāra*], he shows it by inserting it into the midst of his discourse on the Dhamma when the questions have been brought forward.
Those wise men become delighted, thinking: "It is indeed better for us that we did not ask these questions.
For even if we had asked them, the ascetic Gotama would have left us without a foothold and cast us aside."
Moreover, when the Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they pervade the assembly with loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Through this pervasion of loving-kindness, the minds of the great multitude find confidence in the Ten Powers (*dasabala*) of the Buddhas. Indeed, the Buddhas have attained the perfection of form; they are endowed with vision, possess sweet voices, soft tongues, and well-polished lips and teeth.
As if sprinkling the heart with the Deathless (*amata*), they discourse on the Dhamma. In that regard:
As their hearts were thus purified by the pervasion of loving-kindness, it occurred to them:
"We shall not be able to maintain an opposing stance against the Blessed One, who speaks such words that are free from duplicity, not in vain, and leading to liberation.
Thus, precisely because of their state of confidence, they did not ask questions.

"Expounded and answered" means that by the recitation of questions not previously asked—[with the words] "Thus you should ask"—those very questions have been expounded by the Blessed One. And just as they were to be answered, so too have they been answered.
"With the reasons demonstrated" means that it is with this reason and this cause that such-and-such occurs; thus, it is stated with its underlying cause.
By means of their answers, those questions become precisely the reasons pointed out by the Blessed One. And they "become cast into the presence of the Blessed One" (*upakkhittakā*);
that is to say, through the Blessed One’s answering of the questions, those wise kṣatriyas and others become "cast" (*khittakā*) or "thrown into" (*pakkhittakā*) the presence of the Blessed One;
the meaning is that they become either disciples (*sāvaka*) or lay followers (*upāsaka*).
"They attain either the excellence of a disciple (*sāvaka-sampatti*) or the excellence of a lay follower (*upāsaka-sampatti*)," this is what is meant.
"Then" (*atha*) has the sense of immediate succession; the meaning is: immediately after those aforementioned excellences. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that place or in that context.
"Shines forth" (*atirocati*) means it shines and is made manifest exceedingly. "By means of which wisdom" (*yadidaṃ paññāya*) refers to that wisdom of the Blessed One...
"By that wisdom, the Blessed One alone shines forth pre-eminently"—this is the meaning. The word *iti* has the sense of a reason;
the meaning is "for this reason. The rest is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the Pasūra Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta 70.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], in the exposition of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, first, concerning the initial verse: at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, various forms...
Having created [this form] and seeing that the daughter of Māra had approached with longing desire, he felt not even a trace of craving, aversion, passion, or lust for sexual union.

He thought: "What could come of this? Upon seeing the body of this girl, which is filled with urine and excrement, one would not wish to touch her even with the feet; how much less could one live together with her?"
"Full of urine" means filled with urine that remains filling the interior of the bladder according to the quantity of food and drink consumed.

"Full of dung" means full of feces situated within the receptacle known as the large intestine, between the navel and the base of the spinal column, occupying a depth of eight finger-breadths at the end of the intestines.
"Full of phlegm" means [full] with a quantity measuring one bowlful situated on the surface of the stomach.

It is filled with phlegm. "Full of blood" refers to that which fills the lower part of the liver, which remains dripping little by little over the heart, kidneys, and lungs, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs;

and it includes the accumulated blood known as *saṇṇicita-lohita*, which amounts to filling a single bowl, as well as [the blood] at the sites where the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth are detached from the flesh.
Setting aside the stiff, dry skin, it remains pervading the entire acquired body (upādiṇṇaka) following the network of veins,
and is filled with two kinds of blood known as circulating and stagnant.
As for the "collection of bones," there are more than three hundred bones situated above the bones at the base of the entire body.
It is constructed from those bones. "Bound together by sinews" means it is bound and fastened by nine hundred sinews that remain binding the bones throughout the entire body.
"Smeared with blood and flesh" means it is smeared with more than three hundred bones covered by circulating blood, and with nine hundred pieces of flesh.
The body. "Bound with skin" (*cammavinaddha*) means that which stands beneath the outer skin over the visible flesh and sinews, having completely enveloped the entire body;
it is bound and wrapped by that skin. The reading *cammāvanaddha* also occurs in the Pāḷi.
"Covered by skin" (*chaviyā paṭicchanna*) means covered and concealed by the exceedingly delicate skin. "Full of holes" (*chiddāvachidda*)...
It has many openings. "Oozing" means oozing from the eyes, mouth, and so forth. "Dripping" means dripping from the lower part.
"Inhabited by swarms of worms" means frequented by various multitudes of living beings such as needle-mouthed insects.
"Filled with various kinds of filth" means filled with many types of impure substances.
71. Then Māgaṇḍiya thought, “Those who have gone forth indeed renounce human sensual pleasures and go forth for the sake of divine sensual pleasures;
yet this man does not even desire divine sensual pleasures. This is truly a jewel among women—what could his view be?
Thinking thus, he spoke the second verse in order to question him. Therein, the phrase “such a jewel as this” refers specifically to the divine jewel of a woman.
"Nārī" refers to his own daughter. "Diṭṭhigataṃ sīlavataṃ nu jīvitaṃ" means [his] view, virtue, observance, and livelihood.
"Bhavūpapattiṃ ca vadesi kīdisaṃ" means: what kind of rebirth for yourself do you declare? 72.
The two verses following this proceed by way of questions and answers, and thus their connection is evident. Among them:

The summary meaning of the first verse is as follows: O Māgandiya, among the sixty-two types of speculative views, there is nothing that has been grasped by me after investigating them and deciding, "Only this is true;
all else is false. Why is that? Because, seeing the danger in views, I have not accepted any view whatsoever.
Discerning the truths, they saw only Nibbāna—designated as "internal peace"—by virtue of the absence of passion and other defilements within.
"Calamity" means misfortune. "Accompanied by suffering" means accompanied by bodily suffering. "Accompanied by vexation" means possessed of mental suffering.
"Accompanied by despair" means possessed of despair. "Accompanied by fever" means possessed of distress. "Not for disenchantment" means not for...
For the sake of disenchantment with the round; "not for dispassion" means not for the sake of dispassion toward the round; "not for cessation" means not for the sake of the cessation of the round;
"not for peace" means not for the sake of the pacification of the round; "not for direct knowledge" means not for the sake of directly knowing the round;
"not for enlightenment" means not for the sake of awakening from the round by means of the departure from the sleep of the defilements.
"Not for the sake of Nibbāna" means not for the sake of the deathless Nibbāna. Herein, however, "for the sake of disenchantment" refers to insight (*vipassanā*);

"for the sake of dispassion" refers to the path (*magga*); "for the sake of cessation and peace" refers to Nibbāna; "for the sake of direct knowledge and full enlightenment" refers to the path; and "for the sake of Nibbāna" refers to Nibbāna itself.
Thus, in one instance insight is mentioned, in three instances the path, and in three instances Nibbāna is stated. In this way...

The discourse on the analysis [of these terms] should be understood. However, by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*), all of these are indeed synonyms for the Path (*magga*) and also synonyms for Nibbāna.
"The peace of internal lust": through the state of being peaceful and the state of being extinguished (*nibbuta*) regarding internal lust, I beheld Nibbāna, which is designated as "internal peace.
The same method applies to "the peace of hatred," and so forth. This is the summary statement (*uddesapada*) for the subsequent detailed exposition (*niddesa*).
"Vicinanto" means increasing and clarifying the truths. "Pavicinanto" means clarifying each of those individually.
Some explain it as "seeking. "Adassaṃ" means I looked upon them. "Adakkhiṃ" means I penetrated them.
"Aphassiṃ" means I touched them with wisdom. "Paṭivijjhiṃ" means I made them directly manifest through knowledge.

73. The brief meaning of the second verse: Those "theories" (*diṭṭhigata*) are called "determinations" (*vinicchaya*) because they have been grasped after being determined by various beings, and they are called "constructed" (*pakappita*) in the sense that they are conditioned by their own respective causes.
The Sage, having not grasped those phenomena of speculative views, is "peaceful within"—this is the meaning.
"You say, 'Tell me, how has that which is proclaimed by the wise been explained by the wise?'—thus he speaks.
The commentary on this verse is clear in meaning, with the exception of the term *paramattha*. In that context, "the ultimate" (*paramattha*) refers to the supreme *nibbāna*.
74. Then the Blessed One [explained] the means by which that state was explained by the wise, along with its opposite.

Teaching this, he spoke the verse beginning with “Not by view. Therein, by the words “not by view” and so forth, he rejects views, learning, the eight attainments, knowledge, and external rules and observances (*sīlabbata*).
Regarding the word “says” (*āha*) used here in the phrase “one says purity,” one should understand the meaning as follows:
by joining that word “says” with the negative particle *na* throughout all instances and applying it to the first three terms, it means: “I do not say, nor do I speak, of purity through view.”
And as it is here, so it is in the subsequent sections as well. In that context, "not by view" means I do not speak [of liberation] without the right view consisting of ten bases.

Likewise, "by non-hearing" means without the hearing of the ninefold [scripture]. "By ignorance" means without the knowledge that accords with the truth of the ownership of one's own karma (*kammassakatā*).
"By lack of virtue" means without the restraint of the *pātimokkha*. "By lack of vows" means without the vows of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). "Nor by that" means...

The meaning should be understood as follows: "I do not speak even by way of each one of those [views] individually, such as the view and so forth. And "having relinquished these and not grasping them" means:
having relinquished these preceding states belonging to the dark side (kaṇhapakkhika), which are differentiated by view and so forth, through their complete eradication;
and having not grasped even the subsequent states belonging to the bright side (sukkapakkhika), which are differentiated by non-view and so forth, by attaining non-identification (atammayatā).
The peaceful one, not depending on existence, does not long for it through this practice;

by the subsiding of lust and other defilements, being peaceful, he does not depend on any phenomenon among the eye and so forth, nor would he be capable of longing for or praying for even a single existence.
This is the intended meaning of his "inner peace."
"Listening is also to be desired" means that hearing by way of the discourses and so forth is also to be wished for.
