"These factors are the requisites" means that these factors, beginning with right view, constitute requisites in the sense of being supportive. "Of those belonging to the dark side" means of those existing on the unwholesome side.
"Abandonment through eradication is to be desired" means abandonment through complete destruction, that is, through thorough elimination.

It should be desired. Regarding "wholesome states pertaining to the three realms": this refers to those wholesome phenomena belonging to the three planes—comprising the sense-sphere, the fine-material, and the immaterial realms—that have arisen through skill (*kosalla*). "Non-identification" (*atammayatā*) means the state of being free from craving.
When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya, failing to perceive the meaning of these words, recited the verse beginning with "If indeed... (*no ce kira*). Therein:
"Seen" and so forth are exactly as described by the method already stated. However, he spoke regarding those things belonging to the dark side (kaṇhapakkhika) in both instances.
But the word "said" (āha) should be understood in connection with the word "if not" (no ce), such that the meaning is: "If indeed he did not say, if indeed he did not speak.
"Momūha" means utterly deluded, or that which causes delusion. "Pacenti" means they know. The exposition of this verse is also straightforward.
76. Then the Blessed One, rejecting his question on the basis of that view, spoke this verse: “And relying upon a view.

Its meaning is as follows: O Māgaṇḍiya, you who ask again and again by relying upon a view have fallen into delusion regarding those very speculative positions you have grasped; and from this [delusion], by me...

"Because you do not perceive even the slightest notion of consistency—whether from the perspective of what has been stated regarding internal peace, from the perspective of practice, or from the perspective of the teaching of the Dhamma—for that reason you view this Dhamma through sheer delusion.
'Hanging on by means of hanging on' refers to clinging to the hanging on of views; 'bondage' refers to the bondage of views; 'impediment' refers to the impediment of views."
"You have entered into darkness" means you have entered into dense darkness. "One with a perception of the yoke" means one who has a perception regarding the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
"One with a perception of attainment" means one who has acquired a perception regarding the duty of a recluse. "One with a perception of clinging" means one who has a perception of what is perceived.

"One with a perception of cause" means one who has a perception of the reason. "One with a perception of basis" means one who has a perception of the cause. "You do not obtain" means you do not find. "From where [comes] knowledge? means...
But for what reason will you obtain knowledge of the path? The five aggregates are impermanent in the sense of being non-existent after having come to be.
"In conformity with the perception of impermanence" means that the perception which has arisen as "the five aggregates are impermanent" is the perception of impermanence;

that which is in conformity with—that is, not repugnant to—that perception is "in conformity with the perception of impermanence. What is that? It is insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). Of the two...
The same method applies to the insight-knowledges (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that accord with the perceptions of suffering and non-self.
Having thus shown how Māgaṇḍiya fell into dispute due to delusion regarding those things thus grasped,
he now uttered the verse beginning with "equal" and "distinguished" to demonstrate his own freedom from dispute concerning those and other phenomena, being devoid of delusion.

The meaning of this is as follows: whoever thus conceives in these three ways—by means of pride (*māna*), or by means of a view (*diṭṭhi*), or by means of a person (*puggala*)—he would dispute on account of that pride, or that view, or that person.
But for one such as we are, who does not waver among these three modes, there is no thought of being "equal" or "superior";
nor, [as the textual supplement implies], is there the thought of being "inferior. The exposition of this verse is also quite clear.
78. Furthermore: “*Saccanti so*,” etc., is the verse. Its meaning is as follows:

Such a person, who has abandoned conceit and wrong views—thinking, “One like me is a *brāhmaṇa* because of having cast out evil, and so forth; this alone is the truth”—what could he say? What subject matter could he speak of?
Or for what reason would he speak, thinking with pride, “My [view] is the truth, yours is false”?

One might dispute with a view or with a person. But in one such as I, an arahant whose taints are destroyed, there is no conceiving—whether equal through the occurrence of the thought "I am like him," or unequal through the occurrence of the other two modes—that there could be a dispute or a counter-argument regarding equality and so forth.
Thus, the exposition of this verse is also clear.
79. Is it not the case that such a person is [described] with absolute certainty? [This is shown in] the verse beginning, “Having abandoned his home.

Therein, “having abandoned his home” (*okaṃ pahāya*) means having discarded the dwelling-place of consciousness, such as the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), by abandoning desire and lust for them. “Wandering without a home” (*aniketasārī*) means not wandering about due to craving toward the signs of forms and other such dwellings.
“The sage who does not form intimacy in the village” (*gāme akubbaṃ muni santhavāni*) means one who does not engage in intimacy with householders in the village.

"Empty of sensual pleasures" (*kāmehi ritta*) means being detached from all sensual pleasures due to the absence of desire and lust for them. "Not looking forward [to future existence]" (*apurakkharāna*) means not producing a new personal existence in the future.
"How should one not engage in dispute with people? (*kathaṃ na viggayha janena kayirā*) means that one should not speak contentious speech with others.
"Hāliddakāni" refers to a householder of that name. "Went where the Venerable Mahākaccāna was" (*yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkamī*); here, *yena* is used in the locative sense.
This is an expression of the instrument (karaṇavacana). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "He approached him where Mahākaccāna was.
Or alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "He approached for that very reason for which Mahākaccāna should be approached by gods and humans.
And for what reason should Mahākaccāna be approached? It is with the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities.
Like a great tree that bears fruit constantly because of the desire of flocks of birds to enjoy its sweet fruit.
"He approached" (*upasaṅkami*) means that he had gone; "having approached" (*upasaṅkamitvā*) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, it may also mean that having gone in this manner, he went to a place even closer than that, namely, the vicinity of Mahākaccāna.
"Having paid homage" means having worshipped by prostrating with the five points of the body touching the ground.

Now, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come into the presence of Mahākaccāna, he placed his hands together in a bright añjali—resplendent with the joining of ten fingernails—at his head and sat down to one side.
"To one side" is a neuter locative designation, as in such expressions as "the moon and sun move unevenly."
...as it were. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "he sat down" in such a way that he was seated to one side.
Alternatively, this accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. "He sat down" means he took his seat.
For wise gods and humans, having approached one who is worthy of honor, sit to one side out of skill in the use of seats. And this householder—
One among them sat down to one side.
And how did he sit down to one side? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. What are they?
Too far away, too near, to the windward side, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind. Sitting too far away...
For if he wishes to speak, he must speak in a loud voice. Sitting too close, he causes physical contact.
Sitting upwind, he is troubled by the odor of the body. Sitting on high ground, he manifests disrespect.
Sitting directly in front, if he wishes to look at him, he must gaze with eye meeting eye.
[If one sits] too far back, if one wishes to see [the Teacher], one must stretch out one's neck to see.
Therefore, he too sat down, avoiding these six faults of sitting. Thus it is said: "He sat to one side.

"He said this" means he spoke this. This was stated, venerable Kaccāna, by the Blessed One in the *Māgaṇḍiya-ppañha* within the *Aṭṭhakavaggiya*; there is a section in the *Aṭṭhakavaggiya* called the *Māgaṇḍiya-ppañha*, and [this was said] in that question.

“The form element” (rūpadhātu) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). “Bound by craving for the form element” means bound by greed (*rāga*) toward the form element. “Consciousness” (*viññāṇa*) refers to kamma-consciousness. “One who wanders through abodes” (*okasārī*) means one who wanders through houses or wanders through attachments (*ālaya*). Why, then, is it not stated here as “the consciousness element, householder”? It is for the purpose of dispelling delusion; for in meaning, “abode” (*oko*)— [The text continues: ...is [synonymous with] *okāsa* (space/room), and *okāsa* is synonymous with *okāsaka* (one who occupies space); thus, the Blessed One said, “It is the consciousness element, householder. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the agent of wandering. For it is said: “Consciousness, householder, is the wanderer; name-and-form is the abode. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the basis for wandering. For it is said: “With consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be. Moreover, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the cause of wandering. For it is said: “If consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb... Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the destination of wandering. For it is said: “Wherever consciousness finds a footing, there it attains growth. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the support of wandering. For it is said: “When consciousness is supported, there is a descent of name-and-form. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the sustenance of wandering. For it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for name-and-form. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the resort of wandering. For it is said: “Wherever consciousness finds a resort, there it attains growth. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the root of wandering. For it is said: “From the root of consciousness, householder, this suffering mass arises. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the seed of wandering. For it is said: “Consciousness, householder, is the seed; name-and-form is the field. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the leader of wandering. For it is said: “Consciousness leads the way, consciousness goes first. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of wandering. For it is said: “Consciousness precedes, consciousness arrives first. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the guide of wandering. For it is said: “Consciousness guides, consciousness leads. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of rebirth. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of rebirth, the precursor of birth. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the future. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the future, the precursor of renewed existence. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the cycle of existence. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the cycle of existence, the precursor of the round of rebirths. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the continuity of existence. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the continuity of existence, the precursor of the stream of becoming. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of existences. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of existences, the precursor of the lineage of beings. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the series of existences. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the series of existences, the precursor of the chain of births. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of aggregates. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of aggregates, the precursor of the continuity of the five aggregates. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of elements. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of elements, the precursor of the continuity of the eighteen elements. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of bases. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of bases, the precursor of the continuity of the twelve bases. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of sense-spheres. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of sense-spheres, the precursor of the continuity of the eighteen sense-spheres. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of realms. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of realms, the precursor of the continuity of the nine realms. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of destinies. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of destinies, the precursor of the continuity of the five destinies. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of births. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of births, the precursor of the continuity of the four modes of birth. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of lives. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of lives, the precursor of the continuity of the three periods of time. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of kamma. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of kamma, the precursor of the continuity of volitional formations. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of results. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of results, the precursor of the continuity of the fruit of kamma. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of defilements. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of defilements, the precursor of the continuity of the floods, bonds, and latent tendencies. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of aggregates. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of aggregates, the precursor of the continuity of the five aggregates. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of elements. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of elements, the precursor of the continuity of the eighteen elements. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of bases. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of bases, the precursor of the continuity of the twelve bases. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of sense-spheres. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of sense-spheres, the precursor of the continuity of the eighteen sense-spheres. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of realms. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of realms, the precursor of the continuity of the nine realms. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of destinies. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of destinies, the precursor of the continuity of the five destinies. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of births. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of births, the precursor of the continuity of the four modes of birth. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of lives. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of lives, the precursor of the continuity of the three periods of time. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of kamma. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of kamma, the precursor of the continuity of volitional formations. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of results. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of results, the precursor of the continuity of the fruit of kamma. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of defilements. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the succession of defilements, the precursor of the continuity of the floods, bonds, and latent tendencies. Also, it is for the purpose of showing that consciousness is the precursor of the succession of aggregates. For it is said: “Consciousness is the precursor of the
A condition is said [to exist] such that pre-arisen kamma-consciousness is a condition for both subsequently arisen kamma-consciousness and resultant consciousness;
and resultant consciousness is a condition for both subsequent resultant consciousness and kamma-consciousness. Therefore, confusion might arise as to which consciousness is meant here.
To dispel that [confusion], without taking that [consciousness] into account, [the consciousness referred to is] indeed unmixed.
"The teaching has been given. Furthermore, it was stated that there are four stations of consciousness through the formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) [of kamma] by way of resultant objects;
in order to show those as well, consciousness is not included here.

"Application and clinging" (*upaya-upādāna*): there are two types of application, namely the application of craving (*taṇhūpaya*) and the application of views (*diṭṭhūpaya*); and there are four types of clinging, namely the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), and so forth.
"Of the mind": these are the mental determinations (*adhiṭṭhāna*), misapprehensions (*abhinivesa*), and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of unwholesome consciousness.

"Of the Tathāgata" means of the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). For although these have indeed been abandoned by all those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it is said here with reference to the highest limit because the Teacher’s state of having destroyed the taints is most renowned in the world.
Regarding the phrase "the consciousness element": why is consciousness included here? It is for the purpose of showing the abandoning of the defilements (*kilesa*).
For the defilements are not abandoned only within the four aggregates; they are indeed abandoned within all five. Thus it is included for the purpose of showing the abandoning of the defilements.
"In this way, householder, one is a wanderer without a home" means that by not wandering toward a home through karmic consciousness, one is called a wanderer without a home.
"Expansion and confinement by the sign of form as a dwelling-place": form itself is the "sign" (*nimitta*) of the defilements in the sense of being their condition;

it is the "dwelling-place" (*niketa*) in the sense of being an abode, defined as the activity of the object. Thus, it is the "sign of form as a dwelling-place. Expansion (*visāra*) and confinement (*vinibandha*) together constitute "expansion and confinement.
By both terms, the spreading nature and the binding nature of the defilements within that sign of form as a dwelling-place are expressed.
"Spreading and binding" means spreading and binding toward the sign of form as a dwelling; therefore, the meaning is:
by both the spreading of defilements and the binding of defilements that have arisen toward the sign of form as a dwelling. "A wanderer in a dwelling" (niketasārī) is said:
it is called a "wanderer in a dwelling" in the sense of a place of residence by way of making it an object. "Abandoned" refers to those [defilements] in the dwelling of the sign of form.
The obstructions of the spreading of defilements have been abandoned.

But why, in this context, are the five aggregates called the "dwelling" (*oka*) and the six objects the "home" (*niketa*)? It is because of the relative strength and weakness of desire and lust (*chandarāga*).

For although these [aggregates and objects] are equal in their status as objects in the sense of being a basis for attachment (*ālaya*), the term "dwelling" is used in its primary sense [for the aggregates].

The "pure" is said to be the house itself; the "abode" (*niketa*) refers to pleasure gardens and the like, which are places of residence for those who have made an appointment, thinking, "Today we shall play in such-and-such a place.
Just as desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) are powerful toward a house filled with children, wife, wealth, and grain, so too are they toward the internal aggregates (*khandhas*).
However, toward places such as pleasure gardens, that [desire] is weaker than it is [toward the house].
"Thus, regarding the six external objects": it should be understood that this teaching was given according to the strength or weakness of one's desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).

"Among those who are happy, he is happy": when his attendants are happy by way of obtaining wealth, grain, and so forth, he becomes happy with the happiness pertaining to the household, thinking, "Now I shall receive pleasing robes and pleasing food. Through them, he attains prosperity...
He conducts himself as if experiencing it himself. "Suffering with those who suffer" means that when suffering arises for them due to some cause, he himself becomes afflicted by a twofold suffering.

"In matters of duty and service" (*kiccakaraṇīyesu*) means in those duties designated as tasks to be performed. "He applies himself" (*vōyogaṃ āpajjati*) means he personally undertakes the application, that is, the necessity of performing those duties.

"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means in objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāmesu*). "In this way, householder, one is destitute of sensual pleasures" (*evaṃ kho gahapati kāmehi aritto hoti*) means that in this way one is destitute of defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāmehi*).
One is not empty because of the presence of sensual pleasures within; on the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), one should be understood as destitute and empty because of their absence.

"Placing it before oneself" (*purakkharāno*) means making the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) the foremost. Regarding the phrases "one might be of such a form," etc., [this refers to] long, short, dark, fair, and so forth.
One aspires: "May I be such-and-such a person among forms. Among feelings such as pleasure, one aspires: "May I be such-and-such a feeler.
Among perceptions such as the perception of blue, one aspires: "May I be such-and-such a perceiver. Among volitional formations such as meritorious formations, one aspires:
"May I be such-and-such a formator. Among consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness, one aspires: "May I be such-and-such a conscious being."
"Apurakkharāno" means not placing the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) before oneself. "Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te":
your speech is unsuitable and unpolished, whereas mine is suitable, polished, sweet—like a drink of honey. "Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ":
that which has been practiced by you for a long time and is well-mastered is overturned by my argument.
"Everything that has come [to you] has in an instant been overturned and turned back. 'The charge has been laid upon you' means: the fault has been attributed to you by me.
'Go for the sake of releasing yourself from the charge' means: go and wander about, approaching various teachers and seeking a superior argument for the purpose of escaping this charge.
'Or unravel it, if you are able' means: if you yourself are capable, then unravel it right here."
80. Thus is the verse beginning with “secluded from those by which. Therein, “by which” means by which wrong views and so forth.

“Secluded, one should wander” means one should wander empty [of them]. “An elephant would not speak having grasped those” means that an elephant (*nāga*), in the manner described by the phrase “it does not commit an offense,” would not wander having grasped those wrong views. “In the *elambuja*” means in the water known as *ela*.
"Born in the water, a lotus with a thorny stalk"—this is what is meant by "lotus.
Just as it is unsullied by water and mud—meaning that lotus is not defiled by either water or mud—so too is the sage who speaks of peace;
thus, the sage who speaks of inner peace is "unattached" (*agiddho*) due to the absence of greed. And he is "unsullied" (*anūpalitto*) by both kinds of things: sensual pleasures and the world.
In the realm of sense-pleasures and in the world of the states of woe, he remains unsullied by the two kinds of clinging.
"He does no harm" means he commits no fault such as unwholesome deeds. "He does not go" means he does not go by way of a miserable rebirth.
"He does not come back" means he does not return to defilements already abandoned. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome" means produced by lack of skill.
"He does not bring back those defilements" means that those defilements which have been abandoned do not return again. "He does not relish them" means he does not approach them again.
"He does not go back to them" means he does not turn back toward them again.
"A harsh staff" means a staff with a rough blade, a cruel staff. "One whose greed is cast off" means one who has relinquished greed. "One whose greed is overcome" means...
"Vomit-like craving": craving that has been vomited out. "Released craving": craving whose bonds have been severed. "Abandoned craving": craving that has been relinquished. "Renounced craving":
craving that has been cast off in such a way that it never again ascends into the mind.
The same method applies to the subsequent terms beginning with "free from lust. All of these are synonyms for the state of having released what was previously grasped.
81. Furthermore: the verse beginning with “not a master of knowledge” (*na vedagū*).

Therein, “not a master of knowledge who is a driver by means of views” (*na vedagū diṭṭhiyāyako*) means that one such as I, a master of the four paths, is not a driver by means of views; nor does he go by means of views, nor does he regard them as essential.
The etymological meaning therein is as follows: “he drives” (*yāyati*) is *yāyaka*. By means of the instrumental case, “he drives by means of views” (*diṭṭhiyā yāyati*) is *diṭṭhiyāyaka*.
In the sense of "utility" (*upayoga*), he is also called *diṭṭhiyāyako* because he goes by means of view (*diṭṭhi*). He does not go to conceit by means of wisdom (*muti*);
that is, even by means of wisdom—which is distinguished by the [knowledge of] the liberated form and so forth—he does not go to conceit.

For he is not "made of that" (*tammaya*); he is not made of that nor intent upon that through craving and views, but this one is not like that. He is not to be led by action (*kamma*) nor by learning (*suta*); that is, not by the formative activity of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth.
He cannot be led by action, nor by learning such as purification through hearing (*sutasuddhi*), or by other forms of study.
"He is not led into dwellings" means that because he has abandoned both approaches, he is not led into any dwelling of craving or views. Regarding the phrase "or in the form of what is released":

here, "the form of what is released" refers to odors, tastes, and tangibles. "He does not lead to conceit" means he does not resort to the conceit "I am. "He does not approach" means he does not go near. "He does not draw near" means having approached, he does not remain there. "Consisting of that" means made of that.

82. And for such a person as this, there is the verse beginning with “one who is detached from perception. In that context, “detached from perception” (*saññāviratta*) means one for whom perceptions of sensual desire and so forth have been abandoned through meditation preceded by the perception of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*).
By this term, the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*) who is a follower of serenity (*samatha-yānika*) is intended.
“Liberated by wisdom” (*paññāvimutta*) means one who is liberated from all defilements through meditation preceded by insight (*vipassanā*). By this...
The one practicing dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka) is intended here. Regarding the verse, "Those who have grasped at perception and views wander about clashing with one another in the world":
those who have grasped at perceptions such as sensual perception (*kāmasaññā*) are primarily householders, who clash on account of sensual pleasures;
and those who have grasped at views are primarily renunciants, who clash on account of the Dhamma. Thus they wander about, clashing with one another.
"One who develops the Noble Path preceded by serenity" means that person who, having made serenity the precursor—that is, the forerunner—develops the Noble Path together with insight;
the sense is that they first arouse concentration and subsequently arouse the Noble Path together with insight.
"From its beginning" means from the first jhāna of that person. "Taking [it] as the basis" means...
"Depending on" means having relied upon. "The fetters are suppressed" means the fetters have been put at a distance.
"When he has attained Arahantship" means when he has attained the fruit of Arahantship. "An Arahant" refers to one established in the fruit of Arahantship.
All defilements, such as the fetters and delusions, are abandoned.
"One who develops the Noble Path preceded by insight" means that person who, having made insight the precursor—that is, the forerunner—develops the Noble Path;
the meaning is that having first produced insight, they subsequently develop concentration associated with the Noble Path.
"From its beginning for him" means from the starting point of that person's insight.
"Dependent upon insight. Regarding the phrase "delusion is suppressed": here, "suppressed" means it has been driven far away by means of perception (*saññā*).

"They strike" (*ghaṭṭenti*) means that those which grasp at perceptions of sensual desire and so forth oppress by means of perception. "They clash" (*saṅghaṭṭenti*) means they oppress from this and that direction.
Now, in order to show how they strike, he says: "Even kings dispute with kings," and so forth.
The detailed explanation has been stated. Regarding the phrase "they attack one another even with their hands": here, they strike one another with their hands.
"With clods" means with fragments of skull. "With sticks" means with half-sticks. "With weapons" means with double-edged swords.

"Because of the non-abandonment of volitional formations" means because of the state of not having abandoned meritorious and other types of volitional formations. "They collide in their destiny" means:
They are oppressed, that is, they encounter a collision, with respect to the destination that is to be gone to and serves as a foundation. This same method applies to the hells and so forth as well.
The rest here is clear because it follows the method already stated.
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Māgaṇḍiya-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the exposition of the *Purābheda-sutta*. 83.
Regarding the tenth [sutta], the exposition of the *Purābheda-sutta*, [the phrase] "how does he see? refers to this sutta and the five that follow it.

The general origin [of this sutta] should be understood in the same manner as was stated in the commentary on the *Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta*, regarding the *Kalahavivāda*, *Cūḷabyūha*, *Mahābyūha*, *Tuvaṭaka*, and *Attadaṇḍa* suttas. Specifically, however, just as on that great occasion,
in order to teach the Dhamma in a way suitable for deities of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), he had himself questioned by means of a manifested Buddha (*nimmitabuddha*).

He preached the *Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta*. Thus, at that very same great assembly, having understood the minds of those deities whose thoughts had arisen as to "What indeed should be done before the breaking up of the body?", and for the sake of favoring them, he brought a manifested Buddha accompanied by a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty monks through the air;
having had himself questioned by that [manifested Buddha], he preached this sutta.

How so? These called Buddhas are great beings; there is nothing whatsoever in the world with its devas—whether seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or explored by the mind—that is not surpassed by them in any respect, whether it be an object of form analyzed as blue and so forth among objects of form, or an object of sound analyzed as the sound of a drum and so forth among objects of sound.
Or there may be objects such as sounds and so forth that do not come within the range of these doors of knowledge. As it is said:

"Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas... including gods and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or pondered by the mind—that I know, that I have directly realized. Thus it is in all cases.
The Blessed One, whose knowledge is unimpeded, divided all those deities into two classes according to their capacity and incapacity.
Those beings described by the method beginning with "endowed with an obstruction of karma" are called incapable; even though they dwell in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not look upon them.
Conversely, those who are the opposite are called capable; even if they dwell at a distance, the Buddhas go to them and gather them in.
In that assembly of deities, he set aside those who were incapable and took hold of those who were capable.

Having taken hold of them, he divided them into six groups according to their temperaments (*carita*), noting: "So many here are of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*); so many are of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*) and so forth.
Then, considering the teaching of the Dharma appropriate for each, [he thought]: "For the deities of lustful temperament, the *Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta*..."
“I shall teach the *Kalahavivāda Sutta* for those of a hateful temperament; the *Mahāvyūha Sutta* for those of a deluded temperament; the *Cūḷavyūha Sutta* for those of a discursive temperament;
the *Tuvaṭaka Sutta* for those of a faithful temperament; and the *Purābheda Sutta* for those of an intellectual temperament.
Having thus determined his teaching, he again turned his mind toward that assembly, considering: “Is this according to their own inclinations?”
“He would know it by means of another’s underlying intention, by means of the origin of the matter, or by means of a question.
Then, having understood that he would know it by means of a question, [the Buddha] considered:

“Is there anyone capable of asking a question according to their own inclination and conduct, having grasped the underlying intention of the deities? He saw that not even one among those five hundred bhikkhus was capable. Then...
Having brought to mind his eighty great disciples and his two chief disciples, and seeing that even they were unable [to do so], he thought:

"If he were a Paccekabuddha, would he perhaps be able? Knowing that he too would not be able, he considered whether anyone among Sakka, Suyāma, and the others might be able. For if anyone among them were able, he would have [known it].
Having had the question asked, he himself would have answered it; yet not even one among them was able to do so. Then this thought occurred to him:
"Only a Buddha such as I could be capable of this; but is there another Buddha anywhere?
Spreading out his infinite knowledge across the infinite world-systems and surveying the world, he saw no other Buddha. And this is not surprising.
Now, seeing no one equal to himself—even on the day of his birth, as described in the *Brahmajāla-vannanā*—he uttered an irreversible lion’s roar, saying, "I am the foremost in the world.
Having thus seen no other equal to himself, he thought: "If I were to ask questions and I myself were to provide the answers, then..."
“Those deities will not be able to penetrate [the truth]. However, if another Buddha were to ask the questions and I were to provide the answers, it would be a marvel;
the deities would be able to penetrate it. Therefore, I shall create a manifested Buddha.
Having thus entered the meditative absorption (jhāna) that serves as the basis for the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and having emerged from it, he performed the act of taking up the bowl and robe.

Having performed the preliminary work with sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) thoughts, thinking, "May my looking forward, looking around, contracting, and extending be exactly like [the Buddha's]," he made a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) with a fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) thought, saying:
"May it come as if breaking through the moon’s disk while leaping over the enclosure of Pācīnayugaṃdhara. When the host of devas saw him, they...
“Master, has another moon risen? he asked. Then, as it drew closer, [he said], “It is not the moon; the sun has risen.
When it drew even closer, [he said], “It is not the sun; this is a celestial mansion of the gods. When it drew even closer still, [he said], “It is not a celestial mansion of the gods;
this is a son of the gods. When it drew even closer still, [he said], “It is not a son of the gods; it is Mahābrahmā.”
“Is this he? When he was seen even closer, he said, “This is not Mahābrahmā; another Buddha has arrived, sirs!
Thereupon, the ordinary deities (puthujjana-devatā) thought: “If such a gathering of deities occurs for just one Buddha, how great will it be for two?
The noble deities (ariya-devatā) thought: “Two Buddhas in a single world-system...”
"There is no one like him; surely the Blessed One has manifested another Buddha equal to himself.

Even as that host of devas looked on, the manifested Buddha approached; instead of bowing to the One of Ten Powers, he took a seat prepared directly opposite him, making it exactly level with his own.
The thirty-two marks of a Great Man were present on the Blessed One, and they were likewise present on the manifested one.
Six-colored rays issued forth from the Blessed One’s body and from the body of the emanation as well.
The rays from the Blessed One’s body struck against the body of the emanation, and the rays from the emanation’s body struck against the Blessed One’s body.
Rising from the bodies of both Buddhas, they reached the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), then turned back from there and passed over the very tops of the heads of the deities.
Having descended, they settled upon the rim of the Cakkavāḷa. The entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa shone like a shrine-hall covered with golden curved rafters.
The deities of ten thousand Cakkavāḷas gathered together in a single Cakkavāḷa, entered within the radiance of the two Buddhas, and stood there.
As soon as the created being sat down, [he thought]: "How shall I see..."
By means of the method beginning with “Of what character, and how tranquil is he called? he spoke this verse while inquiring about higher wisdom and the other trainings.

Therein, regarding the inquiry: first, by asking “How does he see? he asks about higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*); by “Of what character? he asks about higher virtue (*adhisīla*); and by “How tranquil? he asks about higher mind (*adhicitta*). The rest is self-evident.
For the purpose of explaining the emanated Buddhas and others, it is said in the *Peṭaka*:
“He who approaches the Dhamma by inquiring about what is wholesome and beneficial for his welfare—neither living, nor extinguished, nor dead—what kind of person do the Buddhas call him?
“One whose wandering in saṃsāra is exhausted, yet who has not cast off passion; who is neither a trainee (sekha) nor one who has seen the Dhamma.”
Whom do the Buddhas call that person who has not exhausted the taints yet bears his final body?
“One who is not possessed of the truth of suffering, nor of the truth of the path, much less of cessation;
who is very far indeed from the truth of the origin—whom do the Buddhas call that person?”
“It is neither causeless nor dependent on form; it is neither without condition nor unconditioned;
it does not have the unconditioned as its object, nor is it material—what kind of person do the Buddhas say that is?
Thus it was said.

In this context, it should be understood that the first verse refers to a manifested Buddha (nimmitabuddha), the second verse refers to a Bodhisatta in his final existence (pacchimabhavika), the third verse refers to one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphalatta), and the fourth verse is spoken with reference to one who possesses the mind that precedes the mental-door reviewing of Nibbāna in the formless realm (arūpa).
"By what kind of seeing" means by what sort of seeing; "of what shape" means...
"Of what likeness" (*kiṃsarikkhena*): by what kind? "Of what nature" (*kiṃpakārena*): of what sort? "Of what appearance" (*kiṃpaṭibhāgena*):
of what aspect? "Whomever I ask" (*yaṃ pucchāmi*): that person whom I ask, explain him to me. "I entreat" (*yācāmi*): I implore. "I beseech" (*ajjhesāmi*):
I command. "I gladden" (*pasādemī*): I produce joy within your continuum. "Speak! (*brūhi*): this is the introductory phrase for the detailed exposition.
"Explain" means: speak by way of names, saying "these are their names," regarding those things that are to be taught. "Teach" means: show. "Make known" means: cause to be understood;
for one who establishes absorption (*appanā*) by way of the doors of knowledge (*ñāṇamukha*) is said to "make known.
"Set forth" means: make known; the meaning is "cause to proceed," or "place within the doors of knowledge. "Reveal" means: make it open.
"Having opened, show it"—this is the meaning. "Analyze" (*vibhaja*) means making clear by means of the act of analysis; "show it"—this is the meaning.
"Make manifest" (*uttānīkaro*) means make it evident.
Alternatively, "explain" (*ācikkha*) is the root term for the six terms beginning with "teaching. These six terms, beginning with "teaching," [derive] from this.

These were spoken for the purpose of explaining the meaning. Therein, "teach" means: first, teach by way of a brief summary (*uddesa*) for the sake of those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*);
for those who understand through a condensed statement penetrate what is first stated in brief. "Explain" means:
[teach] for the sake of those who understand through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), by gladdening their hearts and sharpening their intellects.
And first, explain it by way of a detailed exposition of what was stated briefly. "Establish" means:
establish it by way of a further exposition (paṭiniddesa) of that very exposition already given—that is, expand upon it.
"Reveal" means: reveal it by repeating what has already been expounded. "Analyze" means: analyze it by further breaking down what has already been repeatedly stated.

"Analyze it. "Make it clear" means: make it clear by means of a more detailed explanation for that which has been opened up, and by means of an illustrative statement for that which has been analyzed.
This teaching serves for the penetration of those who are to be led (*neyya*).

84. But in the response, the Blessed One, without explicitly answering regarding higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*) and so forth in their specific forms, [answered] by means of the radiance of higher wisdom and so forth.

Because he is called "peaceful" due to the subsiding of those defilements, he spoke the verses beginning with "free from craving" (vītataṇho) in order to demonstrate that very subsiding in accordance with the inclinations of various deities.
Therein, the connection of the first eight verses should be understood through this verse: "Him I call peaceful.
Following that, [the connection] of the subsequent verses is through the line: "He indeed is called 'peaceful'."
By this final phrase. The method of commentary on each word (*anupada-vaṇṇanā-naya*):
"One whose craving has vanished before the breaking up" means one who has abandoned craving even prior to the dissolution of the body.
"Not dependent on the prior limit" means not dependent on the past limit, which is divided into the past time and so forth. "Not to be reckoned in the middle" means...
In the present time as well, he is not to be described by such methods as "one who is lustful" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "for him there is nothing placed before":
because the Arahant lacks the two types of preferential concern (*purekkhāra*), there is for him nothing placed before even in the future time.
"I call him 'peaceful'"—this is how the construction should be understood here. This same method applies everywhere.
"Before the breaking up of the body" means before the breaking up of the body born of karma (*karajakāya*). "Of the personal existence" means of the entire personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"At the casting off of the carcass" means at the casting off of the carcass, that is, from the laying down of the physical frame.
"Before the cutting off of the life-faculty" means even prior to the cutting off of the two-fold life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

The "past" (*pubbanta*) is called the past time-period; it refers to the prior portion or section designated as "the past," which is described as "the past time-period" or "elapsed time. "With reference to the past time-period" means that craving was abandoned in dependence upon the past time.
Furthermore, showing another method for the "Single Fortunate Night" (*bhaddekaratta*), he said, "Or else," and so forth.
In that context, "I was such-and-such a form" means: even though [my body] was black, it was the color of a sapphire; thus, by way of its beautiful appearance, "I was such-and-such a form."

"Thus-feeling" means by way of wholesome feeling, pleasant or joyful feeling (*sukha-somanassa-vedanā*). "Thus-perceiving," "thus-forming," and "thus-conscious" are by way of the perception and other mental factors associated with that [feeling].
Regarding the phrase "I was thus-feeling, thus-perceiving, thus-forming, and thus-conscious in the past time, he does not take delight therein":
this means he does not allow craving (*taṇhā*) for those [aggregates] such as form, or the view associated with craving, to continue. According to another method:
In demonstrating the *Mahākaccāna-bhaddekaratta-pariyāya*, he said, "Or else, 'my eye was thus,'" and so forth.
Therein, "eye" (*cakkhu*) refers to the sensitive eye-organ (*cakkhupasāda*). "Forms" (*rūpa*) refers to forms produced by the four [causes].

By this method, the remaining sense bases (*āyatana*) are also to be understood. "Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers to the dependent consciousness. "He does not delight in that" means he does not delight in both that eye and the form.
He does not rejoice by way of craving or views. Regarding the passage, "Thus my mind was, thus were the phenomena":

here, "mind" (*mano*) refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*). "Phenomena" (*dhammā*) refers to the objects of the three planes of existence. "Smiling, talking, and playing": these are smiling, which is the showing of teeth;
talking, which is vocal chatter; and playing, such as physical play—these are "smiling, talking, and playing. "He does not relish them" means he does not take pleasure in those smiles and so forth.
"He does not rejoice in it" means he does not make it dear. "He does not find satisfaction in it" means he does not attain contentment through it.
"Arisen in dependence on this or that condition" means present. "Red" means not to be reckoned as such; rather, it is "red with lust."
It should not be brought into calculation. The same method applies to what follows as well.

In such passages as "might it be so," *nandī*—defined as the occurrence of craving and views—should be understood as the act of bringing together (*samannānayanā*) by way of the excellence and agreeability of form and so forth.
"Does not intend" means he does not establish [it] by way of aspiration. "By reason of non-intention" means by reason of not establishing an aspiration.
85. *Asantāsa* means not being afraid due to various kinds of non-attainment. *Avikatthī* means one whose nature is not to boast about virtue and so forth.
*Akukkucō* means free from physical fidgeting and the like. *Mantabhāṇī* means one who speaks words after having reflected with wisdom.
*Anuddhata* means free from restlessness. *Sa ve vācāyato* means he is restrained by speech; he is one who speaks words that are free from the four faults.
"Non-angry" (*akkodhana*): Regarding what was said—"one who is not angry, non-angry, free from anger"—first, wishing to explain anger (*kodha*), he said, "Furthermore, anger must first be discussed.
"Anger must first be discussed" means that anger should be explained first. "Anger arises in ten ways" means through ten causes.
Anger arises. "He has done me harm," "he has brought about my ruin"—in this manner, the meaning should be understood for all the phrases.
Or else, anger arises on an improper occasion; that is, anger arises without cause.
For a certain person becomes angry thinking, "The rain is falling too much," or he becomes angry thinking, "It is not raining," or he becomes angry thinking, "The sun is scorching."
“He is not vexed” means he does not become angry. He becomes angry even when the wind blows, and he becomes angry even when it does not blow.
Being unable to sweep, he becomes angry at the Bodhi-leaf trees; being unable to put on his robe, he becomes angry at the wind;
tripping over, he becomes angry at the stump. It is with reference to this that it was said: “But anger arises in an improper place. In that regard:
Because it arises directed toward sentient beings in the nine lower instances, there is a breach of the courses of kamma (*kammapatha*).
However, resentment (*aṭṭhānaghāta*) arising toward formations (*saṅkhāra*) does not constitute a breach of the courses of kamma.

It is called "resentment of the mind" (*cittassa āghāto*) because it arises while causing resentment within the mind; "aversion" (*paṭighāto*) is stronger than that; and "hostility" (*paṭighaṃ*) is so called by way of striking back.
"Pativirujjhati" means "opposition" (paṭivirodha). "Kopa" is so called by way of being agitated. "Pakopa" and "sampakopa" are extensions of the term through the addition of prefixes.
"Dosa" is so called by way of being corrupt. "Padosa" and "sampadosa" are extensions of the term through the addition of prefixes.
"Byāpatti of the mind" refers to the mind's state of corruption or its mode of perversion. It arises as that which defiles the mind.
*Manopadoso*: corruption of mind. *Kodho*: anger by way of being angry. *Kujjhanā*: the state of being angry. *Kujjhitattaṃ*: the condition of one who has become angry. *Doso*: that which corrupts;
*dussanā* is the state of corrupting. *Dussitattaṃ*: the condition of having been corrupted. *Byāpajjanaṃ*: becoming afflicted in the sense of abandoning one's natural state;
*byāpatti* is the same. *Byāpajjanā*: the state of becoming afflicted. *Virodho*: that which opposes; it obstructs again and again.
"Contradicts" (*virujjhati*) means opposition (*paṭivirodha*). Or rather, this is stated by way of the mode of being contradictory and the mode of being opposed.
"Caṇḍika" refers to one who is fierce (*caṇḍa*), a stubborn person; the state of such a person is "fierceness" (*caṇḍikka*).

Because speech that is well-uttered does not occur through this [fierceness], but is instead ill-spoken and incomplete, it is called "not well-uttered" (*asuropa*). For at the time of anger, there is no such thing as complete speech.
It does not exist; even if it were to exist in anyone, it would be immeasurable.

Others, however, say that it is "mental distress" (*assuropo*) because it causes tears (*assu*) to arise and because it leads to the state of being distressed (*assuropana*); but that is not the reason, since joy (*somanassa*) also causes tears to arise.

It is "non-mental-satisfaction" (*anattamanatā*) because it is the opposite of the mental satisfaction mentioned above. Since that, moreover, belongs to the mind alone and not to a sentient being (*satta*), it is stated as "of the mind."
“Excessive slightness should be understood” means the state of being excessive and the state of being slight; the meaning is the state of being strong and the state of being weak.
“At some time” means once in a while. There is also a reading: “kañci kālaṃ. “It is merely a cause for turbidity of the mind” means it is of the measure that causes turbidity of the mind;
the meaning is that it is of the measure that causes defilement of the mind. There is also the reading: “cittālasakaraṇamatto.”
That reading is not good; its meaning is "merely causing weariness of mind.
"And he does not yet have the contraction and expansion of the mouth" means that there is as yet no closing or opening of the mouth.
"And he does not yet have the movement of the jaws" means that there is as yet no shifting back and forth of the two jaws. "And he does not yet have the utterance of harsh speech."
"It does not yet come forth" means that by merely emitting harsh speech from the mouth— which cuts to the quick of others—
it has not yet actually gone outside. "It does not yet look around in all directions and intermediate points" means that for the purpose of insulting another or for the sake of a staff and so forth,
it does not yet repeatedly look toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.
"And he does not yet take up staff or weapon" means that he does not yet take hold of a staff for the purpose of execution, nor a one-edged blade or other such weapon.
"And he does not yet brandish staff or weapon" means that he does not yet raise and strike with the aforementioned staff or weapon. "And he does not yet bring down staff or weapon..."
"It occurs" means this twofold [action] has not yet reached the stage of hurling for the purpose of striking another.

"It has not yet become a maker of severed and mangled parts" means that by the hurling of sticks, weapons, and so forth, it has not yet become a maker of two-fold divisions in the body of another, nor a maker of wounds in various ways.
There is also a reading: "a maker of perforated and mangled parts. "It has not yet become a breaker and a complete shatterer."
"He does not yet break up the body" means he has not yet reduced it to powder and dust.
"He does not yet drag out limb by limb" means he has not yet seized and dragged away each individual member of the body.
"He does not yet deprive of life" means he has not yet deprived it of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "Not yet for the sake of relinquishing everything" [means...].
"He stands firm" means that although he has destroyed the life of another, he does not yet stand firm for the purpose of destroying his own life.

This is what is meant: when, having deprived another of life, one stands for the purpose of depriving oneself of life, then it is called the relinquishment of everything. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily; having cut off anger, one does not grieve.
O Brahmin, the Noble Ones praise the slaying of anger, which has a root as bitter as poison but a tip that is sweet; for having cut it off, one does not grieve.”
"Yato" means when. "Having destroyed another person" means having ruined another person. "He destroys himself" means he kills himself.
"Reached the highest degree" means having attained a state of extreme intensity. "Attained the highest fullness" means having reached a state of extreme magnitude.
"By the abandoning of anger" means by the state of having abandoned anger of the type described as being eliminated by the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga).
"Because the basis for anger has been fully understood" means that the basis of anger— consisting of the objects of affection and aversion which serve as its foundation and cause—
has been known through the modes of full understanding consisting of knowledge and investigation.
"Because the cause of anger has been cut off" means that the arising of a state of consciousness accompanied by displeasure, which is the generative cause of anger, has been severed.
*Tāsī* means one who has the habit of being afraid. *Uttāsī* means one who has the habit of being excessively afraid. *Parittāsī* means one who has the habit of being afraid on all sides.
*Bhāyati* means fear arises. *Santāsaṃ āpajjati* means one reaches a state of agitation.
*Katthī* means one who has the habit of speaking in praise of oneself. *Vikatthī* means one who has the habit of speaking in praise in various and manifold ways.
"By birth" means by the excellence of birth such as the status of a khattiya. "By clan" means by a noble clan such as the Gotama clan.
"By family lineage" means by the state of belonging to a great family. "By beauty of complexion" means by the possession of a beautiful body;
for the body is called "a lotus" (*pokkhara*), and the meaning is: by the state of being handsome through the perfection of its color.
The phrases beginning with "by wealth" (*dhanena*) have meanings that are already evident.
"Remorse" (*kukkucca*) is the term of the summary (*uddesa*) for the detailed exposition (*niddesa*). In this context, "remorse" (*kukkucca*) means that which is badly done (*kukata*);
its state is "remorse. It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; its function is to grieve over what has been done and what has not been done; it is manifested as remorse (*vippaṭisāra*).
The state of what has been done and what has not been done should be regarded as a form of servitude. "Hand-worry" (*hatthakukkucca*) means that which is done with the hands in a contemptible way;
its abstract state is "hand-worry. The same method applies to "foot-worry" (*pādakukkucca*) and so forth.
"Perceiving what is unallowable as allowable" means, for example, eating dog meat thinking it is pork, or eating leopard meat thinking it is deer meat.
He eats; he eats what is an unallowable food thinking it is an allowable food; he eats at an improper time perceiving it as the proper time;
he drinks what is an unallowable drink thinking it is an allowable drink. This is "perceiving what is unallowable as allowable.
Regarding "perceiving what is allowable as unallowable": he eats pork thinking it is bear meat; he eats deer meat thinking it is leopard meat; [he eats] an allowable food...
"Improper food": he eats it; he eats at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time;

he drinks what is an improper drink with the perception that it is a proper drink. This is "perceiving what is proper as improper. "Perceiving what is blameless as blameworthy" means perceiving fault where there is no fault.

"Perceiving what is blameworthy as blameless" means perceiving no fault where there is fault. "The state of being scrupulous" refers to the manner of being scrupulous. "The state of having been scrupulous" [refers to the result of that].
The state of being remorseful; "regret of the mind" means a state of improper retrospection of the consciousness. "Mental anguish" means the anguish of the consciousness.
"By what was done and what was not done" refers to the state of having performed bodily misconduct and so forth, and the state of not having performed bodily good conduct and so forth.
"I have committed bodily misconduct" means that a bad action (*duṭṭhu carita*) was performed by the body because it was defiled by the mental corruptions (*kilesa*).
"Good bodily conduct was not done by me" means that what should have been well-performed with the body was not performed.
The same method applies to verbal misconduct, verbal good conduct, and so forth, up to their cessation.
"Of the mind" means of the mind, not of a being or a person. "Agitation" is the state of being agitated. "Non-quiescence" is the absence of quiescence.
"The mind is distracted" means mental distraction (*cetaso vikkhepo*), which is the wavering of the mind; it is the state of being unsteady in the mind, like a wavering carriage or a wavering ox.
By this, the quivering within a single object is described. For restlessness (*uddhacca*) quivers within a single object, whereas doubt (*vicikicchā*) [quivers] among various objects.
"This is called restlessness" refers to this state of being agitated.
"Having abandoned false speech": here, "false" (*musā*) refers to a verbal or bodily application that destroys the welfare of another by one who has the intention to deceive.
False speech (*musāvāda*), however, is the volition (*cetanā*) that, with the purpose of deceiving, originates a bodily or verbal application intended to deceive another.
According to another method: "false" (*musā*) is an unreal and untrue matter; "speech" (*vāda*) is the making known of that [matter] as real and true.
As for its characteristic: lying is the volition that originates the communication of something as being thus, by one who wishes to make another understand a thing as it is not to be thus;
that is lying. "Having abandoned" means having abandoned this immorality consisting of the volition of lying.
"Abstaining" means that from the moment it is abandoned, one is indeed refrained from that immorality. "There is no transgression of it"—that is, [the thought] "I shall violate it."
The meaning should be understood in this manner for other similar passages as well: "states cognizable by the eye and ear, let alone those cognizable by the body.
One who speaks the truth is a "truth-speaker" (*saccavādī*). One who joins or connects truth with truth is "consistent in truth" (*saccasandho*), not being inconsistent in between.
The meaning is: "he speaks falsely. For a man who sometimes speaks falsely and sometimes the truth, because his truth is interrupted by falsehood, his truth does not cohere with truth;
therefore, he is not one whose word is truth. But this person is not like that;
even for the sake of his life, he does not speak falsely, but rather joins truth with truth—thus he is "one whose word is truth" (*saccasandha*).
"Theteo" means firm; the meaning is "one of firm speech.

For one person is not of firm speech, like turmeric dye, like a post driven into a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed upon the back of a horse; another, however, is of firm speech, like a line carved in stone or like a city gatepost.
Even when his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not utter two different words; such a person is called "theteo."
*Paccayiko* means one who is to be trusted; the meaning is "one who is to be believed. For a certain person is not trustworthy (*apaccayiko*);
when it is said, "This was spoken by whom? By so-and-so," he becomes subject to being told, "Do not believe his word.
Another is trustworthy (*paccayiko*); when it is said, "This was spoken by whom? By so-and-so," [he responds], "If it was spoken by him..."
"This alone is the authority; there is nothing further to be examined now; it is exactly thus"—when one falls into such a state of speaking, this is called "one who relies on conditions" (paccayika).
"One who does not deceive the world" means that by virtue of his truthful speech, he does not deceive the world.

Regarding the phrases "having abandoned slanderous speech" and so forth: that speech by which, when one speaks it to someone, it creates a sense of being dear to oneself in that person's heart while making them feel empty (or alienated) toward oneself—that is slanderous speech.
Furthermore, that speech by which one makes both oneself and another harsh, or which is itself harsh—neither pleasant to the ear nor reaching the heart—that is harsh speech.

By speech. That by which one prattles nonsense is frivolous talk (*samphappalāpa*). The volition (*cetanā*) that is the root of these [actions] also receives the very name "malicious speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) and so forth;
it is precisely this that is intended here.
"For the sake of dividing these" means for the sake of dividing those from whom one has heard what was spoken here. Or, "for the purpose of reconciling those who are divided."
One who, having approached each individual among two friends or those such as co-residents under the same preceptor who have become estranged for some reason,
speaks such words as, "For those born in such noble families and so highly learned,
this is not fitting," and thereby acts as a reconciler and a peacemaker.

"Anuppadātā" means one who provides continuity. The meaning is that, seeing two people in harmony, one should perform a strengthening act by saying such things as, "For those born into such a family and endowed with such qualities as these, this is appropriate.
One whose monastery (ārāma) is harmonious is "samaggārāmo"; however, where there is no harmony, even to dwell there...
The meaning is "he does not desire. There is also a textual reading, *samaggarāmo*, which has this very same meaning.

*Samaggarato* means "delighting in concord"; the meaning is that he does not even wish to go elsewhere after abandoning them. He rejoices upon seeing or hearing of those in concord; thus, he is *samagganandī*.
"He speaks words that create concord" refers to that speech which makes beings indeed concordant.
One speaks only words that illuminate the qualities of harmony, and not otherwise.
Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal applications which cut into the vital parts of another.
"Nela" is so called because "ela" means fault; thus "nelā" means "without *ela*," i.e., faultless—as in the phrase "the white-canopied chariot with faultless parts."
It is like salt mentioned in this context. "Pleasant to the ear" means it is pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of its phrasing (*byañjana*);

it does not produce ear-ache, as if pierced by a needle. It is "endearing" (*pemanīyā*) because, through the sweetness of its meaning (*attha*), it generates affection rather than irritation throughout the entire body.
It is "heart-reaching" (*hadayaṅgamā*) because, proceeding unhindered, it enters the mind with ease.
It is called *porī* because it exists in the city (*pure*) due to its perfection of qualities; it is also called *porī* because it is as delicate as a woman raised in the city;
and it is called *porī* because it belongs to the city—meaning it is the speech of the city-dwellers. For the city-dwellers are speakers of appropriate discourse;
they say "father" to one who is merely a paternal relative, and "brother" to one who is merely a brotherly relative. Such speech is dear to many people, hence it is called *bahujanakantā*.
"Agreeable to many people" (*bahujanamanāpā*) means that by its very nature as something lovely, it is pleasing to many people and brings about the growth of the mind.
"Frivolous chatter" (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) that communicates what is harmful and originates from the application of body and speech.

"One who speaks at the right time" (*kālavādī*) means one who speaks having observed the appropriate time for what is to be said. "True" (*bhūtaṃ*), "actual" (*tathaṃ*), "real" (*tacchaṃ*), and "in accordance with reality" (*sabhāvameva*).

He speaks thus, therefore he is a speaker of truth (*bhūtavādī*). He speaks having based himself solely on what is beneficial for this life and the life to come, therefore he is a speaker of benefit (*atthavādī*).

He speaks having based himself on the nine supramundane states (*dhamma*), therefore he is a speaker of Dhamma (*dhammavādī*). He speaks having based himself on the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment, therefore he is a speaker of Vinaya (*vinayavādī*).
“Nidhāna” means a place for depositing; “nidhānavatī” means that which possesses such a place. The meaning is:

she speaks words that ought to be deposited in the heart. “At the proper time” (kālena): even while speaking such words, she does not speak at an improper time with the thought, “I shall speak words that ought to be deposited”;
rather, the meaning is that she speaks only after considering the appropriate occasion. “With reasons” (sāpadesaṃ):...
"With a simile" means with a reason. "With a limit" means he speaks in such a way that the limit of the matter is made known by demonstrating its boundary.
"Connected with the goal" means he speaks in a manner endowed with meaning, because it cannot be exhausted even when analyzed through numerous methods;
or rather, by that very goal which the speaker, being a proponent of the goal, declares.
Because he is composed, he speaks speech that is meaningful; what is meant is that he does not set aside one thing and speak another.
"He speaks speech free from the four faults" means he speaks speech devoid of the four faults beginning with false speech (*musāvāda*).
"Of the thirty-two kinds of low talk" refers to talk that is like a bypath (*tiracchāna*) leading away from heaven and liberation.
The "ten bases for talk" (*dasa kathāvatthūni*) are the ten causes—beginning with fewness of desires—that serve as the foundation for talk concerning the turning away from the round of existence.
Regarding "talk on fewness of desires": here, one who has "few desires" (*appiccha*) is one devoid of longing, without desire, and without craving.

In this context, while the phrasing (*byañjana*) seems to leave something remaining, the meaning (*attha*) is exhaustive; for in one whose taints are destroyed, there is not even the slightest thing called "desire."

Furthermore, in this context, the distinction between "excessive desire" (*atricchātā*), "evil desire" (*pāpicchātā*), "great desire" (*mahicchātā*), and "fewness of desires" (*appicchatā*) should be understood as follows:
there, the longing for the gains of others while being unsatisfied with one's own entire gains is called "excessive desire.
For one possessed of that [desire], even a cake cooked in a single vessel appears, when it falls into his own bowl, as if not well-cooked and as if small; yet for that very same person...
It appears as if well-cooked when placed in another’s bowl, and even though it is small, it seems large.
However, the concealing of non-existent qualities, lack of moderation in receiving, and evil desire—this is what is called *pāpicchatā*. This is indeed mentioned right here in the passage beginning:
"In this case, someone who is faithless thinks, 'May people know me to be faithful,'" and so forth. A person endowed with these [qualities] engages in hypocrisy (*kohañña*).

It is established. Furthermore, the desire for the recognition of one's virtuous qualities, as well as lack of moderation and great greed in receiving gifts, is indeed what is called "great desire" (*mahicchatā*).
This is included under the same principle as: "Here, someone being faithful desires, 'May people know me as faithful'; being virtuous, he desires, 'May people know me as virtuous'.
A person endowed with these qualities is difficult to satisfy.
Even when she has given birth, he is unable to win her heart over. Therefore, this is said:
“The mass of fire, the ocean, and the person of great desire— even if one were to provide these three with requisites by means of a cart, they could not be satisfied.”
However, the concealment of one’s own virtues and moderation in receiving gifts is what is called fewness of desires (*appicchatā*).
A person endowed with this quality, though possessing faith, does not wish for others to know him as "faithful" out of a desire to hide the virtues existing within himself.
[Likewise,] he who is virtuous... secluded... learned... energetic... and perfected in concentration... [does not wish for others to know these things].
Being wise and having exhausted the taints, he does not desire that people know him as "one whose taints are exhausted," just like the Elder Majjhantika.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu who is thus of few desires generates unarisen gain, makes what has arisen stable, and gratifies the minds of donors;
for in whatever way he takes little because of his own fewness of desires, in that same way—
Likewise, people who have confidence in his conduct give much to him.

There is another fourfold kind of one who has few desires: one who has few desires regarding requisites, one who has few desires regarding the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), one who has few desires regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti*), and one who has few desires regarding spiritual attainments (*adhigama*).
Among these, one who has few desires regarding the four requisites is "one who has few desires regarding requisites. He knows the disposition of the donor and [the nature] of the gift.
He knows the [donor's] disposition; he knows his own strength. For if the gift to be given is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, he takes little according to the donor’s wish.
If the gift to be given is small but the donor wishes to give much, he takes little according to the gift.
If both the gift to be given is abundant and the donor wishes to give much, [he takes much] according to his own strength.
Having understood this, he takes only what is measured.

One who does not wish to make known the existence of the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) within himself is called "one who has few desires regarding ascetic practices" (dhutaṅga-appiccha).

However, one who does not wish to make known his state of being well-versed in the scriptures is called "one who has few desires regarding the scriptures" (pariyatti-appiccha). Furthermore, [one who does not wish to make known] among those such as stream-enterers (sotāpanna)...
One who, having become such, does not wish to make known his status as a stream-enterer and so forth, is called "one who has few desires regarding attainment" (*adhigamappiccha*).

However, one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is called "one who has few desires" because he has abandoned excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire, and is endowed with that pure state of fewness of desires known as non-greed (*alobha*), which is the direct opposite of craving. "Friend..."

When one says, "Having shown the danger in these states—namely, lack of fewness of wishes, evil wishes, and great wishes—one should undertake and abide in such fewness of wishes," one is indeed speaking the discourse on fewness of wishes (*appicchakathā*).

Regarding the discourse on contentment (*santuṭṭhīkathā*) and so forth, we shall clarify only their specific meanings; the method of application, however, should be understood in the same manner as already stated.
The "Discourse on Contentment" is discourse based on contentment with whatever requisites are obtained. This contentment, moreover, is of twelve kinds.
Namely: regarding robes, there is threefold contentment—contentment with what is obtained, contentment with what is suitable to one's strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
The same applies to almsfood and the other requisites.
This is the detailed explanation of its classification: here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether it be beautiful or ugly.
He makes do with that very one; he does not long for another, and even if he receives one, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with whatever robe is obtained (*yathālābhasantosa*).
Furthermore, there is the case of one who is naturally weak, or is overcome by illness or old age, and while putting on a heavy robe...
He becomes weary. Having exchanged that [robe] with a fellow monk of similar standing, he remains content even while wearing a light one.
This is his contentment regarding robes according to his strength. Another person obtains excellent requisites;
having received a costly robe such as one made of fine cloth (*pattuṇṇa*) or several robes, he thinks: "This is for the elders who have long been gone forth."
Having given [robes] with the thought, "May this be suitable for those who are learned; may this be for the sick;
may this be for those who receive little," he remains content even while wearing a robe made from old rags or scraps gathered from rubbish heaps and sewn together into a saṅghāṭi.
This is his contentment with robes as they are appropriate.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined;
he sustains himself with that alone, does not long for another, and even if he receives it, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever almsfood is obtained.
However, if he receives almsfood that is contrary to his own nature or contrary to his illness, such that by consuming it—

He becomes uncomfortable; having given that [food] to a fellow monk of similar standing and having eaten suitable food from his hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength.
Another receives much and excellent almsfood; like a robe, he gives it to elders, those long ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick.
Having given them [the choice portion], or having eaten the remainder, or even while eating mixed food obtained by wandering for alms, he remains content.
This is his contentment with what is appropriate regarding almsfood.
Furthermore, in this case, a bhikkhu receives a lodging, whether pleasant or unpleasant; he does not feel elation because of it...
He does not give rise to mental distress; he is content with whatever dwelling place he obtains, even if it is merely a bed of grass.
This is his contentment regarding dwellings according to what is obtained.

However, if he receives a dwelling place that is contrary to his natural disposition or contrary to his illness, such that he finds it uncomfortable while living there, he gives it to a fellow monk who is suited to it.
Even while dwelling in a suitable lodging belonging to him, he remains contented. This is his contentment with respect to lodgings according to his capacity.
Another person of great merit obtains many excellent lodgings, such as caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and so forth;
