yet, giving these away like a robe to elders, those long-ordained, the learned, those who have little gain, and the sick, he dwells wherever he may be.
He is indeed content. This is his contentment with a dwelling as befits him. Furthermore, having reflected:

"An excellent dwelling is a ground for negligence; sloth and torpor descend upon one sitting there, and for one overcome by sleep, evil thoughts manifest upon waking again," he does not accept even such a dwelling when it is offered.
Having rejected that [luxury], even while dwelling in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or elsewhere, he remains content.
This is his contentment with a suitable resting place.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives medicine, whether coarse or refined; whatever he receives, by that alone...
He is contented; he does not long for anything else, and even if he receives something, he does not take it.

This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine. Furthermore, one who needs oil and receives molasses gives that to a fellow bhikkhu, takes oil from his hand, or seeks out something else entirely to prepare as medicine—even then, he remains truly contented.
This is his contentment with whatever strength he has regarding the requisite of medicine.
Furthermore, another person of great merit receives abundant excellent medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses;
yet, giving these away like a robe to elders, those long-ordained, the learned, and those who have received little, even while subsisting on whatever they receive from them, [he remains content].
He is indeed contented. However, when someone places four kinds of sweet substances in one vessel and urine-soaked harītaka in another,
saying, "Venerable sir, take whichever you desire," he rejects the four sweets— thinking, "If his illness can be cured by even one of those,
then urine-soaked harītaka is what has been praised by the Buddha and others"— and instead uses the urine-soaked harītaka.
While preparing medicine, he remains perfectly content. This is his contentment with what is appropriate regarding the requisite of medicine.
Among these three types of contentment for each of the requisites, however, contentment with what is appropriate is the foremost.
An Arahant is indeed content with all three of these regarding each individual requisite.
"Discourse on seclusion" means discourse dependent upon seclusion. For there are three kinds of seclusion: seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*).

In this regard, one goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, departs alone, applies oneself to the walking meditation path alone, and wanders alone.

“To dwell alone” is what is called physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). The eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), however, are called mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). Nibbāna is called seclusion from the substrata of existence (*upadhiviveka*). For it has been said:
“Physical seclusion belongs to those who have withdrawn their bodies and delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and who have attained supreme clarity.
And seclusion from the substrata of existence belongs to persons who are without substrata.”
“...for those who have reached the unconditioned. Regarding the discourse on non-association (*asaṃsaggakathā*), there are five kinds of association here:

association by hearing, association by seeing, association by conversation, association by sharing enjoyments, and physical association. Among these, a bhikkhu here hears: “In such-and-such a village or town...”
or a woman or a maiden who is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion”—having heard this, he becomes despondent and disheartened;
he is unable to maintain the holy life, and without disclosing his weakness in the training, he falls back to the lower state.
Thus, [he is affected] by the excellence of form and so forth described by others, or by the sounds of laughter, talk, singing, or music produced by himself.
The lust that arises in one who hears [such things] by way of the cognitive process of ear-consciousness is called "contact through hearing.

"In this case, a bhikkhu does not merely hear, but rather sees for himself a woman or a girl who is beautiful, lovely, charming, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; having seen her, he becomes dejected..."
He desponds, he is unable to maintain the holy life, and without disclosing his weakness in the training, he falls away to the lower state.
For one who gazes at a form of a different sex, however, the lust that arises by way of the cognitive series of eye-consciousness is called "contact through seeing.
But the lust that arises by way of mutual conversation and chatter is called "contact through talking. [This applies to] the bhikkhu...
Taking what belongs to a bhikkhunī from a bhikkhunī, or what belongs to a bhikkhu from a bhikkhu, with the intent of using it, while lust has arisen, is called "association by sharing.
However, lust arising through taking the hand and so forth is called "physical contact.
An arahant is unassociated with these five kinds of association even when together with the four assemblies; he is like one who has cast off his bonds.
And one who is free from social contact. Speaking in praise of non-contact, he is said to deliver a discourse on non-contact.

Regarding the "discourse on the arousal of energy": herein, one who has exerted energy and possesses perfect physical and mental energy does not allow a defilement that has arisen while walking to reach the standing posture, nor a defilement that has arisen while standing to reach the sitting posture.
It does not allow a defilement that has arisen while sitting to reach the state of lying down;
it moves about like one seizing a black snake by squeezing it with a staff, or like one treading upon the neck of an enemy.
To speak in praise of such a person who has initiated energy is what is called "discourse on the arousal of energy."

Regarding the phrases "discourse on virtue" (*sīlakathā*) and so forth: "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "Concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*).
"Wisdom" (*paññā*) refers to mundane and supramundane knowledge. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*).

"Knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) refers to the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). One is said to "deliver a discourse on virtue and so forth" when one explains the qualities (*guṇa*) of virtue and the other factors.

The sections beginning with "The discourse on the foundations of mindfulness" and ending with "that sage transcends the net of attachments" are to be understood according to what was stated previously.

86. "Free from longing" (*nirāsatti*) means without craving. "Seeing seclusion in contacts" (*vivekadassī phassesu*) means he sees the seclusion of selfhood and so forth within present contacts such as eye-contact and the rest.
"And not led by views" (*diṭṭhīsu ca na nīyati*) means he is not led by any of the sixty-two types of views.

"He does not grieve over a changed object" means that when any object has lost its natural state and perished, he does not fall into sorrow. "Or over a changing object" means while the object is in the process of perishing.
"Eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*) is contact born together with eye-consciousness, having the eye as its basis.

The same method applies to the others as well. And here, the former [contacts] have only the sensitivity of the eye and so forth as their bases, whereas mind-contact (*manosamphassa*) also has the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) as its basis.

All contact belonging to the four planes, even when without a physical basis (*avatthuka*), indeed receives the name "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-samphassa*) by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*).
For the three immaterial aggregates, acting as their own support, confer upon their co-nascent contact the name "designation-contact.
However, "resistance-contact" (*paṭigha-samphassa*) is [so called] in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*).
“Name-contact” is contact pertaining to the five doors. “Designation-contact” is contact pertaining to the mind door.
“Contact to be experienced as pleasant” is contact that is beneficial to and productive of pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the other two [types of feeling].

“Wholesome contact” is contact co-arising with the twenty-one wholesome types of consciousness. “Unwholesome” is contact co-arising with the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. “Indeterminate” is...
Contact co-arising with the fifty-five indeterminate [states]. "Sense-sphere" refers to contact co-arising with the fifty-four sense-sphere [states].

"Fine-material-sphere" refers to that associated with the fifteen wholesome and other fine-material-sphere states. "Immaterial-sphere" refers to that associated with the twelve immaterial-sphere states by way of the wholesome and indeterminate.
"Empty" (*suññato*) refers to the path that has arisen for one who is practicing insight by way of the contemplation of non-self;
the contact co-nascent with that is "empty contact. The same method applies to the other two as well.

"Signless" (*animittato*) refers here to the path that has arisen for one who is practicing insight by way of the contemplation of impermanence. "Desireless" (*appaṇihito*) refers to [the path] for one who is practicing insight by way of the contemplation of suffering.
The path that has arisen is wishless (*appaṇihita*). "Worldly" (*lokiya*): the world (*loka*) is said to be the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating;

because it is included within that, it is "connected to the world," thus worldly—the phenomena belonging to the three planes. "Supramundane" (*lokuttara*): it is supramundane because it is superior to the world and has crossed over the world;
it is also supramundane by virtue of not being included within the world. "By means of a self" (*attena vā*): by means of a personal identity (*attabhāva*).
Or, "by means of what belongs to oneself" (*attaniyena*) means by means of that which is under one's own control (*attāyattena*).

87. "Withdrawn" (*paṭilīno*) means having departed from those [defilements] because greed and so forth have been abandoned. "Not fraudulent" (*akuha-ko*) means not deceiving by means of the three bases of hypocrisy (*kuhana-vatthu*).

"Not envious" (*apihālu*) means having a nature free from envy; it is said to be devoid of the craving of longing (*patthanā-taṇhā*). "Not stingy" (*amaccharī*) means being free from the five kinds of stinginess (*macchariya*).
"Free from immodesty" means being devoid of physical immodesty and so forth. "Not loathsome" means not to be shunned because of his perfection in virtue and other qualities;
he is unsullied and pleasing. "And not intent on slander" means he is unfit for the act of slandering, which should be applied here in two ways.

"Because of the abandoning of lust" means by way of the state of having abandoned the defilement of lust through the path of Arahantship. "The conceit 'I am' is abandoned" means the pride of inflation consisting in the thought "I am" is abandoned by way of total eradication.
The three bases of hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*) are the three causes for deception. Regarding the phrase "the base of hypocrisy consisting in the acceptance of requisites" and so forth:
when one who is invited with robes and other requisites and actually has need of them, out of a desire for gain (*pāpicchatā*), refuses them;
and then, perceiving that those householders have well-established confidence in him, says to them again, "Oh, the venerable one is so modest (*appiccha*)," and so on.

Thinking, "If he would accept even a small thing, it would be a great gain for us," those who offer excellent robes and other requisites through various means do not abandon their desire to assist him;

rather, by accepting them, from that time forward, the act of using the requisites— which serves as the cause for others to bring offerings even in wagonloads— is what is termed the "acceptance of requisites" (*paccaya-paṭisevana*).

It should be understood as a ground for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the deception practiced through a deportment (*iriyāpatha*) performed with the intention of gaining esteem while one still possesses evil desires is the ground for hypocrisy known as deportment.

Moreover, it should be understood that the deception practiced through speech that falsely indicates the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) while one still possesses evil desires is what is known as "hinting" (*sāmantajappana*).
It should be understood as a basis for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*).
What is meant by "reckoned as the acceptance of requisites"? Here, "acceptance of requisites" refers to that which is reckoned as such; thus it is "reckoned as the acceptance of requisites.
"Invite" means that here householders invite the monks, saying, "Please accept almsfood. Or rather, this very [phrase]...
Regarding the reading: some read it as "invites" (*nimanteti*) or "speaks" (*vadati*). One should understand that the possibility of the reading "they cause to invite" (*nimantāpenti*) exists.
"He renounces the robe" (*cīvaraṃ paccakkhāti*) means he rejects the robe. "This is fitting" (*etaṃ sāruppaṃ*):
that which a recluse (*samaṇo*) does—namely, the wearing of robes—is fitting and appropriate for him. A shopkeeper (*pāpaṇikā*).
"Or endless pieces" means rags without borders found at the edge of a marketplace. "Having gathered" means having collected together. "By way of gleaning" means by wandering for alms.
"By a morsel of food" means by a morsel obtained after collecting [food] into a lump. "Or with putrid urine" means with cow-urine.
"He should make medicine" means he should perform the function of a remedy. "Starting from that" means beginning from that point.
“Proponent of the ascetic qualities” (*dhutavāda*) means one who speaks of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*). “Inviting more and more” means inviting repeatedly, again and again.
“By way of presence” (*sammukhībhāvā*) means by way of being present; the meaning is “by way of existing. “Produces” means obtains.
He said, “It is possible to do so by way of the presence of faith,” and so forth. Objects to be given are easily obtained, and those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*) are...
Furthermore, faith is difficult to find. For the faith of an ordinary person is unstable; it varies from step to step.
For this very reason, even a chief disciple such as Mahāmoggallāna, being unable to act as a guarantor for him, said:
"Friend, I can be a guarantor for two things—wealth and life—but you must be the guarantor for faith."
"In this way you will be excluded from merit"—here, "by means of merit" (*puññena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of an ablative.
You will be deprived of merit and turned away from it. "Frowning" (*bhākuṭika*): by showing the state of being preeminent or foremost in frowning, it means the act of frowning;
that is, the contraction of the face. One whose nature is the act of frowning is "frowning" (*bhākuṭika*).
The state of being frowning is *bhākuṭiyaṃ*. *Kuhanā* means deception. *Kuhāyanā* is the practice (*āyanā*) of one who is deceptive (*kuha*).
The state of being deceptive is *kuhitattaṃ*. *Pāpiccha* is one who desires to display non-existent qualities. *Icchāpakata* means overcome by desire; the meaning is "afflicted" (*upadduta*).
*Sambhāvanādhippāya* is one whose intention is to gain esteem. "He composes his gait" means he deliberately constructs his movement, such as advancing and so forth.
It means he acts with a pleasing demeanor; the same method applies to the others as well. "He goes with aspiration" means he goes having established a resolve.
The same method applies to the rest as well. "He goes as if concentrated" means he goes as if having attained access concentration (upacāra).
The same method applies to the rest as well.
"He is like one who meditates on what is near at hand" means that he displays a state of tranquility as if he were entering a jhāna for people who have come into his presence.
"Of the postures" (iriyāpathassa) means of the four postures. "Setting up" (āṭhapanā) means initial setting up, or setting up with care.
"Establishing" (ṭhapanā) is the manner of establishing. "Re-establishing" (saṇṭhapanā) is the act of composing; it is said to be the making of oneself attractive.
It exists. "Dependent on noble qualities" means connected with supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
"Key" means a lock-opening tool. "Friends" means those possessing affection. "Seen" means merely seen. "Companions" means firm friends.
"Uddaṇḍa" is a particular type of lodging. "Korajika-korajika" means shrinking back, shrinking back; that is, extremely shrinking back. [Another reading is] "koracaka-koracaka."
Or this is another reading. *Bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko* means one who is excessively prone to contorting the face. *Kuhakakuhako* means one who is excessively deceptive.
*Lapakalapako* means one who is excessively talkative. *Mukhasambhāviko* means one who, by means of his own mouth, seeks to be esteemed by others;
some say it means "one whose mind is fixed. *Santānaṃ* means a continuity due to the continuity of defilements (*kilesa*). Regarding *samāpattīnaṃ*:
Of those things to be attained. "Profound" means the depth of its foundation. "Hidden" means difficult to show. "Subtle" means delicate.
"Concealed" means that its intended meaning is difficult to penetrate by way of the literal sense of the words. "Supramundane" means illuminating the Dhamma.
"Associated with emptiness" means associated with Nibbāna. Alternatively, it means "associated with supramundane emptiness."
Connected with Nibbāna, which is the supramundane state (lokuttaradhamma).
"Bodily insolence" (kāyika-pāgabbhiya) means existing in the body; the same method applies to verbal and mental [insolence].
"One who shows no respect" means one devoid of acts of great reverence. "Of those walking without sandals" means of those walking while deprived of sandals.
The term *sāmīvacana* (honorific) is used here either in the sense of proximity or as a mark of disrespect. "Wearing sandals" means he walks about having put on sandals.
"While those walking on a low walkway" refers to those walking on ground that has not been demarcated;
it includes even those walking on a low walkway that has been constructed by making a boundary, scattering sand, and installing a support. "He walks on a high walkway" [is explained as follows].
He walks the walking-path (caṅkama) which is well-constructed with brickwork, surrounded by a railing, and elevated.

If it is enclosed by a wall provided with a gate-tower, or if it is well-sheltered by mountains, forests, or ground-level enclosures, it is permissible to walk on such a walking-path; even if it is not sheltered, it is permissible provided one maintains a respectful distance from others. Even while making physical contact...
"He stands" means he stands too close. "He stands even in front" means he stands even in the space directly ahead.
"Even while standing, he speaks" means he speaks without bending over, like a stump. "Waving his arms" means he speaks while repeatedly waving his arms.

"Pushing in" means entering into the place where everyone is seated. "He obstructs even new bhikkhus from their seats" means that, instead of sitting on his own assigned seat, he enters either before or after [others] and thus obstructs them from their seats.

"He throws wood into [the fire] even without asking permission" means that he casts a piece of wood into the fire without having asked or sought leave. "He closes the door" means he closes it in the bathhouse (*jantāghara*).
"He enters" means he goes down to a bathing place. "He bathes" means he washes his body. "He emerges" means he comes up from the bathing place onto the bank.
"Even by going around" means even by passing by. "Small rooms" refers to bedchambers situated within inner apartments.
"Secret" (*gūḷhāni*) means concealed. "Concealed" (*paṭicchannāni*) means hidden from others.
"Without being asked" (*anajjhiṭṭho vā*) means neither commanded nor requested by the elders to "recite the Dhamma. "Of evil nature" (*pāpadhammo*) means of base character.
"Of impure and suspicious conduct" (*asucisaṅkasarasamācāro*) means that others suspect him, thinking, "This man is immoral."
One whose conduct is to be suspected—that is, one whose conduct is associated with impurity—is called *asucisaṅkasarasamācāra*.
They also recite it as *saṅkassarasamācāra*, having joined the letter *s* [with the preceding *ka*]. One whose actions are concealed is one whose bodily and verbal actions are hidden.

A non-recluse (*assa-maṇo*) is one who is not a recluse. One who claims to be a recluse (*samaṇapaṭiñño*) is one who professes, "I am a recluse. One who does not live the holy life (*abrahmacārī*) is one who lacks the supreme conduct.

"Devoid of the claim to be a brahmacārī" is the opposite of what was previously stated. "Internally rotten" means having become rotten within due to being devoid of wholesome qualities (*kusaladhamma*).
"Lustful" means soaked with passion (*rāga*). "Become like dregs" means having the nature of refuse.
"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" refers here to a bhikkhu who is respectful and reverential, endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, well-robed and well-clad, and inspiring confidence.
In going forth and returning, in looking ahead and looking aside, in bending and stretching his limbs, he was accomplished in deportment; with downcast eyes,
he was one whose sense doors were guarded, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness,
endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, of few wishes, contented, energetic, diligent in the details of proper conduct, and full of deep respect.
He dwells [thus]; this is called conduct (*ācāra*). In this way, first, conduct is to be understood.

Furthermore, resort (*gocara*) is threefold: the resort as support (*upanissaya-gocara*), the resort as protection (*ārakkha-gocara*), and the resort as anchoring (*upanibandha-gocara*). Therein, what is the resort as support?
It is a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of discourse, depending upon whom one hears what has not been heard...
One hears [the Dharma], clarifies what has been heard, overcomes doubt, straightens one’s view, and gladdens the mind;
or else, by training in accordance with him, one grows in faith, in virtue, in learning, in generosity, and in wisdom.
This is called the object of resort as a decisive support (*upanissaya-gocara*).
What is the range of protection? Here, a bhikkhu, having entered among the houses and set out upon a street, goes with eyes cast down, looking only the distance of a yoke’s length, well-restrained;
he does not look at an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a foot soldier, nor a woman, nor a man; he does not look upward, nor look downward.
He goes about looking in every direction and intermediate direction. This is called the range of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*).
What is the range of anchoring (*upanibandha-gocara*)? It is the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) where the mind is anchored.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s own range, his ancestral domain? That is to say, the four [foundations of mindfulness]."
“the foundations of mindfulness”—this is called the domain of close attachment. Thus, being endowed with this conduct and this domain...
[as above] ...being possessed of them. For that reason also he is called “one perfected in conduct and domain.

“Seeing fear in even the slightest faults”: in those things of minute measure, such as the various types of unwholesome mental states, the training rules (*sekhiya*), and so forth, which may be transgressed unintentionally.

One who has the nature of seeing danger in the things to be avoided (*vajja*). "Having undertaken, he trains in the precepts of training" means that whatever is to be trained in among the precepts of training, he undertakes all of that correctly and trains in it.

And here, by the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is shown through a teaching focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). The passage beginning with "endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*)... [and so forth].
However, it should be understood that this was said in order to demonstrate the practice by which that virtue is accomplished for one who has practiced accordingly.

88. "Not failing among things desired" means being free from intimacy with craving toward the strands of sensual pleasure, which are the objects of desire. "Gentle" means being endowed with gentle bodily actions and so forth.
"Possessing presence of mind" means being endowed with the presence of mind derived from mastery of the scriptures, inquiry, and realization.
"Not faithful" means he does not have faith in anyone regarding the Dhamma he has realized for himself.
"He does not become dispassionate" means that because he is already dispassionate through the destruction of lust, he does not now become dispassionate [further].
"Of whomsoever this [is]" refers to those persons whose desire and craving for the strands of sensual pleasure—the objects of intimacy—has not been abandoned; it is associated with familiarity.

Craving has not been abandoned by the path of Arahantship. "In them, craving for forms flows from the eye" means that in these individuals, craving with form as its object arises in conjunction with the impulsion process proceeding from the eye-door.

"It flows" (*savati*) means it flows spatially as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) and phenomenally as far as the state of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*). "It streams" (*sandati*) means it streams downward like the current of a river.
"It occurs" means it occurs by way of repeated arising. The same method applies to the remaining doors as well.

In the bright side (the path), craving is completely abandoned by the path of Arahantship through the reverse process of what was stated [in the dark side]. For them, craving for forms does not flow from the eye.
"Endowed with gentle bodily action" means being possessed of, or unified with, non-harsh and soft bodily action.

The same method applies to verbal action and the others as well. In phrases such as "by means of the subtle foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the foundations of mindfulness and so forth are a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

One who possesses the three types of wisdom—known as the varieties of *paṭibhāna* (readiness of wit)—which are capable of performing the functions of discerning, manifesting, and defining through the mastery of study, questioning regarding the meaning, and the attainment of mundane and supramundane states, is called *paṭibhānavā*. His mastery...
"Depending on it, one answers" means that by relying upon the mastery of that person's [teaching], knowledge arises and knowledge becomes manifest.
The "four foundations of mindfulness" are stated as the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) by way of a mixture of mundane and supramundane states.
The "paths and fruits" are stated by way of the supramundane states that have been produced. The "four analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidā*) and the "six direct knowledges" (*abhiññā*).
It should be understood that this is stated by way of liberation (*vimokkhantika*).

In that context, "the four analytical knowledges" (*catasso paṭisambhidāyo*) means the fourfold classification of knowledge. There are six additional types of knowledge, beginning with the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha*) and ending with the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).
"Of him" (*tassa*) refers to another person; the connection is that "meaning occurs to him" (*attho paṭibhāyati*). "Meaning" (*attho*) is, in brief, [the purpose].
It is cause-and-effect. For since that is realized, attained, and reached by following the cause, it is therefore called "the goal" (*attha*).

As for its classification, whatever has arisen from conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what was spoken, fruition, and functional [consciousness]—these five phenomena should be understood as "the goal.
When one reflects upon that goal, that goal is [to be understood] by way of its classification.
It is known and manifest. "Dhamma" is, in brief, a condition. For it is called "dhamma" because it ordains, causes to proceed, and brings about this or that [result];

therefore it is called dhamma. In detail, however, any cause whatsoever that produces a fruit—namely, the Noble Path, speech, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five things should be understood as "dhamma. That dhamma...
For one who reviews it, that phenomenon becomes known and manifest in its diversity; and regarding the meaning and the phenomenon,
whatever is the natural expression, the non-deviating convention— in the uttering, speaking, and articulating of that,
for one who reviews it by taking as an object that spoken, uttered, and articulated sound of natural expression, that language becomes known and manifest.
Regarding the phrase "when the meaning is known, the meaning becomes manifest":

now, having brought forward its verbal expression, when the various kinds of meanings have become clear, the various kinds of meanings become manifest—that is, they come face-to-face with knowledge—to that person.
Regarding the phrase "when the phenomenon (dhamma) is known, the phenomenon becomes manifest": when the various kinds of phenomena have become clear, the various kinds of phenomena become manifest.
"Through the knowledge of language, language manifests": when language of the aforementioned classification has become clear, the language of the aforementioned classification manifests.

Among these three kinds of knowledge, "knowledge" refers to the knowledge that has reached its full differentiation regarding these three—namely, meaning, phenomena, and language—for one who reviews them by taking all-encompassing knowledge as their object within those three;
or, alternatively, [it refers to the knowledge] regarding those very things as they have been described.
The knowledge that has become detailed by way of the range, function, and so forth, regarding the three types of knowledge, is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
"By means of this analytical knowledge of perspicuity" means by means of this aforementioned kind of wisdom, which has been described in detail as stated above; he is thus "endowed.

Concluding, he says: "He is called 'perspicacious' (*paṭibhānavā*). "For whom there is no mastery of the scriptures" (*pariyatti*)—here, "mastery of the scriptures" refers to the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*).
For one who masters that [scripture], the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become clear. As for the person for whom such a mastery of the scriptures does not exist:

"there is no thorough inquiry" (*paripucchā*); "thorough inquiry" refers to the discussion of knotty points, the meaning of words, and their determination within the Canon (*pāḷi*), the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), and so forth.
For one who explains the meaning of the Canon and other texts that have been mastered, the analytical knowledges become clear. "There is no realization" (*adhigama*)...
"Attainment" (adhigama) refers to the realization of Arahantship. For one who has attained Arahantship, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) become clear.
Since this person lacks the threefold excellence described above, what will appear to him? For what reason will the knowledge that has reached differentiation manifest to such a person?
"By himself" means by his own self. "Known by himself" means understood by him through that very knowledge.

"A Dhamma realized by oneself" means a Dhamma penetrated and reflected upon by oneself. "He does not believe anyone else" means that because he has realized it for himself, he does not rely on others;
he does not proceed by faith alone. This is said by way of showing the twelvefold mode of dependent origination, beginning with "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise."

It has been stated. The phrases beginning with "with the cessation of ignorance" and so forth are spoken with reference to the turning back of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). The passage beginning with "This is suffering" and so forth is by way of the vision of the truths (*sacca*).
The passages beginning with "These are the taints" (*āsava*) and so forth are, by another method, by way of the defilements (*kilesa*) and by way of the demonstration of conditions (*paccaya*).

The passages beginning with "These phenomena are to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth are by way of the demonstration of those phenomena that are to be directly known, fully understood (*pariññeyya*), abandoned (*pahātabba*), developed (*bhāvetabba*), and realized (*sacchikātabba*).
The phrases beginning with "of the six bases of contact" are by way of showing the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the bases of contact.
Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, there is the arising and the falling away in twenty-five ways;
therein, the gratification is by way of desire and lust for them, while the danger is their transformation.

And Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the escape. These phenomena have been stated by way of such vision as the origin of the four great elements through ignorance and so forth, and their subsiding and disappearance upon the cessation of ignorance and so forth.
These phenomena are to be understood according to the method explained in various places.
"Plunged into the Deathless" (amatogadhaṃ): there is no death, reckoned as dying, for this; thus it is the Deathless (amata). Because it is the antidote to the poison of the defilements...
It is also called "plunged into the deathless" (*amata-ogadha*) because of its inclination toward that [deathless]. "Having the deathless as its supreme goal" (*amataparāyana*):

it has the deathless—of the kind already described—as its supreme resort, destination, and foundation; thus, it is "having the deathless as its supreme goal. "Having the deathless as its consummation" (*amatapariyosāna*):
that deathless is its consummation because it constitutes the final end of saṃsāra; thus, it is "having the deathless as its consummation."
89. “He does not train out of desire for gain” means that he does not train in the Suttantas and so forth out of a longing for gain.
“Not at odds with craving, nor greedily attached to flavors”: being unopposed because of the absence of conflict, he does not fall into greed for the root-flavors and so forth of craving.

“For what reason indeed? (*kena nu kho*): this is a particle used in the search for the cause of the longing for gain. “For the production of gain” (*lābhābhinibbattiya*): for the arising of the four requisites through their excellence. “Bringing gain to maturity” (*lābhaṃ paripācento*): while bringing the requisites to full development.
"For the sake of self-taming" means for the sake of taming oneself by means of wisdom associated with insight (*vipassanā*).
"For the sake of self-composure" means for the sake of composing oneself by means of wisdom associated with concentration (*samādhi*).

"For the sake of self-extinction" means for the sake of the extinction of oneself through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*) by means of both kinds of knowledge. For this has been said: "Indeed, it is for the sake of extinction through non-clinging..."
"Friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase "relying on contentment alone," there are four kinds of contentment:
contentment with requisites, contentment with attainment, contentment with the scriptures, and contentment with the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
Their distinct meanings have already been explained in detail below; it means having clung to that contentment. Regarding "contentment with the four requisites": [the text continues].

Having resorted to these three kinds of contentment—the analysis of which has already been explained in detail above—one resorts to and relies upon "only effacement" (*sallekhaññeva*), which means the scraping away of the defilements (*kilesa*).

One resorts to and relies upon "only this state of purpose" (*idamatthitaññeva*); "this state of purpose" (*idamatthitā*) refers to the fact that there is "this" (*idaṃ*) by means of these wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), and it is precisely by depending on and resorting to that state of purpose that one proceeds.
"Juice" (*raso*) is the summary term for the detailed explanation. "Root juice" (*mūlaraso*) is any juice produced in dependence upon a root.

The same method applies to "stem juice" (*khandharaso*) and the others as well. "Sour" (*amblaṃ*) refers to buttermilk and the like. "Sweet" (*madhuraṃ*) refers exclusively to cow’s ghee and the like.

However, honey that has been kept for a long time becomes astringent when mixed with astringent substances; treacle that has been kept for a long time becomes alkaline when mixed with alkaline substances. Ghee (*sappi*).
However, even when kept for a long time, although it loses its color and fragrance, it does not lose its taste;
thus, that alone is exclusively sweet. "Bitter" refers to neem leaves and the like. "Pungent" refers to ginger, black pepper, and the like. "Salty" refers to sea salt and the like.
"Astringent" refers to the shoots of the vātiṅgaṇa plant and the like. "Acid" refers to jujube, myrobalan, kapiṭṭha, sāla-vā, and the like. "Astringent" (kasāva) refers to—
*Harītakādi*. All these tastes have been stated according to their respective bases (*vatthu*).
However, it should be understood that here the taste associated with each particular base is expressed by names such as "sour" (*ambilādi*) and so forth. "Palatable" (*sādu*) means a desirable taste;
"unpalatable" (*asādu*) means an undesirable taste. By these two terms, every taste is encompassed. "Cold" (*sīta*) means a cold taste; "hot" (*uṇha*) means a hot taste. Thus, this...

Although taste is divided by distinctions such as primary tastes (*mūlarasa*) and so forth, it is nonetheless non-different in its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and other attributes. For all of this has the characteristic of impinging upon the tongue;

its function (*rasa*) is to serve as the objective domain for tongue-consciousness; and its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) is the range of that same consciousness. "With the tips of their tongues" means with the sensitive parts of their tongues.
"Supreme tastes" refers to the finest flavors. "Seeking" means searching for them. "Wandering about" means...
They wander here and there. "Having obtained something sour, they seek what is not sour" means that having obtained something sour such as *takkā* (sour gruel), they search for what is not sour.
Thus, everything has been applied by way of repeated permutation.

"He consumes food with wise reflection" means that having known through the wisdom of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-paññā*), he consumes food by means of the proper method. Now, in order to show that method, it is said: "Neither for sport," and so forth.
In this context, "not for amusement" means he does not take food for the sake of diversion. In this regard, actors, acrobats, and the like are said to take food for the sake of amusement.

For when a certain meal appears more attractive to one who has eaten than the diversion consisting of dancing, singing, music, and poetry, they seek out and consume that food by unrighteous and improper means. But this bhikkhu does not consume food in such a manner.
"Not for intoxication" means he does not consume food for the purpose of increasing pride, arrogance, and the intoxication of manhood.

In this regard, kings, royal ministers, and great officials are said to eat for the sake of intoxication; for they partake of refined foods such as rich, savory meals in order to increase their own pride, arrogance, and the intoxication of manhood.
But this bhikkhu does not consume food in such a manner.
"Not for adornment" means he does not consume food for the purpose of adorning the body.
In this regard, women who live for the sake of beauty, such as those in the inner apartments, drink ghee, molasses, and the like, and consume smooth, soft, and delicate food, thinking:
"In this way our limbs will become well-proportioned, and the complexion of the skin on our bodies will become radiant. But this bhikkhu does not consume food in such a manner.
"Not for the sake of adornment" means he does not consume food for the purpose of adorning the body with flesh.

In this regard, wrestlers, boxers, and actors swell their bodies with very succulent fish, meat, and so forth, thinking, "In this way our flesh will become well-developed for the sake of enduring blows.
But this bhikkhu does not consume food in such a manner for the purpose of adorning the body with flesh.
"Only as much as" (*yāvadeva*) is a demonstration of the limitation and determination of the purpose for taking food.
"For the maintenance of this body" (*imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā*) means he takes food for the sake of sustaining this physical body composed of the four great elements;

this is the purpose of his taking food. "For its subsistence" (*yāpanāya*) means he takes food for the sake of maintaining the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "For the allaying of affliction" (*vihiṃsūparatiyā*)...
"Violence" (*vihiṃsā*) means hunger that arises due to the lack of food; he eats for the sake of its cessation and pacification.
"For the support of the holy life" (*brahmacariyānuggahāya*): the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the three trainings, which constitute the entire teaching;
he eats for the sake of supporting that. "Thus" (*iti*) is an indication of the means; the meaning is, "by this means. "And I shall ward off old feeling": "old feeling" (*purāṇavedanā*)...
He partakes of food thinking, "I shall ward off the feeling that arises due to the condition of under-eating. And he partakes of food thinking, "I shall not give rise to new feeling";
for "new feeling" refers to the feeling that would arise due to the condition of over-eating, and he partakes of food thinking, "I shall not give rise to that.
Alternatively, "new feeling" refers to the feeling that does not arise due to the condition of having eaten [in moderation]; since that has not yet arisen—
One consumes food solely for the purpose of non-arising [of afflictions].
"There will be sustenance for me" means there will be maintenance for me. Regarding the phrase "and blamelessness":
here, there is that which is blameworthy and there is that which is blameless. In this context, "blameworthy" refers to unrighteous seeking, unrighteous acceptance, and unrighteous enjoyment.
This is called blameworthy. However, seeking by right means, receiving by right means, reflecting, and then consuming is called blameless.
A certain person makes even what is blameless blameworthy: thinking "I have obtained it," he consumes beyond measure;
being unable to digest it, he resorts to emetics, purgatives, and so forth.
He suffers; the monks throughout the entire monastery apply themselves to his care for the body, the search for medicine, and so forth.
When asked, "What is this?", they say, "Such-and-such a person's belly has become bloated," and so on.
They criticize him, saying, "This man is always of such a nature; he does not even know the capacity of his own stomach."
They censure him. This person is said to commit what is blameworthy even when it is blameless. Instead of acting thus, he consumes food [thinking], "There will be blamelessness for me.
Regarding the phrase "and a comfortable dwelling": here too there is a comfortable dwelling and there is not a comfortable dwelling. In that regard, Āharahatthaka—
The food of these five brahmins—the *alaṃsāṭaka*, the *tatravaṭṭaka*, the *kākamāsaka*, and the *bhuttavamitaka*—is not called a "pleasant dwelling.

For among them, the one called the *āharahatthaka*, having eaten much and being unable to rise by his own nature, says, "Bring it to my hand" (*āhara hatthaṃ*). The *alaṃsāṭaka* is so named because of his excessively bloated and loathsome belly.
Even when he has risen, he is unable to put on his garment. One who "rolls right there" (vaṭṭaka) is one who, being unable to rise, merely rolls about in that very spot.
One who "eats as much as a crow can peck" (kākamāsaka) consumes food up to the opening of the mouth, just enough so that it can be pecked at by crows.
One who "vomits what he has eaten" (bhuttavamitaka) is one who, being unable to hold it in his mouth, vomits it right back there. Thus...
He consumes food not with the thought, "May there be a comfortable dwelling for me," but rather with the thought, "There will be a comfortable dwelling for me.
A "comfortable dwelling" means moderation in eating, being satisfied with four or five morsels. For when one has eaten this much and drinks water, the four postures proceed with ease.
Therefore, the General of the Dhamma spoke thus:
“Having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
At this point, however, the factors [of the practice] should be brought together. For “not for sport” is one factor, and “not for intoxication” is another.
One [purpose] is: "not for adornment"; one is: "not for beautification"; one is: "only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body"; one is:
"for the cessation of affliction and for the support of the holy life"; one is: "thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings"; one is: "and there will be for me sustenance."
The benefit of the meal here consists in these factors: the sustenance of the body, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "The four factors mentioned above are indeed a negation; furthermore, the eight factors [of the Noble Eightfold Path] should be combined [with them].
In that context, "only for the maintenance of this body" is one factor, and "for its sustenance" is...
One [portion] for the subsiding of affliction; one for the assistance of the holy life (*brahmacariya*); one with the thought, "I shall terminate old feeling";
one with the thought, "I shall not give rise to new feeling"; one with the thought, "There shall be sustenance for me";
one for blamelessness; and the benefit of food is a comfortable dwelling. Thus, he consumes food endowed with these eight factors.
90. "Equanimous" means endowed with sixfold equanimity. "Mindful" means possessed of mindfulness such as that of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*).
Regarding the phrase "equanimous means endowed with sixfold equanimity," what is the dhamma called sixfold equanimity here?
It is knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and so forth. When "knowledge" is mentioned, four types associated with knowledge are obtained from the perspective of activity; [and] "constant abiding" (*satatavihāra*).
When it is stated [simply as "seeing"], eight great types of consciousness (mahācitta) are obtained; when it is stated that "there is no lust or hatred," ten types of consciousness are obtained.
Mental joy (somanassa) is obtained by way of repetition (āsevana). "Having seen a form with the eye" means:
having seen a form with the visual consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa), which is capable of seeing forms and is conventionally designated as "the eye" by way of its instrument. The Ancients [say]:
They say: "The eye does not see form because it is devoid of consciousness; the consciousness, too, does not see because it is devoid of the eye.

Rather, one sees by means of a consciousness based on the sensitive organ (pasāda), through the impact of the door and the object. In such instances, there is what is called a "figurative expression" (sasambhārakathā), as in the case of phrases like "he pierces with a bow.
Therefore, the meaning here is simply this: "having seen the form by means of eye-consciousness."
"He is neither glad" means that he does not experience mental joy (*somanassa*) through the arising of greed or the arising of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).
"Neither dejected" means that he does not have a corrupted mind through the arising of aversion (*paṭigha*). "Equanimous" means that he observes from a neutral standpoint;
remaining impartial, he carries out his bodily postures. "Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being possessed of mindfulness and endowed with wisdom (*ñāṇa*).
"He does not crave what is pleasing" means he does not hanker after or long for a desirable object that increases the mind.
"He does not rejoice" means he does not find satisfaction. "He does not generate lust" means he does not produce attachment toward this or that.
"His body remains steady" means that the body of that one whose taints are destroyed remains firm and motionless because it is free from trembling.
"Unpleasant" means an undesirable object. "He does not become dejected" means he does not become afflicted with mental distress (*domanassa*).

"With an unestablished mind" means his mind is not fixed in the manner of anger. "With an undaunted mind" means one whose mind is not cowed. "With a mind free from ill will" means one whose mind is devoid of malice (*byāpāda*).
"He is not lustful toward what is lust-inducing" means he does not give rise to greed (*rāga*) regarding an object that incites lust. "He is not hateful toward what is hate-inducing" means...

Regarding a basis that arouses hatred, he does not arouse hatred. Regarding that which leads to delusion, he is not deluded; thus, regarding a basis that leads to delusion, he does not arouse delusion.
Regarding that which leads to anger, he is not provoked; thus, regarding a basis that leads to anger, he does not waver. Regarding that which leads to intoxication, he is not intoxicated;
thus, regarding a basis that leads to intoxication, he does not sink. Regarding that which leads to defilement, he is not defiled; thus, regarding a basis that leads to burning...

He is not tormented regarding the objective basis. "In what is seen, merely what is seen" means: regarding a visible-object object seen by eye-consciousness, he is merely one who has seen what is seen.

"In what is heard, merely what is heard" means: regarding the sphere of sound heard by ear-consciousness, he is merely one who has heard what is heard. "In what is sensed, merely what is sensed" means:

regarding that which is reached and grasped by nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, he is merely one who has sensed what is sensed. "In what is cognized, merely what is cognized" means: by mind-consciousness...
"In what is known, merely knowing": when one has seen with eye-consciousness a visible object as an objective field (*rūpārammaṇa*), one is not smeared by the stain of craving or views.
"In what is seen, unattached": one is free from craving toward the objective field of form. "Unfallen": one whose mind is not corrupted. "Is found" means it is obtained. "Sees" means he looks upon.

"Lust and passion" means affectionate attachment (*sineha*). "Delighting in form" (*rūpārāma*): that for whom form is a pleasure-ground (*ārāma*) is "delighting in form. "Rejoicing in form" (*rūparata*): one who finds delight in form. "Contented with form" (*rūpasantuṭṭhi*): one who is gladdened by form.

“They lead the tamed one to the assembly”: when going into the midst of a great crowd at places such as pleasure gardens or circular arenas, they lead only a tamed breed of ox or horse, having yoked it to a vehicle. “The king”:
even a king, when going to such places, mounts only one that is tamed. “Among men”: even among men, one who is tamed by the four noble paths is indeed free from cruelty.
"Best": "Yotivākya" means one who, even when such transgressive speech is spoken to him again and again, endures it, does not resist, and is not distressed;
such a tamed person is "best"—this is the meaning.
"Mules" (*assatara*) are those born from a mare and a donkey. "Noble steeds" (*ājānīya*) refers to those whom a trainer of tame horses causes to perform their task.
They are capable of knowing it quickly. "Sindhava" means horses born in the kingdom of Sindhu. "Great elephants" refers to great tuskers known as *kuñjara*.
"Self-tamed": these—whether they be thoroughbred mules, noble breeds, Sindhu horses, or great tuskers—are excellent when tamed, not when untamed.
But he who is self-tamed through the taming by the four paths, being free from worldly desires, is truly self-tamed.
This is even better than that; the meaning is that it is superior to all of these.

For by means of these vehicles—namely, those vehicles such as elephant-vehicles and so forth—no person whatsoever has ever before gone, even in a dream, to that place reckoned as the "untravelled," which is the direction of Nibbāna. Therefore, one would not go to that state by means of these vehicles.
Just as a person who has been tamed by the restraint of the faculties in the prior stage, and later further tamed by the cultivation of the Noble Path,
being thus tamed, free from worldly trappings, and possessed of wisdom, goes toward that direction never before reached and attains the ground of the tamed—
therefore, the meaning is that they hold self-taming alone to be the best.
"Unshaken by the modes" means they do not waver or tremble amidst the various forms of conceit, such as "I am superior to those who are superior.
"Completely liberated from renewed existence" means they are thoroughly freed from, and have stood having escaped, the repeated arising through the rebirth-linking of renewed existence.
"Having reached the stage of the tamed" means having attained the stage of the fruit of arhatship, which is absolute self-mastery.
They are established. "Those who have conquered in the world" refers to those Arahants who, having achieved victory over the world of beings, are called "victorious ones.
Since one whose faculties are cultivated becomes fearless, unshakable, and self-controlled, the Blessed One spoke this verse, "Whose faculties... to demonstrate that point.

Its meaning is as follows: for whomsoever the six faculties—the eye and so forth—[have been developed] through the cultivation of their objects regarding the three characteristics such as impermanence...

Having established them through the cultivation of latent tendencies and having caused them to take up the fragrance of mindfulness and clear comprehension, they are cultivated by means of internal-object meditation;

yet, in this way, both externally and throughout the entire world—in whatever place there is deficiency of the faculties or the arising of such deficiency—they are cultivated by means of non-covetousness and so forth.
Having thus become disillusioned, known, and penetrated this, [he proceeds].

Having tamed both this world and the other world—the world of the aggregates of one’s own continuity and the world of the aggregates of another’s continuity—one who desires to die awaits the time, looks forward to it, and honors the arrival of the moment when life is exhausted; he does not fear death. As it is said:
“I have no fear of death, nor do I have attachment to life.”
“I do not long for death, nor do I long for life;
I await my time as a servant awaits his wages.
Thus, one whose faculties are developed is “tamed. In this way, he whose sense-faculties have been cultivated is tamed.
91. *Nissayatā* means dependence upon craving and views. *Ñatvā dhammaṃ* means having known the Dhamma by way of its aspects, such as impermanence and so forth.
*Anissito* means not dependent upon those aforementioned dependencies. By this, he illuminates that apart from the knowledge of the Dhamma, there are no dependencies because of their absence.
*Bhavāya vibhavāya vā* means for existence or for non-existence—that is, for eternalism or for annihilationism. The exposition of this verse is straightforward.

92. "I call him 'peaceful'"—I speak of one such as this, described by each individual verse, as being "peaceful. "He has crossed over craving"—he has crossed over this great craving, known as *visattikā* (clinging) because of its state of being attached and so forth.
"Lust for one's own view is the bodily tie of covetousness"—the lust consisting of the passion for the view one has adopted oneself is the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*).
"Malice toward the doctrines of others is resentment"—anger toward the counter-arguments of others' doctrines.

The bodily tie of ill will is the state of being uncontented. "One’s own virtue or observance" refers either to the virtue consisting in one’s own undertaking of abstinence from sexual misconduct, or to observances such as the cow-vow and so forth.
"Virtue and observance" refers to both of these together. "Adherence" means that one clings to them as something external, thinking, "By this [virtue or observance] there is purity," and so on.
"One’s own view, the dogmatic insistence that 'this alone is the truth,' is the bodily tie" refers to the view personally adopted by oneself.
“The insistence on ‘only this is true, all else is false’ through improper reflection is the bodily tie of insistence on ‘this is truth.
For him, no ties exist means that for that one whose taints are destroyed, the two ties of views do not exist by way of the path of stream-entry;
the bodily tie of ill will [does not exist] by way of the path of non-returning; and the bodily tie of covetousness [does not exist] by way of the path of arhatship.”
93. Now, praising that very same one who is tranquil, he said: “He has no sons,” and so forth.

In this context, “sons” refers to the four types beginning with those born of one’s own loins (*atraja*). Furthermore, it should be understood that here the possession of sons and so on are expressed by the names of the sons themselves.
For these [possessions] do not exist for him; or, because of their absence, the sons and so forth do not exist. Regarding “self”: “The self exists.”
There is no grasping at the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). "Ceased" (*niratta*) refers to the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), which is grasped as "it is annihilated.
There is nothing to be grasped; there is nothing to be released—that is, nothing to be liberated from.
"For whom there is nothing grasped" means for that person in whom nothing grasped by way of craving (*taṇhā*) or views (*diṭṭhi*) exists. For such a one, there is nothing to be released.
For that person, there is nothing to be released. "One who has transcended grasping and releasing" means one who has passed beyond both seizing and letting go.
"One who has transcended increase and decrease" means one who has gone beyond both growth and decline.
94. "That by which ordinary people would describe him, as well as recluses and brahmins"—by which fault, such as passion and so forth, ordinary people [would describe him]...
All gods and humans, as well as recluses and brahmins outside of this [teaching], might say of him that he is "lustful" or "corrupt.
That [fault] is not present before him; that is to say, those faults such as lust are not present before that Arahant. Therefore, he is not led away by words;
for that reason, he does not waver amidst words of censure.
"Nejati" is the summary phrase for the detailed exposition. "Na iñjati" means it does not move. "Na calati" means it does not incline toward that [object].
"Na vedhati" means it does not quiver, due to its being impossible to shake. "Nappavedhati" means it does not tremble.
"Na sampavedhati" means it does not roll about.
95. He does not speak among superiors—that is, among distinguished persons—by including himself therein and saying, "I am distinguished," out of a sense of overweening pride (*atimāna*).
The same method applies to the other two [categories]. He does not conform to what is allowable (*kappa*); that is, he does not conform to either of these two kinds of what is allowable.
Why? Because he is unallowable (*akappiya*); what is meant is that he has abandoned what is allowable. The commentary on this verse is also quite clear.
96. "Sakanti mayhan" means that which has been grasped as "mine. "And does not grieve over what is non-existent" means he does not grieve over what is non-existent because it is not found.
"And does not go among phenomena" means he does not proceed among all phenomena by way of desire and so forth.
"He indeed is called 'peaceful'" means such a supreme person is called "the peaceful one. This is the exposition of this verse as well.

As if [turning over] what was face-upward, he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, one hundred thousand times ten million deities attained Arahantship;
there is no counting those who became stream-enterers and so forth.
Thus ends the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the Purābheda Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the exposition of the Kalahavivāda Sutta: 97.
In the eleventh [sutta], the exposition of the Kalahavivāda Sutta, regarding the phrase "whence have quarrels and disputes arisen," both quarrel and its...
From where have these arisen: "the preliminary stage" and "dispute"? From where have "lamentation and sorrow" together with "envy" arisen?
From where have "conceit and overweening pride" together with "slander" arisen?
"Those"—all eight of these defiled states—"expound that indeed": explain that very matter which I have asked about.
"Speak, I entreat you," he said; for the particle *iṅgha* has the sense of "entreaty.
"In one way" means by one cause; "in another way" means by another cause. "Householders who are bastinadoed" refers to householders being tormented.
"Monastics who incur an offense" refers to those who have gone forth among the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
"Committing one or another [offense]. "Whence arisen?
means from what source they have come into being. "Whence born? means from what they have acquired their existence.

"Whence produced?"—this is a word expanded by the prefix (*upasagga*). "Whence manifested? means from what they have attained the characteristic of manifestation. Having expanded the word with the prefix...
It was asked: “From where have they arisen? From where have they become manifest? From where have they appeared?
Regarding the phrases beginning with “What is their cause,” that which indicates its own fruit is the *nidāna* (cause). That from which the fruit emerges is the *samudaya* (origin).
That from which the fruit is born is the *jāti* (birth). That from which the fruit originates is the *pabhava* (source). He asks for the root; he asks for the reason for the quarrel.
For a cause (*kāraṇa*) is a root (*mūla*) in the sense of being a foundation. It is a cause (*hetu*) because it moves (*hinoti*) or proceeds toward the production of its own fruit.
It is a source (*nidāna*) because it points out its own fruit as if saying, "Come, take this!
It is an origin (*sambhava*) because from it the fruit arises. It is a provenance (*pabhava*) because the fruit originates (*pabhavati*) from it. The fruit emerges (*samuṭṭhāti*) therein.
It arises by means of this, thus it is an "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*). It brings its own fruit, thus it is "nutriment" (*āhāra*).

In the sense of not being rejected, it delights in its own fruit, thus it is an "object" (*ārammaṇa*). Depending on this, the fruit comes forth—that is, it occurs—without being rejected, thus it is a "condition" (*paccaya*).
From this, the fruit arises, thus it is an "origination" (*samudaya*). In this way, the meaning of these terms should be understood.
Referring to this, the teaching was spoken in the manner beginning with, "He asks about the root of quarreling and disputing.

98. *Piyappahūtā* means born from a source of affection. By the phrase "quarreling and disputing are joined with stinginess," he shows that stinginess is not only a cause for quarrels and disputes, but also a condition for them. And here, by way of the heading "quarrel and dispute,"...
It should be understood that all these states have been mentioned. Just as there is stinginess regarding these things, so too is there slander and dispute.
Therefore he said: "And slanders amidst those who have fallen into dispute. The explanation of this verse is indeed plain in meaning. 99.
From what source in the world do dear things arise, and from what source do those cravings that wander through the world [arise]? [The answer is: "From an abundance of dear things come quarrels."
"Those who are mentioned here as dear in the world—whence is their source?
And not only those who are dear, but also those such as the kṣatriyas and others who wander about in the world, overcome by greed—whence is that greed of theirs?

With this single question, he asks two matters. Here, "whence is their source" (*kutonidāna*) means "what is their source" (*kiṃnidāna*), "what is their cause" (*kiṃhetuka*); it is thus the singular form used for the plural.
The substitution [of *jāta* for *nidāna*] is to be understood, and there is no elision in the compound. Alternatively, "sources" (*nidāna*) means "born" (*jātā*), that is, "arisen" (*uppannā*).
Therefore, what is meant is: "from where born? from where arisen? "Hope and fulfillment" (*āsā ca niṭṭhā ca*) means hope and the success of that hope.
"Those which exist for a man for the sake of the future life" (*ye samparāyāya narassa hontīti*) means those which are the future supports (*parāyanā*) for a man.
"It is" means "it exists. This question is also one and the same.

"They are islands" means they are supports. "They are refuges" means they are the destruction of suffering. "They have reached the ultimate goal" means they have reached the perfection of success. 100.
"Caused by desire" means caused by the desires such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth. And "those cravings that wander about" means those which...
Kṣatriyas and others wander about due to greed (*lobha*); since even their greed has its source in desire (*chanda*), he answers both meanings together.
"From this source" (*ito-nidāna*) means precisely "from desire as its source. For when he says "from this source," he is referring to desire; for greed and the rest have desire as their source.
As for the grammatical derivation of the term "from this source" (*ito-nidāna*), it is the same as in the case of "from what source? (*kuto-nidāna*).
They are to be understood according to the method already stated. "The fulfillment of hope" refers to the attainment of the realization of one's underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).

101. "Decisions" (*vinicchaya*) refers to decisions regarding craving and views. "And those states which have been spoken of by the ascetic" refers to other unwholesome states associated with anger and so forth, or similar unwholesome states spoken of by the Buddha-ascetic;

from where have these arisen? "Of another nature" means having a different intrinsic character (*sabhāva*). "Arranged otherwise" means existing in a different manner. "By one who has stilled evil" means by one who has extinguished evil.
"By one who has cast off evil states" means by one who has abandoned base qualities. "By one whose roots of defilement are split" means by one who stands having split the roots of defilement.
"Released from the bonds of all unwholesome roots" means by one who stands having liberated himself from the twelve unwholesome bonds.
"Spoken" means uttered. "Fully spoken" means spoken in detail.

102. "Depending on that, desire arises": depending on that pleasant and painful feeling—which consists of the two bases [of pleasure and pain]—desire arises by way of the longing for union and separation.
To this extent, the question, "From what source, then, does desire in the world arise? has been answered. Having seen existence and non-existence in forms...
Having seen both decay and arising in forms, a person makes a determination regarding the world—meaning in the world of the states of woe and so forth.
For the sake of acquiring wealth, this person makes a determination based on craving, thinking, "I have been reborn," and so forth, according to the method of determining views.
By this much, the question, "And from where did these determinations arise? has been answered.

"Depending on the pleasant and the unpleasant" means making both the sweet and the unsweet the proximate cause (*upanissaya*). "The desirable and the undesirable" refers to both desirable objects and undesirable objects.

Regarding "devotion to the use of intoxicants, spirits, wine, and maddening things that lead to negligence": here, "spirits" (*surā*) refers to five types: flour-spirit, cake-spirit, rice-spirit, that mixed with grain-powder, and that prepared from various ingredients.
"Wine" (*meraya*) refers to spirit distilled from flowers, spirit distilled from fruits, and spirit distilled from honey.
The five *āsava*s (taints) include *guḷāsava* (molasses-ferment), which is associated with the ingredients. All of these are *majja* (intoxicant) by virtue of their capacity to cause intoxication.
"A basis for negligence" (*pamādaṭṭhāna*) means a cause of negligence; it is a designation for that volition by which one drinks that intoxicant.
"Devotion" (*anuyoga*) means devotion to, or repeated engagement in, that practice of liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are bases for negligence. And because—
For one devoted to that [practice], wealth already arisen declines and that which has not yet arisen does not arise;
therefore, he knows: "My wealth is going to exhaustion, to a state of depletion. This applies in all cases.

"Devotion to wandering through streets at improper times" means being devoted to wandering through streets at the wrong time. "Frequenting fairs" means going to fairs for the purpose of watching dancing and other such performances.
"Devotion to indolence" means being engaged in physical laziness. "He does not resort to the doors of ruin" means he does not resort to the channels for the destruction of wealth.
"By agriculture" means by the work of farming. "Or by trade" means by righteous commercial activity. "Or by cattle-rearing."
"By means of herding cattle" means by the work of a cowherd. "By archery" means by the skill of the bow. "By royal service" means by the work of a king's servant.
"By one or another craft" means by one or another of the crafts such as pottery and so forth. "Practices" means he applies himself to the exertion.
"When the eye has arisen, he knows" means when the eye together with its constituent parts has arisen, he knows. "My self..."
"He has arisen"—thus one adopts such a view. "The eye has vanished" means that it has perished. "My self has vanished"—one adopts the view, "my self is destroyed.
"My self has departed"—my self has passed away. The same method applies to the ear and so forth. 103. "These states are also only a pair":
these states, such as anger and the rest, exist only when there is the pair of the pleasant and the unpleasant.

They exist; they arise. To this extent, the third question has also been answered. Now, showing the means for abandoning doubt for one who might still be wavering regarding these questions thus answered, he said: “One who is doubtful should train in the path of knowledge.
This means that for the sake of attaining the knowledge and vision of knowledge, one should train in the three trainings. Thus it was said.
Why is this so? Because the teachings have been proclaimed by the ascetic after he had understood them. For the Buddha-ascetic has proclaimed the teachings after understanding them;

there is no ignorance regarding these teachings on his part. However, one who does not understand them through the power of his own knowledge would not know them—not because of any fault in the teaching itself.
Therefore, one who is full of doubt should train for the sake of the path of knowledge, thinking: "The teachings have been proclaimed by the ascetic after he had understood them."
"Bound by the binding of confinement" means bound by the binding of city-prisoners. "Or by the binding of enclosure" means by the binding of a fence-enclosure.

Regarding "by the binding of a village" and so forth, one is said to be "bound by the binding of a village" and so on when one is unable to depart from that particular place. "For the sake of release from that binding" refers to this...
For the purpose of releasing one from the aforementioned kind of bondage.
Knowledge is also called the "path of knowledge" (ñāṇapatha): the knowledge that arose previously is the path for subsequent knowledge as it arises one after another;
thus, knowledge is the path of knowledge. The object of knowledge is also the "path of knowledge": the condition for knowledge, having been taken as its support (ālambita), [is likewise so called].

It is the path of knowledge because it arises [therein]. Even those phenomena that coexist with knowledge are the "path of knowledge"; thus, the remaining mental states and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*) that arise together with knowledge are also the path of knowledge.
Now, establishing this by means of a simile, he says: "Just as the Noble Path is the Noble Path," and so forth.

A person who is "full of doubt" (*kathaṃkathī*) is a person possessing uncertainty (*vicikicchā*). "Full of longing" (*sakaṅkho*) means possessing hesitation (*dveḷhaka*). "Full of remorse" (*savilekho*)...

“Possessing ripples of mind” means having waves of thought. “Having doubts” means having hesitations. “Full of perplexity” means having uncertainty. “For the attainment of knowledge” means for the sake of acquiring knowledge.
“For the touching of knowledge” means for the sake of penetrating knowledge; or else, for the sake of finding knowledge.
“For the realization of knowledge” means for the sake of making knowledge directly manifest. “With its source” means together with its cause. “I” [refers to] myself as one possessing a source.
I give the teaching of the Dhamma having made it conditional; "with demonstration" means having made it leading to liberation.
"Not without demonstration" means I do not give the teaching of the Dhamma by making it non-leading to liberation.
104. Regarding the question "From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?": here, "the pleasant and the unpleasant" refers specifically to the feelings of pleasure and pain.
"They do not exist as causes" means "these do not exist. Regarding this matter of both non-existence (*vibhava*) and existence (*bhava*), tell me that from what source it arises.
Here, there is a change of gender in the case endings. This is what is meant:
regarding this matter of the non-existence and existence of the pleasant and unpleasant, tell me that— [The text continues: ...from what source it arises. Tell me that to me.

"Tell me from what source [it arises]. Herein, the views of non-existence (*vibhava*) and existence (*bhava*), which have as their basis pleasant and unpleasant [feelings], should be understood in meaning as "non-existence" and "existence" themselves.
For indeed, in the answer to this question, he will state later in the exposition:
"The view of existence has contact as its source; the view of non-existence also has contact as its source. By means of this verse...
There is nothing further to be said in the exposition.
105. "From this source" means from contact as the source. There is also nothing further to be said regarding this.

106. "When what has disappeared do they not touch? means when what has passed away do the five contacts, beginning with eye-contact, no longer touch? There is also nothing further to be said regarding this.

107. "Dependent on name and form" means dependent on the associated name and the form consisting of the physical basis and the object. "When form has disappeared, contacts do not touch" means that when form has passed away, the five kinds of contact do not touch.
"The meeting of the three is contact" means that contact arises from the meeting of the three:
the eye, the form, and consciousness. "The eye and forms are in the form-factor" means that the sensitive eye and the forms as objects are placed within the category of form, the division of form.
"Excluding eye-contact" means setting aside the contact that arises from the meeting of the three.
"Associated states in the mental" refers to the remaining factors such as feeling, which arise simultaneously with contact and belong to the mental category.
The same method applies to the passages beginning with "dependent on the ear," and so forth.
"Form is manifested in four ways" means that form is transcended by way of four causes.

"By manifestation through knowledge" means by having transcended it after making it evident. "By manifestation through investigation" means by having transcended it after investigating it as impermanent and so forth.
"By manifestation through abandoning" means by having transcended it through the abandoning of desire and lust. "By manifestation through surmounting" refers to the four formless attainments.

"By means of having transcended through acquisition. (108) "How for one who has come together? means how for one who has practiced. "Form ceases" (*vibhoti rūpaṃ*) means form ceases, or it would not exist. "Pleasure and pain" refers specifically to desirable and undesirable forms.

"May we know" means we shall know. "May we understand" means we shall know in detail. "May we discern" means we shall know in manifold ways. "May we penetrate" means we shall know correctly. "May we pierce through" means we shall awaken by means of the mind.
109. “Neither percipient of perception”: just as for one who has attained [the attainment of cessation], form disappears, he is not even a percipient by way of natural perception (*pakatisaññā*).
“Nor non-percipient of perception”: even by way of a distorted perception (*visaṅñā*), he is not a non-percipient of perception, like one who is insane or deranged. “Nor yet non-percipient”:
he is not even devoid of perception, like one who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*) or a non-percipient being (*asaññasatta*). Nor...

"One who perceives the fading away" means that he is not even one who has transcended perceptions by way of the method beginning with "all perceptions of form," yet he is an attainer of the immaterial jhānas.
For one who has thus attained, instead of remaining in this state of "perception-perceived-ness" and so forth—wherein "form fades away"—it was said:
"When his mind is thus concentrated... he directs his mind toward the attainment of the base of infinite space."
For one who has thus attained the formless path, form disappears.
