By the statement, "Proliferation (papañca) and conceptualization (saṅkhā) have perception (saññā) as their source," it is shown that even for one practicing in this way, the proliferation of craving and views, which have that perception as their source, remains unabandoned.

Those who have entered the attainment of cessation are called "non-percipient" (asaññino); having ceased both perception and feeling, those who have entered the attainment of cessation are spoken of as "non-percipient" by virtue of the absence of perception. "Non-percipient beings" (asaññasatta) are those reborn in the non-percipient realm (asaññabhava) entirely devoid of all forms of perception.
"Thus, when his mind is thus concentrated": herein, "his" refers to that bhikkhu. "Thus" is an indication of the sequence of the fourth jhāna;
what is meant is that he has attained the fourth jhāna by this sequence. By the word "concentrated," it means concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna.
Regarding "purified" and so forth: it is purified by way of the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness. Precisely because it is purified...
It is said to be "purified" and "luminous. It is "stainless" because the stains of lust and so forth have been struck down by the destruction of their conditions, such as pleasure and the like.
And precisely because it is stainless, it is "free from defilement"; for it is through the stain that the mind becomes defiled.
Because it has been well-cultivated, it is "made malleable," which means it has attained mastery. For a mind that functions under one's control is called "malleable."
"And it is pliant" means it is workable, capable of being worked upon, and fit for action.
For the mind that is pliant is workable, like gold purified in its core. And both of these qualities arise precisely from being well-developed. As it was said:
"Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other thing that, when developed in this way, becomes so workable as the mind, bhikkhus."

For it is said to be "steadfast" (*ṭhita*) because it stands firm due to its state of being purified and so forth among these qualities. Precisely because it is steadfast, it is described as "unshakable" (*āneñjappatta*), "immovable" (*acala*), and "undisturbed" (*niriñjana*).
Alternatively, it is "steadfast" because it stands under its own control through its softness and wieldiness (*mudukammaññabhāva*).
It is "unshakable" because it is embraced by faith and the other [faculties]. For a mind embraced by faith is not shaken by lack of faith; one embraced by energy...
It is not moved by laziness; being embraced by mindfulness, it is not moved by negligence; being embraced by concentration, it is not moved by restlessness;
being embraced by wisdom, it is not moved by ignorance; having reached illumination, it is not moved by the darkness of the defilements.
When embraced by these six qualities, it has attained imperturbability. Thus, it is endowed with eight factors.
The mind becomes capable of directing its aspiration for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of infinite space.
Another method: [the mind is] concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna; purified by the removal of the hindrances; cleansed by the surmounting of applied thought and so forth;
and free from blemish due to the absence of evil states that are adverse to the attainment of jhāna and to the sphere of desire.
“Icchāvacarānaṃ” means belonging to the range of desire; the meaning is: of the various kinds of causes for anger that have descended through the power of desire and are active.
“Vigatūpakkilese” means with the mental defilements such as covetousness having been removed by their disappearance.
Both of these [terms] should be understood according to the *Aṅgaṇa-sutta* and the *Vattha-sutta*. “Mudubhūte” means made pliant through the attainment of mastery (*vasi*).

By means of attaining the state of the bases of psychic power, it becomes wieldy; by means of reaching a refined state through the perfection of development, it stands having attained imperturbability.
The meaning is that it stands in such a way that its state is imperturbable and it has attained imperturbability.
Thus, through the possession of these eight factors, the mind becomes capable of being directed toward the attainment of the base of infinite space, serving as its foundation and proximate cause.
"One who possesses the path of the formless" means one who has not fallen away from the path leading to the attainment of the formless realms (*arūpasamāpatti*).
"Proliferation itself is the designation for proliferation" means that craving and the like are themselves the designations for proliferation. 110.

"Some wise ones here say that purification for a being is at this extent; or do they say there is something more than this?"—do some wise recluses and brahmins here say that purification for a sentient being is the highest at this extent?
Or rather, he asks whether they also speak of something else beyond this attainment of the formless (*arūpasamāpatti*).
"Beyond this attainment of the formless" means from this very attainment of the formless.
"Some say that even this much is the limit" refers to certain eternalist ascetics and brahmins who consider themselves wise; they maintain that even this much is [the limit].

They declare this to be the supreme purity. "Some among them speak of annihilation" means that some among those very people, being proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), speak of annihilation as their "annihilation.
"Those who advocate for the wholesome in the state of no-residue" means they are those who maintain that there is a wholesome state in the absence of the residue of clinging (*anupādisesa*).
"Terrified by existence" means afraid of becoming. "They rejoice in non-existence" means they find satisfaction in dependence upon annihilation.
"They are stilled" means they are those who advocate the annihilation of the person (*puggala*). "They are calmed" means they speak of the non-arising of the person.
"They are utterly stilled" means they are exceedingly calm. "They are extinguished" means they are peaceful. "They cease" means there is no further arising.
"They subside" means there is no further rebirth. 112. "And knowing these to be dependent": this means that these proponents of views are dependent upon the views of eternalism and annihilationism.
"Having known": having known the bases, that wise sage is "investigating. The Buddha-sage is wise because he has investigated after knowing the bases. "Having known, he is liberated":
having known the phenomena—such as suffering and impermanence—he is liberated. "He does not come together for becoming after becoming":
he does not undergo repeated rebirth. "Not grasping": not grasping; the meaning is that he does not fall into the habit of clinging.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Kalahavivāda-sutta* in the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the sub-commentary to the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed. 12.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Cūḷabyūha-sutta*.

In the twelfth section, the exposition of the Cūḷabyūhasutta, regarding the phrase "adhering to their own respective views," this refers to certain individuals who, at that very same great assembly, had thoughts arisen such as:
"All these proponents of views say, 'We are truly excellent. Now, are these truly excellent ones established only in their own views, or do they also adopt other views?"
This was spoken by the Buddha after having himself questioned a manifested Buddha (nimmitabuddha) in the same manner as before, in order to explain that matter to the deities. 113.
Therein, the first two verses are indeed verses of inquiry. In them, "clinging each to their own view" (*sakaṃ sakaṃ diṭṭhiparibbasānā*) means being under the sway of their respective views.
"Disputing, the experts speak variously" (*viggayha nānā kusalā vadanti*) refers to grasping those views with forceful insistence.
Having grasped [their own views], they each speak individually, asserting, "We are experts in that," yet they do not speak with one voice.

Regarding the statement, "He who knows thus has known the Dhamma; he who contradicts this is incomplete," they say that this refers to the view held by one who knows in such a way—that he has realized the Dhamma—and that one who contradicts this is inferior.
"They speak variously" means they speak with diverse reasons. "They speak in manifold ways" means they speak in many different manners.
"They speak one thing after another" means that instead of saying one thing, they say this or that, taking up various points. "He is incomplete" refers to one who is unwholesome.
"Not fulfilled" means not complete. "Not perfected" means not fully accomplished.
114. "A fool" means inferior. "Unskilled" means ignorant.
115. Now there are three verses of exposition. These stand by expanding upon the meaning stated in the first half [of the prose] with the second half.
Because this expansion is brief compared to the subsequent suttas, this sutta is called the "Cūḷabyūha" (The Shorter Exposition).
It received that name. Regarding this, first, in the initial verse: "If [one holds] another's doctrine" means another's view (*diṭṭhi*).
"All these are fools"—the intention is that, such being the case, all these people are indeed fools. For what reason? Because "all these are steeped in views.
(116) "Neither purified by their own view, nor cleansed; they are not of pure wisdom, skillful, or wise," [referring to those who are] steeped in their own view.
If they are not clear, not bright, and are indeed defiled, yet they possess purified wisdom, are skillful, and are wise;
or alternatively, if the reading is "sanditṭhiyā ce vadātā," its meaning is as follows:
if, by their own view, they are bright, possess purified wisdom, are skillful, and are wise—then, such being the case, there is no one [to blame] for them.
Not even one among them is of inferior wisdom; for what reason? Because their views are held with such conviction, just as those of the others.

117. The summary meaning of the verse beginning "Na vāhametaṃ" is as follows: That which those two pairs of people have mutually called each other a "fool," I do not say that this is true. For what reason? Because all of them [regard] their own...
They established their own view as "this alone is true, all else is false," and for that reason they regarded others as "fools.
In this context, both *tathiyaṃ* and *tathaivaṃ* are readings; *tacchaṃ* means not empty (*atucchaṃ*).
*Tathaṃ* means non-erroneous (*aviparītaṃ*), and *bhūtaṃ* means existing (*santaṃ*). *Yāthāvaṃ* means being found as it is (*saṃvijjamānaṃ*). *Aviparitaṃ* means not deceptive (*na visaṅketaṃ*).
118. Regarding the question verse beginning with *yamāhu*: some say, "That which is the truth of view (*diṭṭhisacca*) is the real.

119. Regarding the response verse beginning with *ekaṃ hi saccaṃ*: there is indeed one truth, namely cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*magga*). "In which people do not dispute" means that when people understand that truth, those who understand it would not dispute among themselves.

"They praise it themselves" means they speak of it by their own [authority]. 120. Regarding the question verse beginning with *kasmā nu*: "Those who propound" refers to the proponents (*vādino*). "Or do they follow their own reasoning? means do those proponents merely follow their own individual logic?

“Struck by reasoning” (*takkapariyāhata*) means thoroughly struck by initial application of thought (*vitakka*). “Followed by investigation” (*vīmaṃsānucarita*) means investigated by one’s own established wisdom (*paññā*). “One’s own inspired flash” (*sayaṃpaṭibhāna*) means one’s own spontaneous intuition.

121. In the verse of the response, “Not indeed so,” [the phrase] “except for perception, they are permanent” refers to those graspings that are taken as permanent merely by way of perception, setting aside perception itself.
“Having fashioned reasoning among views” (*takkañ ca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā*) means having generated within oneself a mere conceptualization of permanence regarding various views.
But because those who generate thought regarding views produce [further] views, it is therefore said:
"They generate and produce speculative views," and so forth. "Generate" means they produce successive views.
"Produce" and the other terms are stated by augmenting the word with prefixes (*upasagga*). "My truth" means my statement is correct.

122. Now, in order to show the error of those proponents of views (*diṭṭhigatika*) who, while these various truths do not exist, merely rely on ratiocination, the Teacher spoke the verses beginning with "In what is seen and heard.
Therein, "the seen" (*diṭṭhe*) means the seen; the intention is "purification through the seen.
This same method applies to "the heard" (*sute*) and so forth. And "relying on these, one sees celestial mansions" (*vimānadassī*) means relying upon these phenomena of views (*diṭṭhidhamma*).
Even one who sees a celestial mansion (vimāna) known as a state of purity, yet remains in that judgment and laughs, saying,
"The other is a fool and unskilled," even such a beholder of the mansion, standing in that doctrinal judgment,
becomes filled with satisfaction and laughter and speaks thus: "The other is inferior and ignorant."
"He does not honor" means he looks upon with contempt; that is, he does not show great respect. Thus, "one who looks with contempt" is one who does not look with great respect.

"He generates mental distress" means that after first clinging to a reliance on views and experiencing mental distress, he subsequently produces joy at the time when he stands firm in his resolution regarding those views. This is the meaning.
“Standing by a view of judgment” means standing by a view that has been adopted through the process of reaching a definitive conclusion.

123. Regarding the verse beginning with “When this is so, by whatever...”: therein, “himself alone” (*sayamattano*) means himself indeed. “He despises” (*vimāneti*) means he reviles. “That very thing, O Pāvā” (*tadeva pāvā*)—he speaks of that very speech as a view, or [he speaks of] that person.

124. Regarding the meaning of the verse beginning with “By a view of excessive transgression” (*atisāradiṭṭhiyā*): he, by means of that very view of excessive transgression which exceeds the [proper] characteristic (*lakkhaṇātisārinī*), [acts in such a way].
It is complete, full, and bloated; and intoxicated by that view and conceit, thinking "I am complete, I am an omniscient one," he thus possesses the conceit of being complete.
He himself mentally anoints himself with the thought, "I am wise. For what reason?
Because that view of his is so thoroughly completed.
All those views transcend characteristics (*lakkhaṇātikkantā*); thus, all those sixty-two views have passed beyond and transcended characteristics. "Anoma" means not deficient (*anūna*).
125. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with "And of another" (*parassa ca*)—what more is there?
Furthermore, he who, standing in his own judgment, laughing, says, "The other is a fool, unskilled," if indeed by the speech of that other person he is being addressed [in return]...
He is inferior; he is dull-witted and possesses inferior wisdom, and thus he too is of inferior wisdom along with him.
For he also calls that person a "fool. If his word were not authoritative, then he himself would indeed be both a master of knowledge and wise.
This being the case, there would be no fool among the recluses, for they would all be wise according to their own desires.

*Vācāya* means by speaking. *Vacanena* means by what has been uttered. *Ninditakāraṇā* means by reason of censure. *Garahitakāraṇā* means by reason of contempt. *Upavaditakāraṇā* means by reason of reproach. 126.
Regarding the connection and meaning of the verse beginning with *Aññaṃ ito*:
"But if there is a wise man who is a master of knowledge (*vedagu*), there is no fool among the recluses"—even when this has been said, someone might ask, "Why? To that, it is replied:
—Because they profess a doctrine other than this, they have missed the way to purity;
they are incomplete. Thus do the various sectarians speak. Those who profess a view other than this have missed and failed regarding the path to purity;
they are incomplete. This is what is meant by "because the various sectarians speak thus. But why do they speak in this way?
Why? Because they are delighted by the lust for their own views; for it is said that those [heretics] are delighted by their own lust for views.
They [claim it is] the path of purity (*suddhimagga*), meaning the undefiled path. The path of purification (*visuddhimagga*), meaning the faultless path.
The path of complete purity (*parisuddhimagga*), meaning the bright path. The path of cleansing (*vodātamagga*), meaning the white path. The path of total cleansing (*pariyodātamagga*)—
The radiant path. *Viraddhā*: having missed it by deviating from the method prescribed for the path.
*Aparaddhā*: having failed by transgressing it. *Khalitā*: having fallen away. *Galitā*: having slipped down from that. *Aññāya*: through ignorance.
*Aparaddhā*: having met with defeat. Alternatively, there is also the reading *ñāyāparaddhā*. The meaning is: having missed the path by way of the method (*ñāya*).
127. And thus, being so delighted—“In this very world there is purity,” etc. Therein, *sakāyane* means in one’s own doctrine. *Daḷhaṃ vadānā* means those who speak firmly.
*Thiravādā* means those who speak with certainty. *Balikavādā* means those who speak powerfully. *Avaṭṭhitavādā* means those who speak having established themselves [in their position]. 128.
Among those who speak thus firmly, whichever sectarian (*titthiya*) speaks firmly in his own doctrine, let him here...

"A fool would burn another"—in brief, regarding those known as eternalism and annihilationism, and in detail, regarding one's own various systems such as nihilism, theism, creatorism, fatalism, and so forth, when one speaks firmly, saying "this alone is the truth," whom among those holding such views could one here rightly regard as a "fool" along with the Dhamma?
For according to his own view, would not everyone else be wise and well-practiced? Thus...
While being virtuous himself, he would bring strife upon himself by speaking of another as a fool of impure nature.
He too, by saying of another, "This person is a fool and of impure nature," would bring strife upon himself. Why?
Because, according to his own view, everyone else is indeed wise and indeed well-practiced.
129. Thus, having himself fallen into error by standing upon all kinds of doctrinal determinations, he enters into dispute with the world above;
and having himself measured the Teacher and others by means of his own views, he enters into even greater dispute.
But having understood the danger in such determinations and having abandoned all determinations through the Noble Path, a person does not create a conflict.
In the word *loke*, he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of *arahantship*.
*Sayaṃ pamāya* means having measured by oneself. *Paminitvā* means having made a measurement. There is also a reading *pavinetvā*, but that is not good.
*Uddhaṃ vādena saddhiṃ* means together with one who speaks above [him], that is, with one who speaks superior to himself. At the conclusion of the teaching...
The realization was exactly as described in the Purābheda Sutta.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of the Cūḷabyūha Sutta within the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*.
13. Explanation of the Discourse on the Great Array (Mahābyūhasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā) 130.
Regarding the thirteenth [section], the explanation of the Discourse on the Great Array, concerning the phrase "those who are obsessed by views":
one might ask, "Do these people obsessed by views receive only censure from the wise, or do they also receive praise?"
In order to reveal this matter to certain deities who had arisen [in that state], it was spoken by having himself questioned through a manifested Buddha (nimmitabuddha) in the same manner as before.
In that context: *anvānayanti* means they lead along, that is, they bring back again and again.
*Nindameva anventi* means they pursue only blame; they approach only censure.

131. Now, since even those proponents of speculative views who say, "This alone is the truth," occasionally receive praise somewhere—and that fruit of their doctrine known as praise is meager, being incapable of pacifying passion and the other defilements—let alone the second fruit, which is blame;
therefore, showing this point, [the Blessed One said] this:
Then he spoke the verse of response: “For this is trifling; it is not enough for equanimity; I declare that there are two fruits of dispute.
In this context, “the two fruits of dispute” refers to blame and praise, or victory and defeat, and so forth, which are of that same nature.
“Seeing even this” means seeing the danger in the fruits of dispute, namely: “Blame is indeed undesirable, and praise is not enough for equanimity.”
"Having seen": beholding Nibbāna as the ground of security and the state free from dispute. "Appakam" means meager; "parittakam" means trifling;
"omakam" means inferior; "lāmakam" means base or evil. "Samāyā" is for the purpose of calming passion and the other defilements;
"upasamāyā" is for the purpose of bringing them further and further under control; "vūpasamāyā" is for the purpose of making them completely subsided.
"For the sake of Nibbāna" means for the sake of the great Nibbāna, which is the Deathless. "For the sake of relinquishment" means for the sake of abandoning the defilements by means of the Path.
"For the sake of subsiding" means it is not sufficient for the non-arising of those [defilements] that have been subsided by means of the Fruit.
132. Thus, without disputing, he recited the verse beginning with "Whatever... Therein, "conventional designations" (*sammutiyo*) refers to views (*diṭṭhiyo*). "Ordinary people" (*puthujjā*)...

"Arising from worldlings. "How could he approach? means: in what sense would he approach even a single phenomenon among form and the rest—since "approach" (upāya) signifies that which is to be approached—and for what reason would he approach?
"Not forming an acceptance toward what is seen or heard" means: not feeling affection for purity based on what is seen or heard.
"Produced by worldlings" means: generated by worldlings. "Designations" means: views. [They are called] "worldlings" (puthu) because they belong to various individuals (nānājana).

"Produced" means generated by various types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigatika*). "It leads" means it does not go [toward liberation]. "It does not approach" means it does not come near. "It does not draw near" means it turns back.
"It does not adhere" means that having entered, it does not remain established.
As for those outside of this [teaching], the verse beginning with "Those who hold virtue as supreme" has the following meaning: they imagine that virtue alone is "supreme."
"Virtue is supreme"—so say some venerable ones; they claim purification comes through mere restraint, having undertaken ascetic practices such as the elephant-girdle and others.
Remaining within this very view, they speak of purification for their teacher, being devoted to existence and clinging to existence;
moreover, they are proponents of "skillfulness," speaking thus: "We are skillful."
134. "And whoever among those supreme in virtue practices accordingly—'if he should pass away,' etc. This is the meaning:

if, due to the interference of others or because he is unable to fulfill it, he passes away from that virtuous practice, he fails in that work of virtue and observances or in the formative action of merit and the like, and he suffers. And he does not merely suffer;...
Moreover, he yearns for that purification of virtue and observances, he prattles about it, and he longs for it.

How so? Just as one who has left his home and is traveling with a caravan, having departed from home, might—while away from home—long for either his home or the caravan, being deprived of them. Thus it is.
"By cutting through another" means being obstructed by another. "Failing to accomplish" means not fulfilling that practice.
"Having missed the goal" means having fallen away from Nibbāna or from the Path. "He follows that same sword" means he goes behind that same sword everywhere.
135. Thus, having abandoned even all rules and observances—which are the cause of wavering for those who hold virtue to be supreme—the noble disciple...
Verse. Therein, "the blameworthy and the blameless" refers to all unwholesome states and worldly wholesome states.
"Not desiring this purity or impurity" means not desiring purity consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth, nor impurity consisting of the unwholesome and so forth.
"One should wander detached" means one should wander detached from both purity and impurity. "Without grasping at views" means without adopting [wrong] views.

"Black with black result" refers to unwholesome karma that yields an unwholesome result. "White with white result" refers to mundane wholesome karma that yields a white result corresponding to itself.

"Entering the fixed course" means entering the path. "Those in training" (sekkhā) refers to the seven types of trainees. "The supreme state" (aggadhamma) refers to the highest state, the fruit of arhatship. 136.
Thus, regarding those outside this [teaching] who possess the highest virtue, who speak of purity through restraint, and who abandon both virtue and ascetic observances, as well as their results—
Having thus shown the practice of the Arahant, he now speaks the verse beginning with “Tamūpanissāya” to demonstrate other ways in which outsiders (bāhiraka) maintain their doctrine of purity.

Its meaning is as follows: there are also other recluses and brahmins who, depending on either the doctrine of “not killing” (amarantapa) which they loathe, or one of the various forms of purity through views such as purity through seeing, or else becoming proponents of nihilism (uddhaṃsara) through the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi), remain with craving unabated amidst successive states of existence.
“They praise purity” means they speak and talk about it.

“Proponents of asceticism and disgust” means those who speak of shame regarding evil through asceticism such as bodily mortification. “Those for whom asceticism and disgust are the essence” means those who possess the essence of shame by means of that very asceticism. “Proponents of upward purification” means those who speak of purification through the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
137. Thus, while those who have not transcended craving are praising purity, even one who considers himself to have attained purity—

The intention is that for one who would thus imagine, because craving has not been abandoned, there will indeed be repeated yearnings as they long for this or that object among various states of existence. For craving, when practiced, only increases craving;
and it is not only yearnings, but also "trembling" (pavedhita) regarding things fashioned by craving and views. Regarding those objects fashioned by craving and views:

"It is also trembling" is what is meant. But for one who, due to being free from craving for various states of existence (*bhava*), has no future passing away and rebirth here, by what could he be shaken, or where would he yearn? This is the connection of that verse. "Coming" means coming again.

"Going" means going elsewhere from here. "Coming and going" means returning after having gone from here. "Time" means death. "Destiny" (*gati*) refers to the destination to be reached by way of going.
138. "That which they call Dhamma" is the question verse. 139.

Now, since not even a single doctrine here is true, for they speak merely out of their own views, he spoke this reply-verse beginning with "For their own" (*sakaṃ hi*) to demonstrate that point. Therein, "convention" (*sammutiṃ*)...
*Diṭṭhiṃ*: [meaning] view. *Anomaṃ*:

meaning not deficient. 140. Thus, while these [teachers] were proclaiming their own doctrine as complete, yet declaring the doctrine of another to be inferior—for anyone among them—[there follows] the verse beginning:
"If, by means of disparaging another... The meaning of this is: if, for the sake of censuring another...
One would become inferior; no one at all would excel or be supreme in regard to the teachings. For what reason?
Because many speak of another’s teaching as inferior, yet they are all firm in their own [teachings], being merely those who speak firmly regarding their own doctrines.

"Causes for disparagement" means causes for wearing away. "Causes for censuring" means causes for doing what is base. "Causes for reviling" means causes for abusing. "One's own body" means one's own path.
141. Furthermore: "The worship of the True Dhamma" is the verse. Its meaning is as follows:
Just as those sectarians praise their own respective systems, so too does the worship of the True Dhamma proceed for them. For they are exceedingly devoted to their teachers and the rest.
If they were to be considered authoritative in this matter, then, such being the case, all doctrines would be true. Why is that?
For their purity is indeed purely individual. It is not accomplished elsewhere, nor is it established from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
For those whose intellects are led by others, that [purity] is merely a grasping at views regarding the self. "Purely individual" means exclusively for each one. 142.
But as for the brahmin who has become so through having expelled evil in the opposite sense, for that brahmin there is no dependence on others.

Verse. Its meaning is as follows: For the brahmin, because he has clearly seen [the truth] by way of such principles as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," there is no knowledge to be led by another.
Among the phenomena of views, there is nothing that he has grasped firmly after deciding, "This alone is the truth.
For that reason, he has transcended disputes over views; indeed, he does not regard any other phenomenon as supreme.
Apart from the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.

"Not led by another" means he is not one who must be led or made to understand by another. "Not dependent on others, not subject to others" means he is not one whose conviction depends on others. "Not subservient to others" means he is not one whose movement is constrained by others.
143. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with "I know" are as follows: thus, first of all, the ultimate brāhmaṇa is not [superior] merely by way of being a *seṭṭha* (a social class).

One sees another phenomenon; however, other sectarians—even though they know and see through such means as the knowledge of others' minds—though they say, "I know and I see it exactly as it is," nevertheless maintain that purity comes through their views. Why?
Because even if one among them has indeed seen or perceived the matter as it truly is by means of that knowledge of others' minds and so forth, what [is the point]?

What has been accomplished by this or that seeing of yours? Has the full comprehension of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*) been achieved, or perhaps one of the others, such as the abandoning of the origin (*samudayappahāna*)?

For in every respect, those sectarians speak of purity in a way entirely different from the Noble Path, and likewise, having transcended those sectarians, the Buddhas and others speak of purity in a way entirely different [from theirs].
144. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with “The man who sees” (passaṃ naro) are as follows—what more is there to say?
That person who has seen by means of the knowledge of others’ minds and so forth—that seeing man will see name-and-form (nāmarūpa), but nothing beyond that.
Or, having seen, he will know these very same name-and-forms as permanent or as pleasant, but not otherwise. Seeing in this way, let him see much or little as he pleases.
Or if one regards name-and-form as permanent and as pleasant, then, because of such a view, the wise say that there is no purification through it.
145. Regarding the connection and meaning of the verse beginning with *nivissavādī*:

even in the absence of purification through that view, one who speaks dogmatically (*nivissavādī*), saying, "I know, I see; it is exactly thus," or who, relying on that very view, [holds] a [wrong] view...
One who asserts purification, saying "this alone is the truth," and thus holds to a fixed doctrine, is not easily disciplined;
for he places before him that very view which has been preconceived and constructed.
Indeed, relying on a particular teacher or system, he speaks of beauty therein, speaking of purification, thinking of himself: "I am one who speaks of purity, or one who sees purity."
Thinking thus, he saw it exactly as it was there; he saw it precisely according to his own view without error.
The intention is that he saw it just as that view functions, and did not wish to see it otherwise.
"One who speaks with conviction" means one who speaks having established a firm position. "Difficult to discipline" means difficult to train. "Difficult to instruct" means...
"Difficult to make known" means it is difficult to cause [others] to obtain [the truth] through the mind.

"Difficult to contemplate" means it is difficult to cause [others] to contemplate again and again after having examined it with the mind for the sake of grasping it. "Difficult to make see" means it is difficult to make [others] see.
"Difficult to inspire confidence in" means it is difficult to produce confidence in the mind.
"Appassī" means he attained penetration by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Paṭivijjhi" means he attained awakening by means of the mind (*citta*). 146.
Regarding those sectarian teachers (*tīrthika*) who hold such preconceived views: "The Brahmin does not enter upon a conceptual construction (*saṅkhā*)," is the verse.

In this context, "saṅkhā" means by way of reckoning (*saṅkhāya*), that is, having known. Nor is he a "kinsman of knowledge" (*ñāṇabandhu*) by means of the knowledge of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*) and so forth.
"Without bonds of craving or views. Herein, the analysis is as follows: "Not even a bond made by knowledge exists for him," thus he is "not bound by knowledge" (*na pi ñāṇabandhu*).
"Conventional designations" (*sammutiyo*) means conventional views (*diṭṭhisammutiyo*). "Arising among worldlings" (*puthujjāti*) means arising among ordinary people (*puthujjana*).
"'Grasping,' they think": others [think] it is grasping; what is meant is that others grasp those conventional designations.
"He looks on with equanimity" (*upekkhati*) means that, having become impartial and not falling into any side, he sees.

147. Furthermore: "Having cast off the bonds," this is the verse. Therein, "without grasping" (*anuggaho*) means devoid of grasping; that which is not his grasping is "without grasping. Or, "he does not grasp" is "without grasping.
"Having cast off the bonds" means having abandoned the bonds such as covetousness and the like. "Having cast off" (*vissajja*) means by way of not taking them up again.
"Having abandoned. "Attached" (*gadhitā*) means joined together. "Bound" (*ganthitā*) means bound as if gathered together by a thread.
"Tied" (*bandhe*) means well-tied. "Fastened" (*vibandhe*) means variously tied. "Obstructed" (*palibuddhe*) means bound by a binding on all sides.

"In bondage" (*bandhane*) refers to the bondage of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Having shaken off" (*phoṭayitvā*) means having brushed away. "Making truth their release" (*saccaṃ vissajjaṃ karonti*) means having dismantled [the bonds].
They make it unfit for use. "They spoil it" means they reduce it to powder and fragments.
Furthermore: "Such as this—one who [destroys] past taints," etc., is the verse.
Therein, "past taints" refers to the defilements liable to arise with reference to past form and so forth. "New" refers to those liable to arise with reference to present form and so forth.
"Not led by desire" means he does not proceed by way of desire and the like. "Not reproaching himself" means not reproaching oneself on account of what has been done or left undone.
149. Thus, regarding the verse beginning with "He who, being one who does not reproach himself... among all phenomena":

therein, "among all phenomena" refers to the sixty-two types of views, categorized as "whatever is seen," and so forth. "One whose burden has fallen" means one whose burden has been laid down. "He does not construct" means he does not [mentally construct].
"Kappiya" means that he does not perform even the two kinds of allowable things (*kappa*).

"Not one who has ceased above" (*nūparato*) means he is not possessed of cessation like the virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) or those in training (*sekkha*). "Not one who desires" (*na patthiyo*) means he is free from craving;

for craving is called "desiring" (*patthiyā*) because it desires, and since he has no such desire, he is "not one who desires. Beyond this and below, the meaning is self-evident, as the method has been explained in various places.

Thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship; at the end of the teaching, there occurred a realization (abhisamaya) exactly as described in the Purābheda Sutta.
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the Commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the Mahābyūha Sutta is finished.
14. Commentary on the exposition of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta. 150.
Regarding the fourteenth [sutta], in the exposition of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta, the phrase "I ask you" (*pucchāmi taṃ*) refers to that very same Great Assembly (*mahāsamaya*). "Kā... [and so forth].

This was spoken by having the emanated Buddha ask himself the question— just as in the previous method— in order to clarify that matter for certain deities who had thought, "Is this indeed the practice for attaining Arahatship?

Therein, regarding the first verse of questions, the term "I ask" (*pucchāmi*) refers to the classification of questioning according to such categories as the inquiry for the sake of revealing what has not been seen.
"Kinsman of the Sun" (*Ādiccabandhu*) means a kinsman by lineage of the sun. "Seclusion and the state of peace" (*vivekaṃ santipadañca*) refers to both seclusion and the state of peace.
"Having seen how" (*kathaṃ disvā*) means for what reason having seen; it is said to mean "having become one who sees how things proceed.
"Three questions" (*tisso pucchā*) is a delimitation by number. "Demonstrating the unseen" (*adiṭṭhajotanā*) refers to that which has not been seen or penetrated.
The inquiry is for the purpose of making [the meaning] clear. "Corroboration with what has been seen" means for the purpose of connecting that which was seen by the eye of knowledge.

"Severing of doubt" means for the purpose of cutting through whatever uncertainty exists. "The characteristic is not known by nature" means that the characteristic of reality (*tathalakkhaṇa*) of phenomena is not known by way of its inherent nature.
"Not seen" means it has not been seen. There is also a reading: "not reached" (*na niṭṭha*).
*Atulitaṃ* means not weighed, as if it were weighed by a scale. *Atīritaṃ* means not scrutinized by way of investigation.
*Avibhūtaṃ* means not manifest. *Avibhāvitaṃ* means not developed by wisdom. *Tassa ñāṇāya* means for the sake of knowing the characteristics of that Dhamma.
*Dassanāya* means for the sake of seeing. *Tulanāya* means for the sake of weighing. *Tīraṇāya* means for the sake of investigating. *Vibhāvanāya* means...
For the purpose of making a division. "By other wise ones" means by others endowed with intelligence.

"Fallen into doubt" means having entered into uncertainty. "Questions of humans" means questions asked by human beings. "Questions of non-humans" means questions asked by *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and so forth.

"Householders" refers to the remaining householders. "Those who have gone forth" is stated by way of their outward appearance (*liṅga*). "Nāgas" refers to *nāgas* such as Supassa and others. "Supaṇṇas" refers to...
[The section] on the Supaṇṇas is according to the *Supaṇṇa-saṃyutta*. "Yakkhas" should be understood as being according to the *Yakkha-saṃyutta*.
"Asuras" refers to Pahārāda and others. "Gandhabbas" refers to Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba, and others. "Mahārājās" refers to the four Great Kings.
"With unimpaired faculties" means having faculties that are not deficient in terms of their physical form. "He was created by him" means he was created by the Blessed One, the Buddha.
An inquiry concerning purification is an inquiry concerning distinguished phenomena. An inquiry concerning the past is an inquiry directed toward phenomena of the past;

the same method applies to the future and so forth. An inquiry concerning the wholesome is an inquiry concerning blameless phenomena. An inquiry concerning the unwholesome is an inquiry concerning blameworthy phenomena.
An inquiry concerning the indeterminate is an inquiry concerning phenomena that are the opposite of both.

"I enjoin you" (*ajjhesāmi tan ti*): I command you. "Tell me" (*kathayassu me ti*): speak to me. "A kinsman by clan" (*gottañātako*): one who is known as a relative through lineage. "A relative by clan" (*gottabandhū*): one who is intimate through lineage.

"In one way" (*ekenākārena*): by means of a single category. "The state of peace" (*santipadaṃ*): the state of Nibbāna, which is designated as peace. "Those states for the attainment of peace" (*ye dhammā santādhigamāya*): those states such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, for the purpose of obtaining Nibbāna.
"For the touching of peace" (*santiphusanāya*): for the purpose of touching Nibbāna by means of the contact of knowledge (*ñāṇaphassa*).

"By way of realization" means for the purpose of making it directly manifest. "The great aggregate of virtue" means the great mass of virtue. The same method applies to the aggregate of concentration and the others.
The aggregates of virtue and so forth are both mundane and supramundane; however, the knowledge and vision of liberation is exclusively mundane.
"The shattering of the mass of darkness" means the destruction of the mass of ignorance. "The breaking up of the perversion" refers to the fourfold perversion.

Breaking apart. "Uprooting the arrow of craving" means pulling out the thorn of craving. "The subsiding of volitional formations" means the extinguishing of meritorious and other volitional formations.
"The laying down of the burden" means setting aside the burden of the five aggregates.
"The cutting off of the cycle of saṃsāra" means the severing of the process of saṃsāra. "The extinguishing of the fever."
The extinction of the fever of the defilements; the allaying of the burning heat means the settling of the agitation caused by the defilements.
"God of gods" means the god who transcends all other gods. 151.
Then the Blessed One, seeing in such a way that he suppresses the defilements, and having seen them thus, proceeded with his vision accordingly.

Having offered the sacrifice, he attains final Nibbāna; therefore, revealing that meaning and urging that assembly of devas toward the abandonment of the defilements in various ways, he spoke five verses beginning with "The root of the conceptual proliferation (*papañca-saṅkhā*).
Therein, first, the summary meaning of the initial verse is as follows: "Conceptual proliferation" (*papañca-saṅkhā*) refers to "proliferations" (*papañcā*) because they are so designated.
Such is the conceptual proliferation (*papañca-saṅkhā*). Ignorance and the other defilements are its root.
One should restrain with wisdom all that proceeds as "I am," which is the root of that conceptual proliferation.
Whatever cravings might arise within, one should train in their discipline and abandonment, always mindful, training by being established in mindfulness.
"Arising internally" means arisen in the mind. "Before the meal" means before the time for the midday meal.
The accusative case is used here in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*), yet in meaning it is simply the locative;
this is the same principle for "after the meal" and so forth. "After the meal" means after the time for the midday meal. "The first watch" means the first division of the night.
The middle watch is the second division of the night. The last watch is the third division of the night. In the dark fortnight means during the waning moon.
In the bright fortnight means during the waxing moon. In the rains means the four months of the rainy season. In the winter means the four months of the cold season.
In the summer means the four months of the hot season. In the first stage of life means in the first period of one’s youth.
The meaning is "in the first stage of life. For a man with a lifespan of one hundred years, each of the three stages of life consists of thirty-three years and four months. 152.
Thus, having first taught the discourse associated with the three trainings according to the peak of Arahantship by means of the first verse—
Furthermore, in order to teach by way of the abandoning of conceit (*māna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Whatever phenomenon...
In this context, "whatever phenomenon one might recognize within oneself" means that one might know some personal quality of one's own, such as being born into a high-born family;
or "or even externally" means that one might know the qualities of one's teachers or preceptors. "One should not take strength from that" means...
One should not take pride because of that quality.

"Of the good" (satānaṃ) means of those possessing peaceful qualities. "The peaceful" (santānaṃ) means those whose mental continuum is extinguished. "Not spoken" (na vuttā) means not uttered. "Not proclaimed" (nappavuttā) means not expounded.
Now, showing the method for not performing [such pride], he spoke the verse beginning with "Better not by that. Its meaning is as follows: by that...
And by means of pride, one should not conceive of oneself as "I am superior," or "I am inferior," or even "I am equal.
Furthermore, when touched by various qualities such as being born of a high-born family, one should not remain conceptualizing oneself in various ways,
such as "I have gone forth from a high-born family," and so forth.
154. Having thus taught by way of the abandoning of conceit (*māna*), he now spoke the verse beginning with “ajjhattameva” in order to teach by way of the pacification of all defilements (*kilesa*).
Therein, “he pacifies within himself alone” means that he should pacify all defilements such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth within his own self.
“The bhikkhu would not seek peace from another” means that, setting aside the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, he would not seek peace through any other means.
One should not seek it. "From where is it relinquished? means from exactly where is it relinquished?

"One should not search for it" means one should not pursue it by means of rules and observances (*sīlabbata*) and so forth. "One should not look for it" means one should not gaze upon it. "One should not seek it" means one should not look at it again and again. 155.
Now, showing the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) of one whose taints are destroyed and who is inwardly calmed, [the text says] "just as in the middle."

He spoke this verse. Its meaning is as follows: Just as in the midst of the great ocean—at its center, measuring four thousand yojanas, which is reckoned as the middle between the upper and lower parts—waves do not arise for one standing amidst the mountains or in the middle of the sea, but he remains steady and unshaken;
even so, the one who is free from agitation and whose taints are exhausted should remain steady and unshaken when faced with gain and the like.
Thus, such a bhikkhu would not allow an excess of lust and other defilements to arise anywhere.
"In depth" means by its lower part. "Deep" means eighty-four thousand yojanas deep from the surface of the water.
There is also a reading "height" (*ubbedho*), but that is not good. "Below" refers to the water within; "above" refers to the water on top.
"In the middle" means in the center. "Does not shake" means it does not move from its place of stability. "Does not waver" means it does not move hither and thither.
"Does not tremble" means it becomes motionless. "Does not quiver" means it does not throb.
"Does not quiver greatly" means it does not turn over. "Does not quiver intensely" means it does not whirl around. "Unshaken" means not moved. "Unstruck" means...
"Unshakeable" means it does not tremble. "Undisturbed" means it does not become turbid.
"No waves arise there" means that no ripples emerge in that place.
"In the intervals between the seven mountains" means in the spaces between the seven mountains, beginning with Yugandhara.
"Sīdantaratā" means that even down to a tuft of *simbali* cotton, whatever falls among them sinks; thus they are "sīdā.
Because they are born between mountains, they are "antarā. There is also a reading, "Antarasīdā.
Now, expressing his appreciation for this Dhamma teaching taught with Arahatship as its pinnacle, [he reflects] upon that Arahatship...
The emanated Buddha, being asked about the primary practice (*ādipaṭipadā*), spoke this verse beginning with "He proclaimed" (*akittayi*). Therein, "he proclaimed" (*akittayi*) means he explained.
"One with open eyes" (*vivaṭacakkhu*) means endowed with the five eyes that are open and unobstructed.

"The Dhamma realized by oneself" (*sakkhidhamma*) means the Dhamma that is one's own domain, personally directly known, and witnessed by oneself. "The removal of perils" (*parissayavinaya*) means the warding off of dangers.
"Speak of the practice (*paṭipadā*)" means: speak now of the way of conduct. "Venerable Sir" (*bhaddante*)—he addressed the Blessed One, saying, "May there be welfare for you.
Alternatively, it is also said: "Speak of your auspicious and beautiful practice.
"The *pātimokkha* or else concentration"—by this he asks, having divided that very practice. Or, by "practice," he refers to the Path (*magga*).
He asks. By the others, he asks about virtue and concentration.
"Even by the fleshly eye" means even by the fleshly eye together with its constituent parts. "Even by the divine eye": it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine;
for the eye of the devas, produced by well-performed kamma, is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth, due to its freedom from defilements.

The divine eye of clarity (*pasādacakkhu*) is capable of receiving objects even at a distance. This eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*), produced by the power of the development of energy (*vīriyabhāvanā*), is exactly like that;

thus, it is "divine" because it resembles the divine. It is "divine" also because it is obtained through the mode of divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*), and because it is itself supported by divine abiding.
It is "divine" also because of its great radiance due to its mastery over light. [It is so called] because of seeing forms situated beyond walls and other such obstacles.
It is also "divine" because it possesses a great destiny. All of this should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). It is "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing;
or it is "eye" because it performs the function of an eye, as if it were an eye. And since it is both divine and an eye, it is the "divine eye" (*dibbacakkhu*).
By means of that divine eye, he is one whose eye is opened. Now, in order to explain the fivefold eye in detail:
“How is it that the Blessed One has opened eyes even with his fleshly eye?”— this is what he said. Regarding the statement,
“Five colors are found in the Blessed One’s fleshly eye,” here it means that within the Buddha, the Blessed One’s eye— which includes its constituent parts and so forth—
five distinct components are each individually perceived.
"Blue color" means the color of an umā flower. "Yellow color" means the color of a kaṇikāra flower. "Red color" means the color of an indragopaka insect.
"Black color" means the color of collyrium. "White color" means the color of a medicinal star-plant.
"And where the eyelashes are established" means the place at which the eyelashes, having been established, have grown up.
Regarding the phrase "that is blue, beautifully blue": here, "blue" is stated in a way that encompasses all [shades of blue].
"Beautifully blue" means a deep blue, free from any internal gaps. "Pleasing" means producing confidence. "Worthy of being seen" means beautiful to behold.
"Equal to the flax flower" means resembling the *dakasītala* flower. "Beyond that" means on the outer side surrounding it. "Yellow" is stated as a comprehensive term for all shades of yellow.
"Very yellow" (*supītakan*) means it is well-yellowed without any gaps. "The two eye-sockets on both sides" (*ubhayato ca akkhikūṭāni*) refers to the two corners of the eyes.
"Red" (*lohitakāni*) is stated in a way that includes all [parts]. "Very red" (*sulohitakāni*) means they are intensely red, with no visible openings.
"Black in the middle" (*majjhe kaṇhan*) means the central part of the eyes is black like collyrium. "Very black" (*sukaṇhan*)...
"Without internal gaps" (*antaravirahitaṃ*) means very black. "Lustrous" (*alūkhaṃ*) means pleasing to the eye. "Glossy" (*siniddhaṃ*) means refined.

"Like a bhadra-ariṭṭhaka fruit" means similar to a bhadra-ariṭṭhaka fruit from which the rind has been removed. There is also a textual reading, *addāriṭṭhakasamānaṃ*; its meaning is "like a ripe ariṭṭhaka fruit.
"White" (*odātaṃ*) is stated by way of including all [the qualities]. "Very white" (*suodātaṃ*) means without internal gaps, like a silver disk.
"Very white. By the two terms "white" and "pale," he shows an extreme whiteness.
"By the natural flesh-eye" means by the ordinary flesh-eye. "Included within the personal existence" means dependent upon the personal existence.
"Produced by kamma consisting of good conduct of body and so forth, generated in previous personal existences arisen here and there" means produced by such kamma. "All around..."
"He sees for a yojana" means that within a yojana extending four gāvutas on all sides, he perceives with his natural fleshly eye forms situated beyond walls and so forth, free from obstruction.
"Both by day and by night" means during the portion of the day and during the portion of the night. "Endowed with four factors" means [endowed] with four...
Endowed with all its parts, it was filled with darkness and devoid of light.

"The sun has set" means that the sun, which had risen producing a state of brilliance, has vanished. "And the dark fortnight, the Uposatha day" refers to the fourteenth-day Uposatha day within the dark fortnight.
"And a dense thicket of forest" refers to a thick mass of trees. "And a great black cloud has arisen" means a massive...
A black cloud and a mass of mist have arisen. A wall means a pile of bricks. A door means a door-panel, a window-lattice, or the like.
A rampart means a rampart made of clay and so forth. A mountain means a mountain of sand and so forth. A thicket means a thicket of young shrubs and the like.
A creeper means a creeper such as the *karavinda* and so forth. "An obstruction for the seeing of forms" means...
There is no prohibition against seeing visible objects as objects of perception.

"If one were to make a single sesame seed the sign" means if one were to take a single sesame seed as a mark of recognition. "One would throw it into a cartload of sesame" means one would cast it into two carts' worth of a heap of sesame.
Some, however, say that "a cartload (vāha) is more than two carts [worth] from a jar. That very same sesame seed—
"Should extract" means that one should extract and take only the sesame seed that was placed there for that purpose.
"With the divine eye" has the meaning already stated. "Purified" means purified because it is the cause for the purification of view through seeing the passing away and rebirth;
for he who sees only the passing away and not the rebirth adopts the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*). He who...
One who sees only rebirth and not passing away adopts the eternalist view that new beings come into existence.
However, one who sees both of these transcends both types of such views;
therefore, his vision becomes a cause for purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*), and it is this very vision that the sons of the Buddha possess. Thus it was said:
“It is ‘purified’ because it is the cause for the purification of view through the seeing of beings passing away and being reborn.

It should be understood as “surpassing the human” because it sees forms after having transcended the human domain; or it is “surpassing the human” because it surpasses the human fleshly eye (*māṃsacakkhu*).
With that divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings—[not] with the human fleshly eye.

He observes beings as if they were [visible]. Regarding the phrase "passing away and being reborn": it is not possible to see with the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) at the precise moment of death (cutikkhaṇa) or the precise moment of rebirth (upapattikkhaṇa).
However, those who are near to death and will pass away shortly are intended by the term "passing away" (cavamāna);

and those who have already taken rebirth-connection (paṭisandhi) and have just been born are intended by the term "being reborn" (upapajjamāna). He [sees] such beings as passing away and being reborn.
And he shows that one "sees. "Inferior" means inferior because they are associated with the outflow of delusion (*moha*). "Superior" means the opposite of that.
"Beautiful" means endowed with a desirable, lovely, and pleasing color because they are associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adveṣa*);

"ugly" is the opposite of that—the meaning is "handsome" or "deformed. "Well-gone" means gone to a good destination; or, because they are associated with the outflow of non-greed (*alobha*), it means "wealthy" or "of great riches."
“Duggate” means those who have gone to a miserable state; or, because they are possessed of the outflow of greed, it refers to the poor who lack food and drink.

“Yathākammūpage” means those who have arrived according to whatever karma has been accumulated. Among these, the function of the divine eye is described by the preceding terms beginning with “passing away”;
however, by this present term, the function of the knowledge of rebirth according to karma is expressed.
And this is the sequence for the arising of that knowledge:
here, a bhikkhu, having extended his light toward the lower hells, sees beings in hell undergoing great suffering; that seeing is precisely the function of the divine eye.
He then attends to it thus: "Having performed what kind of kamma do these beings undergo this suffering?"
Then, the knowledge that takes that kamma as its object arises in him, [knowing], "Having performed this," and so forth.
Likewise, having extended the light upward toward the heavenly worlds, he sees beings in the Nandana Grove, the Missaka Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and so on, experiencing great prosperity.
That seeing, too, is precisely the function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). He reflects thus: "What indeed..."
“Having performed such-and-such karma, these beings experience this success. Then, the knowledge arises in him that “having performed this specific deed,” [this result follows];
this is called the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*). There is no separate preliminary exercise for this.
And as it is with this, so it is with the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*); for both are based solely upon the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
These [qualities] succeed together with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
In phrases such as “these indeed, sirs,” the word “these” is a demonstrative term referring to those things seen by the divine eye. “Vata” is a particle used in the sense of lamentation.
“Bhonto” means “sirs. “Duccarita” means ill-conduct; it is so called because it is conducted badly, or because it is conducted badly due to being rotten with defilements (*kilesa*).
"Bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*) means misconduct committed by the body, or misconduct that has arisen from the body. The same method applies to the others as well.
"Endowed with" (*samannāgatā*) means possessed of.

"Revilers of the noble ones" (*ariyūpavādakā*) refers to the noble ones—namely, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—even including lay followers who have attained the stream-entry fruit (*sotāpanna*).
"Desiring their harm" means being detractors by means of a final ground or by the destruction of their virtues; that is to say, they are abusers and reproachers.
In this context, one who says, "These have no ascetic quality (*samaṇadhamma*); these are not ascetics," detracts by means of a final ground.
One who says, "These have no meditative absorption (*jhāna*), nor liberation (*vimokkha*), nor the path (*magga*), nor the fruit (*phala*)," and so forth—

It should be understood that he reviles by disparaging the virtues [of the noble ones]. Whether he reviles one who possesses jhāna or one who does not possess jhāna, in either case it is indeed a reviling of the noble ones (*ariyūpavāda*).
It is an extremely heavy deed, similar to an immediate offense (*ānantariya-kamma*);
it is an obstruction to heaven and an obstruction to the Path, yet it is remediable. Therefore, if one who reviles a noble one goes [to them] and...
If one is senior to the other, one should sit in a squatting position and ask for forgiveness, saying: "I said this and that to the Venerable One;

may you forgive me for that. But if one is junior, one should pay homage, sit in a squatting position, raise one's joined palms, and ask for forgiveness, saying: "Venerable Sir, I said this and that to you; may you forgive me for that."
If he does not forgive, or has gone away to another region, one should go there oneself or send a student to ask for forgiveness.
If it is impossible to go or to send someone, one should go to those monks who are staying in that monastery;
if they are junior, one should sit on one's heels, and if they are senior, [one should prostrate].
Having approached the elder in the manner already described, one should say, "Venerable sir, I said such-and-such to the venerable one named so-and-so;
may that venerable one forgive me," and thus ask for forgiveness. Even if he does not forgive him in his presence, this same procedure must be followed.
If the monk is a wanderer and neither his place of residence nor his destination can be ascertained, [the following applies].
One should go to a wise bhikkhu and say: "Venerable sir, I spoke thus and so to the venerable one named so-and-so;
as I recall this again and again, remorse arises within me. What should I do?
He will reply: "Do not worry; the elder forgives you. Settle your mind."
Even ten people should raise their joined palms toward the direction where the Noble One has gone and say, "Forgive us.
If he has attained final Nibbāna, they should go to the place of his parinibbāna, and even as far as the charnel ground, ask for forgiveness.
When this is done, there is neither an obstruction to heaven nor an obstruction to the Path; it becomes exactly as it was before.

"Those of wrong view" means those with perverted vision. "Those who undertake actions based on wrong view" refers to those who, by way of wrong view, have undertaken various kinds of kamma, as well as those who encourage others in bodily actions and so forth rooted in wrong view.
And here, by the inclusion of verbal misconduct, the disparagement of the Noble Ones is included; and by the inclusion of mental misconduct, wrong view is included.
It should be understood that even though these two are already included [in the previous categories], they are mentioned again for the purpose of showing their extreme gravity.
For reviling the Noble Ones is extremely grave, being similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. And this has been said:
"Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, in this very life..."
"One might attain final knowledge regarding the Dhamma; I say, Sāriputta, that this is exactly how it is.
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell just as if one had been carried there.
Indeed, there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it has been said:
“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that is so greatly blameworthy as wrong view, monks. Wrong view, monks, is the foremost of things that are greatly blameworthy.
“At the breaking up of the body” means at the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been grasped. “After death” means at the seizing of the aggregates produced immediately thereafter.
Alternatively, “at the breaking up of the body” means the cutting off of the life-faculty. “After death” means subsequent to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).

"Apāya," and so forth—all these are synonyms for *niraya* (hell). Indeed, it is called *apāya* because it is devoid (*apeta*) of "gain" (*āya*)—namely, merit—which is the cause of heaven and liberation;
or because there is an absence of the arrival (*āya*) of happiness. It is called *duggati* because it is a destination (*gati*) of suffering or a refuge (*paṭisaraṇa*) for suffering;
or because it is a destination produced by defiled (*duṭṭha*) karma due to an abundance of hatred. Therein, beings fall down helpless.
"Those who commit wrongdoings" refers to the *vinipāta* (the state of falling away). It is called *vinipāta* because those who are perishing fall into it with their limbs and members shattered.
It is called *niraya* (hell) because there is no (*ni*) essence (*aya*) here that is perceived as a gratification.
Alternatively, by the mention of "the states of loss" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm; for the animal realm is a state of loss because it is departed from the happy destinies (*sugati*).

There is no miserable destination (*duggati*), because high-ranking beings such as the Nāga kings and others can arise there. By the mention of "miserable destination," he indicates the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*);
for that is both a state of loss (*apāya*) and a miserable destination, since it is devoid of happiness and has become a place of suffering.
However, it is not a "fall" (*vinipāta*), because it does not fall [into degradation] in the same way as the host of Asuras. By the mention of "fall," he indicates the host of Asuras.
For indeed, in the sense already stated, it is called a "state of loss" (*apāya*), a "bad destination" (*duggati*), and a "fall" (*vinipāta*) because of its falling away from all elevations.
By the mention of "hell," he illustrates hell itself in its many varieties, such as Avīci and others. "Reborn" (*upapannā*) means having gone there;
the intention is that they have been produced (*abhinibbattā*) therein. The "bright side" (*sukkapa-kkha*) should be understood by reversing what has been said.
However, this is the distinction: therein, by the inclusion of "a happy destination" (*sugatī*), the human destination is also included;

by the inclusion of "heaven" (*sagga*), only the divine destination is meant. Therein, a "happy destination" (*sugati*) is a beautiful destination. A "heaven" (*sagga*) is that which is a supreme (*agga*) state through its objects such as forms and so forth.
All of that is called a "world" (*loka*) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating; such is the etymological meaning. Thus, "with the divine eye," and so forth.
This is the entire concluding statement.

"Thus he sees with the divine eye"—this is the summary of the meaning here: the knowledge of the divine eye operates upon four kinds of objects by way of being limited, present, internal, and external.
The knowledge of the destiny according to deeds operates by way of being limited, sublime, past, internal, and external.

It occurs with respect to five objects. Knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) occurs with respect to eight objects by way of being limited, sublime, immeasurable, a path, the future, internal, external, and indeterminate.
"And the Blessed One, if he so desired" means the Blessed One, if he wished. "He might see even a single world-system" means a single world-sphere (cakkavāḷa).

One should observe. Regarding the phrase "even a thousand [worlds] is a minor [system]," here, as far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating and shining throughout the quarters, so far extends the world-system;
this is called a minor thousandfold system (*sahassacūḷanikā*). "Minor" (*cūḷanikā*) means small.
Regarding "even two thousand [worlds] is a medium world-system," here it is calculated by taking a thousandfold portion of a thousand *cakkavāḷas*.
A system of two thousand middle world-systems, measuring one million four hundred thousand world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*), is called a "second-order intermediate world-system.

By this much, the so-called birth-field (*jātikkhetta*) of the Buddhas is shown. For on the day Bodhisattvas pass away from the deva-world in their final existence and take rebirth in the mother’s womb, as well as on the day they emerge from the mother’s womb and on the day of the Great Renunciation—

And on the days of his full enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the relinquishing of the life-faculty, and the final Nibbāna, this much extent shakes—namely, a *tisahassī* world-system.
Regarding the term "a *tisahassī* world-system": starting from the first thousand, the third [thousand] is called a *tisahassī*;

because the first thousand is calculated by multiplying it tenfold (to form a second thousand), and that middle thousand is then calculated by multiplying it tenfold again, it is called "great" (*mahā*).
"Mahāsahassī" means that which is calculated by thousands. By this much, the world is shown to have the measure of one hundred thousand times ten million *cakkavāḷas*.
However, the Elder Gaṇakaputtatissa said thus: "This is not the measure of a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system (*tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātu*).
For this is merely a place lost from oral tradition based on the teachers' recitations; its measure is actually one hundred thousand times ten million *cakkavāḷas*."
"But the place [of its reach] is called the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system. By this much, the so-called "field of the Blessed One's command" has been shown.

For within this range, the command of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, the Isigili Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Bojjhaṅga Paritta, the Khandha Paritta, the Mora Paritta, the Mettā Paritta, and the Ratana Paritta extends.
"Or as much as he might wish" means however much he may desire. By this, the field of the objective domain is shown.
For there is no limit or measurement to the field of the objective domain of the Buddhas; and regarding its being limitless, they bring forward this simile:
"If one were to fill a hundred thousand million world-systems up to the Brahma-world with mustard seeds..."
Suppose someone were to come along from the eastern direction, dropping a single mustard seed into each world-system (*cakkavāḷa*);
all those mustard seeds would eventually be exhausted. Yet, the world-systems of the eastern direction would not be exhausted. The same applies to the southern direction and the others as well.
In that regard, there is nothing that is beyond the range of the Buddhas. "He would see so much" means he would look over such a vast extent.
Thus he concluded the discourse on the divine eye, stating that the Blessed One’s divine eye is thus completely pure.
How is it that the Blessed One has his eye opened even by the eye of wisdom? In what manner does he have his eye uncovered by the eye of wisdom?
The passage beginning with "He is of great wisdom, of wide wisdom," and ending with "in this respect he surpasses others, namely, by wisdom," has its meaning already explained below.
"By the Buddha-eye" means by the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*) and by the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*).

These two knowledges are named the "Buddha-eye"; the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) is the "Universal Eye" (*samanta-cakkhu*); and the three knowledges of the paths (*magga-ñāṇa*) are the "Dhamma-eye" (*dhamma-cakkhu*).
"Looking over the world, he saw beings" means he beheld beings. Regarding the passage beginning with "with little dust in their eyes," etc.:
Those in whom, by the method already stated, there is little dust of lust and so forth in the eye of wisdom are those with little dust in their eyes (*apparajakkha*).
Those in whom that dust is great are those with much dust in their eyes (*mahārajakkha*). Those whose faculties such as faith are sharp are those with sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*).
Those whose faculties are dull are those with dull faculties (*mudindriya*). Those whose very modes of faith and so forth are beautiful are those of good disposition (*svākāra*).
Those who perceive the reasons that have been stated can easily be made to understand; they are "easy to instruct" (*suviññāpayā*).
Those who view both the next world and moral fault as a source of fear are called "those who see the next world and moral fault with fear.

"In a lotus grove" means in a forest of blue lotuses. The same method applies to the others as well. "Those whose nourishment is submerged within" refers to those whose [roots] are indeed submerged inside.
They will nourish it. "Standing having risen above the water" means they stand having transcended the water.
Among them, those that stand having risen above [the water] are standing awaiting contact with the sun's rays and are destined to flower today.
Those that stand level with the water are destined to flower tomorrow. Those that have not risen above the water...
The *antonimuggaposīni* (those nourished within the mud) are those that bloom on the very third day.
However, there are also other water-born lotuses called *saroga-uppalāni* (diseased lotuses) which will not bloom at all and will become food for fish and turtles;
these have not been included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), but they are explained here after having been brought forward.

Just as there are those four kinds of flowers, even so there are four types of persons: one who gains knowledge through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*), one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*), one who is led to understanding (*neyyo*), and one for whom the words are the limit (*padaparamo*).
That person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs at the very moment it is uttered is called a person who gains knowledge through a brief indication.
That person for whom [realization occurs] when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is being analyzed in detail...
There is the realization of the Dhamma; this person is called one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition.

That person for whom there is realization of the Dhamma by means of recitation, questioning, wise attention, and by serving, associating with, and attending upon spiritual friends—this person is called one who is to be guided.
That person for whom [realization occurs] even though hearing much and speaking much...
Even for one who retains much and recites much, there is no realization of the Dhamma in that very lifetime; such a person is called "one for whom the words are the limit.

In this regard, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world system as if it were a grove of blue lotuses and so forth, [distinguishes] those who are "to be known by a condensed teaching" (*ugghaṭitaññū*) based on those who will flower today, and those who are "to be known by an expanded teaching" (*vipañcitaññū*) based on those who will flower tomorrow; thus he [knows them] in every aspect.
And he saw this. In that regard, for three types of persons, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma accomplishes its purpose within this very lifetime;
for those for whom the words are the limit, it serves as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) for the sake of the future.

Regarding the terms "one of lustful temperament" (*rāgacarita*) and so forth: one who has the quality of moving toward an object by way of lust is "one of lustful temperament. By way of hatred... [the same structure applies].
One who has "wandering" upon an object (*ārammaṇa*) as their characteristic is one of a hating temperament (*dosacarita*).

One who has wandering upon an object through the power of delusion is one of a deluded temperament (*mohacarita*). One who has wandering upon an object through the power of applied thought (*vitakka*) and investigation (*ūhana*) is one of a speculative temperament (*vitakkacarita*).
One who has wandering upon an object through the power of faith consisting in conviction (*okappana-saddhā*) is one of a faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*). Knowledge itself is the wandering.
One who has "conduct through knowledge," "conduct belonging to knowledge," or "conduct originating from knowledge" is called *ñāṇacarita*.
"Of one of lustful temperament" (*rāgacarita*) means one in whom lust is prominent, one who abounds in lust. The same method applies to the following cases as well.
"He speaks a discourse on foulness" means he explains the discourse connected with the ten kinds of foulness, beginning with the bloated (*uddhumātaka*).

For this has been said: “The meditation on the foul (asubha) is to be developed for the abandoning of lust. He explains the development of loving-kindness (mettābhāvanā) means he speaks of the cultivation of affection for the mind.
For this has been said: “Loving-kindness is to be developed for the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda). “Recitation” (uddesa) refers to the rehearsing of the text.
“Inquiry” (paripucchā) refers to the commentary (aṭṭhakathā). “Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time” means at the appropriate and fitting time for further [instruction].
"Listening to the Dhamma of the scriptures. "Discussion of the Dhamma" means discussion with others.
"Living in association with teachers" means attending upon one's teachers. "He establishes them" means he settles them in the presence of the teachers.
"He explains mindfulness of breathing" means he teaches the meditation subject associated with mindfulness of breathing. For this has been said: "Mindfulness of breathing should be developed..."
“For the cutting off of applied thought. “He explains a sign that inspires confidence” means he speaks a discourse that generates confidence, such as the *Cūḷavedalla* or the *Mahāvedalla*.
“The Buddha’s excellent enlightenment” refers to the Blessed Buddha’s penetration of Buddhahood.
“The Dhamma’s excellence as Dhamma” refers to the well-expounded nature of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. “The Saṅgha’s excellent practice” refers to...
He explains the excellent practice of the eightfold Noble Saṅgha, such as their being well-practiced; and "his own virtues" means the virtues belonging to himself.
