He explains the sign of insight—that is, he speaks in connection with arising and passing away, and so forth.

The aspect of impermanence is the aspect of non-existence after having been; the aspect of suffering is the aspect of oppression by arising and passing away; the aspect of non-self is the aspect of lack of mastery.
"Like one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain": this means standing right there on the solid, rock-made summit of a mountain;
for one standing there, there is no need to turn the neck or stretch out the head in order to see.
"Tathūpamaṃ" (like that) means resembling that, comparable to a rocky mountain. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: just as [one sees] from the summit of a rocky mountain...
Just as a man standing might look all around at the people, so too, O Sumedha of beautiful wisdom, may the Blessed One—
the All-Seeing One with the knowledge of omniscience— having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and made of wisdom, himself free from sorrow,
look upon and consider the people who have fallen into sorrow and are overcome by birth and old age. May he take them into account and examine them.

This, however, is the intended meaning here: Suppose, for instance, a man were to clear a large field near the foot of a mountain, build huts there among the field boundaries, and kindle a fire at night; and suppose there were a fourfold darkness [of night, clouds, mist, and smoke];
then, while that man stands on the summit of the mountain and looks down upon the ground with his eyes open—
Neither fields nor field boundaries, nor huts, nor the people sleeping there would be visible;

rather, from the huts, only the flickering of fire-flames would be seen. Thus, for the Tathāgata who has ascended the Palace of Dhamma and surveys the host of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds appear to his Buddha-eye even when they are sitting on their right knees in a solitary dwelling.
Those who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within his range; they are like arrows shot at night.
However, those individuals to be trained who have performed wholesome deeds come within his range even if they are standing far away; they alone are like fire or like Mount Himavanta.
And this has been said:
“The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himālaya mountain;
the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.

Regarding “omniscient knowledge” (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*): herein, one who has known all that is divided into the five paths of guidance is “all-knowing” (*sabbaññū*). [This includes] the divisions of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), and so forth.
For all phenomena (dhammas) consist of five objects of knowledge (neyyapathas): conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), change (vikāra), characteristics (lakkhaṇa), Nibbāna, and designations (paññatti).

The state of being omniscient is omniscience (sabbaññutā); that very omniscience is knowledge, and while it should be called "knowledge of omniscience" (sabbaññutā-ñāṇa), it is stated as "knowledge of omniscience" (sabbaññutaññāṇa). Furthermore, the term "omniscient one" (sabbaññū) refers to one who is omniscient in succession (kama-sabbaññū), one who is omniscient all at once (sakiṃ-sabbaññū), one who is constantly omniscient (satata-sabbaññū), one who is omniscient by power (satti-sabbaññū), and one who is omniscient through knowing (ñāta-sabbaññū).
There would be five kinds of omniscient ones. Among them, *kamasabbaññutā* (gradual omniscience) does not exist because it is impossible for there to be a time when all things are known sequentially;
*sakisabbaññutā* (simultaneous omniscience) does not exist because there is no grasping of all objects at once;

and *satatasabbaññutā* (constant omniscience) [does not exist] because consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness arise according to their respective objects, because it is opposed to the *bhavaṅga*-consciousness, and because there is a lack of logical consistency.

It does not exist; rather, there may be either "power-omniscience" (*satti-sabbaññutā*), due to the capacity to know all things by way of exclusion, or "knowledge-omniscience" (*ñāta-sabbaññutā*), due to having known all phenomena.
It is not tenable to claim that one possessing power-omniscience lacks the state of knowing all things, because it has been said: "There is nothing here that he has not seen...
[and so on]... he is the one with the universal eye. Therefore, only knowledge-omniscience is tenable.
For this being so, omniscience itself exists by way of function, by way of non-delusion, by way of the establishment of the cause, and by way of being bound to adverting.
"By that knowledge" means by that knowledge which knows all.
Again, for the purpose of establishing the state of omniscience through another method, he spoke the verse beginning with "Not of that. Therein:

"There is nothing whatsoever unseen by him": for that Tathāgata, in this world of the three realms (*tedhātuka*) or in this present time, there is not even the slightest thing called "unseen" that does not exist or is not found.
The word *atthi* is a verb expressing the present tense; by this, [it refers to] that which belongs to the present time.
This shows that all phenomena (dhammas) are objects of knowledge. Furthermore, the letter *da* is employed here for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.
Regarding the phrase "and also what is unknown" (*atho aviññātaṃ*): here, *atha* is a particle used for the purpose of taking up the preceding statement.

As for *aviññātaṃ*, it refers to past time; the ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*) is: "there was no class of phenomena whatsoever that was not known. When the indeclinable word *atthi* ("is") is understood, the ellipsis is supplied.
It is indeed appropriate even without [the negative particle]. By this, he shows that all phenomena belonging to the past are objects of knowledge.
"That which is not to be known" means that there will be no class of phenomena belonging to the future that is not to be known;
by this, he shows that all phenomena belonging to the future are objects of knowledge. Or rather, here the vowel *a-* is merely a specific modification of the act of knowing. All...

Regarding the phrase "he directly knew whatever is to be known": here, whatever category of phenomena there is that is to be known (*neyya*)—whether pertaining to the three times or transcending time—the Tathāgata directly knew all of it;
he knew and penetrated it by means of his superior knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
In this context, because both what pertains to the three times and what is timeless are included by the word "is" (*atthi*), the word *atthi* [signifies both existence and the knowable].
He is to be seen as indeed the imperishable (abyayabhūta).
Because his vision extends everywhere—both in terms of time and space—his eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu) functions universally and without limitation; thus he is "all-seeing" (samantacakkhu).
For that reason stated above, it is said that the Tathāgata is all-seeing and omniscient (sabbaññū). This verse is expressed by way of the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
Through this teaching, omniscient knowledge is established.
It is not based on "itihitiha," meaning there is no such thing as "thus, indeed, it was; thus, indeed, it was. It is not based on "itikirā," meaning there is no such thing as "this, indeed, is so.
It is not based on "paramparā," meaning it does not arise even from traditional oral reports. It is not based on "piṭakasampadā" (the acquisition of the Pitakas).
"It does not coincide with our own Piṭaka tradition" means it is not so. "Not because of reasoning" means it is not so even by grasping at logic.
"Not by reflection on modes" means it is not so even by reflecting on a reason such as, "This is a beautiful argument.
"Not by approval through the contemplation of views" means [it is not so] by a view accepted by us after having contemplated and approved it.
Nor does it mean "it comes together with.
Alternatively, regarding the term *samādhi*: here, *samādhi* refers to the one-pointedness of wholesome consciousness. In what sense is it *samādhi*? In the sense of "concentrating" (*samādhāna*).
What is this so-called concentrating? It is the even and correct [state] of consciousness and mental factors upon a single object.

And "placing" (ādhāna) means "establishing. Therefore, that power of a particular state (dhamma) by which the mind and mental factors remain upon a single object—remaining even, rightly, undistracted, and unscattered—this should be understood as "concentration" (samādhāna).
Now, regarding that concentration:
“Non-distraction is its characteristic; the destruction of distraction is its function;
unshakability is its manifestation; and bliss is its proximate cause.

Concentration (samādhi) stands upon the object by way of being undisturbed and immovable; thus it is called “stability” (ṭhiti). The following two words [in the original verse] are due to the addition of prefixes.
It is "increased" (*vaḍḍhita*). Furthermore, it is "stability" (*saṇṭhiti*) because it stands having gathered together the associated states upon the object.
It is "steadiness" (*avaṭṭhiti*) because it stands having plunged into and entered the object. For in the wholesome side, only four factors plunge into the object:
faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, faith is called "conviction" (*okappanā*), and mindfulness is called "non-forgetfulness" (*apilāpanatā*).
Concentration is "stability," and wisdom is "penetration. On the unwholesome side, however, three factors penetrate the object:
craving, views, and ignorance; for that very reason, these are called "floods" (*ogha*). But here, one-pointedness of mind is not strong.
For just as when a place where whitewash has been applied is sprinkled with water and smoothed over, it remains so only for a short time...
Dust settles, and as it dries and dries further, it rises again in its natural state; in the same way, one-pointedness of mind is not strong on the side of the unwholesome.
It is "non-distraction" because it is the opposite of the distracted state that occurs through restlessness and doubt. Precisely by way of restlessness and doubt...
A wandering mind is said to be "distracted. However, since this [state] is not such distraction, it is "non-distraction" (*avikkhepa*).
It is by way of restlessness and doubt that the mind is called "agitated," being dragged here and there;
since this is the state of one whose mind is thus unagitated, it is "unagitated-mindedness" (*avisāhaṭamānasatā*). "Tranquility" (*samatha*) is threefold tranquility.
“Calm of mind, calm of legal issues, and calm of all formations. In this context, one-pointedness of mind within the eight attainments is called “calm of mind.
For by depending upon it, the wavering and agitation of the mind are calmed and stilled;

therefore, it is called “calm of mind. The sevenfold method of settling [legal issues], beginning with resolution in the presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), is [the calm of legal issues]. As for the calm of all formations: [it is the cessation of all conditioned things].
“Settling of legal issues” (adhikaraṇasamatha) means this: by relying upon it, various legal issues are settled and pacified;

therefore, it is called “the settling of legal issues. Furthermore, because all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are settled and pacified by relying upon Nibbāna, it is called “the stilling of all conditioned phenomena” (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha). In this [context]...
Here, tranquility of mind is intended. It is the faculty of concentration because it exercises lordship over the characteristic of concentration.
It is the power of concentration because it is unshakable by restlessness. "Right concentration" refers to concentration according to reality and liberating concentration. 157.
Then the Blessed One [taught] because the restraint of the faculties is the protection of virtue, or because of this sequence...

This teaching being expounded was suitable for those deities; therefore, demonstrating the path of practice beginning with the restraint of the sense faculties, the passage starting with "With the eyes...
is commenced. Therein, "with the eyes he should not be fickle" means that he should not be fickle with his eyes by way of looking at things that ought not to be seen and so forth.
"He should shut his ear to village talk" means that he should close his ear to worldly, trivial conversation.
"By way of the rolling of the eye" means by way of the rolling that arises at the eye-door.

"What has not been seen is to be seen" means it is appropriate to look upon a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) never seen before. "What has been seen is to be transcended" means it is appropriate to transcend a visible object already seen before.
"From garden to garden" means from a flower-garden and so forth to a fruit-garden and so forth, or from a flower-garden and so forth [to another].
"Long journeying" means long walking. "Unsettled journeying" means wandering without reaching a conclusion.
"Is intent upon seeing forms" means he is repeatedly engaged for the purpose of seeing forms as objects.
"Has entered among the houses" means he has entered within the threshold. "Has set out upon the street" means [he has entered] the inner street.
"Immersed. "Looking at the faces of houses" means looking toward the doors of houses. "Gazing upward" means looking upward with one's face turned toward the upper direction.
"Having seen a form with the eye" refers to that which is capable of seeing forms, conventionally designated as "the eye" by way of its causal function.
"Having seen a visible form with eye-consciousness. However, the ancients have said: "The eye does not see the form because it is devoid of consciousness;

the consciousness does not see because it is devoid of the eye. But when there is a convergence of the door and the object, one sees by means of the consciousness that has the sensitive matter as its basis.
This, however, is a 'figurative expression' (sasambhārakathā)—like saying 'one pierces with a bow'—whereby the instrument is used for the agent. Therefore..."
"Having seen a form with eye-consciousness"—this is the meaning here.

"One who grasps at signs" (nimittaggāhī) means that one grasps at a sign—either the sign of a woman or a man, or a sign such as beauty—which serves as a basis for defilements, by way of desire and lust; one does not stop at the mere sight [of the object].

"One who grasps at secondary characteristics" (anubyañjanaggāhī): it is called a "secondary characteristic" (anubyañjana) because it makes the defilements manifest by following after and conforming to them.
It grasps the signs (ākāra) that have acquired conventional designations, which are divided into hand, foot, smile, laugh, speech, looking forward, looking around, and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ," it means: by reason of which, and because of which lack of restraint of the eye-faculty, these covetousnesses and so forth [arise] in this person who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained by the bolt of mindfulness, having left the door of the eye unshut.

“Dhammas might flow in, adhere, and overwhelm him. “He does not practice for its restraint” means he does not practice for the purpose of closing the door of that eye-faculty with the bolt of mindfulness.
One who is thus disposed does not guard the eye-faculty; he is also said to “not attain restraint over the eye-faculty. In this regard:
Furthermore, although there is neither restraint nor non-restraint in the eye-faculty— for mindfulness or forgetfulness does not arise depending on the sensitivity of the eye—
nevertheless, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye,
after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu) performs the function of adverting.
Having arisen, it ceases; then eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing; then the mind-element performs the function of receiving;
then the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element performs the function of investigating;
then the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises and ceases while accomplishing the function of determining; immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) runs its course.
Even there, neither restraint nor non-restraint exists during the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), nor during any of the moments such as adverting (āvajjana).

However, at the moment of impulsion (javana), if immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, or laziness arises, there is non-restraint. When this occurs, it is called "non-restraint in the eye-faculty."

It is so called. Why? Because when that non-restraint exists, not only is the door unguarded, but the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the process-thoughts such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth are also unguarded.

How is this so? Just as when the four gates of a city are left unsecured, even though the inner house doors, gate-towers, inner chambers, and so on are secured, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded. By way of the city gate—

For just as thieves, having entered [a house], would do whatever they desire, even so, when unwholesome states such as immorality arise in the "swift" mind, if there is no restraint, the door is unprotected, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting (āvajjana).
"Given by faith" means given after having faith in karma, its fruit, this world, and the world beyond. "This..."
The meaning is that they were not given with the thought, "He is my kinsman," or "He is my friend," or "He will repay this for me," or "This was done for him by him before.
For when given in such a way, they are not called "gifts of faith" (*saddhādeyya*). Furthermore, the term "foods" (*bhojana*) is merely a heading for the teaching;
in actual fact, however, it refers to those who, having eaten foods that are gifts of faith, having put on robes [that are gifts of faith], and making use of lodgings [that are gifts of faith].
"Consuming medicinal requisites as a support for the sick"—all this has already been explained.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "what is it? Regarding "dancing":
whatever dancing there may be, it is not permitted even for one walking on the road to see it by stretching out the neck. "Singing" means whatever singing there may be. "Instrumental music" means...
Any kind of instrumental music. They watch theatrical performances (*naṭasamajja*). They listen to recitations such as the *Bhārata* and *Rāmāyaṇa*;
it is not even permissible to go to the place where these are being told. *Pāṇissara* refers to cymbals (*kaṃsatāḷa*), though some also call them "hand-clapping" (*pāṇitāḷa*).
*Vetāla* refers to a drum (*ghanatāḷa*), while others say it is "the raising of a dead body by means of a spell. *Kumbhatūṇa*...
The square drum (*caturassa-ambaṇaka-tāḷa*); some also call it the "pot-sound" (*kumbha-sadda*). The *sobhanaka* is the sprinkling of actors;
or, it is that which produces beauty, meaning a brilliant display, as it were. The *caṇḍāla* is a game with iron balls;
they also say it is "the hemp-washing game of the caṇḍālas. The *vaṃsa* is playing by raising up a bamboo pole (*veṇu*).
"Bone-washing" refers to the washing of bones. It is said that in certain regions, when a relative dies, they do not cremate them, but bury them.
Then, perceiving that their bodies have become putrid, they exhume them, wash the bones, smear them with perfumes, and set them aside.
At the time of a festival, they place those bones in one spot... [and so on].
Having set out liquor and other such things in their places, they drink the liquor while weeping and lamenting. And this has also been said:
"Monks, there is among the people of the southern provinces a place called Dhovana;
there one finds food, drink, hard food, soft food, food to be licked, food to be sucked, dancing, singing, and instrumental music. There is, monks, a certain Dhovana..."
"I do not say that this does not exist. However, some say that "washing with a magic trick" refers to washing bones.
In elephant battles and the like, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to fight with elephants and so forth, nor to cause them to fight, nor to watch them fighting.
"Wrestling" (nibbuddha) means boxing. "Combat" (uyyodhika) refers to where there is a clash of arms.
It is given. "Stronghold" (*balagga*) means a place for counting troops. "Array of the army" (*senābyūha*) means the encampment of the army;

it refers to the stationing of the army by way of the chariot-array (*sakaṭabyūha*) and so forth. "Viewing the divisions" (*anīkadassana*) means the viewing of the divisions as described in such passages as, "Three elephants constitute the rear elephant-division," and so on.
"He does not seize upon signs" means that he does not grasp the sign of the kind described above by way of desire and lust.
The remaining phrases should also be understood in the manner opposite to what was stated.

And just as, when unwholesome states such as immorality arise in the sub-consciousness (javana) below, the door remains unprotected due to that lack of restraint, so too do the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), and the other process-consciousnesses remain unprotected.

It has been said: likewise here, when those [virtues] such as moral discipline (*sīla*) have arisen, the sense doors become guarded, as do the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the process-thoughts beginning with adverting (*āvajjana*).

How so? Just as when the city gates are closed, even though the interior houses and so forth may be unsecured, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain well-guarded and well-protected; so too at the city gates...

When the doors are closed, there is no entry for thieves. In the same way, when virtue and the other factors have arisen in the impulsion (javana), the door is guarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the process-thoughts beginning with adverting. Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called "restraint of the eye-faculty.
Beyond this, the meaning should be understood according to the methods explained both below and above.
"Visūkadassanā" means from the sight of spectacles. "Gāmakathā" is the talk of village-dwellers. "Bāttiṃsā" means thirty-two.
Because they do not lead to the paths of heaven or liberation, they are called "tiracchānakathā," meaning talk that is like an animal (or a by-path).
Regarding that, concerning kings, it is in such a manner as: "Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, Dhammāsoka—such was their great majesty," and so forth.

Discourse on kings is "king-talk. This same method applies to discourse on thieves and so forth. Among these, talk concerning the household—such as, "That king is handsome and beautiful to behold"—is indeed "animal-talk" (tiracchāna-kathā).

However, talk that proceeds thus, "Even he, who possessed such great power, has come to destruction," remains within the state of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Regarding thieves as well: "Mūladeva was so powerful..."
To say, “Meghamāla was so greatly powerful,” based on their deeds, or “Oh, what heroes!”—such talk concerning worldly dwellings is frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).

Even regarding battles such as the Mahābhārata war, talk of how “so-and-so was killed by so-and-so in this way” or “pierced in that way,” when conducted out of a desire for sensual gratification (*kāmasādava*), is frivolous talk.
However, talk that proceeds thus: “Even they have indeed come to destruction,” is [not frivolous].
In all cases, it is simply the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, regarding food and so forth, it is not permissible to speak by way of sensual gratification (*kāmasāda*), thinking, "We have eaten, drunk, and enjoyed such food as this, which is thus beautiful in color, fragrant, flavorful, and endowed with pleasant texture"; rather, it should be spoken purposefully (*sātthakaṃ*).
However, after having done so, it is appropriate to say, “In the past, we gave food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, and perfumes—
endowed with such excellence of color and other qualities— to those possessed of virtue, and we performed worship at the cetiya.
But in conversations regarding kinsmen and the like, one may say, “Our kinsmen are brave and capable,” or, “In the past, we traveled about in such various kinds of vehicles.”

It is not permissible to speak of them by way of attachment; however, it is permissible to speak of them for a valid purpose, such as saying, "Those relatives of ours have also met their end," or "In the past, we gave sandals of this kind to the Saṅgha.

Discussion of villages is also permitted when referring to whether they are well-situated or poorly situated, well-supplied with food or lacking in food, and so forth, such as saying, "The inhabitants of that village are brave and capable."

It is not permissible to speak in this way by way of gratification (*assāda*); however, it is permissible to say "faithful and confident" or "gone to destruction and vanishing" provided it is done for a purpose.
The same principle applies to talk concerning cities, towns, and countries. Talk concerning women is also [permissible] based on their complexion, shape, and so forth.

It is not appropriate [to speak] by way of relishing (*assāda*), such as: "The faithful one has passed away. It is only appropriate to say: "He was full of faith; he has reached destruction and passing away. Even regarding talk of heroes, it is not appropriate to say by way of relishing:
"The warrior named Nandamitta was a hero. It is only appropriate to say: "He was full of faith;
he has reached destruction and passing away. Even regarding talk of streets, it is not appropriate [to say]: "Such-and-such a street is well-built, ill-built, or inhabited by heroes..."
“Capable”—this is not permissible by way of attachment (*assāda*). “Faithful, confident, having reached the end of destruction and passing away”—only this is permissible.
Regarding the “story of the water-jar woman”: it is a story about a place with water, also called a “story of a bathing ford,” or a story of a slave-girl carrying a jar.
Even that is not permissible by way of attachment as “graceful, skilled in dancing and singing”; rather, it is permissible by way of such [phrases] as “faithful, confident.”

It is appropriate according to the method. "Talk about the departed" (pubbapetakathā) refers to talk concerning deceased relatives; the determination (vinicchaya) therein is the same as for talk concerning living relatives.
"Talk on diversity" (nānattakathā) refers to various other pointless conversations that are distinct from the preceding and succeeding types of talk.
"Talk on worldly speculation" (lokakkhāyikā) includes such things as: "By whom was this world created? It was created by one named so-and-so," or "The crow is white because of its bones..."
“Because of its own nature, the crane is red; because of the redness of blood, it is red”—such are the frivolous, contentious conversations of the Lokāyata.
As for the so-called "explanations of the ocean": why is the ocean called *sāgara*? It is called *sāgara* because it was dug by the god Sāgara;
it is called *samudda* because he personally announced by means of a hand-gesture, “It has been dug by me”—such are the useless explanations of the ocean.

"Becoming" (*bhava*) means increase; "non-becoming" (*abhava*) means decrease. Thus, whatever useless reason one might state regarding "becoming" or "non-becoming," such talk is called "talk about becoming and non-becoming.
"Would obstruct" (*āvareyya*) means would create an obstruction.
"Would prevent" (*nivāreyya*) means would ward off from the object. "Would restrain" (*saṃvareyya*) means completely and thoroughly.
"Having made a choice" means having selected. "He would guard" means he would provide protection. "He would hide" means he would conceal. "He would cover" means he would make a covering.
"He would cut off" means he would sever the flow.

"They are not satisfied by this or that" means they do not attain contentment with this or that taste, such as sourness and so forth. "They seek further and further" means they search higher and higher.

"158. 'By contact' means by the contact that is a disease. 'And one should not long for existence' means that for the sake of dispelling that contact, one should not yearn for existence such as the existence of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*) and so forth.

'And one should not tremble at fears' means that one should not tremble at fears such as lions, tigers, and so on, which serve as conditions for that contact; or [one should not tremble] at the remaining objects of the nose-faculty and the mind-faculty."
One should not tremble. In this way, the complete restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) is said to be fulfilled.

Alternatively, having shown the restraint of the sense faculties by means of the preceding [passages], he shows by this [passage] that "one dwelling in the forest, upon seeing or hearing something terrifying, should not tremble.
"By one aspect" means by one cause. "Fear and terror are indeed that same thing" means both fear and terror are that very same thing.
And both the small and the large are merely signs of terror. To demonstrate this very point, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth.
"Fear" (bhaya) is the fear arisen on account of that [sign]. "Terrifying" (bhayānaka) is a description of its mode. "Trembling" (chambhitatta) is the shaking of the limbs due to fear.
"Horripilation" (lomahaṃsa) is the bristling or standing up of the body hairs. By these two terms, [the meaning is given] from the perspective of function (kicca).
Having shown fear, he then shows it by way of its intrinsic nature as "agitation and terror of the mind. *Ubbegga* means one who is fearful; *utrāsa* means agitation of the mind.
"Fear of birth" is the fear that arises dependent upon birth. The same method applies to the others as well. "Fear arising from a king" is *rājabhaya*.
The same method applies to the others as well. "Fear of self-reproach" refers to one who has committed evil deeds.
The fear arising from self-reproach. The fear of reproach by others is the fear arising from being reproached by another.
The fear of punishment is the fear arising with respect to the punishment administered by a king for a householder, or the disciplinary punishment of the Vinaya for one who has gone forth.
The fear of an unhappy rebirth is the fear arising with respect to the four states of misery. The fear of waves is...
The fear arising for one descending into the water of the great ocean.
It is said that in the great ocean, the wave called Mahinda rises sixty yojanas, the wave called Taraṅgavīci fifty yojanas, and the wave called Rohaṇavīci forty yojanas.
The fear of waves is that which arises in dependence on such surges. [The fear] arising from the *kumbhīla* (crocodile)...
The fear of crocodiles is *kumbhīlabhaya*. The fear arising from whirlpools in the water is *āvaṭṭabhaya*. A *susukā* is called a fierce fish; the fear arising from that is *susukābhaya*.
The fear regarding livelihood (*ājīvikabhaya*) is the fear concerning one's means of subsistence. The fear of ill-repute (*asilokabhaya*) is the fear of censure.

159. "Having obtained [food], one should not make a store": having obtained any of these things, such as food and so forth, in accordance with the Dhamma, one should not make a store, thinking, "It is difficult to obtain while living in a forest dwelling."

*Odana* (boiled rice) is produced from the grains of the seven types of crops—rice (*sāli*), *vīhi*, barley (*yava*), wheat (*godhuma*), millet (*kaṅgu*), panic seed (*varaka*), and *kudrūsaka*—as well as from grains that are similar to these.
*Kummāsa* (gruel) is produced from barley. *Sattu* (flour) is flour made from rice and other such grains. *Maca* (fish) originates from water.
*Maṃsa* (meat) is well known. *Ambapāna* (mango drink) is a beverage made from mangoes, whether raw or ripe.

In that regard, one making it with raw ingredients should break open young mangoes, place them in water, cook them by the heat of the sun, strain them, and then mix them with honey, sugar, camphor, and so forth, which have been received on that very day.
*Jambupāna* is a drink made from jambu fruits. *Cocapāna* is a drink made from the seeds and the fruit of the plantain (*kadalī*).
*Mocapāna* is a drink made from *kadalī* fruits that have no seeds. *Madhukapāna* is a drink made from the natural juice of *madhuka* flowers;
however, it is permissible when mixed with water, but not when pure.
*Muddikapāna* is a drink made by crushing *muddika* grapes in water, prepared like mango-juice. *Sālūkapāna* refers to the root-bulbs (*sālūka*) of red and blue lotuses and so forth.
"Having crushed [the fruit] and made a drink. "Phārusaka-drink" means a drink made from *phārusaka* mangoes. "Kosamba-drink" means a drink made from *kosamba* fruits.
"Kola-drink" means a drink made from *kola* fruits. "Badara-drink" means a drink made from large *kola*-fruits, like a drink made from mangoes.
These are the eleven drinks; these too are permitted when they have been ripened by the sun.
"Ghatapāna" means drinking ghee. "Telapāna" means drinking sesame oil and so forth. "Payopāna" means drinking milk.
"Yāgupāna" means drinking cooled rice-gruel and so forth. "Rasapāna" means drinking the juices of vegetables and so forth.
"Piṭṭhakhajjaka" refers to the flour of the seven grains, their derivatives, and other foods, such as jackfruit flour and breadfruit flour.
“Flour-based snacks” refers to snacks made from the flours of such things as the *ambāṭaka* (wild plum), the *sāla* tree, and the *khīravalli* (milk-creeping plant).
“Cake snacks” are also made from these very same ingredients. “Root snacks” refers to the roots of radishes, the roots of *khāraka*, the roots of *cuccu*, and so forth.
“Bark snacks” refers to things such as sugarcane bark. “Leaf snacks” refers to leaves such as those of the *nimba*, *kuṭaja*, *paṭola*, and *sulasā*.
"Edible flowers" refers to radish flowers, *khāraka* flowers, white *varaṇa* flowers, *siggu*, blue lotus (*uppala*), red lotus (*paduma*), and so forth. "Edible fruits," however,

refers to the edible fruits of the jackfruit (*panasa*), breadfruit (*labuja*), palm, coconut, mango, *aṭaka*, tamarind (*tintiṇika*), citron (*mātuluṅga*), wood-apple (*kapiṭṭha*), gourd (*alābu*), pumpkin (*kumbhaṇḍa*),
*phussa* fruit, *timbarūsaka*, sesame, *vātiṅgaṇa*, *coca*, *moca*, honey-sugar cane (*madhuka*), and others.
“Not by hypocrisy” means not for the sake of deception. “Not by flattery” means not for the sake of obtaining requisites through flattering speech.
For instance, seeing people who have come to the monastery, one does not invite the bhikkhus by saying, “For what purpose, sirs, have you come? or, “If that is so, go ahead;
I will follow behind and take [the requisites] along. Or else, presenting oneself [as someone special], one says, “I...”
Not by flattery, such as saying, "Three kings have confidence in me," or "Such-and-such a king and such-and-such a high minister of state have confidence in me.
Not by hinting (*nemittikatā*): not by any bodily or verbal action that produces the perception in others that one is a donor of requisites.
Not by belittling (*nippesikatā*): which refers to acts such as reviling others, because of which [the other] is like a bamboo scraper...
It "extracts" (*nippeṣeti*) or wipes away the virtues of another like an ointment;

or, because this pursuit of gain consists in grinding and pulverizing the virtues of others just as one grinds fragrant substances to seek out their scent, it is called "grinding" (*nippesikatā*). One should not [act] with such grinding.
Regarding the phrase "the seeking of gain by means of gain": here, "seeking" (*nijigīsanatā*) means...
"Seeking by way of gain" means seeking gain by means of taking what was obtained from one place and carrying it to another;
it is not such "seeking by way of gain.
"Not by the gift of wood" means not for the sake of requisites; for [wood] that has arisen in a monastery, having been brought from the forest...
It is not permissible to give wood that has been protected and guarded to one's supporters with the thought, "In this way they will provide me with requisites.
For one who makes a living in such a manner lives by wrong livelihood through improper search;
he incurs censure in this very life and becomes a fulfiller of the states of misery in the future life. [However,] one's own private wood may be given for the purpose of grasping wholesome factors.
One who gives [it] incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for being a defiler of families;

one who gives what belongs to another individual with a thieving mind must be dealt with according to the value of the goods. This same principle applies even in the case of what belongs to the Saṅgha.

However, if he gives it because of his status as a lord, he incurs the offense of relinquishing heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa-vissajjana*). Now, which kind of wood constitutes a heavy good, and which does not? First, that which is grown on a plantation...
That which is self-grown is considered heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*) only within the area demarcated by the Saṅgha; beyond that, it is not heavy property.
In the case of planted trees, they are entirely heavy property. By measure, even something as small as the handle of a needle is heavy property.
Regarding the phrases "not by the gift of bamboo," etc., "not by the gift of bamboo" means "not by the gift of bamboo for the purpose of requisites," and so on for all such cases.
This should be understood according to the method already explained in the section on the gift of wood. However, bamboo that is the size of an oil tube is a "heavy article" (*garubhaṇḍa*);
it is not [considered such] if it is smaller than that. When people go to a monastery and ask for bamboo, the monks do not dare to give it because it belongs to the Saṅgha.
If the people then ask repeatedly or even threaten them, at that time the monks [should consider] "punishment" (*daṇḍakamma*).
It is permissible to say, "Having prepared them, take them," but this does not constitute a gift of bamboo.
If they give axes, hatchets, and so forth for the purpose of punishment, or solid food or soft food, it is not permissible to accept them.
However, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "When people whose houses have been burned are taking things away, they should not be stopped."

If bamboo-sprouts arise for the Saṅgha in a bamboo grove, and the bamboo is lost while they do not have it pounded, [the monks] should inform the people during their almsround, saying, "What should be done?
If they do not wish to have it pounded, they should be told, "You will receive an equal share.
If they still do not wish to, they should be told, "You will receive two shares."
Likewise, if they do not wish to comply, there is no purpose in being ruined;
one should tell them, “When you have the opportunity, you may perform the punishment—beat them and take them,” for that is not called a gift of bamboo.
The same principle applies even when a fire breaks out in a bamboo grove or when bamboos are being carried away by water.
Regarding the status of heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*) in the case of a bowl, this is the determination:
even a bowl becomes a heavy good only in such rare circumstances where it is sold, or where perfumers and others take it for the purpose of wrapping perfumes and so forth.

This, first of all, is the determination regarding [ornaments] such as earrings made from *kiṃsuka* leaves, or ornaments made from palm leaves (*tālapatta*). A palm leaf also [is treated] in this very same way.

The proper application [of the rule] should be stated as follows: even a palm leaf is "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa) only within a delimited area by the Saṅgha in a self-grown palm grove, and not beyond that; in the case of planted palms, everything is heavy property.
Its minimum measure is even an empty book measuring eight finger-breadths. Grass also should be included here and thus stated. Where—
However, there is no grass [available], so in that case they cover it even with palm leaves, coconut leaves, and so forth. Therefore, these too are included under "grass.

Thus, any amount of grass measuring a handful from among *muñja* grass, straw, and the like, or even a single leaf from among coconut leaves and such—whether given to the Saṅgha or grown there—within the Saṅgha’s grass-plot outside the monastery grounds, [is considered grass].
Or, grass that has grown or property that has been guarded and protected becomes "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

However, when it has been used for work for the Saṅgha or for work for a shrine (*cetiyakamma*), it is permissible to give the surplus for personal work (*puggalikakamma*). The same principle applies to the timber and bamboo mentioned below regarding giving.
Regarding the gift of flowers: "Having distributed flowers from so many trees, bring them for the sake of rice gruel and alms-food; from so many..."
"Let them bring [the flowers] for the repair of the lodgings"—in this way, flowers designated for such specific purposes are considered "precious goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

If novice monks (*sāmaṇera*) gather flowers and make a heap of them, a monk who distributes the flowers and is endowed with five qualities shall count the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) and divide them into portions.
He must do so without having first asked the assembled company for permission regarding the Saṅgha.

One may receive [flowers] to give. However, if one has not been formally appointed [as a steward], one must give them only after having asked for permission. Regarding which monk it is permissible to give flowers to, and to whom it is not permissible:

even if one brings them to the house of one's mother or father, or even if one has them summoned from their home, it is permissible to give them saying, "Perform an offering to the site (vatthupūjā)";
however, it is not permissible to give them for the purpose of wearing as ornaments. This applies to other relatives as well.
However, one should not take [the flowers] and give them away; rather, having summoned [the recipient], they should be given for the purpose of worship.
When giving to ordinary people who have arrived at a place of worship, one should give without expecting anything in return; this is not called a "gift of flowers.
If many flowers are blooming in a monastery, when a bhikkhu is walking for alms and sees people, he should say: "In the monastery..."
One may say, "Offer many flowers," for there is no fault in merely saying that;
however, one must not say it with the intention, "People will come bringing hard and soft food. If one says it [with such an intention], the hard and soft food must not be consumed.
People, by their own nature, having asked, "Are there flowers in the monastery?"...
“On such-and-such a day we shall come to the monastery; do not let the novices pluck flowers,” they said.
The bhikkhu forgot to tell the novices, and the novices plucked the flowers.
People approached the bhikkhu and said, “We informed you on such-and-such a day that [you should prevent] the novices from plucking flowers.”
"Do not give it," [he says]. "Why did you not stop him? One should say: "My mindfulness failed; I had only just plucked the flowers, and the offering had not yet been made.
One should not say, "Take them and make an offering. If he does say so, the material gift must not be consumed.
Another bhikkhu explains to the novices: "The inhabitants of such-and-such a village [said], 'Flowers..."
"Do not pluck [the flowers]," they said. Then the laypeople, having brought offerings of food and given them as alms, said, "We do not have many people;
please instruct the novices to pluck flowers together with us.
It should be said: "The novices have received their alms. Those who do not go on alms-round will know for themselves, O lay followers."
Having obtained such an arrangement, there is no fault in having a novice—whether a son or a brother—gather flowers;
this is not called a "gift of flowers.
In the case of a gift of fruit, the fruit itself, like the flower, is strictly a heavy article (garubhaṇḍa). [This applies] when there are many monasteries.
When there are fruits and non-fruits, people who are uncomfortable come and make requests; the monks do not venture to give them, thinking, "This belongs to the Saṅgha.
The people, feeling regretful, revile and abuse them. In such a case, what should be done?
One should demarcate the area by means of the fruits or the trees and make a proclamation: "In such-and-such trees and such-and-such trees, there are this many fruits."
"Those who take [fruit], or those taking fruit from so many trees, should not be stopped. Even thieves or lords who take by force should not be stopped;
for if they are angry, they might destroy the entire monastery. However, the danger must be explained. Regarding the gift of bathing facilities:
bath-powders that have been ground are not "precious goods" (garubhaṇḍa); however, the bark of a tree while still on the tree is [considered such].
As for heavy goods, however, it is permissible for one who is not ill to give dye-liquor and powder. For one who is ill, it is indeed permissible to give any kind of powder whatsoever.
"By the giving of powder" refers to the method already stated regarding the giving of *sirīsa* powder and so forth. Regarding the giving of clay:
where clay is difficult to obtain, that very place constitutes a "heavy good. Even that [clay] is limited to a maximum of thirty *palas* in weight, measured by a lump of sugar.
"Below that, it is not a heavy object.
Regarding the giving of tooth-sticks: a tooth-stick that has not yet been cut is indeed a heavy object.
Those novices to whom the turn for tooth-sticks from the Saṅgha falls do not receive permission to give them separately to their own teachers (ācariya) and preceptors (upajjhāya).
However, those who have taken their turn by determining, "So many tooth-sticks are to be brought," are permitted to give the surplus to their teachers and preceptors.
A single bhikkhu must not take many tooth-sticks from the tooth-stick shed; he should take only one each day. This applies even to one living separately.
Having counted the community of bhikkhus, one should take only as many as fall to one’s own share and then depart.
If guests arrive along the way, or if others depart for their respective directions, the items should be brought back and placed in the very place from which they were taken.
"Not by the offering of mouth-water" means not by the offering of water for washing the face.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "not through flattery" (*na cāṭukamyatāya*): "flattery" (*cāṭukamyatā*) refers to speaking with exaggeration out of a desire for affection, while placing oneself in a low position like a slave and smoothing over even another's faulty speech. "Not through bean-soup-like behavior" (*na muggasūpyatāya*) means not being like bean soup.
"Bean-soup-like behavior" refers to making one's livelihood by means of truth mixed with falsehood. This is what it means.

This is a designation. For just as when green gram soup is being cooked, many beans reach full cooking while few do not, even so, in a person who maintains a livelihood through truth and falsehood, the falsehood is great and the truth is small.
Or, just as there is no place for green gram that does not enter [the pot], even so for a person whose conduct consists of truth and falsehood...
There is no such thing as "having no foundation. It finds a footing wherever it desires, like a crossroads. Therefore, that lying of his is called "the condition of being like mung-bean soup.
"Not by way of servitude" means not by the state of being a servant. For the work of a servant is "servitude" (*pāribhaṭya*);
the state of that is "servitude-ness" (*pāribhaṭyatā*), [which occurs] through such acts as performing adornments and the like.
This is a designation for playing with children. "Not by sitting on a seat" means not by entering a house hastily and sitting down on a bench.
Regarding the phrase "not by the science of sites" and so forth:
the "science of sites" (vatthuvijjā) refers to the treatise for knowing whether villages, market towns, cities, and so forth, are well-situated or poorly-situated.

"Tiracchānavijjā" (animal science) refers to all remaining branches of knowledge—such as the science of limbs (*aṅga*), astrology (*nimitta*), and so forth—which, because they do not lead to liberation, are like animals in relation to the paths to heaven and liberation.
"Aṅgavijjā" (science of limbs) refers to the knowledge of the characteristics of women and men that indicate whether they will be fortunate or unfortunate.
"Nakkhattavijjā" (science of constellations) refers to the treatise on knowing the conjunctions of the lunar mansions (*nakkhatta*).
"By going as a messenger" means by going after having performed the duties of a messenger.

"By going on an errand" means by going from house to house having received a message from householders. "By running messages between villages or across districts" means by carrying various messages and counter-messages for those householders.
For this indeed is called "running messages between villages. One's own...
It is permissible to go somewhere after taking a message from one's parents, or from those who attend upon one's parents.
It is also permissible to carry a message for carpenters who are working on behalf of a cetiya, the Saṅgha, or oneself.
When people say, "We shall give a gift; we shall perform an offering; tell the Bhikkhu Saṅgha [where they are]," [it is permissible to go].
And they say, “Give this to the elder named so-and-so,” and they give almsfood, medicine, or robes;
or, saying, “Perform an offering at the monastery,” they present garlands, perfumes, ointments, and the like, or banners and flags.
It is permissible to take all of these; it does not constitute what is called "begging on foot. For one who departs after taking the remaining requisites—
At every step there is an offense.
"Not by means of medical practice" means not by acting as a physician through performing medical treatments such as bodily care and administering medicine.
However, medicine may be prepared for the five who share the same Dhamma: for a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), and a male novice (sāmaṇera).
[It is permissible] for a female novice (sāmaṇerī). For those who possess equal virtue, faith, and wisdom and are devoted to the three trainings, it is not permitted to refuse to provide medicine.

However, it is appropriate to provide it for these five: one's mother and father, those who attend to them, one's own personal attendant, and a "faded leaf" (paṇḍupalāsa) [novice]. [Also for] an elder brother, a younger brother, an elder sister, and a younger sister.

Furthermore, when preparing medicine for these ten—namely, the junior mother, the senior mother, the junior father, the senior father, the paternal aunt, and the maternal aunt—one must take medicine belonging to them alone, compound it, and give it.
If that is not sufficient, one's own medicine may be given on a temporary basis. [This applies] to their line of descendants... up to...

For as long as seven family cycles, for one who causes the four requisites to be brought [for him], there is no offense of *akataviññatti* (directing for what has not been prepared), nor is there an offense of *vejjakamma* (medical practice) for one who prepares medicine, nor is there the offense of being a *kuladūsaka* (a corrupter of families).
Regarding the phrase "not even with alms-food or additional alms-food": to whom should alms-food be given, and to whom should it not be given? [It should be given] to mother and father.
It should be given to those who attend upon him, to his attendant, to one with leaves as pale as a withered leaf, to one who has arrived, to a robber, and even to a lord.
Once it has been given to these, even if alms-food is subsequently obtained, it is no longer called "alms-food" (piṇḍapāta).

"Not by giving again what has already been given" means not by giving again to those to whom one has already given. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means acquired in accordance with the Dhamma. "Equitably" means by means of good bodily conduct and so forth.
"Obtained" means obtained by means of the body (*kāya*). "Having gained" means having reached it by means of the mind (*citta*).

"Having attained" means having fully reached it. "Having found" means having found it through knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Having acquired" means having acquired it again and again. Regarding "the hoarding of food":
here, there are two kinds of discourse on food—namely, from the perspective of the Vinaya and from the perspective of austerity (*sallekha*). From the perspective of the Vinaya...
Whatever food has been received today becomes "stored" (sannidhikāraka) by the following day;
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for consuming it. However, it is permissible to give what one has received oneself to novices, have them set it aside, and eat it on the second day;
yet, in this case, there is no reduction of the offense (sallekha).
The same principle applies to the storage of drinks. Here, "drink" refers to the eight kinds of drinks, beginning with mango juice, as well as those things that are compatible with them.

Regarding the storage of clothes and so forth, if they are neither formally resolved upon nor assigned for specific use, this constitutes both "storage" (*sannidhi*) and an offense against the austerity of effacement (*sallekha*). This is merely an explanatory discourse;
however, from the standpoint of the definitive meaning, one should be content with the three robes alone, and [not keep] a fourth.

Having received it, it must be given to another. If one is unable to give it to anyone at all, but wishes to give it to someone who has gone for the purpose of receiving a recitation or for the purpose of inquiry, it must be given as soon as that person returns; it is not permitted not to give it.
However, if robes are insufficient, it is permitted to set aside the period authorized by expectation of further acquisitions. [This applies] to those who work with needles, thread, and robes.
If it cannot be obtained, it is permissible to set it aside after performing a formal act of the Saṅgha (vinayakamma) for that purpose.

However, it is not permissible to set it aside thinking, "Now that this one is worn out, where else shall I find another such as this? For in doing so, there is the fault of hoarding (sannidhi), and it violates the austerity of simplicity (sallekha).
Regarding the hoarding of vehicles: what is called a "vehicle" includes a draft ox, a chariot, a cart, a carriage, a palanquin, and a sedan chair; this is not [permissible].
A vehicle is for one who has gone forth; however, sandals are indeed a vehicle for one who has gone forth.
For a single bhikkhu, at most two pairs of sandals are permitted—one for going into the forest and one for washing the feet. If a third is obtained, it must be given to another;
it is not permitted to keep it [thinking], "When this one is worn out, where else shall I obtain another?"
There is hoarding, and it violates the austerity of effacement.
Regarding "furniture for lying down," "lying down" refers to a bed. For a single bhikkhu, one bed is permitted in a cell and one during the daytime rest;
at most, two beds are allowed. If more than that is obtained, it must be given to another bhikkhu or to a group.
It is not permissible to take [it] up; for it constitutes both storage and an obstruction to effacement (*sallekha*).
Regarding the storage of scents: when a monk suffers from ailments such as boils, itch, or skin diseases, the use of scent is permitted.

Once that disease has been pacified by means of that scent, or when there are others who are afflicted, it should be given to them. This applies in cases such as the fumigation of the five-fingered chamber at the gate.

Or it should be brought [to him]. It is not permitted to set it aside [thinking], "It will be useful when there is illness again," for that constitutes the storage of perfumes and violates the principle of effacement (*sallekha*).
"Material goods" (*āmisa*) should be understood as everything other than the aforementioned food and so forth; namely, here a certain monk [thinks]: "In such a situation..."
Thinking, "They will be of assistance in due time," he had sesame, rice, mung beans, peas, salt, fish, meat, dried meat, ghee, oil, sugar, vessels, and so forth brought and set aside.

During the rainy season, having had rice-gruel prepared by the novices at an early hour and having eaten it himself, he would say, "Novice, it is difficult to enter the village because of the water and mud; go to such-and-such a family..."
He sent word, saying: "Inform him that I am sitting in my dwelling; bring curd and other provisions from such-and-such a family.
When the monks asked, "Venerable sir, why are you entering the village? he replied, "Friends, the village is difficult to enter at this time.
They said, "Very well, venerable sir, please stay here; we shall go and seek alms and bring them back," and so they departed.
Then the novice, having brought curds and other items and prepared both the rice and the curry, brings them forward;
even as the elder is eating that, his attendants send more food, and he eats what is pleasing and pleasing from that as well.
Then when the monks arrive carrying almsfood, he eats what is pleasing and pleasing from that too, until his neck is full.
In this way he passes even four months. Such a person is called a bhikkhu who "lives the life of a shaven-headed householder, not the life of a recluse.
This is what is known as the accumulation of material goods.
Furthermore, in the dwelling place of a bhikkhu, there might be a single measure of rice, a single lump of sugar, and a quarter-measure of ghee.

It is permissible to store this much for the sake of thieves who might arrive unexpectedly; for if they do not receive even this much hospitality of material goods, they might even deprive one of life.
Therefore, even if one does not already possess this much, it is permissible to have it brought and set aside.
And during times of discomfort, whatever here is allowable (kappiya) may be used by oneself as well. [In] the kitchen (kappiyakuṭi).
But even for one who sets aside much, there is no such thing as "storing up" (sannidhi).

160. "A meditator should not be fickle with his feet": he should be devoted to *jhāna* and not be fickle with his feet. "He should abstain from remorse and not be negligent": he should dispel remorse such as that regarding the hands, and he should not be negligent here through the practice of thoroughness (*sakkacca-kāritā*).

"Devoted to solitude" means devoted to the state of being alone. "One who prizes the ultimate goal" means one who prizes the supreme goal. Alternatively, the reading is "one who prizes his own welfare."

"Delighting in seclusion" (*paṭisallānārāmo*): "delight" (*ārāmo*) means that which is enjoyed; one for whom there is delight in seclusion—that is, in being alone after withdrawing from various objects—is "one who delights in seclusion. "He would be" (*assā*) means he might be. "Rejoicing in that" (*tasmiṃ rato*) means rejoicing in seclusion.
By these [terms], he shows the fulfillment of virtue (*sīla*). Why is that? Because for one deficient in virtue, even one-pointedness of mind (*ekaggatā*) does not come to pass.
"One devoted to internal mental tranquility" means one who is intent upon the tranquility of his own mind. For here, "internally" (*ajjhatta*) and "of oneself" (*attanā*) have the same meaning;
there is only a difference in expression. This [term *ajjhatta*] is used in the accusative case in the sense of a locative.
It is established through its connection with the prefix *anu*.
“With meditation unrepelled” means that his meditation is not struck down externally, or that it is not destroyed.
For this term *nirākaraṇa* (repelling) signifies the sense of removing or destroying; its usage should be seen in such passages as “having repelled stiffness, living in humility.

“Endowed with insight” means being joined with the sevenfold contemplation. The sevenfold contemplation is as follows: [contemplation of impermanence, suffering, non-self, dispassion, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment].

Namely: the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of non-self, the contemplation of disenchantment, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment.
These have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Increasing in empty huts" means expanding [one's practice] in empty huts.
And herein, having taken up a meditation subject by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), day and night...
A bhikkhu who enters and sits in an empty hut should be understood as "one who increases empty huts.
Even one who builds palaces with various levels and so forth should be seen as "increasing empty huts.
Regarding the terms "one who acts with diligence" and so on, [this refers to] the cultivation of wholesome states such as giving, or [the cultivation of] either the person or the object to be given.
Or, one is "one who acts with diligence" (*sakkaccakārī*) by way of performing [the task] thoroughly. *Assa* means "he would be. *Sātacca* is the state of being constant;
one is "one who acts with constancy" (*sātaccakārī*) by way of performing [the task] continuously.

By way of acting without interruption, he is "one who acts without stopping. Just as a crane, having gone a little, stops again and does not go continuously, even so is that person who, having given a gift or performed an offering on a single day...
Or having done it, or having heard the Dhamma, or having performed the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he does it again only after a long time; thus he does not practice it continuously.
He is called "one who acts without persistence" (*asātaccakārī*) and "one who acts with instability" (*ṭhitakārī*). But he who is not like this is "one who acts with stability" (*aṭhitakārī*).
"One whose conduct is not sluggish" (*anolīnavuttiko*): because of the presence of expansion, which consists in acting continuously, his conduct is not sluggish.
"Unrelenting desire" means having unrelenting desire for wholesome activity by virtue of not casting off the desire for energy (*vīriyacchanda*).
"One who has not laid down the burden" means one who does not set aside the burden of energy; the meaning is that his mind does not slacken. "Non-retrogression" means not turning back.
"Resolution" is the state of being established in the performance of what is wholesome. "Application" is the act of devoting oneself to it. "Heedfulness" is non-separation from mindfulness (*sati*).

161. *Tandiṃ* means sloth; *māyaṃ* means deceit; *hassaṃ* means laughter; *khiḍḍanti* means playfulness; and *ālasiyañca māyañca hassañca* refers to physical and verbal playfulness as well as deceit and laughter. *Savibhūsaṃ* means together with adornment.

*Rattindivaṃ chakoṭṭhāsaṃ karitvā* means having divided the night and day into six portions by way of the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night, and likewise for the day—thus making six divisions. *Pañcakoṭṭhāsaṃ paṭijaggeyya* means one should remain awake during five of those portions at night.
Having passed the middle watch, one should not fall asleep during the remaining five portions.
"One should lie down for one portion" means that, being mindful and clearly comprehending, one should lie down and fall asleep during one portion—the middle watch.
Here, by mentioning the morning, midday, and evening, all three divisions of the day are included.

"By means of walking and sitting": by dwelling for the entire day in these two postures alone, one should purify the mind from the five hindrances—those states that obstruct the mind—or from all unwholesome states.
"One should purify the mind": one should cleanse the mind of those states. Although standing is not explicitly mentioned here, it is nonetheless included.
However, it must certainly be taken after relying upon walking meditation and sitting meditation. Regarding "the first watch": this refers to the entire first watch of the night.

Regarding "sleeping": here there are four types of sleeping postures—the posture of those who indulge in sensual pleasures (*kāmabhogī-seyyā*), the posture of the hungry ghosts (*petaseyyā*), the lion’s posture (*sīhaseyyā*), and the Tathāgata’s posture.
Among these, "Bhikkhus, for the most part those who indulge in sensual pleasures lie on their left side" refers to the posture of those who indulge in sensual pleasures.
For among them, there is generally no such thing as lying on one's right side. "Monks, for the most part, ghosts lie on their backs"—this is the posture of the ghosts.
Because they have little flesh and blood, they are unable to lie on one side, being struck by the friction of their skeletal frames;
they lie only on their backs. "Monks, Sīha, the king of beasts, lies on his right side..."
“He lies down on his right side... [and so on] ...he is satisfied”; this is the lion’s posture (*sīhaseyyā*).

For the lion, the king of beasts, being preeminent in vigor, places his two forefeet in one place and his hind foot in another, tucks his tail between his thighs, and having observed the positions where his forefeet, hind feet, and tail rest, he [places] his two forefeet...
He lies down placing his head upon the top [of the bed]. Even after sleeping for the whole day, when he awakens, he does not wake up in terror;
rather, lifting his head, he observes the position where the front feet and so forth were placed.
If anything has been shifted from its place, he becomes dissatisfied, thinking, "This is not worthy of your birth, nor is it befitting your courage."
He lies down right there and does not set out for his range.

However, seeing that he has remained there without abandoning his post, [the lion]—delighted and joyful, thinking, "This is worthy of your birth and your courageous nature"—rises up, stretches with a lion’s yawn, shakes his mane, lets out a lion’s roar three times, and then sets out for his range. As for the reclining posture of the fourth jhāna:

It is called "the reclining posture of the Tathāgata. Among those, the lion’s posture (sīhaseyyā) is what is intended here. For this is indeed called the supreme posture because it is an iriyāpatha (mode of conduct) rich in fiery energy (tejo).
"Placing foot upon foot" means placing the left foot upon the right foot. "Having laid it down" (accādhāya) means having placed it slightly beyond [the other], having gone slightly past it.
For if the ankle were to touch the ankle, or the knee the knee, pain would frequently arise.
The mind is not one-pointed, and the bed is uncomfortable. However, when he places it so that it does not touch [the other], no painful sensation arises;
the mind becomes one-pointed, and the bed is comfortable. Therefore it is said: "Having placed foot over foot.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being endowed with both mindfulness and the wisdom of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
"Having offered. By this, mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) as thorough graspers are explained.
"Having attended to the perception of rising" means having established in the mind the perception of rising that delimits the time for rising, thinking, "I shall rise at such-and-such a time.
For one who lies down after doing so indeed rises at the very time delimited.
In the exposition of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the term "mental factor" (*cetasika*) is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that energy is invariably a mental factor.
For this energy is described in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, whatever is bodily energy, that too is the energy factor of enlightenment;
whatever is mental energy, that too is the energy factor of enlightenment. Thus it is included in the summary. And so forth.

Although it is called "bodily" because it arises in one who is walking back and forth (*caṅkama*) and so forth during the discourses, there is no such thing as a "bodily" [state] like body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*); rather, to show that this is purely mental (*cetasika*), it is stated as "mental.
"Exertion of energy" (*vīriyārambha*) means exertion characterized as energy. For this word *ārambha* [is used] in the sense of action, offense, activity, energy, and violence.
The term *vikopana* occurs in various senses.
For example: “Whatever suffering arises, all of it has its condition in exertion (*ārambha*);
through the cessation of exertions, there is no arising of suffering.”—
For here, "kamma" is given as "ārambha. In the phrase "he undertakes [an action] and feels remorse," it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).
In the phrase "great sacrifices involving great undertakings do not yield great fruit," it refers to the act of erecting a sacrificial post and so forth. In the phrase "Exert yourselves! Strive!
Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching," it refers to energy (*vīriya*). [In the phrase] "with reference to the ascetic Gotama, [one kills] a living being..."

In the phrase "undertaking [harm]," it refers to violence. In the phrase "he abstains from the destruction of seeds and plants," it refers to the disturbance [of living beings] through cutting, breaking, and so forth.
But here, only energy (*vīriya*) is intended. Therefore he said: "The undertaking of energy means an undertaking characterized as energy.
For energy is called an "undertaking" by virtue of its quality of being undertaken. This is its [meaning].

This is the section on essential nature (*sabhāvapada*). It is "striving" (*nikkama*) by way of emerging from indolence. It is "exertion" (*parakkama*) by way of stepping toward higher and higher stages.
It is "effort" (*uyyāma*) by way of rising up and striving. It is "endeavor" (*vāyāma*) by way of making an effort. It is "perseverance" (*ussāha*) by way of exerting oneself.
It is "strenuousness" (*ussoḷhi*) by way of supreme exertion. It is "fortitude" (*thāma*) in the sense of steadfastness. It is [energy] by way of sustaining the mind and mental factors.
It is *dhiti* because it sustains the continuum of the wholesome by way of its uninterrupted occurrence.
According to another method: this is exertion for the removal of sensual desires; this is striving for the cutting of bonds;
this is effort for crossing over the flood; this is endeavor in the sense of going to the further shore; this is enthusiasm in the sense of being the precursor.
This is *ussoḷhi* (exertion) in the sense of being excessive; this is *thāma* (strength) because it overthrows obstacles; this is *dhiti* (fortitude) because of its steadfastness in action.
In the context of the occurrence of the thought, "Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain," it refers to the state of unslackened energy by way of unremitting effort;
the meaning is firm energy, resolute energy. And because this energy...

In the matter of performing wholesome deeds, one does not cast aside desire, does not cast aside the burden, does not let go, does not relinquish, and brings about a state of mind that does not shrink back; therefore, it is said: "not casting aside desire, not casting aside the burden.
Just as, for instance, when oxen used for pulling a load are told "take up the yoke" at a place where the ground is of such a nature and mixed with water, [they do not shrink back].

Just as a bull, pressing its knee against the ground, bears the yoke and does not allow itself to fall, even so does energy not lay down the burden but exerts itself in the performance of wholesome deeds; therefore it is called "the exertion of the burden.

It exercises lordship over that which has the characteristic of exertion, thus it is the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*). It is unshakable by laziness, thus it is the power of energy (*vīriyabala*).
Right effort is the state of wholesome exertion that leads to the goal as it truly is.
*Tandi* means natural laziness. *Tandiyanā* is the manner of being lazy. *Tandimanakatā* is the state of the mind being overcome by laziness.
*Ālasyaṃ* is the nature of one who is idle; *ālasyāyanā* is the manner of behaving idly; *ālasyāyitattaṃ* is the state of having behaved idly.
Thus, by all these phrases, physical indolence due to the influence of the defilements is described.

"Deceitful conduct" means deceitful action. "He speaks the words 'May they not know me'" means that a monk who knowingly transgresses a designation (paṇṇatti) makes it a grave matter, thinking, "But for us, there is no such thing as a point of transgression."
He speaks as if he were peaceful. "He exerts himself with the body" means that thinking, "Let no one know of this evil deed committed by me," he performs his duties with the body.
Because it conceals existing faults, it is like an illusion (*māyā*) that deludes the eye; the state of being possessed of such illusion is *māyāvitā*.
Because a person, having committed an evil deed, subsequently transgresses [the truth] by concealing it through this [deceit], they are called a transgressor (*accasara*).
It is *vañcanā* (deceit) because one deceives by appearing otherwise than one's bodily and vocal actions.

It is *nikati* (guile) because beings ruin themselves by means of it; the meaning is that they act wrongly. It is *nikiraṇā* (concealment) because of casting off evil deeds with the thought, "I did not do this.

It is *pariharaṇā* (evasion) because of avoiding [the truth] with the thought, "I did not do this. It is *gūhanā* (hiding) because of covering up [one's faults] through body and so forth. It is so called because it is partial in every respect.
*Gūhanā* is concealing; *parigūhanā* is thorough concealing. Because one covers over evil with bodily and verbal actions as if with grass and leaves, it is called *chādanā* (covering).
Because it covers on all sides, it is *paricchādanā* (complete covering). Because one does not show [the fault] by making it plain, it is *anuttānīkammaṃ* (not making plain).

Because one does not show it by making it manifest, it is *anāvikammaṃ* (not making manifest). Because it is a very thorough covering, it is *vocchādanā* (extreme covering). This is by way of concealing the evil that has been committed.
Furthermore, it is from the performance of evil that there is "evil-doing.
This is called "deceit" (māyā), which is characterized by the concealment of what has been done.
A person endowed with this is like a coal covered by ashes, like a stump hidden by water, or like a sword wrapped in a cloth. He excessively bares his teeth...
"She laughs" means that she laughs by opening her teeth beyond their normal measure, showing them to others, and thereby producing laughter and joy.
"Bodily play" refers to sport performed with the body. The same method applies to verbal play as well.

"Playing with elephants" means they play for the sake of sporting with elephants, engaging in such activities as running forward and backward, charging, and sitting upon their backs. The same applies here.

The same method applies to horse-chariots as well. Regarding "playing on the eight-square board" (*aṭṭhapada*): because there are eight squares in each row, it is called an "eight-square board" (*aṭṭhapada*);

[they play] on that eight-square board. The same method applies to the ten-square board (*dasapada*) as well. Regarding "in the air": just as on the eight- and ten-square boards, they play in the air itself.
Regarding "on the circuit path" (*parihārapatha*): having fashioned various circular paths on the ground, therein—
They play while avoiding paths that must be avoided. They also "play in proximity" (*santikakīḷā*);
they play by means of this proximity-play, moving pieces made of wood or stone pebbles placed together, shifting them back and forth with their fingernails alone without letting them move.
If any of them moves there, it is a defeat.
"Khalikāya" means they play at dice on a gaming board. "Ghaṭikāya":
a *ghaṭikā* refers to a game played by striking a short stick with a long stick; they play that. "Salākahatthena":
having moistened the hand with lac, red resin, or flour-water, [they mark] it on the ground or on a wall, saying, "What shall it be?"...
Having struck [one another], they play while displaying the forms of elephants, horses, and so forth. "With a ball" means with a guḷa-ball. "With a leaf-whistle" (*paṅkacīra*):

a leaf-whistle is called a leaf-tube; they play by blowing it. "With a hook" (*vaṅkaka*): with a small plough, which is a toy for village children. "With a spinning-top" (*mokkhacikā*): this refers to the game of spinning;
or else, having grasped a staff in the air or placed one's head on the ground.
It is said that they "play" by turning upside down and right side up. Regarding "with a *ciṅgulaka*":
a *ciṅgulaka* is called a wheel made of palm leaves or similar materials that revolves when struck by the wind; they play with that. Regarding "with a *pattāḷhaka*":
a *pattāḷhaka* is called a leaf-measure; they play by measuring sand and such things with it. Regarding "with a chariot": this refers to a small chariot.
"With a bow" means with a small bow. "With letter-guessing" (*akkharikā*): "letter-guessing" is said to be a game for knowing letters either in the air or on the back;
they play with that. "With mind-reading" (*manesikā*): "mind-reading" is said to be a game for knowing what has been thought by the mind;
they play with that. "According to the fault" (*yathāvajjena*): "according to the fault" is said to be whichever fault there is of those who are one-eyed, lame, hunchbacked, and so forth.
Having employed this or that [method], it is a "game of looking," and they play with it. "Mukhabherika" means playing like a drum by means of the sound of the mouth.
"Mukhālambara" means making the sound of a drum smeared on the mouth. "Mukhaḍiṇḍimaka" means making the sound of a drum struck by the mouth.
"Mukhavalimaka" means making a sound by distorting the flesh of the lips.
There is also a reading “mukhatalika,” which means blowing [into a horn] after turning the mouth [sideways]. “Mukhabheruḷaka” means playing the drum with the mouth.
“Nāṭaka” means teaching by demonstrating dramatic performance. There is also a reading “naṭṭaka.
“Lāpa” means making a loud shout. “Gīta” means singing. “Davakamma” means engaging in joking and play. This is verbal [wrong livelihood].
"Play" (*khiḍḍā*) is this sport born of speech, arisen at the door of speech. In the case of "hair and beard," etc.,
it refers to the cutting of the hair with scissors without leaving any remnants on the head,
and the shaving of the beard— except for the mustache— as well as the wearing of garlands such as single-strand jasmine wreaths and the like, and scents such as root-fragrances and the like.
And there is the application of cosmetics and ointments; ornaments and jewelry worn on the neck and other parts; head-dresses, decorations, and ornaments fastened upon the head;
