various garments for the body, as well as the binding of turbans and their adornment. There is also a reading, “parāsana,” which refers to the turban consisting of a cloth wrapped around the head.
Regarding anointing and similar acts: the body odor of infants who have emerged from the mother’s womb disappears at the age of twelve years.
To remove that body odor, people anoint them with fragrant powders and the like; such anointing is not permitted.
However, in the case of meritorious children, one may place them upon one's thighs, smear them with oil, and [massage] their hands, feet, thighs, navel, and so forth.
They massage [the body] for the purpose of shaping it; such massaging is not permitted.
"Bathing" refers to bathing those same children with perfumes and other substances.

"Massaging" (*sambāhana*) refers to the development of the arms by striking the hands and feet with clubs and so forth, as is done by great wrestlers. "A mirror" refers to carrying any kind of mirror.
It is not permitted. "Collyrium" refers specifically to decorative eye-salve. "Garland" means either a strung garland or an unstrung one.
"Ointment" is anything that imparts color to the skin. "Face powder" and "face ointment": they give a clay paste for the purpose of removing black spots and the like on the face.
When the blood has moved [due to that], they give a mustard-seed paste; when the humors have been consumed by that, they give a sesame paste.
They apply red lac to the teeth; when that has settled into the blood, they apply turmeric paste;
when the color of the skin has been restored, they powder the face with facial powder—all of this is not permitted.

Regarding the binding of the hands and so forth: they wander about having bound various items such as conch shells and skull-cups to their hands; whether that or anything else [is done], it is not permitted.
Or even all hand-ornaments are not permitted. Others wander about with their hair tied in a topknot, encircling it with gold leaf, strings of pearls, and so forth; none of that is permitted.
Others wander about carrying a four-cubit staff or some other decorated staff, as well as a medicinal tube variegated with figures of men, women, and the like.
Some held a well-encased sword on their left side; others held a sword with many-colored scabbards that was exceedingly sharp;

some held a parasol decorated with makara-teeth and other motifs and sewn with threads of five colors; others held sandals variegated with gold, silver, and the like, and adorned with peacock feathers and other ornaments;
and some, having displayed the outline of the hairline—four finger-breadths wide and a span in length—at the edge of a cloud, [stood] there.
Tying a turban-cloth on the forehead like a flash of lightning and wearing a crest-jewel, or carrying a yak-tail fan—all that is not permitted.
"Of this putrid body" means of this corpse-like body composed of the four great elements. "Keḷanā" means playing.
*Parikeḷanā* means causing one to play in every way. *Gedhitatā* means the state of longing.
*Gedhitattaṃ* means the state of greed, the state of longing. *Capalatā* means the act of adorning. *Cāpalyaṃ* means the state of being fickle.

In the phrases beginning with *savibhūsaṃ*, *savibhūsaṃ* means together with adornment. *Saparivāraṃ* means together with the retinue known as the application of skin-coloring (cosmetics). *Saparibhaṇḍaṃ* means together with the trimmings. *Saparikkhāraṃ* means together with the requisites.
162. *Āthabbaṇaṃ* refers to the employment of Atharvanic mantras. *Supinaṃ* refers to the science of dreams. *Lakkhaṇaṃ* refers to the characteristics of jewels and so forth.
*No vidaheti*: one should not employ them. *Virutañca*: the cries and calls of deer and other animals. *Āthabbaṇikā* are those who know the mantras for harming others.
It is said that those who employ *āthabbaṇa*—having eaten food without salt for seven days, spread out grass, and slept upon the ground—practice asceticism and on the seventh day...
Having prepared a cemetery ground and standing on the seventh footprint, they roll their hands over and over and mutter the spell with their mouths;
then their ritual succeeds. It is with reference to such practices that he said, "they employ *āthabbaṇa*.
In this context, "they employ" means they are engaged in the application [of the ritual]. Or, "when the city is besieged" means when the city is surrounded on all sides.
"Having hemmed in and surrounded" means having been seized. "When a battle is set before them" means having approached and stood in the fray.
"Against adversaries and enemies" means against hostile foes who have become obstacles. "Causing calamity" means producing bodily trembling and shaking;
they bring about that production. "Affliction" means causing physical pain. "Disease" means illness. "Prajjaraka" means...
"Jaraṃ" means aging. "Sūlaṃ" means a bloated corpse. "Visūcikā" means piercing pain (cholera). "Pakkhandikā" means dysentery with blood. "Karonti" means they produce.
"Supinapāṭhakā" means dream-interpreters. "Ādisanti" means they explain. "Yo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ supinaṃ" refers to a dream seen in the morning time.
In such phrases as "he sees," the accusative case is used to denote continuous connection; the meaning is "at the time of forenoon.
"Thus the result comes to be" means that such a result arises according to whether it is desirable or undesirable. "Lying face down" means lying with the face turned downward;
thus do dream-interpreters explain a dream.
Furthermore, one who sees a dream sees it for four reasons:
either from a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*), from what was previously experienced, from the influence of deities (*devatā*), or from a prognostic sign (*pubbanimitta*).

In this context, one whose elements are disturbed through association with conditions that cause the disturbance of bile and the other humors sees a dream due to a disturbance of the elements; and while seeing, one sees various kinds of dreams.
Contemplating from what was previously experienced, one sees an object that was previously experienced.
Contemplating through the intervention of deities, one sees objects by means of the power of the deities.
Contemplating from a prognostic sign, one sees a dream that serves as a prognostic sign for a future benefit or harm arising through the influence of merit or demerit. In this regard:
A dream that one sees due to a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*) or from what has been previously experienced is not true.
That which one sees due to the influence of deities (*devatā*) may be either true or false; for when deities are angry and desire to destroy [someone] by some means, they show even what is perverted.
However, that which one sees as a portent (*pubbanimitta*) is exclusively true. Of these...
Furthermore, the variety of dreams arises precisely from the variety of the contact and the breaking of the four primary causes.

Moreover, only those who are still in training (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) see these four kinds of dreams, because they have not yet abandoned the perversions (*vipallāsa*). Those beyond training (*asekha*) do not see them, because they have abandoned the perversions.
Now, does one see this while asleep, or while awake, or while neither asleep nor awake?
What is the point here? If, first of all, he sees while asleep, it results in a contradiction with the Abhidhamma.
For one sleeps with the *bhavaṅga*-consciousness, which does not have visible forms or signs as its object, nor is it associated with lust and so forth;
yet such states of consciousness arise for one who is seeing a dream. If, on the other hand, he sees while awake, it results in a contradiction with the Vinaya. For that which...

When one sees while awake, one sees with a mind engaged in worldly activity (*sabbohārika-citta*); and there is no such thing as "non-offense" (*anāpatti*) for a transgression committed with a mind engaged in worldly activity.
However, for a transgression committed by one seeing a dream, there is certainly no offense at all.
Furthermore, if one sees neither while asleep nor while awake, who indeed could see? And this being the case, there would simply be an absence of dreaming.
It is not non-existence. Why? Because one sees while overcome by monkey-sleep. For this has been said:
"O Great King, one who has reached the middle [of the night], overcome by monkey-sleep, sees a dream.
"Overcome by monkey-sleep" means possessed of the sleep of a monkey. For just as the sleep of a monkey is characterized by rapid shifting, so too is this state.

Thus, that sleep which, because it is interspersed with wholesome and other types of consciousness, is light and rapidly shifting—when there is a repeated crossing back from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) during its occurrence, one who is joined with that [sleep] sees a dream. Therefore, this dream may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
In that regard, acts such as worshipping a shrine, hearing the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma occurring within a dream—

It should be understood that when one performs wholesome deeds it is wholesome, when one performs unwholesome deeds such as the taking of life it is unwholesome, and at the moments of adverting and having that as its object, it is neutral (abyākata), being free from both extremes.
Because the volition has a weak basis, this [neutral consciousness] is incapable of drawing forth rebirth-linking;
however, during the course of existence (pavatta), supported by other wholesome or unwholesome states, it yields its result.

The meaning is that in works such as the *Maṇilakkhaṇa* (Characteristics of Gems), they explain the characteristics of gems and so forth by way of their color, shape, and other qualities, stating: "A gem of such a kind is praised; a gem of such a kind is not praised; it is or is not a cause for the master’s health, prosperity, and so on.
In this context, "the characteristics of weapons" refers to all weapons with the exception of the sword and others. The same applies to the characteristics of women and so forth.
The [characteristics] of whichever family men, women, and so forth reside in should be understood solely by way of its increase or decline.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of goats and so on, this distinction should also be understood: "The meat of such goats and so forth may be eaten; that of such others must not be eaten.
Moreover, here, even in the case of the characteristics of the monitor lizard (*godhā*)—such as in paintings, ornaments, and so forth—it is said: "When such a monitor lizard exists, this..."
This too should be understood as a distinction. The characteristics of the *kaṇṇikā* (central nave) should be understood by way of both the jeweled *kaṇṇikā* and the house *kaṇṇikā*.
The characteristics of the tortoise (*kacchapa*) are exactly like those of the monitor lizard (*godhā*).
The characteristics of the deer (*miga*) are comprehensive, being stated by way of the characteristics of all four-footed animals. Thus, the readers of characteristics declare the characteristics.
Thus, those who recite the science of marks (lakkhaṇa) point out and explain the marks.
"Constellations" refers to the twenty-eight constellations, beginning with Kattika.

"By this constellation, the entry into the house should be performed" means that the auspicious ceremony for entering the home should be performed. "The crown should be bound" refers to the auspicious ceremony of adornment.

It should be performed. Regarding "the betrothal": having spoken of the performance of the marriage ceremony by saying, "Bring a girl from such-and-such a family for this boy under such-and-such a lunar mansion," and having spoken of the performance of the wedding ceremony by saying, "Give this girl to the boy named so-and-so under such-and-such a lunar mansion;
in this way their prosperity will come about"—this refers to the auspicious occasion of marriage consisting of the betrothal and the wedding known as *vāreyya*.
"It should be done," they instruct. "The carrying out of seeds" means the removal of seeds outside for the purpose of sowing; "nihāro" is also a reading in the Pāḷi.
"Knowledge of the cries of beasts" is a collective term, stated specifically by way of knowing the sounds of all birds and four-footed animals.
"Reciters of the knowledge of the cries of beasts" refers to those who explain the vocalizations of birds and quadrupeds. "They teach the knowledge of the cries of beasts," etc.
Having heard their sound, they explain it. *Rutaṃ* means sound; or the reading is *rudaṃ*. *Vassitaṃ* means speech.
*Gabbhakaraṇīyo* refers to those who, by administering medicine, effect the stabilization of a fetus that was perishing, so that it does not perish again.
For a fetus perishes due to three causes: wind, parasites, and karma. Among these, regarding that which perishes due to wind:
He gives cooling medicine that destroys wind-disorders (*vāta*). When [diseases] are destroyed by parasites, he provides a remedy for the parasites.

However, when [diseases] are destroyed by karma, even the Buddhas are not able to ward them off; therefore, that is not included here. "Surgery" (*sālākiya*) refers to the medical practice of using probes or lancets (*salāka*).
"Flesh-cutting" (*sallakattiya*) refers to the medical practice of excision with a knife (*sallakatta*). "Body-treatment" (*kāyatikiccha*)...
Having combined root medicines and so forth, it is the medical practice of treating the body. *Bhūtiyaṃ* means the medical practice of exorcism.
*Komārabhaccaṃ* means the medical practice of pediatrics. *Kuhā* means those who deceive. *Thaddhā* means those whose bodies are as rigid as a block of wood.
*Lapā* means those whose speech is dependent on worldly conditions. *Siṅgī* means those whose nature is to adorn themselves. *Unnaḷā* means those whose reed of conceit has risen up high.
"Unconcentrated" means devoid of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
Regarding "should not take up," and so forth: one should not take it up by way of reciting the headings; one should not master it by way of recitation (*sajjhāya*);
one should not retain it by way of fixing it in the mind; one should not attend to it by way of placing it close at hand; [and one should not examine it] by way of investigation.
One should not recognize [it]. One should not employ it by means of instructing others.
163. *Pesuṇiyaṃ* means malicious talebearing (*pesuñña*). The rest of the explanation has already been stated.
164. *Kayavikkaye*: [trading] with five fellow practitioners, either by way of deception or by way of seeking profit.

Or he should not remain [in such a state]. "A bhikkhu should not utter reproach" means that by not producing the defilements that cause reproach, he should not provoke reproach against himself from other recluses and brahmins.
"And he should not be attached in the village" means that he should not be attached in the village through socializing with householders and the like.
"Out of desire for gain, he should not flatter people" means that out of a longing for profit, he should not engage in sycophancy toward others.
“Those acts of buying and selling that are prohibited in the Vinaya” refers to those which are prohibited under the training rule concerning buying and selling by way of receiving gifts;
in order to show the specific kind of buying and selling intended here, he says, “from five [monks] together, whether it be a bowl or a robe,” and so forth.
In that context, “from five” means from five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
Together. "Those belonging to the same Dhamma" (sahadhammika) refers to the five:
bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, sāmaṇeras, and sāmaṇerīs. "Something to be deceived" means something that can be deceived by showing a counterfeit.
"Seeking profit" means seeking increase. "Exchanges" means he performs an exchange.
"Powerful" (*iddhimanta*) means possessing the majesty of success. "Possessing the divine eye" (*dibbacakkhuka*) means possessing the eye of knowledge that is like the divine;

or alternatively, possessing the eye of knowledge obtained by relying on the divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*). "Knowers of others' minds" (*paracittaviduno*) means those who know the minds of others by means of their own mind.
"They see even from afar" means [they see] even from one *yojana*, or a hundred *yojanas*, or even a thousand *yojanas*.
They see and perceive even from a hundred thousand *yojanas*, from a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), or from two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, forty, or even more than forty thousand *yojanas*.
"Even those nearby are not seen" means that even those standing close by or sitting near are not discerned.
"They know the mind with their own mind" means they know the minds of others with their own minds.
They understand. There are indeed deities who possess psychic power (*iddhimantiniyo*); thus there exist deities endowed with the majesty of success.

"Those who know the minds of others" (*paracittaviduniyo*) means those who know the minds of others. "By gross defilements" (*oḷārikehi vā kilesehi*) refers to bodily misconduct and so forth, or by afflictions.
"By middling ones" (*majjhimehi vā*) refers to sensual thoughts and so forth. "By subtle ones" (*sukhumehi vā*) refers to thoughts concerning relatives and so forth.

Alternatively, bodily misconduct and so forth should be understood by way of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*), while sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitakka*) and so forth should be understood by way of the defilements rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-mūlaka-kilesa*).

Regarding thoughts concerning relatives (*ñāti-vitakka*) and so on: a thought that arises with reference to relatives, based on a worldly affection dependent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure, thinking, "My relatives live happily, endowed with prosperity," is a thought concerning relatives. [The thought] "My relatives are subject to destruction... [is also a thought concerning relatives].
However, a reflection that proceeds in the manner of, "We have gone; our faith has gone; those who were confident have passed away," is not what is called *ñātivitakka* (reflection on relatives).

*Janapadavitakka* (reflection on one's country) is the reflection that arises through the influence of domestic affection in one whose mind is delighted by the thought, "Our country is well-supplied with food and abundant in crops.
[The reflection that arises] in one who thinks, "In our country, people who were faithful and confident have come to their end... [is *janapadavitakka*].
However, that which proceeds as "we have gone" is not what is called a reflection on the country (*janapada-vitakka*).
A reflection for the sake of immortality, or a reflection that is immortal, is an "immortality-reflection" (*amaravitakka*).

In this regard, when suffering has been worn away through such practices as the crouching exertion (*ukkuṭikappadhāna*), the self becomes happy in the future life. It is "immortal" because for one who performs such difficult austerities, by that [practice]...
Thought associated with the practice of austerities is called "thought for immortality. However, when one who holds to a speculative view is asked, "Do you say it is eternal?

and so forth, he resorts to evasion, saying, "It is not thus for me, nor is it otherwise for me, nor is it both for me, nor is it neither for me, nor is it not-neither for me. Such thought associated with his speculative view is what is meant.
Just as a fish called "immortal" (amara), when seized in water, cannot be killed and runs hither and thither without falling into a net,
so too, because it does not settle upon any single side, it is called "immortal" (amara) since it does not die;
taking both of these together, it is termed "the thought of immortality" (amaravitakka).
"Connected with lack of compassion for others" means being bound by a worldly affection that is a counterfeit of compassion.
When his attendants rejoice or grieve, he rejoices or grieves twice as much as they do;
when they are happy, he becomes twice as happy, and when they are suffering, he becomes twice as suffering. This occurs when duties and obligations arise.
He applies himself to various tasks; while accomplishing those various duties, he transgresses the formal precepts and violates his own austerity.
Whatever thought connected with the household life arises during that dwelling in association or during that application to tasks, this is called thought associated with concern for others.
"Connected with gain, honor, and renown" means being connected by way of taking as an object both the acquisition of robes and so forth, as well as honor and fame.
"Connected with not being despised" means [being connected] with the aspiration for the state of not being despised, thinking:
"O, may others not despise me; may they speak to me after having purified themselves and cleared themselves."
It is the thought that arises together [with the desire for non-disparagement].

When that thought has arisen—thinking, "May others not despise me"—it is a thought dependent on the house consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and it is a thought associated with non-disparagement.
It clings here and there means it adheres to various objects. It grasps here and there refers to the aforementioned manner.
It enters the object. "Is bound" means it is bound together with, or becomes one with, those various objects.
"Misfortune and ruin" refers to decline and destruction in this or that situation. "Falls into" means he reaches it.
"One who has an eye for material things" means one who is greedy for material goods such as robes and the like. "One who values worldly conditions" means having abandoned the supramundane Dhamma.

For one who lives making only worldly conditions such as forms (rūpa) and so forth their priority. "Addressing" (ālapanā) means that upon seeing people who have come to the monastery, one speaks from the very beginning, saying:
"For what purpose, sirs, have you come? Is it to invite monks? If so, go ahead;
I shall follow after, taking the monks with me. Alternatively, it refers to presenting oneself [to others], saying: "I..."
“Three [people] have confidence in me; such-and-such and such-and-such royal ministers have confidence in me”—this kind of talk directed toward oneself is *ālapanā* (addressing).
*Lapanā* is the speaking in the manner just described when one is questioned.
*Sallapanā* is speaking well after having granted an opportunity to one who is afraid of the householders' dissatisfaction. *Ullapanā*...
“Flattery” (*lapanā*) is speaking by extolling [others] as “great householders,” “great ship-owners,” or “great lords of giving.

“Garrulousness” (*samullapanā*) is speaking by extolling them from every possible aspect. “Pressing” (*unnahanā*) is, for example, saying: “Lay followers, formerly at such a time you gave new offerings;
why do you not give now? and so on, until they say: “We shall give, venerable sir, we simply cannot find the opportunity,” and so forth.
They say that these are successive bindings; what is meant is "wrappings. Alternatively, seeing someone with sugarcane in their hand, he asks:
"Upāsaka, where was this brought from? "From the sugarcane field, Bhante. "Is the sugarcane there sweet, Bhante?
"It can only be known by eating it, Bhante. [He thinks: "It is not proper for me to say, 'Upāsaka, give sugarcane to the bhikkhu.'"

Such talk as this, which involves unraveling even for one who is attempting to unravel [the matter], is *unnahanā* (enticement). *Samunnahanā* (persistent enticement) is enticement from every side, repeated again and again.
*Ukkācanā* (flattering) is the act of lifting up [one’s status] by saying, “This family knows me alone;
if any gift arises here, they will give it only to me”; thus it is called *uddīpanā* (inciting).

Furthermore, repeated praising from every aspect is "constant praise" (*samukkācanā*). "Speaking agreeably" (*anuppiyabhāṇitā*) is the repeated utterance of pleasant words by means of [providing] requisites.
"Gentleness of speech" (*saṇhavācatā*) is the quality of soft speech. "Affability of speech" (*sakhilavācatā*) is the quality of speech that is measured and moderate, or speech that is relaxed.
"Relaxed speech" (*sithilavācatā*) is speech that is conciliatory. "Non-harshness of speech" (*apharusavācatā*) is the quality of sweet speech.
“Ancestral property” (*purāṇa*) means that which arose in the past and belonged to one’s mother and father. “Hidden” (*antarahita*) means concealed or out of sight.
“I know it” means I am aware of it. “A family attendant of such-and-such” means a devotee who frequents the household of such-and-such a minister.
“Of such-and-such” means of such-and-such a female lay follower (*upāsikā*). “Having abandoned me” means having dismissed me.
165. *Payuttaṃ* means connected with robes and so forth, or employed for their sake. The entire explanation of this verse follows the same method as stated above.
166. *Mosavajje na niyyethā* means one should not yield to false speech. *Jīvitena* means by way of livelihood.
*Saṭho* means that which is spoken improperly because it displays non-existent qualities; it is "smooth" (*saṭha*) in every part, thus "completely smooth" (*parisaṭha*). That which...
"In that" (*tattha*) means: in that person. "Craftiness" (*saṭha*) is the act of displaying non-existent virtues; it is hypocrisy (*kerāṭiya*). "Cunningness" (*saṭhatā*) is the state of being crafty.
"Deceitfulness" (*sāṭheyya*) is the quality of being crafty. "Hardness" (*kakkharatā*) is a harshness like that of a lotus stalk, which cannot be touched;

"roughness" (*kakkariya*) is a synonym for that same thing. By the two terms "obstinacy" (*parikkhattatā*) and "obstinate behavior" (*pārikkhattiya*), [the text] refers to having dug in [one's heels].
This is stated as if it were established in the *Daḷhakeraṭiya*. However, some explain the meaning as follows: "The word *kakkaratā* means 'to be esteemed';
the state of being *kakkariya* is 'the state of being esteemed. *Parikkhattatā* is the manner of adorning; *pārikkhattiya* is the state of adorning.
This is called [self-exaltation], which has the characteristic of proclaiming qualities that do not exist in oneself.
What is called "deceit" (sāṭheyya) is that by which a person endowed with it cannot have his belly or his back known. As it is said:
"By the left side he is a boar, by the right an antelope;
by his cry he is a wild ox, and by his horns an old bull."
Thus he is like the aforementioned spirit and the pig. "He despises" means he thinks with contempt.
"But what is this 'one who lives by abundance'?"—who indeed is this person called a *bahulājīvaka*?
"He devours everything" means he eats whatever he obtains. "Of little merit" means one of meager merit. "Of little influence" means devoid of a retinue. "Endowed with wisdom" means...
"Of perfected wisdom" means one whose wisdom is complete. "He answers a question" means he speaks upon or explains a question. 167.
"Having heard much speech uttered in anger, whether by recluses or by ordinary people": "angered" means provoked by others;
[he hears] much undesirable speech from those recluses, or from others such as kṣatriyas and so forth, who are ordinary people.
Having heard [this], one should not respond; one should not retort. For what reason? Because the virtuous do not create an adversary. "Harshly" means cruelly.
"The virtuous" means those whose defilements are extinguished (*nibbuta*). "Adversary" (*paṭiseni*) means an enemy. "Rival" (*paṭimalla*) means an opponent. "Thorn" (*paṭikaṇṭaka*) means an enemy.
"Opponent" (*paṭipakkha*) refers to that which is opposed to the defilements, by way of the defilements.
The meaning is: "They do not form attachments. 168. *Etañca dhammaṃ aññāya*:

having understood all this Dhamma as it has been described. *Vicinanti* means investigating. *Santi*: having known Nibbāna; that is, having known Nibbāna as the stilling (*santi*) of lust and the other defilements.
*Samañca*: bodily good conduct and so forth. *Visamañca*: bodily misconduct and so forth. *Pathañca*: the ten courses of wholesome action.
"And the wrong path" refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasakusalakammapatha*). "Blameworthy" refers to the unwholesome. "Blameless" refers to the wholesome.
"Inferior and superior, dark and bright, censured by the wise and praised by the wise"—this too refers exclusively to the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Among these, bodily good conduct and so forth are "even" because they produce evenness; bodily misconduct and so forth are "uneven" because they produce unevenness. The ten wholesome courses of action...

It is a "path" (*patha*) because it is the way leading to a happy destination (*sugatigamana*). The ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusalakammapatha*) are a "wrong path" (*vipatha*) because they are the opposite of the way leading to a happy destination and are the way leading to states of misery (*apāya*).
The unwholesome is "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) because it is accompanied by defilement (*sadosa*). The wholesome is "blameless" (*anavajja*) because it is free from defilement (*niddosa*).

Likewise, it is "inferior" (*hīna*) because it is associated with delusion (*moha*), or with both hatred and delusion (*dosamoha*), or with greed and delusion (*lobhamoha*). It is [superior] because it is associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion (*alobha-adosa-amoha*).

It is sublime. It is black because it has black fruition; it is white because it has white fruition. It should be understood as "condemned by the wise" because it is censured by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others, and as "praised by the wise" because it is commended by those very same ones.

If one asks for what reason one should not be negligent, it is because of the verse beginning, "For he is a conqueror. In that context, "conqueror" (*abhibhū*) refers to [one who has conquered] form and the other [sense objects].
*Abhibhavitā*: "Unconquered" means not overcome by those [defilements]. *Sakkhidhammam anītiham addasī*:

"He saw the Dhamma, which is directly perceived and not based on tradition," meaning he beheld the Dhamma that is indeed manifest and not mere hearsay. *Sadā namassam anusikkhe*: "Always honoring, one should train in the three trainings," meaning one should train in the three trainings while constantly paying homage.

*Kehici kilesehi*: "By certain defilements," meaning by certain defilements such as lust and so forth that cause affliction. *Abhibhosi ne*: "You have conquered them," meaning you have overcome those defilements. The rest is clear everywhere.
However, herein, the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is shown by such passages as "not fickle with the eyes";

the virtue of using requisites (*paccayapaṭisevana-sīla*) by way of the prohibition of hoarding, by such passages as "of food and drink"; the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkhasaṃvara-sīla*) by such passages as "sexual intercourse, intoxicants, and slander";

the virtue of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla*) by such passages as "divination, dream-interpretation, and physiognomy"; and [the virtue of right conduct] by such passages as "the meditator is not fickle with his feet."

By the phrase "this concentration," concentration is indicated; by "discerning, O bhikkhus," wisdom is indicated; and by "always training with mindfulness," the three trainings are again indicated in brief.

Furthermore, by such passages as "then, in sitting places and sleeping places, the bhikkhu should dwell in quietude and should not indulge in sleep," the assistance, non-assistance, inclusion, and avoidance regarding virtue, concentration, and wisdom have been stated.
Thus the Blessed One, having explained the complete practice for the created being, brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization exactly as described in the *Purābheda Sutta*.
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta is finished.
15. Commentary on the exposition of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. 170.
Regarding the fifteenth [sutta], the Attadaṇḍa Sutta, the meaning of the first verse, "Fear has arisen from the staff of self," is as follows:
"Whatever fear has arisen for the world, whether pertaining to this present life or to the future life, all that has arisen from the rod of self;

it has arisen because of one's own misconduct. Even though this is so, look at the people in conflict—look at these people, such as the Sakyans and others, who are mutually in conflict, harming and oppressing one another. Thus he spoke in opposition to them.

Having rebuked the person who had practiced wrongly, he spoke thus—"I shall proclaim the sense of urgency (saṃvega), just as it was realized by me"—in order to arouse a sense of urgency in him by demonstrating his own right practice. The intention is that [the person] was previously [reborn] as a Bodhisatta himself.
"Three" is the limit of the number. "Sticks" (daṇḍa) refers to misconduct. "The stick of body" (kāyadaṇḍa) is bodily misconduct. This also applies to the stick of speech and so forth.

The same method applies here. "Threefold bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*) refers to the three types of misconduct proceeding from the body, such as the taking of life, which are called "misconduct" because they are evil deeds, or because they are "evil conduct" due to being rotten with defilements (*kilesa*).

"Fourfold" refers to the fourfold [misconduct] beginning with false speech. "Threefold" refers to the threefold [unwholesome states] beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*). "Belonging to this visible world" (*diṭṭhadhammika*)...
"To be experienced in this very life" means to be experienced in this very current existence. "In the future life" means to be experienced in a future existence.
"A wrongdoer" means one who commits evil or commits offenses. "The king rebukes him" means the king rebukes the evildoer and instills fear in him.
"He experiences suffering and grief" refers to bodily suffering.
He experiences mental distress. "This fear, this suffering, this distress"—such is the fear, suffering, and distress.
"From where did it come for him? means from where did it arise for that thief?
It arose from his own punishment, that is, from the misconduct committed by himself.
"Antamaso" means from the very bottom. "He makes [the person] subject to his word" means: "It is not permitted for you to depart from here";
that is, it is not permitted to go from this village or other location. He creates an obstacle and a bond by making it impossible to go outside.
"Even on account of the loss of wealth" means even because of the cause of the depletion of wealth. The king causes various forms of punishment to be inflicted upon him.
"He beats them with whips" means he strikes them with leather thongs. "He beats them with canes" means he strikes them with thorny cane-vines.
"With half-sticks," and so forth, follow the same method explained below.
"He has them devoured by dogs" means that after withholding food for several days, he has hungry dogs devour them; in a mere moment, they become nothing but skeletons of bones.
He performs [these acts]. "He impales on a stake" means he causes him to be placed upon a stake.
"The king is the master of these four punishments" means the king is capable of carrying out these four commands.
"By his own karma" means by the karma performed by himself. Regarding the phrase "the wardens of hell," some elders [hold that] the wardens of hell...
They say, "There is no such thing; it is karma alone that acts as the cause, like a mechanical doll.
However, their position has already been refuted in the Abhidhamma by such methods as: "Are there wardens in the hells? Yes. And are there those who inflict punishment?
For just as there are those who carry out punishments in the human world, so too there are wardens in the hells.

Regarding the "red-hot iron pillar": they force a palm-tree-sized iron stake through the right hand of a person whose body has been laid face up upon a blazing iron ground extending for three gavutas; they do the same with the left hand and so forth.
And just as they lay them face up, they inflict that same torturous punishment even when laying them on their chests, on their left side, or on their right side.
"Having laid him down" means having caused his own body, three *gāvutas* in height, to lie upon the blazing iron earth.
"With axes" means they cut him with great axes as large as a single side of a house roof;
blood flows like a river, flames rise from the iron earth and seize the place where he is being cut, and great suffering arises.
But having fashioned it with saws, they make it eight-sided or six-sided, just like wood.

"With axes" means with axes as large as great winnowing-fans. "Having yoked to chariots" means having yoked them to chariots that are blazing on all sides, complete with yokes, thongs, fittings, wheels, hubs, and poles.
"Large" means the size of a great gabled house. "They mount" means [upon those] that are fully ablaze.
Striking them with iron bars, they throw them up. For a moment, they rise up like rice grains cast into a well-heated frying pan, moving upwards, downwards, and across.
"In the Great Hell" means in the Avīci Great Hell. "Four-cornered" means resembling a square chest. "Divided" means divided by way of four gates. "By parts."
"Divided" means it is partitioned by repeatedly establishing sections according to the gates and streets. "Enclosed" means surrounded.
"Covered with iron" means it is covered on top with a new iron plate nine *yojanas* thick.

"It stands pervading a hundred *yojanas* all around" means it stands having spread out in this way, so that for one standing and looking all around within those hundred *yojanas*, the eyes are like twin marbles.
They emerge as if [from a fire]. As for "the tormentors of the miserly" (*kadariyātapanā*): all those eight great hells, together with their sub-hells (*ussada*), constantly torment the miserly;

thus they are called "the tormentors of the miserly. They are "terrible" (*ghorā*) due to the intensity of their suffering. They are "flaming" (*accimanto*) because of the presence of flames that endure for an eon (*kappa*).
They are "unassailable" (*durāsadā*) because it is difficult to approach or to strike them. Merely seeing or merely hearing of them makes one's hair stand on end.

They are called *haṃsantī* because they cause the hair to stand on end (*lomahaṃsana*). They are *bhīsma* due to their terrifying nature. They are *paṭibhaya* because they produce fear. They are *dukkha* due to the absence of happiness.
Regarding the verses beginning with "On the eastern wall," etc., this is the summary of the meaning, ending with the Avīci hell:
there is no interval (*vīci*) here, whether between the flames of fire, or between the beings themselves, or between their sufferings.
Avīci. For there, masses of flames arise from the eastern walls and so forth, burning the person who has committed evil deeds;
they strike and rebound against the western walls and so forth, and having pierced through those walls, they extend for another hundred yojanas.
Those rising from below strike against the top, and those rising from above strike against the bottom. Thus...
In this place, there is no gap between the nets. Within it, an area of one hundred *yojanas* is filled with beings without any interval, like a tube filled with milk-rice paste;

there is no measure for the number of beings at the boundaries who exist in the four postures, yet they do not obstruct one another, but rather pass away each in their own respective place. Thus it is here.
For sentient beings, there is no such thing as an interval.

However, just as six drops of honey on the tip of the tongue become negligible due to the overwhelming power of the burning of the seventh drop of molten copper, so too, because of the overwhelming power of that burning, the remaining six unwholesome-resultant equanimities become negligible, and only uninterrupted suffering is perceived. Thus it is here.
There is no interval in suffering. It is called "hell" (niraya) in the sense of being devoid of gratification.
Therein, beings are "greatly cruel" means that the beings reborn there are great and cruel. "Committers of great evil deeds" means performers of great and terrible kamma.
"Those whose actions are exclusively evil" means those who are entirely devoted to unwholesome deeds. They are cooked...
And they do not die; they are cooked within six nets, yet they do not perish.
"The body is like fire" means their bodies are similar to a flame. "Of those dwellers in hell" refers to those inhabitants of hell who possess evil karma.
"Behold the firmness of kamma" means look upon the stability of evil deeds. It does not turn to ash, nor...
There is neither soot nor ash, nor even charcoal. "To the east" means that when that gate is opened, they run toward it;

there their skin and other parts are scorched. When they reach the vicinity of the gate, it is closed to them, appearing as if the western gate were open. This same method applies everywhere. [They do so] with the hope of escaping.

"Those who have hope for escape" (*nikkhamitāsā*) are those who possess the desire to emerge from those hells. "Seeking liberation" (*mokkhagavesino*) means seeking and searching for the means of release.

"They do not obtain the opportunity to escape from there due to the condition of their karma" means that those beings do not find an exit door from hell because of the condition of their evil deeds. And as long as their evil karma has not yet ripened...

"Much has been done": there exists much low and cruel karma committed by those beings—of many kinds and various types—which has not yet ripened, has not yet yielded its result, and has been accumulated.
"Terror" (*saṃvega*) means the state of being livid. "Agitation" (*ubbega*) means moving from one's place. "Dread" (*utrāsa*) means being terrified and lacking a sense of certainty.
“Fears” (*bhayanti*) means the terror of the mind. “Affliction” (*pīḷana*) means oppression. “Oppression” (*ghaṭṭana*) means causing affliction.
“Calamity” (*upaddava*) means misfortune. “Misfortune” (*upasagga*) means obstruction. 171.
Now, showing the manner in which he was agitated, he said “trembling,” and so forth. Therein:
"Phandamānaṃ" means trembling due to craving and views. "Appodake" means where there is little water.
"Disvā aññamaññehi byāruddhe" means having seen various beings who are hostile toward one another. "Maṃ bhayamāvisī" means fear has entered me.
"Phandamānaṃ kilesaphandanāya" means trembling due to the agitation of the defilements, such as lust and so forth. "Payogo" refers to the application of body, speech, and mind.
*Viruddhā* means having entered into opposition. *Paṭiviruddhā* means having entered into opposition face-to-face, or being thoroughly opposed.
*Āhatā* means struck or beaten by anger. *Paccāhatā* means struck while acting as an adversary.
*Āghātitā* means provoked. *Paccāghātitā* means especially provoked. *Pāṇīhipi upakkamantī* means they even strike with their hands.
172. "The world is entirely without essence": beginning with the hells, the world on all sides is without essence, devoid of any permanent substance or the like.
"All directions are shaken": all directions are trembling due to impermanence. "Desiring a mere dwelling for myself":
desiring a refuge for oneself. "I saw no place where I could dwell": I did not see any place that was not already inhabited by old age and the other [afflictions].
"Without core" (*asāra*) means not having a core, or being devoid of a core. "Coreless" (*nissāra*) means entirely devoid of a core in every respect.
"Departed from the core" (*sārāpagata*) means gone away from the core. "By means of a constant core-essence" (*niccasārasārena vā*) means by means of an essence reckoned as perpetual.

This same method applies to the following two phrases as well. "Those formations in the eastern direction" (*ye puratthimāya disāya saṅkhārā*) refers to those formations which have come together through conditions in the eastern direction.

"Formed by coming together" means conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*). "They are stirred" means those conditioned phenomena are shaken. "Shaken thoroughly" means completely shaken. "Moved" means they have reached a state of motion.
"Struck" means oppressed by arising and passing away. "By impermanence" means by the state of ceasing after having come to be.
"Followed by birth" means entered into through production. "Pervaded by aging" means overtaken by the state of full ripeness.
"Overcome by disease" means overwhelmed by the disease that has arisen from the fourfold imbalance of the humors.
"Struck down by death" means assailed and smitten by mortality. "Without protection" means devoid of a guardian. "Without refuge" means devoid of a shelter.

"Without a resort" means they have no resort; thus they are without a resort. "Become without a resort" means they themselves do not perform the function of seeking a resort; thus they have become without a resort.
"His own state of being" is the summary phrase for the explanatory passage. "Refuge" means protection. "Cave" means a place of shelter.
"Saranam" (refuge) means the destruction of suffering. "Gati" means a foundation. "Parāyaṇam" means the ultimate resort.
"They saw it as clung-to" means they beheld it as indeed crushed by old age and the like. "All youthfulness" (*yobbañña*): the state of youth is "youthfulness."
All youthfulness of sentient beings is overwhelmed by old age; that is, it is finished and crushed by the ripening of old age. This applies everywhere.

173. “But seeing them at the very end, obstructed, weariness arose in me”—seeing beings whose minds are struck down, obstructed by old age and so forth at the very end, the limit, the point of destruction of youthfulness and the rest, weariness arose in me. Then, in this regard...
“Salla” means, moreover, the dart of lust and so forth among these beings. “Situated in the heart” means dependent upon the mind.
“Youth ends with old age” means that old age brings it to its conclusion, destroys it.
This applies in all cases. If one asks, “What is the power of the dart? it is expressed in the verse beginning, “By which dart one is pierced. In this context, “all directions” refers to...
"It runs about" means it runs toward all directions of misconduct, as well as the eastern and other cardinal directions and the intermediate directions.
"Having extracted that very dart, he neither runs nor sinks" means that having pulled out that very dart, he does not run toward those directions, nor does he sink in the four floods (*oghā*).
Regarding "ignorance" (*aññāṇa*) and so forth: ignorance is non-knowing and non-seeing because it is the opposite of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*); [one who acts] facing toward the Dhamma...

It is called "non-comprehension" (*anabhisamaya*) because it does not coincide with or come together [with reality]. It is called "subsequent awakening" (*anubodha*) because one awakens to phenomena in accordance with their true nature.

It is "non-subsequent awakening" (*ananubodha*) by virtue of being the opposite of that. It is called "non-awakening" (*asambodha*) because one does not awaken by connecting [phenomena] with impermanence and so forth; it is also "non-awakening" because one awakens to what is non-existent and improper.
It is called "non-penetration" (*appaṭivedha*) because one does not penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Regarding form and the other aggregates...
It does not grasp even a single phenomenon by way of its common characteristics, such as impermanence; thus it is "non-grasping" (*asaṅgāhaṇā*). It does not penetrate that very same phenomenon;

thus it is "non-penetration" (*apariyogāhaṇā*). It does not view things with equanimity; thus it is "non-equanimity" (*asamapekkhanā*). It does not look back toward the intrinsic nature of phenomena; thus it is "non-reflection" (*apaccavekkhaṇā*).
Due to its perverted engagement in wholesome and unwholesome kamma, or because of its lack of grasping at their intrinsic nature, not even a single kamma [is understood] by this person.
It is "apaccakkhakamma" because there is no direct perception, or because there is no making of any phenomenon directly perceptible by oneself.
That which would be neutral, pure, or bright in the mental continuum if this [defilement] were not arising, becomes corrupted as neutral by this;
thus it is "dummejjha. The state of fools is "bālya. It deludes, thus it is "moha. It is the more powerful delusion.
Delusion (*pamoha*). It is "complete delusion" (*sammoha*) because it deludes on all sides. It is "ignorance" (*avijjā*) because it is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*).

Its meaning as a flood (*ogha*) and a yoke (*yoga*) has already been stated. It "lies latent" (*anuseti*) in the sense of being firmly established; thus it is a "latent tendency" (*anusaya*). It "obsesses" (*pariyuṭṭhāti*) or overcomes the mind; thus it is an "outburst" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
Due to the absence of grasping at what is beneficial, one is unable to proceed toward the beneficial and instead merely stumbles; thus...
*Laṅgī* means "she who limps" or "she who is lame. Alternatively, she is *laṅgī* in the sense of being difficult to remove.
Just as a *laṅgī*—meaning a great crossbar—is difficult to lift up, so too is this [craving] like a *laṅgī*; thus it is called *laṇgī*. The rest is self-evident.
Regarding the phrase "the doubt that is of such a kind," here "doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) is so called by way of doubting. "Bringing about doubt" is *kaṅkhāyanā*. This refers to the preceding doubt.

For it is called "bringing about doubt" (*kaṅkhaṃ ānayati*). Or rather, this is stated by way of its formal mode (*ākāra*). A consciousness possessing doubt is called "doubtful" (*kaṅkhāyita*) because it has become doubtful;
the state of that is "doubtfulness" (*kaṅkhāyitatta*). "Uncertainty" (*vimati*) means a cognition (*mati*) that has departed [from certainty].
"Perplexity" (*vicikicchā*) means a treatment (*cikicchā*) that has departed; or, one who investigates the true nature (*sabhāva*) suffers and is distressed.

This is called doubt (*vicikicchā*). It should be understood as having the characteristic of uncertainty, the function of wavering, the manifestation of indecision—or the manifestation of grasping at various alternatives—and the proximate cause of improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*);
it is an obstacle to progress. In the sense of wavering, it wavers in two ways, thus it is "doubt" (*dveḷhaka*). Because it obstructs progress, it is like a forked path.
A "twofold path" (*dvedhāpatha*). Because it is unable to settle upon a single mode through such occurrences as "Is this permanent or is it impermanent?", it lies all around;
thus it is "perplexity" (*saṃsayo*). Because it is unable to grasp one side, it is not a "one-sided grasp," hence "non-one-sided grasp" (*anekaṃsaggāho*).
Because it is unable to reach a decision, it retreats from the object; thus it is "retreating" (*āsappanā*). Because it is unable to plunge in, it [remains] all around...
"Sappati" means creeping about. It is "apariyogāhaṇā," meaning an inability to fathom due to an incapacity for deep penetration.
It is "chambhitattaṃ cittassa," meaning a state of paralysis of the mind due to an incapacity to engage with the object through decisive judgment; the sense is a state of rigidity.
For doubt, having arisen, makes the mind rigid; moreover, when it arises, it seizes hold of the object.
It is as if it were scratching the mind; therefore, it is called "mental scratching" (*manovilekho*).
"Pierced" means struck by an arrow. "Touched" means impacted. "Afflicted" means oppressed.
"Runs" means goes forward. "Runs about" means goes in various ways. "Runs hither and thither" means runs with speed. "Wanders" means moves here and there.
*Acelaka* means naked; that is the meaning. *Muttācāra* means one of loose conduct;
devoid of the conduct of worldly sons of good family regarding the acts of defecation and so forth, he defecates, urinates, eats, and consumes while remaining standing.
*Hatthāpalekhana* means that while the alms-food remains in his hand, he scrapes his hand with his tongue; or, having defecated, [he licks] the hand itself.
Perceiving them as sticks, he scrapes them with his hand; for they, it is said, designate a stick as a "living being.

Because, when told "Come, venerable sir" for the sake of receiving alms, he does not come, he is not an *ehibhadantika*. Likewise, because even when told "Stay, venerable sir," he does not stay, he is not a *tiṭṭhabhadantika*.
It is said that in both cases, thinking "I shall do what this person says," he nevertheless does not do it.
“Bringing it” (*abhihaṭa*) refers to alms-food brought after having been taken beforehand.
“Made specifically for one” (*uddissakata*) refers to alms-food announced as, “This was made for you.

“Not an invitation” (*na nimantana*) means he does not consent to nor accept even alms-food invited by saying, “You should enter such-and-such a family, street, or village. “Not from the mouth of a jar” (*na kumbhimukhā*)... [text continues]
He does not accept alms-food being given after it has been lifted from a jar. "Not from the mouth of a basket" means a basket is either a cooking pot or a tray;
he does not accept from that either. Why? Because he thinks, "The jar and the basket will receive a blow with the ladle because of me.
He does not accept what is being given with a threshold placed in between. Why?
“Thinking, ‘This person will gain an interval [for eating] by depending on me. The same principle applies to the staff and the pestle as well.
“Not from two” means that when two people are eating, he does not accept food if one stands up to give it to him. Why? Because it would cause an obstruction to his mouthful (*kabaḷantarāyo*).
Regarding “not from a pregnant woman,” and so forth, [the reason is]: “The child in the womb of a pregnant woman suffers,” and regarding a nursing woman...
He does not accept [food] thinking, "There will be an obstacle to the child’s milk," or "There will be an obstacle to the pleasure of one who has gone to another man.

"Not among those who have mixed [food]" means among those who have prepared a meal by mixing [ingredients). It is said that during a time of famine, disciples of the naked ascetics (acelaka) would collect rice and other grains from here and there for the sake of the naked ascetics and cook a meal; even from such a source, a strict naked ascetic does not accept it.
Wherever a dog stands waiting, thinking, “I shall get a morsel,” he does not take what has been brought there without first giving to it.
Why? Because that would be an obstacle to its getting food. “Moving in groups” means moving in crowds.
For if people, upon seeing a naked ascetic, enter a meal-house thinking, “We shall give alms to him,” [the monk does not accept].
And as they were entering, flies hidden in the openings of the baskets and such flew up and swarmed in clusters.
Therefore, he would not accept alms-food brought from there. Why? Because, "due to me, an obstruction to the flies' range of movement has arisen.
*Thusodaka* is sour gruel made from all kinds of grain ingredients. And herein, it is only the drinking of *surā* that is blameworthy.
But this [person] perceives everything as blameworthy.

An "eater at one house" (*ekāgārika*) is one who returns after receiving alms at only a single house. An "eater of a single mouthful" (*ekālopika*) is one who sustains himself with only a single mouthful (*ālopa*).
The same principle applies to those who eat at two houses, and so forth. "Of even a single *datti*" means of a single *datti*. A *datti*...
There is a certain small bowl in which they place the first alms-food and set it aside. "One-day" means occurring with an interval of one day.
"Fortnightly" means occurring with an interval of half a month. "Eating food by turns" means eating food according to a rotation;
that is, food brought on a one-day turn, a two-day turn, a seven-day turn, or a half-month turn—food brought according to such a daily rotation.
“Eating raw vegetables” (*sākabhakkho*) and so forth have meanings already explained. “Standing upright” (*ubbhaṭṭhako*) means standing on high.

“Devoted to the exertion of squatting” (*ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto*) means devoted to the energy of squatting. Even when walking, he walks by repeatedly springing up while remaining in a squatting posture.
“Using a bed of thorns” (*kaṇṭakāpassayiko*) means having dug iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground and [spreading] leather upon them...
Having spread it out, he performs standing meditation, walking meditation, and so forth. "Lying down" means that even while lying, he makes his bed right there.
"Sleeping on a plank" means sleeping on a wooden plank. "Sleeping on the bare ground" means sleeping on the bare earth, on a high spot of ground.
"Sleeping on one side only" means he sleeps only on one side. "Wearing dust and dirt" means he stands in a dusty place after having smeared his body with oil.
Then dust and dirt cling to his body; he bears that. "One who uses whatever seat is provided" means one whose habit is to sit down right where he finds a seat, without displacing it.
"One who eats refuse" means one whose habit is to eat refuse; "refuse" (vikaṭa) is said to mean excrement.
"One who abstains from drinking" means one who has rejected the drinking of cold water. "Sāyatatiyakaṃ" means that which belongs to the third [meal] in the evening.
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening—three times a day—he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water, thinking, "I shall wash away evil.
"They fashion those arrows" means they produce those seven arrows of lust and so forth. "Fashioning" means producing.
"By way of fashioning the arrows" means by way of the cause for producing the arrows. "He runs toward the eastern direction" means...
He goes toward the eastern direction. "Those formations of the arrow have not been abandoned" means these applications of the arrows of lust and so forth have not been abandoned.
"Because the formations of the arrow have not been abandoned" means by way of the state of those applications of the arrow not having been abandoned.
"He runs in a destination" means he runs within a destination. "From one destination to another destination" means from one state of rebirth to another.

"Does not sink" means does not submerge. "Does not sink down" means does not submerge all around. "Does not settle" means does not retreat. "Does not despond" means does not withdraw. "Does not go under" means does not go downwards. 175.
Regarding beings who have been pierced by such a shaft of great power—the training is sung therein in the verse beginning, "Those things which are clung to in the world.
Its meaning is as follows: those five strands of sensual pleasure in the world which people greedily hanker after for their acquisition...
Having done so, they are called "addicted" (*gadhitāni*); or, because they have been practiced for a long time, they are called "addicted.
In that regard, many trainings such as elephant-training and so forth are explained or mastered with reference to that sign.
Behold how capable this world is, insofar as a wise clansman is devoted to those addictions or to those trainings!
It would not be so; rather, by seeing impermanence and the rest, one becomes disillusioned with all sensual pleasures. One trains for nothing other than one's own Nibbāna.
"Having penetrated" means having emerged by means of knowledge, or having become disillusioned.
176. Now, showing how one should train for the sake of Nibbāna, he said: "One should be truthful," and so forth. Therein:
"Truthful" means endowed with truth in speech, truth in knowledge, and truth in the Path. "Free from slander" means one who has abandoned slander.
"Deceit" means stinginess. 177.

"He should overcome sleep, sloth, and lethargy" means he should master these three states: drowsiness, physical laziness, and mental laziness. "With a mind set on Nibbāna" means one whose heart is inclined toward Nibbāna.
"Unwellness of the body" (*kāyassa akalyatā*) is the state of illness of the mental body (*nāmakāya*), which is comprised of the three aggregates (*khandha*).
For one who is ill is called "unwell. It is also said in the *Vinaya*: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Incapacity" (*akammaññatā*) is the mode of incapacity consisting of bodily illness.
It is called "oppression" (*onāha*) because it oppresses the body, just as a cloud oppresses the sky; it is an oppression from every side.
*Pariyonāho*. It is called *antosamorodho* because it obstructs within. *Middhaṃ* means "it stupefies" (*medhati*); the meaning is that it harms by way of making one unfit for action.
*Suppaṃ* is so called because one sleeps by means of it. *Pacalāyikā* is so called because it causes the eyelids and so forth to droop (*pacala*).
*Suppanā* and *suppitattaṃ* are designations of its mode and state. *Olīyanā* is the mode of sinking (*olīyana*). The second [term] is due to the prefix (*upasagga*).
*Vaḍḍhitaṃ* means increased. *Līnaṃ* means shrunken due to a lack of expansion. The other two terms are descriptions of its mode of manifestation.
*Thinam* means that which exists in a dense state due to a lack of expansion, like a lump of ghee. *Thiyanaṃ* is the description of its mode of manifestation.
*Thiyitattam* is the state of being *thiyita*; the meaning is "stiffness by way of non-expansion."

"Into the realm of all formations" means with a mind inclined toward Nibbāna, within the realm of all formations belonging to the three planes of existence. "Having turned back the mind" means having caused the mind to desist.
"This is peace" refers to this Nibbāna; it is peaceful because of the pacification of the defilements. It is sublime in the sense of being insatiable.
"The wise do not give for the sake of the happiness of acquisitions" means that those of noble character do not give gifts for the sake of sensual pleasure.

And as for the phrase "for the complete destruction of the substrata" (*upadhiparikkhayāya*), these wise ones unilaterally give gifts for the sake of the destruction of sensual desire (*kāmakkhayāya*) and for the purpose of casting off sensual desire.
"For the sake of non-renewal of existence" (*apunarbhavāya*) means for the sake of Nibbāna. "They develop the jhānas" means they increase the first jhāna and so forth.
"For the sake of renewed existence" (*punabbhavāya*) means for the cause of renewed existence. Those wise ones, being oriented toward Nibbāna, give gifts.
178. *Sāhasā* refers to the impulsive acts of one who is passionate, categorized according to their temperament such as those dominated by lust (*rāgacarita*), and so forth.
The explanation is self-evident. 179. *Purāṇaṃ nābhinandeyya*: One should not delight in what is past, namely in past forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.

*Nave*: in what is present. *Hīyamāne*: in what is perishing. *Ākāsaṃ na sito siyā*: One should not be dependent on space; that is, one should not be dependent on craving (*taṇhā*). For craving is called "space" because it provides the opening for forms and other objects.
“Vemāneti” means while it is being measured. “Vigacchamāneti” means while it is passing away.
There are two readings: “ākāsati” and “ākassati.
If one asks, “For what reason would space not be dependent? [The answer is: “Greed, I say,” is the verse. Its meaning is as follows: I indeed...

I call this craving, which is designated as "space," a "greed" because it greedily hankers after forms and so forth; I speak of it as "greed. Furthermore, in the sense of carrying away, it is called an "flood";
in the sense of rushing toward, it is called a "current"; in the sense of being the cause for yearning, "this is mine, this is mine," it is called "longing";
in the sense of being difficult to relinquish, it is called an "object"; and in the sense of causing agitation—
I call it "trembling"; this very thing is called "the mire of sensual pleasures, difficult to cross" in the sense of being an obstacle for the world and in the sense of being difficult to transcend.

It is called *ājavaṃ* because it flows (*ājavanti*) and it rushes and runs (*javati dhāvati*) from the moment of rebirth-linking; this is a designation for craving, which gives rise to rebirth-linking in a future existence due to its being the root of the round of existence.
"Hankering" (*jappanaṃ*) means longing; this is a designation for craving. Craving is also called the "object."
Craving that has arisen toward objects such as visible forms is called an "object" (*ārammaṇa*) in the sense of being impossible to escape.
It is a "mire of sensual pleasure" (*kāmapaṅka*) in the sense of sinking; it is "mud" (*kaddama*) in the sense of clinging; it is a "defilement" (*kilesa*) in the sense of burning;
it is a "quagmire" (*palipa*) in the sense of causing one to stick like resin; it is an "obstruction" (*palirodha*) in the sense of holding one back by blocking the way. Thus it is said.
"Independent of space, free from the sequence beginning with greed.

(181) This is the verse beginning with "The truths do not deviate. Its meaning is as follows: The sage (*muni*), who has attained the state of a sage (*moneyya*) by not deviating from the three kinds of truths previously mentioned, stands upon the ground of Nibbāna;
such a one is called a brahmin. He [the brahmin], being of such a nature, [transcends] all sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Having relinquished [them], one is called "peaceful. There is nothing further to be said in the *Niddesa*.
182. Furthermore: the verse beginning with "He indeed is wise. Therein, "having known the Dhamma" means having understood conditioned phenomena by way of impermanence and so forth.
"He conducts himself rightly in the world" means that, through the abandoning of the defilements that cause wrong conduct, he conducts himself rightly in the world.

183. And thus, not being repelled—“He who here desires” (yo’dha kāmeti)—is the verse. Therein, “attachment” (saṅga) refers to one who has transcended the sevenfold attachment. “Does not covet” (nājjheti) means he does not long for with greed. 184.
Therefore, even among you, to whoever wishes to be of such a nature, I say this: “That which was before” (yaṃ pubbe)—is the verse.
Therein, “that which was before” refers to the defilements subject to arising in relation to past formations, as well as past kamma.
"Let there be nothing for you afterwards" means: let there be no "something" (kiñcana) such as lust and so forth, which is liable to arise in relation to future conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
"If you do not grasp in the middle" means: if you do not grasp even present phenomena such as form (rūpa) and so forth. "Thus you will wander at peace. "Make it seedless" means:
by means of the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa), do not create the seed. "The something of lust" refers to the trembling of lust; the same method applies to the "something of hatred" and so forth.
185. Having thus shown the attainment of Arahatship, he now spoke the following verses by way of praise for the Arahat.
Therein, in the verse beginning with *sabbaso*, "mamāyita" means the act of making something one's own, or an object grasped [with the thought], "This is mine.

"And he does not grieve over what is non-existent" means that he does not grieve on account of what is not found, on account of what is non-existent. "He does not waste away" means that he does not undergo decay.
"Alas, it was mine!"—thus it occurred to me. "Alas, that is no longer mine"—that which existed in the past is not present for me now.
"It might be mine"—regarding that which will be mine in the future, thinking "alas, I do not obtain it," I now certainly do not attain it.
186. Furthermore: “For whom there is nothing” (Kiñca bhiyyo – yassa natthi), etc. Therein, *kiñcana* means any kind of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

*Abhisaṅkhataṃ* means conditioned by karma. *Abhisañcetayitaṃ* means accumulated by the mind. *Avijjāya tveva* means indeed by way of ignorance. *Aseṣavirāganirodhā* means through the cessation without remainder by means of the path known as dispassion (*virāga*).
*Suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu* means either by way of observing that [the world] is not subject to one’s own control, or by way of contemplating it as empty of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"See the world as empty in two ways; having uprooted the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi)," that is, having pulled out the view of a real body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
"Thus one may be a crosser of death," meaning one would become a crosser of death in this way.
"One who thus regards the world"—that is, one seeing the world of the aggregates—"the King of Death does not see him," meaning the King of Death does not look upon or perceive him.

“He desires nothing else at all”: he does not desire or long for anything else, even the slightest bit. “Except for non-relinking” (*aññatra appaṭisandhiyā*): this means excluding *nibbāna*. They also recite it as a single compound:
“*aññatrappaṭisandhiyā*. Furthermore: the verse beginning with “*aniṭṭhurī*. Therein, “*aniṭṭhurī*” means free from envy. Some read it as “*aniṭṭharī*.
“Equal everywhere” (*sabbadhī samo*) means equal in all respects; the intended meaning is that he is equanimous. What has been said?
What is it? When asked about that person who does not grieve, thinking "I have nothing," I describe fourfold benefit in that person as being unshakable:
"not harsh, not greedy, unmoving, and equal in all respects. Here, "harshness" (*niṭṭhuriya*) means envy (*issukī*).
The state of being harsh is "harshness"; based on that, even to say "there is not even this much" is like spitting out phlegm.
The meaning is as follows. "Harsh treatment" (*niṭṭhuriyakamma*) means the act of being harsh.

For when a householder living in dependence upon another householder, or a bhikkhu living in dependence upon another bhikkhu, becomes angry over even a trivial matter and treats that person with harshness—spitting on them while saying, "Not even this much is there from you," and acting as if trampling them with his foot—that is called "harsh treatment. Such an action of his is termed "harsh treatment."

It is so called. *Issā* is a description of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). The two following [terms] are descriptions of its modes of cultivation (*ākāra-bhāvanā*). The remaining three are synonymous expressions (*pariyāya-vacana*).
Furthermore, from the perspective of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, this [envy] has the characteristic of being envious of the success of others;
its function (*rasa*) is dissatisfaction with that; it is manifested as a state of turning away from it; and its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) is the success of others.
"In gain he does not waver" means he does not move at the acquisition of conditions. "In loss as well" means even at the non-acquisition of conditions.
188. Furthermore: "Of the unshakable," etc., is the verse. Therein, "conditioned" (*nisaṅkhata*) refers to any formation whatsoever among the formative forces of merit and so forth;
for it is called "conditioned" because it is conditioned by, or itself conditions.
It is said: "Exertions" (*viyārambhā*) refers to various undertakings, such as the formative volitions of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
"He sees security everywhere" means he sees only fearlessness in all places.

"Undertakings" (*ārambhā*) refers to the initial commencement of kamma; "exertions" (*viyārambhā*) refers to the application of energy through various successive undertakings. This is a designation for those karmas that produce rebirth-linking within the three realms of existence. Therefore, [the Buddha] is "detached from exertions."

189. Thus, regarding the verse beginning with "Seeing thus, not among equals": therein, "he does not speak" means that by way of conceit, such as "I am equal," he does not speak of himself even among equals, nor among those who are inferior or superior.
"He neither takes up nor casts aside" means that he neither grasps nor relinquishes any phenomenon whatsoever, such as form and so forth.
The remainder is clear everywhere, as it follows the method already explained in various places.
Thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely at the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The commentary on the exposition of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta within the *Saddhammappajjotikā*,
the sub-commentary to the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed.
16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta (190).
Regarding the sixteenth [sutta], "He was not seen by me": this is the exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta.
Therein, "prior to this" means prior to his descent here at Saṅkassanagara. "Vagguvada" means one of beautiful speech. "Tusitā gaṇimāgato" means having passed away from the Tusita realm.
Because he has come from the mother’s womb, he is said to have "come from Tusita. Because he is a teacher of a group, he is a "leader" (gaṇī).
Alternatively, in the sense of being contented, he has come from the world of the gods known as Tusita to the leader; or, he has come to the leader of the host of Tusi-ta arahants.
"With this eye" means with this natural eye of flesh included within this personal existence (attabhāva). "With this personal existence" [is the meaning].
"With this final body. "In the abode of the Thirty-three" means in the world of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. "At the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree" means beneath the Koviḷāra tree.
"On the Paṇḍukambala stone" means on the surface of a rock resembling red woolen cloth. "Having spent the rains" means one who has completed the rainy-season retreat.
"Surrounded by a host of gods" means encircled by a multitude of deities. "Descended" means having come down.
"Previously, this vision"—that is, prior to this present vision. "Not seen"—meaning not previously seen at another time.
"Of a khattiya"—meaning that he has not heard it from one who speaks as a khattiya. The same method applies to brahmins and the others as well. Regarding "sweet-spoken" and so forth:
he speaks sweetly, endowed with excellent phrasing, thus he is "sweet-spoken. He speaks what generates affection and is worthy of affection, thus he is "affectionate."
One who speaks thus is "one whose speech is affectionate. One who speaks in a way that is fit to be placed within the heart-reaching mind is "one whose speech is heart-reaching.
One whose voice is sweet like the cry of the karavīka bird is "one whose voice is as lovely as the song of the karavīka.
"Lucid" means unobstructed and free from stumbling here and there. "Intelligible" means easy to understand. "Melodious" means sweet. "Worthy of being heard" [means...]
"Sweet" means pleasant to the ear. "Dripping" means thick. "Non-diffusive" means not spreading out. "Deep" means not shallow.
"Resonant" means possessing a clear tone. "Of him" means of that Teacher. "Outside the assembly" means beyond the circle of followers.
"Does not issue forth" means does not go out. For what reason? Because such a sweet sound [does not arise] without cause.
"May it not perish. Regarding "the voice of Brahmā": others may have voices that are broken, cracked, or like the cawing of a crow;
however, this one is endowed with a voice resembling that of Mahābrahmā. Indeed, because the voice of Mahābrahmā is unobstructed by bile or phlegm, it is pure;
and the work performed by the Blessed One purifies the basis, the basis of...
Because of its purity, the sound arising from the navel upwards arises endowed with all eight qualities; it is thus "pure.
He speaks like a *karavīka* bird, hence he is called *karavīkabhāṇī*; the meaning is that his sweet voice is like the song of the intoxicated *karavīka*.

"He carries across" (*tāreti*) means he causes one to pass beyond a place that is not secure. "He brings safely across" (*uttāreti*) means he carries one across by leading them to the ground of security.

"He rescues" (*nittāreti*) means that while leading [beings] out from an unsafe place, he causes them to cross over. "He brings across" (*patāreti*) means that having grasped them, he causes them to cross;
the meaning is that he causes them to cross as if grasping them with his own hand. All of this—rescuing, bringing across, and so forth—is simply the act of establishing [beings] in a safe place;

thus it is said: "he brings them to the ground of safety" (*khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpeti*). "Beings" (*satta*) refers to those beings who are to be disciplined (*veneyyasatta*). Because of its great density...
Because it is of great harm and difficult to cross, birth itself is a wilderness; thus, it is the "wilderness of birth.
He listens to the group means that the group listens to his words, hears them, and takes note of them.
He lends an ear means that, out of a desire to hear, he lends an ear—that is, he fixes his attention. He establishes a mind desirous of knowing means a mind wishing to understand.
He makes a resolution. "Having raised the multitude from the unwholesome" means having raised the mass of people from the unwholesome states produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*).
"He establishes them in the wholesome" means he places them in the wholesome states produced by skill (*kosalla*). One who possesses a *saṅgha* by way of a collection is a *saṅghin*.
One who possesses a *gaṇa* by way of a retinue is a *gaṇin*. One who is a teacher of a *gaṇa* is a *gaṇācariya*.
191. Regarding the second verse: "As it is seen by the world with its devas" means that it is seen by human beings just as it is seen by the world with its devas.
Or, "as it is seen" means it is seen truly and without error. "Possessing the eye" means possessing the supreme eye.
"Alone" means alone by virtue of such things as the life of renunciation. "Bliss" refers to the bliss of renunciation (*nekkhammarati*) and so forth.
"Resembling gold" means a golden earring. "Like an ear-ring of clay" means like an earring made of clay.
"Like a copper half-māsaka covered with gold" means like a copper coin concealed by gold. "Covered with an outer casing" means concealed by a covering.
"Impure within" means not purified internally due to lust and other defilements. "Shining on the outside" means...
"Beautiful externally with robes and so forth" means [beautiful] by way of robes and other requisites.
"With unassumed postures" means with postures that are not affected by attachment. "Endowed with aspiration" means one whose wishes are fulfilled.
"Pure reputation" means a reputation for complete purity; the sense is a sound of praise according to reality. "Renowned fame and glory" means...
One who is habituated to wandering while taking up fame and renown. Where is his reputation pure?
It is in the places described in detail by way of such passages as, "In the abode of the Nāgas and in the abode of the Supaṇṇas," and so forth. And even more than that:
beyond the manner thus described, he is seen to be even more distinguished according to the needs of those to be trained.
“Every darkness of lust” means the entire darkness of lust. The same method applies to the darkness of hatred and so forth.
