“Causing blindness” means causing the obstruction of the light of wisdom. “Causing sightlessness” means the non-occurrence of the eye of wisdom.

“Causing ignorance” means causing one not to know by means of knowledge. “Obstructing wisdom” means that which destroys the faculty of wisdom. “Belonging to the side of affliction” means belonging to the category of oppression.
"Not conducive to Nibbāna" means it does not lead toward the conditionless, deathless Nibbāna.
"All that was awakened to by that knowledge of enlightenment" means he awakened to all of that by way of the fourfold path-knowledge.
By the first path, he knew and understood; by the second path, he further recognized and penetrated; by the third path...
He attained penetration; he fully awakened. By means of the fourth path, through complete penetration, he rightly awakened.
"He reached, he touched, he realized"—this triad should be applied by way of the fruit. By way of the first and second [paths], he acquired it.
By way of the third, he touched it with the contact of knowledge. By way of the fourth, he made it manifest to direct perception. Then...
Or rather, all three [types of joy] can indeed be obtained for each individual fruit.
"Joy in renunciation" is the joy arising in dependence on going forth and so forth. "Joy in seclusion" is the joy arising in bodily seclusion and so forth.
"Joy in tranquility" is the joy in the subsiding of the defilements. "Joy in enlightenment" is the joy arising in one who is reviewing the Path.
192. Regarding the third verse, "of many bound here": "here" refers to many disciples, such as kṣatriyas and others.
For disciples are called "bound" because their livelihood is dependent upon the teacher. "I have come with a question for the sake of the goal" means: I have come seeking the goal through a question;
or, it is an arrival for the sake of those who seek [the goal] through a question; or, there is an arrival by means of a question for one who seeks [the goal].
Even though the word *Buddha* is absent [in the compound], the phrase "that Buddha" (*taṃ buddhaṃ*) was stated by one wishing to point out that which is the Buddha in the word *buddha*.
"Self-become" (*sayambhū*) means become by oneself without instruction. "Teacherless" (*anācariyako*) is an explanation of the meaning of the word *sayambhū*;
for he who penetrates the Truths without a teacher is called self-become. "In things not heard before," and so forth...

This is the explanation of the meaning of the state of being without a teacher. "In what has not been heard from others" means in truths not heard from a teacher. "By himself" (*sāmaṃ*) means by his own self.
"He fully awakened" (*abhisambujjhi*) means he thoroughly and correctly penetrated [them]. And therein he attained omniscience (*sabbaññutaṃ*);
that is, regarding those truths, he attained the state of an omniscient one. Just as those who penetrate the truths become omniscient.
It is for this reason, because he has penetrated the truths, that it is said thus. There is also a reading: “He attained omniscience. And regarding “mastery over the powers”:
he reached sovereign mastery over the ten powers of a Tathāgata. One who has become such is called a Buddha; this is what is meant.
In that context, his continuum of aggregates is refined by the attainment of the unsurpassed liberation, which is characterized by knowledge unimpeded regarding all phenomena.

The Buddha is a distinguished being designated on the basis of [the attainment of] omniscience, or designated on the basis of the perfect awakening to the Truths which is the foundation for omniscience.
Up to this point, the analysis of the Buddha has been made according to the meaning (*attha*).
Now, analyzing it according to the phrasing (*byañjana*), he says: "In what sense is one called 'Buddha'? and so forth. In that regard, just as in the world...

One who has understood is called "understood"; likewise, one who has awakened to the truths is a Buddha (*buddha*). Just as winds that have withered leaves are called "leaf-withering" (*paṇṇasosa*), so too, one who awakens the world is a Buddha.
He is a Buddha by virtue of omniscience; this means he is a Buddha by means of the wisdom capable of awakening to all phenomena.
He is a Buddha by virtue of all-seeingness; this means [he is a Buddha] by means of the eye of knowledge regarding all phenomena.
Because he has seen [all things], it is said he is "Buddha. Because he is not to be led by others, it is said he is "Buddha" because he has awakened by himself, without being awakened by another.
Because of his blossoming, it is said he is "Buddha" because, like a lotus, he has blossomed with manifold qualities in the sense of unfolding.
By these six modes of expression, beginning with "Buddha in the sense of one whose taints are exhausted," [he is so called].

By the abandoning of those states that cause the contraction of the mind, he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened from the sleep of all defilements (*kilesa*), like a person awakened from sleep.
Since "calculation" (*saṅkhā*) and "that which is calculated" (*saṅkhāta*) are identical in meaning, the word *saṅkhātena* means "by a portion.

By being reckoned as "untainted" (*nirupalepa*) due to the absence of the taints of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*), [he is free] from all defilements together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).

It is stated by distinguishing it with the term "exclusively" because of its having been abandoned. "Exclusively free from defilements" means being free from all defilements, including the remnants of lust, hatred, and delusion.

"One who has gone the path traveled by the One" refers to a Buddha; for since verbal roots meaning "to go" (gamana) also carry the sense of "to awaken" (bujjhana), he is a Buddha because he has awakened.
The verbal roots indeed have the sense of "going"; therefore, because he has gone by the path traveled by only one, he is called "Buddha.
And here, the "path traveled by only one" is as follows: "Path, road, way, track, direct route, course, vehicle;
boat, ford, bridge, raft, float, and crossing."

Among the many names for the path, it is spoken of by the name "way" (*ayana*) and by the name "path" (*magga*). Therefore, the meaning is that it is a path consisting of a single way, not one consisting of a forked road.

Alternatively, it is a "single-way path" (*ekāyana-magga*) because it is to be traversed by one (*eka-ayitabbo*). "By one" means by one who has abandoned association with crowds and dwells in seclusion. "To be traversed" (*ayitabbo*) means to be practiced; or else, it is called a "way" (*ayana*) because one goes (*ayati*) by means of it.
The meaning is: "going from saṃsāra to nibbāna. It is "the way of the one" (ekāyana) because it is the path of the "one" (eka). "Of the one" (esaṃ) means "of the best" (seṭṭhānaṃ).

And since the Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas) are the best of all beings, therefore it is said that this path is the path belonging to the Fully Enlightened Ones, being the way of the "one"—that is, the path traversed by the Fully Enlightened Ones.
Alternatively, it is called "ayana" because it is "traversed" (ayatīti); the meaning is that it goes or proceeds. It is the way in the "one" (ekasmiṃ ayano).
"Maggā" means the path leading to one goal (*ekāyana-magga*). What is meant is that this is the path proceeding only within the teaching of the Buddha, and not elsewhere.

Furthermore, it is called "leading to one" (*ekāyana*) because, although it proceeds in various ways through different methods of cultivation during its earlier stages, it goes to only one thing—Nirvana—in its later stage;
therefore, "the path leading to one" means the path leading to the single Nirvana.

"He is called *Buddha* because he has awakened (*abhisambuddha*) to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*) by himself, and not because he became a Buddha through others. Thus it is said:

"Because he has destroyed non-intelligence (*abuddhi*) and because he has attained intelligence (*buddhi*), he is *Buddha*. *Buddhi*, *buddha*, and *bodha* are synonyms for this. In this regard, just as...

“Just as a cloth is called ‘blue’ or ‘red’ because of its association with the qualities of blue or red, so too it was said in order to make known that he is ‘Buddha’ because of his association with the qualities of a Buddha.
Following that, the passage beginning ‘This name ‘Buddha’ is not [his personal] name’ and so forth was spoken for the purpose of making known that ‘this designation follows from the meaning.
In this context, *mittā* means friends; *amaccā* means ministers; *ñātī* means paternal kinsmen; and *sālohitā* means maternal kinsmen.”
*Śramaṇas* are those who have gone forth into the religious life. *Brāhmaṇas* are those who address others as "bho," or those who have stilled evil and cast out evil.
*Devatās* are [deities] such as Sakka and the Brahmās. Regarding the term *vimokkhantika*: *Vimokkha* is the path to arahantship; the end (*anta*) of that liberation is the fruit of arahantship.
That which exists at the end of that liberation is called *vimokkhantika*. For omniscience is attained through the path to arahantship.
It is perfected; it becomes accomplished at the arising of the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, the state of omniscience occurs at the end of liberation.
Even that which is called "indicative" (nemittika) is what is called "occurring at the end of liberation. Hence it was said: "This [title] of the Blessed Buddhas occurs at the end of liberation.
It is at the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with the acquisition of the knowledge of omniscience—at the root of the Great Bodhi tree.

Simultaneously with the acquisition of omniscient knowledge at the aforementioned moment. "Manifest designation" (*sacchikā paññatti*) refers to the designation arising from the realization of the fruit of arahantship or the realization of all phenomena;
that is to say, the designation "Buddha. This is the analysis of the Buddha according to the phrasing (*byañjana*).
From here on, the conclusion—"Carry this burden"—is [omitted] because it follows the method stated in various other places.
It proceeds exactly according to the commentary. 193.

In the fourth verse, “vijigucchato” means being repelled by birth and so forth. “Rittamāsanaṃ” means a secluded bed or chair. The connection should be understood as: “or in mountain caves,” meaning one should resort to a secluded seat in mountain caves.
“Vijigucchato jātiyā” means being repelled by birth. The same method applies to “jarāya,” “byādhinā,” and so on. “Bhajato” means resorting to.
In such passages as these, *bhajato* means "of one who frequents"; *sevatō* means "of one who serves"; *nisevatō* means "of one who serves properly";

*saṃsevatō* means "of one who serves repeatedly"; *paṭisevatō* means "of one who serves by approaching. *Pabbatapabbhārā* refers to mountain recesses. 194. In the fifth verse, *uccāvacesu* means "in those that are low and high" (inferior and superior).

*Sayanesu* means "in lodgings" such as monasteries (*vihāra*) and so forth. *Kīvanto tattha bheravā* means "how many are the terrifying things there? There is also a reading *kuvanto*, and its meaning is "groaning."
*Kuvanta* means making a sound. *Kūjanta* means making an indistinct sound.
*Nadanta* means shouting. *Saddaṃ karonta* means speaking words. *Kati* is a question regarding number. *Kittaka* is a question regarding measure. *Kīvataka* is a question regarding delimitation.
*Kīvabahu* is a question regarding both measure and delimitation. *Te bheravā* means these terrifying calamities that produce fear.
[The dangers] have fear as their object (*bhayārammaṇā*). When asked, "How many are there?", he answers with "Lions, tigers, leopards," and so forth, in order to show the objects.
195. In the sixth verse, "how many perils" (*kati parissayā*) means how many calamities. "The direction not yet gone to" (*agataṃ disaṃ*) refers to Nibbāna.

For it is "not yet gone to" because it has never been reached before, and it is a "direction" (*disā*) because it is something to be pointed out. Therefore it is said: "the direction not yet gone to. It is the Deathless (*amataṃ*).
"Disānti" is also a reading [for "disāpi"]. "Abhisambhave" means "he would reach. "Pantamhi" means "in a remote place.

"That direction not previously gone to" refers to a direction that has never been gone to even in a dream. "That direction has not been gone to" means that this direction has not been gone to in the manner described. "By this long time" means by this long duration.
"Filled to the brim" means filled level with the rim of the mouth. "Without overflowing" means not spilling over.
Having made it so that no [liquid] spills. "A bowl of oil" means a bowl into which oil has been poured.
"Should carry about" means he should take it and go along. "In this way he guards his own mind":

just as that bowl filled with oil, having placed his own mind between those two—namely, the object of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) and the mindfulness associated with that [mindfulness]—he guards it so that...
For even a moment it does not wander among external objects; thus the wise practitioner of yoga should guard and protect it.
Why is that? Because of this [mind]:
“Of that which is difficult to restrain, light, and falling wherever it pleases...”
“The taming of the mind is excellent; a tamed mind brings happiness.
Therefore—“It is very difficult to see, exceedingly subtle, and it falls wherever it wishes;”
“The wise person should guard the mind; a guarded mind brings happiness. For this [mind] is described thus:
“It travels far, moves alone, is bodiless, and dwells in a cave.”
“Those who will restrain the mind shall be released from the bonds of Māra.
But for the other: “For one whose mind is unsettled, who does not understand the true Dhamma;”
For one whose confidence wavers, wisdom does not reach fulfillment.
But for one who has a steadfast meditation subject as a companion:
“For one whose mind is untainted, whose consciousness is unassailed;”
“For one who has abandoned merit and evil, there is no fear for the wakeful.
Therefore, this was said:
“The mind is flickering and restless, difficult to guard and difficult to restrain;”
“The wise man makes himself straight, like a fletcher straightens his arrow.
Thus, making himself straight, he should guard his own mind.

“Aspiring for a direction never before reached”—having begun the work in this meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), [one should proceed] from the beginningless past...
The meaning is that one should protect one’s own mind according to the method described, aspiring toward a direction in *saṃsāra* never before traversed. But what is this so-called "direction"?
"Parents are the eastern direction; teachers are the southern direction;
wife and children are the western direction; friends and companions are the northern direction."
“Servants and laborers below, ascetics and brahmins above— one should pay homage to these directions; thus a householder is sufficient for his family.
In this context, first of all, mother, father, and so forth are referred to as “directions.”
“The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below— these are the ten directions.
In which direction does the Naga king stand, whom he saw as the six tusks in his dream?”—
here, it is the directions themselves, distinguished as east and so forth, that are referred to by the word “directions.”
“Those who give food, drink, and clothing to householders, they call that direction too;
but this is the supreme direction, O Setaketu, reaching which those who were suffering become happy.”—Here, Nibbāna is spoken of as the “direction.
Here too, that alone is intended [by the term]. By such terms as “the destruction of craving” and “dispassion,”...
It is seen (dissati) and it is looked upon (apadissati); therefore it is called a "direction" (disā).

However, because it has never been traversed even in a dream by any foolish worldling throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), it is called "a direction not previously traversed. One who aspires to that should apply himself to mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). Regarding the words "one who is departing," etc.:
here, "departing" means being near to the arising of the Path; "going" means at the moment of standing still.

"From the arising of the fruit" means from its transcendence. "In the interior" means standing within the interior. "In the remote" means standing in the depths of dense forest thickets. "On the boundary" means standing on the boundary due to distance.
"At the end of the rocks" means at the edge of mountains. "At the end of the woods" means at the edge of forest clusters. "At the end of the rivers" means at the edge of rivers.

"Nearby" (*ante*). "On the edge of water" (*udakante*) means on the boundary of bodies of water. "Where neither plowing nor sowing is done" (*yattha na kasīyati na vapīyati*) means where neither the act of plowing nor the act of sowing is performed.

"Standing beyond the inhabited area" (*janantaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhite*). "In a place not frequented by people" (*manussānaṃ anupacāre*) means in a lodging that is not to be frequented by people through the acts of plowing and sowing.
196. Regarding the seventh verse, *kyāssa byappathayo assū* means "what would his modes of speech be?"—that is, what would his utterances be?
*Musāvādaṃ pahāya* ("having abandoned false speech"): here, *musa* refers to a verbal or bodily exertion that destroys the welfare of another for one who has the intention to deceive.
Furthermore, it is that which, through the intention to deceive, originates the bodily and verbal exertions intended to mislead another.
Volition is lying. According to another method: *musa* is an unreal, untrue matter;

*vāda* is the making known of that [matter] as real and true. By way of its characteristic, however, lying is the volition that originates a communication in such a way by one who wishes to make another understand an unreal matter as being real.
It is so called because of the non-existence (*appatā*) of that purpose which it destroys.

It is slightly blameworthy, yet it becomes greatly blameworthy due to its magnitude. Furthermore, for householders, speaking in the manner of "I have none" and so forth out of a desire not to give away what belongs to oneself is slightly blameworthy;
however, speaking as a witness for the purpose of destroying another's welfare is greatly blameworthy.
For those who have gone forth, having obtained even a small amount of oil or ghee, to say with the intention of joking, "There is oil in the village today... [is slightly blameworthy].

According to the method of Pūraṇa’s discourse, it is slightly blameworthy when one says, "I think the river is flowing"; however, for those who speak according to the method beginning with "the unseen was seen," it is greatly blameworthy.
It has four constituent factors: a non-factual basis, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and [the communication] to another.

"Understanding that meaning": there is one mode of application, namely, acting through oneself. This should be understood as performing an act intended to deceive another, either by means of the body, or by what is connected to the body, or by speech.
If the other person understands that meaning through that act, this volition that originates the act incurs the kamma of lying at the very moment [the volition arises].
One who speaks truth is a "truth-speaker" (*saccavādī*). One who joins and unites truth with truth is a "truth-uniter" (*saccasandho*);

the meaning is that he does not speak falsehood from time to time. For a person who sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes truth, his truth is not joined with truth because it is interrupted by lying;
therefore, such a person is not a truth-uniter. But this one is not like that.
Because one does not speak falsely even for the sake of one’s life, but rather joins truth with truth, one is called "bound by truth" (*saccasaṃdha*).
"Firm" (*theta*) means stable; the meaning is that one whose speech is stable.
One person is not of stable speech, like turmeric dye, like a wooden stake driven into a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on the back of a horse. Another is like a line carved in stone.
He is firm in speech like an indakhīla pillar; even when his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not speak two different words. This is called *theṭho*.
*Paccayiko* means one who is trustworthy, in the sense of being someone to be believed.
For there is a certain person who is not trustworthy; when it is said, "This was spoken by whom? By so-and-so," one must say, "Do not believe his word."
He becomes one who relies on others; when it is said, "By whom was this spoken?
By so-and-so," he falls into the position of saying, "If it was spoken by him, then that alone is the authority; there is nothing further to be examined; it is exactly thus.
Such a person is called one who relies on others (*paccayika*). "One who does not deceive the world" means that by virtue of his truthfulness, he does not deceive the world.

Regarding the phrases "having abandoned slanderous speech" and so forth: that speech by which, when one speaks it to someone, it creates a sense of intimacy for oneself and a sense of emptiness in the other's heart is slanderous speech (*pisuṇavācā*).
However, that speech by which one makes both oneself and another harsh, or which is itself harsh—neither pleasant to the ear nor reaching the heart—is harsh speech (*pharusavācā*).

That by which one prattles nonsense is frivolous talk (*samphappalāpa*). Even the volition (*cetanā*) that is the root of these [other unwholesome actions] receives the very name "malicious speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) and so forth;
it is this [volition] alone that is intended here.
In this context, it is the volition that, arising from a defiled mind, initiates the application of body and speech for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire for one's own favor.

Malicious speech is volition. It is less blameworthy when it causes a rift between those who have few good qualities, and more blameworthy when it causes a rift between those who have great qualities.
It has four constituent factors: another person who is to be divided; the intention to cause division, thinking, "In this way these people will become separate, they will become estranged";
the desire for intimacy, thinking, "In this way I will become dear and trustworthy"; and the corresponding...
"Effort" means the understanding of that purpose.
"For the sake of their division" means for the sake of dividing those from whom one has heard [the words] "it is from them.
Or, "for the reconciliation of those who are divided" refers to two friends, or two who share the same preceptor and so forth, who have become divided due to some cause.
Having approached each one individually, he is a reconciler who says things such as, "For those born into such a family and so very learned, this is not fitting.

As for "one who provides what was given": he is a provider of reconciliation; seeing two people in harmony, he says things such as, "This is appropriate for you who are born into such a family and endowed with such qualities."
The meaning is: "one who performs the strengthening of the bond.
*Samaggārāma* means one for whom the Saṅgha is harmonious; the meaning is that he does not wish to dwell even where there is no harmony.
There is also a Pāli reading, *samaggarāmo*, which has the same meaning. *Samaggarato* means one who delights in those who are harmonious; having abandoned [those who are not],...
The meaning is that he does not even wish to go elsewhere. He rejoices upon seeing or hearing of those who are in harmony; thus, he is "one who rejoices in harmony.
Regarding the phrase "he speaks words that promote harmony": he speaks only those words which cause sentient beings to remain in harmony—words that illuminate the quality of concord—and not others.
Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that originates from bodily or verbal application intended to cut another’s vital parts.
Even when the application is such as to cut the vital parts, it does not constitute harsh speech if there is gentleness of mind.
For instance, parents sometimes say to their children, “May robbers cut you into pieces,” or even [say] regarding them, “An utpala leaf [should fall] upon you.”
They do not wish for [a student] who is falling away. And sometimes teachers and preceptors say to their dependents: "Why do these shameless and unscrupulous ones behave thus?
Expel them! Yet they desire the excellence of their students' mastery of the scriptures and realization.
Just as there is no harsh speech due to gentleness of mind, so too there is no harsh speech due to gentleness of speech.
It does not exist. For one who wishes to cause death, the words "Make this person lie down comfortably" are not harsh speech;

yet, because of the harshness of the mind, it is indeed harsh speech, directed toward that which it intends. It is of slight censure due to the inferiority of the object, and of great censure due to the greatness of the object.
Its three constituent factors are: another person capable of being reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling.
*Neḷā*: *Ela* is said to mean "fault" (*dosa*). That which has no *ela* is *neḷa*, meaning "faultless.
It is like the word *neḷa* used in the phrase, "The white-canopied chariot with faultless wheels. *Ear-pleasing* (*kaṇṇasukhā*): Because of the sweetness of its phrasing, it is pleasant to the ears;
it does not produce earache, as if pierced by a needle. Because of the sweetness of its meaning, it produces affection rather than irritation throughout the entire body.
*Pemaniyā*: It goes to the heart, entering the mind with ease without being obstructed; thus, it is "heart-reaching" (*hadayaṅgamā*). Because it is full of virtues, it is "ancient" (*porī*).
Alternatively, it is "ancient" because it is as delicate as a woman raised in the city.
Or, it is "ancient" because it belongs to the city; the meaning is that it is the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers are speakers of appropriate discourse, possessing a measure of sweetness.
They say, "He shines," or "He is radiant"—such talk is "dear to many" (*bahujanakantā*).
Because it is dear, it is "pleasing to many" (*bahujanamanāpā*), being agreeable to many people and increasing their mental well-being.
Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) that manifests harmful meanings and gives rise to bodily and verbal exertion. Due to its weak habituation...
It is slightly blameworthy, yet becomes greatly blameworthy due to the magnitude of its habitual practice. It has two constituent factors:
the prioritization of useless talk such as the Mahābhārata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual delivery of such talk.

One who speaks at the proper time is a "speaker at the right time" (*kālavādī*); the meaning is that one speaks having discerned the appropriate moment for what ought to be said. That which is factual is *bhūtaṃ*.
He speaks what is true because he speaks exactly according to its own nature; thus he is a speaker of truth (*bhūtavādī*).

He speaks by making it dependent solely upon the welfare pertaining to this life and the life to come; thus he is a speaker of welfare (*atthavādī*). He speaks by making it dependent upon the nine supramundane states (*dhamma*); thus he is a speaker of Dhamma (*dhammavādī*).
He speaks by making it dependent upon the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment; thus he is a speaker of Vinaya (*vinayavādī*). "A treasure-store" (*nidhāna*) is so called.
*Ṭhapanokāsa*: it has a place of storage; thus it is "possessing a store" (*nidhānavatī*).

The meaning is that she speaks words worthy of being stored in the heart. *Kālena*: even while speaking such words, thinking "I shall speak words possessing a store," she does not speak at an improper time;
rather, the meaning is that she speaks only after considering the appropriate time. *Sāpadesaṃ*: with a supporting illustration (*saupamaṃ*).
"With cause" means with a reason. "With a limit" means that he speaks in such a way as to show a boundary so that its limit becomes apparent.
"Beneficial" means endowed with meaning because it cannot be exhausted even when analyzed by means of numerous methods;
or, it is "beneficial" because it is accompanied by that very meaning which the speaker of meaning (atthavādī) expresses.
"He speaks speech" means that he does not set aside one thing and speak another;
this is what is intended. "By means of the four types of verbal good conduct" refers to the four modes of speech described in the sequence beginning with "having abandoned false speech.
"Endowed with" means not having fallen away from them. "He speaks speech free from the four faults" refers to [speech] that is devoid of the unpleasant and so forth.
He speaks speech that is free from the four faults or devoid of them.
Regarding the phrase "there is what is not a resort" (*atthi agocaro*):

although the Elder, desiring to explain the conduct of a recluse and the resort of a recluse, extracted the words "there is what is not a resort, there is what is a resort," it is nevertheless like a man skilled in the path who, while pointing out the way, [says] "the left..."
"Just as one who points out the first path to be abandoned— a dangerous road or a bypath— and afterwards points out the path to be taken—
a safe road or a direct route— so too the General of the Dhamma, like a man skilled in paths,
having first pointed out that which is to be abandoned— the improper resort censured by the Buddha— desires to point out afterwards the proper resort."
He said, beginning with, “What is the improper resort? For a path pointed out by an ordinary person might or might not succeed;
however, the path pointed out by the Tathāgata is infallible—like a diamond released from Indra’s hand—and it leads exclusively to the city of Nibbāna.
Therefore it was said: “‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata.”
“Of the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Or rather, because for a person whose sweat, dirt, and impurities have been removed by bathing, the application of ornaments such as garlands, perfumes, and ointments is appropriate;
so too, for one who has abandoned unwholesome qualities, the possession of wholesome qualities is fitting. Therefore, [the text mentions] the removal of sweat, dirt, and impurities.

Having first explained the improper resort (*agocara*) that is to be abandoned—just as one who has washed away sweat, dirt, and grime would first remove ornaments such as garlands, perfumes, and ointments—he then, wishing to explain the proper resort (*gocara*), said: "What is the improper resort? and so forth.
In this context, "proper resort" (*gocara*) refers to a place suitable for approaching for the sake of alms-food and other requisites; [the opposite] is the unsuitable place.
It is not a proper resort (*agocara*). "One whose resort is prostitutes" (*vesiyāgocaro*) means one who should approach them by way of intimacy with friends;
this is the meaning. In this context, "prostitutes" (*vesiyā*) refers to those who live off their beauty and are easily accessible for illicit conduct.
One who approaches them out of intimacy and affection with friends is said to have prostitutes as his resort. Therefore, it is not proper to approach them in such a manner. For what reason?
Because of failure in protection. For when one approaches in such a manner, even the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*), though long protected and guarded, perishes in just a few days.
Even if it does not perish, one incurs blame. However, one who approaches for the sake of alms (*dakkhiṇā*) should approach having established mindfulness (*sati*).
"Vidhavās" refers to those whose husbands are dead or those whose husbands have gone abroad. "Thullakumāriyo" means grown-up girls who have not yet been married.
"Paṇḍakā" refers to eunuchs—those who are preoccupied with talk about worldly gain, whose defilements are rampant, whose feverish distress is unappeased, and who are neuter.
The danger in approaching any of them should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. It is exactly the same regarding bhikkhunīs.
This is the method. Furthermore, there are monks whose holy life (*brahmacariya*) has flourished, and likewise for the nuns.

Through mutual intimacy, they may in just a few days destroy the protective and guarded nature of their ascetic discipline (*samaṇadhamma*). However, it is permissible to go as one who inquires after the sick.
Moreover, when a monk has obtained flowers, it is indeed permissible for him to go for the purpose of making an offering or for the purpose of giving exhortation (*ovāda*).
"A tavern" means a house for drinking liquor; it is not devoid of those intoxicated by liquor who create obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
It is not permissible to go there impulsively with them out of a desire for intoxication, as that constitutes an obstacle to the holy life.
Regarding the phrases "he dwells in association with kings," and so forth: "kings" refers to those who have been anointed or those who have not been anointed.
"Those who govern the kingdom. "Royal ministers" (*rājamahāmatta*) means those endowed with a great measure of authority similar to that of kings.

"Heretics" (*titthiya*) refers to outside wanderers (*paribbājaka*) who hold perverted views. "Disciples of heretics" (*titthiyasāvaka*) refers to those who provide them with requisites out of devotion;
the meaning is that one becomes associated with them through such contact.

"By improper association": improper association means an association that is contrary to the three trainings, an antagonistic association by which one incurs an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), a transgression of the rules (*paññatti*), and the loss of spiritual refinement (*sallekha*).
For example: associating with kings, royal ministers, and high officials, sharing their griefs, sharing their joys, and sharing in their pleasure and pain.

When duties and obligations arise, it is the state of engaging oneself [in them], or the intimacy consisting of affection, respect, and association that brings about a state of having the same desires, inclinations, and conduct as the followers of other sectarians (*titthiya*).

In this regard, association with kings, royal ministers, and high officials causes an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*); so too does [association] with the other followers of other sectarians.
This refers to adopting their own tenets. However, it is appropriate to approach those who are capable of refuting their doctrine and causing them to adopt one's own tenet.
Now, in order to show another way in which [certain families] are improper resort, the passage beginning with “or those families which... is commenced.

In this context, "lacking faith" means being devoid of faith toward the Buddha and the others; they do not have faith that "the Buddha is omniscient, the Dhamma leads to liberation, and the Saṅgha is well-practiced.
"Lacking confidence" means they are unable to make their minds clear and undisturbed.
"Abusive and insulting" means both abusive and insulting: "You are a thief! You are a fool! and so forth.
"You are deluded, you are a camel, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are one bound for the states of deprivation, you are destined for hell, you are an animal;
there is no happy rebirth for you, only an unhappy destination is to be expected for you"—thus they revile them with these ten grounds of abuse.
"Be off! Now we shall strike you, we shall bind you, we shall kill you"—thus they threaten them by instilling fear; such is the meaning.
"Desiring what is harmful" means they do not desire welfare; they desire only harm. "Desiring what is disadvantageous" means they desire only disadvantage;
they do not desire benefit. "Desiring what is uncomfortable" means they do not desire comfort; they desire only discomfort.
"Desiring what is not security from bondage" means they do not desire the safety and fearlessness that comes from the four bonds; they desire only that which is accompanied by fear.
Regarding "monks," novices are also included here. Regarding "nuns," female trainees (*sikkhamānā*) and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*) are also included.
For all those who have gone forth under the Blessed One and have taken refuge—namely, the four assemblies—it is only those [families] that do not desire their welfare.
"Such families" refers to families such as the kṣatriya clans and so forth. "He frequents" means...
"He lives depending on" means he approaches. "He attends upon" means he approaches again and again.

"This is called" means that these three types—namely, one whose resort consists of prostitutes and so forth (such as a prostitute), one who is associated with kings and so forth (such as a king), and one who serves families lacking faith (such as a family lacking faith)—are all improper resorts to be understood as "non-resort."

By this method as well, his lack of a proper resort (*agocara*) should be understood. First, prostitutes and the like are to be understood as improper resorts because they provide a basis for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
As it is said: "And what, monks, is a monk’s improper resort, another’s domain?

Namely, the five strands of sensual pleasure. Kings and the like are improper resorts because they do not support the practice of meditation and because they produce the cycle of gain, honor, and fame.

Because it is the cause for the failure of right view, and because entering the houses of those lacking faith and so forth brings about a loss of faith and mental corruption, such places are not a proper resort (*agocara*).
Furthermore, the fourfold [unwholesome conduct]—namely, entering the inner quarters of a house and so forth; grasping at signs after seeing a form with the eye and so forth;
indulgence in looking at performances after eating food given in faith; and the pursuit of the five strands of sensual pleasure—is likewise [not a proper resort].
It should be understood as a "non-range" (*agocara*) by way of the arising of defilements.
"Do not, O monks, wander in a non-range" means: do not wander in places unfit for wandering. "In another's domain" means in the domain of an enemy.
"O monks, wandering in a non-range" refers to those wandering in places unfit for wandering. There is also a reading, "wandering" (*caranta*). "He shall obtain" (*lacchati*).
"He will gain, he will see. *Māra* refers both to the son of a deva and to Death. "Opportunities" means flaws, defects, or openings.
In the description of the "range," such statements as "he does not have prostitutes as his range" are to be understood by way of the opposites of what was previously stated.
However, this is the distinction: the four foundations of mindfulness are the "range" in the sense of being the proper place for one to move within; thus, it is the four foundations of mindfulness.
*Gocaro*: within one's own domain. *Pettike visaye*: in the sphere inherited from one's father. *Āraddhavīriyassa*:
of one who possesses the energy of the four right strivings (*sammappadhāna*) properly established. *Thāmagatassa*: of one who has reached firmness.
*Daḷhaparakkamassa*: of one with steadfast effort. *Yassatthāya pesito*: for the sake of which he was sent—that is, for the sake of Arahatship.
The personal existence has been relinquished. "And for one’s own welfare" means for the fruit of Arahantship, which is one's own goal.

"And for the method" means for the Noble Eightfold Path. "And for the characteristics" means for the penetration of the characteristics such as impermanence and so forth. "And for the cause" means for the reason.
"And for the possible and the impossible" means for what is possible and what is impossible; the sense is "for the causal and the non-causal. Now, having explained this in detail:
To demonstrate this, he said, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth.
In the eighth verse, *ekodi nipako* means one whose mind is unified and who is wise.
*Jātarūpassa oḷārikampi malaṃ dhamati* means that one removes even the coarse impurities of gold by means of contact with fire.
“Blows” (*dhamati*) means he blows it out correctly. “Blows away” (*niddhamati*) means he blows it away so that it does not lead to further existence.
Some say, “He burns it” (*jhāpeti*). “Even the medium-sized one” (*majjhimakampi*) means even one subtler than that. “Even the subtle-sized one” (*sukhumakampi*) means even one exceedingly subtle.
“In this very way” (*evameva*) is the application of the simile. “He blows away even his own coarse defilements” (*attano oḷārikepi kilese dhamati*) refers to bodily misconduct and so forth.

One removes gross defilements by means of the heat of energy (*vīriyātapa*). "In the case of middling defilements" refers to thoughts of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth, which are middling among the coarse and the subtle.
"In the case of subtle defilements" refers to extremely delicate defilements such as thoughts of kin (*ñātivitakka*) and so forth.

"One fans away wrong view with right view" means that by means of right view associated with the Path together with insight (*vipassanā*), one fans away wrong view, which is characterized by perversion.
He removes [it]. This same method applies to right intention and the others as well.

198. Thus, having praised the Blessed One with three verses, the Venerable Sāriputta, being asked by five hundred students for the sake of their welfare regarding lodgings, alms-resorts, virtue, vows, and so forth, in order to explain that matter, [spoke as follows]:
The answer is begun by way of the passage beginning with “vijigucchamānassa. Therein, first, the meaning of the initial verse is as follows:

O Sāriputta, for that bhikkhu who desires full awakening, who feels disgust toward birth and so forth, and who resorts to empty seats and beds—whatever comfort there is, whatever pleasant dwelling there is in accordance with the Dhamma, and whatever is the Dhamma itself—that I shall declare to you.
"I speak thus as one who understands, speaking according to how I understand. "A comfortable dwelling" means a dwelling in happiness.

"By seeing unsuitable forms" means by seeing forms such as those of women that are unsuitable for a recluse. "To one desiring to awaken to that awakening" means to one wishing to awaken to that awakening consisting of the knowledge of the four paths.
"Desiring to awaken accordingly" means... [in accordance with] what is suitable.
"To one desiring to awaken through practice" means to one who wishes to pierce through [the truth]. "To one desiring to penetrate" means to one who wishes to break through by making it manifest.
"To one desiring to fully awaken" means to one wishing to correctly awaken by way of not returning to defilements already abandoned.
"To one desiring to attain" means to one wishing to reach [the goal]. "To one desiring to realize" means to one wishing to obtain through the realization of attainment (*paṭilābha-sacchikiriyā*).
Alternatively, "desirous of awakening" means desirous of knowing the knowledge of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*).

"Desirous of further awakening" means desirous of knowing again the knowledge of the once-returning path (*sakadāgāmi-magga-ñāṇa*). "Desirous of penetrating" means desirous of knowing the knowledge of the non-returning path (*anāgāmi-magga-ñāṇa*) by way of penetration.
"Desirous of fully awakening" means desirous of correctly knowing the knowledge of the arahant path (*arahatta-magga-ñāṇa*). "Desirous of attaining" refers to all four kinds [of paths].
"To one desiring to attain" means: to one desiring to touch by means of the contact of knowledge (*ñāṇaphusanā*). "To one desiring to realize" means:
to one desiring to make it manifest through direct personal experience (*paccakkha*) by means of reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*).

"Insight prior to the four paths" refers to the knowledges of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*), such as those concerning arising and passing away, which have arisen during the preliminary stage of the four noble paths (*ariyamagga*).

199. In the second verse, *sapariyantacārī* means one who conducts himself within the four boundaries consisting of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. *Ḍaṃsādhipātānaṃ* refers to brown flies and other kinds of flies;
for they pounce from here and there and bite, and therefore they are called "pouncers" (*adhipātā*).
*Manussaphassānaṃ* refers to the contact of robbers and the like.
“Four boundaries” means four limits or demarcations. “Reflecting on his state of internal putrefaction” means observing the state of corruption within—that is, the state of being devoid of virtue.
“He moves within the boundary of the restraint of virtue” means he moves and conducts himself within the confines of the restraint of virtue. “He does not break the boundary” means...
He does not violate the boundary of virtue nor the limits of virtue.
"Reflecting on the discourse on the burning" means looking upon the teaching concerning what is aflame.

"Reflecting on the similes of the cart-axle grease, the covering of a wound, and the flesh of one's own son" means reflecting on the simile of the cart-driver’s axle-grease, and the simile of the piece of cloth smeared with oil for covering the wounds of a leper.
And observing the simile of the husband and wife traveling through a wilderness who eat the flesh of their own son, he reflects upon the dwelling of the "One Fortunate Night":
"One should not pursue the past, nor should one long for the future;
the peaceful sage indeed declares such a one to be 'possessed of the one fortunate night.'"
Thus it was said while contemplating the dwelling of the "One Fortunate Night. "Flying up again and again, they devour" means that having swooped down repeatedly, they devour.

In the third verse, "those belonging to other doctrines" (*paradhammika*) refers to all those outsiders, excluding those who share the same doctrine (*sahadhammika*). "Seeking what is wholesome" (*kusalānuesī*) means seeking wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).

"Setting aside the seven who share the same Dhamma" means excluding the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, sāmaṇeras, sāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. "There are others yet to be overcome" means there are other things to be crushed that still exist.
201. In the fourth verse, "by the touch of affliction" means by the touch of disease. "Cold and heat" means both cold and heat.
"Touched by those in many ways" means being touched by those various forms such as affliction and the like. "Without a shelter" (anoka) means...
It is that which provides no occasion for the consciousness of volitional formations and so forth.
"By way of the internal elements being disturbed" means by way of the agitation of the water element within the body, or by way of the agitation of another element.

"Heat" means that heat arises within the body due to the agitation of the fire element. "Of the consciousness accompanied by volitional formations" refers to the mind associated with wholesome or unwholesome volition (*cetanā*).
"He does not make room" means he does not provide space or a foothold. "One who has taken it up without stability" refers to one who has descended [into the world] as a grasper.

Having thus answered the question asked in the three verses beginning with "Of a bhikkhu who is disgusted," he now speaks the verse beginning with "He would not commit theft" in order to answer the question asked in the manner of "What would his modes of speech be? and so forth.
In this context, "he touches" means he would touch. "One should know the turbidity of the mind":
whatever turbidity of the mind one might recognize, all that should be dispelled as "the side of the dark.
"Having abandoned taking what is not given": here, taking what is not given is the taking of what has not been given, the seizing of another's property, theft.

"Stealing" (corikā) is what is meant. In that context, "what is not given" (adinna) refers to that which is possessed by another, such that if one were to exercise free will over it, one would incur neither punishment nor blame.

When there is such property belonging to another, the volition of theft—which arises from the undertaking of taking it while perceiving it as belonging to another—is "taking what is not given. This [occurs] when the property of another is inferior...
It is less blameworthy in the case of one who is superior, and more blameworthy in the case of one who is refined. Why? Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*).

When the object is equal, it is more blameworthy in the case of an object belonging to one who possesses superior qualities; conversely, depending on each respective person of superior quality, it is less blameworthy in the case of an object belonging to one whose qualities are inferior to them.
It has five constituent factors: the object belonging to another, the perception that it belongs to another, the intention to steal, the effort, and the taking away by means of that [effort].
"Having abandoned" means having abandoned this immorality consisting of the volition of taking what is not given.
"Abstaining" means that from the moment it is abandoned, one is indeed refrained from that immorality. "He takes only what is given" means:
One who takes what is given. Because one expects only what has been given even by the mind, one is "one who expects what is given" (*dinnapāṭikaṅkhī*).

A thief is one who steals (*theneti*); one who does not steal is "non-thief" (*athena*). By virtue of being non-thieving, one is "purified. "By oneself" (*attanā*) means by way of one's own person (*attabhāvena*);
thus it is said that one dwells having made one's own person non-thieving and purified. From here on, the method is exactly as stated [previously].
Loving-kindness (*mettā*) is by way of loving. The act of loving is *mettāyanā*. The state of a mind that has been made loving, belonging to one possessing loving-kindness, is *mettāyitatta*.
It is called compassion (*anudayā*) because it feels compassion; the meaning is that it protects. The mode of feeling compassion is *anudayanā*.
The state of one who has felt compassion is *anudayitatta*. Seeking the welfare (*hitesitā*) is by way of seeking what is beneficial. By way of commiseration...
Compassion (*anukampā*). By all these terms, loving-kindness (*mettā*) that has reached both access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*) is described.

Herein, "vast" (*vipula*) should be understood in terms of its pervasiveness; however, it is "sublime" (*mahaggata*) by way of its plane, "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) by way of its proficiency, and "immeasurable" also by way of its object, which is sentient beings.
It is "free from enmity" (*avera*) through the abandonment of ill-will (*byāpāda*), and through the abandonment of mental distress (*domanassa*).
"Free from affliction" (*abyāpajja*) means "without suffering. "Turbid" (*āvila*) means "unclear. "Agitated" (*luḷita*) means "muddy.

"Disturbed" (*erita*) means "unsettled. "Struck" (*ghaṭṭita*) means "brought into contact with an object. "Shaken" (*calita*) means "trembling. "Wandering" (*bhanta*) means "straying. "Unappeased" (*avūpasanta*) means "unextinguished. Regarding the phrase "He who is Māra," and so forth:
he is called Māra because, having incited the great multitude toward what is harmful, he causes them to die (*māreti*). He is called Kaṇha because of his dark deeds (*kaṇhakamma*).

Because it is the sovereign over the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), it is the "overlord" (*adhipati*). Because it leads to death, it is the "one who goes to the end" (*antagu*). Because it does not grant release, it is "Namuci.
It is the "Māra’s snare" (*mārabaḷisa*) in the sense of being a trap for Māra. It is the "Māra’s bait" (*mārāmisa*) in the sense of being dependent upon the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
It is the "Māra’s domain" (*māravisaya*) in the sense of being under his control. It is the "Māra’s abode" (*māranivāsa*) in the sense of being his range of activity (*gocara*).

It is the "domain of Māra" (māragocara) in the sense that one wanders according to one's own will within it. It is the "bondage of Māra" (mārabandhana) in the sense that it is difficult to release from.
It is the "suffering-bond" (dukkhabandhana) because it is the source of suffering. 203.
"Having dug up their root, he stands firm": this refers to the root of those [defilements], such as anger and conceit, which begins with ignorance.
"Having dug it up as well, he would stand [there]"—the meaning is that by overcoming this "dear and not dear," one would certainly overcome it in every respect;
one should not exert effort laxly in that regard.

Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the root, etc.: ignorance is the root of anger by way of being its decisive support (*upanissaya*), its co-nascent (*sahajāta*), and so forth. Inappropriate attention (*anupāyamanasikāra*)...

And "self-conceit" (asmimāna)—these two [factors] act solely as decisive supports (upanissaya). Shamelessness (ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), and restlessness (uddhacca)—these three are roots by way of being decisive supports, co-nascent causes (sahajāta), and so forth; the same applies to overweening pride (atimāna). 204.

"Placing wisdom foremost" means making wisdom the precursor. "Possessing noble joy" means being endowed with noble joy. "One should endure the four states that lead to lamentation" means one should endure those states subject to lamentation which are spoken of in the immediately following verse.
"Abounding in investigation" means abounding in thorough examination. "Abounding in analysis" means especially abounding in examination.
"Abounding in observation" means abounding in looking on. "Abounding in scrutiny" means abounding in searching. "Dwelling in the manifest" means dwelling having made [the mind] clear and known.
Regarding the phrase "in advancing and in retreating": here, first, "advancing" refers to going forward; "retreating" refers to turning back.
Both of these are found within the four postures (*īryāpatha*). First, regarding walking: when one moves the body forward, it is called "approaching" (*abhikkamati*);
when turning back, it is called "receding" (*paṭikkamati*). Regarding standing: while remaining standing, leaning the body forward is called "approaching," and drawing it back is called "receding.
Regarding sitting: while remaining seated, facing the front part of the seat...
While wandering in saṃsāra, he is said to "advance. While wandering back toward his final bodily location, he is said to "retreat.
The same principle applies even when lying down.

He is "one who acts with clear comprehension" (sampajānakārī) in the sense that he performs all his duties with clear comprehension, or rather, he is one whose very activity consists of clear comprehension. He...
For indeed, one exercises clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) regarding such things as "going forth" (*abhikkanta*) and so on; one is never devoid of clear comprehension in any situation.
Regarding the terms "looking forward" (*ālokita*) and "looking around" (*vilokita*): here, "looking forward" means gazing ahead; "looking around" means glancing toward the intermediate directions.
Furthermore, there are also "looking down," "looking up," and "looking behind," by way of gazing downward, upward, and backward respectively.
Those [other activities] are not included here. However, these two alone are taken because they are appropriate, or else all of them are indeed included under this heading.
"In bending and stretching" refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. "In wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe"—here:

The use and wearing of the *saṅghāṭi* robe and other robes by way of wearing them as undergarments or outer garments, and the use of the alms-bowl by way of receiving alms-food and so forth, is called "wearing.
Regarding "eating" and the rest: "eating" refers to the consumption of alms-food; "drinking" refers to the drinking of rice-gruel and the like;
"chewing" refers to the chewing of flour-based snacks and the like; "tasting" refers to the tasting of honey, molasses, and the like; and "the work of excrement and urine" refers to excrement...
And in the performance of defecation and urination. Regarding "gone" and so forth: "gone" means in walking; "standing" means in standing;

"seated" means in sitting; "asleep" means in lying down; "awake" means in being awake; "speaking" means in talking. In this context, when the derived form—the sense-sphere of sound—is not occurring, there is no such thing as "one who speaks";
it exists only when that [sound] occurs. Thus the discerning monk [understands].

One is called "acting with clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*) regarding speech. Even when teaching the Dhamma under the heading of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*), or even when engaging in discourse based on the ten topics of talk while abandoning the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk, one is called "acting with clear comprehension" regarding speech.

Regarding silence (*tuṇhībhāva*), which means non-speaking: therein, there is no such thing as "silence" during the occurrence of the sound-base (*saddāyatana*), which is derived form (*upādārūpa*); rather, it exists during its non-occurrence.
"He is one" means that the monk who accepts [the invitation] is called "one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence.

Even one who has taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) according to his own preference among the thirty-eight objects and is seated, or even one who has attained the second jhāna, is called "one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence.
And here, one posture (iriyāpatha) is mentioned in two places; it was previously mentioned under "when approaching," etc.
Regarding the term "having returned": here it is spoken of in terms of the journeying along the road for one going to and coming from the village for alms.

Regarding "having gone and standing": here it should be understood as being spoken of in terms of the removal of dust and footprints within the monastery. The methods beginning with "by means of recollecting the Buddha" have already been explained in various places below.
*Arati* means the negation of delight (*rati*). *Aratitā* is the state of not delighting. *Anabhirati* is the condition of not being delighted.
*Anabhiramanā* is the mode of not being delighted. *Ukkaṇṭhitā* is the mode of longing or yearning. *Paritassitā* is the agitation resulting from that very longing.
"What shall I eat? What will I eat? Where shall they eat? Or where will I eat?"—this is suffering.
"Alas, what a superior way of life! I have slept in suffering this night; where shall I sleep on the night of my arrival tomorrow?
These are the four thoughts: two based on alms-food and two based on lodgings.
"Wandering without a home" means wandering free from obstructions and wandering free from craving.
*Phalake*: on a plank or a seat made of crooked wood and so forth. *Āgāmirattiṃ*: for the sake of warding off the coming night. *Ādevaneyye*: specifically for the purpose of lamenting.
*Paridevaneyye*: for the purpose of lamenting all around. 206. *Kāle*: at the time for alms-food, having obtained food known as alms-food;

or at the time for robes, having obtained clothing known as a robe—this is the intended meaning: "righteously and equitably. *Mattaṃ sa jaññā*: he should know the measure, both in terms of acquisition and in terms of consumption.
"And he should know the measure. *Idha* means "in this teaching," or it is merely a particle. *Tosanatthaṃ* means for the sake of contentment;
what is meant is that he should know the measure for this purpose. *So tesu gutto* means that monk is guarded regarding those requisites.
*Yatacārī* means one who dwells restrained, whose modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*) are protected, and whose doors of body, speech, and mind are guarded.
It has been said. There is also a reading, “one who acts with restraint” (*yat’-ācārī*); the meaning is the same. “Provoked” (*rusito*) means being made angry;
it is synonymous with “assaulted” (*ghaṭṭito*). “One should know the measure by two reasons” means one should know the limit by way of two factors:
either from the time of receiving [the gift] when it is being given by others, or from the time of consumption. Even if it is small...
"Even when given a little" means even when a small amount is being given. "For the non-decline of families" means for the sake of the non-decline of families.
"For the protection of families" means for the purpose of protecting families. "He accepts" means he takes even a small amount.
"Even when given much" means even when a large amount is being given. "He accepts a robe that is conducive to the maintenance of the body": herein, he maintains the body.
“Sustains” means it sustains and nourishes the body; thus it is “body-sustaining. “Stomach-sustaining” means it sustains and nourishes the stomach; thus it is “stomach-sustaining.
For a bhikkhu endowed with contentment regarding various requisites, eight articles are permissible:
the three robes, an alms-bowl, a tooth-stick cutter and razor, a needle, a waist-band, and a water-strainer. And this has been said:
“The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the girdle;
together with the water-strainer—these eight belong to the bhikkhu devoted to yoga.
All of these serve both for the maintenance of the body and for the maintenance of the belly. How so? First, having put on the three robes...
When one wears it and moves about, it protects and nourishes the body; thus, it is "for the protection of the body.
When one strains water with the hem of the robe and drinks, or when one gathers fruits and vegetables to eat, it protects and nourishes the belly;
thus, it is "for the protection of the belly."
A water pot, too, by drawing up water, serves the body at the time of bathing and when decorating the hut;

by taking food and eating, it serves the belly. An axe, too, by cutting tooth-sticks, and by fashioning the parts and legs of beds and stools, as well as robes and the poles for the hut, serves the body; [likewise] by cutting sugarcane, coconut shells, and so forth.
The needle is for the maintenance of the body at the time of sewing robes; it is for the maintenance of the belly when one eats after piercing a cake or fruit;
the waistband is for the maintenance of the body at the time of wearing it while wandering about;
and sugarcane and so forth are for the maintenance of the belly at the time of gathering them after they have been tied up. Having filtered water with a water-strainer...
At the time of bathing and at the time of cleaning the lodgings, it is for the maintenance of the body;
at the time of straining water to remove insects, and at the time of taking sesame, rice, parched grain, and so forth, it is for the maintenance of the belly.
"By means of wise reflection" means having reflected by way of a method or path; the meaning is "having examined. Herein:
And it should be understood that "wise reflection" (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhā*) is precisely the reflection stated in the manner beginning with, "for the warding off of cold," and so forth.

In this context, "robe" (*cīvara*) refers to any one among the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), etc. "He uses" (*paṭisevati*) means he makes use of it, either by wearing it as an undergarment or by putting it on as an upper garment.
"Only for" (*yāvadeva*) is a statement defining the limit and boundary of the purpose. It is only to this extent.
For indeed, this is the purpose for which a practitioner of yoga makes use of robes, namely: "for the warding off of cold," and so forth; there is nothing beyond this.
"Of cold" means of any cold whatsoever that has arisen, either by way of an internal disturbance of the elements or by way of an external change in the weather.
"For the warding off" means for the purpose of repelling. It is for the sake of dispelling it so that no affliction arises in the body;
for when the body is afflicted by cold, one whose mind is distracted is unable to apply oneself with wise effort.
Therefore, the Blessed One authorized the use of a robe "for the warding off of cold. This same method applies everywhere. Only here...
"Of heat" means the heat of fire; its occurrence should be understood in forest fires and the like. Regarding "the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things":
here, *daṃsa* refers to the gadfly (*ḍaṃsanamakkhikā*), which is also called the "blind fly" (*andhamakkhikā*). *Makasa* refers simply to mosquitoes.
*Vāta* refers to the various types of wind, such as those with dust or free from dust. *Ātapa* is the heat of the sun. *Sarīsapā* refers to whatever creatures move by crawling.
There are long-tailed snakes and the like; their contact is twofold: contact by biting and contact by touch.
Even that does not trouble one who is sitting after having put on the robe. Therefore, in such places, one uses it for the purpose of warding them off.
The repetition of the phrase "only so far" (*yāvadeva*) is for the purpose of showing the limit of the fixed necessity.
"For the purpose of concealing the *hirikopīna*" refers to a fixed purpose; the others [the remaining requisites] are occasional.

In this context, *hirikopīna* means each respective private part. For when whichever limb is uncovered, modesty (*hirī*) is disturbed—that is, destroyed—each such part is called *hirikopīna* because it disturbs modesty. And "for the purpose of concealing that *hirikopīna*" means...
For the purpose of covering the private parts. There is also a reading: “for the purpose of covering the shameful parts” (*hirikopīna-paṭicchādanatthaṃ*).
Almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*): any kind of food whatsoever. For whatever food falls into the bowl of a bhikkhu by way of alms-gathering (*piṇḍolya*) is called “almsfood.
Alternatively, almsfood is the gathering (*pāta*) of morsels (*piṇḍa*); that is, the collection of alms obtained here and there.
“Concourse” (*sannipāta*) means a collection (*samūha*). The rest is exactly as explained below.

“Reclining seat” (*senāsana*) means both reclining (*seyyā*) and sitting (*āsana*). For wherever one lies down—whether in a monastery (*vihāra*) or in a gabled house (*aḍḍhayoga*) and so forth—that is “reclining” (*sena*).
Wherever one sits or remains seated, that is “sitting” (*āsana*). Taking these together, it is called “reclining seat” (*senāsana*).

It is said: "For the purpose of warding off the perils of the climate and for delighting in seclusion. In this context, "climate-peril" (*utuparissaya*) refers to the climate itself in the sense of something to be endured.

It is for the purpose of warding off that climate-peril and for the purpose of delighting in seclusion. This means it is for the purpose of warding off any unsuitable climate that causes bodily affliction or mental distraction—which must be dispelled by resorting to a suitable dwelling—and for the sake of the bliss of solitude.
This has been said. Granted that the warding off of climatic dangers such as cold and so forth is indeed already mentioned by the phrase "for the warding off of cold," nevertheless,
just as it was stated regarding the use of robes that "the concealment of the private parts is the constant purpose,
while the others occur only occasionally," so too here this has been said with reference to the constant warding off of climatic dangers.
This should be understood. Alternatively, this aforementioned weather is simply "weather" (*utu*). Obstacles (*parissaya*), however, are of two kinds: manifest obstacles and concealed obstacles.
Among these, manifest obstacles are lions, tigers, and so forth; concealed obstacles are lust, hatred, and so forth.
Wherever these do not cause affliction—either due to a lack of protection or through the sight of unsuitable forms and the like—[that place is suitable].

Having understood and reflected upon that lodging in this way, it should be understood that the bhikkhu who uses it is using the lodging with wise reflection for the purpose of warding off the perils of the climate.
Regarding "requisites for medicinal support for the sick": here, "support" (paccaya) is so called in the sense of counteracting disease, that is, in the sense of going against [it].
“Meaning” (*attha*) is a designation for whatever is suitable. It is called “medicine” (*bhesajja*) because it is permitted as the work of a physician.
“Medicine as a requisite for the sick” (*gilānapaccaya-bhesajja*) means that medicine is indeed a requisite for the sick;
what is meant is any work of a physician suitable for the sick, such as oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding “requisite” (*parikkhāra*), [it is said]: “By seven...”

In such passages as, "It is well-fortified with the requisites for a city," it refers to a retinue. In such passages as, "The chariot has virtue as its equipment, meditation as its axle, and energy as its wheels," it refers to an ornament.
In such passages as, "And these requisites for life that must be procured by one who has gone forth," it refers to provisions.
But here, both provisions and retinue are appropriate. And that medicinal requisite for the sick—
It is a support for life, and it is also a provision because it protects by not allowing an interval for the arising of diseases that destroy life.
It is called "requisite" (*parikkhāra*) because it serves as the cause for its continued occurrence for as long as it lasts.
Thus, medicine as a requisite for the sick is "medicine-requisite-for-the-sick" (*gilānapaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra*). That [is what is meant].

"Requisites for the support of the sick" refers to whatever is suitable for one who is ill and permitted by physicians, such as oil, honey, molasses, and so forth; it is said to be "requisites for life.
"Of those arisen" means of those born, become, and produced. "Afflictive" (*veyyābādhikā*):

here, "affliction" (*byābādha*) is the disturbance of the elements and the skin diseases, swellings, pustules, and so forth that arise from it; they are called "afflictive" because they have arisen from affliction. "Of the feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*).
Painful feeling, unwholesome resultant feeling—these are painful feelings that are afflictive.
"For the sake of supreme non-affliction" means for the sake of supreme freedom from suffering; the meaning is: as long as all that suffering has been abandoned.
"He is content" means he is content with contentment regarding requisites. "With whatever robe" refers to robes that are coarse, fine, rough, excellent, firm, or worn out.
"By whatever means. The meaning is that one is content with whatever is obtained, by whatever method, and by any means whatsoever.
For regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment with what is suitable to one's strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
The same principle applies to almsfood and the other requisites as well.
"One who speaks in praise" means: one person is contented but does not speak in praise of contentment;
another is not contented but speaks in praise of contentment; another is neither contented nor speaks in praise of contentment;
and another is both contented and speaks in praise of contentment. To demonstrate this, [the text says]: "In being content with whatever robe one has..."
And it is said: "one who speaks in praise [of such things]. "Improper search" (*anesana*) refers to various kinds of improper search, such as acting as a messenger, going on errands, and so forth.
"Unbecoming" (*appatirūpa*) means unsuitable. "Without having obtained" (*aladdhā ca*) means not having acquired [robes].
For example, someone might think, "How indeed shall I obtain a robe? and, joining together with monks who possess merit, practices hypocrisy (*kohañña*).
He trembles and is agitated; yet a contented bhikkhu, having thus not obtained a robe, does not become agitated.
"Having obtained" means having acquired it righteously and justly. "Unattached" means one who is free from greed.
"Uninfatuated" means one who has not fallen into a swoon of excessive craving. "Unoverwhelmed" means one who is neither submerged nor enveloped by craving. "One who sees the danger" means...
Seeing the danger in seeking food improperly and in the enjoyment of what has been greedily acquired;
"possessing the wisdom of escape" means understanding that very escape which was stated as: "only for the warding off of cold," and so forth.
"Contentment with whatever robe" means contentment with any kind of robe whatsoever. "He does not exalt himself" means: "I am a wearer of rag-robes; by me, at the very moment of full ordination..."
Having undertaken the practice of wearing rag-robes, he does not engage in self-exaltation, thinking, "Who is there equal to me?

He does not disparage others; that is, he does not disparage others by saying, "But these other bhikkhus are not rag-robe wearers," or "They do not possess even the mere quality of being rag-robe wearers."
"For one who is skillful therein" means one who speaks in praise of contentment with robes, or one who is skillful, clever, and competent in those matters.
"Diligent" means free from laziness due to constant application. "Clearly comprehending and mindful" means endowed with both clear comprehension through wisdom and mindfulness.
"Ancient" means not of recent origin. "Foremost" means that which should be known as "the foremost. [This refers to] the noble lineage.
"Established" means established in the lineage of the Noble Ones (*ariya*). And as for the "noble lineage":

just as there is a lineage of Khattiyas, a lineage of Brahmins, a lineage of Vessas, a lineage of Suddas, a lineage of recluses (*samaṇa*), a lineage of clans, and a lineage of kings—so too this eighth noble lineage is called a noble stream (*ariyatanti*) and a noble tradition (*ariyapaveṇī*).
Furthermore, among these lineages, such as the root-fragrance and so forth, this noble lineage...
It is declared to be supreme, like the fragrance of black aloe-wood (*kāḷānusāri*). But who are those Noble Ones (*ariya*) whose lineage this is?
"Noble Ones" refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata; it is the lineage of these Noble Ones that is the "Ariyavaṃsa" (Noble Lineage).
For prior to this, at the conclusion of four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) beginning from one hundred thousand kappas ago, there appeared Taṇhaṅkara...
The four Buddhas—Meṅkera, Saraṇaṅkara, Dīpaṅkara, and Upapanna—arose; they were noble ones (ariya), and the lineage of those noble ones is the "Noble Lineage" (ariyavaṃsa).
After the final Nibbāna of those Buddhas, after the passing of one incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya), a Buddha named Koṇḍañña arose...
[and so on] ...in this present aeon, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our own [Buddha].
The "Noble Lineage" (ariyavaṃsa) refers to the lineage of those Noble Ones (ariya), the four Buddhas who have arisen, known as the Blessed One Gotama.
Furthermore, it is the lineage of all the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—of the past, future, and present;
he is established in that noble lineage.
"By whatever alms-food" means by any kind of alms-food whatsoever. The same method applies to lodgings and so forth. "In the sense-bases" means in the sense-bases such as the eye and so on.
"Yata" means restrained. "Yatta" means restrained. "Paṭiyatta" means exceedingly restrained.
"Gutta" means guarded. "Gopita" means kept safe like a casket. "Rakkhita" means protected. "Saṃvuta" means closed by the restraint of the doors [of the senses].
"Rebuked" means censured. "Contemned" means disapproved. "Provoked" means brought to a state of provocation. "Despised" means held in contempt. "Reviled" means abused.
"With harshness" means with words that cut to the quick.
"With cruelty" means with what is brutal. "One should not retaliate" means one should not speak back by way of counter-attack.
207. "Devoted to meditation" (*jhānānuyutta*) means devoted to meditation by way of producing what has not yet arisen and cultivating what has already arisen.

"Having attained concentration by undertaking equanimity" (*upekkham ārabbha samāhitatto*) means having produced the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, his mind is concentrated. "He cuts off the tendency toward discursive thought and worry" (*takkāsayaṃ kukkuccañcupacchindeti*):
he should cut off discursive thoughts such as sensual thoughts, the "abode of discursive thought" such as perceptions of sensuality, and worry such as physical fidgeting.

"For the arising of the first jhāna not yet arisen" means for the purpose of producing the first jhāna that has not yet arisen in this present existence, or that which had arisen and was subsequently lost;
it is for the sake of its acquisition within one's own mental continuum.
Regarding the phrases "he cultivates the first jhāna already arisen," and so forth, here he serves it with care, makes it proficient, develops it, and increases it.
*Bahulīkaroti* means he makes it frequent; he does it again and again.
*Upekkhā* refers to the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) that has arisen in the fourth jhāna. *Upekkhā* is a term for its essential nature.
*Upekkhanā* is the mode of viewing from a position of arising. *Ajjhupekkhanā* is viewing while being pre-eminent. *Cittasamatā* is the evenness of the mind...
Equanimity of mind (*cittassa samatā*) is the state of balance, having avoided deficiency and excess. Tranquility of mind (*cittappassaddhatā*) means the mind’s lack of arrogance;
the meaning is its state of being non-stiff. Equanimity of mind (*majjhattatā cittassa*) means not [equanimity] of a being or a person, but the state of neutrality of the mind.
"Taking equanimity as the object in the fourth jhāna" refers to the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) that has arisen in the fourth jhāna.
"Dependent on. "One-pointed mind" means a mind proceeding toward a single object. "Undistracted mind" means a mind free from restlessness (*uddhacca*), not a distracted mind.
The nine types of applied thought (*vitakka*) are exactly as described by the method already stated. Regarding "the underlying tendency (*āsaya*) to sensual perception for sensual thoughts":

when one is thinking sensual thoughts, the sensual perception that arises is the "underlying tendency to sensual perception," meaning it is the dwelling-place or the locus for those thoughts. This same principle applies to ill-will thoughts and the others as well.
208. "Being reproved by words, the mindful one rejoices": being reproved by the words of his preceptor or others, he, being mindful, should rejoice in that reproval.
"He should utter speech that is wholesome": he should utter speech arisen from knowledge.
"Not excessively": however, he should not utter speech that is excessive—that is, speech which transgresses the proper time and the proper occasion for virtuous conduct.
"Regarding the nature of public gossip": this refers to talk that slanders people. "One should not intend" means one should not give rise to the volition [to speak].
