"'This has not been attained by you' means 'this has not been reached by you. 'It is unbecoming' means your conduct is unbecoming.
'It does not stand upon virtue' means your conduct does not rest upon virtue; it is said that for one established in virtue, such conduct does not exist."
...there is. Some read "asiliṭṭhaṃ" and explain the meaning as "smooth speech.
"Of treasures" (nidhīnaṃ) refers to treasure-pots filled with gold, silver, and so forth, which have been buried and deposited here and there.
"A provider" (pavattāraṃ): out of compassion for people living in misery and poverty, [he says], "Come, I shall provide a means for you to live in comfort..."

It is like one who, having led [another] to the location of a hidden treasure, extends his hand and says, "Take this and live happily," to the one who points it out. Regarding "one who sees faults" (*vajjadassin*):
there are two kinds of those who see faults. One is the seeker of flaws, thinking, "By means of this unseemly conduct or lapse, I shall restrain him in the midst of the Saṅgha.

The other is [the teacher] who, for the purpose of making known what is unknown and for the purpose of not neglecting what is already known, [points out faults] by way of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
Furthermore, because of his desire for growth, he is established in a nature that seeks out various faults and proclaims them.

This is what is intended here. For just as a poor man, when shown a treasure even after being threatened and beaten with the words "Take this!", does not become angry but is instead filled with joy, so too, when such a person sees what is unbecoming or a lapse in another...
Upon seeing [this], one should not become angry; rather, one should be pleased. One should even invite them, saying: "Venerable sir, you have done a great service for me.
Standing in the place of my teacher and preceptor and instructing me, please speak to me again. Regarding the term *niggayhavādi*:
some, upon seeing an unseemly act or a lapse by their co-resident disciples and others, [say]: "This one..."
He does not become one who speaks with suppression when he is unable to say, "She attends to me properly with offerings of water for my mouth and other services;
if I speak to her, she will no longer attend to me, and thus there will be a decline for me.
Such a person scatters rubbish upon this Teaching. However, one who, having seen such a fault, rebukes her in accordance with that fault—

One who trains by banishing, imposing penance, or expelling from the monastery is called a "reprover," just like the Perfectly Enlightened One. For this has been said: "Holding them back, Ānanda, I shall speak;
shaking them off, Ānanda, I shall speak; that which is the essence will remain. "Wise" means by means of the wisdom born of the Dhamma-fuel.
"One who possesses [such qualities]. "One such as that" means one should associate with and attend upon a wise person of this kind.
For a resident pupil who associates with such a teacher, it is better and not worse; there is only progress, not decline.
"He should exhort" means that he is said to exhort when speaking once a matter has arisen; even before it has arisen, he exorts by way of saying, "There may be misfortune for you," and so forth.

To instruct by pointing out what is yet to come is called "exhorting. To speak in one's presence is called "admonishing," while sending a messenger or a message in one's absence is called "instructing.
To speak once is called "admonishing," while speaking repeatedly is called "instructing.
Or, one who is admonishing is indeed instructing; thus one should admonish and instruct. "Asabba" means...
The meaning is: "He would restrain unwholesome states and establish one in wholesome states. For he is dear to the virtuous;

such a person is dear to the True Persons, such as the Buddhas and others. But to those who are not virtuous—those who have not seen the Truth, have not transcended the next world, whose eyes are fixed on material gain, and who have gone forth for the sake of a livelihood—he, being their advisor and instructor, says: "You..."
"He is our preceptor, not our teacher; why do you instruct us?"—to those who pierce with such verbal shafts, one becomes unpleasant.

"Single legal act" (*ekakamma*) refers to a single legal act such as a formal motion (*apalokanakamma*). "Single recitation" (*ekuddesa*) refers to a single recitation such as the recitation of the introduction (*nidāna*). "Common training" (*samasikkhatā*) means having the same training.
"State of a wounded mind" (*āhatacittatta*) means the condition of a mind struck by anger. "State of being like a thorn" (*khilajātatā*) means a state of stubbornness.

"The five mental wastelands" (*pañca cetokhilā*) refers to the five states of stiffness or rigidity of the mind toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, and one's fellow practitioners of the holy life.
"Speech arisen from knowledge" (*ñāṇasamuṭṭhitaṃ vācaṃ*) means speech produced by a consciousness associated with knowledge. "Should release" (*muñceyya*) means should utter.
"Connected with the goal" (*atthūpasaṃhitaṃ*) means accompanied by purpose, accompanied by reason. "Connected with the Dhamma" (*dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ*) means consistent with the Dhamma.
"One should not speak words that have transgressed the proper time" means one should not utter speech that has passed its appointed time because that specific time has elapsed.
"One should not speak words that have transgressed the proper occasion" means one should not utter speech that has exceeded its boundary because it has overstepped the limits of verbal decorum.
Both refer to time and occasion.
"When the time has not yet arrived" means when the time for one's own speech has not yet come.
"Exceeding the limit" means speaking in an excessive measure by transgressing the proper time. "He lies struck down" means he lies having been crushed.
"Born of a cuckoo, though raised by a crow" means like a cuckoo chick that, though nurtured by a crow, is born from within a cuckoo.
209. *Atha aparāni*: "Then, furthermore," means now, even beyond this. "The five stains" refers to the five stains beginning with lust for form (*rūparāga*).

"Of which one who possesses mindfulness should train for the sake of their removal" means that, having established mindfulness, one should train in the three trainings (*tisso sikkhā*) for the purpose of removing them.
For by training thus, one would overcome lust for forms... [and so on] ...for contacts, and not otherwise.

“Dust of form” (*rūparaja*) refers to the dust of lust and other defilements that arises dependent upon the object of form. The same method applies to the “dust of sound” (*saddaraja*) and the others as well.
210. Then, training for their removal, he proceeds in due order with the verse: “In these phenomena... (*etesu dhammesu*). Therein, “in these” (*etesu*) means in form and the rest.
“At the proper time, thoroughly investigating the Dhamma” (*kālena so sammā dhammaṃ parivīmaṃsamāno*) refers to that bhikkhu who, regarding what is called “agitation” (*uddhata*), [investigates]...
The time has come for serenity in the mind,” and so forth;
by that time, while thoroughly investigating all conditioned phenomena according to the method of impermanence and so on, one becomes unified and should dispel the darkness.
Thus, with a one-pointed mind, he should dispel all the darkness of delusion and the like—of this there is no doubt.
"In a restless mind" means when the mind is not tranquil due to the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*).
For strong energy overcomes restlessness because of its partiality toward agitation (*uddhacca*) when concentration (*samādhi*) is weak. Thus, "in a restless mind.
"The time for calm" means the time for the cultivation of concentration. "In a concentrated mind" means when the mind is concentrated through access and absorption (*upacāra-ppanā*).
For strong concentration overcomes weak energy because, being on the side of indolence, it succumbs to sloth.
Concentration bound by energy does not permit one to fall into sloth; energy bound by concentration does not permit one to fall into agitation.
Therefore, both should be made equal. For through the equality of both, absorption (*appanā*) occurs.
"The time for insight" means that when one is thus concentrated, it is the time for various kinds of seeing by way of impermanence and so forth;
even strong faith is suitable for one whose task is concentration. One who thus has faith and resolves attains absorption (*appanā*).

However, regarding concentration and wisdom, strong one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) is suitable for one whose task is concentration; for in this way he attains absorption. For one whose task is insight...
However, strong wisdom is required; for it is in this way that one attains penetration of the characteristics.
Even when both [wisdom and energy] are equal, absorption (appanā) certainly occurs.
"He uplifts the mind at the proper time" means that at whatever moment the mind has become sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, [he uplifts it].
At that time, he uplifts the mind by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture.

He restrains it means: at whatever time the mind becomes agitated due to over-exerted energy and so forth, at that time he restrains that mind by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. He gladdens it...

"By the time": when the mind becomes disenchanted due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom or through the disappearance of the bliss of tranquility, at that time one should arouse a sense of urgency by reflecting upon the eight bases for spiritual urgency (*saṃvegavatthu*). The eight bases for spiritual urgency are:
birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the lower realms as the fifth; and in the past...
Suffering rooted in the round [of existence] in the future, suffering rooted in the round in the present, and suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
Through the recollection of the qualities of the Triple Gem, he generates confidence in him. This is called "encouraging at the proper time.
He concentrates the mind at the proper time—at whatever moment faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, [are required].
Equanimity: at that time, one should concentrate the mind evenly.

"He looks on with equanimity at the proper time" means that when, by means of right practice, the mind becomes neither sluggish nor agitated, neither lacking zest nor over-exerted, but proceeds evenly toward the object and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), then, regarding its further exertion, restraint, or encouragement—
He does not exert effort when the horses are proceeding evenly, like a charioteer; this is called "regarding with equanimity at the proper time.

That yogi is "skilled in time" in the sense that he is proficient and competent in the application of the meditation subject regarding the times for exertion, restraint, encouragement, concentration, and equanimity. With the words "At what time?
and so forth, he asks about the time for exertion and the other factors.

Now, explaining the time for exertion and so forth, he says: "When the mind is sluggish," and so on. When the mind has fallen into a state of sluggishness due to excessive laxity of energy and other such factors, there is "exertion" (*paggaha*) by means of arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture.

When the mind is "agitated," there is "restraint" (*viniggaha*) by means of arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, [due to] excessive over-exertion of energy and other such factors.
Restraint. One should gladden the mind that has become devoid of gratification;

that is, one should gladden at that moment the mind that has gone to a state lacking gratification—either due to weakness in the application of wisdom, or due to the disappearance of the bliss of tranquility, or by reflecting on the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), or by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem.
"When the mind is uplifted" means at whatever time the mind has been gladdened in the manner already described.
"It becomes neither sluggish nor agitated" means that because it is restrained by energy and concentration, it is free from both sluggishness and agitation.

"Of the sign of serenity" (samathanimittassa): serenity and the sign are the "sign of serenity"; [it refers] to that sign of serenity. "That time" refers to that time when [the mind] is free from sluggishness and agitation.

That is the time [for this]. "One should delight the mind internally" means one should satisfy and gladden the consciousness associated with meditative absorption (jhāna) within the internal range of the kasiṇa and other objects.
"By this very method" means by the method already described; the letter *ma* is used here for the sake of metrical or phonetic euphony (*padasandhi*). One should look on with equanimity.
"At that time" means when that mind has become concentrated through access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā).
Then, knowing "the mind is concentrated," one should not exert effort in exertion, restraint, or encouragement, but should instead maintain equanimity at that very moment.
Now, concluding the verse asked—"At what time is there exertion?"—he says: "Thus the wise one, knowing the time... and so forth.
"From time to time one should observe the sign of the mind" means that from time to time one should notice and examine the object of the mind associated with concentration;
this is the meaning. The rest is clear everywhere. Thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta within the *Saddhammappajjotikā*,
the commentary on the *Mahāniddesa*, is completed.
The commentary on the *Aṭṭhakavagga* is completed.
The Great Commentary on the Niddesa, titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is completed.
